The setting had high prevalence of multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – It was conducted in **13 Dutch ICUs**.
- B (False) – It was an open-label **cluster-crossover** study, not placebo-controlled or double-blind.
- C (False) – **Both** lowered adjusted 28-day mortality: OR 0.86 (SOD) and 0.83 (SDD); crude 27.5% vs 26.6% vs 26.9%, ~3 percentage points absolute after adjustment.
- D (False) – The Netherlands has a **low** prevalence of resistance.

The trial enrolled 5939 patients.

**EDIC trap:** Its positive results may not generalise to high-resistance ICUs (cf. R-GNOSIS).

**Ref:** de Smet et al., N Engl J Med 2009.

open.q: Your ICU director proposes introducing SDD in a unit with a high prevalence of carbapenem-resistant Gram-negatives. Explain why the results of de Smet, R-GNOSIS and SuDDICU differ and what the evidence implies for this unit.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- de Smet (13 Dutch ICUs, low resistance): SDD/SOD reduced adjusted 28-d mortality (OR 0.83/0.86), ~3 percentage points absolute.
- R-GNOSIS (13 European ICUs, moderate/high resistance, background CHG washing and hand hygiene): no strategy significantly reduced MDR-GN bacteraemia after adjustment; no mortality difference.
- SuDDICU (Australia): mortality 27.0 vs 29.1%, OR 0.91, NS; ↓ bacteraemia and resistant cultures in patients but unit-level non-inferiority for resistant organisms not confirmed.
- Hammond MA: RR 0.91, benefit only with the IV component (RR 0.84 vs 1.01); AMR evidence very low certainty.
- Differences reflect baseline resistance ecology, background care and the presence of the IV component.
- Concern about selection of colistin/aminoglycoside resistance in a high-resistance unit.
- Prioritise multimodal horizontal measures (hand hygiene, CHG, environmental cleaning, stewardship) and screening/contact isolation for CRE/CRAB per ESCMID 2014.

open.q: Compare "horizontal" and "vertical" infection control strategies using the evidence from REDUCE MRSA, BUGG and MOSAR.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Horizontal = universal measures applied to all patients (hand hygiene, CHG bathing, universal decolonisation); vertical = pathogen-specific screening + isolation/targeted decolonisation.
- REDUCE MRSA (74 ICUs): universal decolonisation (mupirocin + CHG) > targeted > screening + isolation; BSI from any pathogen ↓ 44%, NNT 54.
- MOSAR: improved hand hygiene + universal CHG washing reduced acquisition (mainly MRSA); rapid or conventional screening + isolation added no further benefit.
- BUGG: universal gloves/gowns did not reduce MRSA+VRE acquisition (small MRSA reduction secondary), fewer room entries, better exit hand hygiene, no increase in adverse events.
- Climo: daily CHG ↓ MDRO acquisition 23% and BSI 28%; Noto: no reduction in composite HAI – CHG effect strongest for Gram-positives.
- In endemic settings horizontal measures have stronger evidence; in outbreaks and for CRE/CRAB screening + isolation/cohorting remain part of a multimodal approach.

title: W03 · Saturday – weekly review: Infections II

questions.stem: A 66-year-old ventilated patient on day 9 develops fever and hypotension requiring noradrenaline. He has a femoral CVC inserted on day 2; there is purulence at the insertion site. Blood cultures are pending. The most appropriate action regarding the catheter is:
options: Remove the catheter promptly and insert a new one at a different site if still needed
Keep the catheter as long as blood cultures are negative at 24 h
Exchange the catheter over a guidewire at the same site
Start antibiotic lock therapy
Keep the catheter and wait for differential time to positivity
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Septic shock and purulence at the insertion site are each indications for prompt catheter removal (IDSA 2009; Timsit 2020: removal is "always urgent" in shock). A new catheter, if still needed, goes in at a different site, ideally avoiding the femoral route.

**Why not the others:**

- B – Waiting for 24-h cultures in shock with local purulence delays source control.
- C – Guidewire exchange at the same site does not remove the biofilm or the infected tunnel.
- D – Lock therapy is a salvage option only for uncomplicated CRBSI in long-term catheters, never with shock or exit-site pus.
- E – DTP is a diagnostic tool for stable patients; here the indication for removal is already clinical.

**EDIC trap:** In a stable patient without local signs, the catheter may be kept while awaiting cultures – but not in shock.

**Ref:** Mermel, IDSA guideline, Clin Infect Dis 2009; Timsit et al., Intensive Care Med 2020.

questions.stem: Regarding prevention of catheter-related bloodstream infection:
options: Transparent dressings can be left for up to 7 days unless soiled, damp or loose.
In 3SITES, the subclavian site had the most mechanical complications (mainly pneumothorax).
Chlorhexidine–alcohol is preferred over povidone iodine–alcohol for skin antisepsis (CLEAN).
Chlorhexidine-impregnated dressings reduced CRBSI in critically ill adults.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Intact transparent dressings are changed every 7 days, earlier if soiled, damp or loose; the Dressing trial showed 7-day changes non-inferior to 3-day.
- B (True) – In 3SITES the subclavian site had the most mechanical complications, mainly pneumothorax (2.1% vs 1.4% jugular vs 0.7% femoral), despite the fewest CRBSI + DVT.
- C (True) – CLEAN: chlorhexidine–alcohol reduced CRBSI vs povidone iodine–alcohol (0.28 vs 1.32/1000 catheter-days, HR 0.21).
- D (True) – CHG-impregnated sponges reduced CRBSI (0.40 vs 1.3/1000 catheter-days, HR 0.24).

**EDIC trap:** Ultrasound guidance reduces mechanical complications at any site.

**Ref:** Parienti et al., 3SITES, N Engl J Med 2015; Mimoz et al., CLEAN, Lancet 2015; Timsit et al., JAMA 2009.

questions.stem: A patient has candidaemia related to a short-term CVC. Which management is correct?
options: Retain the catheter and give fluconazole for 7 days
Antifungal lock therapy only
Remove the catheter; treat for 14 days from the first negative blood culture, with an echinocandin as empirical choice and fundoscopy
Remove the catheter; no antifungal therapy needed
Treat for 6 weeks in all cases
questions.expl:
**Why C:** *Candida* CRBSI always requires catheter removal. Treatment continues for 14 days from the first negative blood culture in uncomplicated cases, with an echinocandin as the empirical agent and dilated fundoscopy to exclude endophthalmitis. Follow-up blood cultures document clearance.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Retaining the catheter and a 7-day course are both wrong; *Candida* is never managed with catheter salvage.
- B – Lock therapy alone is inadequate; salvage is not recommended for *Candida*.
- D – Candidaemia is always treated, even after catheter removal.
- E – 6 weeks is for complicated disease (endocarditis, osteomyelitis), not all cases.

**EDIC trap:** *Candida* in a single blood culture bottle is never a contaminant.

**Ref:** Mermel, IDSA guideline, Clin Infect Dis 2009; Pappas et al., IDSA candidiasis guideline, Clin Infect Dis 2016.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman presents with fever, confusion (GCS 12) and neck stiffness. CSF shows neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose. Appropriate initial management includes:
options: Ceftriaxone plus amoxicillin (or ampicillin)
Stopping dexamethasone if *S. pneumoniae* is identified
Dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, started with the first antibiotic dose
Therapeutic hypothermia to 33 °C for 48 h if she becomes comatose
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Age > 50 years requires *Listeria* coverage, so amoxicillin/ampicillin is added to ceftriaxone (cephalosporins do not cover *Listeria*).
- B (False) – Dexamethasone is **continued** for the full 4 days when *S. pneumoniae* (or *H. influenzae*) is identified; it is stopped for other pathogens.
- C (True) – Dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 h for 4 days, started before or with the first antibiotic dose.
- D (False) – Therapeutic hypothermia increased mortality in comatose meningitis patients (Mourvillier: 51% vs 31%, trial stopped early).

**EDIC trap:** GCS 12 does not mandate CT before LP (ESCMID threshold GCS < 10).

**Ref:** van de Beek et al., ESCMID guideline, Clin Microbiol Infect 2016; Mourvillier et al., JAMA 2013.

questions.stem: In the de Gans & van de Beek trial, the subgroup with the largest absolute reduction in mortality with dexamethasone was:
options: Meningococcal meningitis
Pneumococcal meningitis
Neonatal meningitis
Viral meningitis
*Listeria* meningitis
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In the de Gans & van de Beek RCT (301 adults), dexamethasone reduced mortality in pneumococcal meningitis from 34% to 14% (unfavourable outcome 52% vs 26%). Overall mortality fell from 15% to 7%. Pneumococcus carries the worst prognosis and the most intense inflammatory response to bacterial lysis.

**Why not the others:**

- A – No significant benefit was shown in meningococcal meningitis.
- C – The trial enrolled adults only; dexamethasone is not recommended in neonates.
- D – Viral meningitis was not studied; only suspected bacterial meningitis was enrolled.
- E – *Listeria* was not a benefit subgroup; ESCMID advises stopping dexamethasone for pathogens other than pneumococcus and *H. influenzae*.

**Ref:** de Gans & van de Beek, N Engl J Med 2002.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with fever, behavioural change and a seizure. MRI shows left medial temporal FLAIR hyperintensity. CSF HSV PCR taken on day 1 is negative. Correct statements:
options: EEG has no role in this patient.
Acyclovir can be stopped because the day-1 PCR is negative.
CSF HSV PCR should be repeated after 3–7 days.
Routine adjunctive corticosteroids are recommended.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – EEG is recommended in all patients with encephalitis, mainly to detect non-convulsive seizures – highly relevant after a seizure.
- B (False) – An early PCR may be falsely negative; with a typical temporal MRI, **acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 h is continued**.
- C (True) – IDSA recommends repeating CSF HSV PCR after 3–7 days when the first is negative but the picture fits.
- D (False) – Routine adjunctive corticosteroids are **not** recommended in HSV encephalitis (only retrospective data).

**EDIC trap:** Medial temporal/inferior frontal FLAIR hyperintensity is the MRI signature of HSV encephalitis; bilateral temporal involvement is almost pathognomonic.

**Ref:** Tunkel et al., IDSA encephalitis guideline, Clin Infect Dis 2008.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man has severe arm pain 24 h after a minor abrasion, with modest erythema, BP 85/50 mmHg, and LRINEC score 5. The most appropriate next step is:
options: MRI before any surgical consultation
IVIG 25 g/day for 3 days as first-line therapy
Broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin, resuscitation and urgent surgical exploration
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy
IV flucloxacillin and reassess in 24 h
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Pain out of proportion to findings plus shock after minor trauma is NSTI (likely type II, GAS) until proven otherwise. LRINEC 5 does not exclude it (sensitivity ~68%). Management is resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin (antitoxin), and urgent surgical exploration – the only way to confirm the diagnosis.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Imaging must not delay surgical consultation in a shocked patient.
- B – IVIG is not first-line; INSTINCT showed no benefit, and it may only be considered in streptococcal TSS.
- D – Hyperbaric oxygen is not recommended and delays debridement.
- E – Flucloxacillin alone is inadequate and a 24-h wait allows fatal progression.

**EDIC trap:** Survival is better with debridement within 6 h.

**Ref:** Stevens et al., IDSA guideline, Clin Infect Dis 2014; Fernando et al., Ann Surg 2019.

questions.stem: Regarding adjunctive therapies in necrotising soft-tissue infection:
options: INSTINCT showed improved 6-month physical function with IVIG.
Adjunctive clindamycin in invasive GAS infection was associated with lower mortality in a large observational cohort.
Clindamycin's efficacy is reduced by a high bacterial inoculum (Eagle effect).
IDSA 2014 does not recommend hyperbaric oxygen.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – INSTINCT found **no difference** in SF-36 PCS at 6 months (36 vs 31, p = 0.81) with IVIG 25 g/day for 3 days.
- B (True) – In Babiker's cohort (1956 patients, 118 US hospitals), adjunctive clindamycin in invasive GAS was associated with lower mortality (aOR 0.44); no RCT exists.
- C (False) – The Eagle effect reduces the efficacy of **β-lactams** at high inoculum (PBP downregulation); clindamycin is unaffected by inoculum size.
- D (True) – IDSA 2014 recommends against hyperbaric oxygen (strong): unproven benefit, risk of delaying resuscitation and debridement.

**EDIC trap:** Clindamycin is never given alone – GAS resistance exists.

**Ref:** Madsen et al., INSTINCT, Intensive Care Med 2017; Babiker et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2021; Stevens et al., IDSA, Clin Infect Dis 2014.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with shock, fever, diffuse erythroderma and vomiting during menstruation. Blood cultures are negative. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Necrotising fasciitis type I
Anaphylaxis
Staphylococcal (TSST-1–mediated) toxic shock syndrome
Meningococcal sepsis
Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Shock, fever, diffuse erythroderma and vomiting during menstruation is classic menstrual staphylococcal TSS, mediated by the TSST-1 superantigen. Blood cultures are usually negative, unlike streptococcal TSS. Treatment: remove the tampon, resuscitate aggressively, β-lactam (anti-staphylococcal) + clindamycin.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Type I NSTI is polymicrobial, occurs in diabetics/perineum and presents with local necrosis, not erythroderma.
- B – Anaphylaxis follows an exposure, causes urticaria/bronchospasm rather than fever, and lacks the menstrual context.
- D – Meningococcal sepsis causes a petechial/purpuric rash, not diffuse erythroderma.
- E – Streptococcal TSS usually has a painful soft-tissue focus and positive blood cultures.

**EDIC trap:** Desquamation of palms and soles appears 1–2 weeks later.

**Ref:** Stevens & Bryant, N Engl J Med 2017.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with lymphoma receiving chemotherapy has temperature 38.5 °C and ANC 0.1 × 10⁹/L. He is known to be colonised with ESBL-producing *E. coli* and is hypotensive. According to ECIL-4:
options: Ceftazidime monotherapy is the preferred choice.
A de-escalation approach starting with a carbapenem is appropriate.
If he later stabilises and is afebrile ≥ 48 h after ≥ 72 h of IV therapy, antibiotics may be stopped even if still neutropenic.
Adding a glycopeptide is contraindicated because of haemodynamic instability.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Septic shock and ESBL colonisation require a de-escalation approach; ceftazidime is inactive against ESBL producers.
- B (True) – ECIL-4: complicated presentation (shock) or known resistant colonisation → start with a carbapenem (± aminoglycoside), then narrow.
- C (True) – Antibiotics may be stopped after ≥ 72 h IV if stable and afebrile ≥ 48 h, regardless of ANC.
- D (False) – Haemodynamic instability is an ECIL-4 **indication** to consider adding a glycopeptide.

**EDIC trap:** Persistent fever > 4–7 days in profound neutropenia → look for invasive fungal infection rather than escalate antibacterials.

**Ref:** Averbuch et al., ECIL-4, Haematologica 2013.

questions.stem: A kidney transplant recipient with PJP and severe hypoxaemia is admitted to the ICU. Which statement is correct?
options: Treatment should be withheld until BAL confirmation
Atovaquone is the preferred first-line agent
TMP-SMX 15–20 mg/kg/day (TMP component) IV for about 3 weeks is first-line
Adjunctive corticosteroids significantly reduced 28-day mortality in non-HIV patients in the PIC trial
Early NIV has been shown to reduce mortality in immunocompromised patients
questions.expl:
**Why C:** First-line treatment of PJP in non-HIV patients is TMP-SMX 15–20 mg/kg/day (TMP component) divided into 3–4 doses, given IV in moderate/severe disease, for about 3 weeks (ECIL-6). Treatment should not be delayed for BAL.

**Why not the others:**

- A – BAL remains diagnostic several days after starting treatment, so therapy is not withheld.
- B – Atovaquone is an alternative for mild disease or intolerance, not first-line in severe PJP.
- D – In PIC, 28-day mortality was 21.5% vs 32.4% – not significant (p = 0.069); ECIL-6 advises against routine steroids in non-HIV PJP.
- E – IVNIctus showed no mortality benefit of early NIV (24.1% vs 27.3%).

**EDIC trap:** Steroids are standard in HIV-PJP with PaO₂ < 70 mmHg, not in non-HIV PJP.

**Ref:** Maschmeyer et al., ECIL-6, J Antimicrob Chemother 2016; Lemiale et al., PIC, Lancet Respir Med 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding acute respiratory failure in immunocompromised patients:
options: In HIGH, high-flow nasal oxygen significantly reduced 28-day mortality.
In Efraim, failure to identify the aetiology was associated with higher mortality.
A positive viral PCR in respiratory samples always proves causality.
Early antibiotics do not affect the yield of microbiological cultures.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – In HIGH, 28-day mortality was 35.6% vs 36.1% – no significant difference.
- B (True) – In Efraim, undetermined aetiology was independently associated with higher mortality (OR 1.43; overall hospital mortality 44%).
- C (False) – Viruses are the second most common cause, but a positive viral test ≠ causality (shedding, co-infection).
- D (False) – Early (recommended) antibiotics **reduce** the yield of pathogen identification to ~50%.

**EDIC trap:** Prefer non-invasive tests first (PCR, β-D-glucan, galactomannan), with targeted BAL if the patient's condition allows.

**Ref:** Azoulay et al., HIGH, JAMA 2018; Azoulay et al., Efraim, Intensive Care Med 2017; Azoulay et al., Intensive Care Med 2020.

questions.stem: A CMV-seropositive, non-immunosuppressed patient with septic shock and ARDS has low-level CMV DNAemia on day 10. Based on GRAIL, which statement is most accurate?
options: Foscarnet is the first-line prophylactic agent
CMV reactivation never occurs in immunocompetent ICU patients
Ganciclovir increased ventilator-free days as the primary outcome
Ganciclovir prophylaxis reduced mortality in such patients
Ganciclovir reduced CMV reactivation but did not change IL-6 levels or mortality
questions.expl:
**Why E:** GRAIL randomised 160 CMV-seropositive immunocompetent adults with sepsis or trauma and respiratory failure to ganciclovir or placebo. Ganciclovir significantly reduced plasma CMV reactivation but did not change the primary outcome (IL-6 change, days 1–14) or mortality. Routine anti-CMV prophylaxis is therefore not recommended.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Foscarnet is reserved for treatment when ganciclovir is limited by myelotoxicity or resistance; it is not a prophylactic agent here.
- B – Reactivation is common in seropositive critically ill patients during sepsis-related immunoparalysis.
- C – Ventilator-free days were a secondary outcome (improved in ITT), not the primary.
- D – No mortality reduction was shown.

**EDIC trap:** CMV reactivation is associated with worse outcome, but association ≠ causality.

**Ref:** Limaye et al., GRAIL, JAMA 2017.

questions.stem: Regarding selective decontamination of the digestive tract:
options: In the Hammond meta-analysis, benefit appeared limited to regimens with an IV antibiotic component.
In R-GNOSIS, conducted in ICUs with moderate-to-high resistance, SDD did not significantly reduce MDR Gram-negative bacteraemia after adjustment.
SuDDICU showed a statistically significant reduction in hospital mortality.
In SuDDICU, bacteraemia was less frequent with SDD.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Hammond: RR 0.84 with an IV component vs 1.01 without (interaction p = 0.02); overall hospital mortality RR 0.91.
- B (True) – R-GNOSIS (13 European ICUs, moderate-to-high resistance) found no significant reduction in MDR-GN bacteraemia after adjustment for SDD, SOD or chlorhexidine mouthwash.
- C (False) – SuDDICU mortality was 27.0% vs 29.1%, OR 0.91 (0.82–1.02) – **not significant**.
- D (True) – Bacteraemia was less frequent with SDD (5.6% vs 8.1%).

**EDIC trap:** Unit-level ecological non-inferiority for resistant organisms was not confirmed in SuDDICU, and AMR evidence in the meta-analysis is very low certainty.

**Ref:** Myburgh et al., SuDDICU, JAMA 2022; Hammond et al., JAMA 2022; Wittekamp et al., R-GNOSIS, JAMA 2018.

questions.stem: Your ICU has endemic MRSA. Which single strategy has the strongest RCT evidence for reducing ICU bloodstream infections?
options: Targeted decolonisation of screen-positive patients only
Universal decolonisation with nasal mupirocin and daily chlorhexidine bathing
Routine decolonisation of all carriers of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales
Rapid PCR screening and isolation of carriers
Universal glove and gown use
questions.expl:
**Why B:** REDUCE MRSA (74 US ICUs, cluster RCT) showed that universal decolonisation – nasal mupirocin plus daily chlorhexidine bathing for all patients – reduced bloodstream infection from any pathogen by 44% (NNT 54) and MRSA clinical cultures by 37%, outperforming targeted decolonisation and screening + isolation.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Targeted decolonisation was inferior to universal decolonisation in REDUCE MRSA.
- C – ESCMID-EUCIC 2019 recommends against routine decolonisation of CRE carriers, and it does not address MRSA.
- D – In MOSAR, rapid PCR screening + isolation brought no further reduction in acquisition.
- E – In BUGG, universal glove and gown use did not reduce MRSA/VRE acquisition (primary outcome).

**EDIC trap:** Horizontal (universal) measures have stronger evidence than vertical (pathogen-specific) ones in endemic settings.

**Ref:** Huang et al., REDUCE MRSA, N Engl J Med 2013.

title: W04 · D1 – Physiology of shock: DO2/VO2, O2 extraction, types of shock

questions.stem: According to the 2014 ESICM consensus on circulatory shock, which statement is correct?
options: Shock requires a systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg
Shock is defined by a lactate > 4 mmol/L
Hypotension is not required to define shock
Shock is defined by a cardiac index < 2.2 L/min/m²
Shock is present only when vasopressors are required
questions.expl:
**Why C:** The 2014 ESICM consensus defines shock as a life-threatening, generalised acute circulatory failure with **inadequate oxygen utilisation by the cells** – so **hypotension is not required** (Level 1, B). Hypoperfusion is recognised from the clinical windows (skin, kidneys, brain) and a lactate typically > 2 mmol/L.

**Why not the others:**

- A – SBP < 90 mmHg (or MAP < 65 mmHg, or a fall ≥ 40 mmHg) defines hypotension when present, not shock itself.
- B – Lactate in shock is typically > 2 mmol/L; 4 mmol/L is not a defining threshold.
- D – A low cardiac index describes low-flow states only; distributive shock often has a normal or high CO.
- E – Vasopressor need belongs to the Sepsis-3 definition of septic shock, not to the general definition of shock.

**EDIC trap:** "Normotensive shock" exists – a MAP ≥ 65 mmHg does not exclude shock.

**Ref:** Cecconi M, et al. Consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring. Task force of the ESICM. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815.

questions.stem: Regarding oxygen delivery and consumption:
options: Arterial oxygen content is determined mainly by haemoglobin concentration and SaO2.
When DO2 falls above the critical DO2, VO2 falls in proportion to DO2.
Below the critical DO2, VO2 remains independent of DO2.
Dissolved oxygen normally contributes about half of arterial oxygen content.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – CaO2 = 1.34 × Hb × SaO2 + 0.003 × PaO2; the haemoglobin-bound fraction makes up almost all of it.
- B (False) – Above the critical DO2, VO2 stays constant (plateau) because O2 extraction rises; it is SvO2 that falls, not VO2.
- C (False) – Below the critical DO2 extraction is exhausted, so VO2 becomes supply-dependent and falls with DO2 → anaerobic metabolism, rising lactate.
- D (False) – Dissolved O2 (0.003 mL/dL per mmHg) is only ~1–2 % of CaO2 at normal PaO2; it matters only with hyperbaric oxygen.

**EDIC trap:** VO2 is supply-independent on the plateau; supply dependency appears only below DO2crit.

**Ref:** Vincent JL, De Backer D. Circulatory shock. *N Engl J Med* 2013;369:1726–1734.

questions.stem: In the large cohort of shock patients cited by Vincent & De Backer (NEJM 2013), the most frequent type of shock was:
options: Anaphylactic
Hypovolaemic
Septic
Obstructive
Cardiogenic
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In the > 1600-patient RCT (De Backer, SOAP II) cited by Vincent & De Backer, **septic shock** was by far the most common type (62 %), followed by cardiogenic (16 %) and hypovolaemic (16 %), other distributive (4 %) and obstructive (2 %). Distributive shock overall therefore accounts for about two-thirds of cases.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Anaphylaxis belongs to the "other distributive" group, only 4 %.
- B – Hypovolaemic shock was 16 %, equal to cardiogenic and far behind septic.
- D – Obstructive shock was the rarest (2 %), although it must be actively excluded because it is rapidly reversible.
- E – Cardiogenic shock was 16 %.

**Ref:** Vincent JL, De Backer D. Circulatory shock. *N Engl J Med* 2013;369:1726–1734. De Backer D, et al. SOAP II. *N Engl J Med* 2010;362:779–789.

questions.stem: Regarding mixed/central venous oxygen saturation in shock:
options: A normal ScvO2 does not exclude tissue hypoxia in septic shock.
It is typically normal or high in distributive shock.
It is typically low in hypovolaemic and cardiogenic shock.
Fever and shivering may decrease SvO2 by increasing VO2.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – In sepsis microcirculatory shunting and mitochondrial dysfunction impair O2 extraction, so dysoxia can coexist with a normal or high ScvO2.
- B (True) – Distributive shock combines high flow with impaired extraction → SvO2 normal or high.
- C (True) – In low-flow states tissues increase extraction to maintain VO2 → wide arteriovenous difference and low SvO2 (also with anaemia).
- D (True) – SvO2 reflects the DO2/VO2 balance; a higher VO2 (fever, shivering, pain, agitation) lowers SvO2 at any given DO2.

**EDIC trap:** A low ScvO2 almost always means DO2 is insufficient; a normal one does not prove adequate tissue oxygenation.

**Ref:** Vincent JL, De Backer D. Circulatory shock. *N Engl J Med* 2013;369:1726–1734. Cecconi M, et al. Consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring. Task force of the ESICM. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old has hypotension, distended neck veins, a low cardiac output and elevated central venous pressure. Clinical examination does not clarify the cause. According to the ESICM consensus, the preferred next step to determine the type of shock is:
options: Pulmonary artery catheter insertion
Echocardiography
Transpulmonary thermodilution
Repeated lactate measurement alone
CT angiography of the chest in all cases
questions.expl:
**Why B:** When clinical examination does not identify the type of shock, ESICM recommends **echocardiography as the preferred modality** (Level 2, B) rather than invasive monitoring. With a high CVP and low CO it rapidly separates cardiogenic shock (poor LV/RV function) from obstructive shock (tamponade, acute cor pulmonale from PE), and it can be repeated at the bedside.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Routine PAC is recommended against (Level 1, A); it is reserved for refractory shock with RV dysfunction or complex cases.
- C – TPTD gives CO, GEDV and EVLW but cannot separate RV from LV failure or show the pericardium.
- D – Lactate confirms hypoperfusion and tracks its course but does not identify the type of shock.
- E – CT may be needed if PE is suspected, but not in all cases and not before bedside echo in an unstable patient.

**Ref:** Cecconi M, et al. Consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring. Task force of the ESICM. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815.

questions.stem: Which statements reflect the 2014 ESICM consensus?
options: Routine use of a pulmonary artery catheter is recommended.
An absolute target for oxygen delivery should be used in all shock patients.
Lactate should be measured in all patients with suspected shock and repeated.
Static measures such as CVP alone should not be used to guide fluid resuscitation.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Routine PAC is recommended against (Level 1, A); PAC or TPTD is suggested only in severe or complex shock, especially with ARDS (Level 2, C).
- B (False) – ESICM recommends against an absolute DO2 target (Level 1, A), after trials of supranormal DO2 such as Gattinoni 1995 showed no benefit.
- C (True) – Measure lactate whenever shock is suspected (Level 1, C) and repeat it (Level 1, C).
- D (True) – Static measures – CVP, PAOP, GEDV – should not be used alone to guide fluids (Level 1, B); use a fluid challenge and dynamic predictors.

**EDIC trap:** The three Level 1 "against" statements – routine PAC, absolute DO2 target, static preload alone – are exam favourites.

**Ref:** Cecconi M, et al. Consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring. Task force of the ESICM. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815.

questions.stem: The 1995 SvO2 Collaborative Group trial (Gattinoni, NEJM) showed that targeting a supranormal cardiac index or a normal SvO2 in critically ill patients:
options: Reduced ICU mortality by about 10 %
Did not reduce morbidity or mortality
Reduced 6-month mortality only in septic patients
Was achieved in nearly all patients of the cardiac index group
Increased mortality significantly in the SvO2 group
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Gattinoni et al. randomised **762 critically ill patients in 56 ICUs** to a normal cardiac index (control), a supranormal cardiac index or a normal SvO2 (≥ 70 %). Mortality to ICU discharge was **48.4 % vs 48.6 % vs 52.1 %** and at 6 months 62.3 % vs 61.7 % vs 63.8 % – all non-significant, with no reduction in organ dysfunction.

**Why not the others:**

- A – No arm reduced ICU mortality.
- C – There was no 6-month mortality benefit, overall or in a septic subgroup.
- D – The supranormal CI target was achieved in only 44.9 % of patients.
- E – Mortality in the SvO2 arm (52.1 %) was not significantly higher.

**EDIC trap:** "Raise DO2 to supranormal values" is wrong; the goal is adequate DO2 relative to demand.

**Ref:** Gattinoni L, et al.; SvO2 Collaborative Group. *N Engl J Med* 1995;333:1025–1032. Cecconi M, et al. Consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring. Task force of the ESICM. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815.

questions.stem: The "three windows" of tissue hypoperfusion include:
options: Altered mental status
Elevated serum troponin
Mottled, cold skin
Hyperglycaemia
questions.expl:
- A (True) – The brain window: confusion, agitation or obtundation.
- B (False) – Troponin reflects myocardial injury and may point to a cardiogenic cause, but it is not a bedside window of tissue hypoperfusion.
- C (True) – The skin window: cold, clammy, mottled skin with prolonged capillary refill from vasoconstriction.
- D (False) – Stress hyperglycaemia is common but nonspecific; the third window is the kidney – urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/h.

**Ref:** Vincent JL, De Backer D. Circulatory shock. *N Engl J Med* 2013;369:1726–1734.

questions.stem: According to the ESICM consensus, inotropic agents in shock should be added when:
options: Ejection fraction is reduced, regardless of perfusion
Cardiac output is low and hypoperfusion persists despite adequate preload
ScvO2 exceeds 80 %
The MAP target of 65 mmHg is not achieved with noradrenaline
Lactate is below 2 mmol/L
questions.expl:
**Why B:** ESICM suggests adding an inotrope (dobutamine first choice) when **cardiac output is low and hypoperfusion persists despite adequate preload** (Level 2, C). The trigger is the combination of low flow and markers of hypoperfusion (lactate, ScvO2, P(cv-a)CO2, skin), and dobutamine is titrated to perfusion, not to a fixed CI.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Inotropes are recommended against for isolated cardiac dysfunction without hypoperfusion (Level 1, B).
- C – A high ScvO2 does not suggest low output; a low ScvO2 would support adding an inotrope.
- D – Failure to reach the MAP target calls for vasopressor escalation (e.g. adding vasopressin), not an inotrope.
- E – A normal lactate argues against hypoperfusion needing inotropic support.

**EDIC trap:** "Low ejection fraction → dobutamine" is wrong unless hypoperfusion persists.

**Ref:** Cecconi M, et al. Consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring. Task force of the ESICM. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815.

questions.stem: Regarding blood pressure targets in the ESICM consensus:
options: Lower blood pressure may be tolerated in uncontrolled haemorrhage with severe traumatic brain injury.
The MAP target should be individualised.
A higher MAP may be considered in septic shock with chronic hypertension.
An initial MAP target of at least 65 mmHg is recommended.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Permissive hypotension in uncontrolled haemorrhage is suggested only **without** severe head injury (Level 2, C); TBI needs adequate cerebral perfusion pressure.
- B (True) – The MAP target should be individualised (Level 1, B).
- C (True) – A higher MAP may be considered with chronic hypertension or if patients improve clinically at higher pressure (Level 2, B); in SEPSISPAM 80–85 mmHg reduced RRT in chronic hypertensives.
- D (True) – The initial MAP target is ≥ 65 mmHg (Level 1, C).

**Ref:** Cecconi M, et al. Consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring. Task force of the ESICM. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815. Asfar P, et al. SEPSISPAM. *N Engl J Med* 2014;370:1583–1593.

open.q: Explain the relationship between DO2 and VO2 as oxygen delivery falls, and why a normal or high ScvO2 does not exclude tissue hypoxia in septic shock.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- DO2 = CO × CaO2; CaO2 ≈ 1.34 × Hb × SaO2 (+ negligible dissolved O2); main adjustable determinant is CO.
- Initially, falling DO2 is compensated by increased extraction → VO2 stays constant (plateau), SvO2 falls.
- Below DO2crit, extraction is exhausted → VO2 becomes supply-dependent → anaerobic metabolism → lactate rises.
- SvO2 reflects the DO2/VO2 balance: falls with ↓ CO, ↓ Hb, ↓ SaO2, ↑ VO2 (fever, shivering, pain).
- In sepsis extraction is impaired (microcirculatory shunting, mitochondrial dysfunction) → dysoxia with normal/high SvO2.
- Therefore no single parameter suffices – combine lactate (repeated), ScvO2, P(cv-a)CO2 and clinical windows (skin, kidneys, brain).

open.q: Outline how you would identify the type of shock in a hypotensive patient whose clinical examination is inconclusive, and the initial treatment principles according to ESICM 2014.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Hypotension is not required; look for hypoperfusion (three windows) and measure lactate (and repeat).
- Echocardiography as preferred modality to determine the type of shock (Level 2, B); distinguishes cardiogenic vs obstructive vs hypovolaemic vs distributive.
- Arterial and central venous catheter if not responding or on vasopressors; ScvO2 and P(cv-a)CO2 to assess type and adequacy of CO.
- No routine PAC (Level 1, A); PAC/TPTD in complex cases or severe shock with ARDS.
- VIP: ventilate, infuse (fluid challenge guided by dynamic predictors, not CVP alone), pump (noradrenaline first line; dobutamine if low CO with persistent hypoperfusion).
- Initial MAP ≥ 65 mmHg, then individualise (lower in uncontrolled haemorrhage without TBI, higher with chronic hypertension).
- No absolute/supranormal DO2 target (Gattinoni 1995: no benefit).

title: W04 · D2 – Fluid responsiveness: PLR, PPV/SVV, EEO, mini-fluid challenge

questions.stem: A sedated patient with septic shock is ventilated in volume control with a tidal volume of 6 mL/kg PBW, in sinus rhythm. Pulse pressure variation is 5 %. What is the best interpretation?
options: A fluid bolus of 2 L should be given
PPV may be falsely negative because of the low tidal volume; perform a tidal volume challenge or PLR
PPV is reliable because the patient is in sinus rhythm
The patient is definitely not fluid responsive
PPV is falsely positive because of low tidal volume
questions.expl:
**Why B:** PPV depends on the size of the cyclic intrathoracic pressure swings; at VT 6 mL/kg the change in preload is too small, so a low PPV may be **falsely negative**. De Backer 2005: a PPV threshold correctly classified only 51 % of patients at VT < 8 mL/kg vs 88 % at ≥ 8 mL/kg. A tidal volume challenge (6 → 8 mL/kg for ~1 min), PLR with real-time CO or EEO resolves the question.

**Why not the others:**

- A – There is no evidence of responsiveness, and a large untested bolus risks fluid overload.
- C – Sinus rhythm is necessary but not sufficient; the low tidal volume remains a limitation.
- D – A PPV below 12–13 % at low VT cannot exclude responsiveness.
- E – Low tidal volume produces false-negative, not false-positive, results.

**EDIC trap:** PPV 5 % at VT 6 mL/kg is not proof of non-responsiveness (LIMITS).

**Ref:** De Backer D, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2005;31:517–523. Monnet X, Shi R, Teboul JL. Prediction of fluid responsiveness. What's new? *Ann Intensive Care* 2022;12:46.

questions.stem: Regarding passive leg raising (PLR):
options: It should start from the semi-recumbent position.
A cardiac output increase ≥ 10 % predicts fluid responsiveness.
Changes in arterial pulse pressure are as sensitive as changes in cardiac output.
Intra-abdominal hypertension has no effect on its reliability.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Starting semi-recumbent mobilises splanchnic as well as leg venous blood, giving a larger preload challenge than starting supine.
- B (True) – A rise in CO/SV ≥ 10 %, measured in real time because the effect peaks within ~1 min, predicts responsiveness (AUROC 0.95).
- C (False) – Pulse pressure changes have a sensitivity of only 0.56 (AUROC 0.77) vs 0.85 (AUROC 0.95) for CO; blood pressure alone is not enough.
- D (False) – Intra-abdominal hypertension impedes venous return from the legs and splanchnic bed and can cause false-negative PLR.

**EDIC trap:** PLR judged by blood pressure alone is a classic wrong answer.

**Ref:** Monnet X, et al. Passive leg raising for predicting fluid responsiveness: a systematic review and meta-analysis. *Intensive Care Med* 2016;42:1935–1947. Monnet X, Shi R, Teboul JL. Prediction of fluid responsiveness. What's new? *Ann Intensive Care* 2022;12:46.

questions.stem: In the original study by Michard et al. (AJRCCM 2000), the threshold of respiratory variation in pulse pressure discriminating responders from non-responders was:
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Michard et al. studied **40 ventilated septic patients** with acute circulatory failure; a respiratory variation in pulse pressure (ΔPP) of **13 %** separated responders from non-responders with **sensitivity 94 % and specificity 96 %**. ΔPP was more accurate than systolic pressure variation and static filling pressures.

**Why not the others:**

- A – 20 % is well above the threshold and would miss many responders.
- B – 10 % is the PLR threshold for the rise in cardiac output, not the ΔPP cut-off.
- D – 5 % is the threshold for the EEO test and the mini-fluid challenge.
- E – 8 is the minimum tidal volume (mL/kg) for PPV to be reliable, not the ΔPP threshold.

**EDIC trap:** Keep the numbers apart: PPV 13 %, PLR 10 %, EEO 5 %, EEO + EIO VTI sum 13 %, VT ≥ 8 mL/kg.

**Ref:** Michard F, et al. *Am J Respir Crit Care Med* 2000;162:134–138.

questions.stem: Conditions that limit the reliability of pulse pressure variation include:
options: Low tidal volume ventilation (< 8 mL/kg)
Open chest
Spontaneous breathing activity
Atrial fibrillation
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Low VT produces small intrathoracic pressure swings and false-negative PPV (De Backer 2005).
- B (True) – With an open chest, ventilation no longer transmits pressure changes to the heart (the "T" in LIMITS).
- C (True) – Spontaneous efforts make pressure swings irregular; respiratory variation in PP had an AUC of only ~0.68.
- D (True) – Irregular beats vary stroke volume independently of ventilation; other limits are a low HR/RR ratio and raised abdominal pressure.

**EDIC trap:** Only a minority of ICU patients meet all conditions for PPV, which is why PLR and EEO were developed.

**Ref:** Monnet X, Shi R, Teboul JL. Prediction of fluid responsiveness. What's new? *Ann Intensive Care* 2022;12:46. De Backer D, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2005;31:517–523.

questions.stem: The end-expiratory occlusion test:
options: Requires a 5-second occlusion and a 15 % rise in cardiac output
Requires an occlusion of about 15 seconds and a rise in cardiac output ≥ 5 %
Is best assessed by changes in central venous pressure
Is unreliable in patients with arrhythmias
Can be performed in non-intubated spontaneously breathing patients on a face mask
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Interrupting ventilation at end-expiration for **~15 s** (> 12 s so the extra preload crosses the pulmonary circulation) removes the cyclic inspiratory impediment to venous return. A **cardiac output rise ≥ 5 %** predicts responsiveness (Monnet 2009: sensitivity 91 %, specificity 100 % with pulse contour CI; Messina 2019 meta-analysis AUROC 0.96).

**Why not the others:**

- A – A 5 s pause is too short for the preload change to reach the LV, and the threshold is 5 %, not 15 %.
- C – CVP is a static pressure, not flow; EEO needs a precise CO measurement.
- D – The original study included patients with arrhythmias, because the effect spans several beats.
- E – EEO requires an intubated patient who tolerates a 15 s pause in ventilation.

**Ref:** Monnet X, et al. End-expiratory occlusion test. *Crit Care Med* 2009;37:951–956. Messina A, et al. Functional hemodynamic tests: EEO and mini-fluid challenge meta-analysis. *Crit Care* 2019;23(1).

questions.stem: Regarding the mini-fluid challenge:
options: Echocardiographic VTI is precise enough to detect a 5 % change reliably in all cases.
It consists of about 100–150 mL given over 1–2 minutes.
Like PLR, its haemodynamic effect is fully reversible in non-responders.
The threshold for a positive response is about a 25 % increase in cardiac output.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – The least significant change of echo VTI is ~12 %, so a 5 % rise cannot be detected reliably; a precise method such as calibrated pulse contour is needed.
- B (True) – The mini-fluid challenge is 100–150 mL over 1–2 min; with 50 mL it is less reliable.
- C (False) – The fluid is actually given and cannot be withdrawn in a non-responder, unlike PLR or EEO.
- D (False) – The threshold is about 5 % (Messina 2019: AUROC 0.91, sensitivity 0.82, specificity 0.83).

**Ref:** Messina A, et al. Functional hemodynamic tests: EEO and mini-fluid challenge meta-analysis. *Crit Care* 2019;23(1). Monnet X, Shi R, Teboul JL. Prediction of fluid responsiveness. What's new? *Ann Intensive Care* 2022;12:46.

questions.stem: In the 2016 meta-analysis by Monnet et al., the pooled area under the ROC curve for PLR-induced changes in cardiac output was approximately:
questions.expl:
**Why B:** The meta-analysis pooled **21 studies and 991 patients**: PLR-induced changes in cardiac output had a pooled sensitivity of 0.85, specificity of 0.91 and **AUROC 0.95**, using a threshold of about 10 %. Accuracy was maintained with spontaneous breathing, arrhythmias and low tidal volume.

**Why not the others:**

- A – 0.85 is the pooled sensitivity for CO changes, not the AUROC.
- C – 0.70 understates PLR; it is closer to PPV accuracy during spontaneous breathing (~0.68).
- D – 0.77 is the AUROC for PLR-induced changes in pulse pressure.
- E – 0.60 would make PLR a poor test, which it is not when CO is measured.

**Ref:** Monnet X, et al. Passive leg raising for predicting fluid responsiveness: a systematic review and meta-analysis. *Intensive Care Med* 2016;42:1935–1947.

questions.stem: Regarding the ESICM 2014 consensus on fluid management in shock:
options: A fluid challenge is recommended before further fluid, except in obvious hypovolaemia such as massive bleeding.
A target CVP of 8–12 mmHg should guide fluid administration.
GEDV alone should not be used to guide fluid therapy.
Static predictors are recommended over dynamic predictors.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – A fluid challenge is recommended before further fluid (Level 1, C), except in obvious hypovolaemia such as massive bleeding, where fluid is given promptly.
- B (False) – The Rivers-era CVP target of 8–12 mmHg is abandoned; static measures alone should not guide fluids (Level 1, B).
- C (True) – GEDV is a static volumetric preload index and, like CVP and PAOP, should not be used alone (Level 1, B).
- D (False) – Dynamic predictors are recommended over static ones (Level 1, B).

**Ref:** Cecconi M, et al. ESICM consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815.

questions.stem: A patient with septic shock and raised intracranial pressure after head injury is mechanically ventilated, in atrial fibrillation, with a calibrated pulse contour monitor. Which test of fluid responsiveness is most appropriate?
options: CVP response to a 1 L bolus
Inferior vena cava collapsibility
End-expiratory occlusion test
Passive leg raising
Pulse pressure variation
questions.expl:
**Why C:** EEO remains valid in **atrial fibrillation** and requires only an intubated patient who tolerates a ~15 s pause. The calibrated pulse contour gives continuous, real-time CO precise enough to detect the ≥ 5 % rise. It is therefore the only listed test not invalidated by this patient's conditions.

**Why not the others:**

- A – CVP change does not predict responsiveness, and 1 L is a treatment rather than a test.
- B – IVC collapsibility has poor accuracy in ventilated patients, and ESICM 2021 recommends against basic ultrasound for this purpose.
- D – PLR lowers the trunk from the semi-recumbent position and is contraindicated in intracranial hypertension.
- E – AF invalidates PPV because stroke volume varies from beat to beat.

**Ref:** Monnet X, et al. End-expiratory occlusion test. *Crit Care Med* 2009;37:951–956. Monnet X, Shi R, Teboul JL. Prediction of fluid responsiveness. What's new? *Ann Intensive Care* 2022;12:46.

questions.stem: Regarding fluid responsiveness:
options: A positive test of fluid responsiveness is by itself an indication for fluid.
In meta-analysed studies only about half of patients were fluid responders.
A classic 500 mL fluid challenge may itself be considered treatment rather than a test.
Respiratory variation of IVC diameter has high sensitivity and specificity in ventilated patients.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Fluid responsiveness is physiological – healthy people are responders; fluid needs hypoperfusion **plus** a positive test **plus** acceptable risk.
- B (True) – The median proportion of responders was 54 % (Messina 2019).
- C (True) – Monnet 2022: a 200–500 mL challenge cannot be taken back in a non-responder, so it is more a treatment than a test.
- D (False) – IVC variability has low sensitivity and specificity in meta-analyses and is distorted by intra-abdominal pressure, low VT and the measurement site.

**EDIC trap:** "Fluid responsive" does not mean "needs fluid".

**Ref:** Monnet X, Shi R, Teboul JL. Prediction of fluid responsiveness. What's new? *Ann Intensive Care* 2022;12:46. Messina A, et al. Functional hemodynamic tests: EEO and mini-fluid challenge meta-analysis. *Crit Care* 2019;23(1).

open.q: A spontaneously breathing, non-intubated patient in atrial fibrillation has septic shock and persistent hypoperfusion after initial fluids. Explain which tests of fluid responsiveness are valid in this patient and which are not, and how you would perform the most suitable one.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- PPV/SVV invalid: spontaneous breathing and irregular rhythm (LIMITS); IVC variability unreliable.
- EEO requires intubation and a 15 s ventilatory pause – not applicable.
- PLR is suitable: works with spontaneous breathing and arrhythmias.
- Technique: start semi-recumbent, move trunk to horizontal and raise legs to 30–45°; measure CO/SV in real time (echo VTI, pulse contour, oesophageal Doppler) within ~1 min.
- Positive if CO rises ≥ 10%; BP alone is not sufficient (PP sensitivity 0.56 vs CO 0.85).
- Check for limitations: IAH (false negative), intracranial hypertension (contraindication).
- Mini-fluid challenge (100–150 mL over 1–2 min, ~5%) is an alternative but needs very precise CO measurement and the fluid cannot be withdrawn.
- A positive test supports fluid only if hypoperfusion persists and the risk is acceptable.

open.q: Explain why pulse pressure variation fails during lung-protective ventilation at 6 mL/kg, and how the tidal volume challenge addresses this.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- PPV relies on cyclic changes in intrathoracic pressure reducing RV preload and, after pulmonary transit, LV SV during positive-pressure breaths.
- With low VT the intrathoracic pressure swing is small → small SV variation even in preload-dependent patients → false negatives.
- De Backer 2005: PPV threshold 12% correctly classified only 51% at VT < 8 mL/kg vs 88% at ≥ 8 mL/kg.
- Low compliance (ARDS) further reduces pressure transmission.
- Tidal volume challenge: transiently increase VT from 6 to 8 mL/kg PBW for ~1 min and observe the absolute change in PPV.
- A significant absolute rise in PPV (published thresholds ~1–3.5%) indicates preload dependence.
- Still requires controlled ventilation and sinus rhythm; alternatives are PLR or EEO.

title: W04 · D3 – Cardiac output measurement: Fick, PAC, transpulmonary thermodilution, pulse contour

questions.stem: In the PAC-Man trial (Lancet 2005), the use of a pulmonary artery catheter in ICU patients:
options: Reduced hospital mortality from 68 % to 66 %
Did not significantly change hospital mortality (68 % vs 66 %)
Was associated with no complications
Increased hospital mortality significantly
Was combined with a strict goal-directed treatment protocol
questions.expl:
**Why B:** PAC-Man randomised **1041 patients in 65 UK ICUs** in whom the clinician considered a PAC indicated, without any treatment protocol. Hospital mortality was **68 % (PAC) vs 66 % (no PAC), p = 0.39**. Complications occurred in 10 % of insertions, none fatal – the PAC is a monitor, and it helps only if the data lead to effective treatment.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Mortality was numerically higher with PAC (68 %), and the difference was not significant.
- C – Complications (haematoma, arterial puncture, arrhythmias) occurred in 10 % of insertions.
- D – The difference was non-significant (p = 0.39).
- E – There was no protocol; clinicians used the data as they wished.

**EDIC trap:** A negative PAC-Man does not mean PAC measurements are inaccurate.

**Ref:** Harvey S, et al. PAC-Man. *Lancet* 2005;366:472–477.

questions.stem: Regarding the Fick principle:
options: The direct Fick method requires mixed venous blood.
Using an estimated rather than measured VO2 introduces negligible error.
Cardiac output equals VO2 divided by the arteriovenous oxygen content difference.
At constant VO2, haemoglobin and SaO2, a fall in cardiac output increases SvO2.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Direct Fick needs measured VO2 (gas exchange) and true mixed venous blood from the pulmonary artery.
- B (False) – Indirect Fick uses tabulated VO2; in critical illness VO2 varies widely (fever, sepsis, sedation), so the error can be substantial.
- C (True) – CO = VO2 / (CaO2 − CvO2) – the Fick principle.
- D (False) – At constant VO2, Hb and SaO2, a lower CO widens the arteriovenous difference, so SvO2 **falls**; this is why SvO2 tracks flow.

**Ref:** Vincent JL, De Backer D. *N Engl J Med* 2013;369:1726–1734. Cecconi M, et al. ESICM consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815.

questions.stem: A patient with ARDS and septic shock has transpulmonary thermodilution: EVLWI 16 mL/kg, PVPI 4.2. The most likely interpretation is:
options: Increased lung water with increased pulmonary vascular permeability
Hydrostatic (cardiogenic) pulmonary oedema
Measurement error, as PVPI cannot exceed 3
Hypovolaemia
Normal lung water
questions.expl:
**Why A:** An EVLWI of 16 mL/kg is more than twice normal (< 7 mL/kg, upper limit ~10), confirming pulmonary oedema. PVPI (EVLW / pulmonary blood volume) **> 3** indicates a leaky alveolocapillary barrier – permeability oedema, as in sepsis-related ARDS.

**Why not the others:**

- B – Hydrostatic oedema has a PVPI ≤ 3, because lung water rises together with pulmonary blood volume.
- C – PVPI can exceed 3; values > 3 are exactly what defines permeability oedema.
- D – Hypovolaemia does not increase lung water; it would lower GEDV, not raise EVLW.
- E – 16 mL/kg is clearly raised.

**EDIC trap:** TPTD volumes quantify oedema but do not predict fluid responsiveness.

**Ref:** Jozwiak M, Teboul JL, Monnet X. Extravascular lung water in critical care. *Ann Intensive Care* 2015;5:38. Monnet X, Teboul JL. Transpulmonary thermodilution: advantages and limits. *Crit Care* 2017;21.

questions.stem: Regarding transpulmonary thermodilution:
options: Cold indicator is injected via a central venous catheter in the superior vena cava territory.
TPTD can separately estimate right and left ventricular function.
GEDV represents the blood volume of the pulmonary circulation.
The thermistor is usually placed in the pulmonary artery.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Cold saline is injected via a CVC in the superior vena cava territory; a femoral venous injection overestimates GEDV.
- B (False) – TPTD gives global values only and cannot separate RV from LV function; use echo or PAC when RV dysfunction is suspected.
- C (False) – GEDV (ITTV − PTV) is the sum of the maximal volumes of all four cardiac chambers, a static preload index; pulmonary blood volume is the denominator of PVPI.
- D (False) – The thermistor-tipped catheter is arterial, usually femoral (axillary or brachial alternatives); a pulmonary artery thermistor belongs to the PAC.

**Ref:** Monnet X, Teboul JL. Transpulmonary thermodilution: advantages and limits. *Crit Care* 2017;21.

questions.stem: The SUPPORT study by Connors et al. (JAMA 1996) on right heart catheterisation was:
options: A randomised trial showing reduced mortality with PAC
A meta-analysis of PAC trials
A randomised trial in high-risk surgical patients
A trial in decompensated heart failure only
A prospective observational cohort showing higher 30-day mortality associated with PAC
questions.expl:
**Why E:** SUPPORT was a **prospective observational cohort** of 5735 critically ill adults in five US teaching hospitals. Using propensity score matching, right heart catheterisation was associated with **higher 30-day mortality (OR 1.24)**, higher costs and longer stay, which triggered the randomised PAC trials.

**Why not the others:**

- A – It was not randomised, and it suggested harm rather than benefit.
- B – It was a single cohort, not a meta-analysis.
- C – The RCT in high-risk surgical patients was Sandham 2003 (1994 patients, 7.8 % vs 7.7 %).
- D – The trial restricted to heart failure was ESCAPE (433 patients).

**Ref:** Connors AF Jr, et al. SUPPORT. *JAMA* 1996;276:889–897.

questions.stem: Regarding PAC randomised trials:
options: PAC-Man enrolled all ICU patients regardless of whether the clinician considered a PAC indicated.
ESCAPE enrolled patients with septic shock.
Sandham (NEJM 2003) found more pulmonary embolism in the PAC group.
ESCAPE showed more days alive out of hospital with PAC.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – PAC-Man was pragmatic: only patients in whom the treating clinician considered a PAC indicated were enrolled.
- B (False) – ESCAPE enrolled 433 patients hospitalised with severe symptomatic heart failure.
- C (True) – Sandham (1994 high-risk surgical patients): mortality 7.8 % vs 7.7 %, but pulmonary embolism 8 vs 0 in the PAC group.
- D (False) – ESCAPE showed no difference in days alive out of hospital and more adverse events with PAC.

**Ref:** Harvey S, et al. PAC-Man. *Lancet* 2005;366:472–477. Sandham JD, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2003;348:5–14. ESCAPE. *JAMA* 2005;294:1625–1633.

questions.stem: According to the 2014 ESICM consensus, in which situation is a pulmonary artery catheter most appropriate?
options: All patients with septic shock on noradrenaline
Shock responding promptly to initial fluids
Refractory shock with right ventricular dysfunction
Routine postoperative monitoring after elective surgery
Hypovolaemic shock from overt bleeding
questions.expl:
**Why C:** ESICM suggests a PAC in **refractory shock with right ventricular dysfunction** (Level 2, C). Only the PAC gives continuous pulmonary artery pressures, PVR, PAOP and true SvO2 to guide fluids, inotropes and pulmonary vasodilators. PAC or TPTD is also suggested in severe shock with ARDS.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Routine PAC is recommended against in shock (Level 1, A).
- B – Patients responding to initial therapy do not need routine CO measurement (Level 1, C).
- D – Routine monitoring after elective surgery is not indicated; Sandham showed no benefit and more PE.
- E – Overt bleeding needs source control and blood products; a PAC adds delay, not benefit.

**Ref:** Cecconi M, et al. ESICM consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815.

questions.stem: Regarding extravascular lung water (EVLW):
options: Normal indexed EVLW is below about 7 mL/kg.
In ARDS, the maximal EVLWI during the course was an independent predictor of 28-day mortality.
A PVPI ≤ 3 suggests hydrostatic pulmonary oedema.
A fall in EVLWI during the first 48 hours of ARDS was associated with survival.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Normal EVLWI is < 7 mL/kg (534 normal lungs: 7.3 ± 2.8 mL/kg), with an upper limit of ~10 mL/kg.
- B (True) – In 200 ARDS patients the **maximal** EVLWI during the illness, not the day-1 value, independently predicted 28-day mortality.
- C (True) – PVPI ≤ 3 suggests hydrostatic oedema; > 3 suggests permeability oedema.
- D (True) – A fall in EVLWI over the first 48 h was associated with survival; a change > ~1 mL/kg is generally significant.

**Ref:** Jozwiak M, Teboul JL, Monnet X. Extravascular lung water in critical care. *Ann Intensive Care* 2015;5:38.

questions.stem: Which condition most typically introduces error in thermodilution cardiac output measured by a pulmonary artery catheter?
options: Severe tricuspid regurgitation
Mild anaemia
Hypothermia of 35 °C
Use of noradrenaline
Sinus tachycardia
questions.expl:
**Why A:** The Stewart–Hamilton method assumes the cold indicator passes the thermistor once, fully mixed. In **severe tricuspid regurgitation** the indicator regurgitates and recirculates, producing a prolonged, flattened curve and an inaccurate CO, usually underestimated. Intracardiac shunts and very low output cause similar errors.

**Why not the others:**

- B – Haemoglobin does not affect a thermal indicator.
- C – Stable mild hypothermia does not invalidate the method, which relies on the injectate–blood temperature difference.
- D – Noradrenaline changes flow, not the validity of thermodilution (unlike uncalibrated pulse contour).
- E – Tachycardia does not distort the curve; three averaged injections are used anyway.

**Ref:** Monnet X, Teboul JL. Transpulmonary thermodilution: advantages and limits. *Crit Care* 2017;21. Cecconi M, et al. ESICM consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815.

questions.stem: Regarding arterial pulse contour analysis:
options: Calibrated systems use thermodilution to calibrate stroke volume estimates.
Uncalibrated systems are less reliable for absolute cardiac output when vascular tone changes rapidly.
Recalibration is unnecessary after major changes in vasopressor dose.
ESICM suggests using less invasive devices only if validated in shock.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Calibrated systems use transpulmonary thermodilution (or indicator dilution) to calibrate pulse contour stroke volume.
- B (True) – Uncalibrated systems estimate arterial impedance from demographics and the waveform, so absolute CO is unreliable with rapid changes in vascular tone; they track short-term trends better.
- C (False) – After a major change in vascular tone, such as a vasopressor dose change, recalibration is required.
- D (True) – Use less invasive devices only if they have been validated in shock (best practice).

**Ref:** Teboul JL, et al. Less invasive hemodynamic monitoring in critically ill patients. *Intensive Care Med* 2016;42(9). Cecconi M, et al. ESICM consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815.

open.q: Explain why the PAC-Man, Sandham and ESCAPE trials found no benefit of the pulmonary artery catheter, and outline the situations in which a PAC is still appropriate according to ESICM 2014.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- A PAC is a monitor, not a treatment; benefit requires an effective treatment protocol that follows from the data.
- PAC-Man (1041 pts, 65 UK ICUs): pragmatic, no protocol; mortality 68 vs 66% (NS); complications in 10%; treatment changed in 80% within 2 h without outcome effect.
- Sandham (1994 high-risk surgical pts): 7.8 vs 7.7%, NS; more PE with PAC (8 vs 0).
- ESCAPE (433 heart failure pts): no difference in days alive out of hospital; more adverse events.
- SUPPORT (observational, 5735 pts) suggested harm (OR 1.24) – prompted the RCTs; confounding possible.
- ESICM: routine PAC not recommended (Level 1, A).
- PAC appropriate in refractory shock with RV dysfunction (Level 2, C), and (or TPTD) in severe shock especially with ARDS and in complex patients (Level 2, C).

open.q: A patient with septic shock and ARDS has TPTD monitoring: EVLWI 15 mL/kg, PVPI 4.0, GEDVI normal, and a positive PLR. Interpret these values and explain how they inform fluid management.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- EVLWI 15 mL/kg is clearly raised (normal < 7, upper limit ~10 mL/kg) → significant pulmonary oedema.
- PVPI > 3 → permeability (ARDS-type) rather than hydrostatic oedema.
- GEDV is a static preload indicator – should not be used alone to guide fluids (ESICM Level 1, B).
- A positive PLR indicates preload responsiveness, but responsiveness ≠ need for fluid.
- High EVLW serves as a safety limit: titrate fluids cautiously and only if hypoperfusion persists (ESICM best practice).
- Maximal EVLWI predicts 28-d mortality in ARDS; a fall during the first 48 h is associated with survival → aim to avoid further rises.
- Use calibrated pulse contour for continuous CO; recalibrate after major changes in vascular tone.

title: W04 · D4 – Perfusion targets: lactate, ScvO2, P(cv-a)CO2, CRT; EGDT and ANDROMEDA-SHOCK

questions.stem: In ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (JAMA 2019), resuscitation targeting capillary refill time compared with lactate:
options: Significantly reduced 28-day mortality (p < 0.01)
Increased fluid overload and mortality
Did not significantly reduce 28-day mortality but was associated with lower SOFA score at 72 h
Was compared with an ScvO2-targeted strategy
Was applied for 24 hours
questions.expl:
**Why C:** ANDROMEDA-SHOCK randomised **424 septic shock patients in 28 ICUs (5 countries)** to an 8-h stepwise protocol targeting normal CRT vs lactate normalisation or a fall > 20 % per 2 h. 28-day mortality was **34.9 % vs 43.4 % (HR 0.75, 95 % CI 0.55–1.02, p = 0.06)**, while SOFA at 72 h was lower with CRT (5.6 vs 6.6, p = 0.045). A Bayesian reanalysis gave > 90 % probability of benefit.

**Why not the others:**

- A – p = 0.06 – the primary outcome was not significant.
- B – CRT targeting was associated with less organ dysfunction, not more harm.
- D – The comparator was a lactate-targeted strategy, not ScvO2.
- E – The protocol lasted 8 hours.

**EDIC trap:** ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (2019) = CRT vs lactate; ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 (2025) = personalised CRT protocol vs usual care.

**Ref:** Hernández G, et al. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK. *JAMA* 2019;321:654–664. Zampieri FG, et al. *Am J Respir Crit Care Med* 2020;201:423–429.

questions.stem: Regarding the original EGDT trial (Rivers, NEJM 2001):
options: Targets included CVP 15–20 mmHg, MAP ≥ 90 mmHg and ScvO2 ≥ 80 %.
If ScvO2 remained low, transfusion to a haematocrit ≥ 30 % and dobutamine were used.
Hospital mortality was similar in both groups.
It enrolled ICU patients up to 24 hours after admission.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Targets were CVP 8–12 mmHg, MAP ≥ 65 mmHg, urine output ≥ 0.5 mL/kg/h and ScvO2 ≥ 70 %.
- B (True) – If ScvO2 stayed < 70 %, red cells were transfused to haematocrit ≥ 30 %, then dobutamine was added.
- C (False) – Hospital mortality was 30.5 % with EGDT vs 46.5 % with standard care (263 patients, single centre).
- D (False) – It enrolled emergency department patients during the first 6 hours, before ICU admission.

**Ref:** Rivers E, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2001;345:1368–1377.

questions.stem: Which trial of early goal-directed therapy had three arms (EGDT, protocol-based standard therapy, usual care)?
options: ARISE
ProCESS
PRISM
ProMISe
ANDROMEDA-SHOCK
questions.expl:
**Why B:** ProCESS (1341 patients, 31 US emergency departments) compared **EGDT, protocol-based standard therapy** (no mandatory CVC or ScvO2) and **usual care**. 60-day in-hospital mortality was 21.0 % vs 18.2 % vs 18.9 % – no significant difference, and also none at 90 days and 1 year.

**Why not the others:**

- A – ARISE had two arms (EGDT vs usual care) in 1600 patients, mainly in Australia and New Zealand.
- C – PRISM was an individual patient meta-analysis of the three trials, not a trial with arms.
- D – ProMISe was a two-arm UK trial (1260 patients).
- E – ANDROMEDA-SHOCK compared CRT- with lactate-targeted resuscitation (two arms).

**Ref:** ProCESS Investigators. *N Engl J Med* 2014;370:1683–1693.

questions.stem: Regarding the PRISM individual patient meta-analysis (NEJM 2017):
options: 90-day mortality was not different between EGDT and usual care.
It pooled ProCESS, ARISE and ANDROMEDA-SHOCK.
EGDT was associated with longer ICU stay and higher costs.
Patients with the highest lactate benefited significantly from EGDT.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Among 3723 patients, 90-day mortality was 24.9 % vs 25.4 % (aOR 0.97).
- B (False) – PRISM pooled ProCESS, ARISE and ProMISe, which were prospectively harmonised; ANDROMEDA-SHOCK is a CRT trial.
- C (True) – EGDT was associated with longer ICU stay, longer cardiovascular support and higher costs.
- D (False) – No subgroup – high lactate, hypotension with hyperlactataemia or high predicted risk – benefited.

**Ref:** PRISM Investigators. *N Engl J Med* 2017;376:2223–2234.

questions.stem: A patient with septic shock after initial resuscitation has MAP 70 mmHg on noradrenaline, ScvO2 74 %, lactate 3.8 mmol/L and a central venous-to-arterial PCO2 difference of 9 mmHg. The most likely interpretation is:
options: Resuscitation is complete
The CO2 gap is normal
Persistent inadequate blood flow despite normal ScvO2
Hyperlactataemia must be due to adrenaline
Cardiac output is adequate because ScvO2 > 70 %
questions.expl:
**Why C:** By the CO2 Fick equation, the P(cv-a)CO2 gap is **inversely related to cardiac output**; **≥ 6 mmHg** means flow is insufficient to wash out tissue CO2. ScvO2 74 % looks reassuring, but a gap of 9 mmHg plus lactate 3.8 mmol/L show persistent hypoperfusion. Ospina-Tascón 2013 (85 patients): a persistently high gap after 6 h predicted higher SOFA and 28-day mortality, even with ScvO2 ≥ 70 %.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Lactate 3.8 mmol/L and a high CO2 gap show that resuscitation is not complete.
- B – A normal gap is < 6 mmHg; 9 mmHg is high.
- D – The patient is on noradrenaline, and septic hyperlactataemia is multifactorial – it cannot be blamed on adrenaline.
- E – A normal ScvO2 does not exclude low flow when extraction is impaired.

**Ref:** Ospina-Tascón GA, et al. *Crit Care* 2013;17:R294.

questions.stem: Regarding ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 (JAMA 2025):
options: The protocol included assessment of fluid responsiveness before fluid boluses.
The intervention was a personalised, tiered protocol targeting capillary refill time for 6 hours.
The primary outcome was a hierarchical composite analysed with a win ratio.
28-day mortality was significantly lower with CRT-targeted resuscitation.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Tier 1 required a fluid responsiveness test before each bolus (up to ~1 L).
- B (True) – CRT-PHR lasted 6 h with hourly CRT; tier 1 used a phenotype from pulse and diastolic pressure, tier 2 echocardiography, a higher MAP trial or a dobutamine test.
- C (True) – Death → duration of organ support → hospital stay; win ratio 1.16 (95 % CI 1.02–1.33, p = 0.04).
- D (False) – 28-day mortality was 26.5 % vs 26.6 %; the benefit came from shorter organ support.

**EDIC trap:** Positive for the hierarchical composite, neutral for mortality (1467 patients, 86 ICUs, 19 countries).

**Ref:** Hernández G, et al. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2. *JAMA* 2025;334:1988–1999.

questions.stem: In the LACTATE study (Jansen, AJRCCM 2010), the intervention group was resuscitated with the target of:
options: ScvO2 ≥ 70 % in 6 hours
A decrease in lactate of at least 20 % every 2 hours during the first 8 hours
Capillary refill time ≤ 3 s
Lactate clearance of 10 % in 24 hours
Lactate < 1 mmol/L within 1 hour
questions.expl:
**Why B:** The LACTATE study randomised **348 ICU patients with lactate ≥ 3 mmol/L**; the intervention targeted a **≥ 20 % decrease every 2 h for the first 8 h**, while control clinicians did not see lactate after admission. Hospital mortality was 33.9 % vs 43.5 % (crude p = 0.067), but **adjusted HR 0.61** was significant, with earlier weaning from inotropes and ventilation.

**Why not the others:**

- A – ScvO2 ≥ 70 % within 6 h was the Rivers EGDT target; in LACTATE ScvO2 only helped decide how to act on lactate.
- C – CRT ≤ 3 s was the target in ANDROMEDA-SHOCK.
- D – A ≥ 10 % lactate clearance was used in the ED trial by Jones (JAMA 2010), over 6 h, not 24 h.
- E – Lactate falls over hours, so normalisation within 1 hour is unrealistic and was never a target.

**Ref:** Jansen TC, et al. *Am J Respir Crit Care Med* 2010;182:752–761.

questions.stem: Causes of hyperlactataemia in a patient with septic shock include:
options: Beta-2-adrenergic stimulation by adrenaline
Reduced hepatic clearance
Thiamine deficiency
Tissue dysoxia from inadequate oxygen delivery
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Adrenaline's β2 effect accelerates aerobic glycolysis in muscle (type B), independent of hypoxia.
- B (True) – The liver clears most lactate (Cori cycle); hepatic hypoperfusion or dysfunction slows clearance.
- C (True) – Thiamine is a cofactor of pyruvate dehydrogenase; deficiency (alcohol, malnutrition) diverts pyruvate to lactate.
- D (True) – Type A hyperlactataemia: below the critical DO2, anaerobic metabolism produces lactate.

**EDIC trap:** Lactate is not synonymous with hypoxia – but a high ScvO2 does not rule out a perfusion problem either.

**Ref:** Garcia-Alvarez M, Marik P, Bellomo R. *Crit Care* 2014;18:503. Kraut JA, Madias NE. *N Engl J Med* 2014;371:2309–2319.

questions.stem: Which statement about the ARISE and ProMISe trials is correct?
options: ARISE enrolled only patients with lactate > 10 mmol/L
ARISE was conducted in the UK
ProMISe showed lower mortality with EGDT
Both showed no reduction in 90-day mortality with EGDT
ProMISe showed EGDT to be cost-effective
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Both trials found **no reduction in 90-day mortality** with EGDT. ARISE (1600 patients, mainly Australia and New Zealand): 18.6 % vs 18.8 %. ProMISe (1260 patients, 56 UK hospitals): 29.5 % vs 29.2 %, with higher costs and no QALY gain.

**Why not the others:**

- A – ARISE enrolled early septic shock (refractory hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L); there was no 10 mmol/L criterion.
- B – ARISE was Australasian; the UK trial was ProMISe.
- C – ProMISe mortality was 29.5 % vs 29.2 % – no difference.
- E – Higher costs without QALY gain mean EGDT was not cost-effective.

**Ref:** ARISE. *N Engl J Med* 2014;371:1496–1506. ProMISe. *N Engl J Med* 2015;372:1301–1311.

questions.stem: Regarding capillary refill time (CRT):
options: A Bayesian reanalysis of ANDROMEDA-SHOCK suggested a high probability that CRT-targeted resuscitation is beneficial.
SSC 2021 suggests CRT as an adjunct to other measures of perfusion.
It responds more slowly to changes in perfusion than lactate.
A value > 1 s is considered abnormal.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Zampieri 2020 found a > 90 % probability that CRT-targeted resuscitation is superior, under all priors tested.
- B (True) – SSC 2021 suggests CRT as an adjunct to other perfusion measures (weak, low quality); SSC 2026 kept this.
- C (False) – CRT changes within minutes of fluid or vasopressors; lactate changes over hours.
- D (False) – CRT > 3 s is abnormal; ≤ 3 s is normal.

**Ref:** Zampieri FG, et al. *Am J Respir Crit Care Med* 2020;201:423–429. Evans L, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021. *Intensive Care Med* 2021;47:1181–1247.

open.q: Explain why the Rivers EGDT trial and the later ProCESS, ARISE and ProMISe trials reached different conclusions, and what this means for modern septic shock resuscitation.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Rivers 2001: single centre, 263 ED patients, 6 h protocol (CVP 8–12 → MAP ≥ 65 → ScvO2 ≥ 70% via transfusion to Hct ≥ 30% and dobutamine); mortality 30.5 vs 46.5%.
- ProCESS (USA, 3 arms), ARISE (ANZ), ProMISe (UK): no mortality benefit (e.g. 18.6 vs 18.8%; 29.5 vs 29.2%).
- PRISM (3723 pts): 24.9 vs 25.4%, aOR 0.97; longer ICU stay, more CV support, higher costs; no subgroup benefited.
- Explanations: lower baseline mortality as "usual care" improved (early recognition, antibiotics, fluids), single-centre vs multicentre design, population differences.
- The core elements (early recognition, antibiotics, fluids) became standard; the rigid CVP/ScvO2/Hct protocol adds nothing.
- Modern approach: individualised targets, dynamic fluid responsiveness, lactate and CRT as perfusion guides (SSC 2021).

open.q: A patient with septic shock has MAP 68 mmHg on noradrenaline, ScvO2 75%, P(cv-a)CO2 8 mmHg, lactate 4.2 mmol/L and CRT 5 s. Interpret these findings and outline your next steps.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- ScvO2 ≥ 70% does not exclude hypoperfusion – impaired extraction/microcirculatory shunting in sepsis.
- P(cv-a)CO2 ≥ 6 mmHg indicates insufficient flow; a persistently high gap is associated with worse SOFA and 28-d mortality (Ospina-Tascón), even with ScvO2 ≥ 70%.
- CRT > 3 s = abnormal peripheral perfusion; responds within minutes (useful for titration), unlike lactate (hours).
- Lactate may be type A and/or B (adrenergic, reduced clearance) – trend it (≥ 20% fall per 2 h target, Jansen).
- Next: assess fluid responsiveness (PLR/EEO) before giving fluid; echocardiography for cardiac dysfunction; consider dobutamine if low CO; consider higher MAP (80–85) trial if chronic hypertension (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 tiered approach).
- Evidence: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (34.9 vs 43.4%, p = 0.06, ↓ SOFA, Bayesian > 90%); ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 win ratio 1.16, mortality unchanged.

title: W04 · D5 – Echocardiography and POCUS in shock

questions.stem: A ventilated patient with ARDS develops shock. Echocardiography shows RV/LV end-diastolic area ratio of 1.1, paradoxical septal motion and a dilated, non-collapsing IVC. The most appropriate immediate step is:
options: Increase PEEP to improve oxygenation regardless of plateau pressure
Start a vasodilator to reduce afterload of the left ventricle
Rapid 1 L crystalloid bolus
Diuresis with high-dose furosemide as the only intervention
Noradrenaline to restore systemic pressure and RV-protective ventilation adjustments
questions.expl:
**Why E:** An RV/LV end-diastolic area ratio **≥ 1** with paradoxical septal motion is **severe acute cor pulmonale**, and the plethoric IVC confirms high right atrial pressure. The pressure-overloaded RV tolerates fluid poorly; **noradrenaline** restores systemic pressure and RV coronary perfusion, while **RV-protective ventilation** (limit driving pressure and hypercapnia, consider prone positioning) lowers RV afterload.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Raising PEEP increases pulmonary vascular resistance and RV afterload, worsening cor pulmonale.
- B – A systemic vasodilator lowers MAP and RV coronary perfusion and can precipitate RV ischaemia.
- C – Fluids dilate the RV further, increase septal shift and impair LV filling.
- D – Diuresis does not correct hypotension or RV ischaemia and is not enough on its own.

**EDIC trap:** Dilated RV + D-shaped LV + plethoric IVC: another fluid bolus is the wrong answer.

**Ref:** Vieillard-Baron A, et al. Acute right ventricle failure. *Intensive Care Med* 2018;44:774–790. Mekontso Dessap A, et al. Acute cor pulmonale in ARDS. *Intensive Care Med* 2016;42(5).

questions.stem: According to the 2021 ESICM consensus on basic ultrasound skills:
options: The consensus used a Delphi process.
Qualitative assessment of LV systolic function is a strong recommendation.
LVOT VTI as an estimate of stroke volume is a strong recommendation.
Ultrasound to determine fluid responsiveness in persistent shock without signs of hypovolaemia is strongly recommended.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – A Delphi process was used; strong = ≥ 84 % agreement, weak = ≥ 74 %.
- B (True) – Qualitative assessment of LV systolic function is a strong recommendation.
- C (False) – LVOT VTI to estimate stroke volume is only a weak recommendation.
- D (False) – There is a strong recommendation **against** basic ultrasound to assess fluid responsiveness in persistent shock without signs of hypovolaemia.

**Ref:** Robba C, et al. ESICM basic ultrasound head-to-toe skills consensus. *Intensive Care Med* 2021;47:1347–1367.

questions.stem: Which echocardiographic finding is most useful to make cardiac tamponade unlikely in a hypotensive patient with a pericardial effusion?
options: Non-dilated inferior vena cava
RV/LV ratio of 0.5
Presence of B-lines
Normal LVOT VTI
Small, hyperdynamic left ventricle
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Tamponade raises intrapericardial and right atrial pressure, so the IVC is almost always **dilated with little respiratory variation**. This makes a plethoric IVC a sensitive sign, and a **non-dilated IVC makes tamponade unlikely**; ESICM 2021 strongly recommends using IVC size to judge its likelihood.

**Why not the others:**

- B – A normal RV/LV ratio excludes RV dilatation, not tamponade, in which the RV is small and compressed.
- C – B-lines indicate interstitial syndrome and say nothing about the pericardium.
- D – A normal VTI does not exclude evolving tamponade.
- E – A small, hyperdynamic LV is consistent with tamponade (underfilling) as well as hypovolaemia.

**EDIC trap:** Chamber collapse signs are specific; a dilated IVC is sensitive, so its absence argues most against tamponade.

**Ref:** Robba C, et al. ESICM basic ultrasound head-to-toe skills consensus. *Intensive Care Med* 2021;47:1347–1367.

questions.stem: Situations in which IVC ultrasound may fail to predict fluid responsiveness include:
options: Hyperinflation with auto-PEEP in COPD exacerbation
Non-invasive ventilation or CPAP
Intra-abdominal hypertension
Severe tricuspid regurgitation
questions.expl:
