Chloride-responsive alkalosis is treated with NaCl and KCl.
Hypertension with hypokalaemic alkalosis suggests mineralocorticoid excess.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – filtered HCO₃⁻ exceeding reabsorptive capacity carries Na⁺ (and K⁺) into the urine, so U-Na⁺ is high despite depletion; U-Cl⁻ is the reliable marker.
- B (True) – a U-Cl⁻ < 20 mmol/L reflects avid Cl⁻ retention (vomiting, NG suction, previous diuretics).
- C (True) – Cl⁻ and volume repletion allow the kidney to excrete HCO₃⁻; KCl removes hypokalaemia as a maintenance factor.
- D (True) – mineralocorticoid excess (Conn's, Cushing's, renovascular disease, liquorice) causes hypertension, hypokalaemia and a chloride-resistant alkalosis.

**Ref:** Emmett M, Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2020;15:1848–1856.

questions.stem: Na⁺ 140, glucose 10, urea 10 mmol/L; measured osmolality 322 mOsm/kg; blood ethanol 0. AG 28 mmol/L, lactate 1.5, ketones negative. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Isopropanol ingestion
Toxic alcohol ingestion (e.g. ethylene glycol)
Uraemic acidosis
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Lactic acidosis type B
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Calculated osmolality = 2 × 140 + 10 + 10 = 300 mOsm/kg. OG = 322 − 300 = **22** (> 10). Together with an unexplained HAGMA (AG 28, normal lactate, negative ketones), this means methanol or ethylene glycol until proven otherwise → fomepizole and consider haemodialysis.

**Why not the others:**
- A – isopropanol (→ acetone) raises the OG but causes ketosis without a HAGMA.
- C – urea of 10 mmol/L is too modest to explain an AG of 28, and urea is already counted in the calculated osmolality.
- D – ketones are negative and glucose is only 10 mmol/L.
- E – lactate of 1.5 mmol/L is normal.

**Ref:** Kraut JA, Mullins ME, N Engl J Med 2018;378:270–280.

questions.stem: Regarding bicarbonate therapy in severe metabolic acidaemia:
options: Bicarbonate may raise ionised calcium.
BICARICU-2 showed lower 90-day mortality with bicarbonate.
Both trials showed less need for kidney replacement therapy with bicarbonate.
In BICAR-ICU, bicarbonate improved the primary outcome in the prespecified AKIN 2–3 stratum.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – alkalinisation increases calcium binding to albumin and **lowers** ionised calcium; other risks are hypernatraemia, hyperosmolality and CO₂ generation.
- B (False) – BICARICU-2 found no difference in 90-day mortality (62.1 % vs 61.7 %).
- C (True) – BICAR-ICU showed less RRT overall, and BICARICU-2 showed less KRT by day 28 (35 % vs 50 %).
- D (True) – in BICAR-ICU's prespecified AKIN 2–3 stratum, the composite outcome was 70 % vs 82 %.

**EDIC trap:** SSC 2021 suggests considering bicarbonate only for pH ≤ 7.2 with AKI 2–3, not to improve haemodynamics.

**Ref:** Jaber S et al., Lancet 2018;392:31–40; Jung B et al., JAMA 2025 (doi:10.1001/jama.2025.20231).

questions.stem: Which fluid has an in vivo strong ion difference of zero and is most likely to cause hyperchloraemic acidosis?
options: 20 % albumin
0.9 % sodium chloride
4.2 % sodium bicarbonate
Ringer's lactate
Plasma-Lyte 148
questions.expl:
**Why B:** 0.9 % NaCl contains Na⁺ 154 and Cl⁻ 154 mmol/L, so its SID is **0**. Large volumes dilute plasma SID (~40) towards zero, causing a hyperchloraemic, normal-AG acidosis. In SMART, balanced crystalloids reduced MAKE30 (14.3 % vs 15.4 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – albumin solutions act mainly through ATOT (a weak acid load), not through a zero SID; they are not the classic cause of hyperchloraemia.
- C – 4.2 % NaHCO₃ contains ~500 mmol/L Na⁺ and no Cl⁻, a very high SID that is alkalinising.
- D – Ringer's lactate has an in vivo SID of ~28 once lactate is metabolised.
- E – Plasma-Lyte 148 has an in vivo SID of ~50 once acetate and gluconate are metabolised.

**Ref:** Kellum JA, Crit Care 2000;4:6–14; Semler MW et al. (SMART), N Engl J Med 2018;378:829–839.

questions.stem: A patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor presents unwell after surgery: glucose 9 mmol/L, pH 7.18, HCO₃⁻ 9 mmol/L, β-hydroxybutyrate 5.5 mmol/L. Which statements are correct?
options: Insulin should be withheld because glucose is near-normal.
DKA is excluded because glucose is < 11.1 mmol/L.
This is consistent with euglycaemic DKA.
This DKA is classified as severe.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – insulin is essential to stop ketogenesis; give it with 5–10 % glucose to prevent hypoglycaemia, and stop the SGLT2 inhibitor.
- B (False) – known diabetes meets the glucose criterion whatever the glucose value; this is euglycaemic DKA.
- C (True) – β-OHB ≥ 3.0, pH < 7.3 and HCO₃⁻ < 18 with glucose < 11.1 mmol/L on an SGLT2 inhibitor are typical of euglycaemic DKA (~10 % of cases).
- D (True) – HCO₃⁻ 9 mmol/L (< 10) is enough to classify it as severe.

**Ref:** Umpierrez GE et al., Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257–1275.

questions.stem: Which arterial blood gas is internally inconsistent (likely a sampling or transcription error)?
options: PaCO₂ 40 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 24 mmol/L, pH 7.40
PaCO₂ 60 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 30 mmol/L, pH 7.32
PaCO₂ 20 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 8 mmol/L, pH 7.22
PaCO₂ 30 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 20 mmol/L, pH 7.45
PaCO₂ 48 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 36 mmol/L, pH 7.30
questions.expl:
**Why E:** [H⁺] = 24 × PaCO₂ / HCO₃⁻ = 24 × 48 / 36 = **32 nmol/L** → pH ≈ 7.50. A reported pH of 7.30 corresponds to [H⁺] of 50 nmol/L, so the values cannot all be correct: suspect a sampling or transcription error and repeat the gas.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 24 × 40 / 24 = 40 nmol/L → pH 7.40 ✓.
- B – 24 × 60 / 30 = 48 nmol/L → pH ≈ 7.32 ✓.
- C – 24 × 20 / 8 = 60 nmol/L → pH ≈ 7.22 ✓.
- D – 24 × 30 / 20 = 36 nmol/L → pH ≈ 7.44–7.45 ✓.

**EDIC trap:** between pH 7.20 and 7.50, each 0.01 pH unit ≈ 1 nmol/L of H⁺ in the opposite direction.

**Ref:** Berend K, de Vries AP, Gans RO, N Engl J Med 2014;371:1434–1445.

questions.stem: Regarding mixed acid–base disorders:
options: Salicylate poisoning typically causes respiratory alkalosis plus high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
A normal pH excludes an acid–base disorder.
A delta ratio > 2 may indicate a coexisting metabolic alkalosis.
A PaCO₂ below the Winter prediction indicates an additional respiratory alkalosis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – salicylates directly stimulate the respiratory centre (respiratory alkalosis) and uncouple oxidative phosphorylation (lactate, ketoacids → HAGMA).
- B (False) – opposing disorders can cancel out (salicylates, sepsis + vomiting); Fencl found a normal BE and HCO₃⁻ in ~1/6 of patients with severe opposing disorders.
- C (True) – HCO₃⁻ has fallen less than the AG has risen, suggesting a coexisting metabolic alkalosis (or a high baseline HCO₃⁻ from chronic hypercapnia).
- D (True) – a PaCO₂ below the expected 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2 means an additional respiratory alkalosis; above it, a respiratory acidosis.

**Ref:** Berend K et al., N Engl J Med 2014;371:1434–1445; Rastegar A, J Am Soc Nephrol 2007;18:2429–2431.

questions.stem: A ventilated COPD patient with metabolic alkalosis is considered for acetazolamide. Based on DIABOLO, the best statement is:
options: Acetazolamide increased mortality
Acetazolamide did not significantly reduce the duration of invasive ventilation
Acetazolamide significantly reduced the duration of invasive ventilation
DIABOLO compared acetazolamide with hydrochloric acid
Acetazolamide is contraindicated in metabolic alkalosis
questions.expl:
**Why B:** DIABOLO randomised 380 ventilated COPD patients to acetazolamide or placebo. Median duration of invasive ventilation was 136.5 vs 163 h (p = 0.17, NS). Acetazolamide lowered HCO₃⁻ modestly, but this did not translate into faster liberation; the trial may have been underpowered.

**Why not the others:**
- A – there was no significant difference in mortality.
- C – the reduction in ventilation time was not statistically significant.
- D – the comparator was placebo, not hydrochloric acid.
- E – acetazolamide (which inhibits proximal HCO₃⁻ reabsorption) is used to treat metabolic alkalosis; the caution is hypokalaemia.

**Ref:** Faisy C et al. (DIABOLO), JAMA 2016;315:480–488.

title: W06 · D1 – Hypo- and hypernatraemia: algorithm, rate of correction, ODS

questions.stem: A 45-year-old has a generalised seizure; Na⁺ 116 mmol/L, duration unknown. The most appropriate first treatment according to the European guideline is:
options: 150 mL of 3 % saline IV over 20 minutes, repeated as needed with sodium checks
Fluid restriction to 800 mL/day
0.9 % saline 1 L over 1 hour
Tolvaptan 15 mg orally
3 % saline infusion at 0.5 mL/kg/h, aiming for +8 mmol/L in 24 h
questions.expl:
**Why A:** A seizure is a severe symptom, and the guideline recommends 150 mL of 3 % NaCl IV over 20 min immediately, checking Na⁺ after 20 min and repeating up to twice (3 boluses in total). The aim is a rise of about 5 mmol/L in the first hour, whatever the duration.

**Why not the others:**
- B – fluid restriction raises Na⁺ by only a few mmol/L per day, which is far too slow for a patient who is seizing.
- C – 0.9 % saline raises Na⁺ by < 1 mmol/L per litre and can even lower it in SIAD.
- D – vaptans act slowly and unpredictably and are not recommended for severe symptoms.
- E – a slow infusion delays the urgent 5 mmol/L rise.

**EDIC trap:** treat a hyponatraemia of unknown duration as chronic for the correction limits, but severe symptoms still get boluses.

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., ESICM/ESE/ERBP hyponatraemia guideline, Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331 (full version Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1–G47); Baek SH et al. (SALSA), JAMA Intern Med 2021;181:81–92.

questions.stem: Regarding the diagnostic approach to hypotonic hyponatraemia (European guideline):
options: SIAD can be diagnosed while the patient is hypovolaemic.
Urine osmolality ≤ 100 mOsm/kg is typical of SIAD.
Urine sodium ≤ 30 mmol/L suggests a low effective arterial blood volume.
Adrenal insufficiency must be excluded before diagnosing SIAD.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – SIAD requires clinical euvolaemia. Hypovolaemia is itself a non-osmotic stimulus for ADH, so it must be excluded or corrected first.
- B (False) – urine osmolality ≤ 100 mOsm/kg means ADH is suppressed (primary polydipsia, beer potomania, low solute intake); in SIAD it is > 100 mOsm/kg.
- C (True) – urine Na⁺ ≤ 30 mmol/L reflects avid renal Na⁺ retention caused by a low effective arterial volume (extrarenal losses, heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome).
- D (True) – adrenal insufficiency (cortisol deficiency stimulates ADH), hypothyroidism, pituitary and renal insufficiency and recent diuretic use must all be excluded before SIAD is diagnosed.

**EDIC trap:** diuretics raise urine Na⁺ even when the patient is hypovolaemic, so U-Na⁺ > 30 in a patient on a thiazide does not prove SIAD.

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., ESICM/ESE/ERBP hyponatraemia guideline, Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331 (full version Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1–G47).

questions.stem: A 60-kg woman (TBW 0.5 × body weight) has Na⁺ 112 mmol/L. Using the Adrogué–Madias formula, 1 L of 3 % saline (Na⁺ 513 mmol/L) would be expected to raise serum Na⁺ by approximately:
options: 18 mmol/L
13 mmol/L
4 mmol/L
25 mmol/L
8 mmol/L
questions.expl:
**Why B:** TBW = 0.5 × 60 = 30 L. By Adrogué–Madias, ΔNa⁺ = (infusate Na⁺ + K⁺ − serum Na⁺) / (TBW + 1) = (513 + 0 − 112) / (30 + 1) = 401 / 31 ≈ **12.9 mmol/L**. One litre would exceed the 24 h limit even before any aquaresis.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 18 mmol/L would mean dividing 401 by ~22 L instead of TBW + 1 = 31 L, so it overestimates.
- C – 4 mmol/L is roughly the effect of only ~300 mL of 3 % saline (0.3 × 12.9), so it underestimates threefold.
- D – 25 mmol/L would need a TBW of only ~15 L, which nearly doubles the true effect.
- E – 8 mmol/L would need a TBW of ~49 L, i.e. a much heavier patient.

**EDIC trap:** the formula ignores urine output, so with aquaresis the real rise can be much larger. Check Na⁺ every 2–4 h.

**Ref:** Adrogué HJ, Madias NE, N Engl J Med 2000;342:1581–1589; Spasovski G et al., ESICM/ESE/ERBP hyponatraemia guideline, Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331 (full version Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1–G47).

questions.stem: Regarding correction of chronic hyponatraemia:
options: Hypokalaemia, alcoholism and malnutrition decrease the risk of osmotic demyelination.
Overcorrection should be managed by continuing hypertonic saline at a lower rate.
The rise in Na⁺ should not exceed 20 mmol/L in the first 24 hours.
After the first day, the limit is 8 mmol/L per 24 hours until Na⁺ reaches 130 mmol/L.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – hypokalaemia, alcoholism, malnutrition, advanced liver disease and Na⁺ ≤ 105 mmol/L **increase** the risk of osmotic demyelination; in these patients aim for ≤ 8 mmol/L/24 h.
- B (False) – stop the hypertonic saline and actively re-lower Na⁺ with 10 mL/kg of electrolyte-free water (e.g. 5 % glucose) over 1 h ± desmopressin 2 µg IV (no more often than every 8 h), with close Na⁺ monitoring.
- C (False) – the limit is 10 mmol/L in the first 24 h; a 20 mmol/L rise would be dangerous overcorrection.
- D (True) – after the first day, Na⁺ may rise by ≤ 8 mmol/L in every further 24 h until it reaches 130 mmol/L.

**EDIC trap:** ODS appears 2–6 days after the overcorrection, so a well patient on day 1 does not exclude it.

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., ESICM/ESE/ERBP hyponatraemia guideline, Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331 (full version Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1–G47); Sterns RH, N Engl J Med 2015;372:55–65.

questions.stem: A 70-kg man (TBW 0.6 × body weight) has Na⁺ 155 mmol/L. His free water deficit is approximately:
questions.expl:
**Why D:** TBW = 0.6 × 70 = 42 L. Free water deficit = TBW × (Na⁺/140 − 1) = 42 × (155/140 − 1) = 42 × 0.107 ≈ **4.5 L**. This figure leaves out ongoing losses (insensible, urinary, GI), which must be added. Chronic hypernatraemia is traditionally lowered by ≤ 10–12 mmol/L/24 h.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 3.0 L would need a TBW of ~28 L (0.4 × weight), so it underestimates the deficit.
- B – 6.0 L would need a TBW of ~56 L (0.8 × weight), which is physiologically implausible.
- C – 1.5 L is the result of using ECF volume (0.2 × weight = 14 L) instead of total body water.
- E – 7.5 L would match a Na⁺ of ~165 mmol/L in this patient.

**Ref:** Adrogué HJ, Madias NE, Hypernatremia, N Engl J Med 2000;342:1493–1499.

questions.stem: Regarding the SALSA trial:
options: It compared rapid intermittent boluses with slow continuous infusion of hypertonic saline.
Re-lowering therapy was needed more often with rapid intermittent boluses.
Several cases of osmotic demyelination occurred in the bolus group.
Rapid intermittent bolus significantly reduced overcorrection (the primary outcome).
questions.expl:
- A (True) – SALSA randomised 178 Korean patients with moderately severe or severe symptomatic hyponatraemia to rapid intermittent boluses (RIB) or a slow continuous infusion (SCI) of 3 % NaCl.
- B (False) – re-lowering therapy was needed **less** often with RIB (41.4 % vs 57.1 %).
- C (False) – no case of osmotic demyelination occurred in either group.
- D (False) – overcorrection, the primary outcome, did not differ significantly (17.2 % vs 24.2 %); RIB reached the early Na⁺ target more often.

**EDIC trap:** "not superior" does not mean "unsafe". SALSA supports the guideline's bolus strategy.

**Ref:** Baek SH et al., JAMA Intern Med 2021;181:81–92.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man drinking large volumes of beer with poor food intake has Na⁺ 118 mmol/L, serum osmolality 250 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 60 mOsm/kg. The most likely mechanism is:
options: Low solute intake with excess water (beer potomania)
Cerebral salt wasting
SIAD
Primary adrenal insufficiency
Pseudohyponatraemia
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Serum osmolality is 250 mOsm/kg, so the hyponatraemia is hypotonic, and urine osmolality ≤ 100 mOsm/kg means ADH is suppressed. Beer contains little solute, and the kidney can excrete water only with solute: maximal water excretion ≈ daily solute load / minimal U-osm (e.g. 250 mOsm / 50 mOsm/kg ≈ 5 L/day). Beer drunk beyond that volume is retained as free water.

**Why not the others:**
- B – cerebral salt wasting causes hypovolaemia with high urine Na⁺ and concentrated urine (ADH appropriately on).
- C – SIAD requires urine osmolality > 100 mOsm/kg.
- D – primary adrenal insufficiency gives concentrated urine with high urine Na⁺, hypovolaemia and often hyperkalaemia.
- E – pseudohyponatraemia has a normal measured serum osmolality, not 250 mOsm/kg.

**EDIC trap:** once he eats again, solute intake rises and **aquaresis** follows, causing rapid overcorrection. His ODS risk is high (alcohol, malnutrition).

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., ESICM/ESE/ERBP hyponatraemia guideline, Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331 (full version Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1–G47); Sterns RH, N Engl J Med 2015;372:55–65.

questions.stem: Treatment of SIAD with moderate or profound hyponatraemia (no severe symptoms) according to the European guideline:
options: Vasopressin receptor antagonists are recommended in profound hyponatraemia.
Demeclocycline and lithium are recommended against.
Fluid restriction is first-line.
Urea is recommended against.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – the guideline does not recommend vasopressin receptor antagonists in moderate hyponatraemia and recommends **against** them in profound hyponatraemia (risk of overcorrection; tolvaptan is also hepatotoxic).
- B (True) – demeclocycline (nephrotoxic, unpredictable) and lithium are recommended against.
- C (True) – fluid restriction is first-line. It tends to fail when U-osm is > 500 mOsm/kg or (U-Na⁺ + U-K⁺) exceeds serum Na⁺.
- D (False) – urea 0.25–0.50 g/kg/day is a **second-line** option, as is a low-dose loop diuretic with oral NaCl.

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., ESICM/ESE/ERBP hyponatraemia guideline, Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331 (full version Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1–G47).

questions.stem: A patient with DKA has glucose 39.6 mmol/L and measured Na⁺ 125 mmol/L. Using a correction of 1.6 mmol/L per 5.6 mmol/L glucose above 5.6 mmol/L, the corrected Na⁺ is closest to:
options: 145 mmol/L
140 mmol/L
135 mmol/L
130 mmol/L
127 mmol/L
questions.expl:
**Why C:** (39.6 − 5.6) / 5.6 = 6.07 steps of 5.6 mmol/L; 6.07 × 1.6 = 9.7; 125 + 9.7 ≈ **135 mmol/L**. Glucose is an effective osmole that pulls water out of cells (translocational, hypertonic hyponatraemia). As insulin lowers the glucose, water re-enters cells and Na⁺ should rise towards the corrected value.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 145 mmol/L would need a factor of ~3.3 per 5.6 mmol/L, which overestimates.
- B – 140 mmol/L is the result with Hillier's factor of 2.4 per 5.6 mmol/L, not the 1.6 specified in the stem.
- D – 130 mmol/L adds only about half of the correction.
- E – 127 mmol/L corrects for barely one 5.6 mmol/L step.

**EDIC trap:** a corrected Na⁺ that is high-normal or rising during DKA treatment signals a free water deficit. It is not hypotonic hyponatraemia, so do not restrict water or give hypertonic saline.

**Ref:** Katz MA, N Engl J Med 1973;289:843–844; Hillier TA et al., Am J Med 1999;106:399–403.

questions.stem: Regarding hypernatraemia in the ICU:
options: A rise in urine osmolality after desmopressin suggests central diabetes insipidus.
Polyuria with urine osmolality < 300 mOsm/kg suggests diabetes insipidus.
In a retrospective ICU cohort (Chauhan 2019), rapid correction (> 0.5 mmol/L/h) was associated with higher mortality.
Acute hypernatraemia (< 48 h) can be corrected faster than chronic hypernatraemia.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – in central DI the kidney still responds to ADH, so urine osmolality rises markedly after desmopressin; in nephrogenic DI the response is minimal.
- B (True) – in hypernatraemia the urine should be small in volume and maximally concentrated (> 600–800 mOsm/kg). Polyuria with U-osm < 300 mOsm/kg therefore points to DI.
- C (False) – in 449 critically ill adults, correction faster than 0.5 mmol/L/h was **not** associated with higher mortality or with cerebral oedema attributable to the correction.
- D (True) – in acute hypernatraemia (< 48 h) the brain has not yet accumulated organic osmolytes, so faster correction is safe. Chronic hypernatraemia is traditionally lowered by ≤ 10–12 mmol/L/24 h.

**Ref:** Chauhan K et al., Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2019;14:656–663; Adrogué HJ, Madias NE, N Engl J Med 2000;342:1493–1499.

questions.stem: A ventilated trauma patient on day 6 receives high-protein enteral nutrition. Na⁺ has risen from 141 to 154 mmol/L over 5 days despite 2.5–3 L/day of urine. Glucose is normal and no mannitol or diuretics are given. Serum urea has risen to 22 mmol/L; urine osmolality is 720 mOsm/kg, urine Na⁺ + K⁺ = 70 mmol/L. The most likely mechanism is:
options: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Urea-induced osmotic diuresis
Central diabetes insipidus
Primary sodium gain from hypertonic fluids
Insensible water loss with appropriate renal water conservation
questions.expl:
**Why B:** U-osm is high and urine volume large, so total solute excretion is ~720 × 2.75 ≈ 2000 mOsm/day (usual load ~600–900). Na⁺ + K⁺ explain only 2 × 70 = 140 of the 720 mOsm/kg, so most of the osmoles are urea from protein feeding and catabolism (serum urea 22 mmol/L). Electrolyte-free water clearance = 2.75 × [1 − 70/154] ≈ **1.5 L/day** of free water lost, which drives the Na⁺ up.

**Why not the others:**
- A – nephrogenic DI gives dilute or isosthenuric urine, not 720 mOsm/kg.
- C – central DI gives hypotonic urine (often < 150–300 mOsm/kg) that concentrates after desmopressin.
- D – no hypertonic fluids were given, and the low urine electrolyte content argues against a sodium load.
- E – appropriate renal water conservation means a small volume of concentrated urine, not 2.5–3 L/day.

**EDIC trap:** use the **electrolyte-free** water clearance (urine Na⁺ + K⁺), not total free water clearance. Treat with free water and review the protein load.

**Ref:** Lindner G et al., Nephrol Dial Transplant 2012;27:962–967.

questions.stem: Hypernatraemia with a normal or high urine output:
options: In central diabetes insipidus urine osmolality is inappropriately low and increases after desmopressin.
In the polyuric phase of AKI urine osmolality is typically close to plasma osmolality.
After high-dose furosemide, a urine osmolality close to plasma osmolality proves nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
Osmotic diuresis from mannitol or glucose produces urine with an osmolality above plasma.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – without ADH the urine stays hypotonic despite a high plasma osmolality (e.g. after brain death, TBI or pituitary surgery), and it concentrates after desmopressin.
- B (True) – recovering tubules cannot rebuild the medullary gradient, so the urine is isosthenuric (~280–320 mOsm/kg) and copious.
- C (False) – loop diuretics wash out the medullary concentration gradient, so the kidney cannot concentrate urine whatever the ADH level. Reassess after the drug effect has worn off.
- D (True) – the unreabsorbed solute drags water with it. The urine is iso- to hypertonic, but the large volume and low electrolyte content still cause a net loss of free water.

**EDIC trap:** in a hypernatraemic patient, a "normal" urine output is never appropriate. The expected response is a small volume of maximally concentrated urine.

**Ref:** Lindner G et al., Nephrol Dial Transplant 2012;27:962–967; Adrogué HJ, Madias NE, N Engl J Med 2000;342:1493–1499.

open.q: A 65-year-old malnourished alcoholic woman is admitted with vomiting and a seizure; Na⁺ 108 mmol/L, duration unknown. Outline your management over the first 48 hours.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Severe symptoms (seizure, vomiting) → 150 mL 3 % NaCl IV over 20 min, check Na⁺ after 20 min, repeat up to 3 boluses; target +5 mmol/L in the first hour (regardless of acuity).
- Unknown duration → treat as chronic; she has several ODS risk factors (Na⁺ near 105, alcoholism, malnutrition, possible hypokalaemia/liver disease) → cautious limit ~8 mmol/L/24 h.
- Absolute limits: ≤ 10 mmol/L in the first 24 h, ≤ 8 mmol/L per further 24 h until Na⁺ 130.
- Frequent Na⁺ checks (every 2–4 h initially) and urine output monitoring; the Adrogué–Madias formula ignores aquaresis.
- Anticipate aquaresis once the ADH stimulus resolves (volume repletion after vomiting, nausea settling, restored solute intake).
- If overcorrected: 10 mL/kg free water (5 % glucose) over 1 h ± desmopressin 2 µg IV (not more often than every 8 h).
- Diagnostic work-up in parallel: serum/urine osmolality, urine Na⁺, volume status, exclude adrenal/thyroid insufficiency; correct K⁺.

open.q: An 80-kg elderly man after neurosurgery has Na⁺ 160 mmol/L, polyuria and urine osmolality 150 mOsm/kg. Calculate his free water deficit and outline diagnosis and treatment.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Polyuria + urine osmolality < 300 → diabetes insipidus; after neurosurgery most likely central.
- Desmopressin test: a rise in urine osmolality confirms central DI (nephrogenic causes: lithium, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia).
- TBW = 0.5 × 80 = 40 L; deficit = 40 × (160/140 − 1) ≈ 5.7 L.
- 1 L of 5 % glucose lowers Na⁺ by (0 − 160) / 41 ≈ 3.9 mmol/L; ~2.6 L is needed to lower Na⁺ by 10 mmol/L/24 h, plus ongoing (urinary) losses.
- Acute hypernatraemia (< 48 h, DI after neurosurgery) can be corrected faster; for chronic, traditionally ≤ 10–12 mmol/L/24 h.
- Chauhan (CJASN 2019): faster correction (> 0.5 mmol/L/h) was not associated with higher mortality or cerebral oedema; evidence for the limit in adults is weak.
- Frequent Na⁺ monitoring; treat with desmopressin plus free water.

title: W06 · D2 – Potassium and magnesium: hyperkalaemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia

questions.stem: A haemodialysis patient has K⁺ 7.3 mmol/L with broad QRS complexes. The first drug to give is:
options: Calcium chloride 10 % 10 mL IV
Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10 g orally
Furosemide 80 mg IV
Nebulised salbutamol 10 mg
Insulin 10 units with 25 g glucose
questions.expl:
**Why A:** K⁺ 7.3 mmol/L with broad QRS complexes is severe hyperkalaemia (≥ 6.5 mmol/L) with ECG changes. ERC 2025 starts by protecting the heart with 10 mL 10 % CaCl₂ (≈ 6.8 mmol Ca²⁺) IV over 5 min, or 30 mL 10 % Ca gluconate. Calcium stabilises the myocardial membrane within minutes and lasts ~30–60 min, but it does not lower K⁺. Shifting therapies follow, then urgent dialysis, which is the definitive removal in this patient.

**Why not the others:**
- B – SZC removes K⁺ through the gut over hours, so it gives no immediate protection to the myocardium.
- C – furosemide needs residual renal function, which a haemodialysis patient usually lacks.
- D – salbutamol is an adjunct that shifts K⁺; it does not stabilise the membrane, and many dialysis patients respond poorly.
- E – insulin–glucose is the fastest K⁺-lowering drug (onset ~15–30 min), but with ECG changes it comes after calcium.

**Ref:** ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753.

questions.stem: Regarding insulin–glucose for hyperkalaemia (ERC 2025):
options: If pre-treatment glucose is < 7 mmol/L, a 10 % glucose infusion at 50 mL/h for 5 hours is suggested.
Nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg can be added.
Insulin removes potassium from the body.
The dose is 25 units of soluble insulin with 10 g glucose IV.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ERC 2025: if pre-treatment glucose is < 7 mmol/L, follow the bolus with 10 % glucose at 50 mL/h for 5 h (25 g) to prevent delayed hypoglycaemia.
- B (True) – nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg adds to the effect of insulin but is not sufficient on its own.
- C (False) – insulin stimulates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and only **shifts** K⁺ into cells. Total body K⁺ is unchanged, so K⁺ rebounds unless it is removed (SZC, diuretic, dialysis).
- D (False) – the dose is 10 units of soluble insulin with **25 g** glucose IV (= 50 mL 50 %, 125 mL 20 % or 250 mL 10 %).

**EDIC trap:** hypoglycaemia is the most common complication, especially with low baseline glucose and renal failure (slower insulin clearance). Monitor glucose for several hours.

**Ref:** ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753.

questions.stem: You need to give 25 g of glucose and only 20 % glucose is available. The required volume is:
options: 250 mL
50 mL
100 mL
200 mL
125 mL
questions.expl:
**Why E:** 20 % glucose = 20 g per 100 mL = 0.2 g/mL, so 25 g / 0.2 g/mL = **125 mL**. The same 25 g dose is 50 mL of 50 % or 250 mL of 10 % glucose. This is the glucose given with 10 units of insulin for hyperkalaemia.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 250 mL is the volume needed with 10 % glucose.
- B – 50 mL is the volume needed with 50 % glucose.
- C – 100 mL of 20 % glucose provides only 20 g.
- D – 200 mL of 20 % glucose provides 40 g.

**EDIC trap:** 50 % glucose is very irritant to veins. Diluted solutions are kinder to peripheral veins but add volume.

**Ref:** ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753.

questions.stem: Regarding calcium in hyperkalaemia:
options: In hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest, calcium and sodium bicarbonate should not be given together through the same line without flushing.
10 mL of 10 % calcium gluconate contains roughly three times more calcium than 10 mL of 10 % calcium chloride.
Calcium lowers the serum potassium concentration.
Its membrane-stabilising effect lasts about 24 hours, so a single dose suffices.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – calcium and bicarbonate precipitate as CaCO₃, so give them through separate lines or flush in between. In hyperkalaemic arrest ERC 2025 recommends 10 mL 10 % CaCl₂ plus 50 mmol NaHCO₃.
- B (False) – the reverse is true: 10 mL 10 % CaCl₂ contains ≈ 6.8 mmol Ca²⁺ and 10 mL 10 % gluconate ≈ 2.2 mmol, so ~30 mL of gluconate is needed for an equivalent dose.
- C (False) – calcium restores the gap between resting and threshold membrane potential and leaves the serum K⁺ unchanged.
- D (False) – the effect lasts only ~30–60 min. Repeat the dose if ECG changes persist, and always add shifting and removal therapy.

**EDIC trap:** CaCl₂ is more irritant on extravasation, so give it through a large or central vein.

**Ref:** ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753.

questions.stem: A patient on furosemide and long-term omeprazole has K⁺ 2.9 mmol/L that does not improve despite 3 days of IV KCl. The most likely contributing factor is:
options: Metabolic acidosis
Hypercalcaemia
Hypophosphataemia
Hyponatraemia
Hypomagnesaemia
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Loop diuretics (renal Mg²⁺ loss) and long-term PPIs (impaired intestinal absorption via TRPM6/7) both cause magnesium deficiency. Low intracellular Mg²⁺ releases its normal block of the ROMK channels in the collecting duct, so the kidney keeps wasting K⁺. KCl stays ineffective until Mg²⁺ is replaced (e.g. MgSO₄ 2 g ≈ 8 mmol IV, then an infusion).

**Why not the others:**
- A – metabolic acidosis shifts K⁺ out of cells and raises serum K⁺; furosemide usually causes alkalosis.
- B – hypercalcaemia is not a recognised cause of KCl-refractory hypokalaemia in this setting, and loop diuretics tend to lower calcium.
- C – hypophosphataemia often coexists (refeeding, alkalosis) but does not block K⁺ repletion.
- D – hyponatraemia does not cause renal K⁺ wasting.

**EDIC trap:** a normal serum Mg²⁺ does not exclude depletion (< 1 % is in serum), so replace empirically if hypokalaemia is refractory.

**Ref:** Gennari FJ, N Engl J Med 1998;339:451–458; Huang CL, Kuo E, J Am Soc Nephrol 2007;18:2649–2652.

questions.stem: ECG features of hypokalaemia include:
options: ST-segment depression
U waves
T-wave flattening or inversion
Prolonged QT(U) interval with risk of torsades de pointes
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ST-segment depression is a typical repolarisation change of hypokalaemia.
- B (True) – U waves (most prominent in V2–V3) reflect delayed repolarisation and grow as K⁺ falls.
- C (True) – the T wave flattens or inverts, and it may merge with the U wave.
- D (True) – the QT(U) interval lengthens and predisposes to torsades de pointes, especially with hypomagnesaemia, digoxin or QT-prolonging drugs.

**EDIC trap:** peaked T waves, a prolonged PR and a broad QRS point to **hyperkalaemia**. Correlation of the ECG with the K⁺ level is poor in both directions.

**Ref:** Gennari FJ, N Engl J Med 1998;339:451–458; ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753.

questions.stem: In cardiac arrest attributed to severe hypokalaemia, ERC 2025 suggests:
options: Potassium is contraindicated during CPR
KCl 100 mmol as a bolus
KCl 40 mmol over 1 hour
Oral potassium after ROSC only
KCl 20 mmol IV over 2–3 minutes, followed by 10 mmol over 2 minutes
questions.expl:
**Why E:** ERC 2025 recommends KCl **20 mmol IV/IO over 2–3 min, then 10 mmol over 2 min** for hypokalaemic cardiac arrest, followed by an infusion adjusted to repeated K⁺ measurements, with any magnesium deficit corrected at the same time. A rapid potassium bolus is justified only during arrest, where the rhythm is already lethal. Outside arrest, peripheral rates are kept to ~10 mmol/h.

**Why not the others:**
- A – severe hypokalaemia is a reversible cause of arrest (one of the "4 Hs"), and correcting it is part of ALS.
- B – a 100 mmol bolus would cause fatal hyperkalaemia.
- C – 40 mmol over 1 h is too slow during arrest; it is a monitored central-line replacement rate.
- D – waiting until ROSC leaves the cause untreated, and oral potassium is impossible during CPR.

**Ref:** ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753.

questions.stem: Recognised causes of hyperkalaemia include:
options: Metabolic alkalosis
Succinylcholine in a patient with a 2-week-old spinal cord injury
Pseudohyperkalaemia from marked thrombocytosis
Furosemide
questions.expl:
- A (False) – alkalosis shifts K⁺ into cells and increases kaliuresis, which causes **hypo**kalaemia. It is mineral (hyperchloraemic) acidosis that raises K⁺.
- B (True) – denervation up-regulates extrajunctional (including α7) acetylcholine receptors from about 24–72 h after injury, lasting for months. Succinylcholine then causes massive K⁺ efflux and a risk of arrest.
- C (True) – platelets release K⁺ during clotting in a serum tube. A heparinised plasma or whole-blood sample (blood gas analyser) shows the true value.
- D (False) – loop diuretics increase distal Na⁺ delivery and flow, which causes kaliuresis and hypokalaemia. K⁺-sparing diuretics, ACEi/ARB and trimethoprim cause hyperkalaemia.

**Ref:** Martyn JAJ, Richtsfeld M, Anesthesiology 2006;104:158–169; Clase CM et al. (KDIGO), Kidney Int 2020;97:42–61.

questions.stem: A patient with torsades de pointes receives 2 g of magnesium sulphate (MgSO₄·7H₂O). This corresponds to approximately:
options: 2 mmol Mg²⁺
8 mmol Mg²⁺
4 mmol Mg²⁺
20 mmol Mg²⁺
16 mmol Mg²⁺
questions.expl:
**Why B:** MgSO₄·7H₂O has a molar mass of ≈ 246 g/mol, so 1 g ≈ 4.06 mmol Mg²⁺ and 2 g = 2000 / 246 ≈ **8 mmol** (= 16 mEq, because Mg²⁺ is divalent). In torsades de pointes, 2 g IV is given whatever the serum magnesium level.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 2 mmol treats grams as millimoles.
- C – 4 mmol corresponds to 1 g, not 2 g.
- D – 20 mmol is about 5 g of MgSO₄·7H₂O.
- E – 16 is the value in mEq, not mmol.

**EDIC trap:** check whether a question uses mmol or mEq. For a divalent ion, mEq = 2 × mmol.

**Ref:** Soar J et al., ERC Guidelines 2025 Adult Advanced Life Support, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110769.

questions.stem: Regarding magnesium:
options: A normal serum magnesium reliably excludes total body magnesium deficiency.
Severe hypermagnesaemia can cause loss of deep tendon reflexes and respiratory depression.
Hypomagnesaemia may cause hypocalcaemia by impairing PTH secretion and action.
Long-term proton pump inhibitor use can cause hypomagnesaemia.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – < 1 % of total body magnesium is in serum (most is in bone and cells), so a normal serum level does not exclude a deficit.
- B (True) – Mg²⁺ reduces acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction. Deep tendon reflexes disappear at ~3.5–5 mmol/L, followed by respiratory depression, hypotension, bradycardia and heart block. Treat with IV calcium, diuresis and dialysis.
- C (True) – hypomagnesaemia impairs PTH secretion and causes end-organ resistance to PTH, so the hypocalcaemia is refractory until Mg²⁺ is corrected.
- D (True) – long-term PPIs reduce active intestinal Mg²⁺ absorption (TRPM6/7), and the level recovers after the drug is stopped.

**Ref:** Hess MW et al., Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2012;36:405–413; Gennari FJ, N Engl J Med 1998;339:451–458.

open.q: A patient with AKI on an ACE inhibitor and trimethoprim has K⁺ 7.0 mmol/L with peaked T waves and a widened QRS. Outline your management step by step, including doses, and explain the role of each drug.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Severe hyperkalaemia (≥ 6.5 mmol/L, ERC 2025) with ECG changes = urgent treatment; exclude pseudohyperkalaemia only if it does not delay therapy (blood gas analyser sample).
- Protect the heart: 10 mL 10 % CaCl₂ IV over 5 min (or 30 mL 10 % Ca gluconate over 10 min); stabilises the membrane, does not lower K⁺; short effect (~30–60 min) → repeat if ECG changes persist.
- Shift K⁺ into cells: insulin 10 U + glucose 25 g IV (onset ~15–30 min); if pre-treatment glucose < 7 mmol/L, follow with 10 % glucose 50 mL/h for 5 h; monitor for hypoglycaemia.
- Add nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg (additive, insufficient alone).
- Remove K⁺: SZC 10 g orally, loop diuretic if passing urine, dialysis if refractory; insulin/salbutamol only shift K⁺ → rebound.
- Monitor K⁺ and glucose.
- Prevent: stop ACE inhibitor and trimethoprim (ENaC blockade), treat the AKI cause.

open.q: Explain why hypokalaemia may be refractory to potassium replacement in an ICU patient and how you would correct it safely.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- ~98 % of K⁺ is intracellular, so a small fall in serum K⁺ reflects a large total deficit (hundreds of mmol).
- Hypomagnesaemia (diuretics, long-term PPIs, alcohol, refeeding, CRRT…) releases ROMK inhibition → renal K⁺ wasting; without Mg²⁺ correction hypokalaemia remains refractory.
- Serum Mg poorly reflects stores (< 1 % in serum) – a normal level does not exclude deficiency.
- Ongoing shift into cells (insulin, β₂-agonists/adrenaline, alkalosis, refeeding) or ongoing losses (diuretics, mineralocorticoids, amphotericin B) also contribute.
- Give MgSO₄ (2 g ≈ 8 mmol IV, then infusion) alongside KCl.
- IV KCl peripherally up to ~10 mmol/h, higher rates centrally only with ECG monitoring; dilute in glucose-free solution.
- Monitor ECG (U waves, QT(U)) and stop QT-prolonging drugs.

title: W06 · D3 – Calcium and phosphate, refeeding syndrome

questions.stem: Total calcium 1.84 mmol/L, albumin 22 g/L. Using the formula Ca + 0.02 × (40 − albumin), the corrected calcium is:
options: 2.20 mmol/L
1.98 mmol/L
2.10 mmol/L
2.36 mmol/L
2.48 mmol/L
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Corrected Ca = 1.84 + 0.02 × (40 − 22) = 1.84 + 0.02 × 18 = 1.84 + 0.36 = **2.20 mmol/L**. The value looks normal, but in critically ill patients the formula agrees poorly with ionised calcium because of pH changes, complexing anions and hypoalbuminaemia. Measure iCa²⁺ directly.

**Why not the others:**
- B – 1.98 adds only 0.14, as if the albumin deficit were 7 g/L instead of 18 g/L.
- C – 2.10 adds only 0.26 (an arithmetic slip).
- D – 2.36 comes from adding 0.36 to 2.00 instead of to the measured 1.84.
- E – 2.48 would need an albumin of only 8 g/L.

**EDIC trap:** a "normal" corrected calcium can hide true ionised hypocalcaemia.

**Ref:** Aberegg SK, Ionized calcium in the ICU, Chest 2016;149:846–855.

questions.stem: Regarding ionised calcium:
options: Alkalosis decreases ionised calcium.
Albumin-corrected calcium accurately predicts ionised calcium in critically ill patients.
A total/ionised calcium ratio > 2.5 during citrate CRRT suggests citrate accumulation.
About 90 % of plasma calcium is ionised.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – alkalosis increases the negative charge on albumin, so more Ca²⁺ is bound and iCa²⁺ falls (hyperventilation tetany). Acidosis has the opposite effect.
- B (False) – albumin-corrected calcium agrees poorly with iCa²⁺ in the ICU (altered pH, citrate/lactate/phosphate complexes, hypoalbuminaemia), so measure iCa²⁺.
- C (True) – citrate–calcium complexes raise total Ca while iCa²⁺ falls. A total/ionised ratio > 2.5 together with a worsening high-AG acidosis indicates citrate accumulation (liver failure, shock).
- D (False) – about 45–50 % of plasma calcium is ionised, ~40 % is protein-bound and ~10 % is complexed.

**Ref:** Aberegg SK, Ionized calcium in the ICU, Chest 2016;149:846–855; Schneider AG et al., Crit Care 2017;21:281.

questions.stem: In the refeeding syndrome trial by Doig et al. (2015), protocolised caloric restriction in critically ill adults with refeeding hypophosphataemia:
options: Increased mortality
Consisted of stopping all nutrition for 5 days
Was tested only in patients with anorexia nervosa
Significantly increased the primary outcome of days alive after ICU discharge
Did not significantly change the primary outcome but improved 60-day survival
questions.expl:
**Why E:** The trial enrolled 339 critically ill adults (13 ICUs, Australia/New Zealand) with refeeding hypophosphataemia. Restriction meant 20 kcal/h for ≥ 2 days, then a gradual return to target over 2–3 days. The primary outcome (days alive after ICU discharge) improved by 4.9 days, which was not significant (p = 0.19). Survival at day 60 was higher (~91 % vs ~79 %, p = 0.002).

**Why not the others:**
- A – mortality was lower, not higher, with restriction.
- B – energy was reduced to 20 kcal/h, not stopped, and only for ≥ 48 h.
- C – it was a general ICU population, not patients with anorexia nervosa.
- D – the primary outcome did not reach significance.

**EDIC trap:** the survival benefit is a secondary outcome, but it underpins ESPEN's advice to restrict energy for 48 h in refeeding hypophosphataemia.

**Ref:** Doig GS et al., Lancet Respir Med 2015;3:943–952; Singer P et al., ESPEN ICU guideline, Clin Nutr 2019;38:48–79.

questions.stem: Consequences of severe hypophosphataemia include:
options: Hypercalcaemia
Respiratory muscle weakness and difficult weaning
Haemolysis and rhabdomyolysis
Right shift of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve due to increased 2,3-DPG
questions.expl:
- A (False) – hypophosphataemia does not raise calcium. Rapid IV phosphate can instead **lower** iCa²⁺ through Ca–P precipitation.
- B (True) – ATP depletion weakens the diaphragm and other respiratory muscles, which causes weaning failure (and also reduces myocardial contractility).
- C (True) – ATP depletion makes red cells rigid (haemolysis) and injures muscle (rhabdomyolysis), especially when Pi is < 0.32 mmol/L.
- D (False) – low phosphate **reduces** 2,3-DPG, which shifts the curve to the **left** and impairs O₂ release to tissues.

**Ref:** Geerse DA et al., Crit Care 2010;14:R147; Singer P et al., ESPEN ICU guideline, Clin Nutr 2019;38:48–79.

questions.stem: A patient with metastatic lung cancer is confused and dehydrated; total calcium 3.9 mmol/L, creatinine mildly raised. The most appropriate initial management is:
options: Hydrocortisone as first-line therapy
Furosemide alone
Oral calcium restriction only
Calcium gluconate
IV isotonic fluid plus an IV bisphosphonate
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Total Ca 3.9 mmol/L (≥ 3.5 = severe) with confusion in a patient with lung cancer is most likely PTHrP-mediated hypercalcaemia of malignancy. Hypercalcaemia causes nephrogenic DI, and the resulting volume depletion lowers GFR and calcium excretion, so the first step is IV isotonic fluid. An IV bisphosphonate (e.g. zoledronic acid 4 mg) is given at the same time and acts in 2–4 days; calcitonin can bridge the first 48 h.

**Why not the others:**
- A – glucocorticoids work in calcitriol-mediated disease (lymphoma, granulomas, vitamin D intoxication), not in PTHrP-mediated hypercalcaemia from solid tumours.
- B – furosemide alone worsens the dehydration; use it only after volume repletion if the patient is fluid overloaded.
- C – restricting oral calcium does little when bone resorption drives the hypercalcaemia.
- D – calcium gluconate would make the hypercalcaemia worse.

**EDIC trap:** if renal failure limits bisphosphonate use, denosumab is the alternative (watch for hypocalcaemia).

**Ref:** Walker MD, Shane E, JAMA 2022;328:1624–1636; El-Hajj Fuleihan G et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2023;108:507–528.

questions.stem: Regarding refeeding syndrome:
options: Thiamine should be withheld until feeding has reached the energy target.
Insulin release drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium out of cells.
ESPEN 2019 recommends continuing full energy targets despite refeeding hypophosphataemia.
In the Doig trial, refeeding hypophosphataemia was defined as phosphate < 0.65 mmol/L with a fall > 0.16 mmol/L within 72 hours of starting feeding.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – give thiamine (with other B vitamins) **before** the first feed and during the first 10 days. A carbohydrate load uses up thiamine and can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy and lactic acidosis.
- B (False) – insulin drives phosphate, K⁺ and Mg²⁺ **into** cells, which is why their serum levels fall.
- C (False) – ESPEN 2019 recommends restricting energy for 48 h, then increasing it gradually, and measuring phosphate 2–3 times daily.
- D (True) – this is the Doig trial's definition of refeeding hypophosphataemia.

**Ref:** NICE CG32, Nutrition support for adults (2006, updated 2017); Singer P et al., ESPEN ICU guideline, Clin Nutr 2019;38:48–79; Doig GS et al., Lancet Respir Med 2015;3:943–952.

questions.stem: Which patient meets a single criterion for high risk of refeeding problems according to NICE?
options: BMI 17.5 kg/m² alone
Little or no intake for 6 days alone
BMI 15 kg/m²
Weight loss of 8 % over 4 months alone
History of alcohol misuse alone
questions.expl:
**Why C:** NICE CG32 lists four criteria that are each enough on their own: BMI < 16, unintentional weight loss > 15 % in 3–6 months, little or no intake for > 10 days, and low K⁺/PO₄/Mg²⁺ before feeding. A BMI of 15 qualifies alone. Start at ≤ 10 kcal/kg/day (5 kcal/kg/day in extreme cases, e.g. BMI < 14) and give thiamine first.

**Why not the others:**
- A – BMI < 18.5 is a minor criterion and needs a second one.
- B – little intake for > 5 days is minor; the single criterion requires > 10 days.
- D – 8 % weight loss does not even meet the minor threshold (> 10 %).
- E – a history of alcohol misuse is a minor criterion and needs a second one.

**Ref:** NICE CG32, Nutrition support for adults (2006, updated 2017).

questions.stem: Regarding treatment of hypercalcaemia:
options: Glucocorticoids are useful when hypercalcaemia is mediated by vitamin D (e.g. granulomatous disease).
PTHrP is the most common mediator of hypercalcaemia of malignancy.
Denosumab may be used when kidney failure limits bisphosphonate use.
Calcitonin has a durable effect without tachyphylaxis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – granulomas and some lymphomas produce calcitriol through 1α-hydroxylase. Glucocorticoids suppress this, and they also help in vitamin D intoxication.
- B (True) – PTHrP (humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy) causes most cases; osteolytic metastases and ectopic calcitriol cause the rest.
- C (True) – denosumab (a RANKL antibody) is not renally cleared, so it is useful in kidney failure or bisphosphonate-refractory disease. It can cause severe hypocalcaemia.
- D (False) – calcitonin lowers Ca within hours, but tachyphylaxis develops within ~48 h (receptor down-regulation), so it serves only as a bridge.

**Ref:** Walker MD, Shane E, JAMA 2022;328:1624–1636; El-Hajj Fuleihan G et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2023;108:507–528.

questions.stem: A laboratory reports phosphate as 1.5 mg/dL. In mmol/L this is approximately:
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Phosphorus has a molar mass of ≈ 31 g/mol, so 1 mg/dL = 10 mg/L / 31 ≈ 0.323 mmol/L. Therefore 1.5 mg/dL × 0.323 = **0.48 mmol/L**. This is moderate hypophosphataemia (0.32–0.65 mmol/L), below the normal range of ~0.8–1.45 mmol/L.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 1.50 simply relabels mg/dL as mmol/L.
- B – 0.15 divides by 10 instead of applying the molar conversion.
- C – 0.32 mmol/L corresponds to 1.0 mg/dL, the threshold for severe hypophosphataemia.
- D – 0.75 halves the value instead of multiplying by 0.323 (≈ 1/3.1).

**Ref:** Geerse DA et al., Treatment of hypophosphatemia in the ICU, Crit Care 2010;14:R147.

questions.stem: Causes of hypocalcaemia in the ICU include:
options: Hyperphosphataemia
Acute pancreatitis
Hypomagnesaemia
Massive transfusion
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Ca–P precipitates in tissues and calcitriol production falls (AKI, rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis).
- B (True) – free fatty acids in peripancreatic fat necrosis bind calcium (saponification), and hypocalcaemia is a marker of severity.
- C (True) – hypomagnesaemia impairs PTH secretion and action, so correct Mg²⁺ first or at the same time.
- D (True) – citrate in blood products chelates ionised calcium, especially with liver dysfunction, hypothermia or shock. The European bleeding guideline recommends monitoring iCa²⁺ and keeping it in the normal range.

**Ref:** Rossaint R et al., European guideline on management of major bleeding, Crit Care 2023;27:80; Aberegg SK, Chest 2016;149:846–855.

questions.stem: A 46 kg woman (BMI 16.5) with alcohol use disorder and 8 days of minimal intake is ventilated for aspiration pneumonia. Enteral feeding was started at 25 kcal/kg/day. On day 3, phosphate has fallen from 1.10 to 0.40 mmol/L, K⁺ is 3.0 and Mg²⁺ 0.55 mmol/L; she fails a spontaneous breathing trial with rapid shallow breathing. The most appropriate management is:
options: Replace the feed with glucose 10 % infusion to avoid protein overload
Stop all nutrition for 7 days
No change – a fall in phosphate is expected and harmless during refeeding
Reduce energy intake (e.g. 20 kcal/h for ≥ 48 h), give IV phosphate, K⁺, Mg²⁺ and thiamine, then increase feeding gradually
Continue full feeding and give oral phosphate only
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Phosphate fell from 1.10 to 0.40 mmol/L, a fall of 0.70 / 1.10 ≈ 64 % within 5 days of feeding. With organ dysfunction (respiratory muscle weakness → failed SBT), this is **severe** refeeding syndrome by ASPEN 2020 (falls of 10–20 % mild, 20–30 % moderate, > 30 % or organ dysfunction severe). She met NICE high-risk criteria (≥ 2 minor), so feeding should have started at ≤ 10 kcal/kg/day with thiamine. Now restrict energy for 48 h (Doig: 20 kcal/h), replace phosphate, K⁺ and Mg²⁺ IV, give thiamine, then increase feeding gradually.

**Why not the others:**
- A – glucose alone maximises insulin release and the phosphate shift.
- B – stopping nutrition for 7 days prolongs starvation; the evidence supports restriction, not cessation.
- C – Pi 0.40 mmol/L with weaning failure is harmful and needs treatment.
- E – full feeding sustains the shift, and oral phosphate is inadequate for a severe deficit.

See also the PCP/refeeding case in [W03/D4](#W03-D4) and the [EDIC II-style cases workshop](#extra-clinical-cases-workshop).

**Ref:** da Silva JSV et al., ASPEN consensus, Nutr Clin Pract 2020;35:178–195; Doig GS et al., Lancet Respir Med 2015;3:943–952; Singer P et al., ESPEN ICU guideline, Clin Nutr 2019;38:48–79; NICE CG32, Nutrition support for adults (2006, updated 2017).

open.q: A 50-kg woman with BMI 15 has eaten almost nothing for 2 weeks and is admitted to the ICU. Outline how you would start nutrition, and how you would respond if her phosphate falls from 1.0 to 0.50 mmol/L on day 2.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- High risk of refeeding syndrome by NICE CG32 (BMI < 16 and little/no intake > 10 days; one criterion is enough).
- Thiamine and B vitamins before the first feed and during the first 10 days.
- Start cautiously: max. 10 kcal/kg/day (= 500 kcal/day), increase gradually; prophylactic K⁺, PO₄, Mg²⁺ according to levels.
- Monitor phosphate at least daily in the first week (2–3 times daily once refeeding hypophosphataemia develops – ESPEN 2019).
- Day 2: Pi 0.50 (< 0.65) with a fall of 0.50 (> 0.16) within 72 h = refeeding hypophosphataemia (Doig definition).
- Restrict to 20 kcal/h for ≥ 48 h, then return gradually to target over 2–3 days, plus IV phosphate; monitor Ca²⁺ and K⁺ during replacement.
- Evidence: Doig 2015 – primary outcome NS (+4.9 days, p = 0.19) but higher 60-day survival (~91 % vs ~79 %, p = 0.002).

open.q: A septic patient on citrate CRRT has total Ca 2.40 mmol/L, iCa²⁺ 0.85 mmol/L and a worsening high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Interpret these results and explain why the albumin-corrected calcium is unhelpful here.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Total/ionised Ca ratio = 2.40 / 0.85 ≈ 2.8 (> ~2.5) → citrate accumulation.
- Citrate accumulation is typical with citrate CRRT in liver failure/shock: ↓ iCa²⁺, ↑ total/iCa ratio, high-AG metabolic acidosis.
- Only iCa²⁺ (~45–50 % of plasma Ca) is biologically active; complexed Ca (citrate) increases total Ca without raising iCa²⁺.
- Corrected Ca (+ 0.02 × (40 − albumin)) is inaccurate in the ICU (altered pH, complexes, hypoalbuminaemia) → measure iCa²⁺.
- Consequences of low iCa²⁺: tetany, seizures, prolonged QT, hypotension, ↓ contractility, impaired coagulation.
- Management: treat symptomatic/severe hypocalcaemia with IV Ca gluconate, correct Mg²⁺, and reassess the citrate anticoagulation.

title: W06 · Saturday – weekly review: Electrolytes

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with chronic thiazide-induced hyponatraemia (Na⁺ 112 mmol/L) received 3 % saline boluses for confusion. After stopping the thiazide, urine output is 400 mL/h and Na⁺ is 124 mmol/L at 12 hours. The best next step is:
options: Start tolvaptan
Continue observation; the correction is within limits
Give 0.9 % saline to replace urine output
Stop sodium-containing fluids, give electrolyte-free water (about 10 mL/kg over 1 h) and consider desmopressin 2 µg IV
Give furosemide
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Na⁺ rose from 112 to 124 = +12 mmol/L in 12 h, which already exceeds the 10 mmol/L/24 h limit. Stopping the thiazide caused an aquaresis of dilute urine at 400 mL/h and Na⁺ will keep climbing. The guideline advises stopping active treatment and giving 10 mL/kg of electrolyte-free water (e.g. 5 % glucose) over 1 h under close monitoring, ± desmopressin 2 µg IV (no more often than every 8 h).

**Why not the others:**
- A – tolvaptan would increase the aquaresis and worsen the overcorrection.
- B – the limit is already exceeded at 12 h, and the ongoing aquaresis will push Na⁺ higher.
- C – 0.9 % saline (154 mmol/L) is far more concentrated than the dilute urine, so replacing urine with it would raise Na⁺ further.
- E – furosemide produces urine that is hypotonic to plasma, which raises Na⁺ further.

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331; Sterns RH, N Engl J Med 2015;372:55–65.

questions.stem: According to the European hyponatraemia guideline:
options: Hyponatraemia of unknown duration should be treated as acute.
In severe symptoms, the target is a rise of about 5 mmol/L in the first hour.
Profound hyponatraemia is defined as Na⁺ < 130 mmol/L.
Vomiting and somnolence are severe symptoms.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – hyponatraemia of unknown duration is treated as **chronic**, because the brain may already have adapted and rapid correction risks ODS.
- B (True) – with severe symptoms, the aim is a rise of ~5 mmol/L in the first hour (150 mL 3 % NaCl over 20 min, up to 3 times). This usually improves symptoms.
- C (False) – profound is < 125 mmol/L; moderate is 125–129 and mild 130–135.
- D (True) – severe symptoms are vomiting, cardiorespiratory distress, abnormal deep somnolence, seizures and coma (GCS ≤ 8). Nausea without vomiting, confusion and headache are moderately severe.

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331.

questions.stem: A 70-kg man (TBW 42 L) with Na⁺ 120 mmol/L receives 1 L of 0.9 % saline (Na⁺ 154 mmol/L). The Adrogué–Madias formula predicts a rise in Na⁺ of approximately:
options: 12 mmol/L
3.4 mmol/L
5 mmol/L
0.8 mmol/L
8 mmol/L
questions.expl:
**Why D:** ΔNa⁺ = (154 + 0 − 120) / (42 + 1) = 34 / 43 ≈ **0.8 mmol/L**. Isotonic saline hardly raises Na⁺ at all. In SIAD, if urine osmolality exceeds that of saline (~308 mOsm/kg), the infused Na⁺ is excreted in a smaller volume and the water is retained, so serum Na⁺ can even fall ("desalination").

**Why not the others:**
- A – 12 mmol/L is more than even 1 L of 3 % saline would achieve here: (513 − 120) / 43 ≈ 9.1.
- B – 3.4 is a decimal slip (34 / 10).
- C – 5 mmol/L is the first-hour target for 3 % boluses in severe symptoms, not the effect of 0.9 % saline.
- E – 8 mmol/L is the daily correction ceiling for high-risk patients, not the effect per litre.

**Ref:** Adrogué HJ, Madias NE, N Engl J Med 2000;342:1581–1589; Spasovski G et al., Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331.

questions.stem: Regarding emergency treatment of hyperkalaemia:
options: Hypoglycaemia is a common complication of insulin–glucose therapy.
Dialysis has no role in refractory severe hyperkalaemia.
Calcium is given to lower the serum potassium when ECG changes are present.
Salbutamol alone is sufficient treatment for severe hyperkalaemia.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – hypoglycaemia is the most common complication, especially with low baseline glucose or renal failure. ERC 2025 adds a 10 % glucose infusion if pre-treatment glucose is < 7 mmol/L.
- B (False) – dialysis is the definitive treatment to remove K⁺ in refractory severe hyperkalaemia, particularly with renal failure.
- C (False) – calcium stabilises the myocardial membrane but does not change the serum K⁺.
- D (False) – salbutamol 10–20 mg nebulised is an adjunct to insulin–glucose. It is insufficient alone, and some patients do not respond.

**Ref:** ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753.

questions.stem: According to ERC 2025, a serum K⁺ of 6.2 mmol/L is classified as:
options: Life-threatening only if ECG changes are absent
Normal
Moderate hyperkalaemia
Severe hyperkalaemia
Mild hyperkalaemia
questions.expl:
**Why C:** ERC 2025 classifies hyperkalaemia as **moderate at 6.0–6.4 mmol/L** and severe at ≥ 6.5 mmol/L, so 6.2 mmol/L is moderate. Treatment urgency also depends on ECG changes, the rate of rise and the clinical context. Moderate hyperkalaemia is treated with insulin–glucose ± salbutamol and K⁺ removal.

**Why not the others:**
- A – ECG changes make hyperkalaemia more dangerous; their absence does not make it life-threatening.
- B – the normal range is ~3.5–5.0 mmol/L.
- D – severe hyperkalaemia starts at 6.5 mmol/L.
- E – ERC 2025 does not use a separate mild category for this value (the older 5.5–5.9 band); 6.2 falls in the moderate band.

**Ref:** ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753.

questions.stem: Regarding hypokalaemia:
options: Hypomagnesaemia causes renal potassium wasting.
A small fall in serum potassium reflects only a small total body deficit.
IV potassium should preferably be diluted in 5 % glucose.
Metabolic alkalosis shifts potassium into cells.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Mg²⁺ deficiency releases the inhibition of ROMK channels, so renal K⁺ wasting continues until magnesium is replaced.
- B (False) – ~98 % of K⁺ is intracellular, so even a 1 mmol/L fall in serum K⁺ reflects a deficit of the order of 200–400 mmol.
- C (False) – glucose stimulates insulin, which shifts K⁺ into cells and can deepen the hypokalaemia; dilute KCl in 0.9 % saline.
- D (True) – in alkalosis H⁺ leaves cells in exchange for K⁺, and bicarbonaturia increases renal K⁺ loss.

**Ref:** Gennari FJ, N Engl J Med 1998;339:451–458.

questions.stem: An 85-year-old woman, 50 kg (TBW 0.45 × weight), has Na⁺ 168 mmol/L. The free water deficit is approximately:
questions.expl:
**Why B:** TBW = 0.45 × 50 = 22.5 L. Deficit = 22.5 × (168/140 − 1) = 22.5 × 0.2 = **4.5 L**, to which ongoing losses must be added. At ≤ 10–12 mmol/L/24 h, correcting chronic hypernatraemia from 168 to ~145 mmol/L takes about 2–3 days.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 7.0 L would need a TBW of 35 L (0.7 × weight), far too high for an elderly woman.
- C – 2.5 L would match a Na⁺ of only ~155 mmol/L.
- D – 5.5 L assumes a TBW of 0.55 × weight.
- E – 3.5 L would need a TBW of ~17.5 L (0.35 × weight), which underestimates the deficit.

**EDIC trap:** use the TBW fraction for age and sex: 0.6 young men, 0.5 young women and elderly men, 0.45 elderly women.

**Ref:** Adrogué HJ, Madias NE, Hypernatremia, N Engl J Med 2000;342:1493–1499.

questions.stem: Regarding calcium disorders:
options: Primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy account for about 90 % of hypercalcaemia.
Hyperphosphataemia from rhabdomyolysis can cause hypocalcaemia.
Severe hypercalcaemia is defined as total calcium ≥ 3.5 mmol/L.
Hypercalcaemia typically prolongs the QT interval.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – primary hyperparathyroidism (mostly outpatients) and malignancy (mostly inpatients) together cause ~90 % of hypercalcaemia.
- B (True) – Ca–P precipitates in damaged muscle in rhabdomyolysis; rebound hypercalcaemia can occur in the recovery phase.
- C (True) – severe hypercalcaemia is total Ca ≥ 3.5 mmol/L (≥ 14 mg/dL), or iCa²⁺ ≥ 2.5 mmol/L.
- D (False) – hypercalcaemia **shortens** the QT interval (short ST segment); a prolonged QT points to hypocalcaemia.

**Ref:** Walker MD, Shane E, JAMA 2022;328:1624–1636.

questions.stem: A malnourished patient with alcohol use disorder starts parenteral nutrition. On day 3 he fails a spontaneous breathing trial; phosphate is 0.25 mmol/L. The most likely explanation is:
options: Refeeding hypophosphataemia causing respiratory muscle weakness
Critical illness polyneuropathy
Hypermagnesaemia
Hypercalcaemia
Metabolic alkalosis from parenteral nutrition
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Malnutrition and alcohol misuse put him at high risk of refeeding. The glucose in parenteral nutrition triggers insulin release, which shifts phosphate into cells; a Pi of 0.25 mmol/L (< 0.32) is severe. ATP and 2,3-DPG depletion weakens the diaphragm, which explains the failed SBT. Treat with IV phosphate, restrict energy for 48 h (ESPEN), give thiamine and replace K⁺ and Mg²⁺.

**Why not the others:**
- B – critical illness polyneuropathy follows prolonged sepsis or multiorgan failure and does not explain a Pi of 0.25 mmol/L on day 3.
- C – refeeding causes **hypo**magnesaemia; hypermagnesaemia needs renal failure or iatrogenic loading.
- D – hypercalcaemia is not a feature of refeeding, and IV phosphate can even lower calcium.
- E – metabolic alkalosis from PN is uncommon and does not explain severe hypophosphataemia.

**Ref:** Singer P et al., ESPEN ICU guideline, Clin Nutr 2019;38:48–79; da Silva JSV et al., Nutr Clin Pract 2020;35:178–195.

questions.stem: Regarding the Doig refeeding trial (Lancet Respir Med 2015):
options: The primary outcome was significantly improved.
It enrolled critically ill adults in Australia and New Zealand.
The intervention was 20 kcal/h for at least 2 days, then a gradual return to goal.
Fewer patients were alive at day 60 in the restricted group.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – the primary outcome (days alive after ICU discharge) improved by 4.9 days, which was not significant (p = 0.19).
- B (True) – the trial randomised 339 critically ill adults in 13 ICUs in Australia and New Zealand.
- C (True) – the intervention was 20 kcal/h for ≥ 2 days, followed by a gradual return to goal over 2–3 days.
- D (False) – **more** patients were alive at day 60 in the restricted group (~91 % vs ~79 %, p = 0.002), a secondary outcome.

**Ref:** Doig GS et al., Lancet Respir Med 2015;3:943–952.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man, 80 kg (TBW 40 L), has Na⁺ 160 mmol/L. The expected effect of 1 L of 5 % glucose on serum Na⁺ (Adrogué–Madias) is:
options: −2.0 mmol/L
−6.0 mmol/L
−10 mmol/L
−3.9 mmol/L
−1.0 mmol/L
questions.expl:
**Why D:** ΔNa⁺ = (0 − 160) / (40 + 1) = −160 / 41 ≈ **−3.9 mmol/L** per litre of 5 % glucose. To lower Na⁺ by 10 mmol/L in 24 h, about 10 / 3.9 ≈ 2.6 L is needed, plus replacement of ongoing (insensible, urinary) losses.

**Why not the others:**
- A – −2.0 mmol/L is the predicted effect of 1 L of 0.45 % saline: (77 − 160) / 41 ≈ −2.0.
- B – −6.0 mmol/L would need a TBW of only ~26 L.
- C – −10 mmol/L is the daily target, not the effect of one litre.
- E – −1.0 mmol/L underestimates the effect about fourfold; such small changes come from near-isotonic fluids, e.g. Hartmann's (130 − 160) / 41 ≈ −0.7.

**EDIC trap:** the formula ignores urine output, so check Na⁺ frequently, especially with DI or osmotic diuresis.

**Ref:** Adrogué HJ, Madias NE, N Engl J Med 2000;342:1493–1499.

questions.stem: Essential features for diagnosing SIAD include:
options: Effective serum osmolality < 275 mOsm/kg
Urine osmolality > 100 mOsm/kg
Clinical hypervolaemia with oedema
Exclusion of hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency
questions.expl:
- A (True) – an effective serum osmolality < 275 mOsm/kg confirms hypotonicity (exclude glucose, mannitol and pseudohyponatraemia).
- B (True) – urine osmolality > 100 mOsm/kg shows inappropriately concentrated urine, i.e. ADH is active.
- C (False) – SIAD requires clinical **euvolaemia**. Oedema points to hypervolaemic hyponatraemia (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome).
- D (True) – hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency (including secondary) must be excluded, as must recent diuretic use and renal failure. Urine Na⁺ is > 30 mmol/L on a normal intake.

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331.

questions.stem: A patient with essential thrombocythaemia (platelets 1100 × 10⁹/L) has serum K⁺ 6.4 mmol/L, a normal ECG and normal renal function. The best next step is:
options: Arrange urgent dialysis
Start insulin–glucose
Measure potassium in a heparinised whole-blood sample (blood gas analyser)
Give sodium bicarbonate
Give calcium chloride immediately
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Platelets release K⁺ while blood clots in a serum tube, so extreme thrombocytosis produces **pseudohyperkalaemia**. A normal ECG and normal renal function support this. Measure K⁺ in heparinised whole blood (blood gas analyser) or plasma; a serum–plasma difference of > ~0.4 mmol/L confirms it.

**Why not the others:**
- A – dialysis is for confirmed, refractory hyperkalaemia, not an unverified result.
- B – insulin–glucose for an artefactual value risks hypoglycaemia and true hypokalaemia.
- D – bicarbonate is not first-line even for true hyperkalaemia outside acidosis or arrest.
- E – calcium is indicated for severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes; the ECG here is normal and 6.4 mmol/L is moderate.

**EDIC trap:** extreme leucocytosis (e.g. CLL), haemolysis and fist clenching cause the same artefact.

**Ref:** ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753; Clase CM et al. (KDIGO), Kidney Int 2020;97:42–61.

questions.stem: According to NICE CG32, which of the following alone (as a single criterion) places a patient at high risk of refeeding problems?
options: History of alcohol misuse
BMI < 18.5 kg/m²
Little or no nutritional intake for > 5 days
Unintentional weight loss > 15 % within 3–6 months
questions.expl:
- A (False) – a history of alcohol misuse (or drugs such as insulin, chemotherapy, antacids, diuretics) is a minor criterion and needs at least one other.
- B (False) – BMI < 18.5 is minor; the single criterion is BMI < 16.
- C (False) – little intake for > 5 days is minor; the single criterion is > 10 days.
- D (True) – unintentional weight loss > 15 % within 3–6 months is a single high-risk criterion, as are BMI < 16, little intake for > 10 days and low K⁺/PO₄/Mg²⁺ before feeding.

**Ref:** NICE CG32, Nutrition support for adults (2006, updated 2017).

questions.stem: Total calcium 2.00 mmol/L, albumin 25 g/L, ionised calcium 0.92 mmol/L in a septic patient. Which statement is correct?
options: Calcium must be given routinely to all septic patients with this result
Ionised calcium is not affected by pH
Corrected calcium is 2.30 mmol/L, so calcium status is normal
Corrected calcium is 1.70 mmol/L
Corrected calcium is 2.30 mmol/L, but the ionised value shows true hypocalcaemia
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Corrected Ca = 2.00 + 0.02 × (40 − 25) = 2.00 + 0.30 = 2.30 mmol/L, which looks normal. The measured iCa²⁺ of 0.92 mmol/L (normal ~1.1–1.3) shows true hypocalcaemia. The albumin formula performs poorly in critically ill patients, so the ionised value decides.

**Why not the others:**
- A – routine supplementation of asymptomatic mild hypocalcaemia in sepsis has no proven benefit; treat symptomatic or severe cases or specific settings (massive transfusion, hyperkalaemia).
- B – pH changes iCa²⁺: alkalosis lowers it and acidosis raises it.
- C – the arithmetic is right but the interpretation is wrong, because iCa²⁺ is low.
- D – 1.70 subtracts the correction instead of adding it.

**Ref:** Aberegg SK, Ionized calcium in the ICU, Chest 2016;149:846–855.

title: W07 · D1 – Cardiogenic shock: definition, SCAI SHOCK, diagnosis, recommendations

questions.stem: According to the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines, which statement about the definition of cardiogenic shock is correct?
options: A cardiac index < 1.8 L/min/m² must be documented
Pulmonary congestion on chest X-ray is required
It is critical end-organ hypoperfusion due to primary cardiac dysfunction, without a fixed blood pressure cut-off
Lactate must exceed 4 mmol/L
Systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg for ≥ 30 minutes is mandatory
questions.expl:
**Why C:** The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines define cardiogenic shock as critical end-organ hypoperfusion caused by a primary cardiac disorder. Lactate > 2 mmol/L supports the diagnosis, but no blood pressure threshold is required: vasoconstriction can keep BP normal while perfusion fails ("normotensive CS").

**Why not the others:**
- A – a cardiac index ≤ 2.2 L/min/m² was a supportive haemodynamic criterion in trial definitions; the guideline does not require a CI of 1.8.
- B – congestion is common ("cold and wet") but not required; "cold and dry" CS exists, e.g. in RV infarction.
- D – lactate > 2 mmol/L supports the diagnosis; 4 mmol/L is not a diagnostic cut-off.
- E – SBP < 90 mmHg for ≥ 30 min is the classic trial definition (SHOCK, IABP-SHOCK II), not the ESC 2026 one.

**EDIC trap:** a normotensive patient with hypoperfusion from a cardiac cause still has CS.

**Ref:** Køber L et al., 2026 ESC Guidelines for the management of heart failure, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457; Hochman JS et al., SHOCK, N Engl J Med 1999;341:625–634.

questions.stem: Regarding the SCAI SHOCK classification (2022 update):
options: Stage C can be assigned without hypotension if hypoperfusion requires intervention.
A lactate ≥ 8 mmol/L is typical of stage E.
Stage B describes haemodynamic instability (relative hypotension or tachycardia) without hypoperfusion.
The cardiac arrest modifier applies to patients who are comatose after cardiac arrest.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – stage C is defined by hypoperfusion that needs one intervention beyond fluids (a drug or a device). Hypotension is typical but not mandatory.
- B (True) – lactate ≥ 8 mmol/L, often with CPR, ECMO or profound hypotension despite maximal support, is typical of stage E (Extremis).
- C (True) – stage B (Beginning) means relative hypotension (SBP < 90, MAP < 60 or a fall > 30 mmHg) or tachycardia, with normal lactate and preserved perfusion.
- D (True) – the cardiac arrest modifier applies to comatose patients after arrest (typically GCS < 9), because the risk of hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury independently worsens prognosis.

**EDIC trap:** B = hypotension without hypoperfusion; C = hypoperfusion with or without hypotension.

**Ref:** Naidu SS et al., SCAI SHOCK Stage Classification Expert Consensus Update, J Am Coll Cardiol 2022;79:933–946.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with anterior STEMI has BP 96/60 mmHg, cool extremities and lactate 3.4 mmol/L, requiring dobutamine to maintain urine output. One hour later he is stable on the same dose. His SCAI stage is:
options: A
B
D
C
E
questions.expl:
**Why D:** The patient has hypoperfusion (cool extremities, lactate 3.4 mmol/L) that needs one intervention beyond fluids (dobutamine), and he remains stable on the same dose after an hour. That is SCAI stage C (Classic), which is option D.

**Why not the others:**
- A – stage A (At risk) has neither haemodynamic instability nor hypoperfusion; a large STEMI alone would be A.
- B – stage B needs normal lactate and preserved perfusion, which a lactate of 3.4 and cold extremities rule out.
- C – stage D (Deteriorating) needs initial support to fail, with rising lactate or escalation of drugs or MCS, and this has not happened.
- E – stage E means circulatory collapse, CPR or ECMO, or lactate ≥ 8 mmol/L.

**EDIC trap:** the option letters do not match the SCAI letters. Read the label, not the position.

**Ref:** Naidu SS et al., SCAI SHOCK Stage Classification Expert Consensus Update, J Am Coll Cardiol 2022;79:933–946.

questions.stem: Regarding haemodynamic assessment in cardiogenic shock:
options: Cardiac power output is calculated as MAP × CO / 451.
The ESICM 2025 guidelines consider echocardiography the first-line tool to determine the type of shock.
Mixed venous oxygen saturation is typically high in cardiogenic shock.
A high pulmonary artery pulsatility index (PAPi) suggests right ventricular failure.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – CPO (W) = MAP × CO / 451. It combines pressure and flow, and a low CPO (< ~0.6 W) is one of the strongest haemodynamic predictors of mortality in CS.
- B (True) – ESICM 2025 recommends echocardiography as the first-line tool to identify the type of shock, repeated even when CO is monitored invasively.
- C (False) – SvO₂ is typically **low** in CS, because low CO increases O₂ extraction. Normal or high values are more typical of septic shock.
- D (False) – PAPi = (sPAP − dPAP) / RAP. It is a **low** PAPi (roughly < 1 in AMI) that signals RV failure.

**EDIC trap:** low SvO₂ + high PCWP + low CI = classic CS profile.

**Ref:** Monnet X et al., ESICM guidelines on circulatory shock 2025, Intensive Care Med 2025;51:1971–2012; Fincke R et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2004;44:340–348.

questions.stem: In the SHOCK trial (NEJM 1999), emergency revascularisation compared with initial medical stabilisation in AMI-related cardiogenic shock:
options: Was stopped early for harm
Increased mortality at 6 months
Showed benefit only with fibrinolysis
Did not significantly reduce 30-day mortality but reduced 6-month mortality
Significantly reduced 30-day mortality
questions.expl:
**Why D:** SHOCK randomised 302 patients with AMI-related CS to emergency revascularisation (PCI or CABG) or initial medical stabilisation. The primary endpoint, 30-day mortality, was not significantly lower (46.7% vs 56.0%, p = 0.11), but 6-month mortality was (50.3% vs 63.1%, p = 0.027). The benefit persisted long-term and underpins the class I recommendation for immediate revascularisation.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the trial completed enrolment and was not stopped for harm.
- B – 6-month mortality was lower, not higher, with revascularisation.
- C – the benefit came from mechanical revascularisation; fibrinolysis was part of the medical stabilisation arm.
- E – the 30-day difference was not statistically significant.

**EDIC trap:** SHOCK was "negative" for its primary endpoint but positive at 6 months.

**Ref:** Hochman JS et al., N Engl J Med 1999;341:625–634; Byrne RA et al., 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720–3826.

questions.stem: Regarding vasoactive drugs in cardiogenic shock:
options: In SOAP II, dopamine was associated with more arrhythmic events than norepinephrine.
In the cardiogenic shock subgroup of SOAP II, dopamine was associated with higher 28-day mortality.
The 2026 ESC guidelines give a class I recommendation for norepinephrine in cardiogenic shock.
An individual-patient meta-analysis associated epinephrine with higher short-term mortality in cardiogenic shock.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – SOAP II (1679 patients with all types of shock) found arrhythmias in 24.1% with dopamine vs 12.4% with norepinephrine, mostly AF.
- B (True) – in the prespecified CS subgroup (n = 280), dopamine was associated with higher 28-day mortality, although overall mortality did not differ (52.5% vs 48.5%).
- C (False) – ESC 2026 gives norepinephrine **IIb, C** as the preferred vasopressor. No vasopressor carries class I in CS.
- D (True) – Léopold et al. (individual-patient data, 2583 patients) linked epinephrine to higher short-term mortality. The data are observational and cannot prove causality.

**EDIC trap:** "preferred" does not mean class I; read the class carefully.

**Ref:** De Backer D et al., N Engl J Med 2010;362:779–789; Léopold V et al., Intensive Care Med 2018;44:847–856; Køber L et al., 2026 ESC Guidelines for the management of heart failure, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457.

questions.stem: According to the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines, which recommendation regarding temporary mechanical circulatory support carries class I?
options: Routine IABP in all cardiogenic shock
Microaxial flow pump in all AMI-related cardiogenic shock
A multidisciplinary Shock Team to guide device selection
VA-ECMO in all patients with lactate > 4 mmol/L
Temporary MCS in unselected AMI-CS
questions.expl:
**Why C:** ESC 2026 recommends a multidisciplinary shock team (interventional cardiologist, intensivist, cardiac surgeon, HF specialist) for patients who are candidates for MCS, with class **I, C**. Team-based care in hub-and-spoke networks aims to match the right device to the right patient at the right time.

**Why not the others:**
- A – routine IABP in unselected CS is class III, B1 (IABP-SHOCK II showed no mortality benefit).
- B – the microaxial pump is IIa, B1 only in selected STEMI-CS with LV dysfunction and no risk of hypoxic brain injury (DanGer Shock), not in all AMI-CS.
- D – no lactate threshold triggers routine VA-ECMO; ECLS-SHOCK (lactate > 3) showed no benefit and more complications.
- E – temporary MCS in unselected AMI-CS is class III, B1 because of the risk of harm.

**Ref:** Køber L et al., 2026 ESC Guidelines for the management of heart failure, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457.

questions.stem: Haemodynamic profiles of cardiogenic shock:
options: The "cold and wet" profile is the most common.
Results of AMI-CS device trials can be directly extrapolated to non-ischaemic HF-related shock.
Isolated right ventricular failure typically shows low right atrial pressure with a high PCWP.
A "warm and wet" profile suggests low systemic vascular resistance, e.g. a systemic inflammatory response after MI.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – "cold and wet" (low CI, high PCWP) is the classic and most common CS profile.
- B (False) – IABP-SHOCK II, ECLS-SHOCK and DanGer Shock all enrolled AMI-CS only. HF-related shock differs in pathophysiology and course, so their results should not be extrapolated automatically.
- C (False) – isolated RV failure shows **high** RAP/CVP with a normal or low PCWP, i.e. a high RAP/PCWP ratio (> ~0.8).
- D (True) – "warm and wet" (relatively preserved CI, low SVR, high PCWP) is the "mixed" phenotype, e.g. SIRS or sepsis after MI. Look for infection.

**EDIC trap:** "cold and dry" can be RV infarction or hypovolaemia with LV dysfunction, so assess preload before giving diuretics.
