**Ref:** Naidu SS et al., SCAI SHOCK Stage Classification Expert Consensus Update, J Am Coll Cardiol 2022;79:933–946; Køber L et al., 2026 ESC Guidelines for the management of heart failure, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457.

questions.stem: A patient with NSTEMI develops cardiogenic shock. According to the 2023 ESC ACS guidelines, the appropriate invasive strategy is:
options: Fibrinolysis first, then angiography within 24 hours
Invasive strategy within 72 hours
Early invasive strategy within 24 hours
Immediate invasive strategy
Selective invasive strategy after non-invasive testing
questions.expl:
**Why D:** In NSTE-ACS, haemodynamic instability or cardiogenic shock is a very-high-risk criterion. ESC 2023 recommends an **immediate** invasive strategy (< 2 h), as in STEMI (I, C), with PCI of the culprit lesion or emergency CABG if the anatomy is unsuitable.

**Why not the others:**
- A – fibrinolysis has no role in NSTE-ACS (no benefit, more bleeding).
- B – the 72-hour window came from older guidelines and does not apply to very-high-risk patients.
- C – the 24-hour window is for high-risk patients (confirmed NSTEMI, dynamic ST changes, GRACE > 140, transient ST elevation).
- E – a selective strategy is for patients without high-risk features, the opposite of shock.

**EDIC trap:** a raised troponin without ST elevation does not mean "within 24 h" when the patient is in shock.

**Ref:** Byrne RA et al., 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720–3826.

questions.stem: Regarding the 2022 SCAI SHOCK update:
options: Mortality increases progressively across stages A to E in validation studies.
It was endorsed by the ESC Association for Acute CardioVascular Care.
Age and frailty are considered modifiable risk factors.
It introduced a three-axis model including shock severity, phenotype/aetiology and risk modifiers.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – large validation cohorts (e.g. Mayo Clinic CICU) showed a stepwise rise in mortality from stage A to E, which gives the scheme prognostic value.
- B (True) – the 2022 update was endorsed by the ESC Association for Acute CardioVascular Care (ACVC) and by SCCM, among others.
- C (False) – age, frailty and comorbidity are **non-modifiable** risk modifiers. They change prognosis but not the stage.
- D (True) – the three axes are shock severity (stage A–E), clinical phenotype/aetiology, and risk modifiers (including cardiac arrest with coma).

**EDIC trap:** the stage describes current severity and is reassessed over time; risk modifiers sit on a separate axis.

**Ref:** Naidu SS et al., SCAI SHOCK Stage Classification Expert Consensus Update, J Am Coll Cardiol 2022;79:933–946; Jentzer JC et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2019;74:2117–2128.

open.q: A 58-year-old man with anterior STEMI arrives with BP 92/58 mmHg, cool mottled extremities, oliguria and lactate 4.1 mmol/L. Outline your initial diagnostic work-up and management during the first hours.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Recognise CS (hypoperfusion from a primary cardiac cause; lactate > 2 supports it, no fixed BP cut-off) and stage it – hypoperfusion needing intervention = at least SCAI C; reassess for deterioration (D).
- ECG, troponin, lactate, ABG, creatinine, liver tests, NT-proBNP; echocardiography as first-line tool – LVEF, regional wall motion, mechanical complications (VSD, acute MR, tamponade), RV function.
- Immediate coronary angiography and PCI of the infarct-related artery (SHOCK trial: ↓ 6-month mortality); emergency CABG if PCI not feasible; culprit-only PCI in multivessel disease.
- Arterial line; consider PAC/TPTD if CO monitoring needed (CPO, PAPi, SvO₂).
- Norepinephrine as preferred vasopressor, initial MAP target ≥ 65 mmHg individualised to perfusion; avoid dopamine and routine epinephrine.
- Inotrope (e.g. dobutamine) if hypoperfusion persists despite standard treatment incl. fluid challenge – lowest dose, shortest time.
- Activate the shock team (I, C); consider microaxial pump only in selected STEMI-CS without risk of hypoxic brain injury (IIa); no routine IABP or unselected MCS (III).
- Monitor perfusion targets: lactate clearance, CRT, urine output, mental status.

open.q: Explain why mixed venous saturation helps distinguish cardiogenic from septic shock, and how PAC-derived indices help identify right ventricular failure.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- In CS, low CO leads to increased O₂ extraction → SvO₂/ScvO₂ typically low.
- In septic shock ScvO₂ is often normal or high.
- Low SvO₂ + high PCWP + low CI = classic CS profile.
- PAPi = (sPAP − dPAP) / RAP; a low value signals RV failure.
- High RAP/PCWP ratio = predominant RV failure; isolated RV failure shows ↑ CVP/RAP with normal or low PCWP.
- CPO = MAP × CO / 451 integrates pressure and flow and is a strong predictor of mortality.

title: W07 · D2 – Mechanical circulatory support in cardiogenic shock

questions.stem: In IABP-SHOCK II, intra-aortic balloon pump support in AMI-related cardiogenic shock:
options: Reduced 30-day mortality by 25 %
Did not reduce 30-day mortality
Was only tested in patients not undergoing revascularisation
Increased the stroke rate significantly
Increased major bleeding significantly
questions.expl:
**Why B:** IABP-SHOCK II randomised 600 patients with AMI-CS who were planned for early revascularisation to IABP or no IABP. 30-day mortality was 39.7% vs 41.3% (RR 0.96; 95% CI 0.79–1.17; p = 0.69), and there was still no difference at 1 and 6 years. As a result, routine IABP in CS is class III (ESC 2023 ACS; ESC 2026 HF III, B1).

**Why not the others:**
- A – there was no reduction; the confidence interval spans 1.
- C – all patients were planned for early revascularisation, mostly PCI.
- D – stroke rates were low and did not differ significantly.
- E – major bleeding was 3.3% vs 4.4%, not significantly different.

**EDIC trap:** IABP still has a role as a bridge in mechanical complications (acute MR, VSR).

**Ref:** Thiele H et al., N Engl J Med 2012;367:1287–1296; Thiele H et al., Circulation 2019;139:395–403.

questions.stem: Regarding the ECLS-SHOCK trial:
options: Peripheral ischaemic vascular complications were more frequent with ECLS.
30-day mortality was significantly lower with early ECLS.
It enrolled patients with AMI-related cardiogenic shock with lactate > 3 mmol/L planned for revascularisation.
Moderate or severe bleeding was less frequent with ECLS.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – peripheral ischaemic vascular complications needing surgical or interventional treatment occurred in 11.0% with ECLS vs 3.8% without.
- B (False) – 30-day mortality was 47.8% vs 49.0% (RR 0.98; 0.80–1.19), with no difference.
- C (True) – 420 patients with AMI-CS (STEMI or NSTEMI), planned early revascularisation and lactate > 3 mmol/L; most had been resuscitated before randomisation.
- D (False) – moderate or severe bleeding (BARC 3–5) was **more** frequent with ECLS: 23.4% vs 9.6%.

**EDIC trap:** ECLS-SHOCK argues against *routine early* ECMO, not against individualised rescue ECMO in refractory shock.

**Ref:** Thiele H et al., ECLS-SHOCK, N Engl J Med 2023;389:1286–1297.

questions.stem: Which patient best matches the population in which DanGer Shock showed a mortality benefit?
options: 62-year-old comatose after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with STEMI and shock
66-year-old with isolated right ventricular infarction
45-year-old with fulminant myocarditis and biventricular failure
70-year-old with NSTEMI, LVEF 55 %, lactate 1.5 mmol/L
58-year-old with anterior STEMI, LVEF 25 %, lactate 4 mmol/L, awake, on norepinephrine
questions.expl:
**Why E:** DanGer Shock enrolled STEMI-CS (SBP < 100 mmHg or vasoactive support, lactate ≥ 2.5 mmol/L, LVEF < 45%) and excluded patients who were comatose after OHCA. Impella CP lowered 180-day mortality from 58.5% to 45.8% (HR 0.74). An awake patient with anterior STEMI, EF 25%, lactate 4 and on norepinephrine matches this population exactly.

**Why not the others:**
- A – comatose OHCA survivors were excluded, because hypoxic brain injury drives their outcome; ESC 2026 restricts IIa to patients without this risk.
- B – a left-sided microaxial pump does not support a failing RV; the trial studied LV failure.
- C – myocarditis is non-ischaemic HF-CS, outside the trial population, although MCS may be used on an individual basis.
- D – EF 55% with lactate 1.5 is not CS by trial criteria, and the trial did not include NSTEMI.

**Ref:** Møller JE et al., DanGer Shock, N Engl J Med 2024;390:1382–1393; Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457.

questions.stem: Regarding DanGer Shock (NEJM 2024):
options: The composite of adverse events was more frequent with the pump.
Limb ischaemia requiring intervention was more frequent with the pump.
Renal replacement therapy was less frequent in the pump group.
All-cause death at 180 days was 45.8 % with the microaxial flow pump vs 58.5 % with standard care.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – the composite safety endpoint (severe bleeding, limb ischaemia, haemolysis, device failure, worsening aortic regurgitation) occurred in 24.0% vs 6.2%.
- B (True) – limb ischaemia needing intervention occurred in 5.6% vs 1.1%.
- C (False) – RRT was **more** frequent with the pump: 41.9% vs 26.7%.
- D (True) – 45.8% vs 58.5% (HR 0.74; 0.55–0.99; p = 0.04). This was the first RCT of MCS in AMI-CS to show a mortality benefit.

**EDIC trap:** the survival benefit came at the cost of more complications, so careful patient selection is essential.

**Ref:** Møller JE et al., N Engl J Med 2024;390:1382–1393.

questions.stem: A patient on femoral VA-ECMO for cardiogenic shock with severe ARDS shows recovering LV function. Right radial PaO₂ is 6 kPa, femoral arterial PaO₂ 35 kPa. The most appropriate intervention is:
options: Improve native lung gas exchange and consider conversion to V-AV ECMO
Increase FiO₂ on the oxygenator
Increase sweep gas flow
Reduce ECMO flow to the minimum
Insert a distal perfusion cannula
questions.expl:
**Why A:** With femoral VA-ECMO, oxygenated blood returns retrogradely up the aorta. The recovering LV ejects deoxygenated blood from the failing lungs into the aortic root, which supplies the coronaries, carotids and right subclavian artery. A right radial PaO₂ of 6 kPa against a femoral PaO₂ of 35 kPa is Harlequin (differential) hypoxaemia. The fix is to treat the source: optimise ventilation (PEEP, FiO₂, recruitment) and/or add a jugular return cannula (V-AV ECMO).

**Why not the others:**
- B – oxygenator FiO₂ only raises the saturation of ECMO blood, which already goes to the lower body.
- C – sweep gas mainly removes CO₂ from ECMO blood and does nothing for blood leaving the native lungs.
- D – lower ECMO flow lets more hypoxic native output into the aorta and moves the mixing zone distally.
- E – a distal perfusion cannula prevents limb ischaemia and does not affect upper-body oxygenation.

**Ref:** Lorusso R et al., ELSO interim guidelines for VA-ECMO in adult cardiac patients, ASAIO J 2021;67:827–844.

questions.stem: Signs suggesting left ventricular distension on peripheral VA-ECMO include:
options: Aortic valve remaining closed on echocardiography
Loss of arterial pulse pressure
Spontaneous echo contrast ("smoke") in the left ventricle
Rapid resolution of pulmonary oedema
questions.expl:
- A (True) – the weak LV cannot generate a pressure above the aortic pressure raised by retrograde flow, so the aortic valve stays closed.
- B (True) – a pulse pressure falling towards 0 (flat arterial trace) means the LV is no longer ejecting.
- C (True) – spontaneous echo contrast ("smoke") in the LV or aortic root shows stasis and a high risk of thrombus.
- D (False) – LV distension raises LVEDP, LA pressure and PCWP, so pulmonary oedema **progresses**.

**EDIC trap:** treat promptly: lower ECMO flow, start an inotrope, reduce afterload, then IABP, Impella or a vent.

**Ref:** Lorusso R et al., ELSO interim guidelines for VA-ECMO in adult cardiac patients, ASAIO J 2021;67:827–844; Kim MC et al., EARLY-UNLOAD, Circulation 2023;148:1570–1581.

questions.stem: The haemodynamic effect of a transvalvular microaxial flow pump (Impella) on the left ventricle is:
options: Increase in LV afterload
Right ventricular unloading
Direct LV unloading with reduced end-diastolic pressure
Full biventricular and respiratory support
Diastolic augmentation only
questions.expl:
**Why C:** The Impella aspirates blood from the LV through a cannula across the aortic valve and ejects it into the ascending aorta, so it works in series with the LV. This directly unloads the ventricle, lowering LVEDP, wall stress and myocardial O₂ consumption while increasing forward flow (Impella CP about 3–4 L/min).

**Why not the others:**
- A – a rise in LV afterload is the problem with peripheral VA-ECMO (retrograde flow).
- B – a left-sided pump does not unload the RV and may increase RV preload; RV support needs Impella RP or an RVAD.
- D – full biventricular and respiratory support is provided by VA-ECMO.
- E – diastolic augmentation is how the IABP works.

**EDIC trap:** contraindications include LV thrombus, a mechanical aortic valve, severe AS/AR and severe PAD.

**Ref:** Møller JE et al., N Engl J Med 2024;390:1382–1393; Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457.

questions.stem: Regarding left ventricular unloading during VA-ECMO:
options: Inotropes are contraindicated because they prevent aortic valve opening.
In EARLY-UNLOAD, early routine transseptal left atrial venting reduced 30-day mortality.
In ECLS-SHOCK, active LV unloading was used in the majority of ECLS patients.
An IABP or microaxial flow pump cannot be used to unload the LV.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – inotropes (e.g. dobutamine) increase contractility so the aortic valve opens, and are a first step against LV distension together with reducing ECMO flow.
- B (False) – EARLY-UNLOAD (116 patients) found 30-day mortality of 46.6% with early routine transseptal LA venting vs 44.8% (NS); the control arm allowed rescue unloading.
- C (False) – only ~6% of ECLS patients received active LV unloading, a frequent criticism of the trial.
- D (False) – both are used: the IABP reduces afterload and the microaxial pump ("ECPELLA") unloads the LV directly; septostomy or an LA vent are alternatives.

**EDIC trap:** no RCT shows a benefit from routine early unloading; unloading is reactive, guided by echo and pulse pressure.

**Ref:** Kim MC et al., Circulation 2023;148:1570–1581; Thiele H et al., N Engl J Med 2023;389:1286–1297.

questions.stem: Which statement about the IPD meta-analysis of VA-ECMO trials in infarct-related cardiogenic shock (Lancet 2023) is correct?
options: It included only observational studies
It showed benefit only in patients older than 75 years
VA-ECMO reduced 30-day mortality by about one third
VA-ECMO did not reduce 30-day mortality and increased major bleeding and vascular complications
It found fewer vascular complications with VA-ECMO
questions.expl:
**Why D:** The individual-patient-data meta-analysis pooled 4 RCTs (ECLS-SHOCK, ECMO-CS, EURO SHOCK and the ECLS-SHOCK pilot), 567 patients with AMI-CS. VA-ECMO did not reduce 30-day mortality (OR 0.93; 0.66–1.29), but it increased major bleeding (OR 2.44) and peripheral vascular complications (OR 3.53).

**Why not the others:**
- A – only randomised trials were included.
- B – no subgroup, including age, showed a significant benefit.
- C – mortality was not reduced.
- E – vascular complications were more than three times as frequent with VA-ECMO.

**EDIC trap:** do not read "no routine ECMO" as "no ECMO"; rescue ECMO, ECPR and bridging remain individual decisions.

**Ref:** Zeymer U et al., Lancet 2023;402:1338–1346.

questions.stem: According to the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines:
options: IABP is not recommended in unselected cardiogenic shock.
Temporary MCS is not recommended in unselected AMI-related cardiogenic shock.
Temporary MCS should be considered as a bridge in mechanical complications of MI.
Routine use of microaxial flow pumps in all cardiogenic shock is recommended.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – IABP in unselected CS is class III, B1, based on IABP-SHOCK II.
- B (True) – temporary MCS in unselected AMI-CS is class III, B1 (ECLS-SHOCK, IPD meta-analysis: no benefit, more bleeding and vascular complications).
- C (True) – temporary MCS as a bridge in mechanical complications of MI is IIa, C. It stabilises the patient until surgical or percutaneous repair.
- D (False) – the microaxial pump is IIa, B1 only in **selected** STEMI-CS with LV dysfunction and no risk of hypoxic brain injury. Routine use is not recommended.

**EDIC trap:** the one class I recommendation in this area is the shock team, not a device.

**Ref:** Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457.

open.q: Explain why ECLS-SHOCK was negative while DanGer Shock showed a mortality benefit, and what this means for device selection in AMI-related cardiogenic shock.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Different devices and physiology: VA-ECMO gives full circulatory support but increases LV afterload; Impella directly unloads the LV.
- ECLS-SHOCK: unselected AMI-CS (STEMI and NSTEMI), lactate > 3, large proportion after CPR; 30-d mortality 47.8 vs 49.0% (NS).
- ECLS-SHOCK: more BARC 3–5 bleeding (23.4 vs 9.6%) and vascular complications (11.0 vs 3.8%); active LV unloading in only ~6%.
- DanGer Shock: carefully selected STEMI-CS, LVEF < 45%, lactate ≥ 2.5, comatose OHCA patients excluded; 180-d mortality 45.8 vs 58.5% (HR 0.74).
- DanGer Shock benefit came at the cost of more adverse events (24.0 vs 6.2%), limb ischaemia and RRT.
- Implication (ESC 2026): microaxial pump IIa only in selected STEMI-CS without risk of hypoxic brain injury; unselected MCS and routine IABP III; shock team I.
- Rescue/individualised VA-ECMO still has a role (refractory CS, ECPR, myocarditis, bridge to transplant/VAD).

open.q: A patient on femoral VA-ECMO shows loss of arterial pulse pressure and worsening pulmonary oedema. Explain the mechanism and outline your management.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Retrograde femoral return increases LV afterload; a weak LV cannot open the aortic valve.
- Result: ↑ LVEDP and LA pressure → pulmonary oedema, LV/aortic root stasis and thrombus, subendocardial ischaemia.
- Confirm with echo: aortic valve not opening, "smoke" in the LV; rising PCWP.
- Reduce ECMO flow to the minimum that maintains perfusion.
- Inotrope to open the aortic valve; vasodilation to reduce afterload.
- Unload with IABP or Impella (ECPELLA), or surgical/percutaneous vent (transseptal LA cannula, septostomy).
- Note: EARLY-UNLOAD showed no benefit of early routine unloading (46.6 vs 44.8%).

title: W07 · D3 – ACS in the ICU: STEMI/NSTEMI, CULPRIT-SHOCK, mechanical complications of MI

questions.stem: In CULPRIT-SHOCK, culprit-lesion-only PCI compared with immediate multivessel PCI in AMI-related cardiogenic shock:
options: Enrolled only patients with single-vessel disease
Reduced the 30-day composite of death or severe renal failure requiring RRT
Showed no difference at 30 days
Increased the 30-day composite of death or renal replacement therapy
Was associated with more renal replacement therapy
questions.expl:
**Why B:** CULPRIT-SHOCK randomised 706 patients with AMI-CS and multivessel disease to culprit-only PCI (with optional staged revascularisation) or immediate multivessel PCI. The 30-day composite of death or severe renal failure needing RRT was 45.9% vs 55.4% (RR 0.83; 0.71–0.96). Mortality drove the result (43.3% vs 51.6%), and the benefit persisted at 1 year (50.0% vs 56.9%).

**Why not the others:**
- A – multivessel disease was an inclusion criterion.
- C – the 30-day difference was significant.
- D – the composite was lower, not higher, with culprit-only PCI.
- E – RRT was numerically less frequent with culprit-only PCI (11.6% vs 16.4%, NS).

**Ref:** Thiele H et al., N Engl J Med 2017;377:2419–2432 and 2018;379:1699–1710; Byrne RA et al., 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720–3826.

questions.stem: Regarding revascularisation strategies in STEMI with multivessel disease:
options: In haemodynamically stable STEMI, COMPLETE showed that complete revascularisation did not reduce cardiovascular death or MI.
In CULPRIT-SHOCK, the mortality difference was no longer present at 1 year.
In cardiogenic shock, PCI during the index procedure should be restricted to the infarct-related artery.
CULPRIT-SHOCK and COMPLETE studied the same population.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – COMPLETE (4041 stable STEMI patients) showed that complete revascularisation **reduced** CV death or new MI: 7.8% vs 10.5% (HR 0.74).
- B (False) – the benefit persisted at 1 year, with mortality of 50.0% (culprit-only) vs 56.9%.
- C (True) – ESC 2023 restricts PCI during the index procedure in CS to the infarct-related artery. Routine immediate PCI of non-IRA lesions is not recommended (III, B); other lesions are staged.
- D (False) – CULPRIT-SHOCK studied AMI-CS (STEMI or NSTEMI); COMPLETE studied haemodynamically stable STEMI without shock.

**EDIC trap:** the trials do not contradict each other. Shock means culprit-only; stable STEMI means complete (staged) revascularisation.

**Ref:** Mehta SR et al., N Engl J Med 2019;381:1411–1421; Thiele H et al., N Engl J Med 2017;377:2419–2432; Byrne RA et al., 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720–3826.

questions.stem: Three days after a late-presenting inferior STEMI, a patient develops sudden pulmonary oedema and hypotension. No new murmur is heard. PCWP tracing shows large v waves. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Dressler syndrome
Ventricular septal rupture
Right ventricular infarction
Papillary muscle rupture with acute mitral regurgitation
Free wall rupture
questions.expl:
**Why D:** A late-presenting inferior STEMI, followed days later by abrupt pulmonary oedema and shock with large v waves on the PCWP trace, points to papillary muscle rupture with acute MR. The posteromedial papillary muscle has a single blood supply (PDA, usually from the RCA), so it is vulnerable in inferior or posterior MI. The murmur is often soft or absent because LV and LA pressures equalise quickly.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Dressler syndrome is a late (weeks) pericarditis with pain, fever and a rub, not acute pulmonary oedema.
- B – VSR causes a new harsh holosystolic murmur and an O₂ saturation step-up between RA and PA.
- C – RV infarction causes hypotension with raised JVP and **clear** lungs.
- E – free wall rupture presents with tamponade or PEA.

**Ref:** Damluji AA et al., Mechanical complications of AMI (AHA scientific statement), Circulation 2021;144:e16–e35; Byrne RA et al., 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720–3826.

questions.stem: Regarding ventricular septal rupture after MI:
options: A new harsh holosystolic murmur is a common finding.
It causes a right-to-left shunt.
A step-down in oxygen saturation between the right atrium and pulmonary artery is typical.
IABP or temporary MCS can be used as a bridge to closure.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – most patients have a new harsh holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border, often with a thrill, along with CS and biventricular failure.
- B (False) – LV pressure exceeds RV pressure, so the shunt is **left-to-right**, causing pulmonary overcirculation (Qp/Qs > 1) and RV volume overload.
- C (False) – oxygenated LV blood enters the RV, so O₂ saturation **steps up** between the RA and the PA.
- D (True) – afterload reduction with an IABP or temporary MCS reduces the shunt and bridges the patient to surgical or percutaneous closure (ESC 2026: MCS as a bridge IIa, C). The Heart Team decides the timing.

**EDIC trap:** inferior MI causes basal septal rupture, which carries a worse prognosis than apical (anterior) rupture.

**Ref:** Damluji AA et al., Mechanical complications of AMI (AHA scientific statement), Circulation 2021;144:e16–e35; Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457.

questions.stem: A patient with NSTEMI develops recurrent ventricular tachycardia and acute heart failure. According to ESC 2023, coronary angiography should be performed:
options: Only after non-invasive ischaemia testing
After 6 weeks of medical therapy
Immediately
Within 24 hours
Within 72 hours
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In ESC 2023, life-threatening arrhythmias (recurrent VT/VF) or cardiac arrest, and acute HF presumed to be ischaemic, are very-high-risk features of NSTE-ACS. They call for an **immediate** invasive strategy (< 2 h, I, C), as do haemodynamic instability, refractory pain, mechanical complications and recurrent dynamic ST changes.

**Why not the others:**
- A – non-invasive testing first is only for low-risk patients managed with a selective strategy.
- B – there is no "6 weeks of medical therapy" strategy, and delay is dangerous with ongoing ischaemia and VT.
- D – angiography within 24 h is for high-risk patients (confirmed NSTEMI, dynamic ST changes, GRACE > 140).
- E – the 72-hour window came from older guidelines and is not used for very-high-risk patients.

**Ref:** Byrne RA et al., 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720–3826.

questions.stem: Regarding right ventricular infarction:
options: ST elevation in V4R supports the diagnosis.
Maintenance of AV synchrony is important.
It is typically associated with inferior STEMI due to proximal RCA occlusion.
Nitrates are the first-line treatment of the associated hypotension.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ST elevation ≥ 1 mm in V4R is the most useful ECG sign. Record right-sided leads in every inferior STEMI.
- B (True) – the ischaemic RV depends on preload and atrial kick. AV block is common, so use AV-sequential pacing if needed and cardiovert AF early.
- C (True) – occlusion of the proximal RCA, before the RV marginal branches, causes RV infarction alongside inferior STEMI.
- D (False) – nitrates (and diuretics) reduce preload and can cause profound hypotension. Treatment is reperfusion, a cautious fluid challenge, inotropes and, if refractory, RV MCS.

**EDIC trap:** the triad is hypotension + raised JVP + **clear** lungs.

**Ref:** Byrne RA et al., 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720–3826; Harjola VP et al., Eur J Heart Fail 2016;18:226–241.

questions.stem: Regarding mechanical complications of MI, the ESC 2023 ACS guidelines state that:
options: IABP is contraindicated in mechanical complications
Surgery is regarded as the treatment of choice, with strategy decided by the Heart Team
Fibrinolysis is the preferred reperfusion strategy
Medical therapy alone is the treatment of choice
Revascularisation should never be performed at the time of surgery
questions.expl:
**Why B:** ESC 2023 regards surgery as the treatment of choice for mechanical complications (VSR, papillary muscle rupture, free wall rupture), with the Heart Team deciding strategy and timing. An IABP should be considered while awaiting surgery, and if revascularisation is needed, CABG is done at the same time as the repair. ESC 2026 adds temporary MCS as a bridge (IIa, C).

**Why not the others:**
- A – the IABP is not contraindicated; it reduces afterload and regurgitant or shunt flow and is the classic bridge.
- C – fibrinolysis does not treat a structural lesion; a mechanical complication must be excluded before lysis in CS.
- D – medical therapy alone carries very high mortality without repair.
- E – concomitant CABG is recommended when revascularisation is needed.

**Ref:** Byrne RA et al., 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720–3826; Damluji AA et al., Mechanical complications of AMI (AHA scientific statement), Circulation 2021;144:e16–e35.

questions.stem: In STEMI management (ESC 2023):
options: Routine oxygen is recommended irrespective of SpO₂.
If the anticipated time from diagnosis to PCI exceeds 120 minutes, fibrinolysis should be considered.
Before fibrinolysis in cardiogenic shock, a mechanical complication should be excluded.
Primary PCI is the preferred reperfusion strategy within 12 hours of symptom onset.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – oxygen is given only if SpO₂ < 90%. Routine oxygen in normoxaemic patients brings no benefit (DETO2X-AMI) and is not recommended.
- B (True) – if the anticipated time from diagnosis to PCI exceeds 120 min, fibrinolysis is given within 10 min of diagnosis, followed by transfer: rescue PCI if it fails, otherwise angiography at 2–24 h.
- C (True) – in CS, when PCI is not available in time, fibrinolysis may be considered after echocardiography excludes a mechanical complication.
- D (True) – primary PCI is the preferred reperfusion strategy within 12 h of symptom onset.

**Ref:** Byrne RA et al., 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720–3826; Hofmann R et al., DETO2X-AMI, N Engl J Med 2017;377:1240–1249.

questions.stem: A patient presents 6 days after an untreated anterior MI with sudden pulseless electrical activity. Bedside echo shows a large pericardial effusion with tamponade. The most likely cause is:
options: Right ventricular infarction
Papillary muscle rupture
Dressler syndrome
Left ventricular thrombus
Free wall rupture
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Sudden PEA with a large effusion and tamponade days after an untreated (non-reperfused) transmural anterior MI is typical of free wall rupture with haemopericardium. It usually occurs within the first week; risk factors include absent reperfusion, a first MI, older age and female sex. Pericardiocentesis is only a bridge to emergency surgical repair.

**Why not the others:**
- A – RV infarction complicates inferior MI and causes hypotension without tamponade.
- B – papillary muscle rupture causes acute MR and pulmonary oedema, mostly after inferior MI.
- C – Dressler syndrome occurs weeks later, with pericarditis and usually a small effusion, not sudden PEA.
- D – LV thrombus after anterior MI causes systemic embolism (stroke), not tamponade.

**EDIC trap:** PEA after a recent MI means do bedside echo immediately and look for tamponade.

**Ref:** Damluji AA et al., Mechanical complications of AMI (AHA scientific statement), Circulation 2021;144:e16–e35; Byrne RA et al., 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720–3826.

questions.stem: Regarding acute coronary syndromes in the ICU:
options: Oral P2Y12 inhibitor absorption may be delayed in shocked, ventilated patients receiving opioids.
Type 2 MI is caused by supply–demand imbalance, e.g. shock or tachyarrhythmia.
An LV thrombus is a contraindication to Impella insertion.
Type 2 MI always requires an immediate invasive strategy.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – opioids, gut hypoperfusion and intubation delay absorption of oral ticagrelor or prasugrel. Options are crushed tablets via an NG tube or IV cangrelor.
- B (True) – type 2 MI results from supply–demand imbalance (shock, anaemia, tachyarrhythmia, hypoxaemia) without acute atherothrombosis, and is very common in the ICU.
- C (True) – LV thrombus is a contraindication to Impella (risk of embolisation), as are a mechanical aortic valve, severe AS/AR and severe PAD.
- D (False) – treat the precipitating cause; invasive coronary assessment is selective, not automatic.

**Ref:** Byrne RA et al., 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720–3826; Thygesen K et al., Fourth Universal Definition of MI, Eur Heart J 2019;40:237–269.

open.q: Explain why CULPRIT-SHOCK and COMPLETE reached different conclusions about multivessel PCI, and how you would apply them in practice.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Different populations: CULPRIT-SHOCK = AMI-CS with multivessel CAD (n = 706); COMPLETE = haemodynamically stable STEMI after successful culprit PCI (n = 4041).
- CULPRIT-SHOCK: culprit-only reduced death or RRT at 30 d (45.9 vs 55.4%, RR 0.83); 1-year mortality 50.0 vs 56.9%.
- COMPLETE: complete revascularisation reduced CV death or MI (7.8 vs 10.5%, HR 0.74).
- In shock, extra lesions add contrast load, procedure time and ischaemia during further interventions.
- The trials do not conflict – presence of shock decides.
- Practice: in CS treat only the IRA during the index procedure, stage other lesions; in stable STEMI aim for complete (staged) revascularisation.
- If anatomy unsuitable for PCI in CS → emergency CABG.

open.q: Four days after a late-presenting MI, a patient becomes acutely hypotensive. Outline how you would differentiate the possible mechanical complications at the bedside and their management.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Urgent echocardiography for any sudden deterioration or new murmur.
- VSR: new holosystolic murmur with thrill, biventricular failure, left-to-right shunt, O₂ saturation step-up RA→PA, Qp/Qs > 1.
- Papillary muscle rupture (posteromedial, inferior MI, single PDA supply): sudden pulmonary oedema, murmur may be absent, flail leaflet, large v waves on PCWP.
- Free wall rupture: tamponade, PEA, sudden death → pericardiocentesis as bridge and emergency surgery.
- Also consider RV infarction (hypotension, raised JVP, clear lungs, V4R) – preserve preload, avoid nitrates.
- Surgery is the treatment of choice, decided by the Heart Team; CABG at the same time if needed.
- Bridge with afterload reduction, IABP or temporary MCS (ESC 2026 IIa, C).

title: W07 · D4 – Acute (decompensated) heart failure, inotropes, NIV

questions.stem: In the DOREMI trial (NEJM 2021), milrinone compared with dobutamine in cardiogenic shock:
options: Significantly reduced in-hospital mortality
Did not significantly differ in the primary composite outcome
Caused significantly more arrhythmias
Was compared in an open-label design
Was tested only in SCAI stage E
questions.expl:
**Why B:** DOREMI randomised 192 patients with CS (SCAI B–E, mostly C and D), double-blind, to milrinone or dobutamine. The primary composite (in-hospital death, resuscitated arrest, MCS or transplant, MI, stroke/TIA, RRT) occurred in 49% vs 54% (RR 0.90; 0.69–1.19), with no significant difference. Neither inotrope is superior, so choose according to the patient's profile.

**Why not the others:**
- A – in-hospital mortality was 37% vs 43% (RR 0.85), not significant.
- C – arrhythmias did not differ significantly between the two drugs.
- D – the trial was double-blind.
- E – it enrolled SCAI stages B–E, mainly C and D.

**Ref:** Mathew R et al., DOREMI, N Engl J Med 2021;385:516–525.

questions.stem: Regarding the 3CPO trial:
options: NIPPV was superior to CPAP for death or intubation.
Non-invasive ventilation did not improve acidosis or hypercapnia faster than oxygen.
Non-invasive ventilation reduced 7-day mortality.
It compared CPAP with high-flow nasal oxygen in acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – death or intubation at 7 days was 11.7% with CPAP vs 11.1% with NIPPV (NS); the two modes are equivalent.
- B (False) – NIV improved acidosis, hypercapnia, heart rate and dyspnoea **faster** than oxygen in the first hour.
- C (False) – 7-day mortality was 9.5% with NIV vs 9.8% with oxygen, with no difference.
- D (False) – 3CPO (1069 patients in UK emergency departments) compared standard oxygen, CPAP and NIPPV; high-flow nasal oxygen was not tested.

**EDIC trap:** NIV remains recommended (IIa, B2) despite neutral mortality, because it corrects physiology and symptoms faster.

**Ref:** Gray A et al., 3CPO, N Engl J Med 2008;359:142–151; Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457.

questions.stem: Which statement about the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines is correct?
options: Inotropes carry a class I recommendation in cardiogenic shock
HFmrEF is defined as LVEF 41–49 %
Heart failure with LVEF < 50 % is classified as HFrEF
Routine opioids are recommended in acute pulmonary oedema
The term "acute heart failure" was retained
questions.expl:
**Why C:** ESC 2026 abolished HFmrEF: HFrEF is now LVEF < 50% and HFpEF LVEF ≥ 50%. The guideline also renamed "acute" HF as "decompensated" HF, replaced GDMT with "foundational medical therapy" and introduced the B1/B2 levels of evidence.

**Why not the others:**
- A – inotropes are IIb, C (SBP < 90 mmHg with hypoperfusion that does not respond to standard treatment), at the lowest dose for the shortest time.
- B – HFmrEF (LVEF 41–49%) was the 2021 category and has been abolished.
- D – routine opioids are III, C because of respiratory depression.
- E – "acute HF" became "decompensated HF", because many patients deteriorate gradually.

**Ref:** Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457; McDonagh TA et al., Eur Heart J 2021;42:3599–3726.

questions.stem: Regarding levosimendan:
options: In SURVIVE, it significantly reduced 180-day mortality compared with dobutamine.
It sensitises troponin C to calcium.
It blocks ATP-sensitive potassium channels, causing vasoconstriction.
ESC 2026 notes it may be preferred over dobutamine in patients on beta-blockers.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – in SURVIVE (1327 ADHF patients), 180-day mortality was 26% vs 28% (HR 0.91; 0.74–1.13), with no significant difference.
- B (True) – it binds troponin C in a calcium-dependent way and increases contractility without raising intracellular Ca²⁺, so O₂ consumption rises little and relaxation is preserved.
- C (False) – it **opens** K-ATP channels in vascular smooth muscle, causing **vasodilation** (hence hypotension).
- D (True) – ESC 2026: levosimendan or a PDE-3 inhibitor may be preferred over dobutamine in patients on β-blockers, because their action does not depend on the β-receptor.

**EDIC trap:** the active metabolite OR-1896 (t½ ~80 h) prolongs the effect for days after a 24-hour infusion.

**Ref:** Mebazaa A et al., SURVIVE, JAMA 2007;297:1883–1891; Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with acute pulmonary oedema, BP 190/105 mmHg, RR 32/min, SpO₂ 86 % on oxygen. Besides NIV, the most appropriate initial drug therapy is:
options: Intravenous nitrate (vasodilator)
Intravenous morphine as routine
Dobutamine infusion
Milrinone
Norepinephrine
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Hypertensive acute pulmonary oedema is mainly fluid **redistribution** caused by high afterload, not total volume overload. IV nitrates quickly reduce preload and afterload; ESC 2026 suggests IV vasodilators as initial therapy when SBP > 110 mmHg (IIb, C), together with early NIV (IIa, B2). High, titrated doses are often needed.

**Why not the others:**
- B – routine opioids are III, C (respiratory depression, association with more mechanical ventilation).
- C – dobutamine is for hypoperfusion with low SBP; it raises HR and O₂ demand.
- D – milrinone is an inodilator for low-output states, not for hypertensive APO.
- E – norepinephrine would raise afterload even further.

**EDIC trap:** APO needs vasodilators first and fewer diuretics, while left-sided congestion from fluid retention needs diuretics first.

**Ref:** Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457; Gray A et al., N Engl J Med 2008;359:142–151.

questions.stem: Regarding decongestion in decompensated heart failure (ESC 2026):
options: IV loop diuretics are recommended for patients admitted with fluid overload.
Adding acetazolamide or hydrochlorothiazide may be considered in patients already on loop diuretics.
In ADVOR, acetazolamide did not increase successful decongestion.
SGLT2 inhibitors should be avoided during hospitalisation.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – IV loop diuretics are I, A for all patients with fluid overload. The initial IV dose is typically 1–2 × the daily oral dose (20–40 mg furosemide if diuretic-naïve).
- B (True) – IIa, B1: short-term IV acetazolamide (ADVOR) or oral hydrochlorothiazide (CLOROTIC) for persistent congestion despite a loop diuretic.
- C (False) – ADVOR (519 patients) **increased** successful decongestion at 3 days: 42.2% vs 30.5% (RR 1.46), with a shorter hospital stay.
- D (False) – SGLT2 inhibitors should be **started** during hospitalisation once the patient is stable (I, B1).

**EDIC trap:** ESC 2026 adds a IIb recommendation to guide diuretic dosing by urinary sodium.

**Ref:** Mullens W et al., ADVOR, N Engl J Med 2022;387:1185–1195; Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457.

questions.stem: The STRONG-HF trial showed that rapid up-titration of heart failure therapy before and shortly after discharge:
options: Increased mortality
Had no effect on outcomes
Was associated with fewer adverse events overall
Was tested only in outpatients with stable HF
Reduced death or heart failure readmission at 180 days
questions.expl:
**Why E:** STRONG-HF randomised 1078 patients hospitalised for acute HF to high-intensity care (rapid up-titration to full doses within 2 weeks of discharge, with 4 visits over 6 weeks monitoring clinical status, labs and NT-proBNP) or usual care. Death or HF readmission at 180 days was 15.2% vs 23.3% (adjusted RR 0.66), and the trial was stopped early for efficacy. ESC 2026 makes this class I, B2.

**Why not the others:**
- A – mortality was not increased.
- B – the primary outcome was significantly reduced.
- C – adverse events (hypotension, hyperkalaemia, renal dysfunction) were **more** frequent, while serious events were similar.
- D – patients were enrolled while hospitalised, before discharge.

**Ref:** Mebazaa A et al., STRONG-HF, Lancet 2022;400:1938–1952; Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457.

questions.stem: Regarding inotropes and vasopressors in cardiogenic shock:
options: Milrinone acts independently of beta-adrenergic receptors.
Dobutamine's effect may be attenuated by beta-blockade.
Inotropes have been shown to improve long-term survival.
Milrinone accumulates in renal failure.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – milrinone inhibits PDE-3 and raises cAMP downstream of the β-receptor, so it works despite β-blockade. It is an inodilator that lowers both PVR and SVR.
- B (True) – dobutamine is a β1-agonist, and competitive β-blockade blunts its effect, so higher doses are needed.
- C (False) – no inotrope has been shown to improve long-term survival, and prolonged use is associated with harm (arrhythmias, ischaemia). They are bridging drugs.
- D (True) – milrinone is renally excreted and accumulates in renal failure, causing hypotension and arrhythmias, so reduce the dose.

**EDIC trap:** inodilators (milrinone, levosimendan) often need norepinephrine to maintain MAP.

**Ref:** Mathew R et al., N Engl J Med 2021;385:516–525; Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457.

questions.stem: According to ESC 2026, non-invasive positive pressure ventilation in decompensated HF is suggested in patients with:
options: Only when PaCO₂ exceeds 8 kPa
Cardiogenic shock with SBP < 70 mmHg as first-line therapy
Only after failure of high-flow nasal oxygen
Respiratory distress (RR > 25/min, SpO₂ < 90 %), started early
Any dyspnoea, regardless of oxygenation
questions.expl:
**Why D:** ESC 2026 (table 9) suggests NIV in patients with respiratory distress (RR > 25/min, SpO₂ < 90%), started early to reduce the risk of intubation (IIa, B2). Positive pressure improves oxygenation and work of breathing and lowers LV preload and afterload.

**Why not the others:**
- A – there is no PaCO₂ threshold; hypoxaemic, normocapnic patients also benefit.
- B – in severe CS, positive pressure can worsen venous return and hypotension, and intubation is often needed instead.
- C – there is no requirement to try high-flow nasal oxygen first.
- E – NIV is not for dyspnoea alone; oxygen is given only if SpO₂ < 90% or PaO₂ < 60 mmHg (I, C).

**EDIC trap:** intubate if respiratory failure persists or progresses despite oxygen or NIV (I, C).

**Ref:** Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457; Gray A et al., N Engl J Med 2008;359:142–151.

questions.stem: Regarding the SURVIVE and SOAP II trials:
options: SOAP II showed significantly lower overall 28-day mortality with dopamine.
SURVIVE compared levosimendan with dobutamine.
SOAP II found more arrhythmic events with dopamine than norepinephrine.
Levosimendan produced a greater reduction in BNP.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – 28-day mortality was 52.5% with dopamine vs 48.5% with norepinephrine (NS), and dopamine was associated with higher mortality in the CS subgroup.
- B (True) – SURVIVE compared levosimendan with dobutamine in 1327 patients with ADHF who needed inotropic support.
- C (True) – arrhythmias occurred in 24.1% vs 12.4%, mostly AF, and more patients stopped dopamine because of them.
- D (True) – levosimendan lowered BNP more, but caused more AF and hypokalaemia and did not improve survival.

**EDIC trap:** a greater fall in a biomarker does not mean better survival.

**Ref:** De Backer D et al., SOAP II, N Engl J Med 2010;362:779–789; Mebazaa A et al., SURVIVE, JAMA 2007;297:1883–1891.

open.q: A 72-year-old woman presents with acute pulmonary oedema, BP 190/105 mmHg, RR 32/min and SpO₂ 86%. Outline your management according to ESC 2026 and the supporting evidence.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Recognise APO: mainly fluid redistribution with ↑ afterload, not total volume overload.
- O₂ for SpO₂ < 90% (I, C); early NIV (CPAP or NIPPV) for RR > 25/min and SpO₂ < 90% (IIa, B2).
- 3CPO: NIV did not reduce mortality but improved dyspnoea, acidosis and hypercapnia faster; CPAP = NIPPV.
- IV vasodilators (nitrates) since SBP > 110 mmHg (IIb, C) – fewer intubations; caution with severe AS/RV infarction.
- IV loop diuretic if fluid overloaded (I, A) – but fewer diuretics needed than in left-sided DHF.
- No routine opioids (III, C).
- Intubate if respiratory failure persists/progresses despite O₂ or NIV (I, C).

open.q: Compare dobutamine, milrinone and levosimendan and explain how you would choose between them in a hypoperfused patient on chronic beta-blocker therapy.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Dobutamine: β1 agonist; arrhythmias, ischaemia; effect attenuated by β-blockade.
- Milrinone: PDE-3 inhibitor acting independently of β-receptors; inodilator, ↓ PVR; hypotension; accumulates in renal failure.
- Levosimendan: Ca²⁺ sensitisation of troponin C + K-ATP opening; long-acting metabolite; hypotension, hypokalaemia, AF.
- DOREMI: milrinone = dobutamine (composite 49 vs 54%, NS); SURVIVE: levosimendan = dobutamine (180-d mortality 26 vs 28%).
- ESC 2026: levosimendan or PDE-3 inhibitor may be preferred over dobutamine in patients on β-blockers.
- Inodilators often need norepinephrine to counter hypotension.
- Inotropes do not improve survival – use for SBP < 90 with hypoperfusion (IIb, C), lowest dose, shortest time.

title: W07 · D5 – Right heart failure and pulmonary hypertension in the ICU

questions.stem: According to the 2022 ESC/ERS guidelines, pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension is defined as:
options: mPAP ≥ 25 mmHg, PAWP ≤ 15 mmHg, PVR ≥ 3 WU
sPAP > 40 mmHg on echocardiography
mPAP > 30 mmHg irrespective of PAWP
mPAP > 20 mmHg, PAWP ≤ 15 mmHg, PVR > 2 WU
mPAP > 20 mmHg, PAWP > 15 mmHg, PVR ≤ 2 WU
questions.expl:
**Why D:** ESC/ERS 2022 defines PH as mPAP > 20 mmHg at rest on right heart catheterisation. Pre-capillary PH also requires PAWP ≤ 15 mmHg and PVR > 2 WU. These thresholds were lowered from mPAP ≥ 25 mmHg and PVR > 3 WU on the basis of the upper limit of normal in healthy subjects.

**Why not the others:**
- A – this is the older (2015-era) definition.
- B – echocardiography estimates the probability of PH (e.g. peak TR velocity > 2.8 m/s) but cannot define it; diagnosis requires RHC.
- C – no such threshold exists, and PAWP is needed to separate pre- from post-capillary PH.
- E – this is isolated post-capillary PH (IpcPH).

**Ref:** Humbert M et al., 2022 ESC/ERS PH Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3618–3731.

questions.stem: Regarding ventricular interdependence:
options: Volume loading of a failing, dilated RV reliably increases cardiac output.
It can reduce left ventricular filling and stroke volume despite normal LV contractility.
Systemic hypotension may worsen RV function by reducing RV coronary perfusion.
A pressure-overloaded right ventricle shifts the septum towards the left ventricle.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – volume loading a dilated, failing RV raises wall tension, worsens TR and pushes the septum to the left, compressing the LV. CO may **fall**, and most patients need a negative balance.
- B (True) – diastolic interdependence (shared septum, stiff pericardium) reduces LV compliance and filling, so stroke volume falls despite normal LV contractility. PCWP may even be falsely high.
- C (True) – RV coronary perfusion pressure ≈ aortic pressure − RV pressure. Hypotension causes RV ischaemia, which closes the vicious circle.
- D (True) – leftward septal shift gives paradoxical septal motion and a D-shaped LV in the short axis.

**EDIC trap:** in acute RV failure, fluids "to raise CO" are mostly ineffective and potentially harmful.

**Ref:** Vieillard-Baron A et al., Intensive Care Med 2018;44:774–790.

questions.stem: Which factor was NOT part of the risk score for acute cor pulmonale in ARDS (Mekontso Dessap, ICM 2016)?
options: PaCO₂ ≥ 48 mmHg
Age > 65 years
Pneumonia as the cause of ARDS
PaO₂/FiO₂ < 150 mmHg
Driving pressure ≥ 18 cmH₂O
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In 752 patients with moderate/severe ARDS on protective ventilation, acute cor pulmonale occurred in ~22%. Four independent risk factors formed the score: pneumonia as the cause of ARDS, driving pressure ≥ 18 cmH₂O, PaO₂/FiO₂ < 150 mmHg and PaCO₂ ≥ 48 mmHg. ACP prevalence rose steeply with each point, and severe ACP was associated with higher mortality. Age was not part of the score.

**Why not the others:**
- A – PaCO₂ ≥ 48 mmHg is in the score; hypercapnia raises PVR.
- C – pneumonia is in the score (direct lung and vascular injury, hypoxic vasoconstriction).
- D – PaO₂/FiO₂ < 150 mmHg is in the score.
- E – driving pressure ≥ 18 cmH₂O is in the score and is the main modifiable factor.

**Ref:** Mekontso Dessap A et al., Intensive Care Med 2016;42:862–870.

questions.stem: Regarding inhaled nitric oxide:
options: It acts predominantly in ventilated lung units, improving V/Q matching.
It causes marked systemic hypotension.
It can be stopped abruptly without risk of rebound pulmonary hypertension.
It improves survival in ARDS.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – iNO reaches only ventilated alveoli and dilates the vessels supplying them. This lowers PVR and redirects flow towards ventilated units, improving V/Q matching.
- B (False) – it is rapidly bound and inactivated by haemoglobin (forming methaemoglobin and nitrate), so it has negligible systemic effect.
- C (False) – abrupt withdrawal can cause rebound PH, hypoxaemia and RV collapse, so wean gradually.
- D (False) – in ARDS, iNO improves oxygenation only transiently and does not improve survival (it may increase AKI). It is not used routinely.

**EDIC trap:** in severe LV dysfunction, iNO can worsen pulmonary oedema by increasing flow into a high-pressure LA.

**Ref:** Gebistorf F et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;(6):CD002787; Vieillard-Baron A et al., Intensive Care Med 2018;44:774–790.

questions.stem: A patient with known pulmonary arterial hypertension is admitted with pneumonia, BP 82/50 mmHg, CVP 18 mmHg, lactate 3.5 mmol/L and a dilated RV with D-sign. The most appropriate initial haemodynamic intervention is:
options: Urgent intubation to reduce work of breathing
1 L crystalloid bolus
Norepinephrine to restore systemic pressure, with consideration of an inotrope
Intravenous nitroglycerin
Beta-blocker to control heart rate
questions.expl:
**Why C:** This is decompensated PAH with shock (BP 82/50 mmHg, lactate 3.5 mmol/L), a high CVP and a D-sign. The priority is to restore systemic pressure, which preserves RV coronary perfusion and breaks the vicious circle. ESC/ERS 2022 advises keeping MAP > 60 mmHg with norepinephrine or vasopressin, adding an inotrope for low output, treating the trigger and aiming for a negative balance.

**Why not the others:**
- A – intubation (induction plus positive pressure) carries a high risk of circulatory collapse and should be avoided whenever possible.
- B – with CVP 18 mmHg and a dilated RV, more fluid worsens septal shift and LV underfilling.
- D – IV nitroglycerin is a systemic vasodilator that lowers BP and RV perfusion.
- E – with a fixed RV stroke volume, CO depends on heart rate, so a β-blocker would lower output.

**Ref:** Humbert M et al., 2022 ESC/ERS PH Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3618–3731; Hoeper MM, Granton J, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2011;184:1114–1124.

questions.stem: According to the ESC/ERS 2022 guidelines on ICU management of PAH with right heart failure:
options: Intubation should be avoided whenever possible.
Most patients require a positive fluid balance.
VA-ECMO is never used in PAH.
Norepinephrine or vasopressin may be required for persistent hypotension.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – intubation in severe PH/RV failure carries a high risk of collapse and death. If it is unavoidable, start a vasopressor before a haemodynamically gentle induction.
- B (False) – most patients need a **negative** balance (diuretics, possibly RRT or ultrafiltration) to reduce RV dilatation and TR.
- C (False) – VA-ECMO is used as a bridge to transplantation in irreversible failure, or to recovery when the trigger is reversible, decided case by case.
- D (True) – norepinephrine or vasopressin is used for persistent hypotension. Vasopressin raises SVR with little effect on PVR.

**Ref:** Humbert M et al., 2022 ESC/ERS PH Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3618–3731; Hoeper MM, Granton J, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2011;184:1114–1124.

questions.stem: In a mechanically ventilated patient, pulmonary vascular resistance is lowest at:
options: Lung volumes associated with atelectasis
Maximal PEEP
Functional residual capacity
Total lung capacity
Residual volume
questions.expl:
**Why C:** PVR is the sum of the resistances of alveolar vessels, which are compressed as the lungs inflate, and extra-alveolar vessels, which narrow at low volumes as radial traction is lost and hypoxic vasoconstriction sets in. The result is a "U"-shaped curve with its lowest point at FRC.

**Why not the others:**
- A – in atelectasis, extra-alveolar vessels collapse and hypoxic vasoconstriction raises PVR.
- B – maximal PEEP overdistends the alveoli and compresses alveolar capillaries, raising PVR and RV afterload.
- D – at TLC, compression of alveolar vessels is maximal.
- E – at residual volume, extra-alveolar vessels narrow and hypoxic vasoconstriction increases PVR.

**EDIC trap:** both too little and too much PEEP harm the RV, so titrate it and check the RV on echo.

**Ref:** Vieillard-Baron A et al., Intensive Care Med 2018;44:774–790; Hoeper MM, Granton J, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2011;184:1114–1124.

questions.stem: "RV-protective" ventilation in ARDS includes:
options: Maximising PEEP to the highest tolerated level
Avoiding hypercapnia
Prone positioning
Limiting driving pressure
questions.expl:
- A (False) – excessive PEEP overdistends alveoli, compresses alveolar vessels and raises PVR and RV afterload. Titrate PEEP to recruit without overdistension.
- B (True) – hypercapnia and acidosis cause pulmonary vasoconstriction; target PaCO₂ < 48 mmHg (~6.4 kPa).
- C (True) – prone positioning recruits lung, lowers driving pressure and PaCO₂, and relieves acute cor pulmonale.
- D (True) – driving pressure ≥ 18 cmH₂O is an ACP risk factor, so keep it < 18 cmH₂O and limit plateau pressure.

**EDIC trap:** for refractory ACP, VV-ECMO allows ultra-protective ventilation and correction of hypercapnia.

**Ref:** Mekontso Dessap A et al., Intensive Care Med 2016;42:862–870; Vieillard-Baron A et al., Intensive Care Med 2018;44:774–790.

questions.stem: Which echocardiographic finding is most typical of RV pressure overload?
options: Paradoxical septal motion with a D-shaped LV in short axis
Small RV with hyperdynamic LV
Isolated LV apical akinesia
Collapsible inferior vena cava
Mitral valve systolic anterior motion
questions.expl:
**Why A:** In RV pressure overload, RV pressure approaches or exceeds LV pressure, which flattens the septum (most at end-systole). This produces a D-shaped LV in the parasternal short axis with paradoxical septal motion. Other findings are RV/LV > 1 in the apical 4-chamber view, low TAPSE and a dilated, non-collapsing IVC.

**Why not the others:**
- B – a small RV with a hyperdynamic LV suggests hypovolaemia.
- C – isolated apical akinesia suggests LAD infarction or takotsubo.
- D – RV failure with high RAP gives a dilated IVC with little respiratory variation.
- E – SAM of the mitral valve indicates dynamic LVOT obstruction (HCM, hypovolaemia, inotropes, takotsubo).

**EDIC trap:** septal flattening mainly in diastole suggests RV **volume** overload.

**Ref:** Vieillard-Baron A et al., Intensive Care Med 2018;44:774–790; Humbert M et al., 2022 ESC/ERS PH Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3618–3731.

questions.stem: Regarding acute right ventricular failure in the ICU:
options: Venous congestion does not affect liver or kidney function.
The right ventricle tolerates acute increases in afterload better than volume load.
Pulmonary embolism and RV infarction should be excluded in right-sided decompensated HF.
Hypoxaemia, hypercapnia and acidosis increase pulmonary vascular resistance.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – venous congestion causes congestive hepatopathy (↑ bilirubin, transaminases) and congestive nephropathy, because high renal venous pressure lowers renal perfusion pressure.
- B (False) – the opposite is true: the thin-walled RV tolerates volume well but an acute rise in afterload (e.g. PE) poorly, and acutely it cannot generate a high mPAP.
- C (True) – ESC 2026: in decompensated right-sided HF, exclude PE and RV infarction, which have specific reperfusion treatments.
- D (True) – hypoxaemia, hypercapnia and acidosis all raise PVR, so correcting them is central to RV-protective care.

**Ref:** Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457; Vieillard-Baron A et al., Intensive Care Med 2018;44:774–790.

open.q: A patient with known PAH is admitted with pneumonia, BP 82/50 mmHg, CVP 18 mmHg, lactate 3.5 mmol/L and a dilated RV with D-sign. Outline your management and explain the physiological rationale.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Vicious circle: ↑ RV afterload → dilatation, TR → ↓ LV filling → hypotension → ↓ RV coronary perfusion → ischaemia.
- Treat the trigger (pneumonia – antibiotics; check arrhythmia, anaemia, interrupted PAH therapy).
- Restore systemic pressure – MAP > 60 mmHg with norepinephrine or vasopressin (vasopressin raises SVR without marked rise in PVR).
- Avoid fluid boluses – dilated RV compresses the LV; most need negative balance (diuretics, RRT/ultrafiltration).
- Inotrope for low output (dobutamine, milrinone; levosimendan alternative), with vasopressor if inodilator causes hypotension.
- Reduce RV afterload: correct hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, acidosis; inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (iNO, inhaled prostacyclins).
- Maintain sinus rhythm/AV synchrony; avoid intubation if possible (if needed: vasopressor running before induction, gentle induction).
- Consider VA-ECMO as a bridge to transplantation or recovery.

open.q: A ventilated ARDS patient has driving pressure 20 cmH₂O, PaCO₂ 55 mmHg and a D-sign on echo. Explain why the RV is failing and describe RV-protective ventilation.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Acute cor pulmonale occurs in ~22% of moderate/severe ARDS; this patient has risk factors (DP ≥ 18, PaCO₂ ≥ 48).
- Positive pressure ↑ RV afterload and ↓ preload; hypercapnia and acidosis ↑ PVR.
- PVR–lung volume relationship is U-shaped – lowest at FRC; atelectasis and hyperinflation both raise PVR.
- Limit plateau and driving pressure (target < 18 cmH₂O).
- Keep PaCO₂ < 48 mmHg; correct hypoxaemia.
- Titrate PEEP – enough to recruit, avoid overdistension; do not simply increase PEEP or give fluids.
- Prone positioning unloads the RV; consider VV-ECMO for refractory ACP; vasopressor to maintain RV perfusion.

title: W07 · Saturday – weekly review: Cardio I

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with anterior STEMI has BP 88/56 mmHg and HR 112/min, warm extremities, normal mentation, urine output 1 mL/kg/h and lactate 1.4 mmol/L. His SCAI SHOCK stage is:
options: C
A
E
B
D
questions.expl:
**Why D:** The patient is hypotensive (88/56 mmHg) and tachycardic (112/min) but well perfused: warm extremities, normal mentation, urine output 1 mL/kg/h and lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Haemodynamic instability without hypoperfusion is SCAI stage B (Beginning), which is option D.

**Why not the others:**
- A – stage C needs hypoperfusion (lactate ≥ 2, cold periphery, oliguria) that requires intervention.
- B – stage A (At risk) has no haemodynamic instability, but this patient is hypotensive and tachycardic.
- C – stage E means collapse, CPR or ECMO, or lactate ≥ 8 mmol/L.
- E – stage D means hypoperfusion that worsens despite initial therapy.

**EDIC trap:** stage B is a warning stage with a high risk of progression; reassess perfusion often.

**Ref:** Naidu SS et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2022;79:933–946.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman is in AMI-related cardiogenic shock with three-vessel disease. Regarding revascularisation:
options: Emergency CABG has no role, even if coronary anatomy is unsuitable for PCI.
All significant lesions should be treated during the index procedure.
CULPRIT-SHOCK showed a lower 30-day rate of death or RRT with culprit-only PCI.
Immediate coronary angiography with PCI of the infarct-related artery is recommended.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – emergency CABG is recommended in AMI-CS when the coronary anatomy is unsuitable for PCI.
- B (False) – immediate multivessel PCI increased death/RRT in CULPRIT-SHOCK, and routine immediate non-IRA PCI in CS is III, B. Non-culprit lesions are staged.
- C (True) – 45.9% vs 55.4% (RR 0.83), driven by mortality (43.3% vs 51.6%) and sustained at 1 year.
- D (True) – immediate angiography with PCI of the infarct-related artery is class I, based on the SHOCK trial (lower 6-month mortality).

**Ref:** Byrne RA et al., 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720–3826; Thiele H et al., N Engl J Med 2017;377:2419–2432.

questions.stem: Five days after an inferior STEMI treated late, a patient becomes hypotensive with a new harsh holosystolic murmur. PAC shows SpO₂ 62 % in the right atrium and 84 % in the pulmonary artery. The diagnosis is:
options: Acute mitral regurgitation
Ventricular septal rupture
Free wall rupture
Pulmonary embolism
Right ventricular infarction
questions.expl:
**Why B:** O₂ saturation rises from 62% in the RA to 84% in the PA, a step-up of > 20%. That means oxygenated blood is entering the right heart between the RA and the PA, i.e. a left-to-right shunt at ventricular level: ventricular septal rupture. Together with a new harsh holosystolic murmur and shock 5 days after a late-treated inferior MI (basal septum, worse prognosis), the diagnosis is clear. Confirm with colour-Doppler echo, bridge with IABP/MCS, then close.

**Why not the others:**
- A – acute MR causes large v waves without a saturation step-up, and its murmur is often soft.
- C – free wall rupture causes tamponade or PEA, with no murmur or step-up.
- D – PE causes no shunt, so saturation does not rise from RA to PA.
- E – RV infarction causes high RAP and clear lungs, with no murmur or step-up.

**Ref:** Damluji AA et al., Circulation 2021;144:e16–e35.

questions.stem: Regarding mechanical circulatory support trials in infarct-related cardiogenic shock:
options: Both ECLS-SHOCK and DanGer Shock showed more bleeding complications with the device.
ECLS-SHOCK showed no reduction in 30-day mortality with early routine VA-ECMO.
DanGer Shock showed lower 180-day mortality with a microaxial flow pump in STEMI-related shock.
IABP-SHOCK II showed no reduction in 30-day mortality with IABP.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ECLS-SHOCK: BARC 3–5 bleeding 23.4% vs 9.6%. DanGer Shock: moderate or severe bleeding 21.8% vs 11.9%.
- B (True) – 30-day mortality was 47.8% vs 49.0% (RR 0.98), with more bleeding and vascular complications.
- C (True) – 180-day mortality was 45.8% vs 58.5% (HR 0.74) in STEMI-CS with LVEF < 45%, excluding comatose OHCA survivors.
- D (True) – 30-day mortality was 39.7% vs 41.3% (RR 0.96), with no difference at 6 years either.

**EDIC trap:** only DanGer Shock was positive, in a highly selected population and at the cost of more complications.

**Ref:** Thiele H et al., N Engl J Med 2012;367:1287–1296 and 2023;389:1286–1297; Møller JE et al., N Engl J Med 2024;390:1382–1393.

questions.stem: A patient on peripheral femoral VA-ECMO for refractory cardiogenic shock develops progressive pulmonary oedema. The arterial line shows a flat trace without pulsatility, and echo shows a closed aortic valve with spontaneous contrast in the LV. The most appropriate next step is:
options: Increase ECMO flow to maximum
Convert to VV-ECMO immediately
Give a fluid bolus
Increase PEEP to 20 cmH₂O and continue unchanged
Start an inotrope and consider LV unloading (IABP or microaxial pump)
questions.expl:
**Why E:** A flat arterial trace, a closed aortic valve, spontaneous contrast in the LV and worsening pulmonary oedema indicate LV distension, caused by the afterload that retrograde flow imposes on peripheral VA-ECMO. The steps are an inotrope to open the valve, ECMO flow reduced to the minimum that maintains perfusion, afterload reduction and, if distension persists, LV unloading with an IABP, microaxial pump ("ECPELLA") or an LA vent. This is urgent because of the risk of thrombus.

**Why not the others:**
- A – higher flow raises afterload further and worsens distension.
- B – VV-ECMO gives no circulatory support in refractory CS.
- C – fluid increases preload and worsens distension.
- D – PEEP may ease the oedema but does not address the cause, and leaving things unchanged allows thrombus to form.

**Ref:** Lorusso R et al., ELSO VA-ECMO interim guidelines, ASAIO J 2021;67:827–844; Kim MC et al., Circulation 2023;148:1570–1581.

questions.stem: A patient on femoral VA-ECMO with severe lung injury has a recovering left ventricle. Regarding differential (Harlequin) hypoxaemia:
options: Increasing FiO₂ on the oxygenator corrects cerebral hypoxaemia.
Conversion to V-AV ECMO is a possible solution.
Oxygenation should be monitored from a femoral arterial line.
The upper body, including the brain and coronaries, may be perfused by poorly oxygenated blood.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – oxygenator FiO₂ affects only ECMO blood, which already goes to the lower body. The upper body receives native cardiac output from the failing lungs.
- B (True) – in V-AV ECMO, an additional return cannula in the internal jugular vein sends oxygenated blood through the RA, lungs and LV to the aortic root. Other options are optimising ventilation or changing the cannulation site.
- C (False) – monitor from the **right radial** artery (ABG, right-hand SpO₂) and with cerebral NIRS. Femoral blood mainly reflects the ECMO circuit.
- D (True) – depending on the mixing zone, the coronaries, carotids and right subclavian artery receive poorly oxygenated native output.

**Ref:** Lorusso R et al., ELSO VA-ECMO interim guidelines, ASAIO J 2021;67:827–844.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old on long-term bisoprolol is admitted with low-output heart failure (SBP 92 mmHg, cold extremities, lactate 3 mmol/L) and remains hypoperfused after cautious fluids. According to ESC 2026, which inotrope may be preferred over dobutamine?
options: Isoprenaline
Dopamine
Vasopressin
Phenylephrine
Levosimendan or a PDE-3 inhibitor
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Long-term β-blockade (bisoprolol) blunts β1-agonists such as dobutamine. Levosimendan (troponin C sensitisation plus K-ATP vasodilation) and PDE-3 inhibitors such as milrinone (cAMP rise downstream of the receptor) work independently of the β-receptor, and ESC 2026 notes they may be preferred. Both are inodilators, so with SBP 92 mmHg norepinephrine is often needed and a bolus is usually omitted.

**Why not the others:**
- A – isoprenaline is a non-selective β-agonist that β-blockade blunts just as much, and it causes tachycardia and vasodilation.
- B – dopamine also depends on the β-receptor and caused more arrhythmias, with higher mortality in the CS subgroup of SOAP II.
- C – vasopressin is a vasopressor with no inotropic effect.
- D – phenylephrine is a pure α1-agonist that raises afterload and can lower CO.

**Ref:** Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457; Mebazaa A et al., JAMA 2007;297:1883–1891.

questions.stem: Regarding trials of inotropes:
options: In SURVIVE, 180-day mortality did not differ significantly.
DOREMI compared milrinone with dobutamine in cardiogenic shock.
SURVIVE compared levosimendan with dobutamine in acute decompensated heart failure.
DOREMI found a significant mortality benefit with milrinone.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 180-day mortality was 26% vs 28% (HR 0.91), not significant.
- B (True) – DOREMI was a double-blind trial in 192 CS patients (SCAI B–E).
- C (True) – SURVIVE enrolled 1327 patients with ADHF who needed inotropic support.
- D (False) – in-hospital mortality was 37% vs 43% (RR 0.85, NS), and the primary composite was 49% vs 54% (NS).

**EDIC trap:** no inotrope has shown a survival benefit over another; choose according to the haemodynamic profile and β-blocker use.

**Ref:** Mathew R et al., N Engl J Med 2021;385:516–525; Mebazaa A et al., JAMA 2007;297:1883–1891.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman presents with acute pulmonary oedema, BP 200/110 mmHg, RR 34/min, SpO₂ 84 %, pH 7.24, PaCO₂ 7.5 kPa, alert and cooperative. The best initial respiratory support is:
options: Heliox
Non-invasive ventilation (CPAP or NIPPV)
Intravenous morphine and oxygen
Immediate intubation
Low-flow oxygen 2 L/min only
questions.expl:
**Why B:** This is hypertensive APO with hypoxaemia, tachypnoea and respiratory acidosis (pH 7.24, PaCO₂ 7.5 kPa) in an alert, cooperative patient, so NIV (CPAP or NIPPV) is indicated. In 3CPO, NIV corrected acidosis, hypercapnia and dyspnoea faster than oxygen, and CPAP and NIPPV were equivalent. ESC 2026 suggests early NIV (IIa, B2). Add IV nitrates for the hypertension, and intubate if NIV fails.

**Why not the others:**
- A – heliox has no role in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
- C – routine morphine is III, C and risks respiratory depression in a hypercapnic patient.
- D – an alert, cooperative patient deserves an NIV trial; intubation is for NIV failure, coma or exhaustion.
- E – low-flow oxygen is inadequate with SpO₂ 84% and does not reduce work of breathing.

**Ref:** Gray A et al., N Engl J Med 2008;359:142–151; Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457.

questions.stem: Regarding the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines:
options: The term "decompensated heart failure" replaces "acute heart failure".
HFmrEF remains a separate category.
Vasopressors, preferably norepinephrine, may be considered in cardiogenic shock.
Intensive rapid up-titration of foundational therapy before and after discharge is recommended.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – "decompensated HF" replaces "acute HF", because many patients deteriorate gradually rather than suddenly.
- B (False) – HFmrEF was abolished: LVEF < 50% is HFrEF and ≥ 50% is HFpEF.
- C (True) – norepinephrine is the preferred vasopressor (IIb, C); dopamine causes more arrhythmias.
- D (True) – rapid up-titration of foundational therapy is I, B2, based on STRONG-HF (death or HF readmission at 180 days 15.2% vs 23.3%).

**Ref:** Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457; Mebazaa A et al., Lancet 2022;400:1938–1952.

questions.stem: A patient with ARDS from pneumonia has driving pressure 19 cmH₂O, PaO₂/FiO₂ 110 mmHg and PaCO₂ 52 mmHg (7 kPa). Echo shows a dilated RV with paradoxical septal motion. Which measure is most likely to help the right ventricle?
options: Fluid bolus of 1 L
Increase PEEP to maximal tolerated values
Start a beta-blocker
Prone positioning with reduction of driving pressure and PaCO₂
Permissive hypercapnia with PaCO₂ target 8 kPa
questions.expl:
**Why D:** All four ACP risk factors are present: pneumonia, driving pressure ≥ 18 (19 cmH₂O), PaO₂/FiO₂ < 150 (110 mmHg) and PaCO₂ ≥ 48 (52 mmHg). A dilated RV with paradoxical septal motion confirms acute cor pulmonale. Prone positioning recruits lung, lowers driving pressure and PaCO₂ and unloads the RV; combine it with a lower tidal volume and correction of hypercapnia (e.g. less dead space). Consider VV-ECMO if this is not enough.

**Why not the others:**
- A – fluids worsen RV dilatation and septal shift.
- B – maximal PEEP overdistends the lung and raises PVR.
- C – a β-blocker lowers contractility and heart rate, and so CO in RV failure.
- E – a PaCO₂ of 8 kPa (60 mmHg) worsens pulmonary vasoconstriction; the target is < 48 mmHg (~6.4 kPa).

**Ref:** Mekontso Dessap A et al., Intensive Care Med 2016;42:862–870; Guérin C et al., PROSEVA, N Engl J Med 2013;368:2159–2168.

questions.stem: Regarding pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure:
options: In PAH with right heart failure, intubation should be avoided whenever possible.
Group 2 PH is associated with lung disease and/or hypoxia.
Pulmonary hypertension is defined by mPAP > 20 mmHg (ESC/ERS 2022).
Isolated post-capillary PH has PAWP > 15 mmHg and PVR > 2 WU.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ESC/ERS 2022 advises avoiding intubation whenever possible. If it is unavoidable, start a vasopressor before induction.
- B (False) – group 2 is left heart disease (the most common group); lung disease and/or hypoxia is group 3.
- C (True) – PH is defined as mPAP > 20 mmHg at rest on right heart catheterisation (previously ≥ 25 mmHg).
- D (False) – isolated post-capillary PH has PAWP > 15 mmHg and PVR ≤ 2 WU. A PVR > 2 WU defines combined post- and pre-capillary PH.

**Ref:** Humbert M et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3618–3731.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with inferior STEMI is hypotensive (82/50 mmHg) with distended neck veins and clear lungs. ST elevation is present in V4R. Which initial treatment should be avoided?
options: Temporary pacing for complete AV block
Cautious fluid challenge
Primary PCI of the right coronary artery
Dobutamine if hypoperfusion persists
Intravenous nitrates
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Inferior STEMI with hypotension, raised JVP, clear lungs and ST elevation in V4R is RV infarction. The ischaemic RV depends on preload, so nitrates (and diuretics), which dilate veins, can cause profound hypotension and should be avoided.

**Why not the others:**
- A – AV block is common with proximal RCA occlusion; pacing (ideally AV-sequential) restores rate and atrial kick.
- B – a cautious fluid challenge is reasonable if the patient is not volume-overloaded; avoid large volumes.
- C – primary PCI of the RCA is the key treatment of the cause.
- D – dobutamine supports RV contractility if hypoperfusion persists after preload is optimised.

**EDIC trap:** record right-sided leads in every inferior STEMI before giving nitrates.

**Ref:** Byrne RA et al., 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720–3826.

questions.stem: Regarding diagnostics in cardiogenic shock:
options: ESICM 2025 considers echocardiography the first-line tool to determine the type of shock.
Mixed venous saturation is typically low.
Large v waves on PCWP tracing suggest acute mitral regurgitation.
A lactate ≥ 2 mmol/L is required for SCAI stage B.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ESICM 2025 recommends echocardiography as the first-line tool to identify the type of shock.
- B (True) – low CO increases O₂ extraction, so SvO₂ is typically low (unlike septic shock).
- C (True) – large v waves reflect regurgitant flow into a non-compliant LA. They are suggestive, not specific (also seen in VSR or a stiff LA).
- D (False) – stage B has **normal** lactate; lactate ≥ 2 mmol/L with hypoperfusion is stage C.

**Ref:** Monnet X et al., Intensive Care Med 2025;51:1971–2012; Naidu SS et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2022;79:933–946.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with anterior STEMI and cardiogenic shock (LVEF 25 %, lactate 5 mmol/L) is awake and was not resuscitated. He remains hypoperfused despite norepinephrine after primary PCI. According to ESC 2026, which option has class IIa support?
options: Dopamine as first-line vasopressor
No mechanical support should be considered
Routine VA-ECMO for all AMI-CS
Microaxial flow pump
Routine IABP
questions.expl:
**Why D:** An awake, non-resuscitated patient with anterior STEMI-CS, LVEF 25% and lactate 5 mmol/L despite norepinephrine after PCI matches the DanGer Shock population (180-day mortality 45.8% vs 58.5%). ESC 2026 gives a microaxial flow pump IIa, B1 in selected STEMI-CS with LV dysfunction and no risk of hypoxic brain injury. Weigh this against bleeding, limb ischaemia and RRT, and involve the shock team (I, C).

**Why not the others:**
- A – dopamine causes more arrhythmias; norepinephrine is the preferred vasopressor (IIb, C).
- B – this patient fits the only population with a proven mortality benefit from MCS.
- C – routine VA-ECMO in unselected AMI-CS is III, B1 (ECLS-SHOCK).
- E – routine IABP is III, B1 (IABP-SHOCK II).

**Ref:** Møller JE et al., N Engl J Med 2024;390:1382–1393; Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457.

title: W08 · D1 – Arrhythmias in the ICU: AF, VT/electrical storm, bradyarrhythmias

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with septic shock on noradrenaline develops new atrial fibrillation at 165/min. BP falls to 70/40 mmHg with rising lactate despite adequate filling. According to ERC 2025, the most appropriate immediate step is:
options: IV digoxin loading
Synchronised cardioversion with an initial shock at maximum defibrillator output
Synchronised cardioversion starting at 50 J with stepwise escalation
Wait 48 hours for spontaneous conversion
IV diltiazem bolus
questions.expl:
**Why B:** AF with shock, ischaemia or acute heart failure is an indication for emergency synchronised electrical cardioversion (ESC 2024, class I C). ERC 2025 changed the energy advice for AF: the first synchronised shock should be delivered at **maximum defibrillator output** instead of escalating, because the first-shock success is higher and repeated shocks are avoided. If it fails, give amiodarone 300 mg IV and shock again.

**Why not the others:**
- A – digoxin acts slowly (hours) and does not treat shock caused by the arrhythmia.
- C – a low start with stepwise escalation is the old approach; ERC 2025 recommends maximum energy for AF (70–120 J is for flutter/SVT).
- D – "wait-and-see" within 48 h is only for haemodynamically stable patients.
- E – diltiazem is negatively inotropic and a vasodilator, so it would worsen the hypotension.

**Ref:** Soar J et al., ERC Guidelines 2025 Adult ALS, Resuscitation 2025;215:110769; Van Gelder IC et al., 2024 ESC AF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3314–3414.

questions.stem: Regarding rate control of atrial fibrillation according to the 2024 ESC guidelines:
options: Lenient rate control with a resting heart rate < 110/min should be considered as the initial target.
Diltiazem and verapamil should be avoided when LVEF is ≤ 40 %.
Digoxin can be used irrespective of left ventricular ejection fraction.
In haemodynamic instability, IV amiodarone, digoxin, esmolol or landiolol may be considered.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ESC 2024 recommends lenient rate control (resting HR < 110/min) as the initial target (IIa B), based on RACE II.
- B (True) – non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are negatively inotropic and can cause decompensation in HFrEF, so they are used only if LVEF > 40%.
