- B (True) – TTM compared 33 °C with 36 °C (950 patients) and found mortality of 50% vs 48%, not significant.
- C (True) – arrhythmias with haemodynamic compromise were 24% vs 17% with hypothermia in TTM2.
- D (True) – the TTM2 control arm was normothermia with active fever treatment (device at ≥ 37.8 °C, target 37.5 °C), not "no temperature management".

**Ref:** Nielsen N, et al. TTM, N Engl J Med 2013; Lascarrou JB, et al. HYPERION, N Engl J Med 2019; Dankiewicz J, et al. TTM2, N Engl J Med 2021.

questions.stem: A comatose patient 18 hours after ROSC has a core temperature of 38.3 °C. According to ERC-ESICM 2025, the most appropriate action is:
options: No action until temperature exceeds 39 °C
Actively treat the fever, targeting ≤ 37.5 °C, with a feedback-controlled device if needed
Start empirical antibiotics as the only measure
Cool to 32 °C for 48 hours
Give 30 mL/kg of cold saline
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Fever after cardiac arrest is common and is associated with worse neurological outcome. ERC-ESICM 2025 recommends **active fever prevention with a target of ≤ 37.5 °C** for 36–72 h in patients who remain comatose. Use antipyretics, and a surface or endovascular device with feedback and continuous core temperature monitoring if needed.

**Why not the others:**
- A – waiting for > 39 °C allows harmful hyperthermia.
- C – antibiotics may be needed if infection is suspected, but they do not control temperature.
- D – cooling to 32 °C for 48 h is not recommended after TTM2.
- E – a large volume of cold saline risks pulmonary oedema and gives poor control.

**Ref:** Nolan JP, et al. ERC-ESICM 2025 Post-Resuscitation Care, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: A patient remains unconscious (GCS motor 2) 96 h after OHCA, sedation stopped 48 h ago, normothermic, no NMB. Which findings would together make a poor outcome likely according to ERC-ESICM 2025?
options: Burst-suppression on EEG and diffuse anoxic injury on CT
Bilaterally absent N20 SSEP and NSE 110 µg/L at 72 h
A single NSE of 45 µg/L at 24 h
Absent corneal reflex on one side only
questions.expl:
The preconditions are met: ≥ 72 h, M ≤ 5 and confounders excluded. Poor outcome is likely when **≥ 2 of 6 predictors** are present.
- A (True) – burst-suppression (a highly malignant EEG) and diffuse anoxic injury on CT are two independent predictors.
- B (True) – bilaterally absent N20 and NSE > 60 µg/L at 72 h are two predictors.
- C (False) – the NSE threshold is > 60 µg/L at **48 and/or 72 h**, so 45 µg/L at 24 h does not qualify.
- D (False) – the predictor is **bilaterally** absent pupillary **and** corneal reflexes, and a single unilateral sign would not be enough anyway.

**Ref:** Nolan JP, et al. ERC-ESICM 2025 Post-Resuscitation Care, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the main reason neuroprognostication is delayed to at least 72 h after ROSC?
options: Because SSEP is unreliable at any time before 7 days
To reduce the risk of false-pessimistic predictions due to confounders such as residual sedation
NSE cannot be measured earlier
Because CT is impossible in the first 72 h
Because legal rules forbid earlier decisions
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Residual sedation (with drug clearance reduced by hypothermia and organ failure), NMB and metabolic disturbances can mimic severe brain injury early on. Waiting **≥ 72 h** and excluding confounders reduces **false-pessimistic** predictions. These matter because withdrawal based on them produces a self-fulfilling prophecy.

**Why not the others:**
- A – SSEP can be interpreted from 24 h and resists sedation.
- C – NSE can be measured at any time; it is interpreted at 48/72 h.
- D – CT can be done at any time; early CT is often used to find the cause of arrest.
- E – the timing comes from clinical evidence, not legal rules.

**Ref:** Nolan JP, et al. ERC-ESICM 2025 Post-Resuscitation Care, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding ECPR trials in refractory OHCA:
options: ERC 2025 suggests ECPR may be considered as rescue therapy in selected patients where it can be implemented.
Prague OHCA met its primary endpoint of 180-day good neurological outcome.
INCEPTION found a significant improvement in 30-day survival with favourable neurological outcome.
ARREST was a single-centre trial with 30 patients.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ERC 2025 says ECPR may be considered as rescue therapy in selected patients when conventional CPR is failing and the system can deliver it.
- B (False) – Prague OHCA missed its primary endpoint: 180-day CPC 1–2 was 31.5% vs 22.0%, p = 0.09. Only 30-day outcomes favoured ECPR.
- C (False) – INCEPTION found 20% vs 16% (OR 1.4), not significant, with a long time to flow (~74 min).
- D (True) – ARREST was a single-centre trial (Minnesota) with 30 patients: 43% vs 7% survival, stopped early for efficacy.

**Ref:** Soar J, et al. ERC 2025 ALS, Resuscitation 2025; Belohlavek J, JAMA 2022; Suverein MM, N Engl J Med 2023; Yannopoulos D, Lancet 2020.

questions.stem: In PARAMEDIC2, adrenaline compared with placebo in OHCA:
options: Increased mortality
Did not change ROSC or survival
Significantly improved survival with favourable neurological outcome only
Was given only to patients with shockable rhythms
Increased 30-day survival but did not significantly improve survival with favourable neurological outcome
questions.expl:
**Why E:** PARAMEDIC2 (8014 OHCA patients, double-blind) found that adrenaline increased **30-day survival from 2.4% to 3.2%** (adjusted OR 1.47; NNT ~112). Survival with **favourable neurological outcome** (mRS ≤ 3) was **2.2% vs 1.9%**, not significant. Severe neurological impairment among survivors was more frequent with adrenaline (31.0% vs 17.8%).

**Why not the others:**
- A – mortality was lower with adrenaline.
- B – ROSC and survival to admission rose markedly (23.8% vs 8.0%).
- C – neurological outcome was the endpoint that did **not** improve significantly.
- D – adrenaline was given for all rhythms.

**Ref:** Perkins GD, et al. PARAMEDIC2, N Engl J Med 2018.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old climber is found in cardiac arrest with core temperature 26 °C. Correct statements (ERC 2025):
options: Transport to the nearest hospital is preferred, regardless of ECPR/VA-ECMO capability.
If VF persists after 3 shocks, further shocks should be delayed until > 30 °C.
Give adrenaline 1 mg every 3–5 minutes from the start.
The HOPE score can help estimate the probability of successful rewarming.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – transfer a hypothermic patient in arrest **directly to an ECPR/VA-ECMO centre**, even if it is further away. Rewarm without ECLS only if a centre cannot be reached in reasonable time (e.g. ~6 h).
- B (True) – if VF persists after 3 shocks, delay further shocks until core temperature is > 30 °C.
- C (False) – **no adrenaline below 30 °C**, because it accumulates. At 30–35 °C, give it every 6–10 min.
- D (True) – the HOPE score estimates the probability of surviving in-hospital ECLS rewarming.

**EDIC trap:** hypothermia protects the brain, so good outcomes are possible after very prolonged CPR.

**Ref:** Lott C, et al. ERC 2025 Special Circumstances, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: A patient on VA-ECMO after ECPR is comatose at 72 h. NSE is 80 µg/L with visible haemolysis; SSEP shows bilaterally present N20; EEG has a continuous background. The most appropriate interpretation is:
options: NSE is likely confounded by haemolysis; with no other predictor, prognosis is indeterminate
Present N20 guarantees full recovery
Repeat NSE is not useful
Withdraw therapy because of ECMO dependence alone
Poor outcome is certain because NSE > 60 µg/L
questions.expl:
**Why A:** NSE is present in erythrocytes, so **visible haemolysis on ECMO falsely raises it**, and 80 µg/L cannot be taken at face value. Present N20 and a continuous EEG background are not predictors of poor outcome. With **no valid second predictor**, prognosis is **indeterminate**: continue treatment, repeat tests and watch the trend.

**Why not the others:**
- B – present N20 is common in patients who do badly (low sensitivity) and does not guarantee recovery.
- C – serial NSE and haemolysis indices help interpret it.
- D – ECMO dependence on its own says nothing about brain prognosis.
- E – a single confounded predictor cannot make poor outcome certain; ≥ 2 valid predictors are required.

**Ref:** Nolan JP, et al. ERC-ESICM 2025 Post-Resuscitation Care, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding coronary angiography and diagnostics after ROSC (ERC-ESICM 2025):
options: Persistent ST elevation after ROSC warrants emergent catheterisation.
A dual-phase whole-body CT is prioritised in patients without ST elevation.
Coma is a contraindication to emergent angiography in STEMI.
In OHCA without ST elevation, catheterisation should be delayed unless acute coronary occlusion is strongly suspected.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – persistent ST elevation after ROSC means emergent catheterisation, with PPCI if needed.
- B (True) – new in 2025: without ST elevation, a dual-phase (biphasic) whole-body CT, head to pelvis including CTPA, is prioritised to find non-coronary causes and CPR injuries.
- C (False) – coma is **not** a contraindication to emergent angiography in STEMI, because early neurological prognosis is unreliable.
- D (True) – without ST elevation, catheterisation is delayed unless acute occlusion is strongly suspected (COACT, TOMAHAWK).

**Ref:** Nolan JP, et al. ERC-ESICM 2025 Post-Resuscitation Care, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman develops urticaria, wheeze and BP 70/40 mmHg minutes after an IV antibiotic; she has a palpable pulse. The first drug to give is:
options: Chlorphenamine 10 mg IV
Adrenaline 1 mg IV bolus
Lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg
Adrenaline 500 µg IM, repeated after 5 minutes if no improvement
Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Urticaria, bronchospasm and hypotension after a drug exposure mean anaphylaxis. The first drug is **IM adrenaline 500 µg** (anterolateral thigh), repeated after 5 min if there is no improvement, together with an IV crystalloid bolus and high-flow oxygen. Its α- and β-effects reverse vasodilatation, bronchospasm and mediator release.

**Why not the others:**
- A – antihistamines treat skin symptoms only and are not first line.
- B – an IV 1 mg bolus is for cardiac arrest only; with a pulse it risks arrhythmia and severe hypertension.
- C – lipid emulsion treats local anaesthetic toxicity.
- E – corticosteroids act slowly, have no proven acute benefit and are not first line.

**Ref:** Lott C, et al. ERC 2025 Special Circumstances, Resuscitation 2025.

title: W10 · D1 – ARDS: Berlin vs new global definition, pathophysiology, phenotypes

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with pneumococcal pneumonia is on high-flow nasal oxygen 50 L/min, FiO₂ 0.7, PaO₂ 63 mmHg (SpO₂ 92 %). Chest radiograph shows bilateral opacities; echocardiography is normal. Which statement is correct?
options: He meets the new global definition of ARDS (non-intubated category)
He meets the Berlin definition of moderate ARDS
ARDS cannot be diagnosed without a CT scan
He cannot have ARDS until he is intubated
He meets the global definition of severe ARDS
questions.expl:
**Why A:** P/F = 63/0.7 = 90 mmHg on HFNO ≥ 30 L/min, with bilateral opacities, a clear risk factor (pneumonia) and a normal echo – this fulfils the non-intubated category of the 2024 global definition.

**Why not the others:**
- B – Berlin requires PEEP/CPAP ≥ 5 cmH₂O; HFNO has no defined PEEP, so Berlin criteria are not met.
- C – chest X-ray (or lung ultrasound in the global definition) is sufficient; CT is never mandatory.
- D – both Berlin (NIV/CPAP) and the global definition (HFNO, NIV) allow ARDS without intubation.
- E – non-intubated patients are not stratified into mild/moderate/severe, because FiO₂ on HFNO is imprecise.

**EDIC trap:** a P/F < 100 tempts "severe", but severity grading applies only to intubated patients.

**Ref:** Matthay MA et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2024;209:37–47.

questions.stem: Regarding the Berlin definition of ARDS:
options: The term "acute lung injury" was abandoned.
Four ancillary variables for severe ARDS improved predictive validity and were retained.
A minimum PEEP or CPAP of 10 cmH₂O is required when assessing PaO₂/FiO₂.
A pulmonary artery wedge pressure ≤ 18 mmHg is required.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – "acute lung injury" (P/F 200–300 in AECC) was replaced by "mild ARDS".
- B (False) – the ancillary variables (compliance ≤ 40 mL/cmH₂O, PEEP ≥ 10, corrected minute ventilation ≥ 10 L/min, radiographic extent) added no predictive validity and were dropped.
- C (False) – the minimum is PEEP/CPAP ≥ 5 cmH₂O (CPAP allowed only in mild ARDS).
- D (False) – the PCWP criterion was removed, because ARDS and raised left atrial pressure can coexist; oedema must only be "not fully explained" by cardiac failure or fluid overload.

**EDIC trap:** PCWP ≤ 18 mmHg belongs to the AECC 1994 definition, not Berlin.

**Ref:** ARDS Definition Task Force, JAMA 2012;307:2526–2533.

questions.stem: In the new global definition of ARDS, the SpO₂/FiO₂ ratio may replace PaO₂/FiO₂ only if:
options: SpO₂ is ≤ 97 %
SpO₂ is ≥ 98 %
The patient is intubated
Haemoglobin is above 100 g/L
The patient is in a high-income country
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Above SpO₂ 97 % the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve is flat, so a large range of PaO₂ values corresponds to almost the same SpO₂ and S/F no longer reflects oxygenation. The global definition therefore accepts S/F ≤ 315 only when SpO₂ is ≤ 97 %; FiO₂ should be titrated down until SpO₂ ≤ 97 % before calculating it.

**Why not the others:**
- B – SpO₂ ≥ 98 % is exactly the range in which S/F is invalid.
- C – S/F is allowed in all categories, including non-intubated and resource-limited settings.
- D – haemoglobin concentration is not a criterion (dyshaemoglobinaemias such as COHb/MetHb are the caveat).
- E – S/F is allowed in any setting; in resource-limited settings it is simply the main tool.

**Ref:** Matthay MA et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2024;209:37–47.

questions.stem: Regarding the modification of the global ARDS definition for resource-limited settings:
options: Lung ultrasound may not be used for imaging.
SpO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 400 is used.
A minimum PEEP is not required.
A minimum oxygen flow rate is not required.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – bilateral B-lines and/or consolidations on lung ultrasound by a trained operator are acceptable imaging in every category, and are especially useful where X-ray or CT is unavailable.
- B (False) – the oxygenation criterion is SpO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 315, valid only with SpO₂ ≤ 97 %.
- C (True) – neither PEEP nor any specific respiratory support is required in resource-limited settings.
- D (True) – no minimum oxygen flow rate is required, unlike the non-intubated category (HFNO ≥ 30 L/min).

**EDIC trap:** the "no PEEP, no flow" relaxation applies only to the resource-limited category; elsewhere HFNO < 30 L/min does not qualify.

**Ref:** Matthay MA et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2024;209:37–47.

questions.stem: In the data used to validate the Berlin definition, hospital mortality for severe ARDS was approximately:
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In the 4188-patient validation cohort of the Berlin definition, mortality rose with severity: 27 % (mild), 32 % (moderate) and 45 % (severe). Median duration of ventilation in survivors also increased (5, 7 and 9 days). Predictive validity was only marginally better than AECC (AUROC 0.577 vs 0.536).

**Why not the others:**
- A – 15 % is far below even the mild category.
- C – 32 % is the mortality of moderate ARDS.
- D – 70 % overstates mortality in contemporary severe ARDS cohorts.
- E – 27 % is the mortality of mild ARDS.

**EDIC trap:** do not confuse with LUNG SAFE hospital mortality (34.9 / 40.3 / 46.1 %).

**Ref:** ARDS Definition Task Force, JAMA 2012;307:2526–2533.

questions.stem: Findings of the LUNG SAFE study include:
options: ARDS accounted for about 10 % of ICU admissions.
Plateau pressure was measured in about 90 % of patients.
Prone positioning was used in a minority (about 16 %) of severe ARDS.
ARDS was recognised by clinicians in nearly all severe cases (> 95 %).
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ARDS represented 10.4 % of ICU admissions and 23.4 % of mechanically ventilated patients across 459 ICUs in 50 countries.
- B (False) – plateau pressure was measured in only about 40 % of patients with ARDS.
- C (True) – prone positioning was used in only 16.3 % of patients with severe ARDS.
- D (False) – clinician recognition ranged from 51 % in mild to 79 % in severe ARDS; overall ARDS was under-recognised.

**EDIC trap:** LUNG SAFE is the source for "under-recognised and under-treated" – fewer than two thirds received VT ≤ 8 mL/kg PBW.

**Ref:** Bellani G et al. (LUNG SAFE), JAMA 2016;315:788–800.

questions.stem: The main mechanism of hypoxaemia in early ARDS that responds poorly to increasing FiO₂ is:
options: Low inspired oxygen pressure
Hypoventilation
Diffusion limitation
Intrapulmonary shunt
Increased alveolar dead space
questions.expl:
**Why D:** In early ARDS, flooded and collapsed alveoli remain perfused but are not ventilated, creating a true intrapulmonary shunt. Blood passing through shunt units never meets alveolar gas, so raising FiO₂ barely improves PaO₂ once the shunt fraction exceeds ~30 %. Recruitment (PEEP, prone positioning) rather than FiO₂ treats this mechanism.

**Why not the others:**
- A – low inspired PO₂ (altitude) is not the mechanism in ARDS and is fully FiO₂-responsive.
- B – hypoventilation causes hypercapnic hypoxaemia correctable by modest FiO₂.
- C – diffusion limitation plays a minor role and also responds to extra oxygen.
- E – increased dead space mainly causes hypercapnia; it is prognostic but not the main cause of refractory hypoxaemia.

**Ref:** Gattinoni L, Pesenti A, Intensive Care Med 2005;31:776–784.

questions.stem: Regarding the "baby lung" concept:
options: The low respiratory system compliance mainly reflects a small amount of aerated lung rather than intrinsically stiff lung.
Even a tidal volume of 6 mL/kg PBW may cause excessive strain when the aerated lung is very small.
In the supine position, collapse predominates in dependent (dorsal) regions.
Ventilator-induced lung injury includes volutrauma, atelectrauma and biotrauma.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – CT studies show that compliance correlates with the size of the aerated lung; the "baby lung" itself has near-normal specific compliance.
- B (True) – strain = VT / end-expiratory aerated lung volume, so even 6 mL/kg PBW may overdistend a very small baby lung (the rationale for limiting driving pressure).
- C (True) – the weight of the oedematous lung (superimposed pressure) produces dorsal, dependent atelectasis supine, with ventral hyperinflation.
- D (True) – VILI comprises volutrauma, barotrauma, atelectrauma and biotrauma (mediator release contributing to MODS).

**EDIC trap:** all-true K′ items exist; judge each statement separately.

**Ref:** Gattinoni L, Pesenti A, Intensive Care Med 2005;31:776–784; Slutsky AS, Ranieri VM, N Engl J Med 2013;369:2126–2136.

questions.stem: Compared with the hypoinflammatory subphenotype, the hyperinflammatory ARDS subphenotype is characterised by:
options: Less frequent vasopressor use
Higher mortality
Exclusively pulmonary (direct) aetiology
Higher serum bicarbonate
Lower plasma IL-6 and IL-8
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In the latent class analysis of ARMA and ALVEOLI, the hyperinflammatory subphenotype (about one third of patients) had markedly higher mortality and fewer ventilator- and organ-failure-free days. It was also associated with higher plasma IL-6, IL-8 and sTNFR-1, more vasopressor use, lower bicarbonate and more sepsis.

**Why not the others:**
- A – vasopressor use was more frequent, not less.
- C – the hyperinflammatory subphenotype is enriched for indirect (extrapulmonary) causes such as sepsis, not exclusively direct injury.
- D – serum bicarbonate is lower (more metabolic acidosis).
- E – IL-6 and IL-8 are higher; they are among the defining biomarkers.

**Ref:** Calfee CS et al., Lancet Respir Med 2014;2:611–620.

questions.stem: Regarding ARDS phenotyping and the ESICM 2023 guidelines:
options: In ALVEOLI, the effect of higher versus lower PEEP appeared to differ between subphenotypes.
Subphenotypes were first identified by latent class analysis of the LUNG SAFE cohort.
ESICM 2023 gave no graded recommendation on the definition of ARDS.
ESICM 2023 strongly recommends routine phenotype-guided PEEP selection.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – in ALVEOLI a significant interaction was found (p = 0.049 for mortality): hyperinflammatory patients appeared to benefit from higher PEEP; this is a post-hoc finding.
- B (False) – subphenotypes were first identified by latent class analysis of ARMA and ALVEOLI data (Calfee 2014), not LUNG SAFE.
- C (True) – ESICM 2023 discussed the definition (HFNO, S/F, ultrasound) without issuing a graded recommendation.
- D (False) – ESICM 2023 considers phenotyping hypothesis-generating and makes no recommendation to use it for routine PEEP or other treatment decisions.

**EDIC trap:** phenotype ≠ severity by P/F; it is based on biomarkers and clinical variables.

**Ref:** Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023;49:727–759; Calfee CS et al., Lancet Respir Med 2014;2:611–620.

open.q: A patient with pneumonia is on HFNO 40 L/min, FiO₂ 0.6, PaO₂ 75 mmHg, with bilateral B-lines on lung ultrasound and a normal echocardiogram. Calculate the P/F ratio and explain whether the patient meets the Berlin and the new global definitions of ARDS.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- P/F = 75 / 0.6 = 125 mmHg.
- Berlin: requires PEEP/CPAP ≥ 5 cmH₂O; HFNO has no defined PEEP → Berlin criteria not met.
- Global definition 2024: non-intubated category allows HFNO ≥ 30 L/min with P/F ≤ 300 (or S/F ≤ 315 if SpO₂ ≤ 97%) → met.
- Imaging criterion satisfied by bilateral B-lines/consolidations on lung ultrasound (trained operator).
- Risk factor present (pneumonia), onset within 1 week, oedema not primarily cardiogenic (normal echo).
- Non-intubated patients are not stratified into mild/moderate/severe.
- On HFNO < 30 L/min the global definition would not be met (outside the resource-limited category).

open.q: Explain the "baby lung" concept and its implications for setting tidal volume in ARDS.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- In severe ARDS the normally aerated part of the lung is the size of a small child's lung.
- Low compliance reflects a small amount of aerated lung rather than intrinsically stiff lung.
- VT scaled to predicted body weight may still be excessive for a small aerated lung → excessive strain (volutrauma).
- Hence the logic of driving pressure (VT normalised to compliance).
- Gravitational distribution: dorsal atelectasis supine, ventral hyperinflation → rationale for prone positioning.
- VILI mechanisms: volutrauma, barotrauma, atelectrauma, biotrauma (→ MODS).

title: W10 · D2 – Protective ventilation: ARMA, plateau and driving pressure, PBW

questions.stem: A 165-cm tall woman weighing 95 kg is intubated for ARDS. Her predicted body weight and the corresponding tidal volume at 6 mL/kg PBW are approximately:
options: 50 kg and 300 mL
57 kg and 340 mL
75 kg and 450 mL
95 kg and 570 mL
62 kg and 370 mL
questions.expl:
**Why B:** For women PBW = 45.5 + 0.91 × (height cm − 152.4) = 45.5 + 0.91 × 12.6 = 57.0 kg. At 6 mL/kg PBW the tidal volume is 57 × 6 ≈ 342 mL. Lung size depends on height and sex, not on actual weight, so the 95 kg is irrelevant.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 50 kg would correspond to a shorter woman (~157 cm); 300 mL underventilates slightly.
- C – 75 kg is the PBW of a 180-cm man, not a 165-cm woman.
- D – 95 kg is the actual weight; 570 mL equals ~10 mL/kg PBW, i.e. injurious.
- E – 62 kg results from using the male formula (50 + 11.5).

**EDIC trap:** short, obese women are the patients most often over-ventilated when VT is set by actual weight.

**Ref:** ARDS Network (ARMA), N Engl J Med 2000;342:1301–1308.

questions.stem: Regarding the ARMA trial (ARDS Network, 2000):
options: Mortality was 31.0 % vs 39.8 % in favour of low tidal volume.
The trial was stopped early for futility.
The low tidal volume group was ventilated with 6 mL/kg actual body weight and plateau pressure ≤ 30 cmH₂O.
The control group received 12 mL/kg predicted body weight with plateau pressure up to 50 cmH₂O.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – mortality before discharge home with unassisted breathing was 31.0 % vs 39.8 % (ARR ~9 %, NNT ~11).
- B (False) – the trial was stopped early for benefit after the fourth interim analysis (861 patients).
- C (False) – low VT was 6 mL/kg predicted (not actual) body weight, with Pplat ≤ 30 cmH₂O and VT down to 4 mL/kg if needed.
- D (True) – the control arm received 12 mL/kg PBW with Pplat ≤ 50 cmH₂O.

**EDIC trap:** a criticism of ARMA is that 12 mL/kg PBW exceeded usual practice of the time (~10 mL/kg actual weight).

**Ref:** ARDS Network (ARMA), N Engl J Med 2000;342:1301–1308.

questions.stem: A ventilated ARDS patient has VT 450 mL, PEEP 10 cmH₂O, peak pressure 38 cmH₂O and plateau pressure 28 cmH₂O. Which statement is correct?
options: Driving pressure is 28 cmH₂O
Driving pressure is 18 cmH₂O and static compliance is 25 mL/cmH₂O
The 10 cmH₂O difference between peak and plateau reflects lung elastance
Driving pressure is 10 cmH₂O
Static compliance is 45 mL/cmH₂O
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Driving pressure = Pplat − PEEP = 28 − 10 = 18 cmH₂O. Static respiratory system compliance = VT/ΔP = 450/18 = 25 mL/cmH₂O. A ΔP of 18 exceeds the commonly quoted ~15 cmH₂O threshold even though Pplat is below 30.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 28 cmH₂O is the plateau pressure itself, not Pplat minus PEEP.
- C – Ppeak − Pplat (10 cmH₂O) is the resistive component (tube, secretions, bronchospasm), not elastance.
- D – 10 cmH₂O is the peak–plateau difference or the PEEP, not the driving pressure.
- E – 45 mL/cmH₂O would require ΔP of 10 cmH₂O.

**Ref:** Amato MBP et al., N Engl J Med 2015;372:747–755.

questions.stem: Regarding driving pressure (Amato, NEJM 2015):
options: An increase of one standard deviation (~7 cmH₂O) was associated with a relative risk of death of about 1.4.
Changes in PEEP were associated with survival only when they decreased driving pressure.
It was derived from individual data of 3562 patients from nine randomised trials.
The association disappeared in patients already receiving protective plateau pressures.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – each 1-SD increase in ΔP (~7 cmH₂O) was associated with RR of death 1.41 (95 % CI 1.31–1.51).
- B (True) – changes in VT or PEEP were associated with survival only when they lowered ΔP (mediation analysis).
- C (True) – individual data of 3562 patients from nine RCTs; it is an observational, not a randomised, analysis.
- D (False) – the association persisted in patients already receiving "protective" Pplat ≤ 30 and VT ≤ 7 mL/kg (RR 1.36).

**EDIC trap:** no RCT has yet tested a ΔP-targeted strategy, and ESICM 2023 makes no recommendation on ΔP.

**Ref:** Amato MBP et al., N Engl J Med 2015;372:747–755.

questions.stem: According to the ESICM 2023 ARDS guidelines, the tidal volume recommendation for ARDS not due to COVID-19 is:
options: No recommendation because of insufficient evidence
Tidal volume titrated to driving pressure < 10 cmH₂O, strong recommendation
4–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, strong recommendation
6 mL/kg actual body weight, conditional recommendation
8–10 mL/kg predicted body weight, strong recommendation
questions.expl:
**Why C:** ESICM 2023 recommends low tidal volume ventilation (4–8 mL/kg PBW) rather than larger VT in ARDS not due to COVID-19 – strong recommendation, high level of evidence. The same strong recommendation applies to COVID-19 ARDS with moderate certainty because of indirectness.

**Why not the others:**
- A – a strong recommendation exists, based on ARMA and subsequent meta-analyses.
- B – driving pressure is listed as a research question; no ΔP target is recommended.
- D – VT is always scaled to predicted, not actual, body weight.
- E – 8–10 mL/kg PBW is above the recommended range.

**Ref:** Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023;49:727–759.

questions.stem: Regarding plateau pressure measurement:
options: It requires an end-inspiratory pause in a patient without active breathing effort.
Active inspiratory effort may cause plateau pressure to underestimate lung stress.
In morbid obesity, a plateau pressure slightly above 30 cmH₂O may correspond to an acceptable transpulmonary pressure.
It reflects mainly airway resistance.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Pplat requires an end-inspiratory hold at zero flow in a relaxed, passive patient, so that airway pressure equals alveolar pressure.
- B (True) – active inspiratory effort lowers pleural pressure, so measured Pplat underestimates the true transpulmonary pressure (lung stress).
- C (True) – with a stiff chest wall (obesity, intra-abdominal hypertension) part of the pressure distends the chest wall; oesophageal pressure can clarify transpulmonary pressure.
- D (False) – Pplat reflects elastic (lung + chest wall) recoil; airway resistance is reflected by Ppeak − Pplat.

**EDIC trap:** a "normal" Pplat with intrinsic PEEP still needs an end-expiratory hold to calculate true ΔP.

**Ref:** Slutsky AS, Ranieri VM, N Engl J Med 2013;369:2126–2136; Amato MBP et al., N Engl J Med 2015;372:747–755.

questions.stem: A 180-cm man with ARDS is ventilated with VT 600 mL. His driving pressure is 19 cmH₂O, plateau pressure 31 cmH₂O. The most appropriate first change is:
options: Increase VT to improve CO₂ clearance
Start inhaled nitric oxide
Increase PEEP by 5 cmH₂O
Reduce VT towards ~450 mL (6 mL/kg PBW) and increase respiratory rate
Switch to pressure support ventilation
questions.expl:
**Why D:** PBW = 50 + 0.91 × (180 − 152.4) = 75.1 kg, so 600 mL ≈ 8 mL/kg PBW. With Pplat > 30 and ΔP 19 cmH₂O, the first step is to reduce VT towards 6 mL/kg (~450 mL) and increase the rate (up to 35/min) to maintain minute ventilation, accepting permissive hypercapnia.

**Why not the others:**
- A – increasing VT worsens volutrauma and raises Pplat further.
- B – inhaled NO improves oxygenation transiently but does not address injurious ventilation or mortality.
- C – raising PEEP at the same VT would push Pplat even higher unless substantial recruitment occurs.
- E – pressure support in early moderate–severe ARDS risks uncontrolled VT and P-SILI.

**Ref:** ARDS Network (ARMA), N Engl J Med 2000;342:1301–1308; Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023;49:727–759.

questions.stem: After increasing PEEP from 10 to 14 cmH₂O at constant VT 420 mL, plateau pressure rises from 26 to 28 cmH₂O. Which statements are correct?
options: Static compliance decreased.
Driving pressure increased from 16 to 18 cmH₂O.
This pattern is consistent with alveolar recruitment.
This pattern suggests that overdistension predominates.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – compliance rose from 420/16 = 26 to 420/14 = 30 mL/cmH₂O.
- B (False) – driving pressure fell from 16 (26 − 10) to 14 (28 − 14) cmH₂O.
- C (True) – a fall in ΔP (rise in compliance) after a PEEP increase at constant VT indicates that recruitment predominates.
- D (False) – overdistension would show a rise in ΔP and fall in compliance.

**EDIC trap:** a rising Pplat after a PEEP increase does not mean overdistension; look at ΔP, not Pplat alone.

**Ref:** Amato MBP et al., N Engl J Med 2015;372:747–755; Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023;49:727–759.

questions.stem: Permissive hypercapnia during lung-protective ventilation is most relevantly limited in a patient with:
options: Type 2 diabetes
Septic shock on low-dose noradrenaline
Community-acquired pneumonia
Raised intracranial pressure after traumatic brain injury
Mild acute kidney injury
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Hypercapnia causes cerebral vasodilatation, increasing cerebral blood volume and intracranial pressure; after TBI this can reduce cerebral perfusion pressure. Raised ICP is therefore the main relative contraindication to permissive hypercapnia; severe pulmonary hypertension or RV failure (hypercapnia raises PVR) is the other.

**Why not the others:**
- A – type 2 diabetes does not interact relevantly with hypercapnia.
- B – mild acidosis is generally tolerated in septic shock on low-dose vasopressors.
- C – pneumonia is the commonest cause of ARDS and the typical setting for permissive hypercapnia.
- E – mild AKI impairs bicarbonate retention slightly but is not a contraindication.

**Ref:** ARDS Network (ARMA), N Engl J Med 2000;342:1301–1308.

questions.stem: Mechanisms of ventilator-induced lung injury include:
options: Biotrauma with release of inflammatory mediators contributing to multiorgan failure
Atelectrauma from cyclic opening and closing of unstable alveoli
Volutrauma from excessive strain of the aerated lung
Hypocapnia-induced alveolar collapse as the main mechanism
questions.expl:
- A (True) – biotrauma: mechanical stress releases cytokines (e.g. IL-6) into the circulation, contributing to MODS; ARMA showed lower IL-6 with low VT.
- B (True) – atelectrauma: shear stress from cyclic opening and closing of unstable alveoli, mainly at low PEEP.
- C (True) – volutrauma: overdistension from excessive strain (VT relative to aerated lung volume).
- D (False) – hypocapnia is not a recognised main VILI mechanism; the fourth classical mechanism is barotrauma (pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum).

**Ref:** Slutsky AS, Ranieri VM, N Engl J Med 2013;369:2126–2136.

open.q: A 170-cm man with moderate ARDS is ventilated in volume control with VT 560 mL, PEEP 8 cmH₂O, Ppeak 36 cmH₂O and Pplat 30 cmH₂O. Calculate his PBW, VT per kg PBW, driving pressure and static compliance, interpret the values and outline the changes you would make.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- PBW = 50 + 0.91 × (170 − 152.4) = 66.0 kg; VT 560 mL ≈ 8.5 mL/kg PBW (above the 4–8 mL/kg range; 6 mL/kg ≈ 396 mL).
- ΔP = 30 − 8 = 22 cmH₂O (well above ~15); Crs = 560/22 ≈ 25 mL/cmH₂O.
- Ppeak − Pplat = 6 cmH₂O = resistive component.
- Pplat is at the 30 cmH₂O limit, but a high ΔP means ventilation is not "safe" despite meeting the Pplat limit.
- Reduce VT towards 6 mL/kg PBW (down to 4 mL/kg if Pplat remains > 30), increase rate (up to 35/min) to maintain pH ≥ 7.30; accept permissive hypercapnia (caution with raised ICP/RV failure).
- Recheck Pplat with an inspiratory pause in a relaxed patient, measure total PEEP (end-expiratory hold); reassess ΔP and compliance after each change.

open.q: Explain why driving pressure may be a better marker of lung stress than VT/PBW, and why it is not yet a guideline recommendation.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- ΔP = Pplat − PEEP = VT/Crs, i.e. VT normalised to the size of the functional (baby) lung → reflects strain.
- Amato 2015: individual data of 3562 patients from 9 RCTs; ΔP had the strongest association with survival (RR 1.41 per 1 SD ~7 cmH₂O).
- Association persisted even with "protective" Pplat and VT (RR 1.36).
- Changes in VT or PEEP were associated with survival only if they reduced ΔP.
- However, it is a mediation analysis, not an RCT; the ~15 cmH₂O threshold comes from observational data.
- No prospective RCT targeting ΔP; ESICM 2023 gives no recommendation (research question).

title: W10 · D3 – PEEP and recruitment: ALVEOLI, LOVS, EXPRESS, ART, EPVent

questions.stem: Which trial showed increased 28-day mortality with a strategy of maximal lung recruitment followed by decremental PEEP titration?
options: EXPRESS
EPVent-2
ART
LOVS
ALVEOLI
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In ART (1010 patients with moderate–severe ARDS), a maximal recruitment manoeuvre (PEEP up to 45 cmH₂O, peak up to 60) followed by decremental PEEP titration to best compliance + 2 cmH₂O increased 28-day mortality (55.3 vs 49.3 %, HR 1.20). Barotrauma was also more frequent (5.6 vs 1.6 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – EXPRESS (Pplat-guided high PEEP) showed no mortality difference but more ventilator-free days.
- B – EPVent-2 (oesophageal pressure-guided PEEP) showed no difference versus empirical high PEEP.
- D – LOVS (open-lung, RM 40 cmH₂O × 40 s) showed no mortality difference and less refractory hypoxaemia.
- E – ALVEOLI (high vs low PEEP table) was stopped for futility, with no mortality difference.

**Ref:** Cavalcanti AB et al. (ART), JAMA 2017;318:1335–1345.

questions.stem: Regarding the LOVS trial:
options: The plateau pressure limit in the intervention arm was 30 cmH₂O, as in the control arm.
Hospital mortality was significantly lower in the open-lung group.
Refractory hypoxaemia and use of rescue therapies were less frequent in the open-lung group.
The intervention included recruitment manoeuvres and higher PEEP.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – the open-lung arm allowed Pplat up to 40 cmH₂O, versus 30 cmH₂O in the ARDSNet control arm.
- B (False) – hospital mortality was 36.4 vs 40.4 % (not significant).
- C (True) – refractory hypoxaemia (4.6 vs 10.2 %) and use of rescue therapies (5.1 vs 9.3 %) were reduced.
- D (True) – the strategy combined pressure control, recruitment manoeuvres (40 cmH₂O for 40 s) and a higher PEEP/FiO₂ table, with VT 6 mL/kg PBW in both arms.

**EDIC trap:** better oxygenation and fewer rescue therapies did not translate into lower mortality.

**Ref:** Meade MO et al. (LOVS), JAMA 2008;299:637–645.

questions.stem: In the EXPRESS trial, PEEP in the "increased recruitment" arm was set:
options: According to the ARDSNet higher PEEP/FiO₂ table
As high as possible while keeping plateau pressure at 28–30 cmH₂O
By oesophageal pressure to achieve end-expiratory transpulmonary pressure 0–6 cmH₂O
At best compliance + 2 cmH₂O after a recruitment manoeuvre
By electrical impedance tomography
questions.expl:
**Why B:** EXPRESS compared an "increased recruitment" strategy, in which PEEP was raised as high as possible without Pplat exceeding 28–30 cmH₂O, with "minimal distension" (PEEP 5–9 cmH₂O). Mortality did not differ (27.8 vs 31.2 %), but ventilator-free and organ-failure-free days increased.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the ARDSNet higher PEEP/FiO₂ table was used in ALVEOLI (and the control arm of EPVent-2).
- C – end-expiratory transpulmonary pressure 0–6 cmH₂O was the EPVent-2 target.
- D – best compliance + 2 cmH₂O after a recruitment manoeuvre was the ART protocol.
- E – EIT-guided PEEP has not been tested in any of these large RCTs.

**Ref:** Mercat A et al. (EXPRESS), JAMA 2008;299:646–655.

questions.stem: Regarding the individual-patient meta-analysis by Briel et al. (JAMA 2010):
options: Overall, higher PEEP significantly reduced hospital mortality.
It included ARMA, LOVS and EXPRESS.
In patients with PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 200, higher PEEP was associated with lower mortality.
In patients with PaO₂/FiO₂ > 200, higher PEEP significantly reduced mortality.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – overall hospital mortality was 32.9 vs 35.2 % (adjusted RR 0.94, not significant).
- B (False) – it pooled ALVEOLI, LOVS and EXPRESS (2299 patients); ARMA compared tidal volumes, not PEEP.
- C (True) – with P/F ≤ 200, mortality was 34.1 vs 39.1 % (adjusted RR 0.90, p = 0.049).
- D (False) – with P/F > 200 (mild ARDS / former ALI) there was a non-significant trend towards harm (27.2 vs 19.4 %).

**EDIC trap:** the benefit of higher PEEP is a subgroup finding of an IPD meta-analysis, not of any single RCT.

**Ref:** Briel M et al., JAMA 2010;303:865–873.

questions.stem: According to the ESICM 2023 guidelines, prolonged high-pressure recruitment manoeuvres (≥ 35 cmH₂O for ≥ 1 minute) in ARDS are:
options: Neither recommended nor discouraged
Recommended against (strong recommendation, moderate certainty)
Suggested only in COVID-19 ARDS
Suggested against (conditional recommendation, very low certainty)
Recommended in all patients with moderate–severe ARDS
questions.expl:
**Why B:** ESICM 2023 recommends against prolonged high-pressure recruitment manoeuvres (≥ 35 cmH₂O for ≥ 1 min) to reduce mortality – strong recommendation, moderate certainty – largely on the basis of ART. For brief high-pressure RMs it conditionally suggests against routine use. ATS 2024 also strongly recommends against prolonged RMs.

**Why not the others:**
- A – a clear (strong) recommendation against exists.
- C – there is no COVID-specific endorsement of prolonged RMs.
- D – the conditional "suggest against" applies to brief RMs, and certainty is not very low.
- E – no guideline recommends RMs in all moderate–severe ARDS.

**Ref:** Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023;49:727–759; Qadir N et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2024;209:24–36.

questions.stem: Regarding oesophageal pressure–guided PEEP:
options: EPVent-2 showed a significant reduction in mortality.
In EPVent-2, the control group received an empirical high PEEP/FiO₂ strategy.
Oesophageal pressure is used as an estimate of pleural pressure.
The original EPVent trial showed worse oxygenation with oesophageal pressure–guided PEEP.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – EPVent-2 (200 patients) showed no difference in the composite of death and ventilator-free days; 28-day mortality was 32.4 vs 30.6 %.
- B (True) – the control arm used an empirical high PEEP/FiO₂ table, which narrowed the PEEP difference between arms.
- C (True) – oesophageal pressure approximates pleural pressure, allowing calculation of transpulmonary pressure (Paw − Pes).
- D (False) – EPVent (2008, 61 patients) showed better oxygenation (P/F ~88 mmHg higher at 72 h) and compliance.

**EDIC trap:** Pes may still help individually in obesity, IAH or a stiff chest wall.

**Ref:** Talmor D et al., N Engl J Med 2008;359:2095–2104; Beitler JR et al., JAMA 2019;321:846–857.

questions.stem: A patient with moderate ARDS has PEEP increased from 10 to 16 cmH₂O at constant VT 400 mL. Plateau pressure rises from 24 to 34 cmH₂O, PaCO₂ rises and blood pressure falls. The most likely explanation is:
options: Pneumothorax is excluded by these findings
Improved compliance
Increased airway resistance
Successful alveolar recruitment
Overdistension with haemodynamic compromise in a poorly recruitable lung
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Driving pressure rose from 14 (24 − 10) to 18 (34 − 16) cmH₂O, so compliance fell from 28.6 to 22 mL/cmH₂O – the extra PEEP overdistended already open alveoli rather than recruiting new ones. Rising PaCO₂ reflects increased dead space, and falling blood pressure reflects reduced venous return and higher RV afterload. PEEP should be reduced to the previous level.

**Why not the others:**
- A – a sudden rise in Pplat with hypotension is compatible with pneumothorax, which must be actively excluded, not assumed absent.
- B – compliance decreased, not improved.
- C – resistance is assessed by Ppeak − Pplat; a rising Pplat reflects elastance.
- D – recruitment would lower ΔP and PaCO₂ and improve compliance.

**Ref:** Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023;49:727–759; Amato MBP et al., N Engl J Med 2015;372:747–755.

questions.stem: Regarding the ART trial (JAMA 2017):
options: It enrolled patients with moderate–severe ARDS.
The recruitment protocol was modified to a less aggressive version during the trial because of safety concerns.
Barotrauma and pneumothorax requiring drainage were more frequent with the intervention.
28-day mortality was higher with the intervention.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 1010 patients with moderate–severe ARDS (P/F ≤ 200 after standardised ventilation) in 120 ICUs.
- B (True) – after 556 patients the RM was modified (maximum PEEP 35, peak 50 cmH₂O) after three cardiac arrests attributed to the manoeuvre.
- C (True) – barotrauma 5.6 vs 1.6 % and pneumothorax requiring drainage 3.2 vs 1.2 %.
- D (True) – 28-day mortality 55.3 vs 49.3 % (HR 1.20); 6-month mortality was also higher, and ventilator-free days were not increased.

**EDIC trap:** all-true K′ items exist; judge each statement on its own merits.

**Ref:** Cavalcanti AB et al. (ART), JAMA 2017;318:1335–1345.

questions.stem: Which statement regarding the ALVEOLI trial is correct?
options: Higher PEEP reduced in-hospital mortality significantly
Tidal volume differed between the groups (6 vs 12 mL/kg PBW)
Mean PEEP was about 13 vs 8 cmH₂O, with no significant difference in mortality
It used oesophageal pressure to titrate PEEP
It was stopped early for benefit
questions.expl:
**Why C:** ALVEOLI (549 patients) compared high versus low PEEP/FiO₂ tables with identical VT 6 mL/kg PBW. Mean PEEP on days 1–4 was 13.2 vs 8.3 cmH₂O, and hospital mortality was 27.5 vs 24.9 % (not significant); the trial was stopped for futility.

**Why not the others:**
- A – mortality was not reduced; the numerically higher mortality in the high-PEEP arm reflected baseline imbalance.
- B – VT was 6 mL/kg PBW in both arms; 6 vs 12 mL/kg was ARMA.
- D – PEEP was titrated by PEEP/FiO₂ tables; oesophageal pressure was used in EPVent.
- E – it was stopped for futility, not benefit.

**Ref:** Brower RG et al. (ALVEOLI), N Engl J Med 2004;351:327–336.

questions.stem: Comparing ESICM 2023 and ATS 2024 recommendations on PEEP:
options: ATS 2024 suggests higher PEEP without recruitment manoeuvres in moderate–severe ARDS.
ESICM makes no recommendation for or against routine higher PEEP.
ESICM makes no recommendation for or against mechanics-guided PEEP titration.
Both strongly recommend PEEP titration by oesophageal pressure.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ATS 2024 conditionally suggests higher PEEP without lung recruitment manoeuvres in moderate–severe ARDS (low–moderate certainty).
- B (True) – ESICM 2023 makes no recommendation for or against routine higher PEEP (PEEP/FiO₂ strategy).
- C (True) – ESICM 2023 makes no recommendation on PEEP titration by respiratory mechanics (compliance, oesophageal pressure) versus tables.
- D (False) – neither guideline recommends oesophageal pressure-guided PEEP; EPVent-2 was neutral.

**EDIC trap:** the two guidelines differ on higher PEEP but agree strongly against prolonged RMs.

**Ref:** Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023;49:727–759; Qadir N et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2024;209:24–36.

open.q: A patient with moderate ARDS (P/F 140) is ventilated with VT 6 mL/kg PBW. Outline how you would set and titrate PEEP, and how you would recognise recruitment versus overdistension at the bedside.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Start with PEEP from the PEEP/FiO₂ table, rather the higher end with P/F ≤ 200 (Briel: benefit of higher PEEP only at P/F ≤ 200).
- Assess the response after each PEEP change: ΔP/compliance, P/F, PaCO₂, haemodynamics.
- Recruitment: ΔP falls (compliance rises), oxygenation improves, no haemodynamic deterioration.
- Overdistension/non-recruitable: ΔP and Pplat rise, PaCO₂ rises (↑ dead space), BP falls (↓ venous return, ↑ RV afterload) → return to the previous PEEP.
- No routine recruitment manoeuvres; avoid prolonged high-pressure RM (ART: ↑ mortality and barotrauma; ESICM strong against).
- Consider oesophageal pressure in obesity/IAH/stiff chest wall.
- With P/F < 150 → prone positioning, which has mortality benefit unlike PEEP.

open.q: Explain why ART showed harm while LOVS and EXPRESS were neutral, and how ESICM 2023 and ATS 2024 differ in their PEEP recommendations.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- LOVS (RM 40 cmH₂O × 40 s, high PEEP) and EXPRESS (PEEP to Pplat 28–30) did not reduce mortality but improved secondary outcomes (less refractory hypoxaemia/rescue therapies; more ventilator-free and organ failure-free days).
- ART used a maximal RM (PEEP up to 45, peak up to 60 cmH₂O) plus decremental titration in an unselected population; 28-d mortality 55.3 vs 49.3% (HR 1.20).
- Harm likely due to haemodynamic instability and barotrauma (5.6 vs 1.6%; pneumothorax requiring drainage 3.2 vs 1.2%); protocol softened mid-trial for safety.
- Recruitability varies widely; focal ARDS tends to overdistend with high pressures.
- ESICM 2023: no recommendation for/against higher PEEP or mechanics-guided titration; strong against prolonged RM; conditional against routine brief RM.
- ATS 2024: conditionally suggests higher PEEP without RM in moderate–severe ARDS; strong against prolonged RM.

title: W10 · D4 – Prone positioning, neuromuscular blockade and corticosteroids in ARDS

questions.stem: In PROSEVA, patients were randomised to prone positioning if, after a stabilisation period of 12–24 hours, they had:
options: PaO₂/FiO₂ < 150 mmHg with FiO₂ ≥ 0.6 and PEEP ≥ 5 cmH₂O
PaO₂/FiO₂ < 100 mmHg on ECMO
Plateau pressure > 30 cmH₂O despite VT 4 mL/kg PBW
PaO₂/FiO₂ < 300 mmHg with any PEEP
PaCO₂ > 60 mmHg despite RR 35/min
questions.expl:
**Why A:** PROSEVA enrolled patients ventilated for < 36 h who, after 12–24 h of stabilisation, still had P/F < 150 mmHg with FiO₂ ≥ 0.6, PEEP ≥ 5 cmH₂O and VT ~6 mL/kg PBW. The stabilisation period excluded patients who improved quickly once ventilation was optimised.

**Why not the others:**
- B – ECMO was an exclusion criterion in PROSEVA, and P/F < 100 was not the threshold.
- C – Pplat > 30 at 4 mL/kg was not an inclusion criterion.
- D – P/F < 300 with any PEEP would include mild ARDS, in which earlier prone trials failed.
- E – refractory hypercapnia was not an inclusion criterion.

**EDIC trap:** the threshold is P/F < 150 after stabilisation, not immediately after intubation.

**Ref:** Guérin C et al. (PROSEVA), N Engl J Med 2013;368:2159–2168.

questions.stem: Regarding the PROSEVA trial:
options: 28-day mortality was 16.0 % vs 32.8 %.
Prone sessions lasted at least 8 consecutive hours.
Participating centres had long experience with prone positioning.
Cardiac arrests were more frequent in the prone group.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 28-day mortality 16.0 vs 32.8 % (HR 0.39); 90-day mortality 23.6 vs 41.0 %; NNT ~6.
- B (False) – sessions lasted at least 16 consecutive hours (mean ~17 h).
- C (True) – all 27 centres had more than 5 years' routine experience of prone positioning.
- D (False) – cardiac arrests were less frequent in the prone group (6.8 vs 13.5 %); other complications did not differ.

**EDIC trap:** earlier trials failed because of short sessions, unselected (milder) patients and non-protective ventilation.

**Ref:** Guérin C et al. (PROSEVA), N Engl J Med 2013;368:2159–2168.

questions.stem: The most important difference between the control arms of ACURASYS and ROSE was:
options: ACURASYS controls received ECMO
ROSE controls received cisatracurium as needed every 6 hours
ACURASYS controls received deep sedation, ROSE controls received light sedation
ACURASYS controls were ventilated with 12 mL/kg PBW
ROSE controls were placed in the prone position routinely
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In ACURASYS both arms were deeply sedated, so cisatracurium was compared with deep sedation without paralysis, a state prone to asynchrony. ROSE compared NMB plus deep sedation with a light-sedation strategy (RASS 0 to −1), reflecting modern practice; this, together with high PEEP in ROSE, is the main explanation for the conflicting results.

**Why not the others:**
- A – ECMO was not part of the control arm in either trial.
- B – ROSE controls received no routine NMB; boluses were allowed only as clinically needed, not scheduled every 6 h.
- D – both trials used low-VT ventilation (~6 mL/kg PBW).
- E – prone positioning was not protocolised in either control arm.

**Ref:** Papazian L et al., N Engl J Med 2010;363:1107–1116; Moss M et al. (ROSE), N Engl J Med 2019;380:1997–2008.

questions.stem: Regarding the ROSE trial:
options: A lower PEEP strategy was used in both arms.
Serious cardiovascular events were more frequent in the neuromuscular blockade group.
90-day mortality was significantly reduced by neuromuscular blockade.
It enrolled patients with PaO₂/FiO₂ < 300 mmHg.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – ROSE used a higher PEEP strategy in both arms, which may have reduced atelectrauma and the potential benefit of NMB.
- B (True) – serious cardiovascular adverse events were more frequent with NMB (14 vs 4 events).
- C (False) – 90-day mortality was 42.5 vs 42.8 %; the trial was stopped for futility after 1006 patients.
- D (False) – inclusion required P/F < 150 mmHg on PEEP ≥ 8 cmH₂O within 48 h.

**Ref:** Moss M et al. (ROSE), N Engl J Med 2019;380:1997–2008.

questions.stem: According to the ESICM 2023 ARDS guidelines, routine continuous infusion of neuromuscular blocking agents in moderate–severe ARDS (non-COVID):
options: Is not addressed
Is recommended against (strong, moderate certainty)
Is recommended only during prone positioning
Is recommended (strong, high certainty)
Is suggested (conditional, low certainty)
questions.expl:
**Why B:** ESICM 2023 recommends against routine continuous NMBA infusion to reduce mortality in moderate–severe ARDS not due to COVID-19 – strong recommendation, moderate certainty – mainly because ROSE showed no benefit against light sedation. NMBAs remain an option individually (severe asynchrony, uncontrolled effort, refractory hypoxaemia).

**Why not the others:**
- A – NMBA infusion is explicitly addressed in ESICM 2023.
- C – no recommendation links NMBA infusion to prone positioning.
- D – a strong recommendation for NMBAs contradicts ROSE.
- E – a conditional suggestion for NMBAs in early severe ARDS is the ATS 2024 position, not ESICM.

**EDIC trap:** ESICM and ATS differ; neither supports routine NMB in every moderate–severe ARDS.

**Ref:** Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023;49:727–759; Qadir N et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2024;209:24–36.

questions.stem: Regarding the DEXA-ARDS trial:
options: Patients had PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 200 at 24 h on PEEP ≥ 10 and FiO₂ ≥ 0.5.
It was a double-blind placebo-controlled trial.
It was stopped early because of slow recruitment.
Dexamethasone 20 mg/day was given for 5 days, then 10 mg/day for up to 5 more days.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – inclusion required persistent moderate–severe ARDS: P/F ≤ 200 at 24 h on standardised PEEP ≥ 10 and FiO₂ ≥ 0.5.
- B (False) – it was open-label with no placebo; only outcome assessors were blinded.
- C (True) – it was stopped early for slow recruitment (277 of a planned 314 patients).
- D (True) – dexamethasone 20 mg IV daily on days 1–5, then 10 mg daily on days 6–10 (or until extubation).

**EDIC trap:** open-label design and early stopping are the key limitations to quote.

**Ref:** Villar J et al. (DEXA-ARDS), Lancet Respir Med 2020;8:267–276.

questions.stem: In DEXA-ARDS, 60-day all-cause mortality in the dexamethasone vs control group was approximately:
questions.expl:
**Why D:** In DEXA-ARDS, 60-day mortality was 21 % with dexamethasone versus 36 % with standard care (difference −15.3 %), and ventilator-free days increased by 4.8 (12.3 vs 7.5). Adverse events did not differ significantly.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 31 vs 40 % is the crude 90-day mortality of ACURASYS (31.6 vs 40.7 %).
- B – 42 vs 43 % is the 90-day mortality of ROSE (42.5 vs 42.8 %).
- C – 16 vs 33 % is the 28-day mortality of PROSEVA (16.0 vs 32.8 %).
- E – 29 vs 41 % is RECOVERY mortality in invasively ventilated patients (29.3 vs 41.4 %).

**Ref:** Villar J et al. (DEXA-ARDS), Lancet Respir Med 2020;8:267–276.

questions.stem: Regarding corticosteroids in ARDS:
options: Starting methylprednisolone ≥ 14 days after ARDS onset was associated with increased mortality in LaSRS.
ATS 2024 suggests corticosteroids for patients with ARDS (conditional, moderate certainty).
ESICM 2023 strongly recommends dexamethasone 20 mg/day in all ARDS.
In RECOVERY, dexamethasone 6 mg reduced mortality most clearly in invasively ventilated patients.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – in LaSRS, methylprednisolone started ≥ 14 days after onset was associated with higher 60- and 180-day mortality; overall mortality did not differ.
- B (True) – ATS 2024 suggests corticosteroids in ARDS (conditional, moderate certainty), without a preferred regimen; the SCCM 2024 focused update makes a similar conditional recommendation.
- C (False) – ESICM 2023 does not address pharmacotherapy, including corticosteroids.
- D (True) – in RECOVERY, mortality was 29.3 vs 41.4 % in ventilated patients, with no benefit in those not receiving oxygen.

**Ref:** Steinberg KP et al., N Engl J Med 2006;354:1671–1684; Qadir N et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2024;209:24–36; RECOVERY, N Engl J Med 2021;384:693–704.

questions.stem: A patient with severe ARDS improves in PaO₂/FiO₂ from 90 to 95 mmHg after the first 16-hour prone session. The best interpretation is:
options: Mortality benefit of prone positioning does not depend on the oxygenation response; continue daily sessions while criteria persist
Proceed directly to ECMO without further proning
Shorten sessions to 4 hours
Proning is contraindicated in non-responders
Prone positioning has failed and should be abandoned
questions.expl:
**Why A:** In PROSEVA the mortality benefit of prone positioning was not tied to oxygenation response; it is mediated mainly by more homogeneous stress/strain (less VILI) and RV unloading. Sessions should continue daily (≥ 16 h) until, supine, P/F ≥ 150 with PEEP ≤ 10 and FiO₂ ≤ 0.6 persists for ≥ 4 h.

**Why not the others:**
- B – ECMO is considered for refractory severe ARDS after optimised care including proning, not as the immediate next step after one session.
- C – short sessions (a few hours) explain the failure of older prone trials.
- D – oxygenation non-response is not a contraindication.
- E – the stopping criteria are improvement, a ≥ 20 % P/F fall in two consecutive sessions, or complications – not a small P/F rise.

**Ref:** Guérin C et al. (PROSEVA), N Engl J Med 2013;368:2159–2168.

questions.stem: Mechanisms by which prone positioning benefits patients with ARDS include:
options: Redistribution of most pulmonary perfusion to ventral regions
Reduced ventilator-induced lung injury
More homogeneous distribution of transpulmonary pressure
Increased right ventricular afterload
questions.expl:
- A (False) – pulmonary perfusion remains predominantly dorsal when prone; ventilation becomes more dorsal too, which improves V/Q matching.
- B (True) – more homogeneous distribution of stress and strain reduces ventilator-induced lung injury, the main mechanism of the survival benefit.
- C (True) – the shape match between chest wall and lung makes the pleural (and transpulmonary) pressure gradient more uniform.
- D (False) – proning reduces RV afterload (recruitment, lower PaCO₂ and PVR), which helps acute cor pulmonale.

**EDIC trap:** oxygenation improvement is the visible effect, but less VILI drives survival.

**Ref:** Guérin C et al. (PROSEVA), N Engl J Med 2013;368:2159–2168; Gattinoni L, Pesenti A, Intensive Care Med 2005;31:776–784.

open.q: A 50-year-old with pneumonia-related ARDS has P/F 110 on FiO₂ 0.7 and PEEP 12 cmH₂O, 18 h after intubation, despite VT 6 mL/kg PBW. Outline your management regarding prone positioning, neuromuscular blockade and corticosteroids, justifying each choice with the evidence.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Meets PROSEVA criteria (P/F < 150, FiO₂ ≥ 0.6, PEEP ≥ 5, after 12–24 h stabilisation) → prone positioning ≥ 16 h/session, repeated daily until P/F ≥ 150 with PEEP ≤ 10 and FiO₂ ≤ 0.6 supine.
- PROSEVA: 28-d mortality 16.0 vs 32.8% (HR 0.39), NNT ~6; ESICM strong recommendation, high certainty.
- Check contraindications (unstable spine, ↑ ICP, open abdomen/recent sternotomy, massive haemoptysis, severe instability); prevent pressure sores and tube dislodgement.
- NMB not routinely (ESICM strong against routine infusion; ROSE neutral); consider individually for severe asynchrony, uncontrollable VT/ΔP, refractory hypoxaemia or during proning (ATS conditionally suggests in early severe ARDS).
- Corticosteroids: ATS 2024 conditionally suggests; DEXA-ARDS regimen (dexamethasone 20 mg d1–5, 10 mg d6–10) improved ventilator-free days and 60-d mortality (21 vs 36%), but open-label and stopped early.
- Start early – avoid starting corticosteroids ≥ 14 days after onset (LaSRS: higher mortality).
- Do not judge proning by the oxygenation response; benefit is via ↓ VILI and RV unloading.

open.q: Explain why ACURASYS and ROSE reached different conclusions on neuromuscular blockade in ARDS.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- ACURASYS: 340 patients, cisatracurium 48 h vs placebo, both arms deeply sedated; adjusted HR for 90-d mortality 0.68, crude 31.6 vs 40.7% (p = 0.08).
- ROSE: 1006 patients, NMB + deep sedation vs light sedation (RASS 0 to −1); 90-d mortality 42.5 vs 42.8%, stopped for futility.
- Control arm: deep sedation without NMB in ACURASYS may have caused asynchrony/P-SILI; ROSE reflects modern light-sedation practice.
- ROSE used a high-PEEP strategy in both arms (less atelectrauma) vs low PEEP in ACURASYS.
- ACURASYS primary result was adjusted; ROSE was 3× larger.
- ROSE showed more serious cardiovascular events with NMB (14 vs 4).
- Result: ESICM strongly against routine NMBA infusion; ATS conditionally for in early severe ARDS.

title: W10 · D5 – ESICM ARDS guidelines 2023: summary of recommendations

questions.stem: According to ESICM 2023, in non-intubated patients with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure not due to cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, HFNO compared with conventional oxygen is:
options: Suggested only in COVID-19
Recommended to reduce the risk of intubation (strong, moderate certainty)
Recommended to reduce mortality (strong, high certainty)
Suggested against because of delayed intubation
Not addressed
questions.expl:
**Why B:** ESICM 2023 recommends HFNO over conventional oxygen in AHRF not due to cardiogenic pulmonary oedema to reduce the risk of intubation – strong recommendation, moderate certainty. For mortality the panel made no recommendation, because the evidence showed high certainty of no effect.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the recommendation applies to AHRF in general, not only COVID-19.
- C – HFNO does not reduce mortality; no recommendation was made for this outcome.
- D – concern about delayed intubation is a monitoring issue, not a recommendation against HFNO.
- E – HFNO versus conventional oxygen is explicitly addressed.

**EDIC trap:** HFNO reduces intubation, not death – match the recommendation to the outcome.

**Ref:** Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023;49:727–759.

questions.stem: Which of the following are STRONG recommendations in the ESICM 2023 ARDS guidelines?
options: Against routine continuous infusion of neuromuscular blocking agents in non-COVID ARDS
Higher PEEP strategy using the PEEP/FiO₂ table
Prone positioning for ARDS with PaO₂/FiO₂ < 150 mmHg
Against prolonged high-pressure recruitment manoeuvres
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ESICM recommends against routine continuous NMBA infusion in moderate–severe non-COVID ARDS (strong, moderate certainty), mainly on the basis of ROSE.
- B (False) – there is no recommendation for or against higher PEEP (high certainty of no effect).
- C (True) – prone positioning for P/F < 150 mmHg (PEEP ≥ 5) to reduce mortality is strong, high certainty.
- D (True) – against prolonged high-pressure RM (≥ 35 cmH₂O for ≥ 1 min) is strong, moderate certainty.

**EDIC trap:** "strong" includes strong recommendations against; read the direction and the strength separately.

**Ref:** Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023;49:727–759.

questions.stem: ESICM 2023 makes "no recommendation" regarding higher versus lower PEEP. The certainty of evidence for this question was rated as:
options: Not graded
High certainty of no effect
Moderate certainty of harm
Low certainty of benefit
Very low, because no RCTs exist
questions.expl:
**Why B:** For higher versus lower PEEP (PEEP/FiO₂ strategies), the panel found high certainty that there is no effect on mortality from several large RCTs (ALVEOLI, LOVS, EXPRESS and others). It therefore issued no recommendation for or against – a deliberate statement, not a gap in the evidence.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the question was graded in GRADE format.
- C – harm was shown for prolonged recruitment (ART), not for higher PEEP itself.
- D – the pooled data did not show benefit with sufficient certainty to recommend higher PEEP.
- E – several large RCTs exist on this question.

**EDIC trap:** "no recommendation" ≠ "no data"; here it means high certainty of no effect.

**Ref:** Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023;49:727–759.

questions.stem: Regarding extracorporeal support in ESICM 2023:
options: ECCO₂R is suggested to facilitate ultra-protective ventilation in all moderate ARDS.
The ECMO recommendation is conditional with very low certainty for non-COVID ARDS.
ECCO₂R is recommended against outside randomised trials.
VV-ECMO is recommended for severe ARDS meeting EOLIA criteria, in an ECMO centre meeting organisational standards.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – ECCO₂R is not suggested; ESICM recommends against its use to prevent mortality outside RCTs.
- B (False) – the VV-ECMO recommendation for severe non-COVID ARDS is strong, moderate certainty (strong, low certainty for COVID-19).
- C (True) – against ECCO₂R outside randomised trials, strong recommendation, high certainty of no effect (REST trial).
- D (True) – VV-ECMO is recommended for severe ARDS meeting EOLIA criteria, in an ECMO centre meeting organisational standards, managed as in EOLIA.

**Ref:** Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023;49:727–759; Combes A et al. (EOLIA), N Engl J Med 2018;378:1965–1975.

questions.stem: A patient with ARDS on VT 6 mL/kg PBW and PEEP 14 cmH₂O, after optimisation, has PaO₂/FiO₂ 70 mmHg for 7 hours. Which statement is correct?
options: ECCO₂R is the recommended next step
He meets the EOLIA criterion of PaO₂/FiO₂ < 80 mmHg for > 6 h
EOLIA criteria require PaO₂/FiO₂ < 50 for > 12 h
ECMO is contraindicated because PEEP > 10
He does not yet meet any EOLIA criterion
questions.expl:
**Why B:** EOLIA inclusion (after optimisation with VT 6 mL/kg PBW and PEEP ≥ 10) required one of: P/F < 50 mmHg for > 3 h, P/F < 80 mmHg for > 6 h, or pH < 7.25 with PaCO₂ ≥ 60 mmHg for > 6 h despite RR 35/min. P/F 70 for 7 h meets the second criterion. Prone positioning should still be performed first if not done.

**Why not the others:**
- A – ECCO₂R removes CO₂ but does not correct severe hypoxaemia, and ESICM recommends against it outside trials.
- C – the strictest criterion is P/F < 50 for > 3 h, not > 12 h.
- D – PEEP ≥ 10 is part of optimisation in EOLIA, not a contraindication.
- E – the P/F < 80 for > 6 h criterion is met.

**Ref:** Combes A et al. (EOLIA), N Engl J Med 2018;378:1965–1975; Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023;49:727–759.

questions.stem: Regarding COVID-19–specific statements in ESICM 2023:
options: Awake prone positioning is recommended to reduce mortality.
Awake prone positioning is suggested to reduce intubation.
Low tidal volume ventilation is also recommended in COVID-19 ARDS.
CPAP/NIV is suggested over HFNO to reduce intubation.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – awake prone positioning in COVID-19 is not recommended for mortality; no recommendation was made for this outcome.
- B (True) – it is suggested to reduce the risk of intubation (conditional, low certainty).
- C (True) – low VT (4–8 mL/kg PBW) is also strongly recommended in COVID-19 ARDS, with moderate certainty because of indirectness.
- D (True) – in COVID-19 AHRF, CPAP/NIV is suggested over HFNO to reduce intubation (conditional); in non-COVID AHRF there is no recommendation between them.

**EDIC trap:** COVID statements usually mirror non-COVID ones with lower certainty; the non-invasive support items are the exceptions.

**Ref:** Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023;49:727–759.

questions.stem: Which topic was NOT addressed by the ESICM 2023 ARDS guidelines?
options: Prone positioning
Corticosteroids
Neuromuscular blocking agents
High-flow nasal oxygen
VV-ECMO
questions.expl:
**Why B:** The ESICM 2023 scope was definition, phenotyping and respiratory support strategies; pharmacotherapy, including corticosteroids, was deliberately excluded. Corticosteroids are covered by ATS 2024 (conditional, moderate certainty for) and by the SCCM 2024 corticosteroid focused update.

**Why not the others:**
- A – prone positioning is addressed (strong recommendation, high certainty).
- C – NMBAs are addressed (strong recommendation against routine infusion).
- D – HFNO is addressed (strong recommendation to reduce intubation).
- E – VV-ECMO is addressed (strong recommendation per EOLIA criteria).

**EDIC trap:** NMBAs are drugs but count as "respiratory support" in ESICM 2023 – they are included.

**Ref:** Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023;49:727–759; Qadir N et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2024;209:24–36.

questions.stem: Comparing ESICM 2023 and ATS 2024:
options: Both recommend routine prolonged recruitment manoeuvres in moderate–severe ARDS.
ESICM 2023 suggests higher PEEP without recruitment manoeuvres.
ATS 2024 recommends against corticosteroids for ARDS.
ATS 2024 suggests neuromuscular blockade in early severe ARDS.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – both guidelines strongly recommend against prolonged high-pressure recruitment manoeuvres.
- B (False) – higher PEEP without RM is the ATS 2024 conditional suggestion; ESICM gives no recommendation on PEEP level.
- C (False) – ATS 2024 suggests corticosteroids for ARDS (conditional, moderate certainty).
- D (True) – ATS 2024 suggests NMBA in early severe ARDS (conditional, low certainty), whereas ESICM strongly recommends against routine infusion.

**EDIC trap:** guidelines differ on NMBA, PEEP, corticosteroids and the strength of the ECMO recommendation.

**Ref:** Qadir N et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2024;209:24–36; Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023;49:727–759.

questions.stem: According to ESICM 2023, prone positioning in intubated ARDS should be started:
options: Early after intubation, after a period of stabilisation, if PaO₂/FiO₂ remains < 150 mmHg, for at least 16 consecutive hours
Only in patients on ECMO
Only after 7 days of failed supine ventilation
Immediately at intubation in all ARDS, for 4 hours per day
Only in mild ARDS
questions.expl:
**Why A:** ESICM 2023 recommends prone positioning early after intubation, after a period of stabilisation, in patients whose P/F remains < 150 mmHg, for at least 16 consecutive hours – strong recommendation, high certainty. This reproduces the PROSEVA protocol.

**Why not the others:**
- B – prone positioning is not restricted to ECMO; in PROSEVA ECMO was an exclusion criterion.
- C – benefit was shown with early proning (within 36 h of ventilation), not after 7 days.
- D – proning at intubation without stabilisation and for 4 h/day repeats the design of failed earlier trials.
- E – mild ARDS (P/F > 150) is outside the recommendation.

**Ref:** Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023;49:727–759; Guérin C et al. (PROSEVA), N Engl J Med 2013;368:2159–2168.

questions.stem: Regarding the grading language used by ESICM 2023:
options: "We recommend" denotes a strong recommendation.
"We suggest" denotes a conditional (weak) recommendation.
"No recommendation" always means that no randomised trials exist.
Most recommendations include a separate statement for COVID-19 ARDS.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – "we recommend" denotes a strong recommendation (for or against).
- B (True) – "we suggest" denotes a conditional (weak) recommendation.
- C (False) – "no recommendation" may also reflect high certainty of no effect (e.g. higher PEEP, mechanics-guided PEEP) or a balance of benefit and harm, not only absence of RCTs.
- D (True) – most PICO questions have a separate COVID-19 statement, usually the same direction with lower certainty because of indirectness.

**Ref:** Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023;49:727–759.

open.q: A 45-year-old with influenza pneumonia develops acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure, is intubated and progresses to severe ARDS. Outline a stepwise respiratory management plan according to ESICM 2023, indicating the strength of each recommendation.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Before intubation: HFNO over conventional O₂ to ↓ intubation (strong, moderate); no recommendation HFNO vs NIV in non-COVID AHRF.
- After intubation: VT 4–8 mL/kg PBW (strong) with Pplat < 30 cmH₂O (expert opinion); monitor ΔP (no recommendation, research priority).
- PEEP: no recommendation for higher vs lower or mechanics-guided PEEP (high certainty of no effect); table as a starting point and individualise.
- No prolonged high-pressure RM (strong against); suggest against routine brief RM.
- P/F < 150 after stabilisation → prone positioning early, ≥ 16 consecutive hours (strong, high).
- No routine continuous NMBA infusion (strong against); use individually.
- If EOLIA criteria met (P/F < 50 > 3 h, P/F < 80 > 6 h, or pH < 7.25 with PaCO₂ ≥ 60 > 6 h) → VV-ECMO in an ECMO centre (strong, moderate); no ECCO₂R outside RCTs (strong against).
- Corticosteroids not covered by ESICM; ATS 2024 conditionally suggests them.

open.q: Explain why ESICM 2023 and ATS 2024 reach different recommendations on PEEP, NMBA and ECMO despite largely the same evidence.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Differences arise from different interpretation of the same data and a different threshold for a "strong" recommendation.
- PEEP: ESICM no recommendation (high certainty of no effect from PEEP RCTs); ATS conditionally suggests higher PEEP without RM in moderate–severe ARDS (weighting the P/F ≤ 200 subgroup signal).
- NMBA: ESICM strongly against routine infusion (weighting ROSE); ATS conditionally suggests in early severe ARDS (weighting ACURASYS).
- ECMO: ESICM strong recommendation per EOLIA criteria (meta-analysis RR ~0.72, moderate certainty); ATS conditional, low certainty for selected patients.
- EOLIA itself was primarily non-significant (35 vs 46%, p = 0.09) with 28% crossover.
- Agreement: low VT, prone positioning in severe ARDS (ESICM ≥ 16 h; ATS 2017 > 12 h/day), against prolonged RM, ECMO in selected severe patients.

title: Monthly review – January (Sat 30 Jan 2027)

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and tense ascites, not taking diuretics, has Na⁺ 121 mmol/L, serum osmolality 255 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 410 mOsm/kg and urine Na⁺ 12 mmol/L. The most likely mechanism of his hyponatraemia is:
options: SIAD
Secondary adrenal insufficiency
Primary polydipsia
Pseudohyponatraemia
Low effective circulating volume
questions.expl:
**Why E:** The serum is hypotonic (255 mOsm/kg) and a urine osmolality > 100 mOsm/kg shows that ADH is active. A urine Na⁺ ≤ 30 mmol/L without diuretics means the kidney is avidly retaining sodium because the *effective* arterial volume is low (cirrhosis, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome) despite total-body excess. Treat with fluid restriction and the underlying disease.

**Why not the others:**

- A – SIAD requires clinical euvolaemia and a urine Na⁺ > 30 mmol/L.
- B – Secondary adrenal insufficiency (cortisol deficiency) behaves like SIAD, with urine Na⁺ > 30 mmol/L.
- C – Primary polydipsia suppresses ADH, so urine osmolality would be ≤ 100 mOsm/kg.
- D – Pseudohyponatraemia has a normal measured serum osmolality, not 255 mOsm/kg.

**EDIC trap:** an oedematous, "overloaded" patient can still have a low effective circulating volume.

**Ref:** Spasovski G, et al. Clinical practice guideline on hyponatraemia. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:320–331.

Review: [W06/D1](#W06-D1)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has hypotonic hyponatraemia (Na⁺ 124 mmol/L). According to the European guideline (Spasovski 2014):
options: If she has nausea without vomiting and confusion, a single infusion of 150 mL 3 % saline over 20 minutes is appropriate.
After correction of the stimulus for ADH (e.g. restoration of volume), aquaresis may cause an uncontrolled rise in Na⁺.
Vomiting would classify her symptoms as severe.
If she is hypovolaemic without severe symptoms, 0.9 % saline or a balanced crystalloid at 0.5–1 mL/kg/h is appropriate.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Nausea without vomiting, confusion and headache are moderately severe symptoms: a single 150 mL infusion of 3 % saline over 20 min.
- B (True) – Once the ADH stimulus (hypovolaemia, pain, nausea, drugs) is removed, aquaresis can raise Na⁺ uncontrollably – the main cause of overcorrection.
- C (True) – Vomiting, seizures, somnolence, coma or cardiorespiratory distress are severe symptoms: 150 mL 3 % saline over 20 min, repeated until Na⁺ has risen by 5 mmol/L.
- D (True) – In hypovolaemic hyponatraemia without severe symptoms, extracellular volume is restored with 0.9 % saline or a balanced crystalloid at 0.5–1 mL/kg/h.

**EDIC trap:** whatever the protocol, limit the rise to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 h and 8 mmol/L per day thereafter.

**Ref:** Spasovski G, et al. Clinical practice guideline on hyponatraemia. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:320–331.

Review: [W06/D1](#W06-D1)

questions.stem: A 60-kg woman (TBW 0.5 × body weight) develops polyuria after pituitary surgery; urine osmolality is 120 mOsm/kg and Na⁺ is 154 mmol/L. Her free water deficit is approximately:
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Free water deficit = TBW × (Na⁺/140 − 1) = 30 L × (154/140 − 1) = 30 × 0.1 = 3.0 L. Polyuria with dilute urine (< 300 mOsm/kg) after pituitary surgery points to central diabetes insipidus, which responds to desmopressin.

**Why not the others:**

- B – 1.5 L is half the correct value, e.g. from using a TBW of 15 L.
- C – 4.5 L overestimates the deficit; it would need a TBW of 45 L.
- D – 2.0 L underestimates it; with TBW 30 L it corresponds to Na⁺ ≈ 149 mmol/L.
- E – 1.0 L would correspond to Na⁺ ≈ 145 mmol/L.

**EDIC trap:** the formula ignores ongoing losses – add continuing urine output to the replacement plan.

**Ref:** Adrogué HJ, Madias NE. Hypernatremia. *N Engl J Med* 2000;342:1493–1499.

Review: [W06/D1](#W06-D1)

questions.stem: A 75-kg man with rhabdomyolysis has K⁺ 7.0 mmol/L with peaked T waves and a widened QRS. Pre-treatment blood glucose is 5 mmol/L.
options: Nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg removes potassium from the body.
10 mL of 10 % calcium gluconate provides roughly the same amount of calcium as 10 mL of 10 % calcium chloride.
After insulin 10 U with 25 g glucose, a 10 % glucose infusion at 50 mL/h for 5 hours is suggested.
Because hyperphosphataemia is likely, calcium should be given only for symptoms or hyperkalaemia, given the risk of metastatic calcification.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – β₂-agonists only shift K⁺ into cells (onset ~30 min); total-body K⁺ is unchanged and rebound follows, so removal needs dialysis, diuresis or binders.
- B (False) – 10 mL of 10 % CaCl₂ contains 6.8 mmol Ca²⁺ vs ~2.2 mmol in 10 mL of 10 % calcium gluconate; about 30 mL of gluconate is equivalent.
- C (True) – With a pre-treatment glucose < 7 mmol/L, a 10 % glucose infusion at 50 mL/h for 5 h is suggested after insulin–glucose to prevent late hypoglycaemia.
- D (True) – In rhabdomyolysis calcium deposits in damaged muscle and is released during recovery, so it is given only for symptoms or hyperkalaemia – the broad QRS here is such an indication.

**EDIC trap:** calcium stabilises the membrane but does not lower K⁺.

**Ref:** European Resuscitation Council. ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation. *Resuscitation* 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753.

Review: [W06/D2](#W06-D2), [W06/D3](#W06-D3)

questions.stem: A patient with several days of vomiting from gastric outlet obstruction has K⁺ 2.6 mmol/L. The main route of potassium loss is:
options: Direct loss in gastric fluid
Reduced dietary intake alone
Transcellular shift caused by metabolic acidosis
Loss in stool
Renal loss driven by bicarbonaturia and secondary aldosteronism
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Gastric fluid contains only ~5–10 mmol/L K⁺, so direct losses are small.
