- D (True) – an end-expiratory occlusion of 15 s that raises CO by ≥ 5 % predicts responsiveness in ventilated patients.

**EDIC trap:** ESICM 2021 advises against basic ultrasound for fluid responsiveness in shock without obvious hypovolaemia.

**Ref:** Monnet X et al., Ann Intensive Care 2016; Robba C et al., ESICM basic ultrasound consensus, Intensive Care Med 2021. Review: [W04/D2](#W04-D2), [W04/D5](#W04-D5).

questions.stem: Which trial randomised UK ICU patients to a pulmonary artery catheter or no PAC (without a treatment protocol) and found hospital mortality of 68 vs 66 % (NS), with complications in about 10 %?
options: ESCAPE
Sandham
ProCESS
SUPPORT
PAC-Man
questions.expl:
**Why E:** PAC-Man randomised 1041 UK ICU patients to a PAC or no PAC, leaving management to the clinician. Hospital mortality was 68 vs 66 % (NS), and about 10 % had a PAC-related complication. It tested the device, not a treatment protocol.

**Why not the others:**
- A – ESCAPE tested PAC-guided therapy in decompensated heart failure.
- B – Sandham tested PAC-guided goal-directed therapy in high-risk surgical patients.
- C – ProCESS was an EGDT trial in septic shock.
- D – SUPPORT (Connors 1996) was observational and suggested harm.

**Ref:** Harvey S et al., PAC-Man, Lancet 2005. Review: [W04/D3](#W04-D3).

questions.stem: Regarding cardiac output measurement:
options: In thermodilution, CO is inversely proportional to the area under the temperature curve.
GEDV is a dynamic index of fluid responsiveness.
Pulse-contour values stay reliable without recalibration after a major change in vascular tone.
Tricuspid regurgitation can cause errors in thermodilution.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – by the Stewart–Hamilton equation, CO is inversely proportional to the area under the thermodilution curve.
- B (False) – GEDV is a **static** preload variable; it does not predict fluid responsiveness.
- C (False) – after a major change in vascular tone, pulse-contour values drift and must be recalibrated.
- D (True) – tricuspid regurgitation, intracardiac shunts and low-flow states cause thermodilution errors.

**EDIC trap:** static values (CVP, GEDV) describe preload, but only dynamic tests predict response to fluid.

**Ref:** Cecconi M et al., ESICM consensus on circulatory shock, Intensive Care Med 2014. Review: [W04/D3](#W04-D3).

questions.stem: A patient in septic shock after initial resuscitation has MAP 70 mmHg, ScvO₂ 74 %, lactate 4.1 mmol/L and P(cv-a)CO₂ 9 mmHg. The best interpretation is:
options: Oxygen delivery is adequate because ScvO₂ is > 70 %
P(cv-a)CO₂ is only meaningful when ScvO₂ is < 70 %
Resuscitation is complete
Cardiac output is probably inadequate despite the normal ScvO₂
The raised lactate must be type B
questions.expl:
**Why D:** A central venous-to-arterial CO₂ gap ≥ 6 mmHg suggests that blood flow is too low to clear tissue CO₂, even when ScvO₂ is ≥ 70 %. In sepsis, a normal or high ScvO₂ can reflect impaired O₂ extraction rather than adequate delivery. With lactate 4.1 mmol/L, raising cardiac output should be considered.

**Why not the others:**
- A – ScvO₂ > 70 % does not exclude tissue hypoxia in sepsis.
- B – P(cv-a)CO₂ is most useful precisely when ScvO₂ is normal.
- C – persistent hyperlactataemia and a high CO₂ gap show that resuscitation is incomplete.
- E – the lactate may be type A or B; a raised CO₂ gap points to a flow problem.

**Ref:** Cecconi M et al., Intensive Care Med 2014; Ospina-Tascón GA et al., Crit Care 2013. Review: [W04/D4](#W04-D4), [W04/D1](#W04-D1).

questions.stem: Regarding the EGDT trials:
options: ProMISe was conducted in Australia.
ARISE was conducted in Australia and New Zealand.
The PRISM meta-analysis found lower mortality with EGDT.
ProCESS had three arms (EGDT, protocol-based standard care, usual care).
questions.expl:
- A (False) – ProMISe was conducted in England.
- B (True) – ARISE was conducted in Australia and New Zealand.
- C (False) – the PRISM meta-analysis found no mortality benefit of EGDT, with higher costs and longer ICU stay.
- D (True) – ProCESS had three arms: EGDT, protocol-based standard care and usual care.

**EDIC trap:** none of the three trials reproduced the benefit seen by Rivers (30.5 vs 46.5 %), probably because usual care had improved.

**Ref:** PRISM Investigators, N Engl J Med 2017; Rivers E et al., N Engl J Med 2001. Review: [W04/D4](#W04-D4).

questions.stem: In the study by Jansen et al., lactate-guided therapy aimed to lower lactate by:
options: 10 % per hour
50 % in 6 hours
Normalisation within 1 hour
20 % every 2 hours
5 % per 24 hours
questions.expl:
**Why D:** In Jansen 2010, the lactate-guided group aimed to decrease lactate by ≥ 20 % every 2 hours during the first 8 hours. Adjusted hospital mortality was lower, although the unadjusted difference was not significant.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 10 % per hour was not the protocol target.
- B – 50 % in 6 hours is not the Jansen target.
- C – normalisation within 1 hour is unrealistic, because lactate kinetics are slow.
- E – 5 % per 24 hours is far too slow to guide resuscitation.

**EDIC trap:** lactate can be type B (adrenaline, liver failure), so do not chase it with fluid alone.

**Ref:** Jansen TC et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2010. Review: [W04/D4](#W04-D4).

questions.stem: Regarding acute cor pulmonale (ACP) and echocardiography in shock:
options: ACP occurs in about 22 % of patients with ARDS.
ACP is defined as an RV/LV area ratio > 0.6 with septal dyskinesia.
A non-dilated IVC almost excludes cardiac tamponade.
In ACP with hypotension, noradrenaline rather than a fluid bolus is the first-line treatment.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – acute cor pulmonale occurs in about 22 % of patients with moderate–severe ARDS.
- B (True) – ACP is defined by RV dilatation (RV/LV end-diastolic area ratio > 0.6) with septal dyskinesia.
- C (True) – a small, collapsing IVC makes tamponade very unlikely; tamponade almost always causes a plethoric IVC.
- D (True) – fluids worsen RV dilatation and septal shift, so give noradrenaline and treat the cause.

**EDIC trap:** in ACP, protect the RV with lower plateau pressure, avoiding hypercapnia, and prone positioning.

**Ref:** Mekontso Dessap A et al., Intensive Care Med 2016; Robba C et al., Intensive Care Med 2021. Review: [W04/D5](#W04-D5).

questions.stem: A 64-year-old with anterior STEMI has MAP 70 mmHg on noradrenaline and dobutamine, lactate 4 mmol/L and oliguria. His condition is not deteriorating further. The SCAI shock stage is:
options: Stage A
Stage B
Stage C
Stage D
Stage E
questions.expl:
**Why C:** SCAI stage C ("classic") is hypoperfusion (lactate ≥ 2, oliguria) that requires pharmacological or mechanical support beyond volume. This applies whatever the blood pressure. He needs two drugs but is not deteriorating, so he has not progressed to stage D.

**Why not the others:**
- A – stage A is "at risk", without hypotension or hypoperfusion.
- B – stage B is hypotension or tachycardia without hypoperfusion.
- D – stage D requires deterioration despite initial treatment.
- E – stage E is extremis, e.g. refractory collapse, ongoing CPR or lactate ≥ 8 mmol/L.

**Ref:** Naidu SS et al., SCAI SHOCK stage update, J Am Coll Cardiol 2022. Review: [W07/D1](#W07-D1).

questions.stem: Regarding cardiogenic shock (ESC 2026 and trials):
options: In the SHOCK trial, urgent revascularisation reduced 30-day mortality.
The ESC 2026 definition of cardiogenic shock has no fixed BP threshold.
Unselected use of mechanical circulatory support has a class III recommendation.
A microaxial pump has a class IIa recommendation in selected STEMI-related cardiogenic shock.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – SHOCK did not reach significance at 30 days (46.7 vs 56.0 %); the benefit of early revascularisation appeared at 6 months.
- B (True) – ESC 2026 defines cardiogenic shock by hypoperfusion due to cardiac dysfunction, with no fixed BP threshold.
- C (True) – routine, unselected use of mechanical circulatory support is class III.
- D (True) – a microaxial flow pump is IIa in selected STEMI-related cardiogenic shock, based on DanGer Shock.

**Ref:** Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026; Hochman JS et al., SHOCK, N Engl J Med 1999. Review: [W07/D1](#W07-D1), [W07/D2](#W07-D2).

questions.stem: Which patient would have met the main inclusion criteria of DanGer Shock (microaxial flow pump)?
options: Patient with acute myocarditis, LVEF 15 % and lactate 5 mmol/L
Awake patient with STEMI-related cardiogenic shock, LVEF 30 % and lactate 4 mmol/L
Patient with STEMI, LVEF 35 % and lactate 1.8 mmol/L
Patient with STEMI, LVEF 55 % and lactate 3 mmol/L
Comatose survivor of OHCA with STEMI and lactate 6 mmol/L
questions.expl:
**Why B:** DanGer Shock enrolled STEMI-related cardiogenic shock with LVEF < 45 % and lactate ≥ 2.5 mmol/L, excluding comatose OHCA survivors. Impella CP reduced 180-day mortality (45.8 vs 58.5 %). However, it caused more bleeding, limb ischaemia and renal replacement therapy.

**Why not the others:**
- A – myocarditis is not STEMI-related shock.
- C – lactate 1.8 mmol/L is below the inclusion threshold.
- D – LVEF 55 % is above the < 45 % limit.
- E – comatose OHCA survivors were excluded.

**Ref:** Møller JE et al., DanGer Shock, N Engl J Med 2024. Review: [W07/D2](#W07-D2).

questions.stem: Regarding acute coronary syndromes in the ICU:
options: COMPLETE supports immediate complete multivessel PCI in cardiogenic shock.
An O₂ saturation step-up between the right atrium and pulmonary artery suggests a ventricular septal rupture.
The absence of a new murmur excludes papillary muscle rupture.
In CULPRIT-SHOCK, culprit-lesion-only PCI increased death or RRT at 30 days compared with immediate multivessel PCI.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – COMPLETE showed benefit of staged complete revascularisation in **haemodynamically stable** STEMI, not in shock.
- B (True) – an O₂ saturation step-up from right atrium to pulmonary artery indicates a left-to-right shunt through a ventricular septal rupture.
- C (False) – acute severe MR from papillary muscle rupture can be silent; echocardiography is needed.
- D (False) – CULPRIT-SHOCK showed **lower** death or RRT at 30 days with culprit-only PCI (45.9 vs 55.4 %).

**Ref:** Thiele H et al., CULPRIT-SHOCK, N Engl J Med 2017; Mehta SR et al., COMPLETE, N Engl J Med 2019; Byrne RA et al., 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023. Review: [W07/D3](#W07-D3).

questions.stem: A patient with chronic HFrEF on high-dose bisoprolol presents in low-output decompensated HF with hypoperfusion. The inotrope whose effect is most reduced by β-blockade is:
options: Milrinone
Levosimendan
Dobutamine
Vasopressin
Noradrenaline
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Dobutamine is a β₁-agonist, so its inotropic effect is blunted by high-dose β-blockade. Milrinone (PDE3 inhibitor) and levosimendan (calcium sensitiser) act downstream of or independently of the β-receptor and are preferred in this case. Both are inodilators, so noradrenaline is often needed for hypotension.

**Why not the others:**
- A – milrinone acts downstream of the β-receptor.
- B – levosimendan acts by calcium sensitisation and K-ATP channel opening.
- D – vasopressin is a vasopressor (V1), not an inotrope.
- E – noradrenaline is mainly an α-agonist vasopressor; its β₁ effect is minor.

**Ref:** Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026. Review: [W07/D4](#W07-D4).

questions.stem: Regarding trials in acute heart failure:
options: In 3CPO, NIV reduced 7-day mortality compared with standard oxygen therapy.
Opiates are routinely recommended for dyspnoea in acute pulmonary oedema.
In SURVIVE, 180-day mortality was similar with levosimendan and dobutamine.
In DOREMI, milrinone was superior to dobutamine.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – in 3CPO, NIV improved dyspnoea and acidosis faster but did not reduce 7-day mortality.
- B (False) – opiates are not recommended routinely (class III); they are associated with more ventilation and mortality.
- C (True) – in SURVIVE, 180-day mortality was similar with levosimendan and dobutamine.
- D (False) – in DOREMI, milrinone and dobutamine had similar outcomes in cardiogenic shock.

**Ref:** Gray A et al., 3CPO, N Engl J Med 2008; Mebazaa A et al., SURVIVE, JAMA 2007; Mathew R et al., DOREMI, N Engl J Med 2021; Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026. Review: [W07/D4](#W07-D4).

questions.stem: A patient with acute severe RV failure from pulmonary hypertension is worsening and needs intubation. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: A 1-litre fluid bolus before induction to protect preload
Start a vasopressor before induction and use RV-protective ventilation
Induction without vasopressor, with high PEEP and VT 10 mL/kg to recruit the lungs
Permissive hypercapnia up to PaCO₂ 80 mmHg to minimise airway pressures
Avoid noradrenaline because it raises pulmonary vascular resistance
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Induction and positive pressure can cause RV collapse in acute RV failure. Avoid intubation if possible. If it is needed, start a vasopressor before induction to keep systemic pressure (MAP > 60 mmHg) and RV coronary perfusion. Then ventilate with low pressures, while avoiding hypoxaemia and hypercapnia.

**Why not the others:**
- A – a large fluid bolus overdistends the RV and lowers CO through ventricular interdependence.
- C – high PEEP and large VT raise PVR and RV afterload.
- D – hypercapnia and acidosis cause pulmonary vasoconstriction.
- E – noradrenaline is first-line, because it restores coronary perfusion with little effect on PVR.

**Ref:** Harjola VP et al., HFA/ESC statement on acute RV failure, Eur J Heart Fail 2016. Review: [W07/D5](#W07-D5).

questions.stem: Regarding new-onset atrial fibrillation in the ICU:
options: Diltiazem is a suitable rate-control drug when LVEF is 30 %.
ESC 2024 uses CHA₂DS₂-VA, which no longer counts female sex.
Cardioversion without anticoagulation or TEE is acceptable only within 24 h of onset.
The rate-control target is < 110/min.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – diltiazem and verapamil are negatively inotropic and are used only when LVEF is > 40 %; use a β-blocker, amiodarone or digoxin instead.
- B (True) – ESC 2024 uses CHA₂DS₂-VA, which drops female sex as a risk factor.
- C (True) – early cardioversion without prior anticoagulation or TEE is acceptable only within 24 h of onset.
- D (True) – lenient rate control (< 110/min) is the initial target.

**EDIC trap:** treat the trigger first – sepsis, hypovolaemia, K⁺/Mg²⁺ and catecholamines.

**Ref:** Van Gelder IC et al., 2024 ESC AF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024. Review: [W08/D1](#W08-D1).

questions.stem: A patient has a QTc of 560 ms and recurrent runs of polymorphic VT with a twisting axis (torsade de pointes). Between episodes BP is stable. The first-line drug is:
options: Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV
Sotalol
Adenosine 6 mg
Procainamide
Amiodarone 300 mg IV
questions.expl:
**Why A:** IV magnesium sulfate 2 g is first-line for torsade de pointes, whatever the serum magnesium level. Also stop QT-prolonging drugs, correct K⁺ and raise the heart rate (isoprenaline or overdrive pacing). Defibrillate if it degenerates into sustained VF.

**Why not the others:**
- B – sotalol prolongs QT and can cause torsade.
- C – adenosine has no role in polymorphic VT.
- D – procainamide is a class Ia drug that prolongs QT.
- E – amiodarone prolongs QT further.

**Ref:** Zeppenfeld K et al., 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias, Eur Heart J 2022. Review: [W08/D1](#W08-D1).

questions.stem: Regarding acute pulmonary embolism:
options: In intermediate-high risk PE, anticoagulation with monitoring and rescue thrombolysis if the patient deteriorates is recommended.
In high-risk PE, systemic thrombolysis (e.g. alteplase 100 mg over 2 h) is indicated.
Fluid loading in RV failure from PE should be limited (≤ 500 mL).
PEITHO showed lower mortality with tenecteplase in intermediate-high risk PE.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – intermediate-high risk PE: anticoagulation with monitoring, and rescue reperfusion if the patient deteriorates.
- B (True) – high-risk PE needs systemic thrombolysis (e.g. alteplase 100 mg over 2 h); surgery or catheter therapy is used if it is contraindicated or fails.
- C (True) – cautious fluid (≤ 500 mL) only; more fluid worsens RV dilatation.
- D (False) – PEITHO reduced death or haemodynamic decompensation, but not mortality, at the cost of more major bleeding and haemorrhagic stroke.

**Ref:** Konstantinides SV et al., 2019 ESC PE Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2020; Meyer G et al., PEITHO, N Engl J Med 2014. Review: [W08/D2](#W08-D2).

questions.stem: CT angiography shows an intimal tear in the descending aorta, with the dissection extending retrogradely into the ascending aorta. The classification and management are:
options: Stanford B – medical therapy
Stanford B – TEVAR
DeBakey III – medical therapy
Stanford A – emergency surgery
Stanford A – medical therapy because the entry tear is distal
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Stanford classification depends on involvement of the ascending aorta, wherever the entry tear lies. A descending tear with retrograde extension into the ascending aorta is type A, which needs emergency surgery. Untreated type A has a mortality of about 1–2 % per hour early on.

**Why not the others:**
- A – this is not type B, because the ascending aorta is involved.
- B – TEVAR is for complicated type B dissection.
- C – DeBakey III involves only the descending aorta.
- E – the entry site does not change the type or the need for surgery.

**Ref:** Mazzolai L et al., 2024 ESC Guidelines on peripheral arterial and aortic diseases, Eur Heart J 2024. Review: [W08/D3](#W08-D3).

questions.stem: Regarding acute aortic dissection and tamponade:
options: A pulsus paradoxus > 10 mmHg supports tamponade.
The targets in dissection are SBP < 120 mmHg and HR ≤ 60/min.
In tamponade from type A dissection, complete pericardial drainage to normotension is the goal before surgery.
A vasodilator should be started before the β-blocker.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – pulsus paradoxus (fall in SBP > 10 mmHg on inspiration) supports tamponade.
- B (True) – in acute dissection, target SBP < 120 mmHg and HR ≤ 60/min.
- C (False) – in haemopericardium from type A dissection, the aim is a bridge to theatre: small-volume controlled drainage with permissive BP, not full drainage to normotension.
- D (False) – give the IV β-blocker **first**; a vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia and increases aortic wall stress.

**Ref:** Mazzolai L et al., 2024 ESC aortic guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024; Menger J et al., 2025 ESC myocarditis and pericarditis guidelines, Eur Heart J 2025. Review: [W08/D3](#W08-D3).

questions.stem: A patient with an acute intracerebral haemorrhage, presenting within 2 h, has SBP 230 mmHg. The most appropriate BP strategy is:
options: Target SBP 160–180 mmHg only after 24 h
Target SBP 140–160 mmHg within 6 h, avoiding a fall > 70 mmHg in 1 hour
Do not treat BP in ICH
Lower MAP by 50 % in the first hour
Lower SBP to < 110 mmHg within 1 hour
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In acute ICH, lowering SBP to 140–160 mmHg within 6 h should be considered (IIa). When SBP is ≥ 220 mmHg, avoid a fall of more than 70 mmHg within the first hour. Too rapid or too deep a fall has been linked to renal and neurological harm.

**Why not the others:**
- A – waiting 24 h misses the early window when haematoma expansion occurs.
- C – BP is treated in ICH.
- D – a 50 % fall is not a recommended target.
- E – ATACH-2 (target 110–139 mmHg) gave no benefit and caused more AKI.

**Ref:** McEvoy JW et al., 2024 ESC Hypertension Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024; Qureshi AI et al., ATACH-2, N Engl J Med 2016. Review: [W08/D4](#W08-D4).

questions.stem: Regarding hypertensive emergencies:
options: In cocaine-induced hypertensive crisis, a β-blocker alone is the first choice.
In most emergencies, MAP is lowered by about 50 % within the first hour.
A hypertensive emergency requires BP ≥ 220/130 mmHg.
After mechanical thrombectomy, an SBP target < 120 mmHg improves outcome.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – in cocaine or phaeochromocytoma crisis, use α-blockade (phentolamine) or benzodiazepines; a β-blocker alone causes unopposed α-vasoconstriction.
- B (False) – in most emergencies, MAP is lowered by 20–25 % over the first hours; faster falls are reserved for aortic dissection and pulmonary oedema.
- C (False) – a hypertensive emergency is defined by acute hypertension-mediated organ damage, usually with BP ≥ 180/110 mmHg.
- D (False) – in ENCHANTED2/MT, an SBP target < 120 mmHg after thrombectomy worsened functional outcome.

**Ref:** van den Born BJH et al., ESC Council on Hypertension position, Eur Heart J Cardiovasc Pharmacother 2019; Yang P et al., ENCHANTED2/MT, Lancet 2022. Review: [W08/D4](#W08-D4).

questions.stem: A patient with aortic valve endocarditis develops acute severe aortic regurgitation and cardiogenic shock. Which intervention is contraindicated?
options: Emergency cardiac surgery
Noradrenaline
Transoesophageal echocardiography
Intra-aortic balloon pump
Dobutamine
questions.expl:
**Why D:** An intra-aortic balloon pump inflates in diastole, so it increases regurgitant volume in aortic regurgitation. It is contraindicated in significant AR and in aortic dissection. Acute severe AR from endocarditis needs emergency surgery.

**Why not the others:**
- A – emergency surgery is the definitive treatment.
- B – noradrenaline may be needed for hypotension, although excess afterload increases regurgitation.
- C – TEE is essential to assess vegetations, abscess and valve damage.
- E – dobutamine is helpful, because a higher heart rate shortens diastole and limits regurgitation.

**EDIC trap:** in acute AR, bradycardia is harmful – avoid β-blockers.

**Ref:** Delgado V et al., 2023 ESC Endocarditis Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023; Praz F et al., 2025 ESC/EACTS Valvular Heart Disease Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2025. Review: [W08/D5](#W08-D5).

questions.stem: Regarding drugs in ALS (ERC 2025):
options: In VF/pVT, adrenaline 1 mg is given after the third shock.
PARAMEDIC2 showed better survival with a favourable neurological outcome after adrenaline.
A low ETCO₂ alone is enough to decide to stop CPR.
Lidocaine 100 mg is an alternative to amiodarone after the third shock.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – in shockable rhythms, give adrenaline 1 mg after the third shock, then every 3–5 min.
- B (False) – PARAMEDIC2 improved 30-day survival (3.2 vs 2.4 %), but not survival with a favourable neurological outcome.
- C (False) – low ETCO₂ alone must not be used to decide to stop CPR.
- D (True) – lidocaine 100 mg is an alternative to amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock.

**Ref:** Soar J et al., ERC 2025 ALS, Resuscitation 2025; Perkins GD et al., PARAMEDIC2, N Engl J Med 2018; Kudenchuk PJ et al., ALPS, N Engl J Med 2016. Review: [W09/D1](#W09-D1).

questions.stem: A ventilated patient after ROSC (ERC-ESICM 2025) should be managed with:
options: Hyperventilation to PaCO₂ 3.5 kPa
PaO₂ > 20 kPa to protect the brain
SpO₂ 94–98 %, PaO₂ 10–13 kPa and PaCO₂ 4.7–6.0 kPa
SpO₂ 88–92 % and PaCO₂ 6.0–7.5 kPa
SpO₂ 100 % for the first 24 h
questions.expl:
**Why C:** ERC-ESICM 2025 recommends normoxia (SpO₂ 94–98 %, PaO₂ 10–13 kPa) and normocapnia (PaCO₂ 4.7–6.0 kPa) after ROSC. Ventilate with VT 6–8 mL/kg PBW. Both hypoxaemia and hyperoxia are avoided.

**Why not the others:**
- A – hyperventilation causes cerebral vasoconstriction and ischaemia.
- B – PaO₂ > 20 kPa is hyperoxia, which has no proven benefit.
- D – SpO₂ 88–92 % applies to hypercapnic COPD, and mild hypercapnia is not the post-ROSC target.
- E – 100 % SpO₂ only briefly while it cannot be measured reliably; then titrate FiO₂ down.

**Ref:** Nolan JP et al., ERC-ESICM 2025 Post-Resuscitation Care, Resuscitation 2025. Review: [W09/D2](#W09-D2).

questions.stem: Regarding temperature control after cardiac arrest:
options: Large volumes of cold IV fluid are recommended prehospital.
HYPERION enrolled patients with shockable rhythms.
ERC-ESICM 2025 advises against actively rewarming patients with mild hypothermia after ROSC.
In TTM2, the normothermia arm received active fever prevention, with a device started at ≥ 37.8 °C.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – large volumes of cold IV fluid prehospital are not recommended (more re-arrest and pulmonary oedema).
- B (False) – HYPERION enrolled **non-shockable** rhythms (CPC 1–2: 10.2 vs 5.7 %, a fragile result).
- C (True) – mildly hypothermic patients after ROSC should not be actively rewarmed.
- D (True) – in TTM2, the normothermia arm received active fever prevention, with a device started at ≥ 37.8 °C.

**EDIC trap:** ERC-ESICM 2025: actively prevent fever, target ≤ 37.5 °C for 36–72 h.

**Ref:** Nolan JP et al., ERC-ESICM 2025, Resuscitation 2025; Lascarrou JB et al., HYPERION, N Engl J Med 2019; Dankiewicz J et al., TTM2, N Engl J Med 2021. Review: [W09/D3](#W09-D3).

questions.stem: A comatose patient 72 h after OHCA has NSE 80 µg/L at 48 h, but the laboratory reports that the sample was haemolysed. Which statement is correct?
options: NSE should be measured only at 24 h
Haemolysis falsely raises NSE, so the value is unreliable
NSE is unaffected by haemolysis but affected by sedation
Haemolysis falsely lowers NSE
NSE > 60 µg/L is diagnostic of a poor outcome on its own
questions.expl:
**Why B:** NSE is present in red blood cells and platelets, so haemolysis falsely raises it. A haemolysed value cannot be used for prognostication. NSE > 60 µg/L at 48–72 h is one predictor; poor outcome is "likely" only with ≥ 2 predictors at ≥ 72 h and no confounders.

**Why not the others:**
- A – NSE is measured serially at 24, 48 and 72 h; the 48–72 h values are the most informative.
- C – sedation affects EEG and clinical examination, not NSE, which is affected by haemolysis.
- D – haemolysis raises, not lowers, NSE.
- E – no single predictor is used alone in the multimodal algorithm.

**Ref:** Nolan JP et al., ERC-ESICM 2025 Post-Resuscitation Care, Resuscitation 2025. Review: [W09/D4](#W09-D4).

questions.stem: Regarding ECPR and special circumstances (ERC 2025):
options: In anaphylaxis without cardiac arrest, the first-line drug is IM adrenaline 0.5 mg.
At a core temperature < 30 °C, adrenaline is withheld and up to 3 shocks are given.
In ARREST (n = 30), survival was 43 % with ECPR vs 7 % with standard ACLS.
INCEPTION showed a significant survival benefit of ECPR.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – in anaphylaxis without arrest, IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (anterolateral thigh) is first-line, repeated after 5 min if needed.
- B (True) – below 30 °C, adrenaline is withheld and up to 3 shocks are given; drug intervals are doubled at 30–34 °C.
- C (True) – in ARREST (n = 30), survival to discharge was 43 % with ECPR vs 7 % with standard ACLS.
- D (False) – INCEPTION showed no significant benefit (20 vs 16 %, NS), partly due to a long time to flow.

**EDIC trap:** ERC: consider ECPR only in selected patients in experienced systems.

**Ref:** Lott C et al., ERC 2025 Special Circumstances, Resuscitation 2025; Yannopoulos D et al., ARREST, Lancet 2020; Suverein MM et al., INCEPTION, N Engl J Med 2023. Review: [W09/D5](#W09-D5).

title: W14 · D3 – Review: respiratory

questions.stem: A non-intubated patient with pneumonia has bilateral opacities. On HFNO at 50 L/min and FiO₂ 0.5, SpO₂ is 94 %. No arterial blood gas is available. Which statement is correct?
options: He meets the Berlin definition of moderate ARDS
He meets the 2024 global definition (S/F 188 ≤ 315 on HFNO ≥ 30 L/min), but not the Berlin definition
He meets the global definition only if lung ultrasound is normal
He cannot be classified without a PaO₂
He meets neither definition, because ARDS requires intubation
questions.expl:
**Why B:** The 2024 global definition extends ARDS to non-intubated patients on HFNO ≥ 30 L/min. It accepts SpO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 315 when SpO₂ ≤ 97 %. Here S/F = 94/0.5 = 188, so he qualifies. Berlin requires PEEP/CPAP ≥ 5 cmH₂O and a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio, neither of which is available here.

**Why not the others:**
- A – HFNO does not satisfy the Berlin PEEP/CPAP requirement.
- C – lung ultrasound can show bilateral opacities; a normal scan would argue against ARDS.
- D – the global definition allows S/F instead of P/F.
- E – neither definition requires intubation (Berlin accepts NIV/CPAP).

**Ref:** Matthay MA et al., Global definition of ARDS, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2024. Review: [W10/D1](#W10-D1).

questions.stem: Regarding ARDS definitions and phenotypes:
options: In the Berlin definition, mortality for mild, moderate and severe ARDS was about 27, 32 and 45 %.
The Berlin definition requires invasive ventilation.
The 2024 global definition allows bilateral opacities to be shown on lung ultrasound.
The hyperinflammatory phenotype is part of the 2024 global definition.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Berlin mortality was about 27 % (mild), 32 % (moderate) and 45 % (severe).
- B (False) – Berlin accepts non-invasive ventilation or CPAP with PEEP ≥ 5 cmH₂O in the mild category.
- C (True) – the global definition accepts bilateral opacities on chest X-ray, CT or lung ultrasound (in trained hands).
- D (False) – hypo/hyperinflammatory phenotypes are based on biomarkers and clinical variables, and are still a research tool.

**Ref:** ARDS Definition Task Force, JAMA 2012; Matthay MA et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2024; Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023. Review: [W10/D1](#W10-D1).

questions.stem: A woman 165 cm tall and weighing 95 kg is intubated for ARDS. A tidal volume of 6 mL/kg predicted body weight is approximately:
options: 450 mL
300 mL
340 mL
570 mL
400 mL
questions.expl:
**Why C:** For women, PBW = 45.5 + 0.91 × (height in cm − 152.4) = 45.5 + 0.91 × 12.6 ≈ 57 kg. So 6 mL/kg PBW ≈ 340 mL. Lung size depends on height and sex, not on actual body weight.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 450 mL is about 8 mL/kg PBW.
- B – 300 mL is about 5 mL/kg PBW.
- D – 570 mL is 6 mL/kg of actual body weight (95 kg).
- E – 400 mL is about 7 mL/kg PBW.

**EDIC trap:** obesity does not enlarge the lungs – always use PBW.

**Ref:** ARDS Network, N Engl J Med 2000; Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023. Review: [W10/D2](#W10-D2).

questions.stem: A paralysed ARDS patient has VT 420 mL, PEEP 12 cmH₂O and plateau pressure 28 cmH₂O.
options: In Amato's analysis, driving pressure was the variable most strongly associated with survival, but a ΔP-targeted strategy has not been validated in an RCT.
ESICM 2023 strongly recommends VT 4–8 mL/kg PBW.
Driving pressure is 16 cmH₂O.
Static respiratory system compliance is about 26 mL/cmH₂O.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – in Amato's analysis, driving pressure was most strongly associated with survival (RR 1.41 per 7 cmH₂O), but no RCT has validated a ΔP-targeted strategy.
- B (True) – ESICM 2023 strongly recommends low VT (4–8 mL/kg PBW).
- C (True) – ΔP = Pplat − PEEP = 28 − 12 = 16 cmH₂O.
- D (True) – Crs = VT/ΔP = 420/16 ≈ 26 mL/cmH₂O.

**EDIC trap:** a "safe" plateau (< 30) can still mean a high driving pressure (> 15).

**Ref:** Amato MBP et al., N Engl J Med 2015; Grasselli G et al., ESICM ARDS guidelines, Intensive Care Med 2023. Review: [W10/D2](#W10-D2).

questions.stem: Which trial found **higher** mortality (55.3 vs 49.3 %) and more barotrauma with maximal lung recruitment plus PEEP titration?
options: EPVent-2
EXPRESS
ALVEOLI
ART
LOVS
questions.expl:
**Why D:** ART (2017) randomised moderate–severe ARDS to maximal lung recruitment plus PEEP titration or low-PEEP ARDSNet. 28-day mortality was higher (55.3 vs 49.3 %) with more barotrauma. This is why ESICM 2023 strongly recommends against prolonged high-pressure recruitment manoeuvres.

**Why not the others:**
- A – EPVent-2 tested oesophageal-pressure-guided PEEP and was neutral.
- B – EXPRESS compared minimal distension with increased recruitment and was neutral for mortality.
- C – ALVEOLI compared higher with lower PEEP and was neutral.
- E – LOVS tested open-lung ventilation and was neutral for mortality.

**Ref:** ART Investigators, JAMA 2017; Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023. Review: [W10/D3](#W10-D3).

questions.stem: Regarding neuromuscular blockade and corticosteroids in ARDS:
options: ESICM 2023 strongly recommends against routine NMBA infusion.
In ROSE, mortality was significantly lower with NMB plus deep sedation than with light sedation.
In DEXA-ARDS, 60-day mortality was 21 vs 36 %.
Corticosteroids can safely be started ≥ 14 days after ARDS onset.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ESICM 2023 strongly recommends against routine continuous NMBA infusion in moderate–severe ARDS.
- B (False) – ROSE found no difference in 90-day mortality (42.5 vs 42.8 %).
- C (True) – DEXA-ARDS (dexamethasone 20 → 10 mg for 10 days): 60-day mortality 21 vs 36 %, 4.8 more ventilator-free days; open-label and stopped early.
- D (False) – starting corticosteroids ≥ 14 days after ARDS onset increased mortality in LaSRS.

**Ref:** Moss M et al., ROSE, N Engl J Med 2019; Villar J et al., DEXA-ARDS, Lancet Respir Med 2020; Steinberg KP et al., LaSRS, N Engl J Med 2006. Review: [W10/D4](#W10-D4).

questions.stem: ESICM 2023 makes a **strong recommendation against** which intervention in ARDS?
options: NIV rather than HFNO
ECCO₂R outside of RCTs
Higher PEEP
Low tidal volume
Prone positioning in moderate–severe ARDS
questions.expl:
**Why B:** ESICM 2023 makes strong recommendations against prolonged high-pressure recruitment manoeuvres, routine NMBA infusion and ECCO₂R outside RCTs. The REST trial of ECCO₂R was stopped for futility, with more serious adverse events.

**Why not the others:**
- A – no recommendation was made for NIV vs HFNO in non-COVID ARDS.
- C – no recommendation was made for a higher or lower PEEP level.
- D – low tidal volume is strongly recommended.
- E – prone positioning is strongly recommended in moderate–severe ARDS.

**Ref:** Grasselli G et al., ESICM ARDS guidelines, Intensive Care Med 2023; McNamee JJ et al., REST, JAMA 2021. Review: [W10/D5](#W10-D5).

questions.stem: Regarding VV-ECMO trials in ARDS:
options: CESAR tested referral to an ECMO centre, not ECMO itself.
The Bayesian reanalysis showed that EOLIA was a positive trial.
In EOLIA, 60-day mortality was 35 vs 46 % (p = 0.09).
In EOLIA, no control patients crossed over to rescue ECMO.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – CESAR randomised referral to an ECMO centre; only 76 % of referred patients received ECMO.
- B (False) – Goligher's Bayesian reanalysis is post hoc. It gives a high probability of *some* benefit (88–99 %), but the effect size remains uncertain.
- C (True) – EOLIA 60-day mortality was 35 vs 46 % (p = 0.09), so it missed its primary endpoint.
- D (False) – 28 % of controls crossed over to rescue ECMO, diluting the effect.

**Ref:** Peek GJ et al., CESAR, Lancet 2009; Combes A et al., EOLIA, N Engl J Med 2018; Goligher EC et al., JAMA 2018. Review: [W11/D1](#W11-D1).

questions.stem: A patient on VV-ECMO for ARDS has SpO₂ 92 % but PaCO₂ rising to 9 kPa with respiratory acidosis. Circuit flow is stable. The first adjustment is:
options: Add a second drainage cannula
Increase blood flow
Increase FiO₂ on the ventilator to 1.0
Increase the sweep gas flow
Increase tidal volume to 8 mL/kg PBW
questions.expl:
**Why D:** On VV-ECMO, CO₂ removal depends on the sweep gas flow through the oxygenator. Oxygenation depends mainly on blood flow relative to cardiac output. Oxygenation is adequate and circuit flow is stable, so increasing sweep is the first step for hypercapnia.

**Why not the others:**
- A – a second drainage cannula is for insufficient blood flow or recirculation.
- B – increasing blood flow mainly improves oxygenation.
- C – ventilator FiO₂ adds little and does not address CO₂.
- E – larger VT abandons ultraprotective ventilation (Pplat ≤ 24, PEEP ≥ 10).

**EDIC trap:** blood flow → O₂; sweep → CO₂.

**Ref:** Combes A et al., EOLIA, N Engl J Med 2018; Grasselli G et al., Intensive Care Med 2023. Review: [W11/D1](#W11-D1).

questions.stem: Regarding oxygen targets in the ICU:
options: UK-ROX showed lower mortality with SpO₂ 88–92 % in ventilated patients.
The IOTA meta-analysis found that liberal oxygen increases mortality.
In HOT-ICU (PaO₂ 8 vs 12 kPa), 90-day mortality was significantly lower with the 8-kPa target.
LOCO2 was stopped early because of lower 90-day mortality in the conservative arm.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – UK-ROX (n ≈ 16 500) found no difference in 90-day mortality with SpO₂ 88–92 % compared with usual care.
- B (True) – IOTA found higher mortality with liberal oxygen in acutely ill adults.
- C (False) – HOT-ICU 90-day mortality was 42.9 vs 42.4 % (NS).
- D (False) – LOCO2 was stopped early because of **higher** mortality and mesenteric ischaemia in the conservative arm.

**EDIC trap:** IOTA shows harm from **hyperoxia**, which does not prove benefit from a low target.

**Ref:** Martin DS et al., UK-ROX, JAMA 2025; Chu DK et al., IOTA, Lancet 2018; Schjørring OL et al., HOT-ICU, N Engl J Med 2021; Barrot L et al., LOCO2, N Engl J Med 2020. Review: [W11/D2](#W11-D2).

questions.stem: After 12 h of HFNO for pneumonia, a patient has SpO₂ 90 %, FiO₂ 0.9 and RR 35/min. The ROX index and its interpretation are:
options: ≈ 4.9 – low risk of failure
≈ 2.9 – low risk, because a lower ROX is better
≈ 3500 – very low risk (SpO₂/FiO₂ multiplied by RR)
≈ 2.9 – high risk of HFNO failure; do not delay intubation
≈ 9.0 – low risk of failure
questions.expl:
**Why D:** ROX = (SpO₂/FiO₂)/RR = (90/0.9)/35 = 100/35 ≈ 2.86. At 12 h, ROX < 3.85 predicts HFNO failure, whereas ≥ 4.88 predicts success. A ROX of 2.9 means high risk of failure, and intubation should not be delayed.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 4.9 is miscalculated, and it would mean low risk.
- B – a lower ROX is worse, not better.
- C – RR is the denominator, not a multiplier.
- E – 9.0 is miscalculated, and does not match these values.

**Ref:** Roca O et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019. Review: [W11/D3](#W11-D3).

questions.stem: Regarding non-invasive support in hypoxaemic respiratory failure:
options: In FLORALI, 90-day mortality was lowest with NIV.
In FLORALI, intubation rates were significantly lower with HFNO (primary outcome).
HENIVOT (helmet NIV) was positive for its primary outcome.
The HACOR score was developed to predict failure of HFNO.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – in FLORALI, 90-day mortality was lowest with HFNO (12 vs 23 % standard O₂ vs 28 % NIV).
- B (False) – the primary outcome (intubation at day 28) did not differ significantly; benefit was only in the P/F ≤ 200 subgroup.
- C (False) – HENIVOT was neutral for its primary outcome (respiratory-support-free days), although intubation was less frequent with helmet NIV.
- D (False) – HACOR predicts **NIV** failure; ROX predicts **HFNO** failure.

**Ref:** Frat JP et al., FLORALI, N Engl J Med 2015; Grieco DL et al., HENIVOT, JAMA 2021; Duan J et al., HACOR, Intensive Care Med 2017. Review: [W11/D3](#W11-D3).

questions.stem: A patient needed 4 spontaneous breathing trials over 9 days before successful extubation. According to Boles 2007, weaning was:
options: Failed
Simple
Difficult
Prolonged
Short (WIND)
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Boles 2007 classifies weaning by the number of SBTs and time from the first one. Simple = first SBT successful. Difficult = up to 3 SBTs or ≤ 7 days. Prolonged = more than 3 failed SBTs or > 7 days. Four SBTs over 9 days is prolonged weaning.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the patient was successfully extubated.
- B – simple weaning means success at the first SBT.
- C – difficult weaning is limited to ≤ 3 SBTs or ≤ 7 days.
- E – "short" is a WIND category, not a Boles category.

**Ref:** Boles JM et al., Eur Respir J 2007; Béduneau G et al., WIND, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2017. Review: [W11/D4](#W11-D4).

questions.stem: Regarding SBTs and extubation:
options: In Esteban 2004, NIV for established post-extubation respiratory failure increased mortality (25 vs 14 %).
In Subirà 2019, a 30-min SBT on PSV 8 cmH₂O led to more successful extubations than a 2-h T-piece trial (82.3 vs 74.0 %).
In Subirà 2019, reintubation rates were higher after the PSV SBT.
In HIGH-WEAN, HFNO + NIV reduced reintubation compared with HFNO alone in high-risk patients (11.8 vs 18.2 %).
questions.expl:
- A (True) – in Esteban 2004, NIV for established post-extubation respiratory failure increased ICU mortality (25 vs 14 %), probably by delaying reintubation.
- B (True) – in Subirà 2019, a 30-min PSV 8 cmH₂O SBT led to more successful extubations than a 2-h T-piece trial (82.3 vs 74.0 %).
- C (False) – reintubation rates did not differ (11.1 vs 11.9 %).
- D (True) – in HIGH-WEAN, prophylactic HFNO + NIV reduced reintubation compared with HFNO alone in high-risk patients (11.8 vs 18.2 %).

**EDIC trap:** prophylactic NIV helps, rescue NIV harms.

**Ref:** Esteban A et al., N Engl J Med 2004; Subirà C et al., JAMA 2019; Thille AW et al., HIGH-WEAN, JAMA 2019. Review: [W11/D4](#W11-D4), [W11/D5](#W11-D5).

questions.stem: For which patient with a COPD exacerbation is there a strong recommendation for NIV?
options: pH 7.31, PaCO₂ 8.9 kPa, respiratory rate 28/min
pH 7.40, PaCO₂ 7.5 kPa, dyspnoeic
Any patient with chronic hypercapnia on admission
pH 7.45, PaCO₂ 6.0 kPa, SpO₂ 86 %
pH 7.38 after bronchodilators, PaCO₂ 7.0 kPa
questions.expl:
**Why A:** ERS/ATS 2017 strongly recommends NIV (high certainty) for acute or acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure with acidosis (pH ≤ 7.35). This patient has pH 7.31, PaCO₂ 8.9 kPa and tachypnoea. NIV reduces intubation and mortality in this group.

**Why not the others:**
- B – hypercapnia with normal pH is compensated and is not an indication.
- C – chronic hypercapnia without acidosis is not an indication for acute NIV.
- D – this is hypoxaemia without hypercapnia; give controlled oxygen.
- E – pH 7.38 after bronchodilators is no longer acidotic.

**Ref:** Rochwerg B et al., ERS/ATS NIV guideline, Eur Respir J 2017. Review: [W12/D1](#W12-D1).

questions.stem: Regarding COPD exacerbation and severe asthma:
options: In hypercapnic COPD exacerbation, HFNO should be tried before NIV.
ERS/ATS strongly recommends NIV in acute asthma.
The SpO₂ target is 88–92 % in COPD and 93–95 % in asthma.
Prednisone 40 mg for 14 days is required to prevent relapse (REDUCE).
questions.expl:
- A (False) – in hypercapnic COPD, NIV is first-line; ERS 2022 suggests HFNO only if NIV is not tolerated, or after it.
- B (False) – ERS/ATS makes no recommendation for NIV in acute asthma, due to uncertain evidence.
- C (True) – target SpO₂ 88–92 % in COPD (risk of hypercapnia) and 93–95 % in acute asthma.
- D (False) – in REDUCE, 5 days of prednisone 40 mg was non-inferior to 14 days.

**Ref:** Oczkowski S et al., ERS HFNO guideline, Eur Respir J 2022; Rochwerg B et al., Eur Respir J 2017; Leuppi JD et al., REDUCE, JAMA 2013. Review: [W12/D1](#W12-D1).

questions.stem: A patient with severe CAP has a negative urinary *Legionella* antigen. Which statement is correct?
options: *Legionella* is excluded
The test detects only serogroup 1, so other serogroups are not excluded
A macrolide is no longer needed for any CAP
The test detects all *Legionella* species
The test is valid only after 14 days
questions.expl:
**Why B:** The urinary *Legionella* antigen detects only *L. pneumophila* serogroup 1, which causes most cases. A negative test does not exclude other serogroups or species. In severe CAP, also send blood cultures, sputum (including *Legionella* PCR/culture) and pneumococcal urinary antigen.

**Why not the others:**
- A – a negative test does not exclude *Legionella*.
- C – empirical therapy for severe CAP still includes a macrolide.
- D – the test does not detect non-*pneumophila* species or other serogroups.
- E – antigen is detectable within days of onset and can stay positive for weeks.

**Ref:** Metlay JP et al., ATS/IDSA CAP guideline, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019. Review: [W12/D2](#W12-D2).

questions.stem: Regarding severe community-acquired pneumonia:
options: ATS 2025 suggests corticosteroids also in severe influenza pneumonia.
CAPE COD included patients with septic shock and influenza.
MRSA and *Pseudomonas* should be covered routinely in all patients with severe CAP.
Empirical therapy is a β-lactam plus a macrolide.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – ATS 2025 suggests corticosteroids in severe CAP, but this does **not** apply to influenza pneumonia (observational data suggest harm).
- B (False) – CAPE COD **excluded** septic shock and influenza.
- C (False) – cover MRSA or *Pseudomonas* only when individual risk factors are present.
- D (True) – empirical therapy is a β-lactam plus a macrolide (or a respiratory fluoroquinolone).

**Ref:** Jones BE et al., ATS CAP guideline, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2025; Dequin PF et al., CAPE COD, N Engl J Med 2023; Metlay JP et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019. Review: [W12/D2](#W12-D2).

questions.stem: In the INTUBE study (29 countries), the most frequent major adverse peri-intubation event was:
options: Severe hypoxaemia
Aspiration
Cardiovascular instability
Oesophageal intubation
Cardiac arrest
questions.expl:
**Why C:** INTUBE (2964 patients, 29 countries) found major adverse peri-intubation events in 45.2 %. Cardiovascular instability was the most common (42.6 %), ahead of severe hypoxaemia (9.3 %) and cardiac arrest (3.1 %). This supports haemodynamic optimisation and vasopressor readiness before induction.

**Why not the others:**
- A – severe hypoxaemia was second (9.3 %).
- B – aspiration was not among the most frequent major events.
- D – oesophageal intubation was not a main outcome category.
- E – cardiac arrest occurred in 3.1 %.

**Ref:** Russotto V et al., INTUBE, JAMA 2021. Review: [W12/D3](#W12-D3).

questions.stem: Regarding trials of airway management in critically ill adults:
options: In DEVICE, video laryngoscopy increased first-attempt success (85.1 vs 70.8 %).
In BOUGIE, a bougie significantly increased first-attempt success.
In the RSI trial, ketamine caused less cardiovascular collapse than etomidate.
In PREOXI, NIV preoxygenation halved hypoxaemia (9.1 vs 18.5 %).
questions.expl:
- A (True) – in DEVICE, video laryngoscopy increased first-attempt success (85.1 vs 70.8 %).
- B (False) – BOUGIE found no difference in first-attempt success (80.4 vs 83.0 %).
- C (False) – in the RSI trial, mortality was similar, and cardiovascular collapse was **more** common with ketamine (22.1 vs 17.0 %).
- D (True) – in PREOXI, NIV preoxygenation halved hypoxaemia (9.1 vs 18.5 %).

**Ref:** Prekker ME et al., DEVICE, N Engl J Med 2023; Driver BE et al., BOUGIE, JAMA 2021; Casey JD et al., RSI trial, N Engl J Med 2025; Gibbs KW et al., PREOXI, N Engl J Med 2024. Review: [W12/D3](#W12-D3).

questions.stem: A patient with a parapneumonic effusion has pleural fluid pH 7.10. A small-bore drain inserted 2 days ago is draining poorly, and loculations are seen. The patient is clinically stable. The next step supported by MIST2 is:
options: Intrapleural tPA plus DNase
Intrapleural streptokinase
Intrapleural DNase alone
Intrapleural tPA alone
Remove the drain and continue antibiotics only
questions.expl:
**Why A:** pH < 7.2 means complicated parapneumonic effusion, and a poorly draining, loculated collection needs better drainage. In MIST2, only tPA plus DNase improved radiological drainage and reduced surgical referral and hospital stay. Surgery (VATS) is considered if this fails.

**Why not the others:**
- B – in MIST1, streptokinase did not reduce mortality or surgery.
- C – DNase alone was harmful (more surgical referrals).
- D – tPA alone did not help.
- E – a loculated infected effusion will not resolve with antibiotics alone.

**Ref:** Rahman NM et al., MIST2, N Engl J Med 2011; Maskell NA et al., MIST1, N Engl J Med 2005; Roberts ME et al., BTS pleural guideline, Thorax 2023. Review: [W12/D5](#W12-D5).

questions.stem: Regarding tracheostomy and pneumothorax:
options: In TracMan, early tracheostomy (≤ 4 days) did not reduce mortality.
Lung point is a specific ultrasound sign of pneumothorax.
Percutaneous tracheostomy has fewer stoma infections than surgical tracheostomy.
In a laryngectomy patient, oxygen should be applied to the stoma.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – in TracMan, early tracheostomy (≤ 4 days) did not reduce 30-day mortality.
- B (True) – lung point (where sliding lung meets the pneumothorax) is close to 100 % specific.
- C (True) – percutaneous tracheostomy has fewer stoma infections than surgical tracheostomy.
- D (True) – after laryngectomy, the stoma is the only airway, so oxygenate and, if needed, intubate via the stoma, never via the mouth.

**EDIC trap:** distinguish a laryngectomy (no upper airway connection) from a tracheostomy (upper airway still patent).

**Ref:** Young D et al., TracMan, JAMA 2013; McGrath BA et al., NTSP guidelines, Anaesthesia 2012. Review: [W12/D4](#W12-D4), [W12/D5](#W12-D5).

questions.stem: A paralysed patient on volume control has constant flow 60 L/min, VT 500 mL, Ppeak 35, Pplat 25 and PEEP 5 cmH₂O (no PEEPi). Which set of values is correct?
options: R 20 cmH₂O/L/s; Cstat 20 mL/cmH₂O; τ 0.4 s
R 0.17 cmH₂O/L/s; Cstat 25 mL/cmH₂O; τ 0.004 s
R 10 cmH₂O/L/s; Cstat 16.7 mL/cmH₂O; τ 0.17 s
R 10 cmH₂O/L/s; Cstat 25 mL/cmH₂O; τ 0.25 s
R 10 cmH₂O/L/s; Cstat 50 mL/cmH₂O; τ 0.5 s
questions.expl:
**Why D:** 60 L/min = 1 L/s, so R = (Ppeak − Pplat)/flow = (35 − 25)/1 = 10 cmH₂O/L/s. Cstat = VT/(Pplat − PEEP) = 500/20 = 25 mL/cmH₂O = 0.025 L/cmH₂O. τ = R × C = 10 × 0.025 = 0.25 s.

**Why not the others:**
- A – R uses Ppeak − Pplat (10), not Pplat − PEEP (20).
- B – flow must be converted to L/s, and C to L/cmH₂O.
- C – 16.7 mL/cmH₂O is the **dynamic** compliance (500/30).
- E – 50 mL/cmH₂O would need Pplat − PEEP = 10.

**Ref:** Hess DR, Respir Care 2014. Review: [W13/D2](#W13-D2).

questions.stem: Regarding ventilation modes:
options: In VCV, a high inspiratory demand can cause flow starvation.
In PCV, VT ≈ (Pinsp + Pmus) × C, so strong efforts can produce large VTs at a "safe" displayed pressure.
NAVA and PAV+ improve patient–ventilator synchrony, but no mortality benefit has been shown.
In the study by Zhou 2017, APRV reduced mortality.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – in VCV, flow is fixed, so high inspiratory demand causes flow starvation (scooped pressure curve).
- B (True) – in PCV, VT ≈ (Pinsp + Pmus) × C, so strong efforts can produce large VTs at a "safe" displayed pressure.
- C (True) – NAVA and PAV+ improve synchrony, but no mortality benefit has been shown.
- D (False) – in Zhou 2017 (a small trial), APRV gave more ventilator-free days, but mortality did not differ significantly.

**Ref:** Zhou Y et al., Intensive Care Med 2017. Review: [W13/D1](#W13-D1).

questions.stem: A patient on VCV has RR 20/min, VT 0.5 L, Ppeak 30, Pplat 25 and PEEP 10 cmH₂O. Using the simplified Gattinoni formula MP = 0.098 × RR × VT × (Ppeak − ½ ΔP), mechanical power is approximately:
options: 29 J/min
35 J/min
22 J/min
12 J/min
15 J/min
questions.expl:
**Why C:** ΔP = 25 − 10 = 15 cmH₂O, so Ppeak − ½ΔP = 30 − 7.5 = 22.5. MP = 0.098 × 20 × 0.5 × 22.5 ≈ 22 J/min. In observational data (Serpa Neto 2018), MP > ~17 J/min was associated with higher mortality.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 29 J/min would use Ppeak alone (0.098 × 20 × 0.5 × 30).
- B – 35 J/min does not follow from the formula.
- D – 12 J/min omits the PEEP-related component.
- E – 15 J/min uses ΔP instead of the full pressure term.

**EDIC trap:** MP is an observational marker, not a guideline target.

**Ref:** Gattinoni L et al., Intensive Care Med 2016; Serpa Neto A et al., Intensive Care Med 2018. Review: [W13/D4](#W13-D4).

questions.stem: Regarding effort assessment and VILI:
options: Raising PEEP raises mechanical power (linearly).
Pmus can be estimated as about ¾ of the airway occlusion pressure swing (ΔPocc).
P0.1 > 3.5 cmH₂O indicates high inspiratory effort.
Mechanical power is a guideline-recommended titration target.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – in the Gattinoni equation, PEEP contributes a term proportional to VT × PEEP, so MP rises linearly with PEEP.
- B (True) – Pmus can be estimated as about −¾ × ΔPocc (the occlusion pressure swing).
- C (True) – P0.1 > 3.5 cmH₂O indicates high inspiratory drive/effort; < 1 suggests over-assistance.
- D (False) – no RCT has titrated mechanical power, so it is not a guideline target.

**Ref:** Bertoni M et al., Crit Care 2019; Telias I et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2020; Gattinoni L et al., Intensive Care Med 2016. Review: [W13/D4](#W13-D4).

questions.stem: A patient with COPD on PSV 20 cmH₂O (external PEEP 0) has visible inspiratory efforts without ventilator triggering. The ventilator rate is 14/min, but the patient's neural rate is clearly higher. The most appropriate change is:
options: Increase trigger sensitivity to the maximum and increase PS
Switch to SIMV
Deepen sedation and add a neuromuscular blocker
Increase pressure support to 25 cmH₂O
Decrease pressure support and add external PEEP
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Ineffective efforts in COPD on high PS arise because large VTs need a long expiration, so dynamic hyperinflation (PEEPi) develops. The patient then cannot overcome PEEPi to trigger. Reduce PS (smaller VT, longer Te) and add external PEEP below PEEPi (about 70–80 %) to reduce the triggering load.

**Why not the others:**
- A – maximal trigger sensitivity risks auto-triggering, and more PS worsens hyperinflation.
- B – SIMV worsens synchrony and work of breathing.
- C – deep sedation and paralysis treat the symptom, not the cause, and prolong ventilation.
- D – more PS increases VT and PEEPi, causing more ineffective efforts.

**Ref:** Thille AW et al., Intensive Care Med 2006. Review: [W13/D3](#W13-D3), [W13/D5](#W13-D5).

questions.stem: Regarding patient–ventilator asynchrony:
options: In Thille 2006, about a quarter of patients had an asynchrony index > 10 %, which was associated with longer ventilation.
Asynchrony index = asynchronous events / (ventilator cycles + ineffective efforts) × 100.
Premature cycling is corrected by increasing the cycle-off (% of peak flow) threshold.
An asynchrony index > 10 % is considered severe.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – in Thille 2006, about 24 % of patients had an asynchrony index > 10 %, which was associated with longer ventilation.
- B (True) – AI = asynchronous events / (ventilator cycles + ineffective efforts) × 100.
- C (False) – premature cycling is corrected by **decreasing** the cycle-off threshold (% of peak flow); increase it for delayed cycling, as in COPD.
- D (True) – AI > 10 % is considered severe.

**Ref:** Thille AW et al., Intensive Care Med 2006. Review: [W13/D3](#W13-D3).

questions.stem: A ventilated patient has respiratory system resistance 20 cmH₂O/L/s and compliance 0.05 L/cmH₂O. With RR 20/min and I:E 1:2, roughly what fraction of VT is exhaled before the next breath?
questions.expl:
**Why C:** τ = R × C = 20 × 0.05 = 1.0 s. At RR 20/min each cycle lasts 3 s, and with I:E 1:2, Te = 2 s = 2τ. The exhaled fraction is 1 − e⁻² ≈ 86 %, so some air trapping is likely.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 63 % is reached after 1τ.
- B – 99 % needs about 5τ.
- D – 95 % needs about 3τ, i.e. Te 3 s.
- E – 50 % corresponds to about 0.7τ.

**EDIC trap:** to lengthen Te, lower RR or shorten Ti (higher inspiratory flow).

**Ref:** Hess DR, Respir Care 2014; Leatherman J, Chest 2015. Review: [W13/D2](#W13-D2), [W13/D5](#W13-D5).

questions.stem: Regarding mechanical ventilation in status asthmaticus:
options: Plateau pressure should be < 30 cmH₂O, ideally < 25 cmH₂O.
An end-inspiratory lung volume (V_EI) ≥ 1.4 L was associated with complications (Williams).
External PEEP is absolutely contraindicated in asthma.
The goal is normocapnia, so RR should be increased as PaCO₂ rises.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – keep plateau pressure < 30 cmH₂O, ideally < 25 cmH₂O, to limit hyperinflation.
- B (True) – in Williams 1992, V_EI ≥ 1.4 L was associated with barotrauma and hypotension.
- C (False) – external PEEP is not contraindicated; titrate it by the Pplat response to a PEEP trial.
- D (False) – the strategy is permissive hypercapnia; raising RR shortens Te and worsens dynamic hyperinflation.

**Ref:** Williams TJ et al., Am Rev Respir Dis 1992; Leatherman J, Chest 2015. Review: [W13/D5](#W13-D5).

title: W14 · D4 – Review: acid–base + electrolytes

questions.stem: A blood gas report shows HCO₃⁻ 20 mmol/L and pCO₂ 50 mmHg. Which reported pH is internally consistent?
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Henderson equation: [H⁺] = 24 × pCO₂/HCO₃⁻ = 24 × 50/20 = 60 nmol/L. Near pH 7.40 (40 nmol/L) each 1 nmol/L is about 0.01 pH unit, so 60 nmol/L ≈ pH 7.20–7.22. Henderson–Hasselbalch confirms it: 6.1 + log(20/1.5) ≈ 7.22.

**Why not the others:**
- B – pH 7.52 means [H⁺] ≈ 30 nmol/L, which would need a much lower pCO₂ or a higher HCO₃⁻.
- C – pH 7.12 means [H⁺] ≈ 76 nmol/L, too acidic for these values.
- D – pH 7.40 needs a HCO₃⁻/pCO₂ ratio of 24/40 (0.6), not 20/50 (0.4).
- E – pH 7.32 means [H⁺] ≈ 48 nmol/L, too alkaline for a ratio of 0.4.

**EDIC trap:** Check internal consistency before interpreting a gas. A mismatch means a sampling or transcription error.

**Ref:** Berend K, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2014;371:1434–1445. · [W05/D1](#W05-D1)

questions.stem: A patient with septic shock who is becoming exhausted has HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L and pCO₂ 32 mmHg.
options: The expected pCO₂ (Winter) is about 23 mmHg (21–25).
There is a concomitant respiratory acidosis.
Respiratory compensation can overshoot and bring pH above 7.40.
Full respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis takes 3–5 days.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Winter: 1.5 × 10 + 8 = 23 ± 2, so the expected pCO₂ is 21–25 mmHg.
- B (True) – A pCO₂ of 32 is above the expected range, so ventilation is inadequate. This is a concomitant respiratory acidosis and a warning of exhaustion and impending respiratory failure.
- C (False) – Compensation never overshoots and rarely normalises pH. A pH > 7.40 implies a second, alkalotic primary disorder.
- D (False) – Respiratory compensation starts within minutes and is complete within ~12–24 h. Renal compensation is the one that takes 3–5 days.

**EDIC trap:** A pCO₂ of "only" 32 in severe metabolic acidosis is too high. Anticipate the need for ventilatory support.

**Ref:** Berend K, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2014;371:1434–1445; Albert MS, et al. *Ann Intern Med* 1967;66:312–322. · [W05/D1](#W05-D1)

questions.stem: An ICU patient has Na⁺ 136, Cl⁻ 104, HCO₃⁻ 20 mmol/L and albumin 16 g/L. Which interpretation is correct?
options: AG 12 – the low albumin causes acidosis
Corrected AG ≈ 6 – hyperchloraemic acidosis
Corrected AG ≈ 28 – toxic alcohol certain
Normal anion gap; no further work-up is needed
Corrected AG ≈ 18 – a hidden high-AG acidosis (check lactate, ketones, urea)
questions.expl:
**Why E:** AG = 136 − (104 + 20) = 12, which looks normal. Each 10 g/L fall in albumin lowers the AG by ~2.5 mmol/L, so corrected AG = 12 + 0.25 × (40 − 16) = 18 mmol/L. This is a high-AG acidosis hidden by hypoalbuminaemia, so look for lactate, ketones, uraemia and toxins.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 12 is the uncorrected AG, and low albumin alkalinises (less weak acid); it does not cause acidosis.
- B – The correction is added, not subtracted. Subtracting it gives the wrong value of 6.
- C – 28 overstates the correction, and no AG value makes a toxic alcohol "certain".
- D – The uncorrected AG is falsely reassuring, and an HCO₃⁻ of 20 still needs an explanation.

**EDIC trap:** In the ICU, always correct the AG for albumin (Figge).

**Ref:** Figge J, et al. *Crit Care Med* 1998;26:1807–1810. · [W05/D1](#W05-D1)

questions.stem: A patient with DKA who has also had several days of diarrhoea has: Na⁺ 138, Cl⁻ 110, HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L, albumin 40 g/L.
options: The anion gap is 18 mmol/L.
The "corrected HCO₃⁻" (HCO₃⁻ + ΔAG) of 16 mmol/L supports a coexisting normal-AG acidosis.
The delta ratio indicates a mixed high-AG and normal-AG metabolic acidosis.
The delta ratio is about 0.4.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – AG = 138 − (110 + 10) = 18 mmol/L.
- B (True) – ΔAG = 18 − 12 = 6, so corrected HCO₃⁻ = 10 + 6 = 16 mmol/L. A value below ~22 means HCO₃⁻ has fallen more than the AG explains, so a NAGMA (diarrhoea) coexists.
- C (True) – A delta ratio of 0.4–0.8 indicates a combined high-AG and normal-AG metabolic acidosis.
- D (True) – Delta ratio = ΔAG/ΔHCO₃⁻ = 6/14 ≈ 0.43.

**EDIC trap:** Delta ratio < 0.4 = pure NAGMA; 0.4–0.8 = mixed; 1–2 = pure HAGMA; > 2 = HAGMA plus metabolic alkalosis (or a pre-existing high HCO₃⁻).

**Ref:** Rastegar A. *J Am Soc Nephrol* 2007;18:2429–2431. · [W05/D1](#W05-D1)

questions.stem: A patient with liver cirrhosis has pCO₂ 25 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 18 mmol/L and pH 7.48. The best description is:
options: Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic alkalosis
Acute respiratory alkalosis with an additional metabolic alkalosis
Acute respiratory alkalosis with appropriate compensation
Primary metabolic acidosis with appropriate compensation
Chronic respiratory alkalosis with appropriate compensation
questions.expl:
**Why E:** pH 7.48 with pCO₂ 25 means a primary respiratory alkalosis, which is typical of cirrhosis (hormonal and ammonia-driven hyperventilation). pCO₂ fell by 15 mmHg. In chronic respiratory alkalosis HCO₃⁻ falls by ~4–5 per 10 mmHg, so the expected value is ≈ 18, exactly as measured.

**Why not the others:**
- A – HCO₃⁻ is low, not high, so there is no metabolic alkalosis.
- B – An extra metabolic alkalosis would push HCO₃⁻ above the acute prediction (≈ 21), not below it.
- C – Acute compensation predicts HCO₃⁻ ≈ 21; a value of 18 is too low for an acute disorder.
- D – Alkalaemia excludes a primary acidosis, because compensation never overshoots.

**EDIC trap:** If the time course is unknown, the same numbers could be acute respiratory alkalosis plus metabolic acidosis. The history decides.

**Ref:** Berend K, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2014;371:1434–1445. · [W05/D1](#W05-D1)

questions.stem: Regarding the Stewart approach:
options: The independent variables are pCO₂, SID and ATOT.
Hypoalbuminaemia causes a metabolic acidosis.
Albumin is a strong ion.
The SID of 0.9 % NaCl is 0.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – In Stewart's model, pH depends on three independent variables: pCO₂, the strong ion difference (SID) and total weak acids (ATOT, mainly albumin and phosphate).
- B (False) – Hypoalbuminaemia lowers ATOT and causes a metabolic **alkalosis**, which can mask a coexisting acidosis.
- C (False) – Albumin is a weak acid (only partly dissociated) and part of ATOT. Strong ions are fully dissociated (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, lactate).
- D (True) – 0.9 % NaCl contains 154 mmol/L each of Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so its SID is 0. Large volumes dilute plasma SID and cause hyperchloraemic acidosis.

**EDIC trap:** In the Stewart approach, HCO₃⁻ is a dependent variable. It changes only because SID, ATOT or pCO₂ change.

**Ref:** Kellum JA. *Crit Care* 2000;4:6–14. · [W05/D2](#W05-D2)

questions.stem: A septic patient has Na⁺ 140, K⁺ 4, Ca²⁺ 2.2 mEq/L, Mg²⁺ 1.0 mEq/L, Cl⁻ 106, lactate 5 mmol/L, HCO₃⁻ 14 mmol/L, and an albumin + phosphate charge (A⁻) of 8 mmol/L. The strong ion gap (SIG) is about:
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Apparent SID (SIDa) = (Na⁺ + K⁺ + Ca²⁺ + Mg²⁺) − (Cl⁻ + lactate) = 147.2 − 111 ≈ 36 mEq/L. Effective SID (SIDe) = HCO₃⁻ + A⁻ = 14 + 8 = 22. SIG = SIDa − SIDe ≈ 14 mEq/L, which means unmeasured anions **beyond** lactate (ketones, uraemic anions, toxins).

**Why not the others:**
- A – A SIG of 0 would mean no unmeasured anions (SIDa = SIDe).
- B – A SIG of 4 would need a SIDe of ≈ 32, which is incompatible with HCO₃⁻ 14.
- C – 22 is the SIDe, not the SIG.
- E – 36 is the SIDa, not the SIG.

**EDIC trap:** Lactate is a measured strong anion and already sits in SIDa. The SIG is close to 0 in health.

**Ref:** Fencl V, et al. *Am J Respir Crit Care Med* 2000;162:2246–2251. · [W05/D2](#W05-D2)

questions.stem: Regarding the urine anion gap (UAG):
options: The UAG remains reliable with marked ketonuria.
UAG = U-Na⁺ + U-K⁺ − U-Cl⁻.
A negative UAG in normal-AG acidosis points to diarrhoea.
A positive UAG in normal-AG acidosis points to distal RTA.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Ketoacid anions are excreted with NH₄⁺ but are not measured, so the UAG becomes falsely positive. The UAG is unreliable with ketonuria, polyuria or U-Na⁺ < 20 mmol/L.
- B (True) – UAG = U-Na⁺ + U-K⁺ − U-Cl⁻. It is an indirect estimate of urinary NH₄⁺, which is excreted with Cl⁻.
- C (True) – A negative UAG means high NH₄⁺ excretion, which is the appropriate renal response to an extrarenal loss such as diarrhoea ("neGUTive").
- D (True) – A positive UAG means low NH₄⁺ excretion, which points to a renal cause such as distal (type 1) RTA.

**EDIC trap:** With ketonuria or polyuria, use the urine osmolal gap to estimate NH₄⁺.

**Ref:** Kraut JA, Madias NE. *Clin J Am Soc Nephrol* 2012;7:671–679. · [W05/D2](#W05-D2)

questions.stem: Which cause produces **type B** lactic acidosis?
options: Carbon monoxide poisoning
Cardiogenic shock
Severe anaemia
Mesenteric ischaemia
Metformin
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Type B lactic acidosis occurs without evident tissue hypoxia. Metformin inhibits mitochondrial complex I and hepatic lactate uptake for gluconeogenesis, especially when it accumulates in AKI. Other type B causes: adrenaline/β₂-agonists, propofol infusion syndrome, thiamine deficiency, liver failure, malignancy and linezolid.

**Why not the others:**
- A – CO poisoning reduces O₂ carriage and delivery to tissue, so it is type A.
- B – Cardiogenic shock causes global hypoperfusion, so it is type A.
- C – Severe anaemia reduces O₂ content and delivery, so it is type A.
- D – Mesenteric ischaemia is regional hypoperfusion, so it is type A.

**EDIC trap:** In sepsis, types A and B overlap (hypoperfusion, adrenergic glycolysis and reduced clearance).

**Ref:** Kraut JA, Madias NE. *N Engl J Med* 2014;371:2309–2319. · [W05/D2](#W05-D2)

questions.stem: Regarding sodium bicarbonate in severe metabolic acidaemia:
options: Bicarbonate raises ionised calcium.
In BICAR-ICU, the primary composite outcome did not differ significantly (66 vs 71 %).
In BICARICU-2 (AKI KDIGO 2–3), 90-day mortality was significantly lower with bicarbonate.
In BICARICU-2, more patients received kidney replacement therapy with bicarbonate.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Bicarbonate increases calcium binding to albumin and **lowers** ionised Ca²⁺, which can depress contractility. Monitor iCa²⁺ and replace it.
- B (True) – BICAR-ICU: the composite of day-28 death and day-7 organ failure was 66 vs 71 %, NS. Benefit was seen only in the prespecified AKIN 2–3 stratum.
- C (False) – BICARICU-2 (AKI KDIGO 2–3): 90-day mortality was 62.1 vs 61.7 %, with no difference.
- D (False) – **Fewer** patients needed KRT with bicarbonate (35 vs 50 %).

**EDIC trap:** In severe acidaemia with AKI, bicarbonate reduces the need for dialysis, not mortality. Other risks are hypernatraemia, hyperosmolality and a CO₂ load.

**Ref:** Jaber S, et al. *Lancet* 2018;392:31–40; Jung B, et al. BICARICU-2. *JAMA* 2025. · [W05/D2](#W05-D2)

questions.stem: After a week of vomiting, a patient has pH 7.52, pCO₂ 47 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 34 mmol/L, K⁺ 2.8 mmol/L and urine Cl⁻ 10 mmol/L. The best management is:
options: 0.9 % NaCl with KCl
Acetazolamide
Hydrochloric acid infusion as first-line
Intubation for hypoventilation
Spironolactone
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Expected pCO₂ in metabolic alkalosis ≈ 40 + 0.7 × (34 − 24) = 47 mmHg, so compensation is appropriate. A U-Cl⁻ < 20 mmol/L means a chloride-responsive (Cl⁻- and volume-depleted) alkalosis. Giving Cl⁻ as 0.9 % NaCl with KCl lets the kidney excrete HCO₃⁻, and correcting K⁺ removes a driver of H⁺ loss.

**Why not the others:**
- B – Acetazolamide worsens volume depletion and hypokalaemia; it is for alkalosis with fluid overload.
- C – HCl infusion (central line) is reserved for severe, refractory, life-threatening alkalosis.
- D – A pCO₂ of 47 is appropriate compensation and does not need intubation.
- E – Spironolactone treats mineralocorticoid excess, a chloride-resistant alkalosis.

**EDIC trap:** In vomiting, assess volume with U-Cl⁻, not U-Na⁺.

**Ref:** Emmett M. *Clin J Am Soc Nephrol* 2020;15:1848–1856. · [W05/D3](#W05-D3)

questions.stem: Regarding metabolic alkalosis:
options: In vomiting, urine Na⁺ is a better marker of volume status than urine Cl⁻.
Mineralocorticoid excess causes chloride-responsive alkalosis (U-Cl⁻ < 20) with hypotension.
In DIABOLO, acetazolamide significantly shortened mechanical ventilation in COPD.
"Paradoxical aciduria" results from Cl⁻/K⁺ depletion and aldosterone activation.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – In vomiting, bicarbonaturia drags Na⁺ and K⁺ into the urine, so U-Na⁺ can be high despite hypovolaemia. **U-Cl⁻** is the better marker.
- B (False) – Mineralocorticoid excess causes a **chloride-resistant** alkalosis (U-Cl⁻ > 20) with **hypertension** and hypokalaemia.
- C (False) – DIABOLO: ventilation lasted 136.5 vs 163 h, NS (the trial was underpowered).
- D (True) – Cl⁻ and K⁺ depletion plus aldosterone drive distal H⁺ secretion, so the urine is acidic despite alkalaemia ("paradoxical aciduria").

**EDIC trap:** U-Cl⁻ < 20 = saline-responsive. U-Cl⁻ > 20 = saline-resistant, or an ongoing diuretic effect.

**Ref:** Faisy C, et al. DIABOLO. *JAMA* 2016;315:480–488; Emmett M. *Clin J Am Soc Nephrol* 2020;15:1848–1856. · [W05/D3](#W05-D3)

questions.stem: A patient after an overdose has pH 7.44, pCO₂ 24 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 16, Na⁺ 141 and Cl⁻ 103 mmol/L. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Pure respiratory alkalosis
Salicylate poisoning – respiratory alkalosis + high-AG metabolic acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis + respiratory acidosis
Normal acid–base status
Compensated metabolic acidosis
questions.expl:
**Why B:** AG = 141 − (103 + 16) = 22, so there is a HAGMA. Winter predicts pCO₂ 32 ± 2; the measured 24 is lower, so there is also a primary respiratory alkalosis. Delta ratio = 10/8 = 1.25, a pure HAGMA. A near-normal pH with these two disorders is classic for salicylate poisoning, which stimulates the respiratory centre and uncouples oxidative phosphorylation.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Respiratory alkalosis alone cannot explain an AG of 22.
- C – Both HCO₃⁻ and pCO₂ are low, which is the opposite pattern.
- D – A normal pH can hide two opposing disorders.
- E – Compensation does not fully normalise pH, and pCO₂ is below the Winter range.

**EDIC trap:** Normal pH with abnormal pCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ is a mixed disorder until proven otherwise.

**Ref:** Berend K, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2014;371:1434–1445. · [W05/D3](#W05-D3)

questions.stem: Regarding ketoacidoses (2024 DKA consensus):
options: In alcoholic ketoacidosis, the nitroprusside test overestimates ketosis.
Bicarbonate is indicated when pH is < 7.1.
DKA with pH 7.23 and HCO₃⁻ 8 mmol/L is "moderate", because pH is between 7.0 and 7.25.
A β-hydroxybutyrate ≥ 3.0 mmol/L is one of the diagnostic criteria.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – In AKA, the high NADH/NAD⁺ ratio makes β-hydroxybutyrate the main ketone. Nitroprusside detects only acetoacetate (and acetone), so it **underestimates** ketosis. Measure β-OHB.
- B (False) – The 2024 consensus supports bicarbonate only when pH is < 7.0.
- C (False) – Severity follows the worst parameter. An HCO₃⁻ < 10 mmol/L alone makes this DKA **severe**, even with a pH of 7.23.
- D (True) – Diagnosis needs hyperglycaemia (≥ 11.1 mmol/L) or known diabetes, ketonaemia (β-OHB ≥ 3.0 mmol/L), and acidosis (pH < 7.3 and/or HCO₃⁻ < 18 mmol/L).

**EDIC trap:** With SGLT2 inhibitors, DKA can be euglycaemic. Ketones and pH make the diagnosis, not glucose.

**Ref:** Umpierrez GE, et al. *Diabetes Care* 2024 (ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus). · [W05/D3](#W05-D3)

questions.stem: A patient in hyperglycaemic crisis has Na⁺ 126 mmol/L and glucose 39.2 mmol/L. Using the Katz correction (1.6 mmol/L per 5.6 mmol/L of glucose above 5.6), the corrected Na⁺ is about:
options: 142 mmol/L
136 mmol/L
131 mmol/L
146 mmol/L
128 mmol/L
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Glucose excess = 39.2 − 5.6 = 33.6 mmol/L, which is 6 × 5.6. Katz correction: 6 × 1.6 = 9.6, so corrected Na⁺ ≈ 126 + 9.6 ≈ 136 mmol/L. Glucose is an effective osmole that pulls water out of cells and dilutes Na⁺, giving a hypertonic (translocational) hyponatraemia.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 142 overcorrects; even the Hillier factor (2.4 per 5.6 mmol/L) gives only ≈ 140.
- C – 131 undercorrects (only ~0.8 per 5.6 mmol/L).
- D – 146 would need a correction of 20 mmol/L, which is far too high.
- E – 128 barely corrects and ignores the osmotic water shift.

**EDIC trap:** Corrected Na⁺ should rise as glucose falls. A falling corrected Na⁺ during treatment signals too much free water and a risk of cerebral oedema.

**Ref:** Umpierrez GE, et al. *Diabetes Care* 2024; Spasovski G, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:320–331. · [W05/D3](#W05-D3) · [W06/D1](#W06-D1)

questions.stem: A confused patient has Na⁺ 135, glucose 10, urea 8 mmol/L, measured osmolality 320 mOsm/kg and undetectable ethanol.
options: The calculated osmolality is 288 mOsm/kg.
Ethylene glycol causes AKI with calcium oxalate crystals and hypocalcaemia; thiamine and pyridoxine are cofactors given in treatment.
A normal osmolal gap would exclude toxic alcohol poisoning.
An osmolal gap of 32 suggests a toxic alcohol.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Calculated osmolality = 2 × 135 + 10 + 8 = 288 mOsm/kg.
- B (True) – Ethylene glycol is metabolised to glycolate (acidosis) and oxalate, which precipitates as calcium oxalate in the tubules (AKI, crystalluria) and lowers Ca²⁺. Thiamine and pyridoxine divert glyoxylate to non-toxic products.
- C (False) – The OG reflects the parent alcohol. As it is metabolised to acids, the OG falls and the AG rises, so a late presenter can have a normal OG.
- D (True) – OG = 320 − 288 = 32 (normal < ~10) with ethanol excluded. Suspect methanol or ethylene glycol, give fomepizole and consider dialysis.

**EDIC trap:** Early: high OG, normal AG. Late: high AG, normal OG.

**Ref:** Kraut JA, Mullins ME. *N Engl J Med* 2018;378:270–280. · [W05/D3](#W05-D3)

questions.stem: A patient found with an empty bottle of rubbing alcohol has a raised osmolal gap, ketonaemia, a normal anion gap and normal pH. The likely toxin is:
options: Propylene glycol
Methanol
Isopropanol
Ethylene glycol
Salicylate
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Rubbing alcohol is usually 70 % isopropanol. Alcohol dehydrogenase converts it to acetone, a ketone rather than an acid. The result is a raised osmolal gap and ketonaemia/ketonuria without acidosis or a raised AG ("ketosis without acidosis"). Treatment is supportive, and fomepizole is not needed.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Propylene glycol (a benzodiazepine vehicle) raises the OG and causes a lactic HAGMA.
- B – Methanol produces formic acid, causing a HAGMA and visual loss.
- D – Ethylene glycol produces glycolic and oxalic acid, causing a HAGMA, AKI and oxalate crystals.
- E – Salicylate causes respiratory alkalosis plus HAGMA, without a raised osmolal gap.

**EDIC trap:** Acetone can falsely raise creatinine measured by the Jaffe method.

**Ref:** Kraut JA, Mullins ME. *N Engl J Med* 2018;378:270–280. · [W05/D3](#W05-D3)

questions.stem: Regarding the diagnosis of hypotonic hyponatraemia (Spasovski 2014):
options: With urine osmolality > 100, a urine Na⁺ ≤ 30 mmol/L suggests SIAD.
A serum Na⁺ of 127 mmol/L is classified as "profound".
Urine osmolality ≤ 100 mOsm/kg suggests SIAD.
Hyponatraemia caused by hyperglycaemia is hypotonic.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – With U-osm > 100, a U-Na⁺ ≤ 30 mmol/L suggests **low effective arterial blood volume** (hypovolaemia, heart failure, cirrhosis). SIAD typically has U-Na⁺ > 30.
- B (False) – Biochemical grades: mild 130–135, moderate 125–129, profound < 125 mmol/L. So 127 is moderate.
- C (False) – U-osm ≤ 100 mOsm/kg means maximally dilute urine with ADH suppressed: primary polydipsia or low solute intake. In SIAD the urine is inappropriately concentrated.
- D (False) – Hyperglycaemia causes a **hypertonic** (translocational) hyponatraemia, which must be excluded first.

**EDIC trap:** Treatment urgency follows the symptoms, not the biochemical grade.

**Ref:** Spasovski G, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:320–331. · [W06/D1](#W06-D1)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old with Na⁺ 112 mmol/L has a generalised seizure. The first treatment is:
options: Fluid restriction to 800 mL/day
0.9 % NaCl 1 L over 1 h
150 mL 3 % NaCl IV over 20 min, recheck Na⁺, and repeat up to twice to achieve a rise of ~5 mmol/L
3 % NaCl infusion aiming for Na⁺ 130 within 6 h
Tolvaptan 15 mg orally
questions.expl:
**Why C:** A seizure is a severe symptom, so hypertonic saline is needed urgently, whatever the chronicity. Give 150 mL of 3 % NaCl over 20 min, recheck Na⁺, and repeat up to twice until Na⁺ has risen by ~5 mmol/L. Then stay within ≤ 10 mmol/L in 24 h and ≤ 8 mmol/L per 24 h afterwards.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Fluid restriction acts over days and is wrong for a seizing patient.
- B – 0.9 % NaCl barely raises Na⁺ and can worsen it in SIAD (desalination).
- D – Reaching 130 within 6 h is a rise of 18 mmol/L, which risks osmotic demyelination.
- E – Tolvaptan is slow and unpredictable, and it is not used for severe symptoms.

**EDIC trap:** Aim for +5 mmol/L in the first hour, not a normal sodium.

**Ref:** Spasovski G, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:320–331. · [W06/D1](#W06-D1)

questions.stem: Regarding the correction of chronic hyponatraemia:
options: In SALSA, rapid intermittent bolus therapy caused significantly more overcorrection than slow continuous infusion.
The limit is ≤ 10 mmol/L in the first 24 h and ≤ 8 mmol/L in each following 24 h.
Hypokalaemia, alcoholism, malnutrition and liver disease increase the risk of osmotic demyelination.
Overcorrection is treated with 10 mL/kg of free water over 1 h, ± desmopressin 2 µg IV.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – SALSA: overcorrection was 17.2 % (bolus) vs 24.2 % (continuous), NS. The bolus group needed relowering less often.
- B (True) – Limits for chronic hyponatraemia: ≤ 10 mmol/L in the first 24 h and ≤ 8 mmol/L in each following 24 h.
- C (True) – Hypokalaemia, alcoholism, malnutrition, advanced liver disease and very low Na⁺ (≤ 105) raise the risk of osmotic demyelination.
- D (True) – To relower Na⁺, give 10 mL/kg of electrolyte-free water (e.g. 5 % glucose) over 1 h, ± desmopressin 2 µg IV, with close monitoring.

**EDIC trap:** K⁺ replacement also raises Na⁺, so include it when you calculate the expected correction.

**Ref:** Baek SH, et al. SALSA. *JAMA Intern Med* 2021; Spasovski G, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:320–331. · [W06/D1](#W06-D1)

questions.stem: A 60-kg woman (TBW = 0.5 × weight) has Na⁺ 118 mmol/L. Using the Adrogué-Madias formula, 1 L of 3 % NaCl (Na⁺ 513 mmol/L) is expected to raise serum Na⁺ by approximately:
options: 17.1 mmol/L
6.6 mmol/L
19.8 mmol/L
9.3 mmol/L
12.7 mmol/L
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Adrogué–Madias formula: ΔNa⁺ = (infusate Na⁺ − serum Na⁺)/(TBW + 1). TBW = 0.5 × 60 = 30 L, so ΔNa⁺ = 395/31 ≈ 12.7 mmol/L per litre. That already exceeds the 24-h limit, so give much less than 1 L. The formula ignores urine output, and once ADH falls, aquaresis can raise Na⁺ much more.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 17.1 is 513/30, which uses the infusate Na⁺ without subtracting the serum Na⁺.
- B – 6.6 is 395/60, which uses body weight instead of TBW.
- C – 19.8 divides by too small a TBW (≈ 20 L).
- D – 9.3 divides by too large a TBW (≈ 0.7 × weight).

**EDIC trap:** Recalculate after each infusion and measure Na⁺ every 2–4 h.

**Ref:** Adrogué HJ, et al. *JAMA* 2022;328:280–291. · [W06/D1](#W06-D1)

questions.stem: Regarding SIAD:
options: Fluid restriction is the first-line treatment.
