**Why C:** Patel randomised 83 ARDS patients on face-mask NIV to continue the face mask or switch to a helmet. Intubation fell from 61.5 % to 18.2 %, and 90-day mortality from 56.4 % to 34.1 %. The trial was small, single-centre and stopped early for efficacy, so it is hypothesis-generating.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 38 vs 47 % are the FLORALI intubation rates (HFNO vs standard O₂).
- B – 30 vs 51 % are the HENIVOT intubation rates (helmet NIV vs HFNO).
- D – 4.9 vs 12.2 % are the reintubation rates in Hernández I (HFNO vs conventional O₂, low-risk patients).
- E – 11.8 vs 18.2 % are the HIGH-WEAN reintubation rates (NIV + HFNO vs HFNO).

**Ref:** Patel BK, et al. *JAMA* 2016;315:2435–2441.

Review: [W11/D3](#W11-D3)

questions.stem: Regarding guidelines for non-invasive respiratory support:
options: ESICM 2023 recommends HFNO to reduce mortality.
ERS 2022 suggests trying NIV before HFNC in hypercapnic COPD exacerbation.
ESICM 2023 recommends HFNO over conventional oxygen in AHRF to reduce intubation (strong recommendation, moderate certainty).
ERS/ATS 2017 strongly recommends NIV or CPAP in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – ESICM 2023 makes no recommendation on HFNO to reduce mortality, because trials show no mortality effect.
- B (True) – ERS 2022 suggests a trial of NIV before HFNC in hypercapnic COPD exacerbation (conditional recommendation).
- C (True) – ESICM 2023 recommends HFNO over conventional oxygen in AHRF to reduce intubation (strong, moderate certainty).
- D (True) – ERS/ATS 2017 recommends bilevel NIV or CPAP in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (strong recommendation).

**EDIC trap:** ESICM 2023 gives no general recommendation on HFNO vs CPAP/NIV in AHRF.

**Ref:** Grasselli G, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2023;49:727–759; Oczkowski S, et al. *Eur Respir J* 2022;59:2101574; Rochwerg B, et al. *Eur Respir J* 2017;50:1602426.

Review: [W11/D3](#W11-D3)

questions.stem: According to the ERS/ATS/ESICM weaning consensus (Boles 2007), weaning success is defined as:
options: Passing a spontaneous breathing trial
Extubation and absence of ventilatory support for 7 days
Extubation and absence of ventilatory support for 24 h
Extubation and absence of ventilatory support for 48 h
Extubation directly onto prophylactic NIV
questions.expl:
**Why D:** The Boles consensus defines weaning success as extubation with no ventilatory support for 48 h. Weaning failure is a failed SBT, reintubation or resumption of ventilatory support, or death within 48 h after extubation.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Passing an SBT is a step towards extubation, not weaning success.
- B – A 7-day window is used by WIND for successful separation, not by Boles.
- C – 24 h is too short; Boles uses 48 h.
- E – A patient extubated onto NIV is classed as "weaning in progress".

**Ref:** Boles JM, et al. *Eur Respir J* 2007;29:1033–1056.

Review: [W11/D4](#W11-D4)

questions.stem: Regarding the spontaneous breathing trial (SBT):
options: ATS/ACCP 2017 suggests that the initial SBT uses inspiratory pressure augmentation of 5–8 cmH₂O rather than a T-piece or CPAP.
In Subirà et al. (JAMA 2019), reintubation was significantly higher after a 30-min PSV SBT than after a 2-h T-piece trial.
In Subirà et al., hospital mortality was lower in the PSV group (10.4 % vs 14.9 %).
Most patients who fail an SBT do so only after the first 90 minutes.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ATS/ACCP 2017 suggests an initial SBT with 5–8 cmH₂O of inspiratory pressure augmentation rather than a T-piece or CPAP (conditional, moderate certainty).
- B (False) – Reintubation was 11.1 vs 11.9 % (NS), and successful extubation was higher after the PSV trial (82.3 vs 74.0 %).
- C (True) – Hospital mortality was 10.4 vs 14.9 %, also favouring the PSV SBT.
- D (False) – Most SBT failures occur early, within the first ~20 minutes.

**EDIC trap:** A shorter, less demanding SBT led to more extubations without more reintubations.

**Ref:** Subirà C, et al. *JAMA* 2019;321:2175–2182; Schmidt GA, et al. ATS/ACCP. *Am J Respir Crit Care Med* 2017;195:115–119.

Review: [W11/D4](#W11-D4)

questions.stem: A patient's first separation attempt (an SBT) fails on day 6 of ventilation. She is successfully extubated 4 days after that first attempt and needs no further support. How is she classified by WIND (Béduneau 2017)?
options: Simple weaning
"No weaning" group
Group 1 – short weaning; ICU mortality ~6 %
Group 3 – prolonged weaning; ICU mortality ~29 %
Group 2 – difficult weaning; ICU mortality ~17 %
questions.expl:
**Why E:** WIND counts from the first separation attempt (an SBT or extubation) to successful weaning: < 1 day = short, 1 to < 7 days = difficult, ≥ 7 days = prolonged. She was weaned 4 days after the first attempt, so she is in Group 2 (difficult weaning), with ICU mortality ~17 %.

**Why not the others:**
- A – "Simple weaning" is a Boles category, not a WIND group.
- B – The "no weaning" group never had a separation attempt.
- C – Short weaning requires success within 1 day of the first attempt.
- D – Prolonged weaning requires ≥ 7 days from the first attempt.

**EDIC trap:** Count from the first separation attempt, not intubation.

**Ref:** Béduneau G, et al. WIND. *Am J Respir Crit Care Med* 2017;195:772–783.

Review: [W11/D4](#W11-D4)

questions.stem: Comparing the Boles (2007) and WIND (2017) weaning classifications:
options: In Boles, "difficult weaning" means failing the first SBT and succeeding within 3 SBTs or 7 days.
The Boles classification starts counting from the first SBT.
WIND defines the start of weaning as the day of intubation.
WIND could classify only about half of ventilated patients.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Boles: difficult weaning = failing the first SBT and succeeding within up to 3 SBTs or 7 days; prolonged weaning needs more than that.
- B (True) – The Boles classification counts from the first SBT.
- C (False) – WIND starts at the first separation attempt (an SBT or extubation without an SBT), not at intubation.
- D (False) – WIND classified 99 % of patients; it was Boles that could not classify about half (no SBT, tracheostomy, death).

**EDIC trap:** WIND was created because Boles left many patients unclassifiable.

**Ref:** Boles JM, et al. *Eur Respir J* 2007;29:1033–1056; Béduneau G, et al. WIND. *Am J Respir Crit Care Med* 2017;195:772–783.

Review: [W11/D4](#W11-D4)

questions.stem: During spontaneous breathing, a patient has RR 30/min and tidal volume 400 mL. What is the RSBI and its interpretation?
options: 75 breaths/min/L: below the 105 threshold, but this does not guarantee successful weaning
12 breaths/min/L: very low, guaranteed success
133 breaths/min/L: predicts weaning failure
75 breaths/min/L: guarantees successful extubation
0.013: uninterpretable
questions.expl:
**Why A:** RSBI = f/V_T in litres = 30/0.4 = 75 breaths/min/L. A value ≤ 105 is associated with weaning success, but specificity is low (~0.64), so a low RSBI does not guarantee success. RSBI is an aid and does not replace an SBT.

**Why not the others:**
- B – 12 is f × V_T (minute ventilation in L/min), not f/V_T.
- C – 133 does not follow from the numbers; the RSBI here is 75.
- D – The value is right, but RSBI never guarantees successful extubation.
- E – 0.013 is V_T/f, the inverted ratio.

**EDIC trap:** RSBI has high sensitivity and NPV, but low specificity.

**Ref:** Yang KL, Tobin MJ. *N Engl J Med* 1991;324:1445–1450.

Review: [W11/D4](#W11-D4)

questions.stem: Regarding causes of weaning failure:
options: After a failed SBT, the SBT should be repeated after 1 hour.
In weaning-induced pulmonary oedema, the switch to spontaneous breathing increases venous return and LV afterload.
Metabolic alkalosis can contribute through hypoventilation.
Hypophosphataemia can contribute to weaning failure.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – After a failed SBT, look for the cause, rest the patient on comfortable ventilation and repeat the SBT after 24 h.
- B (True) – Negative intrathoracic pressure increases venous return and LV afterload, which can unmask LV dysfunction and cause weaning-induced pulmonary oedema.
- C (True) – Metabolic alkalosis (e.g. after diuretics) depresses ventilatory drive and causes compensatory hypoventilation.
- D (True) – Hypophosphataemia (like hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia) impairs respiratory muscle function.

**EDIC trap:** Repeating the SBT the same day does not speed weaning; treating the cause does.

**Ref:** Boles JM, et al. *Eur Respir J* 2007;29:1033–1056.

Review: [W11/D4](#W11-D4)

questions.stem: In high-risk patients, Hernández et al. (JAMA 2016) compared HFNO with NIV for 24 h after extubation. Which result is correct?
options: HFNO was inferior to NIV
HFNO was superior, with reintubation 4.9 % vs 12.2 %
HFNO was non-inferior (reintubation 22.8 % vs 19.1 %), with less postextubation respiratory failure (26.9 % vs 39.8 %)
NIV was well tolerated and never interrupted
NIV reduced ICU mortality
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In 604 high-risk patients, 24 h of HFNO after extubation was non-inferior to NIV (margin 10 %), with reintubation 22.8 vs 19.1 %. Postextubation respiratory failure was lower with HFNO (26.9 vs 39.8 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – HFNO met the non-inferiority criterion.
- B – 4.9 vs 12.2 % is Hernández I (low-risk patients, HFNO vs conventional O₂).
- D – NIV was often interrupted because of adverse effects (43 vs 0 %).
- E – ICU mortality did not differ between groups.

**EDIC trap:** Later, in HIGH-WEAN, NIV alternating with HFNO beat HFNO alone in high-risk patients (reintubation 11.8 vs 18.2 %).

**Ref:** Hernández G, et al. *JAMA* 2016;316:1565–1574; Thille AW, et al. HIGH-WEAN. *JAMA* 2019;322:1465–1475.

Review: [W11/D5](#W11-D5)

questions.stem: Regarding postextubation stridor and the cuff leak test (ATS/ACCP 2017):
options: A cuff leak test is suggested for all ventilated patients before extubation.
In the guideline meta-analysis, corticosteroids did not reduce reintubation.
A universally validated cuff-leak volume threshold exists.
Risk factors include traumatic intubation, intubation > 6 days, a large tube and female sex.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – The cuff leak test is suggested only in patients at high risk of postextubation stridor, because blanket testing produces false positives and delays extubation.
- B (False) – In patients who failed a cuff leak test, systemic corticosteroids given ≥ 4 h before extubation reduced reintubation (5.8 vs 17.0 %).
- C (False) – Thresholds varied widely between studies (e.g. 88–283 mL, or 10–24 % of V_T).
- D (True) – Risk factors include traumatic intubation, intubation > 6 days, a large tube, female sex and reintubation after unplanned extubation.

**Ref:** Girard TD, et al. ATS/ACCP. *Am J Respir Crit Care Med* 2017;195:120–133.

Review: [W11/D5](#W11-D5)

questions.stem: A patient with a COPD exacerbation has dyspnoea VAS 7, RR 28/min, HR 110/min, SpO₂ 89 %, CRP 45 mg/L, PaCO₂ 52 mmHg and pH 7.31. Symptoms worsened over 5 days. According to the Rome proposal (adopted by GOLD), the exacerbation is:
options: Not an exacerbation
Mild
Severe
Moderate
Unclassifiable without knowing the place of treatment
questions.expl:
**Why C:** The Rome proposal grades severity by objective variables: dyspnoea VAS ≥ 5, RR ≥ 24/min, HR ≥ 95/min, SpO₂ < 92 % and CRP ≥ 10 mg/L. "Severe" additionally requires hypercapnia with acidosis (PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg and pH < 7.35), which this patient has.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Worsening of symptoms over ≤ 14 days with these features meets the exacerbation definition.
- B – Mild means VAS < 5, RR < 24, HR < 95, SpO₂ ≥ 92 % and CRP < 10.
- D – Moderate would apply if there were hypercapnia without acidosis.
- E – The Rome proposal deliberately abandons classification by place of treatment.

**Ref:** Celli BR, et al. *Am J Respir Crit Care Med* 2021;204:1251–1258; GOLD 2026 Report.

Review: [W12/D1](#W12-D1)

questions.stem: Regarding drug treatment of a COPD exacerbation:
options: Methylxanthines are recommended as an add-on bronchodilator.
In REDUCE, 5 days of prednisone 40 mg was non-inferior to 14 days.
IV corticosteroids are superior to oral corticosteroids even if the patient can swallow.
Antibiotics are indicated whenever NIV or invasive ventilation is required.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Methylxanthines are not recommended, because of adverse effects.
- B (True) – In REDUCE, re-exacerbation within 6 months was 35.9 vs 36.8 %, so 5 days of prednisone 40 mg was non-inferior to 14 days at half the cumulative dose.
- C (False) – Oral corticosteroids are as effective as IV if the patient can swallow.
- D (True) – Antibiotics are indicated when NIV or invasive ventilation is needed, typically for 5 days.

**Ref:** Leuppi JD, et al. REDUCE. *JAMA* 2013;309:2223–2231; GOLD 2026 Report.

Review: [W12/D1](#W12-D1)

questions.stem: In which situation does ERS/ATS 2017 suggest **not** using NIV?
options: Facilitating weaning in a hypercapnic patient
COPD exacerbation with pH 7.30 and RR 26/min despite standard therapy
COPD exacerbation with pH 7.22 that would otherwise need intubation and is not deteriorating rapidly
COPD exacerbation with pH 7.33 and PaCO₂ 60 mmHg
COPD with PaCO₂ 55 mmHg and pH 7.38
questions.expl:
**Why E:** PaCO₂ 55 mmHg with pH 7.38 is compensated hypercapnia without acidosis. For this situation ERS/ATS 2017 suggests not using NIV (conditional, low certainty).

**Why not the others:**
- A – NIV to facilitate weaning in hypercapnic patients is suggested (conditional, moderate certainty).
- B – pH ≤ 7.35 with hypercapnia is a strong recommendation for bilevel NIV (high certainty).
- C – A trial of NIV is recommended even when intubation would otherwise be needed, unless the patient is deteriorating rapidly (strong, moderate).
- D – pH 7.33 with PaCO₂ 60 mmHg is acute respiratory acidosis, a strong indication (high certainty).

**EDIC trap:** NIV treats hypercapnic acidosis, not hypercapnia alone.

**Ref:** Rochwerg B, et al. ERS/ATS. *Eur Respir J* 2017;50:1602426.

Review: [W12/D1](#W12-D1)

questions.stem: Regarding NIV in hypercapnic COPD exacerbation:
options: NIV is absolutely contraindicated when pH is < 7.25.
An arterial blood gas after 1–2 h without improvement in pH/PaCO₂ predicts NIV failure.
EPAP should be set at 0 cmH₂O because it worsens hyperinflation.
In meta-analyses, NIV reduced intubation but not mortality.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – There is no pH below which NIV is absolutely contraindicated; the lower the pH, the higher the risk of failure, so use NIV in the ICU with intubation immediately available.
- B (True) – No improvement in pH and PaCO₂ after 1–2 h predicts NIV failure and should prompt intubation.
- C (False) – EPAP of ~4–6 cmH₂O offsets intrinsic PEEP and reduces the work of triggering.
- D (False) – In meta-analyses NIV reduced both mortality (RR 0.63) and intubation (RR 0.41).

**EDIC trap:** Delaying intubation when NIV is failing worsens outcome.

**Ref:** Rochwerg B, et al. ERS/ATS. *Eur Respir J* 2017;50:1602426; Brochard L, et al. *N Engl J Med* 1995;333:817–822.

Review: [W12/D1](#W12-D1)

questions.stem: Which finding in a patient with acute severe asthma most strongly signals impending respiratory failure?
options: PEF 60 % of predicted
Loud widespread wheeze
PaCO₂ 4.0 kPa in a tachypnoeic patient
PaCO₂ 5.3 kPa (normal) in a tachypnoeic, exhausted patient
SpO₂ 96 % on room air
questions.expl:
**Why D:** In acute asthma, tachypnoea should drive PaCO₂ below normal. A normal (5.3 kPa) or rising PaCO₂ in a tachypnoeic, exhausted patient signals fatigue and impending ventilatory failure, which is a life-threatening feature.

**Why not the others:**
- A – PEF 60 % is a moderate attack; life-threatening attacks have PEF < ~25–30 % of predicted.
- B – Loud wheeze shows air movement, whereas a "silent chest" is the danger sign.
- C – A low PaCO₂ is the expected response to tachypnoea.
- E – SpO₂ 96 % on room air is reassuring.

**EDIC trap:** A "normal" PaCO₂ in severe asthma is an alarm, not reassurance.

**Ref:** Global Initiative for Asthma. GINA 2025 update.

Review: [W12/D1](#W12-D1)

questions.stem: Regarding acute severe asthma (GINA 2025, ERS/ATS 2017):
options: Antibiotics should be given routinely.
In adults, oxygen is titrated to SpO₂ 98–100 %.
IV magnesium sulfate is not recommended in severe exacerbations.
ERS/ATS 2017 strongly recommends NIV in acute asthma.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Antibiotics are given only when there is clear evidence of bacterial infection.
- B (False) – In adults, titrate oxygen to SpO₂ 93–95 %; hyperoxia can raise PaCO₂.
- C (False) – IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 min is used in severe exacerbations not responding to initial treatment.
- D (False) – ERS/ATS 2017 makes no recommendation on NIV in acute asthma because the evidence is insufficient.

**EDIC trap:** The SpO₂ target in asthma (93–95 %) differs from COPD (88–92 %).

**Ref:** Global Initiative for Asthma. GINA 2025 update; Rochwerg B, et al. *Eur Respir J* 2017;50:1602426.

Review: [W12/D1](#W12-D1)

questions.stem: A ventilated COPD patient on volume control with constant flow has a peak pressure that rises from 30 to 45 cmH₂O, while plateau pressure stays at 22 cmH₂O. The most likely cause is:
options: Tension pneumothorax
Progression to ARDS
Bronchospasm, secretions or a kinked tube
Worsening dynamic hyperinflation
Right main bronchus intubation
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In constant-flow VCV, Ppeak − Pplat reflects the resistive pressure (flow × resistance). Here it rose from 8 to 23 cmH₂O while Pplat stayed at 22 cmH₂O, so airway resistance has increased: bronchospasm, secretions, or a kinked or bitten tube.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Tension pneumothorax lowers compliance, so Pplat would also rise.
- B – Progression to ARDS lowers compliance and raises Pplat.
- D – Worsening dynamic hyperinflation raises PEEPi and Pplat.
- E – Endobronchial intubation reduces compliance, raising both Ppeak and Pplat.

**EDIC trap:** Only Ppeak up → resistance; Ppeak and Pplat both up → compliance or hyperinflation.

**Ref:** Hess DR. *Respir Care* 2014;59:1773–1794.

Review: [W12/D1](#W12-D1), [W13/D2](#W13-D2)

questions.stem: Regarding the ATS/IDSA 2019 criteria for severe community-acquired pneumonia:
options: Respiratory rate ≥ 30/min is a minor criterion.
Septic shock requiring vasopressors is a major criterion.
PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 250 is a minor criterion.
Thrombocytopenia < 100 × 10⁹/L is a minor criterion.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Respiratory rate ≥ 30/min is a minor criterion.
- B (True) – Septic shock requiring vasopressors is a major criterion, like the need for invasive ventilation.
- C (True) – PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 250 is a minor criterion.
- D (True) – Thrombocytopenia < 100 × 10⁹/L is a minor criterion, as are confusion, uraemia, leucopenia, hypothermia, multilobar infiltrates and hypotension needing aggressive fluids.

**EDIC trap:** Severe CAP = 1 major or ≥ 3 minor criteria.

**Ref:** Metlay JP, et al. ATS/IDSA. *Am J Respir Crit Care Med* 2019;200:e45–e67.

Review: [W12/D2](#W12-D2)

questions.stem: A 55-year-old returns from a hotel stay with high fever, relative bradycardia, diarrhoea, hyponatraemia and raised CK. He is admitted to the ICU with severe CAP. The urinary Legionella antigen is negative. What is the correct conclusion?
options: Legionella is excluded if the sputum Gram stain is negative
Switch to β-lactam monotherapy, which covers Legionella
Repeat the urinary antigen; if negative, Legionella is excluded
The test detects only *L. pneumophila* serogroup 1, so send PCR/culture from the lower respiratory tract and keep atypical cover
A negative test excludes Legionella; stop the macrolide
questions.expl:
**Why D:** The urinary antigen detects only *L. pneumophila* serogroup 1, so a negative result does not exclude Legionella, especially with this typical picture (hotel stay, hyponatraemia, raised CK, relative bradycardia). Send lower respiratory tract PCR or culture and continue a macrolide or fluoroquinolone.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Legionella stains poorly on Gram stain, so a negative stain excludes nothing.
- B – β-lactams do not cover intracellular atypical pathogens such as Legionella.
- C – Repeating the same test does not overcome its serogroup limitation.
- E – Stopping the macrolide risks untreated Legionnaires' disease.

**EDIC trap:** A negative urinary antigen does not rule out Legionella.

**Ref:** Martin-Loeches I, et al. ERS/ESICM/ESCMID/ALAT. *Intensive Care Med* 2023;49:615–632; Metlay JP, et al. *Am J Respir Crit Care Med* 2019;200:e45–e67.

Review: [W12/D2](#W12-D2)

questions.stem: Regarding the CAPE COD trial (NEJM 2023):
options: Hydrocortisone reduced insulin requirements.
Hydrocortisone was given at 400 mg/day for 7 days.
Patients with septic shock on vasopressors at enrolment were included.
Patients with influenza were included and benefited most.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Hydrocortisone increased insulin requirements.
- B (False) – The dose was 200 mg/day for 4 days, then tapered, for a total of 8 or 14 days.
- C (False) – Septic shock on vasopressors was an exclusion criterion.
- D (False) – PCR-positive influenza was an exclusion criterion.

**EDIC trap:** 28-day mortality fell (6.2 vs 11.9 %) only in sCAP without shock and without influenza.

**Ref:** Dequin PF, et al. CAPE COD. *N Engl J Med* 2023;388:1931–1941.

Review: [W12/D2](#W12-D2)

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the REMAP-CAP corticosteroid domain (ICM 2025)?
options: It used dexamethasone 6 mg/day for 10 days
It showed a significant reduction in 28-day mortality
It used methylprednisolone 40 mg/day for 7 days, with 60-day mortality 16 % vs 18 %
It used hydrocortisone 50 mg 6-hourly for 7 days and was stopped for futility
It excluded patients with influenza and shock
questions.expl:
**Why D:** The REMAP-CAP corticosteroid domain randomised 658 patients (536 : 122) to hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 h for 7 days or no hydrocortisone, and stopped for futility. 90-day mortality was 15 vs 9.8 %; a large benefit is unlikely, but the wide intervals did not exclude a small benefit or harm.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Dexamethasone 6 mg/day for 10 days is the RECOVERY COVID-19 regimen.
- B – There was no significant mortality reduction.
- C – Methylprednisolone 40 mg/day with 60-day mortality 16 vs 18 % describes ESCAPe.
- E – Unlike CAPE COD, REMAP-CAP included patients with influenza and shock.

**Ref:** REMAP-CAP Investigators. *Intensive Care Med* 2025;51:665–680; Meduri GU, et al. ESCAPe. *Intensive Care Med* 2022;48:1009–1023.

Review: [W12/D2](#W12-D2)

questions.stem: Regarding empirical treatment of severe CAP:
options: Routine anaerobic cover is recommended for suspected aspiration pneumonia.
Oseltamivir may be given empirically during influenza season when PCR is unavailable.
ERS/ESICM 2023 suggests adding a macrolide rather than a fluoroquinolone to a β-lactam.
Procalcitonin should be used to decide whether to start antibiotics.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Aspiration pneumonia is treated as standard CAP; anaerobic cover is added only for lung abscess or empyema.
- B (True) – During influenza season, oseltamivir can be started empirically when PCR is unavailable.
- C (True) – ERS/ESICM 2023 suggests adding a macrolide, rather than a fluoroquinolone, to a β-lactam (conditional, low certainty).
- D (False) – Procalcitonin helps to shorten antibiotic duration, not to decide whether to start antibiotics.

**Ref:** Martin-Loeches I, et al. ERS/ESICM/ESCMID/ALAT. *Intensive Care Med* 2023;49:615–632; Metlay JP, et al. *Am J Respir Crit Care Med* 2019;200:e45–e67.

Review: [W12/D2](#W12-D2)

questions.stem: A patient with pneumonia has a moderate parapneumonic effusion that is safely accessible on ultrasound. Pleural pH (blood gas analyser) is 7.30, pleural LDH is 1200 IU/L and he remains febrile. According to BTS 2023, the next step is:
options: Intrapleural streptokinase
Immediate VATS decortication
Consider a chest drain (small-bore, ≤ 14 F, ultrasound-guided)
Intrapleural tPA alone
No drainage; antibiotics alone because pH > 7.2
questions.expl:
**Why C:** BTS 2023 grades pleural pH: < 7.2 means drain, while 7.2–7.4 is intermediate risk, where LDH is measured. With LDH > 900 IU/L and ongoing sepsis, a small-bore (≤ 14 F), ultrasound-guided chest drain should be considered.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Intrapleural streptokinase was ineffective in MIST1.
- B – VATS is reserved for failure of drainage and medical therapy, not a first step.
- D – In MIST2, tPA alone did not work; only tPA + DNase improved drainage of a residual collection.
- E – pH > 7.2 does not rule out drainage when LDH is high and the patient remains septic.

**Ref:** Roberts ME, et al. BTS. *Thorax* 2023;78:1143–1156; Rahman NM, et al. MIST2. *N Engl J Med* 2011;365:518–526; Maskell NA, et al. MIST1. *N Engl J Med* 2005;352:865–874.

Review: [W12/D5](#W12-D5)

questions.stem: Regarding peri-intubation risk in the ICU:
options: In INTUBE, cardiovascular instability (42.6 %) was the most frequent major peri-intubation event.
In INTUBE, first-pass success was only about 80 %.
A MACOCHA score ≥ 3 indicates low risk of difficult intubation.
In the MACOCHA score, Mallampati III–IV scores 1 point.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – In INTUBE, a major peri-intubation event occurred in 45.2 % of patients, most often cardiovascular instability (42.6 %).
- B (True) – First-pass success was only about 80 %.
- C (False) – A MACOCHA score ≥ 3 (range 0–12) indicates high risk of difficult intubation.
- D (False) – In MACOCHA, Mallampati III–IV scores 5 points, the largest single item.

**EDIC trap:** In INTUBE, severe hypoxaemia occurred in 9.3 % and cardiac arrest in 3.1 %, so ICU intubation is a high-risk procedure.

**Ref:** Russotto V, et al. INTUBE. *JAMA* 2021;325:1164–1172; De Jong A, et al. *Am J Respir Crit Care Med* 2013;187:832–839.

Review: [W12/D3](#W12-D3)

questions.stem: An ICU resident (not an anaesthetist) is about to intubate a patient with obstructive sleep apnoea, Mallampati II, mouth opening 4 cm, normal neck mobility, GCS 6 and SpO₂ 75 %. What is the MACOCHA score?
options: 5 – high risk of difficult intubation
questions.expl:
**Why C:** MACOCHA: OSA 2 + coma (GCS < 8) 1 + severe hypoxaemia (SpO₂ < 80 %) 1 + non-anaesthetist operator 1 = 5. Mallampati II, mouth opening ≥ 3 cm and normal neck mobility score 0. A score ≥ 3 means high risk of difficult intubation.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 6 would need one more risk factor, such as limited mouth opening or reduced neck mobility.
- B – 3 omits two points, e.g. the 2 points for OSA.
- D – 4 omits one factor, typically the non-anaesthetist operator.
- E – 2 counts only the OSA.

**Ref:** De Jong A, et al. *Am J Respir Crit Care Med* 2013;187:832–839.

Review: [W12/D3](#W12-D3)

questions.stem: Regarding RCTs of emergency airway management in critically ill adults:
options: In DEVICE, videolaryngoscopy reduced severe complications.
In BOUGIE, a bougie significantly increased first-pass success.
In DEVICE, videolaryngoscopy increased first-pass success (85.1 % vs 70.8 %).
In PreVent, bag-mask ventilation between induction and laryngoscopy significantly increased aspiration.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – In DEVICE, severe complications were 21.4 vs 20.9 % (no difference).
- B (False) – BOUGIE was negative: first-pass success was 80.4 % with a bougie vs 83.0 % with a stylet.
- C (True) – Videolaryngoscopy increased first-pass success (85.1 vs 70.8 %).
- D (False) – In PreVent, bag-mask ventilation halved severe hypoxaemia (10.9 vs 22.8 %) without a significant difference in aspiration (2.5 vs 4.0 %).

**EDIC trap:** Bag-mask ventilation between induction and laryngoscopy is safe and prevents hypoxaemia.

**Ref:** Prekker ME, et al. DEVICE. *N Engl J Med* 2023;389:418–429; Driver BE, et al. BOUGIE. *JAMA* 2021;326:2488–2497; Casey JD, et al. PreVent. *N Engl J Med* 2019;380:811–821.

Review: [W12/D3](#W12-D3)

questions.stem: The RSI trial (NEJM 2025) compared ketamine and etomidate for emergency intubation. Which finding is correct?
options: Ketamine reduced 28-day mortality
Mortality did not differ, and cardiovascular collapse was more frequent with ketamine (22.1 % vs 17.0 %)
Ketamine caused more severe hypoxaemia
Etomidate increased mortality through adrenal suppression
Cardiovascular collapse was similar in both groups
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In the RSI trial, 28-day in-hospital mortality did not differ (28.1 % ketamine vs 29.1 % etomidate), while cardiovascular collapse during intubation was more frequent with ketamine (22.1 vs 17.0 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – Mortality did not differ.
- C – Ketamine did not cause more severe hypoxaemia.
- D – Adrenal suppression by etomidate (11β-hydroxylase) did not translate into higher mortality.
- E – Cardiovascular collapse was more frequent with ketamine.

**EDIC trap:** No induction agent is "haemodynamically safe"; reduce the dose in patients at risk of collapse.

**Ref:** Casey JD, et al. RSI. *N Engl J Med* 2025.

Review: [W12/D3](#W12-D3)

questions.stem: Regarding the "physiologically difficult airway" and drugs for intubation:
options: Succinylcholine is contraindicated in hyperkalaemia and in burns older than 24–72 h.
In a patient with DKA and severe metabolic acidosis, the high pre-intubation minute ventilation must be maintained after intubation.
Sugammadex reverses rocuronium but does not by itself solve a CICO situation caused by oedema or obstruction.
Propofol causes less hypotension than ketamine or etomidate.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Succinylcholine raises K⁺ by ~0.5 mmol/L and can cause life-threatening hyperkalaemia in burns older than 24–72 h, denervation and immobilisation.
- B (True) – In severe metabolic acidosis, a sudden fall in minute ventilation after intubation can cause a precipitous fall in pH and cardiac arrest.
- C (True) – Sugammadex reverses rocuronium, but airway oedema or obstruction persists, so a CICO situation may still need front-of-neck access.
- D (False) – Propofol causes more hypotension than ketamine or etomidate.

**Ref:** Higgs A, et al. DAS/ICS/FICM/RCoA. *Br J Anaesth* 2018;120:323–352.

Review: [W12/D3](#W12-D3)

questions.stem: The SETPOINT2 trial (JAMA 2022) randomised ventilated patients with severe stroke to tracheostomy within 5 days or after day 10. What did it show?
options: Fewer days of sedation, with lower 30-day mortality
Better functional outcome with early tracheostomy
Higher procedural complication rates with late tracheostomy
No improvement in functional outcome (mRS 0–4 at 6 months: 43.5 % vs 47.1 %)
Lower 6-month mortality with early tracheostomy
questions.expl:
**Why D:** SETPOINT2 randomised ventilated patients with severe stroke to tracheostomy within 5 days or after day 10. Survival without severe disability (mRS 0–4) at 6 months did not differ (43.5 vs 47.1 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – Early tracheostomy did not lower 30-day mortality.
- B – Functional outcome was not better with early tracheostomy.
- C – Procedural complications were not higher with late tracheostomy.
- E – 6-month mortality was numerically higher with early tracheostomy (35.0 vs 29.6 %, NS).

**EDIC trap:** Like TracMan, SETPOINT2 found no hard-outcome benefit from early tracheostomy; decide individually, typically at ~10 days.

**Ref:** Bösel J, et al. SETPOINT2. *JAMA* 2022;327:1899–1909.

Review: [W12/D4](#W12-D4)

questions.stem: Regarding tracheostomy technique and complications:
options: An unstable cervical spine favours surgical tracheostomy.
Compared with surgical tracheostomy, percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy was associated with fewer stoma infections (Putensen 2014).
Cuff pressure should be kept at 20–30 cmH₂O.
A tracheo-innominate fistula typically presents within the first 24 hours.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – An unstable cervical spine (no neck extension) favours a surgical approach.
- B (True) – In the Putensen meta-analysis, percutaneous tracheostomy was associated with fewer stoma infections than surgical tracheostomy.
- C (True) – Cuff pressure of 20–30 cmH₂O protects against both microaspiration and mucosal ischaemia.
- D (False) – A tracheo-innominate fistula typically presents in weeks 1–4, often after a "sentinel bleed".

**EDIC trap:** Displacement of an immature stoma is the most dangerous early complication.

**Ref:** Putensen C, et al. *Crit Care* 2014;18:544; McGrath BA, et al. NTSP. *Anaesthesia* 2012;67:1025–1041.

Review: [W12/D4](#W12-D4)

questions.stem: Two weeks after tracheostomy, a patient has a small bleed from the stoma, followed an hour later by brisk arterial bleeding around the tube. The immediate first manoeuvre is to:
options: Perform bronchoscopy to locate the source
Overinflate the tracheostomy cuff; if this fails, apply digital compression of the artery against the sternum through the stoma, and call a vascular/thoracic surgeon
Arrange CT angiography before any intervention
Remove the tracheostomy tube
Give nebulised tranexamic acid and observe
questions.expl:
**Why B:** A sentinel bleed followed by brisk arterial haemorrhage two weeks after tracheostomy suggests a tracheo-innominate fistula. First overinflate the cuff to tamponade the bleeding. If that fails, compress the artery against the sternum digitally through the stoma, secure the airway with an orotracheal tube cuffed distal to the bleed, and call the surgeon immediately.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Bronchoscopy delays haemorrhage control.
- C – CT angiography wastes time in massive bleeding.
- D – Removing the tube loses both the airway and the tamponade.
- E – Nebulised tranexamic acid cannot stop arterial bleeding.

**Ref:** McGrath BA, et al. NTSP. *Anaesthesia* 2012;67:1025–1041.

Review: [W12/D4](#W12-D4)

questions.stem: Regarding pneumothorax and bronchopleural fistula:
options: Absent lung sliding is specific for pneumothorax.
In a ventilated patient with bronchopleural fistula, chest-drain suction should be increased to reduce the air leak.
In Brown et al. (NEJM 2020), conservative management of moderate-to-large primary spontaneous pneumothorax was inferior for re-expansion at 8 weeks.
A lung point on ultrasound is highly specific for pneumothorax.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Absent lung sliding is not specific; it also occurs with endobronchial intubation, pleurodesis, apnoea and ARDS.
- B (False) – In bronchopleural fistula, minimise suction, because it increases flow through the fistula; use the lowest V_T, Pplat and PEEP with a short inspiratory time.
- C (False) – Conservative management was non-inferior for re-expansion at 8 weeks, and ~15 % needed intervention.
- D (True) – A lung point is highly specific for pneumothorax.

**EDIC trap:** Lung sliding rules pneumothorax out at that point; its absence does not rule it in.

**Ref:** Brown SGA, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2020;382:405–415; Lichtenstein DA, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2000;26:1434–1440.

Review: [W12/D5](#W12-D5)

questions.stem: A paralysed patient on VCV has V_T 450 mL, constant inspiratory flow 45 L/min, Ppeak 33 cmH₂O, Pplat 24 cmH₂O, set PEEP 6 cmH₂O and total PEEP 6 cmH₂O. What are the static compliance and airway resistance?
options: C_stat 16.7 mL/cmH₂O; R 9 cmH₂O/L/s
C_stat 25 mL/cmH₂O; R 12 cmH₂O/L/s
C_stat 25 mL/cmH₂O; R 9 cmH₂O/L/s
C_stat 18.75 mL/cmH₂O; R 12 cmH₂O/L/s
C_stat 16.7 mL/cmH₂O; R 12 cmH₂O/L/s
questions.expl:
**Why B:** C_stat = V_T/(Pplat − PEEP_tot) = 450/(24 − 6) = 25 mL/cmH₂O. Flow 45 L/min = 0.75 L/s, so R = (Ppeak − Pplat)/flow = (33 − 24)/0.75 = 12 cmH₂O/L/s.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 16.7 mL/cmH₂O is dynamic compliance (450/(33 − 6)), and R = 9 comes from not converting flow to L/s.
- C – Compliance is correct, but R = 9 comes from not converting flow to L/s.
- D – 18.75 mL/cmH₂O divides V_T by Pplat without subtracting PEEP.
- E – 16.7 mL/cmH₂O is dynamic, not static, compliance.

**EDIC trap:** Always convert flow from L/min to L/s before calculating resistance.

**Ref:** Hess DR. *Respir Care* 2014;59:1773–1794.

Review: [W13/D2](#W13-D2)

questions.stem: Match the waveform description to its interpretation:
options: "Sawtooth" oscillations on the flow–time curve → secretions or water in the circuit.
A concave (downward-bowed) inspiratory pressure–time curve in VCV → alveolar overdistension.
A "scooped" expiratory limb of the flow–volume loop → small-airway obstruction.
In PCV, inspiratory flow that has not reached zero at the end of Ti → Ti shorter than ~3τ, so V_T is not fully delivered.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Sawtooth oscillations on the flow–time curve suggest secretions or water in the circuit.
- B (False) – A concave pressure–time curve in VCV means flow starvation (patient demand exceeds set flow); overdistension shows as "beaking" of the P–V loop.
- C (True) – A scooped expiratory limb of the flow–volume loop indicates small-airway obstruction.
- D (True) – Flow that has not returned to zero at the end of Ti in PCV means Ti < ~3τ, so V_T is not fully delivered.

**EDIC trap:** Flow starvation is a patient–ventilator mismatch, not a lung-mechanics problem.

**Ref:** Mojoli F, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2016;42:914–915; Hess DR. *Respir Care* 2014;59:1773–1794.

Review: [W13/D2](#W13-D2)

questions.stem: A passive patient has airway resistance 20 cmH₂O/L/s and compliance 50 mL/cmH₂O. Expiratory time is 2 s. What is the time constant, and roughly what fraction of V_T is exhaled?
options: τ 1000 s; negligible exhalation
questions.expl:
**Why A:** τ = R × C = 20 cmH₂O/L/s × 0.05 L/cmH₂O = 1.0 s. Te 2 s = 2τ, so ~86 % of V_T is exhaled (1τ ≈ 63 %, 3τ ≈ 95 %, 5τ ≈ 99 %).

**Why not the others:**
- B – τ is 1.0 s, not 2.5 s, and the exhaled fraction is wrong.
- C – τ is right, but 63 % is the fraction after 1τ, not 2τ.
- D – τ is 1.0 s, not 0.4 s, and 99 % requires ~5τ.
- E – τ 1000 s comes from not converting mL to L.

**EDIC trap:** Express compliance in L/cmH₂O when calculating τ.

**Ref:** Hess DR. *Respir Care* 2014;59:1773–1794.

Review: [W13/D2](#W13-D2)

questions.stem: Regarding oesophageal pressure (P_es) monitoring:
options: Chiumello (AJRCCM 2008) found that the ratio E_L/E_rs varied from 0.33 to 0.95.
Absolute P_es values are more reliable than changes in P_es.
In EPVent-2, P_es-guided PEEP reduced mortality compared with an empirical high PEEP/FiO₂ table.
Correct balloon position is confirmed by an occlusion test with ΔP_es/ΔP_aw ≈ 0.8–1.2.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – In Chiumello's study, E_L/E_rs varied from 0.33 to 0.95, so the same Pplat can mean very different lung stress.
- B (False) – Absolute P_es is affected by mediastinal weight and position, so changes in P_es are more reliable.
- C (False) – EPVent-2 found no difference (28-day mortality 32.4 vs 30.6 %).
- D (True) – An occlusion test with ΔP_es/ΔP_aw ≈ 0.8–1.2 confirms correct balloon position.

**EDIC trap:** P_es is better at tracking changes than at measuring absolute pleural pressure.

**Ref:** Chiumello D, et al. *Am J Respir Crit Care Med* 2008;178:346–355; Beitler JR, et al. EPVent-2. *JAMA* 2019;321:846–857; Mauri T, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2016;42:1360–1373.

Review: [W13/D2](#W13-D2)

questions.stem: A passive patient on VCV has V_T 400 mL, Pplat 28 cmH₂O and PEEP 8 cmH₂O. During the breath, oesophageal pressure rises by 8 cmH₂O. What are the dynamic transpulmonary driving pressure (ΔP_L) and the elastance-derived end-inspiratory transpulmonary pressure (P_L,ei)?
options: ΔP_L 12 cmH₂O; P_L,ei 16.8 cmH₂O
ΔP_L 28 cmH₂O; P_L,ei 16.8 cmH₂O
ΔP_L 12 cmH₂O; P_L,ei 28 cmH₂O
ΔP_L 20 cmH₂O; P_L,ei 11.2 cmH₂O
ΔP_L 12 cmH₂O; P_L,ei 11.2 cmH₂O
questions.expl:
**Why A:** ΔP_aw = 28 − 8 = 20 cmH₂O, so E_rs = 20/0.4 = 50 cmH₂O/L. E_cw = 8/0.4 = 20, so E_L = 30 cmH₂O/L. ΔP_L = ΔP_aw − ΔP_es = 20 − 8 = 12 cmH₂O, and P_L,ei = Pplat × E_L/E_rs = 28 × 0.6 = 16.8 cmH₂O.

**Why not the others:**
- B – 28 cmH₂O is Pplat, not a transpulmonary pressure.
- C – P_L,ei 28 cmH₂O ignores the chest-wall component.
- D – 20 cmH₂O is the airway driving pressure, and 11.2 cmH₂O uses E_cw/E_rs instead of E_L/E_rs.
- E – ΔP_L is right, but P_L,ei 11.2 cmH₂O uses the chest-wall ratio.

**Ref:** Mauri T, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2016;42:1360–1373.

Review: [W13/D2](#W13-D2)

questions.stem: An obese patient with ARDS is ventilated with PEEP 10 cmH₂O. End-expiratory oesophageal pressure is 14 cmH₂O and Pplat is 31 cmH₂O.
options: End-expiratory transpulmonary pressure is −4 cmH₂O.
A negative end-expiratory P_L means dependent alveoli tend to collapse at end-expiration.
Raising PEEP to bring end-expiratory P_L to ≥ 0 is physiologically justified.
Pplat 31 cmH₂O necessarily indicates excessive lung stress in this patient.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – P_L,ee = PEEP_tot − P_es,ee = 10 − 14 = −4 cmH₂O.
- B (True) – A negative end-expiratory P_L means dependent alveoli tend to collapse at end-expiration (atelectrauma).
- C (True) – Raising PEEP until end-expiratory P_L is ≥ 0 is physiologically reasonable, especially in obesity.
- D (False) – With a stiff chest wall, part of Pplat distends the chest wall, so Pplat > 30 cmH₂O need not mean excessive lung stress.

**EDIC trap:** In obesity, Pplat overestimates lung stress; P_es helps to separate lung from chest wall.

**Ref:** Mauri T, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2016;42:1360–1373; Talmor D, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2008;359:2095–2104.

Review: [W13/D2](#W13-D2)

questions.stem: A 20-minute recording in a patient on PSV shows 300 ventilator cycles, 50 ineffective efforts and 20 double-triggering events. What is the asynchrony index (AI)?
options: 20 % – severe asynchrony
questions.expl:
**Why E:** AI = asynchronous events/(ventilator cycles + ineffective efforts) × 100 = (50 + 20)/(300 + 50) × 100 = 20 %. An AI > 10 % is severe asynchrony. The patient's true rate is 350/20 = 17.5/min, while the ventilator shows only 15/min.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 6.7 % counts only double triggering, over ventilator cycles alone.
- B – 14.3 % counts only ineffective efforts.
- C – 23.3 % omits ineffective efforts from the denominator.
- D – 16.7 % counts only ineffective efforts, over ventilator cycles alone.

**EDIC trap:** Ineffective efforts belong in both the numerator and the denominator.

**Ref:** Thille AW, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2006;32:1515–1522.

Review: [W13/D3](#W13-D3)

questions.stem: Regarding types of patient–ventilator asynchrony:
options: In low-V_T VCV, double triggering can nearly double the delivered tidal volume (breath stacking).
Reverse triggering occurs only in awake patients on pressure support.
Auto-triggering from cardiac oscillations can mimic respiratory effort during brain-death assessment.
Delayed cycling in COPD is treated by lowering the cycle-off percentage.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – In low-V_T VCV, double triggering stacks two breaths and can nearly double the delivered V_T.
- B (False) – Reverse triggering is typical of deeply sedated patients on controlled modes.
- C (True) – Cardiac oscillations can auto-trigger the ventilator and mimic effort; the apnoea test is therefore done without ventilator triggering.
- D (False) – Delayed cycling in COPD (long τ) is treated by raising the cycle-off threshold (e.g. to 40–50 %) and lowering PS.

**EDIC trap:** Premature cycling → lower cycle-off; delayed cycling → raise cycle-off.

**Ref:** Thille AW, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2006;32:1515–1522; Pham T, et al. *Crit Care* 2021.

Review: [W13/D3](#W13-D3)

questions.stem: A COPD patient on PSV has intrinsic PEEP 6 cmH₂O, and the ventilator pressure trigger is set at −2 cmH₂O. Roughly how much must the patient lower alveolar pressure (inspiratory effort) to trigger a breath?
options: 12 cmH₂O
2 cmH₂O
4 cmH₂O
6 cmH₂O
8 cmH₂O
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Before the airway pressure can fall, the patient's effort must first overcome PEEPi (6 cmH₂O) and then reach the trigger threshold (2 cmH₂O): 6 + 2 = 8 cmH₂O. Smaller efforts are ineffective.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 12 cmH₂O double-counts PEEPi.
- B – 2 cmH₂O ignores the threshold load imposed by PEEPi.
- C – 4 cmH₂O subtracts the trigger from PEEPi instead of adding it.
- D – 6 cmH₂O overcomes PEEPi but does not reach the trigger.

**EDIC trap:** External PEEP (below PEEPi) and lower support (smaller V_T, less PEEPi) reduce ineffective triggering.

**Ref:** Thille AW, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2008;34:1477–1486.

Review: [W13/D3](#W13-D3)

questions.stem: Regarding key studies on asynchrony:
options: Vaporidi 2017: clusters of ineffective efforts were associated with hospital mortality.
Thille 2006: about one quarter of patients had AI > 10 %.
Blanch 2015 proved that asynchrony causes increased mortality.
Thille 2006: AI > 10 % was associated with longer duration of mechanical ventilation.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Clusters of ineffective efforts were associated with higher hospital mortality.
- B (True) – 15 of 62 patients (24 %) had AI > 10 %.
- C (False) – Blanch was observational: AI > 10 % was associated with higher mortality, but causality was not shown.
- D (True) – AI > 10 % was associated with a longer duration of ventilation (median 25.5 vs 7.5 days).

**EDIC trap:** "Associated with" does not mean "causes"; asynchrony may be a marker of severity.

**Ref:** Vaporidi K, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2017;43:184–191; Thille AW, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2006;32:1515–1522; Blanch L, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2015;41:633–641.

Review: [W13/D3](#W13-D3)

questions.stem: Using MP ≈ 0.098 × RR × V_T × (Ppeak − ½ × ΔP), calculate the mechanical power for VCV with V_T 0.5 L, RR 16/min, Ppeak 32 cmH₂O, Pplat 26 cmH₂O and PEEP 12 cmH₂O.
options: 24.3 J/min
11.0 J/min
31.4 J/min
19.6 J/min
9.8 J/min
questions.expl:
**Why D:** ΔP = Pplat − PEEP = 26 − 12 = 14 cmH₂O, so ½ΔP = 7. MP = 0.098 × 16 × 0.5 × (32 − 7) = 0.784 × 25 = 19.6 J/min.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 24.3 J/min is an arithmetic error; the bracket is 25, not 31.
- B – 11.0 J/min uses only ΔP (14) in the bracket.
- C – 31.4 J/min uses Pplat + ΔP (40) instead of Ppeak − ½ΔP.
- E – 9.8 J/min is roughly half the correct value.

**EDIC trap:** In observational data (Serpa Neto 2018), mortality rose above ~17 J/min; MP is not a guideline target.

**Ref:** Gattinoni L, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2016;42:1567–1575; Serpa Neto A, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2018;44:1914–1922.

Review: [W13/D4](#W13-D4)

questions.stem: Regarding mechanical power (Gattinoni, ICM 2016):
options: PEEP does not contribute to mechanical power.
Current guidelines recommend titrating ventilation to keep mechanical power < 17 J/min.
Mechanical power rises linearly with respiratory rate.
Mechanical power rises with the square (exponent 2) of V_T, driving pressure and inspiratory flow.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – PEEP contributes to mechanical power, which rises linearly with PEEP.
- B (False) – MP is an observational marker; no guideline sets an MP target, and no RCT has titrated it.
- C (False) – MP rises with RR to the power 1.4, not linearly.
- D (True) – MP rises with the square of V_T, driving pressure and inspiratory flow.

**EDIC trap:** Lowering V_T while raising RR may not reduce mechanical power.

**Ref:** Gattinoni L, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2016;42:1567–1575.

Review: [W13/D4](#W13-D4)

questions.stem: Using MP ≈ 0.098 × RR × V_T × (PEEP + ΔP_insp), calculate the mechanical power for PCV with RR 25/min, V_T 0.4 L, PEEP 10 cmH₂O and inspiratory pressure 12 cmH₂O above PEEP.
options: 9.8 J/min
11.8 J/min
26.9 J/min
21.6 J/min
43.1 J/min
questions.expl:
**Why D:** MP = 0.098 × 25 × 0.4 × (10 + 12) = 0.98 × 22 = 21.6 J/min.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 9.8 J/min uses only PEEP (10) in the bracket.
- B – 11.8 J/min uses only the inspiratory pressure (12) and omits PEEP.
- C – 26.9 J/min is an arithmetic error.
- E – 43.1 J/min doubles the correct value.

**EDIC trap:** In PCV, ΔP_insp is the pressure above PEEP, and PEEP must be added.

**Ref:** Becher T, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2019;45:1321–1323.

Review: [W13/D4](#W13-D4)

questions.stem: A patient on PSV 10 cmH₂O with PEEP 6 cmH₂O (Ppeak 16 cmH₂O) has an end-expiratory occlusion pressure ΔPocc of −15 cmH₂O. Using P_mus ≈ −¾ × ΔPocc and ΔP_L,dyn ≈ ΔP_aw − ⅔ × ΔPocc:
options: P_mus is about 11 cmH₂O, indicating high effort (> 10 cmH₂O).
Increasing pressure support will necessarily reduce ΔP_L,dyn.
ΔP_L,dyn is about 20 cmH₂O.
ΔP_L,dyn is about 0 cmH₂O because ⅔ × ΔPocc is subtracted from ΔP_aw.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – P_mus ≈ −¾ × (−15) ≈ 11 cmH₂O, above the ~10 cmH₂O threshold for high effort.
- B (False) – Higher PS may reduce effort, but V_T and lung stress can rise, so ΔP_L,dyn need not fall.
- C (True) – ΔP_aw = 16 − 6 = 10, so ΔP_L,dyn ≈ 10 − ⅔ × (−15) = 10 + 10 = 20 cmH₂O.
- D (False) – Because ΔPocc is negative, subtracting ⅔ × ΔPocc adds 10 cmH₂O; ΔP_L,dyn is ~20 cmH₂O, not 0.

**EDIC trap:** Watch the sign of ΔPocc.

**Ref:** Bertoni M, et al. *Crit Care* 2019;23:346.

Review: [W13/D4](#W13-D4)

questions.stem: A patient with severe ARDS has an estimated FRC (aerated "baby lung") of 300 mL and receives V_T 450 mL. Using a specific lung elastance of 13.5 cmH₂O, what are the strain and stress?
options: Strain 1.5; stress ~6.75 cmH₂O
Strain 1.5; stress ~20 cmH₂O, in the range considered injurious
Strain 3; stress ~40 cmH₂O
Strain 0.67; stress ~20 cmH₂O
Strain 0.67; stress ~9 cmH₂O
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Strain = ΔV/FRC = 450/300 = 1.5. Stress = specific elastance × strain = 13.5 × 1.5 ≈ 20 cmH₂O. In experimental models, a strain > 1.5 is clearly injurious, corresponding to a stress of ~20 cmH₂O.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 6.75 cmH₂O is half the correct stress.
- C – A strain of 3 would need V_T 900 mL.
- D – 0.67 is the inverse ratio (FRC/V_T).
- E – 0.67 is the inverse ratio, and so is the stress of ~9 cmH₂O derived from it.

**EDIC trap:** In a small "baby lung", a "normal" V_T can still cause injurious strain.

**Ref:** Chiumello D, et al. *Am J Respir Crit Care Med* 2008;178:346–355; Gattinoni L, et al. *Crit Care* 2017;21:183.

Review: [W13/D4](#W13-D4)

questions.stem: Regarding external PEEP in obstructive lung disease:
options: During controlled ventilation, the response to external PEEP is unpredictable.
In Caramez et al. (CCM 2005), a paradoxical response (fall in Pplat and total PEEP) occurred in 5 of 8 patients at least at one PEEP level.
If Pplat rises during a PEEP trial, the higher PEEP should be kept.
In spontaneously breathing COPD patients with flow limitation, external PEEP set below PEEPi reduces the work of triggering.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – During controlled ventilation, the response to external PEEP is unpredictable.
- B (True) – In Caramez et al., a paradoxical fall in Pplat and total PEEP occurred in 5 of 8 patients at least at one PEEP level.
- C (False) – A rising Pplat means more hyperinflation, so return to the previous PEEP; keep the new PEEP only if Pplat falls or does not change.
- D (True) – Per the "waterfall" concept, external PEEP below PEEPi reduces triggering work without worsening hyperinflation.

**EDIC trap:** Use Pplat to guide a PEEP trial in obstructive disease.

**Ref:** Caramez MP, et al. *Crit Care Med* 2005;33:1519–1528.

Review: [W13/D5](#W13-D5)

questions.stem: A passive COPD patient on VCV has V_T 450 mL, Pplat 26 cmH₂O and set PEEP 6 cmH₂O. An end-expiratory hold shows total PEEP 15 cmH₂O. What are the intrinsic PEEP and the correct static compliance?
options: PEEPi 9 cmH₂O; C_stat 22.5 mL/cmH₂O
PEEPi 6 cmH₂O; C_stat 17.3 mL/cmH₂O
PEEPi 9 cmH₂O; C_stat ≈ 41 mL/cmH₂O
PEEPi 15 cmH₂O; C_stat 30 mL/cmH₂O
PEEPi 21 cmH₂O; C_stat 22.5 mL/cmH₂O
questions.expl:
**Why C:** PEEPi = total PEEP − set PEEP = 15 − 6 = 9 cmH₂O. C_stat must use total PEEP: 450/(26 − 15) = 450/11 ≈ 41 mL/cmH₂O.

**Why not the others:**
- A – PEEPi is right, but 22.5 mL/cmH₂O uses set PEEP and falsely suggests stiff lungs.
- B – PEEPi is 9, not 6, and 17.3 mL/cmH₂O ignores PEEP entirely.
- D – 15 cmH₂O is total, not intrinsic, PEEP.
- E – PEEPi is the difference, not the sum, of total and set PEEP.

**EDIC trap:** Ignoring PEEPi underestimates compliance.

**Ref:** Pepe PE, Marini JJ. *Am Rev Respir Dis* 1982;126:166–170.

Review: [W13/D5](#W13-D5)

questions.stem: Regarding ventilation in status asthmaticus:
options: Reducing RR lengthens expiratory time more than increasing inspiratory flow does.
In Williams (1992), an end-inspiratory volume above FRC (V_EI) ≥ 1.4 L was associated with complications in 65 % of patients.
Normocapnia should be targeted by increasing RR.
A high Ppeak with an acceptable Pplat mainly reflects alveolar overdistension.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – With Ti 1 s, doubling the inspiratory flow gains only 0.5 s of Te, while cutting RR from 20 to 12/min lengthens Te from 2 to 4 s.
- B (True) – Complications occurred in 65 % (11/17) of patients with V_EI ≥ 1.4 L, and in 0 % below it.
- C (False) – Use permissive hypercapnia; raising RR shortens Te and worsens dynamic hyperinflation.
- D (False) – A high Ppeak with an acceptable Pplat is the resistive component, while Pplat (with PEEPi) reflects alveolar pressure.

**EDIC trap:** RR is the most powerful lever for lengthening Te.

**Ref:** Tuxen DV, Lane S. *Am Rev Respir Dis* 1987;136:872–879; Williams TJ, et al. *Am Rev Respir Dis* 1992;146:607–615.

Review: [W13/D5](#W13-D5)

questions.stem: A ventilated asthmatic is on VCV with V_T 600 mL, constant inspiratory flow 60 L/min with no inspiratory pause, and RR 15/min. What are the inspiratory time, expiratory time and I:E ratio?
options: Ti 0.6 s; Te 2.4 s; I:E 1:4
Ti 1.0 s; Te 3.0 s; I:E 1:3
Ti 0.6 s; Te 3.4 s; I:E 1:3
questions.expl:
**Why B:** The cycle is 60/15 = 4 s. Ti = V_T/flow = 0.6 L ÷ 1 L/s = 0.6 s, so Te = 4 − 0.6 = 3.4 s and I:E = 0.6:3.4 ≈ 1:5.7.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Ti 0.36 s does not fit V_T 0.6 L at 1 L/s.
- C – Te 2.4 s corresponds to a 3-s cycle (RR 20/min).
- D – Ti 1.0 s would require a flow of 36 L/min.
- E – Ti and Te are correct, but the I:E ratio is 1:5.7, not 1:3.

**EDIC trap:** Convert flow from L/min to L/s (60 L/min = 1 L/s).

**Ref:** Tuxen DV, Lane S. *Am Rev Respir Dis* 1987;136:872–879.

Review: [W13/D5](#W13-D5)

questions.stem: Regarding ventilation modes:
options: In Demoule (ICM 2016), NAVA reduced the asynchrony index (14.7 % vs 26.7 %) but did not improve the primary outcome.
PRVC increases inspiratory pressure when the patient's effort increases.
In Esteban (NEJM 1995), IMV produced the shortest weaning duration.
NAVA triggers and cycles breaths from the diaphragm's electrical activity (Edi), recorded with an oesophageal catheter.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – In Demoule's trial, NAVA reduced the asynchrony index (14.7 vs 26.7 %), but the primary endpoint (staying in a partial mode for 48 h) did not differ (67.2 vs 63.3 %).
- B (False) – PRVC lowers inspiratory pressure when the patient's effort increases V_T, just when more help may be needed.
- C (False) – In Esteban, IMV was the slowest method; a once-daily SBT was ~2.8× faster.
- D (True) – NAVA triggers and cycles from the diaphragm's electrical activity (Edi), recorded with an oesophageal catheter.

**EDIC trap:** PRVC reduces support when the patient works harder.

**Ref:** Demoule A, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2016;42:1723–1732; Esteban A, et al. *N Engl J Med* 1995;332:345–350.

Review: [W13/D1](#W13-D1)

questions.stem: A 180-cm man with ARDS is ventilated on VCV with V_T 450 mL. Pplat is 30 cmH₂O, PEEP is 14 cmH₂O and there is no intrinsic PEEP. What are his predicted body weight and respiratory-system compliance?
options: PBW 80 kg; C_rs ≈ 28 mL/cmH₂O
PBW 75 kg; C_rs ≈ 15 mL/cmH₂O
PBW 70 kg; C_rs ≈ 32 mL/cmH₂O
PBW ≈ 75 kg; C_rs ≈ 28 mL/cmH₂O
PBW 75 kg; C_rs ≈ 45 mL/cmH₂O
questions.expl:
**Why D:** PBW (men) = 50 + 0.91 × (180 − 152.4) = 50 + 25.1 ≈ 75 kg, so 450 mL ≈ 6 mL/kg PBW. ΔP = Pplat − PEEP = 30 − 14 = 16 cmH₂O, and C_rs = 450/16 ≈ 28 mL/cmH₂O.

**Why not the others:**
- A – C_rs is right, but PBW is 75 kg, not 80 kg.
- B – 15 mL/cmH₂O divides V_T by Pplat instead of by ΔP.
- C – PBW is 75 kg, and 32 mL/cmH₂O divides V_T by PEEP (450/14).
- E – 45 mL/cmH₂O is a miscalculation; ΔP is 16 cmH₂O.

**EDIC trap:** Compliance uses driving pressure (Pplat − total PEEP), not Pplat.

**Ref:** ARDS Network. *N Engl J Med* 2000;342:1301–1308; Amato MBP, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2015;372:747–755.

Review: [W10/D2](#W10-D2), [W13/D2](#W13-D2)

questions.stem: A patient with severe ARDS has P/F 70 mmHg on PEEP 14 cmH₂O and FiO₂ 0.9 after 18 h of optimised ventilation. He was intubated 2 days ago.
options: ESICM 2023 strongly recommends against prolonged high-pressure recruitment manoeuvres.
Prone positioning for ≥ 16 h/day is indicated (P/F < 150 mmHg).
Increasing RR to compensate for a lower V_T increases mechanical power.
VV-ECMO should only be considered once ventilation has exceeded 7 days.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ESICM 2023 strongly recommends against prolonged high-pressure recruitment manoeuvres.
- B (True) – Prone positioning for ≥ 16 h/day is indicated with P/F < 150 mmHg (strong recommendation, PROSEVA).
- C (True) – MP rises with RR (exponent 1.4), so a higher RR can offset the gain from a lower V_T.
- D (False) – In EOLIA, ventilation > 7 days was an exclusion criterion, and CESAR showed the value of early referral.

**EDIC trap:** Refer for ECMO early; late ECMO is less likely to help.

**Ref:** Grasselli G, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2023;49:727–759; Guérin C, et al. PROSEVA. *N Engl J Med* 2013;368:2159–2168; Combes A, et al. EOLIA. *N Engl J Med* 2018;378:1965–1975.

Review: [W10/D4](#W10-D4), [W10/D5](#W10-D5), [W11/D1](#W11-D1), [W13/D4](#W13-D4)

questions.stem: A COPD patient on PSV 18 cmH₂O (cycle-off 25 %) shows a pressure spike at the end of inspiration and frequent ineffective efforts during expiration. Which adjustment is most appropriate?
options: Increase pressure support to 24 cmH₂O
Switch to SIMV
Increase cycle-off to 40–50 % and reduce pressure support
Decrease cycle-off to 10 %
Make the trigger less sensitive
questions.expl:
**Why C:** COPD has a long time constant, so with cycle-off at 25 % insufflation continues into neural expiration (the end-inspiratory pressure spike). Te shortens, PEEPi rises and subsequent efforts become ineffective. A higher cycle-off (40–50 %) and lower PS shorten insufflation, reduce V_T and PEEPi, and reduce ineffective efforts.

**Why not the others:**
- A – More PS increases V_T and PEEPi, which worsens ineffective efforts.
- B – SIMV does not correct delayed cycling and prolongs weaning.
- D – Lowering cycle-off delays cycling even further.
- E – A less sensitive trigger increases ineffective efforts.

**Ref:** Thille AW, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2008;34:1477–1486.

Review: [W13/D3](#W13-D3), [W12/D1](#W12-D1)

questions.stem: Regarding oxygenation targets and respiratory measurements across conditions:
options: Plateau pressure and compliance measured during reverse triggering are reliable, because the patient is deeply sedated.
In hypercapnic COPD, the target SpO₂ is 88–92 %.
HOT-ICU showed that a PaO₂ target of 8 kPa reduced 90-day mortality compared with 12 kPa.
In acute severe asthma in adults, the target SpO₂ is 93–95 %.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – During reverse triggering, muscle effort (median P_mus 8.7 cmH₂O in Pham 2021) makes Pplat and compliance unreliable.
- B (True) – In hypercapnic COPD, target SpO₂ 88–92 %.
- C (False) – HOT-ICU found no difference: 90-day mortality 42.9 vs 42.4 %.
- D (True) – In acute severe asthma in adults, target SpO₂ 93–95 %.

**EDIC trap:** "Deeply sedated" does not mean passive.

**Ref:** Pham T, et al. *Crit Care* 2021; Schjørring OL, et al. HOT-ICU. *N Engl J Med* 2021;384:1301–1311; GOLD 2026 Report; GINA 2025.

Review: [W11/D2](#W11-D2), [W12/D1](#W12-D1), [W13/D3](#W13-D3)

questions.stem: A patient with ARDS is on VCV with V_T 0.42 L, RR 30/min, Ppeak 34 cmH₂O, Pplat 28 cmH₂O and PEEP 12 cmH₂O. The team plans to raise RR to 35/min for hypercapnia. Using MP ≈ 0.098 × RR × V_T × (Ppeak − ½ΔP), which statement is correct?
options: MP ≈ 16.1 J/min, within the range not associated with excess mortality
MP ≈ 32.1 J/min, and raising RR will reduce it
MP ≈ 32.1 J/min, well above ~17 J/min; raising RR will increase it further
MP ≈ 64 J/min
MP ≈ 12.6 J/min
questions.expl:
**Why C:** ΔP = 28 − 12 = 16 cmH₂O, so ½ΔP = 8. MP = 0.098 × 30 × 0.42 × (34 − 8) = 1.2348 × 26 ≈ 32.1 J/min, well above the ~17 J/min associated with mortality in observational data. MP rises with RR (exponent 1.4), so RR 35/min will increase it further.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 16.1 J/min is half the correct value.
- B – The value is correct, but raising RR increases MP rather than reducing it.
- D – 64 J/min is double the correct value.
- E – 12.6 J/min is a miscalculation.

**EDIC trap:** The driving pressure of 16 cmH₂O is also high; MP is an observational marker, not a guideline target.

**Ref:** Gattinoni L, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2016;42:1567–1575; Serpa Neto A, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2018;44:1914–1922.

Review: [W13/D4](#W13-D4), [W10/D2](#W10-D2)

questions.stem: A 70-year-old COPD patient ventilated for 9 days for pneumonia is recovering.
options: By Hernández 2016 criteria, he is at high risk of extubation failure.
The only strong ATS/ACCP 2017 liberation recommendation is extubation to prophylactic NIV in high-risk patients.
Had he received a tracheostomy within 4 days of intubation, TracMan suggests his 30-day mortality would have been lower.
A once-daily SBT liberates patients faster than gradual IMV weaning (Esteban 1995).
questions.expl:
- A (True) – One Hernández criterion is enough, and he has at least two: age > 65 and ventilation > 7 days (moderate/severe COPD would add a third).
- B (True) – Extubation to prophylactic NIV in high-risk patients is the only strong ATS/ACCP 2017 liberation recommendation.
- C (False) – In TracMan, 30-day mortality was 30.8 vs 31.5 % (NS); only sedation days were fewer with early tracheostomy.
- D (True) – Esteban 1995: a once-daily SBT led to extubation ~2.8× faster than IMV.

**EDIC trap:** Early tracheostomy does not reduce mortality.

**Ref:** Hernández G, et al. *JAMA* 2016;316:1565–1574; Schmidt GA, et al. ATS/ACCP. *Am J Respir Crit Care Med* 2017;195:115–119; Young D, et al. TracMan. *JAMA* 2013;309:2121–2129; Esteban A, et al. *N Engl J Med* 1995;332:345–350.

Review: [W13/D1](#W13-D1), [W11/D4](#W11-D4), [W11/D5](#W11-D5), [W12/D4](#W12-D4)

title: W15 · D1 – Traumatic brain injury: ICP, CPP, Brain Trauma Foundation, SIBICC

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with severe TBI (post-resuscitation GCS 6, frontal contusions) has a parenchymal ICP monitor. He is sedated, head up 30°, normothermic, PaCO₂ 39 mmHg. ICP is 26 mmHg (sustained) and MAP, zeroed at the tragus, is 82 mmHg. Which statement is most appropriate?
options: CPP is 108 mmHg; no further action is required
CPP is 56 mmHg; ICP is above the BTF threshold and tier-1 measures (e.g. osmotherapy bolus, deeper sedation) are indicated
CPP is 56 mmHg; immediate bifrontal decompressive craniectomy is the next step
ICP is acceptable because the BTF treatment threshold is 25 mmHg
CPP is 56 mmHg; hyperventilate to PaCO₂ 25 mmHg for the next 24 h
questions.expl:
**Why B:** CPP = MAP − ICP = 82 − 26 = 56 mmHg, below the BTF target of 60–70 mmHg, and a sustained ICP of 26 mmHg exceeds the BTF 4th-edition treatment threshold of 22 mmHg. Tier-0 measures are already in place, so the next step is SIBICC tier 1: deeper analgesia/sedation, an osmotherapy bolus (mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg or hypertonic saline), CSF drainage if an EVD is present and CPP 60–70 mmHg.

**Why not the others:**
- A – CPP is MAP minus ICP, not the sum; 108 mmHg is an arithmetic error.
- C – early bifrontal craniectomy for diffuse injury worsened functional outcome in DECRA; DC is a tier-3 option after surgical lesions are excluded.
- D – the BTF threshold is 22 mmHg (25 mmHg was the RESCUEicp entry criterion).
- E – prolonged hyperventilation to ≤ 25 mmHg is not recommended (BTF IIB), especially in the first 24 h.

**Ref:** Carney N, Neurosurgery 2017; Hawryluk GWJ, Intensive Care Med 2019.

questions.stem: Regarding the Brain Trauma Foundation 4th-edition recommendations for severe TBI:
options: Treatment of ICP above 22 mmHg is recommended because values above this level are associated with higher mortality.
Corticosteroids may be considered to reduce ICP in patients with large contusions.
Systolic blood pressure should be kept at or above 110 mmHg in patients aged 15–49 years or older than 70 years.
Prophylactic hyperventilation to PaCO₂ ≤ 25 mmHg is recommended during the first 24 hours to prevent ICP elevation.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – BTF 4th edition (Level IIB) recommends treating ICP > 22 mmHg, the value above which mortality rises (moved from 20 mmHg).
- B (False) – corticosteroids are **not recommended** in TBI (Level I): CRASH showed higher 2-week mortality (21.1 vs 17.9 %), whatever the lesion type.
- C (True) – SBP ≥ 110 mmHg at 15–49 and > 70 years; ≥ 100 mmHg at 50–69 years (Level III).
- D (False) – prolonged prophylactic hyperventilation to PaCO₂ ≤ 25 mmHg is **not recommended** (IIB) and should be avoided in the first 24 h, when CBF is often critically reduced; it is only a brief bridge for herniation.

**EDIC trap:** older MCQs quote ICP 20 mmHg – BTF 4th edition uses 22 mmHg.

**Ref:** Carney N, Neurosurgery 2017; CRASH Trial Collaborators, Lancet 2004.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman with diffuse TBI and no mass lesion has ICP > 20 mmHg for more than 15 minutes within a 1-hour period on day 1, despite first-tier therapy. The neurosurgeon proposes an early bifrontotemporoparietal decompressive craniectomy. Based on the DECRA trial, compared with continued medical therapy, this operation:
options: halves 6-month mortality
improves 6-month extended Glasgow Outcome Scale
lowers ICP and shortens ICU stay, but increases the proportion with unfavourable outcome
has no effect on ICP
reduces the proportion of survivors in a vegetative state
questions.expl:
**Why C:** DECRA (n = 155) randomised diffuse TBI with early, moderate ICP elevation (> 20 mmHg for > 15 min within 1 h, < 72 h) to bifrontotemporoparietal DC or medical care. Surgery lowered ICP and shortened ventilation and ICU stay, but unfavourable GOS-E at 6 months was more frequent (70 vs 51 %, OR 2.21).

**Why not the others:**
- A – mortality was similar (~19 vs 18 %); halving of mortality (26.9 vs 48.9 %) was seen in RESCUEicp, in late refractory ICP.
- B – GOS-E was worse, not better, with surgery.
- D – ICP fell significantly after DC.
- E – reducing vegetative survivors is not a DC effect; RESCUEicp actually increased the vegetative state proportion.

**EDIC trap:** DECRA = early, bifrontal, diffuse injury, worse function; RESCUEicp = late, refractory ICP, better survival with more disability.

**Ref:** Cooper DJ, N Engl J Med 2011; Hutchinson PJ, N Engl J Med 2016.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with severe TBI and an EVD has an ICP of 27 mmHg. All of the following belong to tier 1 or tier 2 of the SIBICC ICP algorithm EXCEPT:
options: Mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg as an intermittent bolus
Drainage of CSF via the external ventricular drain
Mild hypocapnia with PaCO₂ 32–35 mmHg
Active cooling to 33 °C
A trial of neuromuscular blockade
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Active cooling to 33 °C does not belong to tiers 1–2. SIBICC places only mild hypothermia (35–36 °C) in tier 3 and lists routine cooling below 36 °C among measures not to use. Eurotherm3235 showed worse outcome when 32–35 °C hypothermia was used to treat ICP > 20 mmHg (favourable GOS-E 26 vs 37 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – intermittent mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg is a tier-1 measure (continuous infusion is discouraged).
- B – CSF drainage via an EVD is tier 1.
- C – mild hypocapnia (PaCO₂ 32–35 mmHg) is tier 2; < 30 mmHg is discouraged.
- E – a neuromuscular blockade test dose, then infusion if effective, is tier 2.

**EDIC trap:** temperature control in tiers 0–2 means avoiding fever (36–37.5 °C), not therapeutic hypothermia.

**Ref:** Hawryluk GWJ, Intensive Care Med 2019; Andrews PJD, N Engl J Med 2015.

questions.stem: Regarding the RESCUEicp trial of decompressive craniectomy for traumatic intracranial hypertension:
options: Patients were enrolled with ICP > 25 mmHg for 1–12 hours despite stage 1 and 2 measures.
Six-month mortality was 26.9 % with surgery vs 48.9 % with medical care.
Surgery increased the proportion of survivors in a vegetative state or with lower severe disability.
Surgery significantly increased the rate of upper severe disability or better at 6 months.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – inclusion was ICP > 25 mmHg for 1–12 h despite stage 1 and 2 measures: late, refractory intracranial hypertension.
- B (True) – 6-month mortality 26.9 % with DC vs 48.9 % with medical care (including barbiturates).
- C (True) – vegetative state 8.5 vs 2.1 % and lower severe disability 21.9 vs 14.4 %: more survivors, many dependent.
- D (False) – upper severe disability or better was 42.8 vs 34.6 % at 6 months, **not significant**; the difference became significant only at 12 months (45.4 vs 32.4 %).

**EDIC trap:** RESCUEicp is a trade-off of survival for disability – discuss expected outcome and the patient's values with the family before surgery.

**Ref:** Hutchinson PJ, N Engl J Med 2016.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with severe TBI is on day 3 in the ICU. She is not bleeding; Hb has drifted to 8.4 g/dL. ICP and PbtO₂ are not monitored. Based on current evidence, the most appropriate transfusion approach is:
options: Transfuse to maintain Hb ≥ 9 g/dL
Transfuse only if Hb falls below 7 g/dL, as in general ICU patients
Transfuse to Hb ≥ 10 g/dL, which significantly improved outcome in HEMOTION
Start erythropoietin instead of transfusion
Transfuse only if PbtO₂ falls below 20 mmHg
questions.expl:
**Why A:** TRAIN (n = 820 acute brain injury: TBI, SAH, ICH) compared transfusion triggers of 9 vs 7 g/dL. The liberal strategy reduced unfavourable 6-month neurological outcome (62.6 vs 73.5 %, RR 0.85) and cerebral ischaemia. Her Hb of 8.4 g/dL is below 9 g/dL, so transfusion is reasonable without waiting for neuromonitoring.

**Why not the others:**
- B – the "7 for everyone" message comes from general ICU trials (TRICC, TRISS) and does not apply to acute brain injury.
- C – HEMOTION (10 vs 7 g/dL, n = 742) showed only a non-significant trend (68.4 vs 73.5 %).
- D – erythropoietin is not a substitute for transfusion and has no role in correcting anaemia acutely.
- E – PbtO₂ is not monitored, and guiding transfusion by PbtO₂ remains investigational.

**EDIC trap:** "restrictive transfusion is safe in all ICU patients" is false for acute brain injury.

**Ref:** Taccone FS, JAMA 2024; Turgeon AF, N Engl J Med 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding hyperosmolar therapy in traumatic intracranial hypertension:
options: Mannitol is best given as a continuous infusion to avoid rebound intracranial hypertension.
In the COBI trial, a continuous infusion of 20 % saline improved 6-month neurological outcome.
Mannitol can cause hypovolaemia through osmotic diuresis, and a rising osmolar gap suggests accumulation.
Hypertonic saline is contraindicated once serum sodium exceeds 145 mmol/L.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – mannitol is given as an intermittent **bolus** (0.25–1 g/kg over 15–20 min); SIBICC explicitly discourages continuous infusion, which promotes accumulation and rebound oedema.
- B (False) – COBI (n = 370) found **no difference** in 6-month GOS-E with continuous 20 % saline targeting Na 145–155 mmol/L (adjusted OR 1.02), nor in intracranial hypertension.
- C (True) – osmotic diuresis can cause hypovolaemia and hypotension; a rising osmolar gap (> ~20 mOsm/kg) suggests mannitol accumulation.
- D (False) – sodium is commonly allowed to rise to ~155–160 mmol/L during osmotherapy; Na > 145 is not a contraindication.

**EDIC trap:** both mannitol and hypertonic saline lower ICP, but neither has proven superiority for long-term outcome.

**Ref:** Hawryluk GWJ, Intensive Care Med 2019; Roquilly A, JAMA 2021.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man arrives 90 minutes after a fall. GCS is 12, pupils equal and reactive; CT shows a small subdural haematoma. Regarding tranexamic acid (TXA), the most appropriate statement is:
options: TXA is not indicated because CRASH-3 showed benefit only when GCS ≤ 8
TXA should be given only if the INR is > 1.5
A single 2 g bolus is recommended at any time within 24 h
TXA 1 g over 10 min followed by 1 g over 8 h is indicated because he is within 3 hours
TXA is contraindicated in TBI because it increases vascular occlusive events
questions.expl:
**Why D:** He has mild–moderate TBI (GCS 12) with intracranial blood and is within 3 hours of injury. In CRASH-3, TXA 1 g over 10 min then 1 g over 8 h reduced head-injury death in GCS 9–15 (RR 0.78), with greater benefit the earlier it was given and no excess of vascular occlusive events.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the reverse: no benefit was seen in severe TBI (GCS 3–8) or with bilateral unreactive pupils.
- B – TXA is antifibrinolytic and its indication does not depend on INR.
- C – the regimen is 1 g + 1 g over 8 h, and benefit was limited to treatment within 3 h.
- E – CRASH-3 found no increase in vascular occlusive events.

**EDIC trap:** CRASH-3 overall result in patients treated ≤ 3 h was not significant (RR 0.94); the benefit is in the mild–moderate subgroup.

**Ref:** CRASH-3 trial collaborators, Lancet 2019.

questions.stem: Regarding ventilation targets in patients with acute brain injury (ESICM consensus 2020):
options: A PaO₂ target of 80–120 mmHg is recommended.
PaCO₂ of 35–45 mmHg is recommended in patients without raised ICP.
PEEP must be avoided in every patient with raised ICP.
Brief hyperventilation is contraindicated even during transtentorial herniation.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ESICM consensus recommends PaO₂ 80–120 mmHg, avoiding both hypoxaemia and hyperoxia.
- B (True) – PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg is the target when ICP is not raised.
- C (False) – PEEP can be used in raised ICP, with monitoring; it does not usually raise ICP meaningfully if MAP and PaCO₂ are kept stable.
- D (False) – brief hyperventilation is an accepted **rescue** bridge during transtentorial herniation, while definitive treatment is arranged; only prolonged prophylactic hyperventilation is discouraged.

**EDIC trap:** lung-protective ventilation is recommended when there is no ICP concern; with raised ICP, individualise and monitor rather than avoiding PEEP.

**Ref:** Robba C, Intensive Care Med 2020.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with severe TBI has ICP persistently 25–28 mmHg on day 4 despite tier 1 and tier 2 measures; a repeat CT shows no new surgical lesion. Which of the following is LEAST appropriate?
options: Secondary large fronto-temporo-parietal decompressive craniectomy
Barbiturate coma after a test dose shows ICP response, with haemodynamic monitoring
High-dose methylprednisolone
Mild hypothermia to 35–36 °C
A frank discussion with the family about likely survival with disability after surgery
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Corticosteroids are contraindicated in TBI (BTF Level I). In CRASH (n ≈ 10 000), methylprednisolone increased 2-week mortality (21.1 vs 17.9 %), and SIBICC lists steroids among measures not to use at any tier.

**Why not the others:**
- A – secondary large fronto-temporo-parietal DC for late refractory ICP is a tier-3 option; BTF 2020 update recommends it to reduce mortality (IIA).
- B – barbiturate coma is tier 3, used only if a test dose lowers ICP and with close haemodynamic monitoring.
- D – mild hypothermia 35–36 °C is a tier-3 option (unlike 32–35 °C in Eurotherm3235).
- E – RESCUEicp showed more survivors with severe disability after DC, so an honest discussion of expected outcome is essential.

**EDIC trap:** "LEAST appropriate" stems often hide a harmful but familiar drug among legitimate tier-3 options.

**Ref:** Carney N, Neurosurgery 2017; Hawryluk GWJ, Intensive Care Med 2019.

open.q: A 30-year-old man with severe TBI (GCS 5, diffuse swelling, compressed basal cisterns) has an EVD. Despite sedation and head-up positioning, ICP is 30 mmHg with MAP 85 mmHg. Describe your stepwise management using the SIBICC tiers, including targets and the measures you would avoid.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Calculate CPP = 85 − 30 = 55 mmHg (target 60–70); treat ICP > 22 mmHg (BTF).
- Exclude a surgical lesion (repeat CT) and correct simple causes: neck veins, tube ties, asynchrony, fever, seizures, hypo-Na, hypercapnia.
- Tier 0: head 30–45°, sedation/analgesia, normothermia, SpO₂ ≥ 94 %, Hb > 7 (TRAIN supports ~9), normal Na.
- Tier 1: CPP 60–70, deeper sedation, PaCO₂ 35–38, mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg or HTS bolus, CSF drainage via EVD, EEG.
- Tier 2: PaCO₂ 32–35, NMB trial, MAP challenge, raise CPP if autoregulation intact.
- Tier 3: secondary DC (RESCUEicp – survival with possible disability, discuss with family), barbiturates (test dose, avoid hypotension), 35–36 °C.
- Avoid: steroids, continuous mannitol, lumbar drain, PaCO₂ < 30, CPP > 70 with fluids/pressors (ARDS), hypothermia 32–35 °C (Eurotherm), early bifrontal DC (DECRA).

title: W15 · D2 – Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage: rebleeding, aneurysm securing, DCI, hydrocephalus, sodium

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman presents 3 hours after a sudden severe headache that peaked within seconds during exercise. She is alert (GCS 15) without focal deficit. A non-contrast CT performed 4 hours after onset is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Lumbar puncture immediately, regardless of timing
Lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset to look for xanthochromia
Discharge with analgesia – subarachnoid haemorrhage is effectively ruled out
Repeat non-contrast CT at 24 hours
Start nimodipine empirically and admit to the ICU
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In neurologically intact patients, a modern non-contrast CT performed **within 6 hours** of headache onset and read by an experienced radiologist has a sensitivity close to 100 % for SAH (Perry, BMJ 2011). AHA 2023 accepts that SAH is effectively excluded in this situation, so no LP is needed.

**Why not the others:**
- A – LP is needed only if CT is performed later than 6 h (or is of doubtful quality); early LP gives false positives from traumatic taps.
- B – waiting 12 h for xanthochromia applies when CT is negative but done > 6 h after onset.
- D – repeat CT adds nothing; sensitivity decreases with time.
- E – nimodipine is given only for confirmed aneurysmal SAH.

**EDIC trap:** the 6-hour rule applies to an alert patient with a good-quality scan; a CT at 10 h with a negative result still requires LP.

**Ref:** Perry JJ, BMJ 2011;343:d4277; Hoh BL, Stroke 2023.

questions.stem: Regarding grading of aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage:
options: The WFNS scale is based on the Glasgow Coma Scale and the presence of a focal motor deficit.
The modified Fisher scale is a clinical scale based on the level of consciousness.
A modified Fisher grade 4 (thick cisternal blood with intraventricular haemorrhage) carries the highest risk of symptomatic vasospasm.
Poor-grade patients should be graded definitively on admission, before any external ventricular drainage.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – WFNS I: GCS 15; II: 13–14 without deficit; III: 13–14 with motor deficit; IV: 7–12; V: 3–6.
- B (False) – the (modified) Fisher scale is **radiological** (CT thickness of SAH and presence of IVH).
- C (True) – grade 4 has ~40 % risk of symptomatic vasospasm/DCI.
- D (False) – grade after resuscitation and after treating hydrocephalus; poor grade on admission often improves after EVD and prognosis should be delayed.

**Ref:** Hoh BL, Stroke 2023; Treggiari MM, Neurocrit Care 2023.
