questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with WFNS grade II aneurysmal SAH arrives at a neurovascular centre 2 hours after ictus. The anterior communicating aneurysm is suitable for both coiling and clipping. Which strategy is best supported by current evidence?
options: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV, then 1 g every 8 hours until the aneurysm is secured
Delayed clipping after day 14, when vasospasm has resolved
Prophylactic hypervolaemic haemodilution before aneurysm treatment
IV magnesium sulphate to prevent delayed cerebral ischaemia
Endovascular coiling within 24 hours, together with oral nimodipine
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Rebleeding risk is highest in the first hours, so ESO 2026 suggests securing the aneurysm within 24 h. If both techniques are suitable in a good-grade patient, coiling is preferred (ISAT: death/dependency at 1 year 23.7 vs 30.6 %). Oral nimodipine 60 mg q4h for 21 days is the only DCI-preventive drug with high-quality evidence.

**Why not the others:**
- A – ULTRA: ultra-early TXA did not improve functional outcome (60 vs 64 % good outcome, NS); ESO recommends against routine antifibrinolytics.
- B – delayed surgery leaves the aneurysm exposed during the period of highest rebleeding risk.
- C – prophylactic hypervolaemia (triple-H) has no benefit and causes complications.
- D – MASH-2: magnesium did not improve outcome.

**Ref:** Vergouwen MDI, Eur Stroke J 2026; Molyneux A, Lancet 2002; Post R, Lancet 2021.

questions.stem: Regarding nimodipine in aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage:
options: The usual regimen is 60 mg orally every 4 hours for 21 days.
Its main benefit is a significant reduction in angiographic vasospasm.
In the British aneurysm nimodipine trial, cerebral infarction was reduced from 33 % to 22 %.
If it causes hypotension, the dose may be split into 30 mg every 2 hours.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – standard oral/NG regimen, started early, continued for 21 days.
- B (False) – nimodipine improves outcome **without** a proven effect on large-artery angiographic vasospasm; benefit is attributed to microvascular and neuroprotective effects.
- C (True) – BRANT: infarction 22 vs 33 %, poor outcome 20 vs 33 %.
- D (True) – smaller, more frequent doses limit hypotension; avoid stopping the drug.

**Ref:** Pickard JD, BMJ 1989; Vergouwen MDI, Eur Stroke J 2026.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman on day 6 after coiling of a ruptured MCA aneurysm becomes drowsy and develops new right arm weakness. All of the following are appropriate initial steps EXCEPT:
options: Urgent CT to exclude hydrocephalus or rebleeding
Check serum sodium and glucose
Fluid restriction to 1 L/day because the serum sodium is 129 mmol/L
Ensure euvolaemia and consider a trial of induced hypertension with noradrenaline
CT angiography/perfusion and consideration of endovascular rescue if deficits persist
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Hyponatraemia after SAH is often due to **cerebral salt wasting with hypovolaemia**; fluid restriction aggravates hypovolaemia and increases the risk of DCI. Treat with isotonic/hypertonic saline and consider fludrocortisone.

**Why not the others:**
- A – other causes of deterioration (hydrocephalus, rebleeding) must be excluded before diagnosing DCI.
- B – hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia and seizures mimic DCI.
- D – euvolaemia plus a cautious induced-hypertension trial is accepted practice in a secured aneurysm (AHA/NCS), although evidence is weak (HIMALAIA).
- E – angioplasty or intra-arterial vasodilators are rescue options for refractory symptomatic vasospasm.

**EDIC trap:** a new focal deficit between day 3 and 14 = DCI until proven otherwise, but the diagnosis requires the exclusion of other causes.

**Ref:** Hoh BL, Stroke 2023; Treggiari MM, Neurocrit Care 2023; Vergouwen MDI, Stroke 2010.

questions.stem: Regarding interventions studied to prevent delayed cerebral ischaemia after aneurysmal SAH:
options: Intravenous magnesium improved functional outcome in MASH-2.
Statins are recommended by the ESO 2026 guideline.
Clazosentan reduced angiographic vasospasm without a convincing improvement in functional outcome.
Prophylactic triple-H therapy is recommended in poor-grade patients.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – MASH-2: poor outcome 26.2 vs 25.3 %, no benefit.
- B (False) – ESO 2026 recommends **against** statins (STASH neutral), as well as against magnesium, tirilazad and endothelin antagonists.
- C (True) – CONSCIOUS trials: less angiographic vasospasm, but no improvement in functional outcome; REACT also negative.
- D (False) – prophylactic hypervolaemia/haemodilution/hypertension is not recommended; aim for euvolaemia.

**Ref:** Dorhout Mees SM, Lancet 2012; Vergouwen MDI, Eur Stroke J 2026.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man with modified Fisher grade 4 aneurysmal SAH has had his aneurysm coiled on day 1. In the EARLYDRAIN trial, adding a lumbar CSF drain (5 mL/h) started within 72 hours to standard care:
options: increased the rate of rebleeding
had no effect on outcome but reduced shunt dependency
reduced 6-month mortality by half
reduced unfavourable outcome at 6 months (about 33 vs 45 %) and secondary infarctions
was stopped early because of brain herniation
questions.expl:
**Why D:** EARLYDRAIN (JAMA Neurol 2023): unfavourable outcome (mRS 3–6) at 6 months 32.6 vs 44.8 % (RR 0.73), and secondary infarction 28.5 vs 39.9 %. Mortality was not significantly different.

**Why not the others:**
- A – lumbar drainage was started after aneurysm securing; no increase in rebleeding.
- B – the main effect was on functional outcome; shunt dependency was not the key result.
- C – mortality 13.2 vs 17.5 % (NS).
- E – the trial was completed; herniation was not a significant issue in selected patients without mass effect.

**EDIC trap:** despite this positive trial, ESO 2026 makes **no evidence-based recommendation** on lumbar drainage (single open-label trial) – know both facts.

**Ref:** Wolf S, JAMA Neurol 2023; Vergouwen MDI, Eur Stroke J 2026.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman on day 5 after SAH has an MCA mean flow velocity on transcranial Doppler of 210 cm/s with an extracranial ICA velocity of 30 cm/s.
options: The Lindegaard ratio is about 7, consistent with severe vasospasm.
An MCA velocity above 200 cm/s suggests severe vasospasm.
A Lindegaard ratio below 3 with high MCA velocity suggests global hyperaemia rather than vasospasm.
TCD has excellent sensitivity for vasospasm in the distal anterior cerebral artery territory.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 210/30 = 7; > 6 indicates severe vasospasm.
- B (True) – > 120 cm/s suggests vasospasm, > 200 cm/s severe.
- C (True) – raised velocities in both MCA and ICA (ratio < 3) indicate hyperaemia (high flow), not narrowing.
- D (False) – TCD is reliable for proximal MCA, poor for ACA and distal vessels; CTA/CTP or DSA is needed.

**Ref:** Treggiari MM, Neurocrit Care 2023; Hoh BL, Stroke 2023.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman on day 4 after clipping of an aneurysm develops pulmonary oedema. Troponin is elevated, the ECG shows deep T-wave inversion, and echocardiography shows apical and mid-ventricular hypokinesia with an LVEF of 30 %. Coronary angiography is normal. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Neurogenic stunned myocardium (stress cardiomyopathy)
Acute myocardial infarction due to plaque rupture
Nimodipine-induced cardiomyopathy
Fluid overload from triple-H therapy as the sole cause
Myocarditis
questions.expl:
**Why A:** The catecholamine surge after SAH causes troponin release (20–40 %), ECG changes and Takotsubo-like regional wall motion abnormalities that do not follow a coronary territory. It is usually reversible within days to weeks; supportive treatment with inotropes (dobutamine or milrinone) may be needed if cardiac output falls.

**Why not the others:**
- B – normal coronary arteries argue against type 1 MI.
- C – nimodipine causes vasodilatation and hypotension, not cardiomyopathy.
- D – fluid overload may contribute to pulmonary oedema but does not explain regional wall motion abnormalities with troponin rise.
- E – no clinical context for myocarditis; the timing and pattern fit neurogenic stunning.

**Ref:** Hoh BL, Stroke 2023; Treggiari MM, Neurocrit Care 2023.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with secured aneurysmal SAH is on day 3 with Hb 8.6 g/dL, no bleeding and no signs of DCI. Regarding red cell transfusion, which statement is most accurate?
options: SAHaRA showed that a threshold of 10 g/dL significantly reduced 12-month unfavourable outcome
A threshold of 7 g/dL has been proven superior in SAH
Transfusion is contraindicated during the vasospasm window
In SAHaRA, liberal (Hb < 10) vs restrictive (Hb < 8) transfusion did not significantly change 12-month unfavourable outcome (33.5 vs 37.7 %)
Erythropoietin is the recommended alternative
questions.expl:
**Why D:** SAHaRA (NEJM 2025, n = 725) found a non-significant difference (RR 0.88, 95 % CI 0.72–1.09). Together with TRAIN (which included SAH patients and favoured Hb 9 over 7 g/dL), a threshold of ~8–9 g/dL is reasonable; strict 7 g/dL is not supported in acute brain injury.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the difference was not statistically significant.
- B – no SAH trial showed superiority of 7 g/dL; TRAIN suggested harm from restrictive strategies.
- C – anaemia worsens oxygen delivery during the DCI window; transfusion is not contraindicated.
- E – erythropoietin has no proven role.

**Ref:** English SW, N Engl J Med 2025; Taccone FS, JAMA 2024.

open.q: A 52-year-old woman with WFNS IV aneurysmal SAH (modified Fisher 4) is admitted to your ICU after coiling and EVD placement. Outline your plan for the next 14 days to prevent and detect delayed cerebral ischaemia and medical complications.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Nimodipine 60 mg PO/NG every 4 h for 21 days (30 mg q2h if hypotension).
- Euvolaemia (fluid balance, avoid hypovolaemia; no prophylactic triple-H); normothermia; glucose ~7.8–10 mmol/L; Hb ~8–9 g/dL (SAHaRA, TRAIN).
- DCI surveillance: clinical exam if possible; daily TCD (MCA > 120/200 cm/s, Lindegaard > 3/> 6); cEEG ± PbtO₂/ICP in poor grade; CTA/CTP if suspicion.
- EVD management (ICP, CSF drainage, infection prevention, gradual or rapid weaning); consider lumbar drain if communicating (EARLYDRAIN – guideline caution).
- Sodium: monitor twice daily; CSW vs SIADH – no fluid restriction; saline/hypertonic saline, fludrocortisone.
- Cardiopulmonary: troponin/echo for stunned myocardium; lung-protective ventilation.
- If DCI: exclude other causes; euvolaemia, cautious induced hypertension (noradrenaline), endovascular rescue (angioplasty/IA vasodilators).
- Avoid magnesium, statins, clazosentan; VTE prophylaxis after securing; delay prognostication in poor-grade.

title: W15 · D3 – Spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage: blood pressure, reversal, haemostasis, surgery, ICU care

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man presents 90 minutes after onset of right hemiparesis. CT shows a 20 mL left putaminal haemorrhage. GCS is 14 and BP 196/104 mmHg. He takes no antithrombotic drugs. Which blood pressure strategy is most appropriate?
options: No treatment unless SBP exceeds 220 mmHg, to preserve perihaematomal perfusion
Prompt IV labetalol or nicardipine aiming for SBP ~140 mmHg (avoiding < 130 mmHg), with smooth, sustained control
Target SBP 110–120 mmHg within 2 h to minimise haematoma expansion
Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg, repeated as needed
IV nitroprusside titrated to SBP < 140 mmHg
questions.expl:
**Why B:** For SBP 150–220 mmHg, AHA 2022 recommends targeting 140 mmHg (range 130–150) early, and ESO 2025 supports acute lowering. INTERACT2 showed a favourable ordinal shift, INTERACT3 showed benefit from a bundle including SBP < 140 within 1 h; smooth control with titratable agents limits BP variability.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the 220 mmHg threshold applies to ischaemic stroke not treated with thrombolysis, not ICH.
- C – ATACH-2 (110–139) showed no benefit and more renal adverse events; AHA classes lowering to < 130 mmHg as potentially harmful.
- D – sublingual nifedipine causes unpredictable, precipitous falls.
- E – nitroprusside causes cerebral venodilatation and may increase ICP; it is not first line.

**Ref:** Greenberg SM, Stroke 2022; Steiner T, Eur Stroke J 2025; Qureshi AI, NEJM 2016.

questions.stem: Regarding randomised trials of blood pressure management in acute stroke:
options: In INTERACT2, intensive lowering significantly reduced the primary dichotomous outcome of death or major disability.
In ATACH-2, a target SBP of 110–139 mmHg was associated with more renal adverse events than standard care.
In INTERACT4, prehospital BP lowering improved outcome in patients later found to have ischaemic stroke.
AHA 2022 recommends lowering SBP below 110 mmHg in patients with large haematomas.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – 52.0 vs 55.6 %, p = 0.06; only the ordinal mRS analysis was significant.
- B (True) – renal adverse events within 7 days 9.0 vs 4.0 %, with no functional benefit.
- C (False) – INTERACT4 showed **harm** in ischaemic stroke (OR 1.30) and benefit in ICH (OR 0.75): BP should not be lowered before the stroke type is known.
- D (False) – lowering to < 130 mmHg is potentially harmful; the target is ~140 mmHg.

**Ref:** Anderson CS, NEJM 2013; Qureshi AI, NEJM 2016; Li G, NEJM 2024; Greenberg SM, Stroke 2022.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman taking dabigatran 110 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation (last dose 4 h ago) presents with a 25 mL lobar haemorrhage. Creatinine clearance is 45 mL/min. What is the most appropriate reversal strategy?
options: Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg
Vitamin K 10 mg IV and 4-factor PCC 25 IU/kg
Protamine sulphate 50 mg IV
Idarucizumab 5 g IV
Platelet transfusion and desmopressin
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Idarucizumab is a humanised antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with high affinity and reverses its anticoagulant effect within minutes (RE-VERSE AD). Reduced renal clearance prolongs dabigatran effect, which makes specific reversal more important; haemodialysis is an option if idarucizumab is unavailable.

**Why not the others:**
- A – FFP does not reverse direct thrombin inhibition and requires large volumes.
- B – vitamin K works only for VKA; PCC is a second-line non-specific alternative.
- C – protamine reverses heparin, not dabigatran.
- E – platelets and desmopressin are for antiplatelet-associated bleeding (and platelets are harmful without surgery – PATCH).

**Ref:** Greenberg SM, Stroke 2022; Steiner T, Eur Stroke J 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding andexanet alfa for factor Xa inhibitor–associated intracerebral haemorrhage:
options: In ANNEXA-I, andexanet improved haemostatic efficacy compared with usual care (mostly PCC).
In ANNEXA-I, thrombotic events, including ischaemic stroke, were more frequent with andexanet.
In ANNEXA-I, andexanet significantly reduced 30-day mortality.
Andexanet was withdrawn from the US market in December 2025 after FDA safety concerns about thromboembolism.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 67.0 vs 53.1 % (adjusted difference 13.4 %).
- B (True) – thrombotic events 10.3 vs 5.6 %; ischaemic stroke 6.5 vs 1.5 %.
- C (False) – no difference in 30-day mortality or functional outcome.
- D (True) – voluntary withdrawal of US sales after an FDA safety communication; 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg is widely used instead.

**Ref:** Connolly SJ, NEJM 2024; FDA safety communication 2025.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man taking aspirin 100 mg and clopidogrel 75 mg after coronary stenting has a 15 mL thalamic haemorrhage with GCS 14. Surgery is not planned. All of the following are appropriate EXCEPT:
options: Admission to a stroke unit or neuro-ICU
SBP target of about 140 mmHg
Intermittent pneumatic compression for VTE prophylaxis from admission
Discussion with cardiology about the timing of restarting antiplatelet therapy
Platelet transfusion to counteract the antiplatelet effect
questions.expl:
**Why E:** In PATCH, platelet transfusion for antiplatelet-associated ICH increased death or dependence at 3 months (OR 2.05). ESO 2025 makes a weak recommendation against it; it may be considered only before emergency neurosurgery.

**Why not the others:**
- A – organised stroke-unit care has strong evidence.
- B – early SBP target ~140 mmHg is recommended.
- C – IPC reduces proximal DVT (CLOTS 3); pharmacological prophylaxis can follow after 24–48 h.
- D – RESTART: restarting antiplatelet therapy did not increase recurrent ICH; stent thrombosis risk must be balanced.

**Ref:** Baharoglu MI, Lancet 2016; Steiner T, Eur Stroke J 2025; RESTART, Lancet 2019.

questions.stem: Regarding surgical treatment of spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage:
options: STICH showed that early craniotomy improves outcome in all supratentorial haemorrhages.
In ENRICH, the benefit of minimally invasive endoport evacuation was driven mainly by lobar haemorrhages.
A cerebellar haemorrhage > 15 mL with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus should be evacuated surgically.
In SWITCH, decompressive craniectomy significantly reduced death or severe disability (mRS 5–6) in deep ICH.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – STICH and STICH II found no overall benefit from early surgery.
- B (True) – utility-weighted mRS 0.458 vs 0.374; no benefit in anterior basal ganglia ICH.
- C (True) – EVD alone is not recommended as initial treatment for cerebellar ICH with brainstem compression.
- D (False) – 44 vs 58 %, aRR 0.77 (95 % CI 0.59–1.01), p = 0.057: not significant, "weak evidence".

**Ref:** Pradilla G, NEJM 2024; Beck J, Lancet 2024; Greenberg SM, Stroke 2022.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman has a supratentorial lobar ICH. On CT the haematoma measures 5 × 4 × 4 cm with intraventricular extension. GCS is 11. What are her estimated haematoma volume and ICH score?
options: 80 mL; ICH score 4
40 mL; ICH score 2
40 mL; ICH score 3
20 mL; ICH score 2
40 mL; ICH score 4
questions.expl:
**Why C:** ABC/2 = 5 × 4 × 4 / 2 = 40 mL. ICH score: GCS 5–12 = 1, volume ≥ 30 mL = 1, IVH = 1, supratentorial = 0, age < 80 = 0 → **3** (historical 30-day mortality ~72 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – 80 mL forgets to divide by 2.
- B – omits one point (usually the IVH).
- D – 20 mL divides by 4; score also wrong.
- E – adds a point for age, which applies only at ≥ 80 years.

**EDIC trap:** the score estimates risk; it must not be used alone to withdraw care in the first 24 h.

**Ref:** Hemphill JC, Stroke 2001;32:891–897; Greenberg SM, Stroke 2022.

questions.stem: Regarding haematoma expansion and haemostatic therapy in non-anticoagulated ICH:
options: A CTA "spot sign" predicts haematoma expansion.
In TICH-2, tranexamic acid improved 90-day functional outcome.
In FAST, rFVIIa reduced haematoma growth but did not improve clinical outcome.
In FASTEST, rFVIIa given within 2 hours improved functional outcome in the overall population.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – contrast extravasation within the haematoma predicts growth and poor outcome.
- B (False) – no difference in 90-day function; less expansion and fewer early deaths.
- C (True) – reduced growth, no clinical benefit, more arterial thromboembolic events.
- D (False) – FASTEST was stopped for futility; signals only in very early treatment (~90 min) or spot-sign subgroups.

**Ref:** Sprigg N, Lancet 2018; Steiner T, Eur Stroke J 2025.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man survived a lobar ICH 4 weeks ago while taking aspirin for secondary prevention after a myocardial infarction. Regarding restarting antiplatelet therapy, which statement is best supported by evidence?
options: Restarting antiplatelet therapy did not increase recurrent ICH in the RESTART trial
Antiplatelets must be avoided permanently after any ICH
Dual antiplatelet therapy should replace aspirin to prevent ischaemic events
Warfarin is safer than aspirin after ICH
RESTART showed a threefold increase in recurrent ICH with antiplatelets
questions.expl:
**Why A:** RESTART (n = 537) found recurrent ICH in 4 % vs 9 % (HR 0.51, NS), excluding a large hazard. ESO 2025 makes a weak recommendation for antiplatelet therapy with a licensed indication after ICH.

**Why not the others:**
- B – permanent avoidance exposes patients to ischaemic events without proven benefit.
- C – DAPT increases bleeding and has no indication here.
- D – VKA carries a higher ICH risk than antiplatelets.
- E – the point estimate actually favoured restarting.

**Ref:** RESTART Collaboration, Lancet 2019; Steiner T, Eur Stroke J 2025.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with a 35 mL right frontal lobar ICH is alert (GCS 15) and has not had any seizures. Regarding antiseizure medication, the most appropriate approach is:
options: Phenytoin 20 mg/kg loading for 7 days
No prophylactic antiseizure medication; treat clinical seizures or EEG-confirmed seizures if they occur
Levetiracetam for 3 months because the haemorrhage is lobar
Valproate for 6 months
Prophylactic midazolam infusion for 24 h
questions.expl:
**Why B:** ESO 2025 (weak against) and AHA 2022 do not recommend prophylactic antiseizure medication in ICH; prophylaxis (especially phenytoin) was associated with worse outcomes in observational data. Clinical seizures should be treated, and cEEG is indicated in patients with unexplained depressed consciousness.

**Why not the others:**
- A – phenytoin prophylaxis is a TBI recommendation (BTF), not ICH, and is associated with harm after ICH.
- C – lobar location raises seizure risk but does not justify prophylaxis.
- D – no evidence for valproate prophylaxis.
- E – sedation without indication impairs neurological assessment.

**Ref:** Steiner T, Eur Stroke J 2025; Greenberg SM, Stroke 2022.

open.q: A 68-year-old man taking apixaban arrives 2 hours after onset of left hemiplegia; CT shows a 30 mL right basal ganglia haemorrhage with small IVH. BP 210/110 mmHg, GCS 13. Outline your management in the first 24 hours.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- ABC, neuro-ICU/stroke unit; CTA (spot sign, macrovascular cause); repeat CT at ~6–24 h or with deterioration.
- BP: titratable IV agent (labetalol, nicardipine, clevidipine, urapidil) – SBP ~140 mmHg within 1 h, avoid < 130 and large variability (INTERACT2/3, ATACH-2).
- Reversal: last dose, anti-Xa level if quick; 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg (or andexanet where available, accepting thrombotic risk – ANNEXA-I; withdrawn in the US 2025); activated charcoal if < 2 h from ingestion.
- Bundle (INTERACT3): glucose 6–10 mmol/L, temperature ≤ 37.5 °C, reversal within 1 h.
- No platelets, no routine rFVIIa or TXA, no steroids, no prophylactic ASM.
- Neurosurgical review: EVD if hydrocephalus; consider MIS (ENRICH – mainly lobar) or DC (SWITCH – deep ICH, weak evidence) if deterioration.
- IPC on admission; dysphagia screen; no limitation of care in first 24 h; ICH score for communication, not decisions.
- Later: decide on restarting anticoagulation (~2–8 weeks) or LAA occlusion.

title: W15 · D4 – Acute ischaemic stroke: thrombolysis, thrombectomy, blood pressure, malignant infarction

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man (78 kg) presents 2 hours after onset of aphasia and right hemiplegia (NIHSS 16). CT shows no haemorrhage and ASPECTS 9; CTA shows a left M1 occlusion. BP is 172/95 mmHg, glucose 7 mmol/L, platelets 220 × 10⁹/L. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Thrombectomy only, withholding IV thrombolysis to avoid bleeding
Wait for MRI to confirm DWI–FLAIR mismatch before any treatment
Aspirin 300 mg and admission to the stroke unit
Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (≈ 20 mg) IV bolus, followed by immediate endovascular thrombectomy
Lower BP to < 140/90 mmHg before thrombolysis
questions.expl:
**Why D:** He is within 4.5 h with a disabling deficit and no contraindication, so IVT is indicated; tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) is an accepted alternative to alteplase (AHA 2026, ESO 2023). An M1 occlusion with ASPECTS ≥ 6 within 6 h is a class I indication for EVT, and IVT should not delay transfer to the angiography suite.

**Why not the others:**
- A – direct-to-EVT has not convincingly been shown non-inferior; eligible patients should receive bridging IVT.
- B – MRI mismatch is needed only for unknown-onset stroke; it delays treatment here.
- C – antiplatelets are given 24 h after IVT; this patient needs reperfusion therapy.
- E – the threshold before IVT is < 185/110 mmHg; his BP already qualifies.

**Ref:** Prabhakaran S, Stroke 2026; Goyal M, Lancet 2016.

questions.stem: Regarding intravenous thrombolysis for acute ischaemic stroke:
options: Alteplase is dosed at 0.9 mg/kg (maximum 90 mg), with 10 % as a bolus and the remainder over 60 minutes.
Blood pressure must be below 185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis and kept below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours afterwards.
Orolingual angioedema after alteplase is more frequent in patients taking ACE inhibitors.
In the WAKE-UP trial, patients with a DWI–FLAIR mismatch benefited from alteplase despite an unknown time of onset.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – standard alteplase regimen.
- B (True) – limits for reducing sICH risk.
- C (True) – angioedema 1–5 %, more common with ACE inhibitors (bradykinin) and insular infarction.
- D (True) – mRS 0–1 53.3 vs 41.8 %.

**EDIC trap:** all-true K′ items exist – judge each statement on its own.

**Ref:** Berge E, Eur Stroke J 2021; Thomalla G, NEJM 2018.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman was last seen well 14 hours ago and now has a right ICA terminus occlusion, NIHSS 18 and a small core (12 mL) on CT perfusion. The most appropriate treatment based on the DAWN trial is:
options: Endovascular thrombectomy, which increased functional independence (mRS 0–2) from ~13 % to ~49 %
IV alteplase alone, because she is outside the thrombectomy window
Thrombectomy is contraindicated after 6 hours
Decompressive hemicraniectomy now
Supportive care, because the benefit of thrombectomy after 6 h is limited to basilar occlusion
questions.expl:
**Why A:** DAWN enrolled patients 6–24 h after last known well with a mismatch between clinical deficit and small infarct core; thrombectomy raised mRS 0–2 from 13 % to 49 %. DEFUSE 3 (6–16 h, perfusion mismatch) confirmed the benefit.

**Why not the others:**
- B – standard IVT is limited to 4.5 h (or imaging-selected up to 9 h); EVT is the effective treatment for LVO.
- C – the 6-h limit is outdated.
- D – hemicraniectomy is for malignant oedema, not as a first treatment with salvageable tissue.
- E – late-window benefit applies to anterior circulation LVO (DAWN, DEFUSE 3), and basilar occlusion (BAOCHE).

**Ref:** Nogueira RG, NEJM 2018; Prabhakaran S, Stroke 2026.

questions.stem: Regarding endovascular thrombectomy trials published since 2022:
options: In LASTE, thrombectomy for large infarcts (ASPECTS 0–5) reduced mortality.
In ESCAPE-MeVO, thrombectomy for medium-vessel occlusion improved the proportion with mRS 0–1.
SELECT2 and ANGEL-ASPECT showed no benefit of thrombectomy in large-core stroke.
In ATTENTION, thrombectomy for basilar artery occlusion improved functional outcome.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – mortality 36.1 vs 55.5 % with better functional shift.
- B (False) – mRS 0–1 41.6 vs 43.1 %; mortality (13.3 vs 8.4 %) and sICH were higher. DISTAL also neutral.
- C (False) – both trials were positive for functional outcome (stopped early for efficacy).
- D (True) – mRS 0–3 46 vs 23 %.

**Ref:** Costalat V, NEJM 2024; Goyal M, NEJM 2025; Sarraj A, NEJM 2023; Tao C, NEJM 2022.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man has undergone successful thrombectomy (mTICI 3) for a left M1 occlusion and is admitted to the ICU. All of the following are appropriate EXCEPT:
options: Keeping BP below 180/105 mmHg
Avoiding hypotension and hypovolaemia
Glucose target of 7.8–10 mmol/L
Supplemental oxygen only if SpO₂ falls below ~94 %
Intensive lowering of SBP to below 120 mmHg to prevent reperfusion haemorrhage
questions.expl:
**Why E:** ENCHANTED2/MT (SBP < 120) and OPTIMAL-BP (SBP < 140; mRS 0–2 39.4 vs 54.4 %) showed worse functional outcome with intensive lowering after EVT. AHA 2026 does not recommend SBP < 140 mmHg even after complete reperfusion.

**Why not the others:**
- A – standard post-EVT limit.
- B – hypotension reduces collateral and penumbral perfusion.
- C – SHINE: intensive glucose control adds no benefit and causes hypoglycaemia.
- D – SO2S: routine oxygen gives no benefit.

**Ref:** Nam HS, JAMA 2023; Prabhakaran S, Stroke 2026.

questions.stem: Regarding blood pressure in acute ischaemic stroke:
options: In a patient not treated with reperfusion therapy, BP below 220/120 mmHg is usually not lowered in the first 24 hours unless there is another indication.
Prehospital BP lowering before imaging improves outcome in ischaemic stroke.
Intensive SBP lowering to 130–140 mmHg after IV thrombolysis significantly improves functional outcome.
Nitroprusside is the drug of choice to reduce BP before thrombolysis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – permissive hypertension; lower cautiously (~15 %) if > 220/120 mmHg.
- B (False) – INTERACT4: harm in ischaemic stroke (OR 1.30).
- C (False) – ENCHANTED: no improvement in function; AHA 2026 confirms no benefit of intensive lowering after IVT.
- D (False) – labetalol, nicardipine, clevidipine or urapidil are first line.

**Ref:** Prabhakaran S, Stroke 2026; Li G, NEJM 2024.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a left MCA infarction involving > 2/3 of the territory. Thirty hours after onset her GCS falls from 13 to 9 and CT shows midline shift of 6 mm. Which management is best supported by evidence?
options: High-dose dexamethasone
Decompressive hemicraniectomy with duraplasty within 48 h
Prolonged hyperventilation to PaCO₂ 25–30 mmHg
Therapeutic hypothermia to 33 °C
Mannitol infusion as definitive therapy
questions.expl:
**Why B:** The pooled analysis of DECIMAL, DESTINY and HAMLET (age ≤ 60, surgery ≤ 48 h) showed mortality reduced from 71 % to 22 % and more patients with mRS ≤ 3 (43 vs 21 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – steroids do not reduce cytotoxic oedema and are not recommended.
- C – hyperventilation is only a short bridge; prolonged use causes ischaemia.
- D – hypothermia (DEPTH-SOS) did not improve outcome and increased complications.
- E – osmotherapy is a bridge, not definitive therapy.

**Ref:** Vahedi K, Lancet Neurol 2007.

questions.stem: Regarding decompressive hemicraniectomy for malignant MCA infarction in patients older than 60 years (DESTINY II):
options: Surgery increased survival without severe disability (mRS 0–4).
Most surviving operated patients were independent (mRS 0–2).
Surgery did not change mortality.
The decision should consider the patient's previously expressed values about living with disability.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – mRS 0–4: 38 vs 18 %.
- B (False) – no patient reached mRS 0–2; most survivors were mRS 4.
- C (False) – mortality was markedly reduced (~33 vs 70 %).
- D (True) – survival with disability is a values-based outcome; involve the family.

**Ref:** Jüttler E, NEJM 2014.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents 3 hours after onset of mild left facial droop and dysarthria (NIHSS 2), which he and the team judge non-disabling. CT is normal and there is no large-vessel occlusion. The most appropriate treatment is:
options: Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg
Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg
Aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days, then single antiplatelet therapy
Therapeutic-dose heparin infusion
No antithrombotic therapy for 7 days
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In non-disabling minor stroke, IVT has not shown benefit (PRISMS), and ARAMIS showed DAPT non-inferior to alteplase. CHANCE and POINT support a short course of DAPT (21 days) to reduce early recurrence. AHA 2026 prefers DAPT in this group.

**Why not the others:**
- A, B – no benefit and a small bleeding risk in non-disabling deficits.
- D – heparin increases bleeding without reducing recurrence in non-cardioembolic stroke.
- E – delaying antiplatelets increases early recurrence.

**Ref:** Prabhakaran S, Stroke 2026.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes after the start of alteplase for an ischaemic stroke, a 71-year-old woman develops headache, vomiting and a fall in GCS from 14 to 10. What is the most appropriate first action?
options: Stop the alteplase infusion and obtain an urgent CT
Continue the infusion and give IV mannitol
Give protamine sulphate 50 mg
Give 4 units of platelets immediately
Give vitamin K 10 mg IV
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Neurological deterioration during thrombolysis suggests symptomatic ICH. Stop the infusion, perform urgent CT and send coagulation tests including fibrinogen; if ICH is confirmed, give cryoprecipitate (10 U, fibrinogen target > 1.5 g/L) and consider TXA 1 g, with haematology and neurosurgical review.

**Why not the others:**
- B – continuing the drug may enlarge a haemorrhage.
- C – protamine reverses heparin, not alteplase.
- D – platelets are not first line unless thrombocytopenia.
- E – vitamin K reverses VKA, not fibrinolysis.

**Ref:** Prabhakaran S, Stroke 2026; Berge E, Eur Stroke J 2021.

open.q: A 64-year-old woman wakes at 07:00 with right hemiplegia and aphasia (last seen well 23:00). NIHSS 18, no haemorrhage on CT, left M1 occlusion on CTA. Describe how you decide on reperfusion therapy and her first 24 hours of ICU care.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Onset unknown/ > 4.5 h: imaging selection – CT perfusion (core vs Tmax > 6 s penumbra) or MRI (DWI–FLAIR mismatch). If mismatch: IVT can be considered (WAKE-UP, EXTEND; TNK up to 24 h only where EVT unavailable – TRACE-III).
- EVT up to 24 h with clinical-core/perfusion mismatch (DAWN, DEFUSE 3); large core does not exclude EVT (SELECT2, ANGEL-ASPECT, LASTE).
- Peri-procedure: GA or sedation per local practice; avoid hypotension, hypocapnia.
- ICU: BP < 180/105, no SBP < 140 target (OPTIMAL-BP, ENCHANTED2/MT); glucose 7.8–10; SpO₂ ≥ 94 %; normothermia; dysphagia screen; IPC; repeat CT at 24 h before antithrombotics.
- Watch for malignant oedema (days 2–5): neuro checks, early hemicraniectomy discussion (≤ 48 h; age and values – DESTINY II).
- Secondary prevention: aspirin after 24 h, aetiology work-up, early DOAC if AF (ELAN).

title: W15 · D5 – Status epilepticus: definitions, staged treatment, refractory SE, NCSE in the ICU

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man (80 kg) with known epilepsy has a generalised tonic–clonic seizure that has lasted 6 minutes on arrival of paramedics. There is no IV access. What is the most appropriate first treatment?
options: Rectal paracetamol and observation for another 5 minutes
IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg after obtaining access
Oral lorazepam 1 mg
IM phenytoin 20 mg/kg
IM midazolam 10 mg
questions.expl:
**Why E:** For convulsive SE, treatment starts at t1 = 5 min with a full-dose benzodiazepine. RAMPART showed that IM midazolam 10 mg (> 40 kg) given by paramedics stopped seizures before ED arrival more often than IV lorazepam (73.4 vs 63.4 %), mainly because it is given faster.

**Why not the others:**
- A – waiting exceeds t1 and benzodiazepine efficacy falls with time.
- B – second-line ASMs follow benzodiazepines (ESETT used them after benzodiazepine failure).
- C – oral route and 1 mg dose are inadequate.
- D – IM phenytoin is erratically absorbed and is not a first-line drug.

**Ref:** Silbergleit R, NEJM 2012; Glauser T, Epilepsy Curr 2016.

questions.stem: Regarding the ILAE 2015 definition of status epilepticus:
options: For tonic–clonic SE, time point t1 (when treatment should start) is 30 minutes.
For focal SE with impaired awareness, t2 (risk of long-term consequences) is 10 minutes.
Super-refractory SE is defined as SE persisting for more than 1 hour after the first benzodiazepine dose.
Refractory SE requires failure of at least two anaesthetic agents.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – t1 = 5 min; **t2 = 30 min** for tonic–clonic SE.
- B (False) – for focal SE with impaired awareness t1 = 10 min and t2 > 60 min.
- C (False) – SRSE = SE continuing or recurring ≥ 24 h after starting anaesthetic therapy.
- D (False) – RSE = failure of a benzodiazepine and one adequately dosed second-line ASM.

**EDIC trap:** all-false K′ items exist – do not assume at least one statement is true.

**Ref:** Trinka E, Epilepsia 2015.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman's convulsive seizures continue after two doses of IV lorazepam 4 mg. She is haemodynamically stable. In the ESETT trial, which statement about second-line therapy is correct?
options: Fosphenytoin was significantly more effective than levetiracetam
Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate had similar efficacy (~45–47 % seizure cessation)
Valproate caused significantly more hypotension than fosphenytoin
Phenobarbital was superior to all three
Levetiracetam was harmful in children
questions.expl:
**Why B:** ESETT (n = 384) randomised benzodiazepine-refractory convulsive SE to levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg or valproate 40 mg/kg; the primary outcome (cessation of seizures and improved responsiveness at 60 min) occurred in 47 %, 45 % and 46 %. The choice therefore depends on patient factors (e.g. valproate in pregnancy is avoided; fosphenytoin in arrhythmia risk).

**Why not the others:**
- A – no significant difference.
- C – hypotension and intubation were numerically more frequent with fosphenytoin.
- D – phenobarbital was not included in ESETT.
- E – efficacy was similar in children and adults.

**Ref:** Kapur J, NEJM 2019.

questions.stem: Regarding the pathophysiology and pharmacology of prolonged seizures:
options: During prolonged seizures, synaptic GABA-A receptors are internalised, reducing benzodiazepine efficacy.
NMDA receptor density at the synapse decreases, which is why ketamine loses efficacy late in SE.
Valproate should be avoided in suspected mitochondrial disease (e.g. POLG mutations).
Phenytoin is the drug of choice for tricyclic antidepressant–induced seizures.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – GABA-A receptor endocytosis explains time-dependent benzodiazepine resistance.
- B (False) – NMDA receptors move **to** the synapse, providing the rationale for ketamine in refractory SE.
- C (True) – risk of fulminant liver failure; also avoid in urea-cycle disorders and pregnancy.
- D (False) – sodium-channel blockers like phenytoin are ineffective or harmful in TCA toxicity; use benzodiazepines, sodium bicarbonate and barbiturates/propofol.

**Ref:** Trinka E, Epilepsia 2015; Brophy GM, Neurocrit Care 2012.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman, 34 weeks pregnant, presents with generalised convulsions. BP is 172/112 mmHg and she has proteinuria. All of the following are appropriate EXCEPT:
options: Magnesium sulphate 4–6 g IV loading dose, then infusion
Antihypertensive treatment (e.g. labetalol)
A benzodiazepine if seizures persist despite magnesium
Valproate 40 mg/kg IV as the preferred second-line agent
Urgent obstetric review regarding delivery
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Eclampsia is treated with magnesium sulphate (superior to diazepam and phenytoin for preventing recurrence) plus BP control and delivery. Valproate is teratogenic and avoided in pregnancy; it is not the treatment of eclamptic seizures.

**Why not the others:**
- A – magnesium is first line for eclampsia.
- B – severe hypertension (≥ 160/110) must be treated to prevent ICH.
- C – benzodiazepines are used for persistent seizures.
- E – delivery is the definitive treatment.

**Ref:** Brophy GM, Neurocrit Care 2012.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man remains comatose 2 hours after his generalised convulsions were controlled with lorazepam and levetiracetam. He is intubated and sedated with propofol.
options: Non-convulsive status epilepticus should be excluded with EEG, ideally continuous.
Neuromuscular blockade without EEG monitoring may mask ongoing seizures.
Continuous EEG for 24–48 h increases seizure detection compared with a 30-minute routine EEG.
A normal CT scan excludes ongoing seizures.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – NCSE follows treated convulsive SE in a substantial proportion; persistent coma is a classic indication for cEEG.
- B (True) – NMB abolishes motor signs but not electrical seizures.
- C (True) – about 80–90 % of seizures are detected within 24 h; comatose patients may need 48 h.
- D (False) – imaging cannot exclude electrographic seizures.

**Ref:** Brophy GM, Neurocrit Care 2012; Hirsch LJ, J Clin Neurophysiol 2021.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has refractory convulsive SE despite lorazepam and valproate. He is intubated in the ICU. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Third dose of lorazepam and observe
Neuromuscular blockade to stop the convulsions
Continuous IV midazolam or propofol titrated to seizure suppression, guided by continuous EEG
Therapeutic hypothermia to 33 °C as first-line therapy
Oral topiramate via nasogastric tube as sole therapy
questions.expl:
**Why C:** RSE (failure of benzodiazepine + one second-line ASM) requires continuous anaesthetic infusion (midazolam, propofol, or barbiturate) with cEEG, aiming for seizure or burst suppression for 24–48 h before gradual weaning.

**Why not the others:**
- A – further benzodiazepine boluses delay effective therapy.
- B – NMB only hides motor activity; seizures continue.
- D – HYBERNATUS: hypothermia did not improve functional outcome.
- E – enteral ASMs are adjuncts, too slow as sole therapy.

**Ref:** Brophy GM, Neurocrit Care 2012; Legriel S, NEJM 2016.

questions.stem: Regarding trials and evidence in status epilepticus:
options: In the VA cooperative trial (Treiman 1998), lorazepam was more successful than phenytoin alone as initial therapy.
In HYBERNATUS, hypothermia 32–34 °C improved functional outcome at 90 days.
In TELSTAR, treating rhythmic and periodic EEG patterns after cardiac arrest improved neurological outcome.
In the prehospital trial by Alldredge (2001), both lorazepam and diazepam were more effective than placebo.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 64.9 vs 43.6 %.
- B (False) – GOS 5: 49 vs 43 % (NS); it only reduced progression to EEG-confirmed SE on day 1.
- C (False) – poor outcome 90 vs 92 % – no benefit.
- D (True) – termination 59.1 % (lorazepam) and 42.6 % (diazepam) vs 21.1 % (placebo).

**Ref:** Treiman DM, NEJM 1998; Legriel S, NEJM 2016; Ruijter BJ, NEJM 2022; Alldredge BK, NEJM 2001.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man being treated for tuberculosis is brought in after an overdose of his medication. He has recurrent generalised seizures that do not respond to two doses of IV lorazepam. In addition to supportive care, which treatment is most specific?
options: IV pyridoxine
IV thiamine
IV phenytoin
IV naloxone
IV flumazenil
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Isoniazid depletes pyridoxal-5-phosphate, a cofactor for GABA synthesis, causing benzodiazepine-resistant seizures and metabolic acidosis. Pyridoxine (gram for gram of isoniazid ingested, or 5 g empirically) restores GABA production.

**Why not the others:**
- B – thiamine is for Wernicke encephalopathy/alcohol-related states, not isoniazid.
- C – phenytoin is ineffective in isoniazid toxicity.
- D – naloxone reverses opioids.
- E – flumazenil may precipitate seizures.

**Ref:** Brophy GM, Neurocrit Care 2012.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with no history of epilepsy develops refractory SE after a febrile flu-like illness. CT, CSF cell count, toxicology and metabolic tests are unremarkable. Seizures persist after 48 hours of midazolam infusion. Which statement is most appropriate?
options: This is simple refractory SE; increase the midazolam dose and await recovery
This is new-onset refractory SE (NORSE/FIRES phenotype); start a search for autoimmune causes and consider early immunotherapy alongside ketamine or additional ASMs
Withdraw anaesthetics because the prognosis is invariably fatal
Fosphenytoin is contraindicated and the patient should receive only benzodiazepines
Prognosis depends mainly on the dose of benzodiazepine given in the first 5 minutes
questions.expl:
**Why B:** New-onset refractory SE without an evident cause in a previously healthy adult (NORSE; FIRES when preceded by fever) is often autoimmune or cryptogenic. Persistence ≥ 24 h on anaesthetics defines SRSE; management includes autoimmune antibody screening (serum/CSF), tumour search (e.g. ovarian teratoma), early immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange) and additional agents such as ketamine.

**Why not the others:**
- A – this is super-refractory SE, not simple RSE; escalation and a cause search are needed.
- C – many patients survive with good recovery; early withdrawal is inappropriate.
- D – fosphenytoin is not contraindicated here.
- E – prognosis is driven mainly by aetiology, age and duration.

**Ref:** Trinka E, Epilepsia 2015; Brophy GM, Neurocrit Care 2012.

open.q: A 55-year-old man is brought to the ED with convulsive seizures lasting 15 minutes. Describe a time-based treatment algorithm up to refractory SE, including drugs, doses and investigations.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- 0–5 min: ABC, O₂, lateral position, monitoring, IV access, glucose (thiamine first if alcohol/malnutrition), electrolytes incl. Ca/Mg, ASM levels, toxicology, CK, ABG.
- 5–20 min: benzodiazepine full dose – IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (4 mg) or IV diazepam 0.15–0.2 mg/kg or IM midazolam 10 mg (RAMPART); repeat once.
- 20–40 min: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4.5 g) or valproate 40 mg/kg (max 3 g) or fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg (max 1.5 g) – equivalent in ESETT; adjust to comorbidities.
- 40–60 min: RSE – intubate, midazolam or propofol infusion (± barbiturates), cEEG, target seizure/burst suppression 24–48 h, maintenance ASMs, slow wean.
- SRSE: ketamine, additional ASMs, immunotherapy if NORSE/autoimmune; no routine hypothermia (HYBERNATUS).
- Investigate cause: CT/MRI, LP, EEG; specific antidotes (pyridoxine for isoniazid, magnesium for eclampsia).
- Complications: aspiration, rhabdomyolysis, hyperthermia, lactic acidosis; avoid NMB without EEG.

title: W15 · Saturday – weekly review: Neuro I (TBI, SAH, ICH, ischaemic stroke, status epilepticus)

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with severe diffuse TBI has an ICP of 24 mmHg and MAP of 80 mmHg (zeroed at the tragus) on day 2, despite sedation, head elevation and normocapnia. There is no surgical lesion on repeat CT. Which is the most appropriate next measure?
options: Hypertonic saline bolus (or mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg) and CSF drainage if an EVD is present
Early bifrontal decompressive craniectomy
Hyperventilation to PaCO₂ 25 mmHg for 24 h
Cooling to 33 °C
Dexamethasone 10 mg IV
questions.expl:
**Why A:** ICP > 22 mmHg (BTF) with CPP 56 mmHg needs tier-1 SIBICC measures: osmotherapy bolus, CSF drainage, deeper sedation, PaCO₂ 35–38 mmHg and CPP 60–70 mmHg.

**Why not the others:**
- B – DECRA: early bifrontal DC worsened functional outcome.
- C – prolonged hyperventilation to ≤ 25 mmHg is not recommended (ischaemia).
- D – Eurotherm3235: 32–35 °C was harmful.
- E – steroids increase mortality in TBI (CRASH).

**Ref:** Carney N, Neurosurgery 2017; Hawryluk GWJ, Intensive Care Med 2019. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: Regarding transfusion and temperature management in acute brain injury:
options: In TRAIN, a haemoglobin threshold of 9 g/dL was associated with fewer unfavourable neurological outcomes than 7 g/dL.
In HEMOTION, a threshold of 10 g/dL significantly improved outcome in TBI.
In POLAR, prophylactic early hypothermia improved favourable outcome after severe TBI.
In SAHaRA, liberal transfusion (Hb < 10 g/dL) significantly reduced 12-month unfavourable outcome after aneurysmal SAH.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 62.6 vs 73.5 % unfavourable outcome.
- B (False) – 68.4 vs 73.5 %, not significant.
- C (False) – 48.8 vs 49.1 % favourable outcome, no benefit.
- D (False) – 33.5 vs 37.7 %, RR 0.88, not significant.

**Ref:** Taccone FS, JAMA 2024; Turgeon AF, NEJM 2024; English SW, NEJM 2025. → [D1](D1.md), [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman with WFNS grade I aneurysmal SAH had her aneurysm coiled on day 1. She is on day 7. Which treatment has the strongest evidence for improving her functional outcome?
options: IV magnesium sulphate infusion
Simvastatin 40 mg daily
Oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days
Clazosentan infusion
Prophylactic hypervolaemia
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Nimodipine reduced cerebral infarction (22 vs 33 %) and poor outcome (20 vs 33 %) in BRANT and is the only drug recommended on high-quality evidence by ESO 2026.

**Why not the others:**
- A – MASH-2 neutral.
- B – STASH neutral; ESO recommends against statins.
- D – clazosentan reduced vasospasm but not poor outcome; ESO recommends against endothelin antagonists.
- E – no benefit and more complications.

**Ref:** Pickard JD, BMJ 1989; Vergouwen MDI, Eur Stroke J 2026. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: Regarding complications after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage:
options: Hyponatraemia is common and may be due to cerebral salt wasting with hypovolaemia.
Fluid restriction is the treatment of choice for hyponatraemia after SAH.
Delayed cerebral ischaemia typically occurs between days 3 and 14.
Acute hydrocephalus is treated with an external ventricular drain when symptomatic.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – CSW (natriuresis + volume depletion) or SIADH, often mixed.
- B (False) – fluid restriction increases DCI risk; use saline/hypertonic saline and fludrocortisone.
- C (True) – peak days 5–10.
- D (True) – EVD is first line for symptomatic acute hydrocephalus.

**Ref:** Hoh BL, Stroke 2023; Treggiari MM, Neurocrit Care 2023. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman on warfarin (INR 3.4) has a 22 mL lobar ICH, GCS 14, 1 hour after onset. What is the most appropriate reversal?
options: Fresh frozen plasma 10 mL/kg alone
Vitamin K 10 mg orally alone
Recombinant factor VIIa
Platelet transfusion
4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus vitamin K 10 mg IV
questions.expl:
**Why E:** 4F-PCC corrects INR faster than FFP and reduced haematoma expansion (INCH); IV vitamin K prevents rebound once the PCC effect wanes. INTERACT3 included reversal to INR < 1.5 within 1 h in its successful care bundle.

**Why not the others:**
- A – FFP is slower, requires large volumes and thawing.
- B – oral vitamin K alone takes many hours.
- C – rFVIIa does not replace all factors and is not recommended for VKA reversal.
- D – platelets are not indicated; she is not thrombocytopenic.

**Ref:** Greenberg SM, Stroke 2022; Ma L, Lancet 2023. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man has a cerebellar haemorrhage of 22 mL with compression of the fourth ventricle and early hydrocephalus. GCS falls from 14 to 11. What is the most appropriate management?
options: External ventricular drain alone
Surgical evacuation of the haematoma (suboccipital decompression), with EVD if needed
Mannitol and observation
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV
Minimally invasive catheter evacuation with alteplase (MISTIE)
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Cerebellar ICH > 15 mL with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus and neurological deterioration should be evacuated surgically. EVD alone is not recommended as initial therapy because it does not relieve brainstem compression and risks upward herniation.

**Why not the others:**
- A – insufficient as sole treatment.
- C – osmotherapy is only a bridge.
- D – TICH-2 showed no functional benefit of TXA.
- E – MISTIE III studied supratentorial ICH.

**Ref:** Greenberg SM, Stroke 2022; Steiner T, Eur Stroke J 2025. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: Regarding acute blood pressure management in intracerebral haemorrhage:
options: A target SBP of around 140 mmHg, achieved early and smoothly, is recommended.
Lowering SBP to below 130 mmHg is potentially harmful.
Large fluctuations in blood pressure are associated with worse outcome.
The INTERACT3 care bundle included control of glucose and temperature in addition to blood pressure.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – AHA 2022 and ESO 2025.
- B (True) – AHA 2022 (class 3: harm), based on ATACH-2 renal adverse events and lack of benefit.
- C (True) – BP variability is a recognised predictor of poor outcome.
- D (True) – SBP < 140, glucose targets, temperature ≤ 37.5 °C and anticoagulation reversal.

**Ref:** Greenberg SM, Stroke 2022; Ma L, Lancet 2023. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man presents 18 hours after last known well with a right M1 occlusion, NIHSS 17 and ASPECTS 4 on CT. Based on recent trials, which statement is most accurate?
options: Thrombectomy is contraindicated because ASPECTS is below 6
Only IV tenecteplase is indicated
Thrombectomy can be considered: large-core trials (SELECT2, ANGEL-ASPECT, TENSION, LASTE) showed better functional outcome
Thrombectomy is indicated only if the occlusion is in a medium vessel
Decompressive hemicraniectomy should be performed immediately instead of thrombectomy
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Large-core trials (ASPECTS 3–5 and in LASTE 0–5, up to 24 h) showed improved functional outcome, and LASTE reduced mortality (36.1 vs 55.5 %). AHA 2026 extends EVT to selected patients with large cores.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the ASPECTS ≥ 6 rule is outdated.
- B – at 18 h, IVT is not standard (TNK only where EVT is unavailable – TRACE-III).
- D – medium-vessel occlusion trials (ESCAPE-MeVO, DISTAL) were negative.
- E – hemicraniectomy is considered when malignant oedema develops, not instead of reperfusion.

**Ref:** Sarraj A, NEJM 2023; Costalat V, NEJM 2024; Prabhakaran S, Stroke 2026. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: Regarding intravenous thrombolysis in ischaemic stroke:
options: Tenecteplase is given as a single bolus of 0.25 mg/kg (maximum 25 mg).
A platelet count of 80 × 10⁹/L is a contraindication.
Patients with non-disabling minor deficits benefit more from alteplase than from dual antiplatelet therapy.
In EXTEND, patients with perfusion mismatch 4.5–9 hours after onset benefited from alteplase.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – the stroke dose is lower than the MI dose.
- B (True) – platelets < 100 × 10⁹/L contraindicate IVT.
- C (False) – PRISMS/ARAMIS: no benefit of IVT; DAPT is preferred.
- D (True) – mRS 0–1 35.4 vs 29.5 % (adjusted benefit).

**Ref:** Berge E, Eur Stroke J 2021; Prabhakaran S, Stroke 2026. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman has a malignant right MCA infarction and deteriorates 36 hours after onset. Which statement about decompressive hemicraniectomy is LEAST accurate?
options: In patients ≤ 60 years operated within 48 h, mortality falls from ~71 % to ~22 %
It increases the proportion with mRS ≤ 3 in patients ≤ 60 years
In patients > 60 years, it increases survival but most survivors are moderately severely disabled
It improves outcome only when the dominant hemisphere is spared
The family should be informed that survival with disability is likely
questions.expl:
**Why D:** The pooled trials showed benefit regardless of hemisphere; aphasia is not a contraindication, and hemisphere side is a values question, not an evidence-based exclusion.

**Why not the others:**
- A – pooled DECIMAL/DESTINY/HAMLET: 71 → 22 %.
- B – mRS ≤ 3 43 vs 21 %.
- C – DESTINY II: mRS 0–4 38 vs 18 %, no patient mRS 0–2.
- E – correct and important for shared decision-making.

**Ref:** Vahedi K, Lancet Neurol 2007; Jüttler E, NEJM 2014. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has convulsive SE; seizures persist 10 minutes after IV lorazepam 4 mg, repeated once. Weight 75 kg, normal renal and liver function, history of atrial fibrillation with bradycardia. Which second-line therapy is most appropriate?
options: Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (maximum 4500 mg)
Phenytoin 20 mg/kg at 100 mg/min
A third and fourth dose of lorazepam
Oral carbamazepine via nasogastric tube
Neuromuscular blockade and intubation without further ASM
questions.expl:
**Why A:** In ESETT, levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate were equally effective (~45–47 %). Given his bradyarrhythmia, levetiracetam avoids the cardiac effects of phenytoin; NICE NG217 prefers levetiracetam as first-choice second-line agent.

**Why not the others:**
- B – phenytoin causes bradycardia, arrhythmia and hypotension, and the maximum rate is 50 mg/min.
- C – further benzodiazepines delay effective therapy.
- D – enteral route is too slow.
- E – NMB masks seizures; it is not a treatment.

**Ref:** Kapur J, NEJM 2019; NICE NG217 2022. → [D5](D5.md)

questions.stem: Regarding status epilepticus:
options: ILAE defines t1 for convulsive SE as 5 minutes.
In RAMPART, IM midazolam was at least as effective as IV lorazepam for prehospital SE.
Non-convulsive SE is rare in comatose ICU patients and EEG is rarely useful.
HYBERNATUS showed that hypothermia improved good functional outcome.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – t1 = 5 min, t2 = 30 min.
- B (True) – 73.4 vs 63.4 % seizure cessation before ED arrival.
- C (False) – NCSE occurs in ~8–10 % of comatose ICU patients; cEEG is essential.
- D (False) – GOS 5: 49 vs 43 %, not significant.

**Ref:** Trinka E, Epilepsia 2015; Silbergleit R, NEJM 2012; Legriel S, NEJM 2016. → [D5](D5.md)

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man with TBI (GCS 10, small subdural haematoma) arrives 2 hours after injury. Which statement about tranexamic acid is most accurate?
options: CRASH-3 showed benefit only in patients with bilateral unreactive pupils
TXA increases vascular occlusive events in TBI
TXA is effective up to 24 h after injury
CRASH-3 showed reduced head-injury death in mild–moderate TBI when given within 3 hours
TXA should be given only after CT confirms no haematoma
questions.expl:
**Why D:** CRASH-3: TXA (1 g over 10 min + 1 g over 8 h) within 3 h reduced head-injury death in mild–moderate TBI (RR 0.78); no benefit in severe TBI or with bilateral unreactive pupils, and earlier was better.

**Why not the others:**
- A – no benefit in that group.
- B – no increase in vascular occlusive events.
- C – the benefit is limited to ≤ 3 h and falls with each delay.
- E – a haematoma is not a contraindication; it is the target population.

**Ref:** CRASH-3 collaborators, Lancet 2019. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: Regarding intracerebral haemorrhage associated with antithrombotic therapy:
options: Platelet transfusion improves outcome in antiplatelet-associated ICH without surgery.
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran.
In ANNEXA-I, andexanet reduced 30-day mortality compared with usual care.
Restarting antiplatelet therapy after ICH did not increase recurrent ICH in RESTART.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – PATCH: death or dependence increased (OR 2.05).
- B (True) – 5 g IV.
- C (False) – better haemostasis, more thrombotic events, no mortality benefit.
- D (True) – 4 vs 9 %, HR 0.51.

**Ref:** Baharoglu MI, Lancet 2016; Connolly SJ, NEJM 2024; RESTART, Lancet 2019. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: Regarding the SIBICC consensus for severe TBI with ICP monitoring:
options: Mannitol should be given as a continuous infusion.
Lumbar CSF drainage is recommended for raised ICP.
Barbiturate coma is a tier-3 intervention.
Routine cooling below 36 °C is a tier-1 intervention.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – bolus only; continuous mannitol is on the "do not" list.
- B (False) – lumbar drainage is on the "do not" list.
- C (True) – with a test dose and haemodynamic monitoring, alongside secondary DC and mild hypothermia (35–36 °C).
- D (False) – mild hypothermia 35–36 °C is tier 3; routine < 36 °C is discouraged.

**Ref:** Hawryluk GWJ, Intensive Care Med 2019. → [D1](D1.md)

title: W16 · D1 – Analgesia and sedation (PADIS 2018 + 2025 focused update), ABCDEF bundle

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with Child–Pugh C cirrhosis and oliguric AKI (not yet on RRT) is intubated for pneumonia. He requires an opioid infusion to tolerate the ventilator. Which opioid's elimination is LEAST affected by his organ dysfunction?
options: Morphine
Fentanyl
Hydromorphone
Remifentanil
Oxycodone
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Remifentanil is an ester hydrolysed by non-specific plasma and tissue esterases, so its offset (3–10 min, context-insensitive) is independent of liver and kidney function. Its metabolite (remifentanil acid) is almost inactive, making it the most predictable opioid in combined hepatic and renal failure.

**Why not the others:**
- A – morphine is glucuronidated; M6G (active) and M3G (neuroexcitatory) accumulate in renal failure.
- B – fentanyl depends on hepatic CYP3A4 and accumulates with prolonged infusion (large volume of distribution).
- C – hydromorphone-3-glucuronide accumulates in renal failure (neuroexcitation).
- E – oxycodone depends on hepatic CYP3A4/2D6 metabolism and renal excretion of metabolites.

**EDIC trap:** "least affected by organ dysfunction" = esterase metabolism (remifentanil, also cisatracurium among NMBAs).

**Ref:** Devlin JW, Crit Care Med 2018 (PADIS).

questions.stem: A 66-year-old intubated woman on day 2 after laparotomy cannot self-report pain. Regarding pain assessment and management according to PADIS:
options: A Behavioural Pain Scale (BPS) score of 7 indicates significant pain.
Tachycardia and hypertension are valid stand-alone indicators of pain in this patient.
Low-dose ketamine may be used as an adjunct to reduce postoperative opioid consumption.
A Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT) score of 1 indicates significant pain.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – BPS ranges 3–12; a score > 5 indicates significant pain.
- B (False) – PADIS states vital signs should **not** be used alone to assess pain; tachycardia/hypertension are only a cue to perform a validated behavioural assessment (BPS or CPOT).
- C (True) – low-dose ketamine is suggested as an adjunct to opioids after surgery to reduce opioid consumption (conditional).
- D (False) – CPOT ranges 0–8; significant pain is a score > 2, so 1 is not.

**EDIC trap:** know the cut-offs – BPS > 5, CPOT > 2; NRS ≥ 4 if the patient can self-report.

**Ref:** Devlin JW, Crit Care Med 2018 (PADIS).

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with severe TBI has been sedated with propofol 5 mg/kg/h for 3 days together with noradrenaline. Lactate rises to 6 mmol/L, CK is 12,000 U/L, potassium 6.1 mmol/L and the ECG shows coved ST elevation in V1–V2. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Add dexmedetomidine to reduce the propofol requirement
Give intravenous dantrolene
Stop propofol and switch to an alternative sedative with supportive care
Start a lipid emulsion bolus
Increase noradrenaline and continue propofol at the same dose
questions.expl:
**Why C:** This is propofol-related infusion syndrome (PRIS): high dose (> 4 mg/kg/h) for > 48 h with catecholamines in TBI, producing lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia and a Brugada-like ECG. Management is to stop propofol immediately, switch to another sedative and give supportive care (RRT for hyperkalaemia/acidosis, pacing or ECMO if refractory).

**Why not the others:**
- A – any continued propofol perpetuates the mitochondrial injury; reducing the dose is insufficient.
- B – dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia, not PRIS.
- D – propofol is already a lipid emulsion; lipid rescue is for local anaesthetic toxicity.
- E – escalating catecholamines while continuing propofol worsens the syndrome.

**EDIC trap:** risk factors are dose, duration, catecholamines/steroids, TBI and low carbohydrate intake; monitor CK, lactate and triglycerides.

**Ref:** Devlin JW, Crit Care Med 2018 (PADIS).

questions.stem: Regarding randomised trials of sedation strategy in mechanically ventilated adults:
options: In the trial by Kress et al. (2000), daily interruption of sedative infusions shortened the duration of mechanical ventilation.
In the ABC trial (Girard 2008), pairing a spontaneous awakening trial with a spontaneous breathing trial was associated with lower 1-year mortality.
In NONSEDA (2020), a non-sedation strategy significantly reduced 90-day mortality compared with light sedation.
In the trial by Strøm et al. (2010), a no-sedation strategy increased days without ventilation but was associated with more agitated delirium.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Kress (n = 128): daily interruption shortened mechanical ventilation (4.9 vs 7.3 days) and ICU stay.
- B (True) – ABC trial: SAT paired with SBT reduced 1-year mortality (44 vs 58 %, HR 0.68).
- C (False) – NONSEDA (n = 700): 90-day mortality 42.4 vs 37.0 % with non-sedation vs light sedation – **not significant**, and not a reduction.
- D (True) – Strøm (single centre): no sedation gave more ventilator-free days (13.8 vs 9.6) but more agitated delirium (20 vs 7 %).

**EDIC trap:** the benefit of protocolised light sedation does not extend to proven mortality benefit of "no sedation" (NONSEDA).

**Ref:** Kress JP, N Engl J Med 2000; Girard TD, Lancet 2008; Strøm T, Lancet 2010; Olsen HT, N Engl J Med 2020.

questions.stem: In the SPICE III trial (4000 patients), early sedation with dexmedetomidine compared with usual care resulted in:
options: Lower 90-day mortality
Similar 90-day mortality, with more bradycardia and hypotension
Fewer days of mechanical ventilation and lower mortality in patients younger than 65 years
Achievement of deep sedation targets without additional sedatives in most patients
Higher 90-day mortality in all age groups
questions.expl:
**Why B:** SPICE III (n = 4000) compared early dexmedetomidine-based sedation with usual care. 90-day mortality was identical (29.1 % in both groups), while bradycardia and hypotension were more frequent with dexmedetomidine.

**Why not the others:**
- A – mortality did not differ.
- C – in patients ≤ 65 years there was a signal of **higher**, not lower, mortality (heterogeneity by age).
- D – most dexmedetomidine patients needed supplemental propofol, midazolam or both to reach targets.
- E – a possible benefit was seen in older patients (> 65 years), so higher mortality was not universal.

**EDIC trap:** dexmedetomidine is a light-sedation drug; it does not reduce mortality.

**Ref:** Shehabi Y, N Engl J Med 2019 (SPICE III).

questions.stem: Regarding the 2025 PADIS focused update (Society of Critical Care Medicine):
options: It strongly recommends benzodiazepines for anxiety in ventilated adults.
It suggests melatonin to improve sleep in critically ill adults.
It makes no recommendation for or against antipsychotics for delirium.
It suggests enhanced mobilisation/rehabilitation over usual care.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – the panel made **no recommendation** on benzodiazepines for anxiety (insufficient evidence); it advises validated assessment and non-pharmacological measures.
- B (True) – melatonin is suggested to improve sleep (conditional, low certainty).
- C (True) – no recommendation for or against antipsychotics for delirium (low certainty, minimal effect on outcomes).
- D (True) – enhanced mobilisation/rehabilitation is suggested over usual care (conditional, moderate certainty).

**EDIC trap:** every 2025 recommendation is conditional or "no recommendation" – a statement containing "strongly recommends" is false. The update also conditionally suggests dexmedetomidine over propofol for light sedation.

**Ref:** Lewis K, Crit Care Med 2025.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man is ventilated for pneumonia. He is agitated (RASS +2) on a low dose of propofol. Heart rate is 48/min with first-degree AV block. Which sedative choice is LEAST appropriate?
options: Treat pain first with an opioid bolus and reassess
Titrate propofol to RASS −1 to 0
Assess for delirium with the CAM-ICU
Look for causes of agitation such as hypoxaemia, urinary retention or withdrawal
Start dexmedetomidine infusion
questions.expl:
**Why E:** He is already bradycardic (48/min) with first-degree AV block. α2-agonists lower heart rate; in A2B severe bradycardia (HR < 50/min) was ~1.6 times more frequent with dexmedetomidine or clonidine than with propofol. Starting dexmedetomidine is therefore the least appropriate choice.

**Why not the others:**
- A – analgesia first: pain is a common cause of agitation in ventilated patients.
- B – light sedation (RASS −1 to 0) with propofol is consistent with PADIS.
- C – agitation may be hyperactive delirium; screen with CAM-ICU.
- D – treat reversible causes (hypoxaemia, retention, withdrawal) before adding drugs.

**EDIC trap:** the PADIS 2025 suggestion of dexmedetomidine over propofol is conditional – baseline bradycardia or conduction disease favours alternatives.

**Ref:** Walsh TS, JAMA 2025 (A2B); Lewis K, Crit Care Med 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding the A2B (2025), MENDS2 (2021) and SESAR (2025) trials:
options: In A2B, dexmedetomidine significantly shortened time to successful extubation compared with propofol.
In A2B, α2-agonist sedation was associated with more agitation than propofol.
In MENDS2, dexmedetomidine increased days alive without delirium or coma in septic patients.
In SESAR, inhaled sevoflurane reduced 90-day mortality in ARDS compared with propofol.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – A2B (n = 1404): time to successful extubation was not significantly shorter with dexmedetomidine (sHR 1.09) or clonidine (sHR 1.05) than propofol.
- B (True) – α2-agonist sedation caused more agitation (RR ~1.5) and more severe bradycardia (RR ~1.6).
- C (False) – MENDS2 (sepsis, n = 438): no difference from propofol in days alive without delirium or coma, ventilator-free days, 90-day mortality or 6-month cognition.
- D (False) – SESAR (n = 687): inhaled sevoflurane **increased** 90-day mortality (52.9 vs 44.3 %) and reduced ventilator-free days.

**EDIC trap:** none of the newer sedative strategies (dexmedetomidine, clonidine, volatile agents) has outperformed propofol on hard outcomes.

**Ref:** Walsh TS, JAMA 2025; Hughes CG, N Engl J Med 2021; Jabaudon M, JAMA 2025.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with moderate–severe ARDS (PaO₂/FiO₂ 110 mmHg) on day 1 needs deep sedation for prone positioning and neuromuscular blockade. Which approach is best supported by current evidence?
options: Inhaled sevoflurane via an anaesthetic conserving device
Dexmedetomidine as sole agent targeting RASS −5
IV propofol with an opioid, targeting deep sedation during blockade
No sedation, opioid boluses only
Neuromuscular blockade with light sedation (RASS 0)
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Neuromuscular blockade requires deep sedation to prevent awareness, and IV propofol plus an opioid is the standard, evidence-supported approach. During prone positioning with NMB, target deep sedation (e.g. RASS −5) and monitor with clinical signs ± processed EEG.

**Why not the others:**
- A – SESAR: inhaled sevoflurane in early moderate–severe ARDS caused fewer ventilator-free days and higher 90-day mortality (52.9 vs 44.3 %).
- B – dexmedetomidine cannot reliably achieve deep sedation as a sole agent.
- D – opioid boluses alone cannot provide amnesia/hypnosis during paralysis.
- E – light sedation during NMB risks awareness under paralysis – a never event.

**EDIC trap:** "light sedation for all" has an exception – NMB, refractory ICP, status epilepticus and severe ARDS need deep sedation.

**Ref:** Jabaudon M, JAMA 2025 (SESAR); Devlin JW, Crit Care Med 2018 (PADIS).

questions.stem: Regarding the ABCDEF bundle and early mobilisation:
options: "B" stands for both spontaneous awakening and spontaneous breathing trials.
In the ICU Liberation Collaborative (> 15,000 adults), complete bundle performance was associated with lower hospital mortality.
The association between bundle performance and outcome was demonstrated in a large randomised controlled trial.
In the TEAM trial, early active mobilisation increased days alive and out of hospital at 180 days.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – B = Both spontaneous awakening and spontaneous breathing trials (A = assess pain, C = choice of sedation, D = delirium, E = early mobility, F = family).
- B (True) – in > 15 000 adults, complete bundle performance was associated with lower hospital mortality (adjusted HR 0.32) and less delirium, coma and restraint use.
- C (False) – the ICU Liberation Collaborative was a **prospective cohort**, not an RCT; residual confounding is possible.
- D (False) – TEAM (n = 750): early active mobilisation did not increase days alive and out of hospital at 180 days, and adverse events were more frequent.

**EDIC trap:** PADIS 2025 still suggests enhanced mobilisation – TEAM tested an intense early protocol, not rehabilitation per se.

**Ref:** Pun BT, Crit Care Med 2019; TEAM Study Investigators, N Engl J Med 2022.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with AKI (creatinine 420 µmol/L) received midazolam and morphine infusions for 5 days. Both were stopped 36 h ago, but he remains unresponsive with pinpoint pupils and slow respiratory rate on pressure support. CT brain is normal. The most likely explanation is:
options: Accumulation of active metabolites of morphine and midazolam
Hypoactive delirium
Propofol infusion syndrome
Non-convulsive status epilepticus
Critical illness polyneuropathy
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Morphine-6-glucuronide (active μ-agonist) and α-hydroxymidazolam glucuronide are renally excreted and accumulate in AKI, causing prolonged sedation, miosis and respiratory depression long after the infusions stop. A naloxone trial is diagnostic and therapeutic; switch to drugs not dependent on renal clearance.

**Why not the others:**
- B – hypoactive delirium does not cause pinpoint pupils and bradypnoea.
- C – he never received propofol, and PRIS presents with acidosis, rhabdomyolysis and arrhythmias.
- D – NCSE should be excluded with EEG if he fails to wake, but miosis and slow breathing point to opioid effect.
- E – polyneuropathy causes weakness, not unresponsiveness with miosis.

**EDIC trap:** benzodiazepine metabolites accumulate in renal failure too – avoid prolonged midazolam infusion in AKI.

**Ref:** Devlin JW, Crit Care Med 2018 (PADIS).

questions.stem: According to PADIS, which target best defines "light sedation" in a mechanically ventilated adult without a specific indication for deep sedation?
options: RASS −4 to −3
RASS +1 to +2
RASS −2 to 0
SAS 1–2
questions.expl:
**Why D:** PADIS defines light sedation as being arousable with purposeful response to voice – roughly RASS −2 to +1 (or SAS 3–4); most protocols target RASS −2 to 0. Light sedation is associated with shorter ventilation and ICU stay.

**Why not the others:**
- A – RASS −4 to −3 is deep/moderate sedation, reserved for specific indications.
- B – RASS +1 to +2 is restless/agitated, not a target.
- C – BIS 40–60 corresponds to general-anaesthetic depth.
- E – SAS 1–2 is unarousable/very sedated; light sedation is SAS 3–4.

**EDIC trap:** RASS 0 = alert and calm; negative scores describe sedation, positive scores agitation.

**Ref:** Devlin JW, Crit Care Med 2018 (PADIS).

open.q: Describe an evidence-based approach to analgesia and sedation for a mechanically ventilated adult on day 2 of septic shock without ARDS. Include monitoring tools, drug choices and the role of daily awakening, citing key trials.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Analgesia-first: assess pain with NRS (if possible) or BPS (> 5) / CPOT (> 2); opioid (fentanyl/remifentanil) ± paracetamol; vital signs are only a cue.
- Light sedation target RASS −2 to 0 with RASS/SAS every shift; deep sedation only if specific indication.
- Prefer propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines (PADIS 2018); PADIS 2025 conditionally suggests dexmedetomidine over propofol when light sedation/less delirium is the priority – caution with bradycardia (A2B: more bradycardia and agitation, no faster extubation).
- Daily SAT paired with SBT: Kress 2000 (MV 4.9 vs 7.3 d), ABC 2008 (VFD 14.7 vs 11.6; 1-year mortality 44 vs 58 %).
- No-sedation strategy not superior to light sedation (NONSEDA).
- Dexmedetomidine: no mortality benefit (SPICE III), no advantage over propofol in sepsis (MENDS2).
- Integrate into ABCDEF bundle: delirium screening (CAM-ICU/ICDSC), early mobilisation, family engagement; complete bundle associated with lower mortality (Pun 2019).

open.q: List the risk factors, clinical features and management of propofol-related infusion syndrome.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Risk factors: dose > 4 mg/kg/h for > 48 h, young age, TBI, catecholamines, corticosteroids, low carbohydrate intake, critical illness.
- Mechanism: impaired mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation and respiratory chain.
- Features: unexplained metabolic/lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis (high CK), hyperkalaemia, AKI, hypertriglyceridaemia, hepatomegaly, Brugada-like ECG (coved ST elevation V1–V3), arrhythmias, bradycardia, cardiovascular collapse.
- Monitoring: triglycerides, CK, lactate during prolonged high-dose infusions.
- Management: stop propofol immediately, alternative sedation, supportive care, RRT for hyperkalaemia/acidosis, pacing for bradyarrhythmias, VA-ECMO in refractory shock.

title: W16 · D2 – Delirium: diagnosis, prevention and treatment

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman on day 4 of ventilation for pneumonia has RASS −1. She fails to squeeze on 4 of the 10 letters in "SAVEAHAART". Her nurse reports she was alert yesterday and drowsy today. Which conclusion is correct?
options: CAM-ICU cannot be assessed because she is intubated
CAM-ICU is negative because Feature 4 has not been tested
CAM-ICU is positive
She is in coma and delirium cannot be assessed
An ICDSC score is needed before CAM-ICU can be interpreted
questions.expl:
**Why C:** CAM-ICU is positive with Feature 1 (acute change or fluctuating course – alert yesterday, drowsy today) plus Feature 2 (inattention: > 2 errors on the letters test; she made 4) plus either Feature 3 (altered level of consciousness, any RASS ≠ 0 – she is −1) or Feature 4. Features 1 + 2 + 3 are present, so she is delirious.

**Why not the others:**
- A – CAM-ICU was designed and validated for intubated, non-verbal patients.
- B – Feature 4 is tested only if Feature 3 is absent.
- D – coma is RASS −4/−5; at −1 she is assessable.
- E – the ICDSC is an alternative tool, not a prerequisite.

**EDIC trap:** RASS −1 counts as altered consciousness for Feature 3 – only RASS 0 is "normal".

**Ref:** Ely EW, JAMA 2001 (CAM-ICU).

questions.stem: Regarding screening tools for ICU delirium:
options: A patient with RASS −4 should be scored as CAM-ICU negative.
The ICDSC is scored over a whole shift, and a score of 4 or more indicates delirium.
In the original validation, the CAM-ICU had sensitivity and specificity above 90 % in ventilated patients.
Inattention is required for a CAM-ICU diagnosis of delirium.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – RASS −4/−5 is coma: the patient is "unable to assess", not CAM-ICU negative; reassess when sedation lightens.
- B (True) – the ICDSC has 8 items scored over a shift; ≥ 4 = delirium, 1–3 = subsyndromal delirium.
- C (True) – original validation: sensitivity 93–100 % and specificity 98–100 % in ventilated patients (lower in later routine-care studies).
- D (True) – Features 1 (acute onset/fluctuation) and 2 (inattention) are both mandatory.

**EDIC trap:** a sedated patient at RASS −4 is never "delirium-free" – coma and delirium are separate brain-dysfunction states.

**Ref:** Ely EW, JAMA 2001; Bergeron N, Intensive Care Med 2001.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is extubated after cardiac surgery. He lies quietly, answers slowly, is disoriented and cannot follow a conversation. Nurses describe him as "settled". Which statement is most accurate?
options: Hypoactive delirium is uncommon in the ICU and carries a better prognosis than hyperactive delirium
This presentation excludes delirium because there is no agitation
Low-dose haloperidol should be started to shorten delirium duration
This is likely hypoactive delirium, the most common ICU subtype
A benzodiazepine at night will help restore the sleep–wake cycle
questions.expl:
**Why D:** A quiet, slow, disoriented patient who cannot follow a conversation has inattention and altered consciousness – the picture of hypoactive delirium. Hypoactive and mixed forms dominate in the ICU; pure hyperactive delirium is uncommon. Without routine CAM-ICU/ICDSC screening it is frequently missed.

**Why not the others:**
