options: Prognostication is considered in patients who remain unconscious with a GCS motor score ≤ 5 at ≥ 72 hours after ROSC.
Poor outcome is considered very likely when at least two predictors of poor outcome are present.
A bilaterally absent N20 SSEP wave can be used from 24 hours after ROSC.
MRI for diffuse hypoxic–ischaemic injury is most informative between 2 and 7 days.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – after excluding confounders (sedation, NMBA, hypothermia, hypotension, hypoglycaemia, sepsis, metabolic derangement).
- B (True) – predictors: absent pupillary and corneal reflexes ≥ 72 h, status myoclonus ≤ 72 h, absent N20 ≥ 24 h, highly malignant EEG > 24 h, NSE > 60 µg/L at 48/72 h, diffuse anoxic injury on CT/MRI.
- C (True) – very specific, but only ~50 % sensitive.
- D (True) – diffuse restricted diffusion predicts poor outcome; its absence favours a good outcome.

**Ref:** Nolan JP, Intensive Care Med 2025; Sandroni C, Intensive Care Med 2020. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is sedated and ventilated 10 hours after ROSC from an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. On noradrenaline 0.08 µg/kg/min her MAP is 67 mmHg, lactate 1.4 mmol/L and urine output 1 mL/kg/h. What is the most appropriate haemodynamic strategy?
options: Increase noradrenaline to reach MAP 85–90 mmHg to improve cerebral perfusion
Add dobutamine to increase cardiac output by 20 %
Continue the current therapy, keeping MAP above 60–65 mmHg
Stop noradrenaline and accept MAP 55 mmHg
Give a 2 L crystalloid bolus
questions.expl:
**Why C:** The 2025 guideline targets MAP > 60–65 mmHg; in BOX, MAP 77 vs 63 mmHg made no difference to death or severe disability (34 vs 32 %). She has no signs of hypoperfusion, so no escalation is needed.

**Why not the others:**
- A – higher targets did not improve outcome and need more vasopressor; consider them only for individual reasons (e.g. chronic hypertension with hypoperfusion).
- B – inotropes are indicated only for low cardiac output with hypoperfusion.
- D – hypotension (MAP < 60 mmHg) worsens hypoxic–ischaemic injury, especially with impaired autoregulation.
- E – she is not fluid-responsive by any stated criterion; fluid overload worsens oxygenation.

**Ref:** Kjaergaard J, N Engl J Med 2022; Nolan JP, Intensive Care Med 2025. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: Regarding the treatment of cerebral venous thrombosis:
options: Anticoagulation is indicated even in the presence of a haemorrhagic venous infarct.
In TO-ACT, endovascular treatment improved functional outcome in severe CVT.
Corticosteroids are recommended to reduce vasogenic oedema.
In CVT associated with antiphospholipid syndrome, warfarin is preferred over a DOAC.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – the haemorrhage is caused by venous hypertension; LMWH is preferred over UFH.
- B (False) – mRS 0–1 at 12 months 67 vs 68 %; stopped for futility.
- C (False) – steroids are not recommended and may be harmful (ISCVT), except for underlying inflammatory disease.
- D (True) – DOACs are associated with more thrombotic events in APS; VKA is preferred.

**Ref:** Ferro JM, Eur J Neurol 2017; Coutinho JM, JAMA Neurol 2020; Saposnik G, Stroke 2024. → [D5](D5.md)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with metastatic colon cancer receiving bevacizumab presents with headache, two seizures and cortical blindness. BP is 182/104 mmHg. MRI shows bilateral parieto-occipital subcortical FLAIR hyperintensities with increased ADC and patent venous sinuses on MR venography. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome
Cerebral venous thrombosis
Bilateral posterior cerebral artery infarction
Brain metastases
Herpes simplex encephalitis
questions.expl:
**Why A:** An anti-VEGF drug, acute hypertension, seizures, cortical blindness and bilateral parieto-occipital vasogenic oedema (increased ADC) are typical of PRES. Management is gradual BP reduction, stopping bevacizumab and treating seizures.

**Why not the others:**
- B – MR venography shows patent sinuses.
- C – arterial infarction shows restricted diffusion (low ADC) in a vascular territory.
- D – metastases are usually enhancing lesions with surrounding oedema, not symmetrical subcortical oedema.
- E – HSV encephalitis affects the medial temporal and inferior frontal lobes, with fever and CSF pleocytosis.

**Ref:** Fugate JE, Lancet Neurol 2015. → [D5](D5.md)

questions.stem: Regarding cerebral venous thrombosis:
options: Thrombosis of the deep venous system can cause bilateral thalamic oedema and decreased consciousness.
Seizures are less frequent in CVT than in arterial ischaemic stroke.
In ISCVT, about one-third of patients had died at 16 months.
Acetazolamide is recommended routinely in the acute phase to lower intracranial pressure.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – internal cerebral veins and straight sinus drain the thalami; deep CVT is a predictor of poor outcome.
- B (False) – seizures occur in ~40 % of CVT, far more often than in arterial stroke.
- C (False) – mortality was 8.3 %, and 79 % recovered completely.
- D (False) – acetazolamide is not recommended routinely in acute CVT.

**Ref:** Ferro JM, Stroke 2004; Ferro JM, Eur J Neurol 2017. → [D5](D5.md)

title: W18 · D1 – Acute kidney injury: KDIGO definition and staging, pathophysiology, biomarkers, prevention

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man (80 kg) with pneumonia has a baseline creatinine of 90 µmol/L. On day 2 his creatinine is 190 µmol/L and his urine output has been 0.4 mL/kg/h for the last 14 hours. What is his KDIGO AKI stage?
options: No AKI – the creatinine has not tripled
Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
Cannot be staged without a 24-hour urine collection
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Creatinine 190/90 = 2.1 × baseline (stage 2), and urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥ 12 h is also stage 2. Patients are staged by whichever criterion gives the highest stage.

**Why not the others:**
- A – AKI requires only a 1.5 × rise in 7 days or 0.3 mg/dL (26.5 µmol/L) in 48 h.
- B – both criteria exceed stage 1 (1.5–1.9 × or UO < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 h).
- D – stage 3 needs ≥ 3 ×, SCr ≥ 354 µmol/L, KRT, UO < 0.3 mL/kg/h for 24 h or anuria for 12 h.
- E – KDIGO staging uses hourly urine output and serum creatinine; no timed collection is needed.

**Ref:** KDIGO AKI Work Group, Kidney Int Suppl 2012.

questions.stem: Regarding serum creatinine as a marker of kidney function in the ICU:
options: Sepsis reduces creatinine production, so creatinine may underestimate the severity of AKI.
Trimethoprim can raise serum creatinine without reducing the glomerular filtration rate.
A large positive fluid balance tends to raise serum creatinine concentration.
Creatinine rises within 2 hours of a tubular injury.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – reduced muscle perfusion and production in sepsis blunt the creatinine rise.
- B (True) – trimethoprim (and cimetidine) inhibits tubular creatinine secretion.
- C (False) – fluid overload dilutes creatinine and can mask AKI; correction for fluid balance is advised.
- D (False) – creatinine is a late marker, lagging 24–48 h; damage biomarkers rise within hours.

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012; Ostermann M, JAMA Netw Open 2020.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman had coronary artery bypass grafting 4 hours ago. Creatinine and urine output are normal, but urinary [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] is 0.9 (ng/mL)²/1000. Which action is best supported by randomised evidence?
options: Start a furosemide infusion to keep urine output > 1 mL/kg/h
Start low-dose dopamine 2 µg/kg/min
Start early haemodiafiltration
Implement the KDIGO bundle (stop nephrotoxins and ACE inhibitors, optimise haemodynamics, monitor creatinine and urine output)
Give N-acetylcysteine
questions.expl:
**Why D:** A [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] > 0.3 identifies high risk of moderate–severe AKI. In PrevAKI, applying the KDIGO bundle in biomarker-positive cardiac surgery patients reduced AKI within 72 h (55.1 vs 71.7 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – diuretics do not prevent AKI (KDIGO 1B).
- B – low-dose dopamine is recommended against (1A).
- C – there is no indication for KRT; early KRT does not improve outcome.
- E – NAC does not prevent AKI.

**Ref:** Meersch M (PrevAKI), Intensive Care Med 2017.

questions.stem: Regarding acute kidney injury biomarkers and tests:
options: [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] reflects G1 cell-cycle arrest of tubular cells.
Plasma NGAL is highly specific for kidney injury in septic patients.
Cystatin C is a marker of glomerular filtration that is less dependent on muscle mass than creatinine.
In the furosemide stress test, a urine output of less than 200 mL in 2 hours predicts progression to KDIGO stage 3.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – both are cell-cycle arrest markers ("tubular stress"); a cut-off > 0.3 identifies high risk.
- B (False) – plasma NGAL is released by neutrophils and rises in sepsis and inflammation, so its specificity is limited.
- C (True) – a functional marker, useful in sarcopenia; affected by steroids and thyroid disease.
- D (True) – furosemide 1.0–1.5 mg/kg; < 200 mL in 2 h had ~87 % sensitivity and ~84 % specificity.

**Ref:** Kashani K, Crit Care 2013; Chawla LS, Crit Care 2013; Ostermann M, JAMA Netw Open 2020.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with septic shock is resuscitated with fluids and noradrenaline; he has KDIGO stage 1 AKI. All of the following are recommended to prevent progression of AKI EXCEPT:
options: Furosemide to convert oliguric to non-oliguric AKI
Avoiding aminoglycosides when an alternative is available
Using isotonic crystalloids rather than hydroxyethyl starch
Targeting an adequate mean arterial pressure with vasopressors
Avoiding a large positive fluid balance
questions.expl:
**Why A:** KDIGO recommends against diuretics to prevent or treat AKI (1B/2C); converting oliguria to non-oliguria improves the numbers, not the kidney. Diuretics are used only for fluid overload.

**Why not the others:**
- B – nephrotoxin avoidance is part of the KDIGO bundle.
- C – starches increase KRT (6S, CHEST); crystalloids are preferred.
- D – vasopressors with fluids are recommended in vasomotor shock (1C).
- E – fluid overload and venous congestion worsen kidney outcomes.

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012; Joannidis M, Intensive Care Med 2017.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman has severe metabolic acidaemia (pH 7.12, HCO₃⁻ 11 mmol/L, lactate 3 mmol/L) and KDIGO stage 2 AKI after abdominal sepsis. Which statement about sodium bicarbonate is best supported by the BICARICU-2 trial (2025)?
options: It significantly reduced day-90 mortality in the whole trial population
It did not reduce day-90 mortality
It reduced day-28 mortality from 63 % to 46 %
It is contraindicated in AKI
It increased mortality because of hypernatraemia
questions.expl:
**Why B:** BICARICU-2 randomised 640 ICU patients with severe metabolic acidaemia and moderate–severe AKI; day-90 mortality was 62.1 % with bicarbonate vs 61.7 % without. The hypothesis generated by the BICAR-ICU subgroup was not confirmed.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the primary end point was neutral (absolute difference 0.4 percentage points, P = .91).
- C – 46 vs 63 % was the AKIN 2–3 stratum of BICAR-ICU (2018), not BICARICU-2.
- D – bicarbonate is not contraindicated; it may still be used for selected indications.
- E – no excess mortality was found.

**Ref:** Jaber S (BICARICU-2), JAMA 2025; Jaber S (BICAR-ICU), Lancet 2018.

questions.stem: Regarding the KDIGO definition and timeline of acute kidney injury:
options: A creatinine rise of 26.5 µmol/L (0.3 mg/dL) within 48 hours is sufficient to diagnose AKI.
Starting kidney replacement therapy automatically classifies the patient as stage 3.
Acute kidney disease describes kidney dysfunction persisting between 7 and 90 days.
Anuria for 6 hours is a stage 3 criterion.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – the AKIN-derived absolute criterion.
- B (True) – initiation of KRT is a stage 3 criterion regardless of creatinine.
- C (True) – AKD bridges AKI (≤ 7 days) and CKD (> 90 days).
- D (False) – stage 3 requires anuria ≥ 12 h (or UO < 0.3 mL/kg/h for ≥ 24 h).

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man develops AKI on day 3 after emergency laparotomy for perforated diverticulitis. His intra-abdominal pressure is 24 mmHg, MAP 70 mmHg and CVP 14 mmHg. Which mechanism most directly explains the falling urine output?
options: Acute interstitial nephritis from piperacillin–tazobactam
Reduced renal perfusion pressure and venous congestion due to intra-abdominal hypertension
Obstruction of the ureters by the drains
Contrast-associated nephropathy
Glomerular hyperfiltration
questions.expl:
**Why B:** IAP 24 mmHg is grade III intra-abdominal hypertension. Renal perfusion pressure ≈ MAP − IAP (here ~46 mmHg), and raised renal venous pressure and parenchymal compression reduce GFR; oliguria is an early sign of abdominal compartment syndrome.

**Why not the others:**
- A – AIN is possible with β-lactams but does not fit the clear haemodynamic picture.
- C – ureteric obstruction by drains is rare; ultrasound would exclude it.
- D – no contrast exposure is mentioned.
- E – hyperfiltration raises, not lowers, GFR.

**Ref:** Joannidis M, Intensive Care Med 2017.

questions.stem: Regarding the pathophysiology of AKI in the critically ill:
options: In septic AKI, total renal blood flow is often preserved or even increased.
The outer medulla is particularly vulnerable to ischaemia because of its low tissue oxygen tension.
A fractional excretion of sodium < 1 % reliably distinguishes pre-renal from intrinsic AKI in ICU patients on diuretics.
Extensive tubular necrosis is the typical histological finding in septic AKI.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – septic AKI is driven by microcirculatory dysfunction, inflammation and tubular metabolic adaptation rather than global ischaemia.
- B (True) – the S3 segment and thick ascending limb work in a low-PO₂ environment.
- C (False) – urinary indices are unreliable in the ICU, especially with diuretics and sepsis.
- D (False) – histology usually shows patchy, mild changes with little necrosis.

**Ref:** Joannidis M, Intensive Care Med 2017; KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman (45 kg, sarcopenic) has a creatinine of 70 µmol/L on day 4 of septic shock, unchanged from admission, but her urine output has been 0.25 mL/kg/h for 26 hours. What is the most accurate interpretation?
options: Stage 3 AKI by urine-output criteria; creatinine underestimates the injury
Stage 1 AKI
No AKI, because creatinine is normal
Pre-renal state only – AKI cannot be diagnosed on urine output
Stage 2 AKI
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Urine output < 0.3 mL/kg/h for ≥ 24 h meets stage 3. In low muscle mass and sepsis creatinine production is reduced, so a "normal" creatinine is falsely reassuring.

**Why not the others:**
- B – the urine output criterion gives a higher stage; the highest stage applies.
- C – urine output criteria alone define AKI.
- D – oliguria is a full KDIGO criterion and carries excess mortality.
- E – stage 2 is < 0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥ 12 h; she exceeds it.

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is discharged from the ICU after septic shock with KDIGO stage 3 AKI that did not require dialysis; creatinine at discharge is 140 µmol/L (baseline 85). What does KDIGO recommend for follow-up?
options: No follow-up because he did not need dialysis
Lifelong avoidance of all RAAS inhibitors
Routine kidney biopsy at 4 weeks
Repeat creatinine only if symptoms develop
Evaluation at 3 months for resolution, new or worsening chronic kidney disease
questions.expl:
**Why E:** AKI survivors are at markedly increased risk of CKD, ESKD and cardiovascular events. KDIGO recommends evaluation 3 months after AKI; the 2026 draft extends follow-up recommendations for acute kidney disease.

**Why not the others:**
- A – risk of CKD is increased even without KRT.
- B – RAAS inhibitors are restarted when the patient is stable, as indicated (e.g. heart failure, proteinuria).
- C – biopsy is reserved for suspected intrinsic renal disease.
- D – CKD is usually asymptomatic.

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012; KDIGO 2026 AKI/AKD draft.

open.q: Define AKI according to KDIGO and list the staging criteria. What are the limitations of serum creatinine in critically ill patients?
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **Definition:** SCr ↑ ≥ 0.3 mg/dL (26.5 µmol/L) in 48 h, or ≥ 1.5 × baseline within 7 days, or UO < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h.
- **Stages:** 1 = 1.5–1.9 × or ≥ 0.3 mg/dL, UO < 0.5 for 6–12 h; 2 = 2.0–2.9 ×, UO < 0.5 for ≥ 12 h; 3 = ≥ 3 ×, SCr ≥ 4.0 mg/dL (354 µmol/L), KRT, UO < 0.3 for ≥ 24 h or anuria ≥ 12 h; highest criterion applies. AKD 7–90 days, CKD > 90 days.
- **Limitations:** late and functional (lag 24–48 h, > 50 % GFR loss), non-steady state; reduced production (sepsis, sarcopenia, liver disease); dilution by fluid overload; assay interference (ketones, flucytosine); drugs blocking secretion (trimethoprim, cimetidine); unknown baseline.
- **Alternatives:** urine output, cystatin C, measured clearance, damage biomarkers ([TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7], NGAL) – subclinical AKI (ADQI), integrated in the KDIGO 2026 draft.

open.q: Describe the evidence-based measures to prevent AKI or its progression in a high-risk ICU patient.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Identify risk: clinical risk factors, e-alerts, damage biomarkers ([TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] > 0.3) and implement the **KDIGO bundle** (PrevAKI: AKI 55.1 vs 71.7 %).
- Haemodynamics: individualised MAP ≥ 65 mmHg (higher in chronic hypertension), functional assessment of fluid responsiveness, avoid venous congestion and fluid overload; treat intra-abdominal hypertension.
- Fluids: isotonic, preferably balanced crystalloids; avoid starches (and gelatins).
- Nephrotoxins: avoid/stop NSAIDs, aminoglycosides (or once daily with levels), vancomycin levels/AUC dosing, lipid amphotericin, minimise contrast; pause ACEi/ARB for 48 h after high-risk surgery.
- Glycaemic control (avoid hyperglycaemia), adequate protein (no restriction).
- Not effective: diuretics (except fluid overload), low-dose dopamine, fenoldopam, ANP, NAC; bicarbonate does not improve survival (BICARICU-2).

title: W18 · D2 – Timing of kidney replacement therapy: STARRT-AKI, AKIKI, AKIKI 2, ELAIN, IDEAL-ICU

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with septic shock from pneumonia has KDIGO stage 3 AKI (creatinine 3.4 × baseline, urine output 0.2 mL/kg/h for 18 h). K⁺ is 5.2 mmol/L, pH 7.31, PaO₂/FiO₂ 260; he is on noradrenaline 0.2 µg/kg/min. What is the most appropriate approach to kidney replacement therapy?
options: Start CRRT within 6 hours because he has stage 3 AKI
Start intermittent haemodialysis immediately to clear inflammatory mediators
Start CRRT when urea exceeds 20 mmol/L
Start high-volume haemofiltration at 70 mL/kg/h
Watchful waiting with close monitoring, starting KRT if an urgent indication or prolonged oligo-anuria develops
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Without an urgent indication, accelerated KRT did not reduce mortality in AKIKI, IDEAL-ICU or STARRT-AKI and increased adverse events and KRT dependence. About 40–50 % of patients in delayed arms never needed KRT.

**Why not the others:**
- A – stage 3 alone is not an indication (AKIKI: 48.5 vs 49.7 %).
- B – removal of mediators is not proven and IHD is poorly tolerated in shock.
- C – a single urea threshold of 20 mmol/L is not an indication; AKIKI used BUN > 112 mg/dL (urea > 40 mmol/L).
- D – high-volume haemofiltration did not improve survival in septic shock (IVOIRE).

**Ref:** Bagshaw SM (STARRT-AKI), N Engl J Med 2020; Gaudry S (AKIKI), N Engl J Med 2016.

questions.stem: Regarding the STARRT-AKI trial (2020):
options: More than 2,900 patients were included in the analysis.
Accelerated KRT reduced 90-day mortality compared with the standard strategy.
Dependence on KRT at 90 days was more frequent in the accelerated group.
All patients in the standard arm eventually received KRT.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 3,019 randomised, 2,927 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis.
- B (False) – 43.9 vs 43.7 % (RR 1.00).
- C (True) – 10.4 vs 6.0 %; adverse events were also more frequent (23.0 vs 16.5 %).
- D (False) – 38 % of the standard arm never received KRT.

**Ref:** Bagshaw SM, N Engl J Med 2020.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has been anuric for 80 hours with septic AKI. Her urea is 46 mmol/L (BUN ≈ 129 mg/dL), K⁺ 5.6 mmol/L and pH 7.24; she is haemodynamically stable on low-dose noradrenaline. According to AKIKI 2, what is the best decision?
options: Wait until urea exceeds 50 mmol/L (BUN 140 mg/dL) or K⁺ > 6 develops
Start KRT now
Give furosemide 250 mg to induce diuresis and avoid KRT
Start KRT only if she develops pericarditis
Give sodium bicarbonate and reassess in 72 hours
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In AKIKI 2, among patients with oliguria > 72 h or BUN > 112 mg/dL, further postponement ("more-delayed", until mandatory criteria) did not increase KRT-free days and was associated with higher 60-day mortality (55 vs 44 %, adjusted HR 1.65).

**Why not the others:**
- A – this is the "more-delayed" strategy that appeared harmful.
- C – diuretics do not treat AKI or avoid KRT (KDIGO 2C).
- D – waiting for uraemic complications is unsafe.
- E – BICARICU-2 showed no mortality benefit of bicarbonate, and a further 72 h delay is too long.

**Ref:** Gaudry S (AKIKI 2), Lancet 2021.

questions.stem: Regarding randomised trials of KRT timing:
options: In AKIKI, about half of the patients in the delayed group never received KRT.
ELAIN was a large multicentre trial in medical septic patients.
IDEAL-ICU compared early KRT with a strategy of delaying KRT for 7 days.
In AKIKI, catheter-related bloodstream infections were less frequent with the early strategy.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 49 % of the delayed group avoided KRT.
- B (False) – ELAIN was single-centre (n = 231), mostly cardiac surgery patients at KDIGO stage 2 with raised NGAL.
- C (False) – the delayed arm waited 48 h (septic shock, RIFLE "failure"); 90-day mortality 58 vs 54 %; stopped for futility.
- D (False) – they were more frequent with early KRT (10 vs 5 %).

**Ref:** Gaudry S, N Engl J Med 2016; Zarbock A, JAMA 2016; Barbar SD, N Engl J Med 2018.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with stage 3 AKI after aortic surgery has K⁺ 5.8 mmol/L, pH 7.27, urine output 0.3 mL/kg/h for 20 h and stable haemodynamics. Which of the following would be an ABSOLUTE indication to start KRT now?
options: Serum creatinine of 400 µmol/L
Positive [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] test
Pulmonary oedema with PaO₂/FiO₂ 150 not responding to furosemide
Urea 25 mmol/L
KDIGO stage 3 by creatinine criteria
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Diuretic-resistant fluid overload with hypoxaemia (STARRT-AKI used PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 200) is a conventional indication. Others are K⁺ ≥ 6 mmol/L, pH ≤ 7.20 with HCO₃⁻ ≤ 12 mmol/L and uraemic complications.

**Why not the others:**
- A – a creatinine value alone is not an indication.
- B – biomarkers predict risk but have not been shown to improve outcome as triggers.
- D – urea 25 mmol/L is below AKIKI criteria (> 40 mmol/L).
- E – stage 3 alone did not justify early KRT (AKIKI, STARRT-AKI).

**Ref:** Bagshaw SM, N Engl J Med 2020; KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has been on CRRT for 9 days for septic AKI. Shock has resolved. Her urine output over the last 24 hours, without diuretics, was 650 mL. Which statement best guides discontinuation of KRT?
options: KRT must continue until creatinine normalises
Furosemide infusion should be started to hasten renal recovery
Urine output cannot be used while on CRRT
Spontaneous urine output above about 400–500 mL/day without diuretics predicts successful discontinuation
Discontinuation should only be attempted after 21 days
questions.expl:
**Why D:** In BEST Kidney, urine output > 436 mL/day without diuretics was the strongest predictor of successful cessation of CRRT; the threshold is much higher (~2,300 mL/day) if diuretics are given.

**Why not the others:**
- A – creatinine is cleared by CRRT and lags; full normalisation is not required.
- B – KDIGO suggests not using diuretics to enhance kidney recovery or shorten KRT (2B).
- C – urine output is the main clinical marker of native recovery during CRRT.
- E – there is no minimum duration.

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012.

questions.stem: Regarding potential harms associated with KRT in critically ill patients:
options: Hypophosphataemia is a frequent complication of continuous KRT.
KRT can remove antibiotics and lead to underdosing.
Intradialytic hypotension may delay renal recovery.
Hypothermia and hypomagnesaemia can occur during continuous KRT.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – phosphate is removed effectively; replacement fluids with phosphate are used.
- B (True) – hydrophilic, low-protein-bound drugs (β-lactams, vancomycin) are cleared – dose by effluent rate and levels.
- C (True) – repeated ischaemic hits are a proposed reason for higher KRT dependence after accelerated KRT in STARRT-AKI.
- D (True) – extracorporeal heat loss (may mask fever) and loss of magnesium, especially with citrate, are common.

**Ref:** Bagshaw SM, N Engl J Med 2020; Gaudry S, N Engl J Med 2016.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is admitted after a cardiac arrest from hyperkalaemia (K⁺ 8.2 mmol/L) and has anuric AKI. ROSC was achieved after calcium, insulin–glucose and bicarbonate. Repeat K⁺ is 6.9 mmol/L with peaked T waves. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Emergency haemodialysis
Repeat insulin–glucose every 4 hours and wait for urine output
Oral calcium polystyrene sulphonate and reassess tomorrow
Watchful waiting according to STARRT-AKI
Furosemide 40 mg IV
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Refractory life-threatening hyperkalaemia in anuric AKI is an emergency indication for KRT; intermittent haemodialysis removes potassium fastest. Medical therapy only shifts K⁺ temporarily.

**Why not the others:**
- B – insulin–glucose is a temporising shift, effective for only 4–6 h.
- C – resins act slowly (hours to days) and are not suitable for emergencies.
- D – STARRT-AKI excluded patients with urgent indications such as K⁺ ≥ 6.0.
- E – an anuric kidney does not respond to diuretics.

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012; Bagshaw SM, N Engl J Med 2020.

questions.stem: Regarding the 2020 individual patient data meta-analysis of KRT timing (Gaudry, Lancet):
options: It included 10 randomised trials with more than 2,000 patients.
It showed that early KRT reduces 28-day mortality.
It identified a subgroup (cardiac surgery) with a clear survival benefit from early KRT.
It found that the delayed strategy reduced exposure to KRT.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 10 RCTs, 2,143 patients.
- B (False) – 28-day mortality 44 vs 43 % (RR 1.01).
- C (False) – no subgroup showed a benefit of early initiation.
- D (True) – many patients randomised to the delayed strategy never needed KRT.

**Ref:** Gaudry S, Lancet 2020.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with bipolar disorder is admitted with confusion and coarse tremor; serum lithium is 4.6 mmol/L and creatinine 280 µmol/L (baseline 80). Which is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Activated charcoal and observation
Forced diuresis with furosemide
Intermittent haemodialysis
CVVH at 20 mL/kg/h only if lithium rises above 8 mmol/L
Wait for AKIKI criteria before KRT
questions.expl:
**Why C:** EXTRIP recommends extracorporeal treatment for lithium > 4.0 mmol/L with impaired kidney function, or for reduced consciousness, seizures or life-threatening dysrhythmias at any level; intermittent haemodialysis is preferred. Dialysable intoxication is an urgent KRT indication.

**Why not the others:**
- A – charcoal does not bind lithium.
- B – forced diuresis is ineffective and may worsen AKI; give isotonic saline.
- D – a low-dose CRRT is less efficient and the threshold is wrong.
- E – timing trials excluded urgent indications such as intoxications.

**Ref:** Decker BS (EXTRIP), Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2015.

questions.stem: Early KRT reduced 90-day mortality in the ELAIN trial but not in AKIKI, IDEAL-ICU or STARRT-AKI. Which feature of ELAIN best explains why its result (lower mortality with early KRT) differed from later trials?
options: It used intermittent haemodialysis only
It enrolled only patients with chronic kidney disease
It started KRT at KDIGO stage 3 in both arms
It was a multicentre trial with 3,000 patients
It was a single-centre trial, mostly in cardiac surgery patients, starting at KDIGO stage 2
questions.expl:
**Why E:** ELAIN (n = 231) was single-centre, predominantly post-cardiac-surgery, enriched by NGAL > 150 ng/mL and started early KRT within 8 h of stage 2 – a different population and a fragile effect size (39.3 vs 54.7 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – ELAIN used CVVHDF.
- B – patients with advanced CKD were excluded.
- C – the early arm started at stage 2; the delayed arm within 12 h of stage 3.
- D – that describes STARRT-AKI.

**Ref:** Zarbock A (ELAIN), JAMA 2016.

open.q: Summarise the evidence on the timing of KRT initiation in critically ill patients with severe AKI and give a practical approach.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **Trials:** ELAIN (single centre, cardiac surgery, early benefit 39.3 vs 54.7 %); AKIKI (stage 3, 48.5 vs 49.7 %, 49 % of delayed never needed KRT, more CRBSI with early); IDEAL-ICU (septic shock, 58 vs 54 %); STARRT-AKI (n ≈ 3,000, 43.9 vs 43.7 %, more KRT dependence 10.4 vs 6.0 % and adverse events with accelerated); IPD meta-analysis (2,143 patients, RR 1.01); AKIKI 2 (more-delayed waiting harmful: 55 vs 44 %).
- **Approach:** start emergently for urgent indications (refractory K⁺ ≥ 6, pH ≤ 7.15–7.20, diuretic-resistant fluid overload with hypoxaemia, uraemic complications, dialysable toxins); otherwise watchful waiting with close monitoring; do not postpone beyond oliguria > 72 h/BUN > 112 mg/dL; individualise on trajectory, demand–capacity mismatch and goals of care.
- **Harms of KRT:** catheter infection, hypotension, electrolyte loss, drug removal, bleeding/anticoagulation, cost.

title: W18 · D3 – Kidney replacement therapy: modalities, dose, vascular access and citrate anticoagulation

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with traumatic brain injury (ICP monitor, ICP 22 mmHg) develops rhabdomyolysis-associated anuric AKI requiring KRT. Which modality is most appropriate?
options: Intermittent haemodialysis, 4-hour sessions with high dialysate flow
Continuous kidney replacement therapy
Peritoneal dialysis
Slow continuous ultrafiltration (SCUF) only
Daily sustained low-efficiency dialysis with high-efficiency membrane
questions.expl:
**Why B:** KDIGO suggests CRRT rather than intermittent therapy in patients with acute brain injury or raised ICP (2B). Gradual solute removal avoids the rapid fall in plasma osmolality that drives water into brain cells (dialysis disequilibrium).

**Why not the others:**
- A – rapid urea clearance with IHD can raise ICP.
- C – PD is inefficient and poorly controllable in a hypercatabolic trauma patient.
- D – SCUF removes fluid but provides negligible solute clearance.
- E – SLED is a reasonable compromise elsewhere, but continuous therapy gives the most stable osmolality.

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012.

questions.stem: Regarding the physical principles of kidney replacement therapy:
options: Diffusion is more efficient than convection at removing middle molecules such as β₂-microglobulin.
Predilution replacement fluid reduces the clearance achieved for a given effluent rate.
In postdilution haemofiltration, the filtration fraction should be kept below about 20–25 %.
Convection requires a replacement (substitution) fluid to maintain volume.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – convection (solvent drag) clears middle molecules better; diffusion favours small solutes.
- B (True) – blood is diluted before the filter, so solute concentration in the ultrafiltrate falls (~15–20 % loss of efficiency).
- C (True) – higher filtration fraction haemoconcentrates blood in the filter and causes clotting.
- D (True) – large ultrafiltrate volumes must be replaced; net removal is the difference.

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012.

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient is started on CVVHDF for septic AKI. Which prescription best follows KDIGO recommendations on dose?
options: Prescribe 25–30 mL/kg/h effluent so that the delivered dose is 20–25 mL/kg/h
Prescribe 40 mL/kg/h to improve survival
Prescribe 70 mL/kg/h (high-volume haemofiltration) for septic shock
Prescribe 15 mL/kg/h to protect residual renal function
Dose is irrelevant as long as urea falls
questions.expl:
**Why A:** KDIGO recommends a delivered effluent of 20–25 mL/kg/h (1A). Because of downtime and predilution, a somewhat higher prescription is usually needed, and the delivered dose should be monitored.

**Why not the others:**
- B – RENAL: 40 vs 25 mL/kg/h, 90-day mortality 44.7 vs 44.7 %.
- C – IVOIRE: 70 vs 35 mL/kg/h, no benefit.
- D – underdosing risks inadequate control of solutes and acidosis.
- E – delivered dose matters for K⁺, acid–base and drug dosing.

**Ref:** Bellomo R (RENAL), N Engl J Med 2009; Palevsky PM (ATN), N Engl J Med 2008.

questions.stem: Regarding regional citrate anticoagulation during CRRT:
options: Citrate chelates ionised calcium, which is required for the coagulation cascade.
The target post-filter ionised calcium is about 1.0–1.2 mmol/L.
Metabolism of one citrate molecule generates three bicarbonate molecules.
Severe liver failure is an absolute contraindication to citrate.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – the circuit is anticoagulated; systemic iCa is restored by calcium infusion.
- B (False) – post-filter iCa is targeted at 0.25–0.35 mmol/L; 1.0–1.2 mmol/L is the systemic target.
- C (True) – citrate acts as a buffer; replacement fluids therefore contain less bicarbonate.
- D (False) – it is a relative contraindication; citrate can be used at lower doses with close monitoring of the total/ionised Ca ratio.

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012; Zarbock A (RICH), JAMA 2020.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with alcoholic hepatitis and septic shock (lactate 9 mmol/L) is on CVVHDF with citrate. Over 12 hours, systemic ionised calcium falls to 0.85 mmol/L despite increasing calcium infusion; total calcium is 3.1 mmol/L; anion gap is 22 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Citrate overdose with metabolic alkalosis
Filter clotting
Hypoparathyroidism
Citrate accumulation due to impaired metabolism
Laboratory error
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Total/ionised Ca ratio = 3.1/0.85 ≈ 3.6 (> 2.5), falling iCa despite more calcium and a high-anion-gap acidosis indicate that citrate is not being metabolised (liver failure, shock with high lactate). Reduce or stop citrate and change anticoagulation.

**Why not the others:**
- A – excess citrate delivery with normal metabolism causes metabolic **alkalosis**, not acidosis with a high Ca ratio.
- B – clotting does not lower systemic iCa or widen the anion gap.
- C – hypoparathyroidism would not raise total calcium.
- E – the pattern is internally consistent.

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman needs CRRT; she has no bleeding risk and no history of HIT. Which statement about the RICH trial (2020) comparing citrate with systemic heparin is correct?
options: Citrate reduced 90-day mortality by 10 %
Heparin prolonged filter life
Bleeding complications were more frequent with citrate
Infections were less frequent with citrate
Citrate prolonged filter life (47 vs 26 h) without a difference in 90-day mortality
questions.expl:
**Why E:** RICH (n = 638, stopped early) showed median filter life 47 vs 26 h and 90-day mortality 51.2 vs 53.6 % (not significant), with less bleeding (5.1 vs 16.9 %). Citrate is therefore the default anticoagulant for CRRT.

**Why not the others:**
- A – mortality was not significantly different.
- B – citrate, not heparin, prolonged filter life.
- C – bleeding was less frequent with citrate.
- D – new infections were more frequent with citrate (68.0 vs 55.4 %).

**Ref:** Zarbock A (RICH), JAMA 2020.

questions.stem: Regarding vascular access for KRT in the ICU (KDIGO):
options: The left internal jugular vein is the preferred first site.
The subclavian vein is preferred because of the lowest infection risk.
Antibiotic lock solutions are recommended for non-tunnelled dialysis catheters.
A 15-cm catheter is typically adequate in the femoral vein.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – the right internal jugular is first; then femoral, then left jugular.
- B (False) – the subclavian is last because of central venous stenosis that compromises future fistulas.
- C (False) – KDIGO suggests against antibiotic locks (and topical antibiotics) for non-tunnelled catheters (2C).
- D (False) – femoral catheters should be 20–25 cm (tip in the IVC); 15–16 cm suits the right IJ.

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man on CVVHDF with heparin develops a platelet fall from 240 to 80 × 10⁹/L on day 7, with a new femoral vein thrombosis; the 4T score is 7. What is the most appropriate anticoagulation?
options: Stop heparin, use citrate for the circuit only
Switch to enoxaparin
Stop all heparin and start argatroban
Continue heparin and transfuse platelets
Run CRRT without anticoagulation
questions.expl:
**Why C:** High pre-test probability HIT with thrombosis requires stopping all heparin (including flushes) and therapeutic non-heparin anticoagulation, e.g. argatroban (hepatic clearance – suitable in AKI). Argatroban can also anticoagulate the circuit.

**Why not the others:**
- A – citrate anticoagulates the circuit but does not treat the systemic HIT-associated thrombosis.
- B – LMWH cross-reacts with HIT antibodies.
- D – heparin continuation and prophylactic platelet transfusion worsen thrombosis.
- E – no anticoagulation ignores the patient's thrombosis.

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012.

questions.stem: Regarding continuous vs intermittent kidney replacement therapy:
options: In the Hemodiafe trial, survival was similar with IHD and CVVHDF in patients with multiple organ dysfunction.
Intermittent haemodialysis lowers serum potassium faster than CRRT.
KDIGO recommends CRRT as the default for all critically ill patients.
Lactate rather than bicarbonate is the preferred buffer for patients in shock.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 60-day survival 31.5 vs 32.6 % with haemodynamic precautions for IHD.
- B (True) – high dialysate and blood flows give fast K⁺ removal, making IHD the choice for life-threatening hyperkalaemia.
- C (False) – CRRT and IHD are complementary; CRRT is suggested for haemodynamic instability and raised ICP.
- D (False) – KDIGO recommends bicarbonate rather than lactate in shock (1B); lactate requires hepatic metabolism.

**Ref:** Vinsonneau C (Hemodiafe), Lancet 2006; KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man on CVVHDF (effluent 30 mL/kg/h) for septic AKI is receiving meropenem. Cultures remain positive on day 3. Which principle of antibiotic dosing during CRRT is correct?
options: Loading doses should be halved during CRRT
Meropenem is not removed by CRRT because it is a small molecule
Doses should follow the anuric (end-stage kidney disease) recommendations
Maintenance doses should account for effluent rate and be guided by therapeutic drug monitoring where available
Protein-bound drugs are removed more efficiently than unbound drugs
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Hydrophilic, low-protein-bound drugs such as β-lactams are cleared in proportion to effluent flow; dosing should be adapted to the delivered dose and checked by drug levels. Underdosing is common in the early phase.

**Why not the others:**
- A – loading depends on volume of distribution, which is unchanged or increased; full loading doses are given.
- B – small molecules are removed efficiently by both diffusion and convection.
- C – anuric dosing ignores extracorporeal clearance and risks underdosing.
- E – only the unbound fraction passes the membrane.

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman on CVVHDF with citrate develops pH 7.53, HCO₃⁻ 35 mmol/L, normal anion gap, normal lactate and a total/ionised calcium ratio of 2.0. Her blood flow was recently increased. What is the most likely cause?
options: Citrate accumulation from liver failure
Excess citrate (buffer) load relative to its removal
Hypoventilation
Contraction alkalosis from diuretics
Inadequate dialysate flow causing acidosis
questions.expl:
**Why B:** With normal metabolism, every citrate becomes three bicarbonates; increasing blood flow (and hence citrate dose) without increasing dialysate/effluent flow causes metabolic alkalosis. Correct by reducing blood flow/citrate or increasing dialysate flow.

**Why not the others:**
- A – accumulation causes a high Ca ratio (> 2.5) and high-anion-gap acidosis.
- C – hypoventilation causes respiratory acidosis.
- D – no diuretics are described; she is on CRRT.
- E – the problem is alkalosis, not acidosis.

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012.

open.q: Explain how regional citrate anticoagulation works during CRRT, how it is monitored, and how you would recognise and manage citrate accumulation.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **Mechanism:** pre-filter trisodium citrate chelates iCa²⁺ → circuit anticoagulation; post-filter iCa 0.25–0.35 mmol/L; Ca–citrate partly removed in effluent; calcium infusion restores systemic iCa 1.0–1.2 mmol/L; returned citrate metabolised (liver, muscle) to bicarbonate (3 HCO₃⁻ per citrate) – citrate is the buffer.
- **Monitoring:** post-filter and systemic iCa every 6–8 h initially, total Ca, total/ionised ratio, pH/HCO₃⁻, anion gap, Na⁺, Mg²⁺.
- **Accumulation:** risk in liver failure, shock with high lactate; signs – ratio > 2.5, falling iCa despite rising Ca infusion, high-AG metabolic acidosis; management – reduce blood flow/citrate, increase dialysate, correct Ca, consider heparin or no anticoagulation.
- **Excess load (normal metabolism):** metabolic alkalosis, hypernatraemia – reduce citrate/blood flow or increase dialysate.
- **Evidence:** KDIGO 2B (preferred for CRRT); RICH – filter life 47 vs 26 h, less bleeding, same mortality, more infections.

open.q: Compare intermittent haemodialysis and continuous KRT in the ICU and state when you would choose each.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Principles: IHD diffusion, high flows, short sessions; CRRT continuous convection/diffusion, low flows.
- IHD: fastest removal of K⁺ and dialysable toxins (lithium, methanol, salicylate), less anticoagulation, mobilisation; risks hypotension and disequilibrium.
- CRRT: haemodynamic stability, steady fluid removal, stable osmolality – preferred in shock and raised ICP/acute brain injury (KDIGO 2B), in fulminant liver failure.
- Equivalent mortality (Hemodiafe 31.5 vs 32.6 % survival); complementary; SLED as hybrid; PD in resource-limited settings.
- Dose: delivered 20–25 mL/kg/h (RENAL/ATN) or Kt/V 3.9 per week.

title: W18 · D4 – Rhabdomyolysis and contrast-associated acute kidney injury

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman is found on her floor after an estimated 36-hour "long lie". CK is 48,000 U/L, K⁺ 5.9 mmol/L, creatinine 190 µmol/L, urine dark brown; dipstick is strongly positive for blood but microscopy shows no red cells. What is the most important initial treatment?
options: Mannitol 1 g/kg IV
Isotonic crystalloid infusion titrated to a urine output of about 200–300 mL/h
Furosemide 80 mg IV to flush the tubules
Immediate high cut-off haemodiafiltration to remove myoglobin
Calcium gluconate to correct the expected hypocalcaemia
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Early, generous isotonic fluid therapy corrects hypovolaemia from muscle sequestration and increases tubular flow, reducing myoglobin cast formation. Urine output is titrated to ~200–300 mL/h while watching for fluid overload.

**Why not the others:**
- A – mannitol has no proven benefit and can cause hyperosmolality and AKI.
- C – loop diuretics acidify urine and do not prevent AKI.
- D – myoglobin removal by extracorporeal techniques is not proven; KRT is for conventional indications.
- E – asymptomatic hypocalcaemia should not be treated (calcium deposition, later hypercalcaemia).

**Ref:** Bosch X, N Engl J Med 2009.

questions.stem: Regarding the pathophysiology of rhabdomyolysis-induced AKI:
options: Myoglobin precipitates with Tamm–Horsfall protein more readily in acidic urine.
Free haem scavenges nitric oxide and promotes renal vasoconstriction.
Myoglobin is too large to be filtered by the glomerulus.
Haem iron promotes oxidative injury of proximal tubular cells.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – the basis for (unproven) urinary alkalinisation.
- B (True) – together with endothelin and hypovolaemia.
- C (False) – myoglobin (17.8 kDa) is freely filtered.
- D (True) – Fenton reaction, lipid peroxidation.

**Ref:** Bosch X, N Engl J Med 2009.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man is admitted after a 6-hour building-collapse entrapment of both legs. Six hours after extrication, his left calf is tense and painful on passive stretch. BP 130/80 mmHg; anterior compartment pressure is 58 mmHg. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Elevate the leg above heart level and repeat pressure in 4 hours
Apply compression bandages
Urgent fasciotomy
Start mannitol to reduce compartment oedema
Hyperbaric oxygen as first-line treatment
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Compartment pressure > 30 mmHg (or ΔP = diastolic BP − compartment pressure < 30 mmHg; here 80 − 58 = 22 mmHg) with clinical signs indicates acute compartment syndrome requiring urgent fasciotomy to prevent further muscle necrosis.

**Why not the others:**
- A – elevation above heart level reduces arterial inflow; delay worsens necrosis.
- B – compression increases compartment pressure.
- D – mannitol is not an alternative to decompression.
- E – hyperbaric oxygen is at most an adjunct.

**Ref:** Bosch X, N Engl J Med 2009.

questions.stem: Regarding biochemical changes in rhabdomyolysis:
options: Hypocalcaemia is typical in the early phase.
Hypercalcaemia may develop during the recovery phase.
CK usually peaks within 2 hours of muscle injury.
Hypophosphataemia is the typical early finding.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – calcium phosphate deposition in necrotic muscle.
- B (True) – mobilisation of deposited calcium and increased calcitriol, especially after AKI.
- C (False) – CK rises after 2–12 h and peaks at 24–72 h.
- D (False) – phosphate is released from muscle: hyperphosphataemia (hypophosphataemia can be a cause of rhabdomyolysis, however).

**Ref:** Bosch X, N Engl J Med 2009.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man is sedated with propofol at 5 mg/kg/h for 3 days for refractory status epilepticus and receives noradrenaline. He develops a new right bundle branch block, lactate 7 mmol/L, CK 25,000 U/L, triglycerides 6 mmol/L and K⁺ 6.2 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Propofol infusion syndrome
Malignant hyperthermia
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Septic shock with myocarditis
Exertional rhabdomyolysis from seizures alone
questions.expl:
**Why A:** High-dose (> 4 mg/kg/h) prolonged (> 48 h) propofol with catecholamines, metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hypertriglyceridaemia, hyperkalaemia and ECG changes (Brugada-like, RBBB) is typical of propofol infusion syndrome. Stop propofol immediately.

**Why not the others:**
- B – malignant hyperthermia follows volatile agents/suxamethonium, with hypercapnia and hyperthermia.
- C – NMS follows dopamine antagonists, with rigidity and hyperthermia.
- D – does not explain hypertriglyceridaemia and the drug exposure.
- E – seizure-related rhabdomyolysis does not explain lipaemia and cardiac changes.

**Ref:** Bosch X, N Engl J Med 2009.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with rhabdomyolysis after a fall (CK 30,000 U/L) has received 6 L of crystalloid. He is now anuric for 8 hours, with bilateral crackles, SpO₂ 90 % on 6 L/min O₂ and K⁺ 6.6 mmol/L. All of the following are appropriate EXCEPT:
options: Calcium chloride IV if the ECG shows hyperkalaemic changes
Insulin–glucose to shift potassium
Starting kidney replacement therapy
Continuing aggressive fluid loading to reach 300 mL/h urine output
Stopping further fluid boluses
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Once the patient is oligo-anuric and fluid overloaded, aggressive fluid loading causes pulmonary oedema without restoring diuresis. Fluids should be stopped and KRT started for hyperkalaemia and overload.

**Why not the others:**
- A – calcium is indicated for hyperkalaemia with ECG changes (even though asymptomatic hypocalcaemia is otherwise not treated).
- B – shifts potassium as a bridge.
- C – refractory hyperkalaemia and diuretic-resistant overload are conventional KRT indications.
- E – correct in an anuric, overloaded patient.

**Ref:** Bosch X, N Engl J Med 2009; KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012.

questions.stem: Regarding contrast-associated and contrast-induced AKI:
options: Contrast-associated AKI implies that contrast was the cause of the AKI.
A meta-analysis of propensity-matched ICU studies showed no significant increase in AKI attributable to contrast.
Intra-arterial contrast with first-pass renal exposure carries a higher risk than intravenous contrast.
Iso-osmolar contrast is clearly superior to low-osmolar contrast in preventing AKI.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – CA-AKI is a temporal association; CI-AKI is the causal subset.
- B (True) – pooled OR 0.95 (Ehrmann, ICM 2017).
- C (True) – the threshold for prophylaxis is eGFR < 45 for intra-arterial first-pass vs < 30 for IV.
- D (False) – no clinically relevant difference between iso- and low-osmolar agents; avoid high-osmolar agents.

**Ref:** Ehrmann S, Intensive Care Med 2017; van der Molen AJ, Eur Radiol 2018.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old diabetic man with eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m² is scheduled for coronary angiography. Which prophylactic strategy is supported by the PRESERVE trial?
options: IV sodium bicarbonate rather than IV saline
Oral N-acetylcysteine 1,200 mg twice daily
Prophylactic haemofiltration after the procedure
Theophylline before contrast
IV isotonic saline; neither bicarbonate nor N-acetylcysteine adds benefit
questions.expl:
**Why E:** PRESERVE (n = 5,177) found no difference in death, dialysis or persistent kidney decline at 90 days between bicarbonate and saline (4.4 vs 4.7 %) or NAC and placebo (4.6 vs 4.5 %), nor in CA-AKI. Isotonic saline remains reasonable for high-risk intra-arterial procedures.

**Why not the others:**
- A – bicarbonate was not superior to saline.
- B – NAC was not better than placebo.
- C – prophylactic KRT is not recommended.
- D – theophylline is not recommended.

**Ref:** Weisbord SD (PRESERVE), N Engl J Med 2018.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man in the ICU with suspected mesenteric ischaemia has an eGFR of 25 mL/min/1.73 m² and heart failure (EF 30 %). Regarding contrast-enhanced CT angiography:
options: The CT should be delayed until renal function improves.
Prophylactic haemodialysis should be planned immediately after the scan.
Oral N-acetylcysteine should be given before the scan.
The lowest diagnostic dose of a low- or iso-osmolar agent should be used.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – contrast should not be withheld for a life-threatening indication.
- B (False) – prophylactic or post-contrast dialysis is not recommended.
- C (False) – NAC is ineffective (PRESERVE).
- D (True) – minimise dose; IV saline is indicated at eGFR < 30 but should be cautious or omitted with heart failure.

**Ref:** Davenport MS (ACR–NKF), Radiology 2020; Weisbord SD, N Engl J Med 2018.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m² needs an outpatient contrast-enhanced CT. Which statement is best supported by the AMACING trial?
options: Withholding prophylactic IV hydration is non-inferior to guideline hydration
IV hydration halves the risk of contrast-associated AKI
Oral NAC is required
Contrast is contraindicated at this eGFR
Haemodialysis should be available after the CT
questions.expl:
**Why A:** In AMACING (n = 660, eGFR 30–59), CA-AKI occurred in 2.7 % without prophylaxis vs 2.6 % with IV hydration; no prophylaxis was non-inferior and avoided hydration complications (heart failure ~5 %) and costs. ACR–NKF: prophylaxis not needed for eGFR ≥ 45.

**Why not the others:**
- B – no difference was shown.
- C – NAC is ineffective.
- D – eGFR 52 is not a contraindication.
- E – no need for dialysis planning.

**Ref:** Nijssen EC (AMACING), Lancet 2017; Davenport MS, Radiology 2020.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with KDIGO stage 2 AKI and suspected aortic dissection needs urgent imaging. She takes metformin. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Delay CT angiography for 72 hours and hydrate first
Use MRI with a linear (group I) gadolinium agent to avoid iodinated contrast
Perform CT angiography now and withhold metformin, rechecking renal function at 48 h
Perform CT angiography and start prophylactic haemodialysis
Give sodium bicarbonate infusion for 6 h before CT
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Life-threatening conditions must not wait for contrast prophylaxis. In AKI (or eGFR < 30), metformin is stopped at the time of contrast and restarted when renal function is confirmed stable after 48 h, because of the risk of metformin accumulation and lactic acidosis.

**Why not the others:**
- A – delaying diagnosis of dissection is dangerous.
- B – linear (group I) gadolinium agents carry the highest risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in AKI and MRI is slower.
- D – prophylactic dialysis is not recommended.
- E – bicarbonate is not superior to saline and delays imaging.

**Ref:** van der Molen AJ (ESUR), Eur Radiol 2018; Davenport MS, Radiology 2020.

open.q: A 30-year-old man is extricated after 8 hours under rubble. Outline the ICU management of crush-related rhabdomyolysis.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **Early fluids** (ideally before/at extrication): isotonic crystalloid 1–2 L/h initially, then titrate to UO ~200–300 mL/h (≈ 3 mL/kg/h) until myoglobinuria clears/CK < 5,000; stop in oligo-anuria/overload.
- **Monitoring:** hourly UO (catheter), CK (peak 24–72 h), K⁺, Ca²⁺, PO₄³⁻, pH, creatinine, coagulation (DIC), compartment pressures.
- **Hyperkalaemia:** ECG, calcium if ECG changes, insulin–glucose, salbutamol; avoid suxamethonium; KRT if refractory.
- **Calcium:** do not treat asymptomatic early hypocalcaemia; watch for late hypercalcaemia.
- **Bicarbonate/mannitol:** no proven benefit; bicarbonate only for severe acidosis/hyperkalaemia.
- **Compartment syndrome:** pressure > 30 mmHg or ΔP < 30 mmHg → fasciotomy; wound/limb care, tetanus, infection.
- **KRT** for conventional indications (IHD for rapid K⁺ removal; CRRT if unstable); myoglobin removal not proven.
- **Risk stratification:** McMahon score; look for cause (drugs, toxins, hyperthermia).

title: W18 · D5 – Hyperkalaemia and urgent dialysis indications

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man on ramipril and spironolactone presents with weakness. K⁺ is 7.4 mmol/L; the ECG shows absent P waves and QRS 160 ms; heart rate 42/min. What is the first drug to give?
options: Sodium bicarbonate 8.4 % 100 mL
Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10 g orally
Furosemide 80 mg IV
10 mL 10 % calcium chloride IV
Atropine 3 mg IV
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes requires immediate membrane stabilisation: 10 mL 10 % calcium chloride (or 30 mL 10 % calcium gluconate). It acts within minutes but does not lower K⁺, so insulin–glucose and salbutamol follow at once.

**Why not the others:**
- A – bicarbonate is not routine; reserved for arrest or severe acidosis.
- B – SZC takes ~1 h; it is a removal step, not an emergency stabiliser.
- C – diuretics are slow and depend on kidney function.
- E – the bradycardia is caused by hyperkalaemia; treat the cause first.

**Ref:** Lott C (ERC), Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding the drugs used to treat acute hyperkalaemia:
options: Calcium chloride lowers the serum potassium concentration by about 1 mmol/L.
Insulin with glucose lowers potassium within 15–30 minutes and the effect lasts about 4–6 hours.
Nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg has an effect additive to insulin–glucose.
Hypoglycaemia after insulin–glucose occurs mainly in the first 10 minutes.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – calcium stabilises the myocardium without changing K⁺.
- B (True) – lowers K⁺ by ~0.6–1.0 mmol/L.
- C (True) – both stimulate Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; together ~1.2–1.5 mmol/L.
- D (False) – hypoglycaemia occurs later (1–6 h) as glucose is consumed; monitor for at least 6 h and give 10 % glucose if baseline < 7 mmol/L.

**Ref:** Lott C (ERC), Resuscitation 2025; Lindner G, Eur J Emerg Med 2020.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman with myelofibrosis (platelets 1,400 × 10⁹/L) has a laboratory serum K⁺ of 6.8 mmol/L; she is asymptomatic and her ECG is normal. Creatinine is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Calcium gluconate and insulin–glucose immediately
Measure potassium on a whole-blood sample with a blood gas analyser
Emergency haemodialysis
Start patiromer
Stop all medications
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Extreme thrombocytosis releases K⁺ from platelets during clotting (pseudohyperkalaemia). A heparinised whole-blood or plasma sample analysed promptly gives the true value; treatment of a spurious result causes hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia.

**Why not the others:**
- A – no ECG changes and suspected artefact; confirm first.
- C – no indication.
- D – potassium binders are unnecessary if the value is spurious.
- E – non-specific and unhelpful.

**Ref:** Lindner G, Eur J Emerg Med 2020.

questions.stem: Regarding drugs and situations causing hyperkalaemia in ICU patients:
options: Trimethoprim blocks the epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct.
Unfractionated heparin can suppress aldosterone production.
Suxamethonium is safe in a patient with 40 % burns on day 5.
β₂-agonists cause hyperkalaemia.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – an amiloride-like effect reduces K⁺ secretion.
- B (True) – even at prophylactic doses, especially with AKI or RAAS inhibitors.
- C (False) – up-regulated extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors after 24–72 h cause massive K⁺ release.
- D (False) – β₂-agonists shift K⁺ into cells (used therapeutically); β-blockers can raise K⁺.

**Ref:** Lindner G, Eur J Emerg Med 2020.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with anuric AKI after cardiac surgery has K⁺ 7.1 mmol/L and QRS widening. After calcium, insulin–glucose and salbutamol, K⁺ is 6.4 mmol/L. He is haemodynamically stable. Which treatment will lower his potassium fastest and most definitively?
options: Intermittent haemodialysis with a low-potassium dialysate
Calcium polystyrene sulphonate enemas
Fludrocortisone
CRRT at 20 mL/kg/h
Repeating insulin–glucose hourly
questions.expl:
**Why A:** IHD with high blood and dialysate flows and low-K⁺ dialysate lowers K⁺ by ~1 mmol/L in the first hour – the fastest method of removal. Recheck after a few hours because of rebound from the intracellular pool.

**Why not the others:**
- B – resins act over hours to days and risk colonic necrosis.
- C – mineralocorticoid has no rapid effect and needs functioning tubules.
- D – CRRT is slower; preferred when unstable or with continuous K⁺ release.
- E – repeated insulin only shifts K⁺ and causes hypoglycaemia.

**Ref:** Lott C (ERC), Resuscitation 2025; KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man on haemodialysis misses two sessions and arrives in cardiac arrest (PEA). Point-of-care K⁺ is 8.9 mmol/L. In addition to standard ALS, all of the following are recommended by ERC 2025 EXCEPT:
options: 10 mL 10 % calcium chloride IV
Insulin 10 units with 25 g glucose IV
Sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol IV
Considering dialysis during CPR for refractory arrest
Oral sodium zirconium cyclosilicate during CPR
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Oral binders cannot be given or act during cardiac arrest. ERC 2025 recommends calcium chloride, insulin–glucose and sodium bicarbonate (separate lines), and consideration of dialysis (or ECPR) in refractory arrest.

**Why not the others:**
- A – calcium stabilises the myocardium.
- B – shifts K⁺ intracellularly.
- C – 50 mmol bicarbonate is recommended in hyperkalaemic arrest.
- D – dialysis during CPR can be life-saving in refractory hyperkalaemic arrest.

**Ref:** Lott C (ERC), Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding potassium binders:
options: Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate begins to lower potassium within about an hour.
Patiromer acts more rapidly than sodium zirconium cyclosilicate.
Sodium polystyrene sulphonate with sorbitol has been associated with colonic necrosis.
Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate can cause oedema because of its sodium content.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – it traps K⁺ in exchange for Na⁺ and H⁺ throughout the gut; HARMONIZE showed rapid lowering within 48 h.
- B (False) – patiromer has an onset of ~7 h.
- C (True) – especially post-operatively or with ileus.
- D (True) – oedema was dose-related in HARMONIZE; caution in heart failure.

**Ref:** Kosiborod M (HARMONIZE), JAMA 2014; Lindner G, Eur J Emerg Med 2020.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman takes 40 tablets of lithium carbonate (modified release). She is drowsy with coarse tremor; serum lithium is 3.6 mmol/L at 8 h and rising; creatinine 160 µmol/L (baseline 70). What is the most appropriate management?
options: Activated charcoal 50 g
Haemodialysis
Forced diuresis with furosemide
Observation and repeat level in 24 h
Sodium bicarbonate infusion
questions.expl:
**Why B:** EXTRIP recommends extracorporeal treatment for lithium when consciousness is decreased (regardless of level) or > 4.0 mmol/L with impaired kidney function; a rising level after a modified-release overdose with AKI makes the expected time to < 1.0 mmol/L long. Lithium has low molecular weight, no protein binding and a small Vd – ideal for haemodialysis.

**Why not the others:**
- A – charcoal does not bind lithium (whole-bowel irrigation may be considered for modified-release tablets).
- C – furosemide increases lithium reabsorption and worsens AKI.
- D – delay risks neurotoxicity (SILENT syndrome).
- E – bicarbonate does not enhance lithium elimination.

**Ref:** Decker BS (EXTRIP), Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2015.

questions.stem: Regarding the properties of drugs that determine removal by haemodialysis:
options: A large volume of distribution (> 5 L/kg) favours removal.
High protein binding favours removal.
Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning is an indication for haemodialysis.
Low molecular weight favours removal.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – only drug in plasma is accessible; a Vd < 1 L/kg favours removal.
- B (False) – only the unbound fraction crosses the membrane.
- C (False) – tricyclics are highly protein bound with a large Vd; treat with bicarbonate and supportive care.
- D (True) – < 500 Da for conventional dialysis; higher for high-flux/convective therapies.

**Ref:** Decker BS (EXTRIP), Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2015.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes on metformin presents with vomiting and AKI (creatinine 450 µmol/L). pH is 6.88, lactate 22 mmol/L, and she needs noradrenaline 0.3 µg/kg/min. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Sodium bicarbonate until pH > 7.30
Insulin–dextrose infusion
Watchful waiting as in STARRT-AKI
Thiamine and observation
Kidney replacement therapy (intermittent haemodialysis or CRRT if unstable)
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Metformin-associated lactic acidosis with lactate > 20 mmol/L, pH ≤ 7.0 and shock is an EXTRIP indication for extracorporeal removal; KRT clears metformin and lactate and corrects acidosis. IHD is preferred; CRRT if haemodynamics do not allow IHD.

**Why not the others:**
- A – bicarbonate alone does not remove metformin or improve survival.
- B – insulin is not indicated.
- C – STARRT-AKI excluded patients with urgent indications such as severe acidaemia and intoxication.
- D – thiamine is reasonable if deficiency is suspected but does not treat metformin toxicity.

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012; Bagshaw SM, N Engl J Med 2020.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with stage 3 AKI (urea 52 mmol/L) has a new pericardial friction rub; echocardiography shows a small pericardial effusion without tamponade. K⁺ is 5.3 mmol/L and pH 7.28. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Pericardiocentesis
Watchful waiting until K⁺ exceeds 6.0 mmol/L
Start kidney replacement therapy
High-dose NSAIDs
Colchicine and review in 72 hours
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Uraemic pericarditis is an absolute indication for KRT, regardless of K⁺ and pH. Heparin should be minimised (risk of haemorrhagic effusion) – regional citrate is attractive.

**Why not the others:**
- A – no tamponade; drainage is for haemodynamic compromise.
- B – uraemic complications are themselves an indication; waiting risks tamponade.
- D – NSAIDs worsen AKI and bleeding.
- E – colchicine does not treat the uraemic cause.

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012.

open.q: Describe the emergency management of a patient with K⁺ 7.2 mmol/L and a wide QRS complex.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **Assess:** ABC, continuous ECG monitoring, IV access, confirm (blood gas K⁺ – exclude pseudohyperkalaemia, but do not delay treatment with ECG changes); identify cause (AKI, drugs, rhabdomyolysis, DKA).
- **Protect the heart:** 10 mL 10 % calcium chloride (or 30 mL 10 % gluconate) IV; repeat if ECG changes persist; effect 30–60 min; does not lower K⁺.
- **Shift:** insulin 10 U + 25 g glucose IV (↓ 0.6–1.0 mmol/L in 15–30 min, 4–6 h); 10 % glucose 50 mL/h for 5 h if baseline glucose < 7 mmol/L; salbutamol 10–20 mg nebulised; bicarbonate only with severe acidosis/arrest.
- **Remove:** SZC 10 g (or patiromer), loop diuretic if responsive; **dialysis** (IHD fastest) if refractory, anuric or ongoing release; expect rebound.
- **Monitor:** K⁺ at 1, 2, 4, 6 h; glucose hourly for 6 h; ECG.
- **Prevent recurrence:** stop RAAS inhibitors, K⁺-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim, K⁺ supplements; review diet/drugs.

open.q: List the indications for urgent kidney replacement therapy in a critically ill patient and the properties that make a toxin dialysable.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **Indications (AEIOU):** refractory hyperkalaemia (K⁺ ≥ 6.0–6.5 or ECG changes despite therapy); severe metabolic acidaemia (pH ≤ 7.15–7.20); diuretic-resistant fluid overload with hypoxaemia; uraemic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding); dialysable intoxication; others – severe dysnatraemia with AKI, hyperthermia, tumour lysis, hypercalcaemia, hypermagnesaemia.
- **Toxin properties:** low molecular weight (< 500 Da for HD), low protein binding, small Vd (< 1 L/kg), water soluble, low endogenous clearance.
- **Examples (EXTRIP):** lithium (> 4.0 mmol/L with impaired kidney function, or reduced consciousness/seizures/dysrhythmias), salicylates (> 7.2 mmol/L), metformin (lactate > 20, pH ≤ 7.0), toxic alcohols (with fomepizole), theophylline, phenobarbital, valproate.
- **Modality:** IHD preferred for speed; CRRT if haemodynamically unstable or raised ICP.

title: Monthly review – March (Sat 27 Mar 2027)

questions.stem: A 35-year-old with severe diffuse TBI has ICP 25 mmHg despite tier 0 and tier 1 measures: deeper sedation, head up 30°, mannitol and hypertonic saline boluses, CSF drainage via an EVD and PaCO₂ 36 mmHg. Repeat CT shows no surgical lesion. According to SIBICC, which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Hyperventilate to PaCO₂ 28 mmHg
Start a barbiturate coma
Change mannitol to a continuous infusion
Give a test dose of a neuromuscular blocker and continue it as an infusion if ICP falls
Insert a lumbar drain for additional CSF drainage
questions.expl:
**Why D:** SIBICC moves up one tier at a time, and only when the lower tier has failed and a surgical lesion has been excluded. Tier 2 includes mild hypocapnia (PaCO₂ 32–35 mmHg), neuromuscular blockade (a test dose, then an infusion if it works), a MAP challenge to assess autoregulation and raising CPP if autoregulation is intact.

**Why not the others:**
- A – SIBICC lists ventilation to PaCO₂ < 30 mmHg among the things not to do; it risks cerebral ischaemia.
- B – Barbiturate coma is tier 3, used only if a test dose lowers ICP and hypotension can be avoided.
- C – Mannitol should be given as intermittent boluses; a continuous infusion is explicitly discouraged.
- E – Lumbar CSF drainage is also on the "not recommended" list (herniation risk).

**Ref:** Hawryluk GWJ, et al. SIBICC. *Intensive Care Med* 2019;45:1783–1794.

Review: [W15/D1](#W15-D1)

questions.stem: Regarding the Brain Trauma Foundation 4th-edition recommendations for severe TBI:
options: ICP above 22 mmHg should be treated.
A CPP target of 60–70 mmHg is recommended, and aggressive attempts to keep CPP above 70 mmHg with fluids and vasopressors carry a risk of ARDS.
Phenytoin prophylaxis is recommended because it prevents late post-traumatic epilepsy.
Prolonged prophylactic hyperventilation to PaCO₂ ≤ 25 mmHg is not recommended, but brief hyperventilation can be used as a temporising bridge.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – BTF 4th edition raised the treatment threshold from 20 to 22 mmHg (Level IIB), because mortality rises above it.
- B (True) – CPP 60–70 mmHg is the target (IIB); pushing CPP above 70 mmHg with fluids and pressors raises the risk of ARDS (III).
- C (False) – Phenytoin is recommended to prevent early seizures (< 7 days, IIA); prophylaxis does not prevent late seizures or epilepsy.
- D (True) – Prophylactic hyperventilation to PaCO₂ ≤ 25 mmHg is not recommended (IIB), especially in the first 24 h; brief hyperventilation is only a bridge (e.g. herniation).

**EDIC trap:** Older trials (DECRA, Eurotherm) use 20 mmHg – read the stem carefully.

**Ref:** Carney N, et al. BTF 4th edition. *Neurosurgery* 2017;80:6–15.

Review: [W15/D1](#W15-D1)

questions.stem: A 28-year-old with TBI has ICP above 25 mmHg for 6 hours despite stage 1 and stage 2 medical therapy. The neurosurgeon proposes a secondary decompressive craniectomy, and the family asks what to expect. Based on RESCUEicp, which statement best describes the effect of surgery at 6 months?
options: Lower mortality, but more patients in a vegetative state or with severe disability
Similar mortality with more favourable functional outcomes
Similar mortality with worse functional outcomes
No effect on ICP but fewer ICU days
Higher mortality but less disability among survivors
questions.expl:
**Why A:** RESCUEicp (n = 408) randomised patients with ICP > 25 mmHg for 1–12 h despite stage 1–2 therapy to last-tier craniectomy or medical care including barbiturates. Six-month mortality was 26.9 vs 48.9 %, but vegetative state (8.5 vs 2.1 %) and lower severe disability (21.9 vs 14.4 %) were more frequent. Surgery means survival, often with disability – a values-based decision with the family.

**Why not the others:**
- B – Upper severe disability or better was not significantly different at 6 months (42.8 vs 34.6 %); the difference became significant only at 12 months.
- C – This describes DECRA (early bifrontal DC for diffuse injury): unfavourable outcome 70 vs 51 %, mortality similar.
- D – Craniectomy lowered ICP in both DECRA and RESCUEicp.
- E – Mortality was lower, not higher.

**Ref:** Hutchinson PJ, et al. RESCUEicp. *N Engl J Med* 2016;375:1119–1130; Cooper DJ, et al. DECRA. *N Engl J Med* 2011;364:1493–1502.

Review: [W15/D1](#W15-D1)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old with moderate–severe TBI is on day 3 in the ICU. He is haemodynamically stable with no active bleeding, and his haemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL. Which transfusion strategy is best supported by the 2024 trials?
options: Transfuse only if Hb falls below 7 g/dL, as in general ICU patients
Transfuse only if PbtO₂ falls below 20 mmHg
Transfuse to keep Hb above 12 g/dL
Transfuse to keep Hb above about 9 g/dL
Give erythropoietin instead of red cells
questions.expl:
**Why D:** TRAIN (n = 820; TBI, SAH and ICH) compared transfusion triggers of 9 and 7 g/dL. Unfavourable neurological outcome was 62.6 vs 73.5 % (RR 0.85), and there was less cerebral ischaemia in the liberal arm. HEMOTION (10 vs 7 g/dL) showed a non-significant trend the same way.

**Why not the others:**
- A – The "7 for everyone" message comes from general ICU trials (TRICC, TRISS) and does not apply to acute brain injury.
- B – No trial validated PbtO₂-triggered transfusion; transfusion is only one late option in the low-PbtO₂ algorithm.
- C – No trial tested a target of 12 g/dL; even 10 g/dL (HEMOTION) was not significantly better.
- E – Erythropoietin is not a substitute for transfusion.

**Ref:** Taccone FS, et al. TRAIN. *JAMA* 2024;332:1623–1633; Turgeon AF, et al. HEMOTION. *N Engl J Med* 2024;391:722–735.

Review: [W15/D1](#W15-D1)

questions.stem: Regarding trials of temperature, tranexamic acid and osmotherapy in TBI:
options: In Eurotherm3235, hypothermia (32–35 °C) for raised ICP improved functional outcome.
In POLAR, early prophylactic hypothermia improved the rate of favourable outcome.
In CRASH-3, tranexamic acid given within 3 hours benefited patients with mild–moderate TBI (GCS 9–15), but not those with bilateral unreactive pupils.
In COBI, a continuous infusion of 20 % saline targeting Na 145–155 mmol/L improved 6-month GOS-E.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Eurotherm3235 was stopped early because outcome was worse with hypothermia (favourable GOS-E 26 vs 37 %).
- B (False) – POLAR (n = 511) found no benefit: favourable outcome 48.8 vs 49.1 %.
- C (True) – CRASH-3 (1 g over 10 min + 1 g over 8 h): RR 0.78 for head-injury death in GCS 9–15; no benefit in severe TBI or with bilateral unreactive pupils; earlier is better.
- D (False) – COBI (n = 370) found no difference in 6-month GOS-E (adjusted OR 1.02) or in intracranial hypertension. Use hyperosmolar boluses for ICP crises.

**EDIC trap:** Aim for controlled normothermia (36–37.5 °C); deeper cooling is tier 3 only.

**Ref:** Andrews PJD, et al. Eurotherm3235. *N Engl J Med* 2015;373:2403–2412; CRASH-3. *Lancet* 2019;394:1713–1723; Roquilly A, et al. COBI. *JAMA* 2021;325:2056–2066.

Review: [W15/D1](#W15-D1)

questions.stem: The SIBICC consensus lists several interventions that should NOT be used in the management of raised ICP after TBI. All of the following are on that list EXCEPT:
options: Mannitol given as a continuous infusion
Lumbar CSF drainage
Ventilation to PaCO₂ below 30 mmHg
Corticosteroids
A test dose of neuromuscular blocker followed by an infusion if effective
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Neuromuscular blockade, after a test dose shows that ICP falls, is a recognised tier 2 intervention in SIBICC. It reduces ICP by abolishing coughing, straining and ventilator asynchrony.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Mannitol must be given as intermittent boluses (0.25–1 g/kg); continuous infusion is explicitly discouraged.
- B – Lumbar CSF drainage is not recommended because of the risk of herniation in a patient with intracranial mass effect.
- C – PaCO₂ < 30 mmHg causes cerebral vasoconstriction and ischaemia; SIBICC allows only mild hypocapnia (32–35 mmHg) in tier 2.
- D – Steroids are not recommended (CRASH: 2-week mortality 21.1 vs 17.9 %, higher with steroids).

**Ref:** Hawryluk GWJ, et al. SIBICC. *Intensive Care Med* 2019;45:1783–1794.

Review: [W15/D1](#W15-D1)

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with aneurysmal SAH (WFNS II) had her aneurysm coiled on day 1. On day 6 she develops new right arm weakness, and her GCS falls from 15 to 13 for more than 1 hour. CT shows no hydrocephalus or rebleeding, Na is 137 mmol/L, and TCD shows a left MCA mean velocity of 170 cm/s with a Lindegaard ratio of 4.5. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Hypervolaemic "triple-H" therapy
Fluid restriction to 1 L/day
Euvolaemia, a cautious trial of induced hypertension with noradrenaline, and endovascular rescue if the deficit persists
Start an intravenous magnesium infusion
Start clazosentan
questions.expl:
**Why C:** This is delayed cerebral ischaemia (new focal deficit or GCS fall ≥ 2 for ≥ 1 h, other causes excluded) with TCD evidence of vasospasm (velocity > 120 cm/s, Lindegaard > 3). Management is euvolaemia, optimised haemoglobin, and a stepwise trial of induced hypertension in a secured aneurysm. Refractory symptomatic vasospasm can be treated with angioplasty or intra-arterial vasodilators.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Prophylactic or therapeutic hypervolaemia gives no benefit and causes pulmonary oedema and hyponatraemia.
- B – Fluid restriction increases the risk of DCI.
- D – Magnesium failed in MASH-2 (poor outcome 26.2 vs 25.3 %); ESO 2026 recommends against it.
- E – Clazosentan reduced angiographic vasospasm but not clinically relevant DCI or poor outcome; it is licensed only in Japan.

**Ref:** Vergouwen MDI, et al. ESO/EANS SAH guideline. *Eur Stroke J* 2026; Hoh BL, et al. AHA aSAH. *Stroke* 2023;54:e314–e370.

Review: [W15/D2](#W15-D2)

questions.stem: Regarding prevention of rebleeding and delayed cerebral ischaemia after aneurysmal SAH:
options: Nimodipine improves outcome mainly by reversing angiographic vasospasm.
If nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours causes hypotension, 30 mg every 2 hours may be given instead.
In ULTRA, ultra-early tranexamic acid before aneurysm securing improved functional outcome.
In ISAT, endovascular coiling reduced death or dependency at 1 year compared with clipping.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – In BRANT, nimodipine reduced cerebral infarction (22 vs 33 %) and poor outcome (20 vs 33 %) without a convincing effect on angiographic vasospasm; the benefit is thought to be neuroprotective or microvascular.
- B (True) – Splitting the dose to 30 mg every 2 h keeps the same 21-day course while limiting hypotension.
- C (False) – ULTRA (n = 955): good outcome 60 vs 64 % (OR 0.86, NS), rebleeding 10 vs 14 % (NS). ESO 2026 recommends against routine antifibrinolytics.
- D (True) – ISAT: death or dependency 23.7 vs 30.6 % (ARR 6.9 %, NNT ~14), with slightly more late rebleeding after coiling.

**Ref:** Pickard JD, et al. BRANT. *BMJ* 1989;298:636–642; Post R, et al. ULTRA. *Lancet* 2021;397:112–118; Molyneux A, et al. ISAT. *Lancet* 2002;360:1267–1274.

Review: [W15/D2](#W15-D2)

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man is on day 5 after a coiled anterior communicating artery aneurysm. Na has fallen from 139 to 128 mmol/L. Urine output is 4 L/day with high urine sodium, he is tachycardic, his weight has fallen by 2 kg and ultrasound shows a collapsing IVC. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Fluid restriction to 800 mL/day
Isotonic or hypertonic saline, with fludrocortisone to reduce natriuresis
Tolvaptan
Furosemide with oral salt tablets
0.45 % saline to match urine losses
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Natriuresis with clinical hypovolaemia points to cerebral salt wasting, a common cause of hyponatraemia after SAH. Hypovolaemia promotes delayed cerebral ischaemia, so the treatment is to replace salt and volume with isotonic or hypertonic saline. Fludrocortisone (or hydrocortisone) reduces natriuresis.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Fluid restriction is the classic SIADH treatment, but it is harmful after SAH because it worsens hypovolaemia and increases DCI risk.
- C – A vaptan causes free-water diuresis and would worsen volume depletion; it is not part of SAH management.
- D – A loop diuretic would increase volume loss in a hypovolaemic patient.
- E – Hypotonic fluid would lower sodium further and worsen cerebral oedema.

**EDIC trap:** After SAH, never fluid-restrict a hyponatraemic patient.

**Ref:** Hoh BL, et al. AHA aSAH. *Stroke* 2023;54:e314–e370; Treggiari MM, et al. NCS aSAH. *Neurocrit Care* 2023;39:1–28.

Review: [W15/D2](#W15-D2)
