- D – AKIKI 2 applies to patients without urgent indications; these indications are present now.
- E – Bicarbonate does not improve survival (BICARICU-2) and is not a reliable K⁺-lowering therapy.

**Ref:** KDIGO AKI guideline. *Kidney Int Suppl* 2012;2:1–138; Zarbock A, et al. RICH. *JAMA* 2020;324:1629–1639.

Review: [W18/D3](#W18-D3), [W18/D2](#W18-D2), [W18/D4](#W18-D4), [W15/D1](#W15-D1)

questions.stem: Regarding haemodynamic and transfusion targets in acute brain injury and after cardiac arrest:
options: In HEMOTION, a transfusion threshold of 10 g/dL significantly improved functional outcome after TBI.
In HIMALAIA, induced hypertension improved outcome in delayed cerebral ischaemia after SAH.
In BOX, a MAP target of 77 mmHg after cardiac arrest improved outcome compared with 63 mmHg.
ESO 2025 supports limiting treatment in the first 24 hours of ICH when the ICH score is 3 or more.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – HEMOTION (n = 742): unfavourable GOS-E 68.4 vs 73.5 % (NS, trend to liberal). TRAIN (9 vs 7 g/dL) did show benefit.
- B (False) – HIMALAIA was stopped early (n = 41) with no benefit on CBF or outcome. ESO 2026 makes no evidence-based recommendation, although AHA/NCS 2023 consider induced hypertension reasonable.
- C (False) – BOX: death or severe disability 34 vs 32 % (HR 1.08). The 2025 guideline recommends MAP > 60–65 mmHg, individualised.
- D (False) – ESO 2025 advises against general policies that limit treatment in the first 24 h. Prognostic scores must not be used alone (self-fulfilling prophecy).

**Ref:** Turgeon AF, et al. HEMOTION. *N Engl J Med* 2024;391:722–735; Kjaergaard J, et al. BOX. *N Engl J Med* 2022;387:1456–1466; Steiner T, et al. ESO/EANS ICH. *Eur Stroke J* 2025;10:1007–1086.

Review: [W15/D1](#W15-D1), [W15/D2](#W15-D2), [W15/D3](#W15-D3), [W17/D4](#W17-D4)

questions.stem: Regarding antiseizure drugs across acute neurological conditions in the ICU:
options: After cardiac arrest, ERC–ESICM 2025 advises against seizure prophylaxis; seizures are diagnosed on EEG and treated (e.g. levetiracetam or valproate).
In spontaneous ICH, prophylactic antiseizure medication is recommended for lobar haematomas.
In cerebral venous thrombosis, primary seizure prophylaxis is recommended for all patients with a parenchymal lesion, even without seizures.
In TBI, phenytoin prophylaxis prevents late post-traumatic epilepsy.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – There is no prophylaxis, and EEG guides treatment. TELSTAR showed that aggressively treating rhythmic or periodic patterns did not improve outcome (poor outcome 90 vs 92 %).
- B (False) – ESO 2025 is weakly against and AHA 2022 found no benefit; even though early seizures occur in ~10–15 %, mostly lobar, treat only clinical or EEG seizures.
- C (False) – ASMs are given only to patients who have had seizures with supratentorial lesions; there is no primary prophylaxis.
- D (False) – Phenytoin prevents early (< 7 days) seizures only. SAH: avoid phenytoin, and use a short course (≤ 7 days) only in high-risk patients.

**Ref:** Nolan JP, et al. ERC–ESICM post-resuscitation care. *Intensive Care Med* 2025; Steiner T, et al. ESO/EANS ICH. *Eur Stroke J* 2025;10:1007–1086; Ferro JM, et al. ESO CVT. *Eur J Neurol* 2017;24:1203–1213; Carney N, et al. BTF 4th edition. *Neurosurgery* 2017;80:6–15.

Review: [W17/D4](#W17-D4), [W15/D3](#W15-D3), [W17/D5](#W17-D5), [W15/D1](#W15-D1)

title: W18 · Saturday – weekly review: Renal (AKI and KDIGO, timing of RRT, RRT modalities and citrate, rhabdomyolysis and contrast, hyperkalaemia)

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man (100 kg) with pancreatitis has a creatinine of 105 µmol/L on admission (baseline 100). Over the next 36 hours it rises to 135 µmol/L; urine output averages 0.6 mL/kg/h. What is his KDIGO status?
options: No AKI – the creatinine has not risen by 50 %
Stage 2 AKI
Stage 1 AKI by the absolute creatinine criterion
AKI cannot be diagnosed without a known baseline from the past year
Stage 3 AKI
questions.expl:
**Why C:** A rise of ≥ 26.5 µmol/L (0.3 mg/dL) within 48 h defines AKI stage 1, even when the relative rise is < 50 % (135 − 105 = 30 µmol/L in 36 h).

**Why not the others:**
- A – the absolute (AKIN-derived) criterion is sufficient.
- B – stage 2 requires 2.0–2.9 × baseline or UO < 0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥ 12 h.
- D – the 48-h absolute criterion uses the admission value.
- E – stage 3 requires ≥ 3 ×, ≥ 354 µmol/L, KRT or severe oliguria/anuria.

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: Regarding AKI biomarkers and prevention:
options: A urinary [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] > 0.3 (ng/mL)²/1000 identifies patients at high risk of moderate–severe AKI.
In PrevAKI, implementing the KDIGO bundle in biomarker-positive cardiac surgery patients reduced AKI.
Low-dose dopamine is suggested to prevent AKI in high-risk patients.
A positive damage biomarker with unchanged creatinine is termed subclinical AKI.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – cell-cycle arrest markers; > 2.0 = very high risk.
- B (True) – AKI within 72 h 55.1 vs 71.7 %.
- C (False) – KDIGO recommends against low-dose dopamine (1A).
- D (True) – ADQI 23 concept, integrated in the KDIGO 2026 draft.

**Ref:** Meersch M, Intensive Care Med 2017; Ostermann M, JAMA Netw Open 2020. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman with septic shock and stage 3 AKI has pH 7.14, HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L and K⁺ 5.4 mmol/L. A colleague proposes sodium bicarbonate "to improve survival". Which trial result is most relevant?
options: BICARICU-2: no reduction in day-90 mortality (62.1 vs 61.7 %)
PRESERVE: bicarbonate reduced contrast nephropathy
RENAL: bicarbonate-buffered CRRT improved survival
BICAR-ICU: bicarbonate reduced mortality in all patients
AKIKI 2: bicarbonate allowed KRT to be delayed safely
questions.expl:
**Why A:** BICARICU-2 (JAMA 2025, n = 640) tested bicarbonate in severe metabolic acidaemia with moderate–severe AKI and found no mortality benefit, refuting the BICAR-ICU subgroup hypothesis.

**Why not the others:**
- B – PRESERVE found bicarbonate no better than saline.
- C – RENAL compared CRRT doses (40 vs 25 mL/kg/h), not buffers.
- D – BICAR-ICU was neutral overall; benefit appeared only in the AKIN 2–3 stratum.
- E – AKIKI 2 compared two delayed KRT strategies; prolonged delay was harmful.

**Ref:** Jaber S, JAMA 2025; Jaber S, Lancet 2018. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with KDIGO stage 3 AKI after septic shock has no urgent indication for KRT. His family asks whether starting dialysis "early" would improve his chances. Which statement best reflects the STARRT-AKI results?
options: Accelerated KRT reduced 90-day mortality by 10 %
Accelerated KRT did not reduce 90-day mortality and was associated with more dialysis dependence
Accelerated KRT reduced dependence on dialysis at 90 days
Accelerated KRT was beneficial only in septic patients
All patients in the standard arm required KRT within 72 hours
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In STARRT-AKI (n ≈ 3,000), 90-day mortality was 43.9 vs 43.7 %; KRT dependence at 90 days was higher with accelerated KRT (10.4 vs 6.0 %) and adverse events were more frequent.

**Why not the others:**
- A – no mortality difference.
- C – dependence was higher, not lower.
- D – no subgroup (including sepsis) benefited.
- E – 38 % of the standard arm never received KRT.

**Ref:** Bagshaw SM, N Engl J Med 2020. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: Regarding trials of KRT timing:
options: AKIKI 2 suggested that waiting beyond oliguria > 72 h or BUN > 112 mg/dL for mandatory criteria may be harmful.
IDEAL-ICU showed a survival benefit of early KRT in septic shock.
ELAIN enrolled mainly cardiac surgery patients at KDIGO stage 2.
In AKIKI, early KRT reduced 60-day mortality.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 60-day mortality 55 vs 44 % (adjusted HR 1.65) with the "more-delayed" strategy.
- B (False) – 58 vs 54 % at 90 days; stopped for futility.
- C (True) – single centre, n = 231, NGAL-enriched; 39.3 vs 54.7 %.
- D (False) – 48.5 vs 49.7 %; half of delayed patients never needed KRT.

**Ref:** Gaudry S, Lancet 2021; Barbar SD, N Engl J Med 2018; Zarbock A, JAMA 2016; Gaudry S, N Engl J Med 2016. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with stage 3 AKI is being managed with watchful waiting. Which new finding is an indication to start KRT now?
options: Creatinine has risen from 380 to 420 µmol/L
Urine output 0.2 mL/kg/h for 20 hours
Urea 28 mmol/L
Diuretic-resistant pulmonary oedema with PaO₂/FiO₂ 140
K⁺ 5.6 mmol/L without ECG changes
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Fluid overload with hypoxaemia (PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 200) not responding to diuretics is a conventional indication for KRT (STARRT-AKI criteria).

**Why not the others:**
- A – rising creatinine alone is not an indication.
- B – oliguria < 72 h is not by itself an indication.
- C – below AKIKI threshold (urea > 40 mmol/L, BUN > 112 mg/dL).
- E – K⁺ ≥ 6.0 mmol/L is the usual threshold.

**Ref:** Bagshaw SM, N Engl J Med 2020; Gaudry S, N Engl J Med 2016. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: Regarding the dose and modality of KRT:
options: RENAL showed lower 90-day mortality with an effluent rate of 40 mL/kg/h than with 25 mL/kg/h.
KDIGO recommends a delivered effluent volume of 20–25 mL/kg/h for CRRT.
KDIGO suggests CRRT rather than intermittent haemodialysis in patients with raised intracranial pressure.
In the ATN trial, more intensive renal support reduced 60-day mortality.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – 44.7 vs 44.7 %; more hypophosphataemia with the higher dose.
- B (True) – 1A; prescribe somewhat more to compensate for downtime.
- C (True) – 2B; avoids rapid osmotic shifts (dialysis disequilibrium).
- D (False) – 53.6 vs 51.5 %; no benefit.

**Ref:** Bellomo R, N Engl J Med 2009; Palevsky PM, N Engl J Med 2008; KDIGO 2012. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman with acute liver failure (INR 4.2, lactate 8 mmol/L) on CVVHDF with regional citrate develops a falling systemic ionised calcium despite higher calcium infusion, an anion gap of 24 mmol/L and a total/ionised calcium ratio of 3.0. What is the best action?
options: Increase the citrate dose to prolong filter life
Increase the blood flow
Add systemic heparin to the citrate
Give sodium bicarbonate and continue unchanged
Stop or reduce citrate and switch to an alternative anticoagulation strategy
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Ratio > 2.5, falling iCa and high-anion-gap acidosis indicate citrate accumulation from impaired hepatic metabolism. Citrate must be reduced or stopped (no anticoagulation, or heparin if bleeding risk allows) and clearance increased.

**Why not the others:**
- A – more citrate worsens accumulation.
- B – higher blood flow increases citrate delivery.
- C – adding heparin does not address accumulation and increases bleeding risk in coagulopathy.
- D – masks the problem; citrate continues to accumulate.

**Ref:** KDIGO, Kidney Int Suppl 2012. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man needs CRRT for septic AKI. He has a platelet count of 70 × 10⁹/L and recent gastrointestinal bleeding; there is no liver failure. According to KDIGO and the RICH trial, which anticoagulation strategy is most appropriate?
options: Systemic unfractionated heparin with aPTT 1.5–2 × normal
Regional citrate anticoagulation
Low-molecular-weight heparin at therapeutic dose
Argatroban
Regional heparin with protamine reversal
questions.expl:
**Why B:** KDIGO suggests citrate rather than heparin for CRRT (2B) and, in increased bleeding risk, citrate rather than no anticoagulation (2C). In RICH, citrate prolonged filter life (47 vs 26 h) and reduced bleeding (5.1 vs 16.9 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – systemic heparin increases bleeding.
- C – therapeutic LMWH accumulates in AKI and increases bleeding.
- D – argatroban is reserved for HIT.
- E – KDIGO suggests against regional heparin (2C).

**Ref:** Zarbock A, JAMA 2020; KDIGO 2012. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man develops severe muscle pain and dark urine after a marathon in hot weather. CK is 85,000 U/L, creatinine 150 µmol/L, K⁺ 5.0 mmol/L, Ca²⁺ 1.9 mmol/L (asymptomatic). Which statement about his management is correct?
options: Calcium gluconate should be given to normalise calcium
Mannitol improves renal outcomes in randomised trials
Urinary alkalinisation with bicarbonate is proven to prevent AKI
Early isotonic fluid targeting a high urine output is the cornerstone of treatment
Prophylactic haemodialysis to remove myoglobin is recommended
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Early, generous isotonic crystalloid (urine output ~200–300 mL/h) corrects hypovolaemia and limits cast formation. Bicarbonate and mannitol have no proven benefit.

**Why not the others:**
- A – asymptomatic early hypocalcaemia should not be treated (calcium deposition, later hypercalcaemia).
- B – no RCT evidence; risk of hyperosmolality.
- C – not proven.
- E – myoglobin removal is not proven; KRT for conventional indications.

**Ref:** Bosch X, N Engl J Med 2009. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: Regarding contrast-associated AKI:
options: In PRESERVE, oral N-acetylcysteine reduced the composite of death, dialysis or persistent kidney decline.
In AMACING, no prophylactic hydration was non-inferior to IV hydration in patients with eGFR 30–59.
Prophylactic haemodialysis after contrast is recommended in patients with eGFR < 30.
Contrast should be withheld in AKI even for suspected life-threatening haemorrhage.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – 4.6 vs 4.5 %; no effect.
- B (True) – CA-AKI 2.7 vs 2.6 %; hydration had complications and cost.
- C (False) – not recommended.
- D (False) – life-saving imaging should not be delayed; prophylactic IV saline for eGFR < 30 or AKI if feasible.

**Ref:** Weisbord SD, N Engl J Med 2018; Nijssen EC, Lancet 2017; Davenport MS, Radiology 2020. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man has crush injury of both thighs after a car accident. On day 2, CK is 60,000 U/L. All of the following are typical findings or complications EXCEPT:
options: Hyperkalaemia
Hyperphosphataemia
Early hypocalcaemia
High-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
Hypouricaemia
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Muscle necrosis releases purines, which are metabolised to uric acid – hyperuricaemia, not hypouricaemia, is typical.

**Why not the others:**
- A – intracellular K⁺ release; may be early and fatal.
- B – phosphate release from muscle.
- C – calcium phosphate deposition in damaged muscle.
- D – release of organic acids and AKI.

**Ref:** Bosch X, N Engl J Med 2009. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman with K⁺ 6.9 mmol/L and peaked T waves receives 10 units of insulin with 25 g glucose. Her pre-treatment glucose was 5.2 mmol/L; she is not diabetic. What is the most appropriate additional measure?
options: 10 % glucose at 50 mL/h for 5 hours with regular glucose checks
No further glucose; check once at 24 h
Repeat insulin without glucose after 30 minutes
Give 50 mL 50 % glucose every hour for 6 hours
Stop all monitoring once K⁺ is < 6.0 mmol/L
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Hypoglycaemia after insulin–glucose is common (up to ~20 %), occurs over the following hours and is more likely with a low baseline glucose and no diabetes. ERC/RCUK 2025 advise 10 % glucose 50 mL/h for 5 h if pre-treatment glucose is < 7 mmol/L, with glucose monitoring.

**Why not the others:**
- B – hypoglycaemia risk lasts up to ~6 h; monitoring is needed.
- C – insulin without glucose causes hypoglycaemia.
- D – excessive glucose causes hyperglycaemia and hyperosmolality.
- E – rebound hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia require continued monitoring.

**Ref:** Lott C (ERC), Resuscitation 2025. → [D5](D5.md)

questions.stem: Regarding urgent indications for extracorporeal treatment in poisoning:
options: Lithium poisoning with decreased level of consciousness is an indication for haemodialysis irrespective of the lithium level.
Metformin-associated lactic acidosis with lactate > 20 mmol/L is an indication for extracorporeal treatment.
Digoxin toxicity is effectively treated by haemodialysis.
Salicylate poisoning with altered mental status is an indication for haemodialysis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – EXTRIP: recommended for decreased consciousness, seizures or dysrhythmias at any level, or > 4.0 mmol/L with impaired kidney function.
- B (True) – also pH ≤ 7.0, shock or failure of standard therapy.
- C (False) – digoxin has a large Vd; treat with digoxin-specific Fab.
- D (True) – also salicylate > 7.2 mmol/L (100 mg/dL), new hypoxaemia, pH ≤ 7.20.

**Ref:** Decker BS (EXTRIP), Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2015. → [D5](D5.md)

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with C6 tetraplegia from a diving accident 10 days ago needs emergency intubation for respiratory failure. K⁺ is 4.8 mmol/L. Which neuromuscular blocker is most appropriate?
options: Suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg
Suxamethonium at half dose after pretreatment with a non-depolarising agent
Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg
Suxamethonium – the risk applies only to burns
Avoid all neuromuscular blockers
questions.expl:
**Why C:** After denervation injury (spinal cord injury, from ~24–72 h onwards), up-regulated extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors cause massive K⁺ release with suxamethonium, which can lead to cardiac arrest. High-dose rocuronium gives rapid-sequence conditions (reversible with sugammadex).

**Why not the others:**
- A – risk of life-threatening hyperkalaemia.
- B – dose reduction or pretreatment does not prevent the receptor-mediated K⁺ release.
- D – the risk also applies to denervation, immobilisation, crush and rhabdomyolysis.
- E – a neuromuscular blocker improves intubating conditions; rocuronium is safe.

**Ref:** Lindner G, Eur J Emerg Med 2020. → [D5](D5.md)

title: W19 · D1 – Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting. Glucose 28 mmol/L, venous pH 7.18, HCO₃⁻ 9 mmol/L, capillary β-hydroxybutyrate 5.2 mmol/L, K⁺ 3.1 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate immediate step after starting fluids?
options: Start fixed-rate insulin 0.1 U/kg/h and recheck K⁺ in 2 hours
Give an insulin bolus of 0.1 U/kg followed by an infusion
Give sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg
Replace potassium and delay insulin until K⁺ is above 3.5 mmol/L
Start subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin every 2 hours
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Total-body potassium is depleted in DKA, and insulin will push K⁺ into cells. With K⁺ < 3.5 mmol/L at presentation, insulin is delayed while potassium is given (about 10–20 mmol/h with ECG monitoring) until K⁺ > 3.5 mmol/L.

**Why not the others:**
- A – starting insulin with K⁺ 3.1 mmol/L risks fatal hypokalaemia and arrhythmia.
- B – a bolus is not required, and insulin must wait here anyway.
- C – bicarbonate is not indicated at pH 7.18 and would worsen hypokalaemia.
- E – subcutaneous insulin is for mild/uncomplicated moderate DKA; this is moderate–severe with hypokalaemia.

**Ref:** Umpierrez GE, Diabetes Care 2024; Dhatariya KK, Diabet Med 2022.

questions.stem: Regarding the diagnostic criteria of hyperglycaemic crises according to the 2024 international consensus:
options: DKA requires a plasma glucose of at least 13.9 mmol/L (250 mg/dL).
A β-hydroxybutyrate of 3.0 mmol/L or more fulfils the ketosis criterion for DKA.
A bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L fulfils the acidosis criterion for DKA, even if the pH is 7.32.
HHS requires an effective serum osmolality of at least 350 mOsm/kg.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – the glucose criterion is ≥ 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) *or* a history of diabetes, so euglycaemic DKA is included.
- B (True) – BHB ≥ 3.0 mmol/L (or urine ketones ≥ 2+).
- C (True) – acidosis is defined as pH < 7.30 *and/or* HCO₃⁻ < 18 mmol/L.
- D (False) – HHS needs effective osmolality > 300 mOsm/kg (or total > 320), with glucose ≥ 33.3 mmol/L.

**Ref:** Umpierrez GE, Diabetes Care 2024.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man on empagliflozin develops vomiting 2 days after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Glucose 9.8 mmol/L, pH 7.15, HCO₃⁻ 8 mmol/L, anion gap 24 mmol/L, β-hydroxybutyrate 6.1 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate management?
options: No insulin because the glucose is below 11 mmol/L; give fluids only
Stop empagliflozin and give IV fluids, fixed-rate insulin and early dextrose
Sodium bicarbonate infusion to pH 7.30
Continue empagliflozin and start metformin
Haemodialysis for unexplained high anion gap acidosis
questions.expl:
**Why B:** This is euglycaemic DKA associated with an SGLT2 inhibitor (fasting, surgery). Treatment is as for DKA – fluids, fixed-rate insulin 0.1 U/kg/h – with dextrose from the start so that enough insulin can be given to clear the ketones, and the SGLT2 inhibitor is stopped.

**Why not the others:**
- A – ketoacidosis is driven by insulin deficiency; insulin is the key therapy whatever the glucose.
- C – bicarbonate is not routinely indicated (2024: only if pH < 7.0).
- D – the SGLT2 inhibitor caused the problem, and metformin is contraindicated in acidosis.
- E – the cause is known and treatable medically.

**Ref:** Umpierrez GE, Diabetes Care 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding potassium, sodium and ketone measurements in DKA:
options: A normal serum potassium at presentation excludes a total-body potassium deficit.
The nitroprusside test detects acetoacetate but not β-hydroxybutyrate.
A measured sodium of 140 mmol/L with glucose 40 mmol/L indicates a free-water deficit.
Insulin therapy tends to raise serum potassium.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – total K⁺ is depleted by 3–5 mmol/kg; serum K⁺ is normal or high because of insulin deficiency and hyperosmolality.
- B (True) – blood BHB should be measured; nitroprusside reactions can paradoxically increase during recovery.
- C (True) – corrected Na⁺ ≈ 140 + 1.6–2.4 × (34/5.6) ≈ 150–155 mmol/L, i.e. hypernatraemic dehydration.
- D (False) – insulin drives K⁺ into cells and lowers serum K⁺.

**Ref:** Umpierrez GE, Diabetes Care 2024; Dhatariya KK, Diabet Med 2022.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old nursing-home resident with type 2 diabetes is confused. Glucose 52 mmol/L, Na⁺ 152 mmol/L, urea 24 mmol/L, β-hydroxybutyrate 0.8 mmol/L, pH 7.36. Which is the best initial management?
options: Insulin bolus 0.1 U/kg, then 0.1 U/kg/h
0.45 % saline 1 L/h to correct hypernatraemia rapidly
Isotonic crystalloid, delaying fixed-rate insulin at 0.05 U/kg/h until glucose stops falling with fluids, plus LMWH prophylaxis
Isotonic crystalloid aiming for a sodium fall of 15 mmol/L in 24 h
Sodium bicarbonate and furosemide
questions.expl:
**Why C:** This is HHS (glucose ≥ 30–33 mmol/L, effective osmolality 2 × 152 + 52 = 356 mOsm/kg, no ketoacidosis). Fluids are the main treatment and lower glucose by themselves; insulin is started at 0.05 U/kg/h once glucose stops falling (JBDS), and LMWH is given because of high VTE risk.

**Why not the others:**
- A – DKA dosing in HHS lowers glucose and osmolality too fast and shifts fluid out of the circulation.
- B – hypotonic fluid is used only if osmolality fails to fall despite adequate isotonic fluid; rapid correction risks cerebral oedema and ODS.
- D – Na⁺ should fall by no more than 10 mmol/L in 24 h.
- E – there is no acidosis; diuretics worsen dehydration.

**Ref:** Mustafa OG, Diabet Med 2023; Umpierrez GE, Diabetes Care 2024.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with DKA has received 0.9 % saline (6 L) and insulin for 14 hours. β-hydroxybutyrate is 0.4 mmol/L, glucose 9 mmol/L, pH 7.31, Na⁺ 141, Cl⁻ 117, HCO₃⁻ 16 mmol/L. What best explains the persistently low bicarbonate?
options: Persistent ketoacidosis needing a higher insulin rate
Lactic acidosis from occult sepsis
Hyperchloraemic normal anion gap acidosis from saline
Renal tubular acidosis type 4
Starvation ketosis
questions.expl:
**Why C:** The anion gap is 141 − (117 + 16) = 8 mmol/L (normal) and ketones have cleared (< 0.6 mmol/L). The residual acidosis is hyperchloraemic, caused by large volumes of 0.9 % saline; it is benign and does not need more insulin. Balanced crystalloids reduce it (SMART/SALT-ED DKA subgroup).

**Why not the others:**
- A – BHB 0.4 mmol/L and pH 7.31 meet resolution criteria.
- B – lactic acidosis would raise the anion gap.
- D – type 4 RTA is a chronic hyperkalaemic state, not explained by this course.
- E – starvation ketosis would raise BHB and the anion gap.

**Ref:** Self WH, JAMA Netw Open 2020; Umpierrez GE, Diabetes Care 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding fluid and insulin management of adult DKA:
options: Long-acting basal insulin should be continued during the intravenous insulin infusion.
Once glucose falls below about 14 mmol/L, the insulin infusion should be stopped.
In the SMART/SALT-ED DKA subgroup, balanced crystalloids shortened the time to DKA resolution compared with saline.
A fall in β-hydroxybutyrate of at least 0.5 mmol/L/h indicates an adequate response to insulin.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – continuing basal insulin prevents rebound ketosis after the infusion stops.
- B (False) – dextrose is added and insulin continued until ketoacidosis resolves.
- C (True) – median 13.0 vs 16.9 h (n = 172).
- D (True) – JBDS targets: BHB ↓ ≥ 0.5 mmol/L/h, HCO₃⁻ ↑ ≥ 3 mmol/L/h, glucose ↓ ≥ 3 mmol/L/h.

**Ref:** Dhatariya KK, Diabet Med 2022; Self WH, JAMA Netw Open 2020.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with severe DKA (pH 6.98) becomes drowsy with headache, bradycardia and hypertension 6 hours into treatment. Glucose is 15 mmol/L, K⁺ 4.2 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Give mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg (or 3 % saline) and reduce the fluid rate
Give sodium bicarbonate
Increase the insulin infusion
Give a 20 mL/kg bolus of 0.45 % saline
Arrange an urgent EEG before any treatment
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Headache, falling consciousness, bradycardia and hypertension during DKA treatment in a young patient suggest cerebral oedema. Treatment should not wait for imaging: hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg or hypertonic saline), head-up positioning, reduced fluid rate and ICU care.

**Why not the others:**
- B – bicarbonate is a risk factor for cerebral oedema in children.
- C – a faster fall in glucose and osmolality could worsen oedema.
- D – hypotonic fluid worsens brain swelling.
- E – this is a clinical diagnosis; treat first, then CT if needed.

**Ref:** Kuppermann N (PECARN FLUID), N Engl J Med 2018; Umpierrez GE, Diabetes Care 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding the hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state:
options: The water deficit is usually larger than in DKA.
A rise in measured sodium during the first hours of treatment is acceptable if osmolality is falling.
Mortality is lower than that of DKA.
Prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin is recommended unless contraindicated.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – about 100–220 mL/kg vs about 100 mL/kg in DKA.
- B (True) – as glucose falls, water moves into cells and Na⁺ rises; what matters is a controlled fall in osmolality (3–8 mOsm/kg/h).
- C (False) – HHS mortality (5–20 %) is much higher than DKA (< 1–2 %).
- D (True) – hyperviscosity and immobility give a high VTE risk.

**Ref:** Mustafa OG, Diabet Med 2023.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is admitted with moderate DKA. All of the following are recommended in the 2024 consensus EXCEPT:
options: Measuring blood β-hydroxybutyrate to monitor response
Adding potassium to fluids when K⁺ is below 5.0 mmol/L
Starting dextrose when glucose falls below 13.9 mmol/L
Routine phosphate replacement
Treating the precipitating cause
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Phosphate falls during treatment, but routine replacement has not improved outcomes; it is given only for severe hypophosphataemia (< 0.32 mmol/L) or symptoms (muscle weakness, cardiac dysfunction, haemolysis).

**Why not the others:**
- A – blood BHB is the preferred monitoring parameter.
- B – K⁺ replacement starts below 5.0 mmol/L (target 4–5).
- C – dextrose allows insulin to continue until ketones clear.
- E – infection, insulin omission and other triggers must be treated.

**Ref:** Umpierrez GE, Diabetes Care 2024.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man is recovering from DKA. β-hydroxybutyrate 0.5 mmol/L, pH 7.34, and he is eating. He has not been on insulin before. What is the safest way to stop the intravenous insulin infusion?
options: Stop the infusion and give subcutaneous insulin when glucose exceeds 15 mmol/L
Stop the infusion and start metformin
Give subcutaneous basal insulin, and stop the infusion immediately in the same minute
Continue the infusion for 24 more hours regardless of eating
Give subcutaneous basal (and prandial) insulin and continue the infusion for 1–2 hours afterwards
questions.expl:
**Why E:** The half-life of IV insulin is only minutes. Subcutaneous basal insulin is given 1–2 h before the infusion is stopped (basal–bolus, about 0.3–0.6 U/kg/day in insulin-naïve patients) to avoid rebound hyperglycaemia and ketosis.

**Why not the others:**
- A – a gap without insulin leads to recurrent DKA.
- B – oral agents are not appropriate for insulin-deficient DKA.
- C – without overlap there is an insulin-free gap while subcutaneous insulin is absorbed.
- D – once resolved and eating, prolonging the infusion has no benefit.

**Ref:** Umpierrez GE, Diabetes Care 2024; Dhatariya KK, Diabet Med 2022.

open.q: Outline the first 6 hours of management of an adult with severe DKA.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **Assessment:** ABC, severity (pH < 7.0, HCO₃⁻ < 5–10, BHB > 6, K⁺ < 3.5, GCS < 12, shock) → HDU/ICU; look for the precipitant (infection, MI, insulin omission, SGLT2 inhibitor); ECG, blood/urine cultures.
- **Fluids:** isotonic, preferably balanced crystalloid 0.5–1 L/h for 2–4 h (bolus 500 mL if SBP < 90), smaller volumes in heart/kidney failure.
- **Potassium:** K⁺ < 3.5 → replace and delay insulin; 3.5–5.0 → 20–40 mmol/L in fluids; > 5.0 → none, recheck at 2 h.
- **Insulin:** FRIII 0.1 U/kg/h, no bolus; continue basal insulin; dextrose when glucose < 13.9–14 mmol/L.
- **Monitoring:** hourly glucose and BHB, venous gas 1–2-hourly; targets BHB ↓ ≥ 0.5/h, HCO₃⁻ ↑ ≥ 3/h; fluid balance, GCS.
- **Avoid:** routine bicarbonate (only if pH < 7.0), routine phosphate; watch for hypoglycaemia, hypokalaemia, cerebral oedema.

open.q: How does the management of HHS differ from that of DKA?
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Diagnosis: glucose ≥ 30–33 mmol/L, osmolality > 300 effective / ≥ 320 mOsm/kg, BHB < 3, pH ≥ 7.30; older patients, larger water deficit (100–220 mL/kg), higher mortality.
- Fluids are the primary therapy; isotonic crystalloid first, positive balance 3–6 L by 12 h; hypotonic only if osmolality stops falling.
- Insulin lower dose (0.05 U/kg/h) and only when glucose stops falling with fluids (unless significant ketonaemia).
- Controlled correction: glucose ↓ 4–6 mmol/L/h, osmolality ↓ 3–8 mOsm/kg/h, Na⁺ ↓ ≤ 10 mmol/L/24 h; a rising Na⁺ is acceptable if osmolality falls (risk of cerebral oedema/ODS).
- LMWH thromboprophylaxis, foot protection, search for MI/stroke/sepsis; mixed DKA–HHS treated as DKA for insulin.

title: W19 · D2 – Glucose control in the ICU: Leuven, NICE-SUGAR, TGC-fast and current targets

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with septic shock on noradrenaline and enteral feeding has repeated arterial glucose values of 12–13 mmol/L. Which insulin strategy is best supported by current guidelines?
options: No insulin until glucose exceeds 15 mmol/L
IV insulin targeting 4.4–6.1 mmol/L
Subcutaneous sliding-scale insulin every 6 hours
IV insulin infusion by protocol, targeting about 7.8–10 mmol/L
Stop enteral feeding to lower glucose
questions.expl:
**Why D:** SSC 2021 (unchanged in SSC 2026) recommends starting insulin at glucose ≥ 10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL), with a typical target of 7.8–10 mmol/L; in an unstable patient on vasopressors an IV infusion with a validated protocol is preferred.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the threshold for starting insulin is 10 mmol/L, not 15.
- B – tight control increased mortality in NICE-SUGAR and showed no benefit in TGC-fast.
- C – subcutaneous absorption is unpredictable in shock; sliding scales alone are discouraged.
- E – withholding nutrition to control glucose is not appropriate.

**Ref:** Prescott HC (SSC 2026), Crit Care Med 2026; Honarmand K, Crit Care Med 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding the NICE-SUGAR trial:
options: It randomised more than 6,000 mixed medical and surgical ICU patients.
Intensive glucose control (4.5–6.0 mmol/L) increased 90-day mortality.
Severe hypoglycaemia (≤ 2.2 mmol/L) was more common with intensive control.
The benefit of intensive control was confined to surgical patients.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 6,104 patients in 42 centres.
- B (True) – 27.5 vs 24.9 % (OR 1.14, P = 0.02).
- C (True) – 6.8 vs 0.5 %.
- D (False) – there was no benefit in the surgical subgroup either; the treatment effect did not differ between surgical and medical patients.

**Ref:** NICE-SUGAR Investigators, N Engl J Med 2009.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman in septic shock (noradrenaline 0.4 µg/kg/min, generalised oedema, Hb 72 g/L) has a capillary fingerstick glucose of 3.4 mmol/L. What is the best next step?
options: Check glucose immediately on arterial blood with a blood-gas analyser, while treating as hypoglycaemia if confirmed
Ignore it – capillary values are always falsely low
Increase the insulin infusion
Repeat fingerstick in 4 hours
Give glucagon 1 mg IM
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Capillary point-of-care meters are inaccurate in shock, vasopressor therapy, oedema and anaemia. An arterial sample on a blood-gas analyser should be checked at once; true hypoglycaemia is treated with IV dextrose and a review of insulin and nutrition.

**Why not the others:**
- B – the error can go either way; hypoglycaemia must not be dismissed.
- C – increasing insulin with possible hypoglycaemia is dangerous.
- D – a 4-hour delay could allow severe neuroglycopenia.
- E – with IV access, IV dextrose is faster and more reliable; glucagon is a fallback.

**Ref:** Evans L, Intensive Care Med 2021; Honarmand K, Crit Care Med 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding the Leuven I trial (Van den Berghe, 2001) and TGC-fast (2023):
options: Leuven I enrolled mainly cardiac surgical patients.
Patients in Leuven I commonly received early parenteral nutrition.
TGC-fast showed that tight glucose control reduced 90-day mortality when early parenteral nutrition was withheld.
TGC-fast used a computerised insulin-dosing algorithm in the tight-control arm.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – about 63 % were cardiac surgery patients.
- B (True) – early IV glucose and parenteral nutrition were standard, producing marked hyperglycaemia in the control arm.
- C (False) – there was no difference in ICU stay (HR 1.00) or 90-day mortality (10.5 vs 10.1 %).
- D (True) – the LOGIC-Insulin algorithm.

**Ref:** Van den Berghe G, N Engl J Med 2001; Gunst J (TGC-fast), N Engl J Med 2023.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man on an insulin infusion (4 U/h) has his enteral feed stopped for a planned tracheostomy. Two hours later his glucose is 2.1 mmol/L. Which is the most likely cause?
options: Relative adrenal insufficiency
Insulinoma
Continuing insulin after interruption of nutrition
Capillary measurement artefact
Sepsis-induced gluconeogenesis
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Interrupting nutrition while the insulin infusion continues is a classic, preventable cause of ICU hypoglycaemia. Protocols must couple insulin to nutrition: reduce or stop insulin, or give dextrose, when feeding stops.

**Why not the others:**
- A – adrenal insufficiency can cause hypoglycaemia but does not explain the timing.
- B – insulinoma is rare and would not appear after a feed stop on an infusion.
- D – artefact is possible but must be confirmed, not assumed; the timing points to insulin.
- E – sepsis *increases* gluconeogenesis (though severe sepsis and liver failure can cause hypoglycaemia).

**Ref:** Honarmand K, Crit Care Med 2024; NICE-SUGAR Investigators, N Engl J Med 2012.

questions.stem: According to the SCCM 2024 guideline on glycaemic control, which statement for critically ill adults is correct?
options: Insulin should be titrated to 4.4–7.7 mmol/L to reduce infections
Continuous glucose monitoring is recommended as the sole monitoring method
Glucose targets should be individualised according to HbA1c
Insulin is recommended only when glucose exceeds 15 mmol/L
Titrating insulin to an intensive range of 4.4–7.7 mmol/L rather than 7.8–11.1 mmol/L is not suggested
questions.expl:
**Why E:** SCCM 2024 makes a conditional recommendation (moderate certainty) against intensive targets (80–139 mg/dL) compared with conventional targets (140–200 mg/dL), mainly because of hypoglycaemia; it also suggests protocols with explicit decision support.

**Why not the others:**
- A – this is exactly what the guideline suggests against.
- B – CGM accuracy in critical illness is not established enough for such a recommendation.
- C – HbA1c-based individualised targets are a research priority (CONTROLING was neutral).
- D – the usual starting threshold is ~10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL).

**Ref:** Honarmand K, Crit Care Med 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding hypoglycaemia in ICU patients:
options: Moderate hypoglycaemia (2.3–3.9 mmol/L) is not associated with mortality.
Sedation and β-blockers can mask the warning signs of hypoglycaemia.
Kidney failure lowers the risk of hypoglycaemia by reducing insulin clearance.
Glucagon is highly effective in patients with acute liver failure.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – in NICE-SUGAR, moderate hypoglycaemia was associated with death (HR ≈ 1.4), severe with HR ≈ 2.1.
- B (True) – adrenergic and neuroglycopenic signs are masked in sedated, ventilated patients.
- C (False) – reduced insulin clearance (and gluconeogenesis) in kidney failure *increases* the risk.
- D (False) – glucagon needs hepatic glycogen; it works poorly in liver failure – use IV dextrose.

**Ref:** NICE-SUGAR Investigators, N Engl J Med 2012.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with acute ischaemic stroke and diabetes has a glucose of 13 mmol/L on admission. Which statement about glucose management is best supported by the SHINE trial?
options: Intensive IV insulin to 4.4–7.2 mmol/L improves functional outcome
Intensive treatment did not improve functional outcome and caused more severe hypoglycaemia
Hyperglycaemia should be left untreated in stroke
Glucose should be kept below 5 mmol/L to protect the penumbra
Dextrose infusions should be given to all stroke patients
questions.expl:
**Why B:** SHINE (n = 1,151) compared IV insulin targeting 4.4–7.2 mmol/L with subcutaneous insulin targeting 4.4–10 mmol/L: favourable outcome 20.5 vs 21.6 % (no difference), with severe hypoglycaemia 2.6 vs 0 %.

**Why not the others:**
- A – no improvement was found.
- C – hyperglycaemia is still treated, to the standard range.
- D – low glucose is harmful to the injured brain (neuroglycopenia).
- E – routine dextrose worsens hyperglycaemia.

**Ref:** Johnston KC (SHINE), JAMA 2019.

questions.stem: Regarding mechanisms and causes of hyperglycaemia in critical illness:
options: Cortisol and catecholamines promote hepatic gluconeogenesis.
Hydrocortisone for septic shock lowers blood glucose.
Neurons and endothelial cells take up glucose largely independently of insulin.
Parenteral nutrition dextrose loads contribute to hyperglycaemia.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – counter-regulatory hormones and cytokines cause hepatic insulin resistance and gluconeogenesis.
- B (False) – hydrocortisone raises glucose (more hyperglycaemia in ADRENAL and APROCCHSS).
- C (True) – insulin-independent uptake (GLUT1/3) exposes them to glucose overload and toxicity.
- D (True) – which is why the early-PN context of Leuven I matters.

**Ref:** Honarmand K, Crit Care Med 2024; Van den Berghe G, N Engl J Med 2001.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man is admitted to the ICU after major abdominal surgery. All of the following increase the risk of insulin-induced hypoglycaemia EXCEPT:
options: Starting continuous kidney replacement therapy
Decompensated cirrhosis
Abrupt cessation of parenteral nutrition while insulin continues
Intensive glucose targets
Starting a hydrocortisone infusion for septic shock
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Hydrocortisone raises glucose and insulin requirements. Hypoglycaemia occurs when steroids are *tapered or stopped* without reducing insulin.

**Why not the others:**
- A – kidney failure reduces insulin clearance; some CRRT fluids are glucose-free and remove glucose.
- B – liver failure impairs gluconeogenesis and glycogen stores.
- C – a classic iatrogenic cause.
- D – tight targets multiplied hypoglycaemia in every trial.

**Ref:** Honarmand K, Crit Care Med 2024.

questions.stem: A peritoneal dialysis patient using icodextrin has a point-of-care glucose of 18 mmol/L but appears clinically hypoglycaemic and sweaty. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Stress hyperglycaemia
Falsely high reading on a glucose dehydrogenase–PQQ meter due to maltose from icodextrin
Pseudohypoglycaemia from leucocytosis
Insulin resistance from uraemia
Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Icodextrin is metabolised to maltose, which GDH-PQQ meters read as glucose. Glucose can be dangerously overestimated, insulin given in error, and true hypoglycaemia missed. Glucose should be checked with a laboratory or blood-gas analyser (glucose oxidase/hexokinase).

**Why not the others:**
- A – stress hyperglycaemia does not explain hypoglycaemic symptoms.
- C – leucocytosis causes falsely *low* lab values in stored samples.
- D – uraemia does not cause sweating with apparent high glucose.
- E – HHS causes dehydration and confusion, not adrenergic sweating, and glucose would be far higher.

**Ref:** Honarmand K, Crit Care Med 2024.

open.q: Explain why the results of Leuven I and NICE-SUGAR differed, and state the current glucose target in the ICU.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Leuven I (2001): single centre, mostly cardiac surgery, early IV glucose/parenteral nutrition (severe hyperglycaemia in the control arm), arterial blood-gas measurements, expert nursing → ICU mortality 4.6 vs 8.0 %.
- NICE-SUGAR (2009): 6,104 mixed patients, 42 centres, mostly enteral feeding, control ≤ 10 mmol/L, variable measurement methods → 90-day mortality ↑ (27.5 vs 24.9 %), severe hypoglycaemia 6.8 vs 0.5 %.
- Hypoglycaemia (dose–response association with death), measurement error, different control targets and nutrition explain the difference; TGC-fast (2023, no early PN) found no benefit.
- Current: start insulin at ≥ 10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL), target 7.8–10 mmol/L (140–180 mg/dL); avoid < 6.1 as a target (SCCM 2024: against 4.4–7.7); validated protocols, arterial samples, avoid hypoglycaemia and variability.

title: W19 · D3 – Thyroid emergencies: thyroid storm, myxoedema coma and thyroid function in critical illness

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with untreated Graves' disease is admitted with pneumonia, temperature 40.1 °C, AF at 160/min, agitation and jaundice. Burch–Wartofsky score is 65. Which treatment sequence is most appropriate?
options: Lugol's iodine first, then propylthiouracil 1 hour later
Radioiodine ablation within 24 hours
Propylthiouracil (or methimazole), then iodide at least 1 hour later, plus β-blockade and hydrocortisone
Aspirin for fever and levothyroxine
Amiodarone loading for AF and observation of thyroid function
questions.expl:
**Why C:** This is thyroid storm (BWPS ≥ 45). The thionamide is given first to block synthesis; iodide is given at least 1 h later to block release without supplying substrate for new hormone. β-blockade (cautious, ideally short-acting IV) and hydrocortisone 300 mg then 100 mg every 8 h complete the treatment, together with antibiotics.

**Why not the others:**
- A – iodide before a thionamide can fuel further hormone synthesis.
- B – radioiodine is a definitive treatment, not for the acute storm, and may worsen thyroiditis.
- D – salicylates displace T4 from binding proteins; levothyroxine is absurd here.
- E – amiodarone is an iodine load and is not first-line; observation is inadequate.

**Ref:** Ross DS, Thyroid 2016; Taylor P, Eur Thyroid J 2026.

questions.stem: Regarding drugs used in thyroid storm:
options: Propylthiouracil inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.
Agranulocytosis occurs with propylthiouracil but not with methimazole.
Cholestyramine reduces enterohepatic recirculation of thyroid hormone.
Iodide acts mainly by inhibiting peripheral deiodinase.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – an advantage of PTU in the acute storm, in addition to blocking synthesis.
- B (False) – agranulocytosis is a class effect of both thionamides; check the neutrophil count if fever or sore throat.
- C (True) – 4 g every 6 h, an adjunct for severe cases.
- D (False) – iodide acts mainly by blocking hormone release (and synthesis, Wolff–Chaikoff); glucocorticoids, PTU and propranolol inhibit deiodination.

**Ref:** Ross DS, Thyroid 2016; Satoh T, Endocr J 2016.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man in thyroid storm has a heart rate of 150/min, BP 85/60 mmHg, lactate 4 mmol/L and on echocardiography a dilated left ventricle with ejection fraction 20 %. Which is the most appropriate approach to heart rate control?
options: Oral propranolol 80 mg every 4 hours
IV metoprolol 15 mg bolus
Verapamil infusion
No rate control ever in thyroid storm
A cautiously titrated short-acting IV β1-selective blocker (esmolol or landiolol) with haemodynamic monitoring, and escalation to mechanical support if shock worsens
questions.expl:
**Why E:** In low-output thyrotoxic cardiomyopathy, tachycardia contributes to failure, but abrupt β-blockade can cause collapse. Short-acting β1-selective IV agents (esmolol, landiolol) can be titrated and stopped quickly; VA-ECMO is an option for refractory thyrotoxic cardiogenic shock.

**Why not the others:**
- A – long-acting non-selective high-dose propranolol is dangerous with EF 20 % and shock.
- B – a large bolus of a longer-acting agent risks cardiovascular collapse.
- C – verapamil is negatively inotropic and vasodilating.
- D – rate control is a key part of treatment; it just must be cautious here.

**Ref:** Satoh T, Endocr J 2016; Taylor P, Eur Thyroid J 2026.

questions.stem: Regarding myxoedema coma:
options: Hyponatraemia is a common feature.
Hydrocortisone should be given before or with thyroid hormone until adrenal insufficiency is excluded.
Aggressive active external rewarming is the preferred method of rewarming.
Hypoventilation with hypercapnia may require mechanical ventilation.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – reduced free-water clearance and inappropriate ADH secretion.
- B (True) – thyroid hormone increases cortisol clearance and can unmask adrenal insufficiency (coexisting autoimmune or pituitary disease).
- C (False) – passive rewarming is preferred; active external rewarming causes peripheral vasodilatation and cardiovascular collapse.
- D (True) – central hypoventilation, respiratory muscle weakness and macroglossia.

**Ref:** Jonklaas J, Thyroid 2014.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman is found at home in January, drowsy, temperature 32.5 °C, HR 44/min, Na⁺ 121 mmol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L, PaCO₂ 9.1 kPa. TSH is 68 mU/L and free T4 is undetectable. Besides supportive care, which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Oral levothyroxine 25 µg daily, increased every 4 weeks
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 8 h, then IV levothyroxine loading 200–400 µg
IV liothyronine 100 µg bolus
Hypertonic saline only; thyroid hormone after the sodium is normal
Dexamethasone and wait for a short Synacthen test before any thyroid hormone
questions.expl:
**Why B:** This is myxoedema coma. ATA 2014 recommends IV levothyroxine 200–400 µg loading (lower in frail/cardiac patients), then about 1.6 µg/kg/day × 0.75 IV, with hydrocortisone 100 mg every 8 h given first until adrenal insufficiency is excluded.

**Why not the others:**
- A – oral low-dose titration is for stable outpatient hypothyroidism; gut absorption is unreliable in myxoedema coma.
- C – T3 may be added in small doses (5–20 µg); a 100 µg bolus risks ischaemia and arrhythmia.
- D – hyponatraemia is secondary; thyroid hormone should not be delayed.
- E – a cortisol sample is drawn, but treatment should not wait for a Synacthen test.

**Ref:** Jonklaas J, Thyroid 2014.

questions.stem: Regarding thyroid function tests in critically ill patients:
options: A low T3 with raised reverse T3 is typical in the early phase of critical illness.
In prolonged critical illness TSH is often low or normal despite low T4.
Dopamine infusion can suppress TSH secretion.
Heparin can raise measured free T4 levels.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – reduced activation (type 1 deiodinase) and increased inactivation (type 3 deiodinase).
- B (True) – a central (hypothalamic) pattern in prolonged illness.
- C (True) – dopamine and glucocorticoids suppress TSH.
- D (True) – heparin activates lipoprotein lipase; free fatty acids displace T4 from binding proteins in the sample.

**Ref:** Fliers E, Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2015.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man on amiodarone for 2 years develops thyrotoxicosis. Thyroid ultrasound shows a normal-sized gland with absent vascularity on colour-flow Doppler. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Prednisolone 40 mg/day
High-dose methimazole alone
Radioiodine
Potassium iodide
Levothyroxine
questions.expl:
**Why A:** A normal gland with absent vascularity suggests type 2 amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis – a destructive thyroiditis releasing preformed hormone. Glucocorticoids (prednisolone ~ 40 mg/day, tapered over 2–3 months) are first-line.

**Why not the others:**
- B – thionamides are for type 1 (increased synthesis); they are ineffective in destructive thyroiditis.
- C – iodine-loaded glands have low uptake; radioiodine is ineffective.
- D – more iodine is unhelpful.
- E – levothyroxine is for hypothyroidism.

**Ref:** Bartalena L, Eur Thyroid J 2018.

questions.stem: Regarding the diagnosis of thyroid storm:
options: Free T4 is usually much higher in thyroid storm than in uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis and is the key diagnostic test.
A Burch–Wartofsky score of 30 indicates that thyroid storm is excluded.
Central nervous system dysfunction is a core element of the Japan Thyroid Association criteria.
Iodinated contrast is a recognised precipitant.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – hormone levels overlap with uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis; the diagnosis is clinical.
- B (False) – 25–44 means impending storm; ≥ 45 is highly suggestive.
- C (True) – CNS manifestations plus fever, tachycardia, heart failure or GI–hepatic signs.
- D (True) – iodine load (contrast, amiodarone) can precipitate thyrotoxicosis (Jod-Basedow).

**Ref:** Satoh T, Endocr J 2016; Ross DS, Thyroid 2016.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with thyroid storm continues to deteriorate despite 24 hours of PTU, iodide, IV esmolol and hydrocortisone, and develops neutropenia 0.4 × 10⁹/L attributed to PTU. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Switch to methimazole
Radioiodine therapy today
Double the PTU dose
Stop PTU and use therapeutic plasma exchange (± lithium) as a bridge to urgent thyroidectomy
Stop all treatment and observe
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Agranulocytosis contraindicates all thionamides (cross-reactivity). For refractory storm or when thionamides cannot be used, plasma exchange removes hormone, and lithium inhibits release, as a bridge to surgery; the 2026 consensus lists these with ECMO and thyroidectomy for refractory disease.

**Why not the others:**
- A – cross-reactivity between PTU and methimazole for agranulocytosis is high; switching is not recommended.
- B – radioiodine is slow, iodide-loaded glands take it up poorly, and it can worsen thyroiditis.
- C – more PTU worsens the agranulocytosis.
- E – untreated storm is fatal.

**Ref:** Ross DS, Thyroid 2016; Taylor P, Eur Thyroid J 2026.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman is on day 14 of septic shock. TSH 0.3 mU/L, free T4 low-normal, free T3 low. She has no history of thyroid disease. All of the following are appropriate EXCEPT:
options: Interpreting the pattern as non-thyroidal illness syndrome
Considering the effect of dopamine or steroids on TSH
Starting levothyroxine to improve outcome
Repeating thyroid tests after recovery if thyroid disease is still suspected
Recognising that a transient TSH rise may occur during recovery
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Low T3 with low-normal T4 and low–normal TSH in prolonged critical illness is NTIS; thyroid hormone treatment has not been shown to improve outcomes and is not recommended.

**Why not the others:**
- A – this is the typical NTIS pattern.
- B – dopamine and glucocorticoids suppress TSH.
- D – retesting after recovery distinguishes NTIS from true disease.
- E – TSH may rise transiently during recovery; this is not primary hypothyroidism.

**Ref:** Fliers E, Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2015.

questions.stem: Regarding amiodarone and the thyroid:
options: Amiodarone contains about 37 % iodine by weight.
In euthyroid patients, amiodarone typically lowers T4 and raises T3.
Glucocorticoids are the first-line treatment of type 1 amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis.
Amiodarone must always be stopped in amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – a large iodine load, causing both hypo- and hyperthyroidism.
- B (False) – it inhibits type 1 deiodinase: T4 and rT3 rise, T3 falls.
- C (False) – type 1 AIT (iodine-driven synthesis in an abnormal gland) is treated with thionamides ± perchlorate; glucocorticoids are first-line for type 2 (destructive) AIT.
- D (False) – it may be continued if essential for arrhythmia control, after a joint decision with cardiology.

**Ref:** Bartalena L, Eur Thyroid J 2018.

open.q: Describe the management of thyroid storm in the ICU.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Clinical diagnosis (BWPS ≥ 45, JTA criteria); do not wait for labs; ICU admission; identify and treat the precipitant (infection, drug withdrawal, iodine, surgery).
- **β-blockade:** propranolol 60–80 mg PO every 4 h or IV esmolol/landiolol (β1-selective, titratable – echo first; caution in low-output failure).
- **Thionamide:** PTU 500–1,000 mg load then 250 mg every 4 h (also blocks T4 → T3) or methimazole 60–80 mg/day.
- **Iodide ≥ 1 h after thionamide:** SSKI 5 drops every 6 h or Lugol's.
- **Hydrocortisone** 300 mg then 100 mg every 8 h; **cholestyramine** 4 g every 6 h.
- Supportive: cooling, paracetamol (no aspirin), fluids, glucose, thiamine, AF rate control and anticoagulation, VTE prophylaxis.
- Refractory: lithium, plasma exchange, VA-ECMO, urgent thyroidectomy; definitive therapy once stable.

title: W19 · D4 – Adrenal insufficiency, adrenal crisis and critical illness–related corticosteroid insufficiency (CIRCI)

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman with known Addison's disease presents with 2 days of vomiting and diarrhoea. BP 70/40 mmHg, Na⁺ 124 mmol/L, K⁺ 6.1 mmol/L, glucose 3.0 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Short Synacthen test, then treat according to the result
Dexamethasone 4 mg IV and fludrocortisone 100 µg orally
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV, then 200 mg/24 h, with rapid IV isotonic fluids and dextrose
Noradrenaline infusion and wait for cortisol results
Oral hydrocortisone 20 mg and antiemetics
questions.expl:
**Why C:** This is adrenal crisis. Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately, then 200 mg/24 h (infusion or 50 mg every 6 h), with isotonic fluid (about 1 L in the first hour) and dextrose for hypoglycaemia. At these doses hydrocortisone also supplies enough mineralocorticoid activity.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the diagnosis is known; testing would only delay life-saving treatment.
- B – dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity, and oral fludrocortisone is unreliable with vomiting.
- D – vasopressors will fail without glucocorticoid; never wait for results.
- E – oral therapy fails with vomiting and shock.

**Ref:** Bornstein SR, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2016.

questions.stem: Regarding primary and secondary adrenal insufficiency:
options: Hyperkalaemia is typical of secondary (pituitary) adrenal insufficiency.
Hyperpigmentation suggests primary adrenal insufficiency.
Withdrawal of long-term exogenous glucocorticoids is the commonest cause of adrenal insufficiency.
Aldosterone secretion depends mainly on ACTH.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – aldosterone is preserved in secondary AI, so hyperkalaemia is typical of primary AI.
- B (True) – high ACTH (POMC-derived MSH) causes pigmentation.
- C (True) – HPA suppression after ≥ 4 weeks of supraphysiological doses.
- D (False) – aldosterone is controlled mainly by renin–angiotensin and potassium.

**Ref:** Bornstein SR, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2016; Beuschlein F, Eur J Endocrinol 2024.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with pneumococcal septic shock has received 3 L of crystalloid and is on noradrenaline 0.35 µg/kg/min for 6 hours. Random cortisol is 720 nmol/L. What is the most appropriate approach to corticosteroids?
options: Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (50 mg every 6 h or infusion), regardless of the cortisol value
No steroids because the cortisol is high
Perform a short Synacthen test and give steroids only if Δ cortisol < 250 nmol/L
Methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3 days
Dexamethasone 6 mg/day for 10 days
questions.expl:
**Why A:** For septic shock with an ongoing vasopressor requirement (noradrenaline ≥ 0.25 µg/kg/min for ≥ 4 h), SSC suggests IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day; the decision does not depend on cortisol levels or stimulation tests. Steroids speed shock reversal (ADRENAL, APROCCHSS).

**Why not the others:**
- B – total cortisol does not reflect tissue corticosteroid activity and does not predict response.
- C – CORTICUS showed that the ACTH test did not identify responders; guidelines do not use it to guide therapy.
- D – SCCM 2024 recommends against high-dose short-course steroids (> 400 mg/day for < 3 days).
- E – dexamethasone 6 mg is the COVID-19 regimen, not septic shock.

**Ref:** Prescott HC (SSC 2026), Crit Care Med 2026; Chaudhuri D, Crit Care Med 2024; Annane D, Intensive Care Med 2017.

questions.stem: Regarding the major trials of corticosteroids in septic shock:
options: ADRENAL showed a significant reduction in 90-day mortality with hydrocortisone 200 mg/day.
APROCCHSS combined hydrocortisone with fludrocortisone.
HYPRESS showed that hydrocortisone prevents progression from sepsis to septic shock.
CORTICUS showed a significant mortality benefit in ACTH non-responders.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – 27.9 vs 28.8 % (NS), though shock resolved faster and ventilation was shorter.
- B (True) – HC 50 mg every 6 h + fludrocortisone 50 µg/day for 7 days; 90-day mortality 43.0 vs 49.1 %.
- C (False) – progression to shock 21.2 vs 22.9 % (NS).
- D (False) – no mortality difference in either responders or non-responders; the ACTH test did not predict benefit.

**Ref:** Venkatesh B, N Engl J Med 2018; Annane D, N Engl J Med 2018.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with severe community-acquired pneumonia (no shock, no influenza) is admitted to the ICU on high-flow oxygen. According to the SCCM 2024 focused update, which statement on corticosteroids is correct?
options: Corticosteroids are recommended against in all CAP
Corticosteroids are recommended (strong recommendation) in severe bacterial CAP
Only methylprednisolone 1 g/day is effective
They are indicated only if adrenal insufficiency is proven
Fludrocortisone alone is recommended
questions.expl:
**Why B:** SCCM 2024 makes a strong recommendation (moderate certainty) for corticosteroids in hospitalised adults with severe bacterial CAP, based largely on CAPE COD (hydrocortisone 200 mg/day, 28-day mortality 6.2 vs 11.9 %). The REMAP-CAP corticosteroid domain (2025) later suggested no large benefit, so the evidence remains debated.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the recommendation is for, not against, in severe CAP.
- C – high-dose pulses are not the evidence-based regimen.
- D – benefit is anti-inflammatory, not replacement.
- E – fludrocortisone has no role in CAP.

**Ref:** Chaudhuri D, Crit Care Med 2024; Dequin PF (CAPE COD), N Engl J Med 2023; REMAP-CAP, Intensive Care Med 2025.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man on long-term prednisolone 15 mg/day for polymyalgia is admitted for emergency laparotomy with peritonitis. Which perioperative steroid strategy is most appropriate?
options: Stop prednisolone because of infection risk
Continue prednisolone 15 mg orally only
Give fludrocortisone instead
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction, then 200 mg/24 h, tapering as he recovers
Dexamethasone 0.5 mg daily
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Chronic use of ≥ 5 mg prednisolone-equivalent for > 4 weeks may suppress the HPA axis. The ESE/ES 2024 guideline recommends stress dosing for major surgery or critical illness – hydrocortisone 100 mg IV then 200 mg/24 h – tapering to the usual dose over days as the stress resolves.

**Why not the others:**
- A – abrupt cessation risks adrenal crisis.
- B – the usual dose is insufficient for major stress, and absorption may fail after laparotomy.
- C – fludrocortisone has no glucocorticoid stress coverage.
- E – a tiny dexamethasone dose is inadequate.

**Ref:** Beuschlein F, Eur J Endocrinol 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding the diagnosis of critical illness–related corticosteroid insufficiency (CIRCI):
options: A Δ cortisol below 9 µg/dL (250 nmol/L) after 250 µg cosyntropin is a suggested diagnostic criterion.
Total cortisol accurately reflects free cortisol in hypoalbuminaemic patients.
Elevated cortisol in critical illness is partly caused by reduced cortisol breakdown.
Routine measurement of plasma free cortisol is recommended.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – or a random total cortisol < 10 µg/dL (276 nmol/L) (conditional, low quality).
- B (False) – low CBG and albumin mean total cortisol underestimates free cortisol.
- C (True) – suppressed hepatic and renal metabolism (Boonen, NEJM 2013), with ACTH often low.
- D (False) – the 2017 guideline suggests against routine free cortisol measurement.

**Ref:** Annane D, Intensive Care Med 2017; Boonen E, N Engl J Med 2013.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with septic shock is to be intubated. Her family asks about etomidate and adrenal suppression. Which statement is best supported by the RSI trial (2025)?
options: Etomidate increased 28-day mortality compared with ketamine
Ketamine caused less peri-intubation cardiovascular collapse
Etomidate must always be followed by 7 days of hydrocortisone
28-day in-hospital mortality did not differ between ketamine and etomidate
Etomidate does not affect cortisol synthesis
questions.expl:
**Why D:** The RSI trial (n = 2,365) found 28-day in-hospital mortality of 28.1 % with ketamine vs 29.1 % with etomidate (no significant difference). Cardiovascular collapse was more frequent with ketamine (22.1 vs 17.0 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – no mortality difference was found.
- B – collapse was more frequent with ketamine.
- C – routine steroid cover after a single dose of etomidate is not required.
- E – etomidate inhibits 11β-hydroxylase for 24–72 h; the clinical significance is what is uncertain.

**Ref:** Casey JD (RSI), N Engl J Med 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding adverse effects and practical use of hydrocortisone in septic shock:
options: Continuous infusion causes more glycaemic variability than bolus dosing.
Hyperglycaemia is a common adverse effect.
High-dose short-course regimens (> 400 mg/day for < 3 days) are recommended in refractory shock.
Fludrocortisone requires enteral absorption.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – infusion gives *less* glycaemic variability.
- B (True) – seen in ADRENAL and APROCCHSS.
- C (False) – SCCM 2024 recommends against them (strong, moderate).
- D (True) – it is given orally/enterally (50 µg/day in APROCCHSS); absorption may be poor in gut failure.

**Ref:** Chaudhuri D, Crit Care Med 2024; Annane D, N Engl J Med 2018.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with meningococcal sepsis develops refractory shock with petechiae and purpura. CT shows bilateral adrenal enlargement with haemorrhage. All of the following are correct EXCEPT:
options: This is consistent with Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome
He requires stress-dose hydrocortisone
Long-term glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement may be needed
Hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia may develop
Fludrocortisone must be added immediately even with hydrocortisone 200 mg/day
questions.expl:
**Why E:** At hydrocortisone doses above 50 mg/day, its mineralocorticoid activity is sufficient; fludrocortisone is added only when the dose is reduced to maintenance in primary AI.

**Why not the others:**
- A – bilateral adrenal haemorrhage in meningococcaemia is Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome.
- B – primary adrenal failure requires stress-dose hydrocortisone.
- C – adrenal destruction may be permanent.
- D – loss of aldosterone gives hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia.

**Ref:** Bornstein SR, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2016.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with sepsis from pyelonephritis is normotensive (MAP 75 mmHg) without vasopressors, lactate 1.8 mmol/L. A colleague suggests hydrocortisone to prevent septic shock. What does the evidence show?
options: Hydrocortisone reduces progression to septic shock by about half
Hydrocortisone improves 28-day survival in sepsis without shock
Hydrocortisone did not prevent progression to septic shock (HYPRESS)
Steroids should be given if random cortisol is < 700 nmol/L
Only fludrocortisone prevents shock
questions.expl:
**Why C:** HYPRESS (n = 380) found no reduction in progression to septic shock (21.2 vs 22.9 %) with hydrocortisone 200 mg/day in sepsis without shock, and more hyperglycaemia. Guidelines restrict corticosteroids to septic shock.

**Why not the others:**
- A – no reduction was found.
- B – there was no survival benefit.
- D – cortisol levels do not guide steroid use in sepsis.
- E – there is no evidence for fludrocortisone alone.

**Ref:** Keh D (HYPRESS), JAMA 2016; Prescott HC (SSC 2026), Crit Care Med 2026.

open.q: Summarise the evidence and recommendations for corticosteroids in septic shock.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Rationale: CIRCI (HPA dysfunction, altered metabolism, tissue resistance), restore vascular responsiveness, anti-inflammatory effect.
- Trials: Annane 2002 (non-responders benefit), CORTICUS (no mortality benefit, ACTH test not predictive), ADRENAL (n = 3,800, HC 200 mg/day – no mortality difference, faster shock reversal), APROCCHSS (HC + fludrocortisone – 90-day mortality 43.0 vs 49.1 %); HYPRESS – no benefit in sepsis without shock.
- Recommendations: SSC 2021/2026 – suggest IV corticosteroids in septic shock (conditional), hydrocortisone 200 mg/day when noradrenaline ≥ 0.25 µg/kg/min ≥ 4 h; SCCM 2024 – against > 400 mg/day for < 3 days; no cortisol testing to decide.
- Adverse effects: hyperglycaemia, hypernatraemia, weakness; fludrocortisone optional.
- Related: severe CAP (strong recommendation, CAPE COD; REMAP-CAP 2025 neutral/possible harm), ARDS (suggested).

title: W19 · D5 – Pituitary emergencies, diabetes insipidus (AVP deficiency) and SIADH

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man is on day 2 after severe traumatic brain injury. Urine output is 450 mL/h for 3 hours, Na⁺ has risen from 142 to 154 mmol/L, serum osmolality 318 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 110 mOsm/kg. He received no mannitol. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Furosemide
Desmopressin and replacement of free-water losses
Fluid restriction
Hydrochlorothiazide
3 % saline
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Large-volume dilute urine (Uosm 110 mOsm/kg) with rising Na⁺ and high serum osmolality after TBI is central DI (AVP deficiency). Desmopressin 1–2 µg IV/SC and replacement of free-water losses (enteral water or 5 % dextrose) are indicated, with frequent Na⁺ checks.

**Why not the others:**
- A – a loop diuretic would worsen water loss.
- C – restriction would cause dangerous hypernatraemia.
- D – thiazides are used in nephrogenic DI, not acute central DI.
- E – hypertonic saline would worsen hypernatraemia.

**Ref:** Christ-Crain M, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2019.

questions.stem: Regarding polyuria in the ICU:
options: A urine osmolality of 450 mOsm/kg in a polyuric patient indicates central diabetes insipidus.
Lithium causes central diabetes insipidus by inhibiting AVP release.
Hypokalaemia protects against nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
Desmopressin is effective in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – polyuria with Uosm > 300 mOsm/kg is a solute diuresis (glucose, mannitol, urea, saline).
- B (False) – lithium enters collecting-duct cells via ENaC and causes AVP resistance (nephrogenic DI).
- C (False) – hypokalaemia (and hypercalcaemia) *cause* nephrogenic DI.
- D (False) – the kidney does not respond to AVP; treatment is thiazides, amiloride, NSAIDs and removal of the cause.

**Ref:** Christ-Crain M, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2019.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man on warfarin develops sudden severe headache, bitemporal visual loss and a right third-nerve palsy. BP 92/60 mmHg, Na⁺ 129 mmol/L, glucose 3.6 mmol/L. MRI shows haemorrhage into a pituitary macroadenoma. What is the most urgent treatment?
options: Levothyroxine 100 µg IV
Desmopressin
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV, then 50 mg every 6 h
Cabergoline
Hypertonic saline 3 % 150 mL
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Pituitary apoplexy causes acute ACTH deficiency in most patients; hypotension, hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia point to it. Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV then 50 mg every 6 h (or infusion) is given immediately; warfarin is reversed and neurosurgery considered for visual loss.

**Why not the others:**
- A – thyroxine before cortisol replacement may precipitate adrenal crisis.
- B – there are no features of DI.
- D – cabergoline treats prolactinoma; it is not the emergency treatment.
- E – hyponatraemia is mild and due to cortisol deficiency; hydrocortisone corrects it.

**Ref:** Rajasekaran S, Clin Endocrinol 2011.

questions.stem: Regarding the criteria for SIADH (European hyponatraemia guideline 2014):
options: Urine osmolality must be above 100 mOsm/kg.
Urine sodium is typically below 20 mmol/L.
The patient must be clinically hypovolaemic.
Adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism must be excluded.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Uosm > 100 mOsm/kg shows inappropriate AVP activity despite hypotonicity.
- B (False) – urine Na⁺ is > 30 mmol/L on normal salt and water intake.
- C (False) – SIADH requires clinical euvolaemia; hypovolaemia suggests salt loss (diuretics, CSW, vomiting).
- D (True) – cortisol deficiency and hypothyroidism cause an identical biochemical picture.

**Ref:** Spasovski G, Eur J Endocrinol 2014.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman on an SSRI is admitted after two seizures. Na⁺ 112 mmol/L, serum osmolality 238 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 420 mOsm/kg, urine Na⁺ 55 mmol/L, euvolaemic. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: Fluid restriction to 800 mL/day
Tolvaptan 15 mg orally
0.9 % saline 1 L over 1 hour
3 % saline 150 mL over 20 minutes, repeated if needed until Na⁺ rises by 5 mmol/L
3 % saline infusion aiming to normalise Na⁺ within 24 hours
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Seizures are a severe symptom. The European guideline recommends 150 mL of 3 % saline over 20 min, checking Na⁺ and repeating (up to twice more) until Na⁺ rises by 5 mmol/L or symptoms improve, then limiting the rise to ≤ 10 mmol/L in the first 24 h.

**Why not the others:**
- A – fluid restriction is too slow for severe symptoms.
- B – vasopressin antagonists are not recommended for acute severe hyponatraemia (overcorrection risk).
- C – in SIADH with Uosm 420, isotonic saline may worsen hyponatraemia (desalination).
- E – normalising Na⁺ in 24 h (+ 23 mmol/L) would risk osmotic demyelination.

**Ref:** Spasovski G, Eur J Endocrinol 2014.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old alcoholic man with Na⁺ 108 mmol/L and K⁺ 2.8 mmol/L has a sodium of 119 mmol/L 12 hours after admission, with a urine output of 600 mL/h of dilute urine. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give 5 % dextrose (e.g. 10 mL/kg over 1 h) and desmopressin 2 µg IV to re-lower sodium
Continue current management; the rise is acceptable
Give furosemide to control urine output
Start 3 % saline
Give fludrocortisone
questions.expl:
**Why A:** He has already risen 11 mmol/L in 12 h, exceeding the 24-h limit, during a water diuresis; he is at very high risk of osmotic demyelination (alcoholism, hypokalaemia, malnutrition, Na⁺ < 110). The guideline advises stopping active treatment and re-lowering Na⁺ with electrolyte-free water and desmopressin.

**Why not the others:**
- B – > 10 mmol/L in 24 h (and 8 in high-risk patients) is overcorrection.
- C – furosemide would increase free-water loss and raise Na⁺ further.
- D – hypertonic saline would increase overcorrection.
- E – fludrocortisone has no role here.

**Ref:** Spasovski G, Eur J Endocrinol 2014.

questions.stem: Regarding copeptin-based diagnosis of polyuria–polydipsia syndrome:
options: Copeptin is released in equimolar amounts with AVP.
Hypertonic saline–stimulated copeptin was more accurate than the water deprivation test.
Arginine-stimulated copeptin was more accurate than hypertonic saline–stimulated copeptin.
A baseline copeptin ≥ 21.4 pmol/L without fluid restriction suggests AVP resistance.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – it is the C-terminal fragment of the AVP precursor and is stable in plasma.
- B (True) – 96.5 vs 76.6 % (cut-off > 4.9 pmol/L = primary polydipsia).
- C (False) – arginine stimulation was simpler but less accurate (74.4 vs 95.6 %).
- D (True) – high baseline copeptin reflects high AVP with renal resistance.

**Ref:** Fenske W, N Engl J Med 2018; Refardt J, N Engl J Med 2023.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman is on day 6 after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. Na⁺ has fallen to 127 mmol/L, urine Na⁺ 120 mmol/L, urine output 4 L/day, negative fluid balance and rising haematocrit. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Fluid restriction to 1 L/day
Tolvaptan
Furosemide and fluid restriction
Desmopressin
Isotonic or hypertonic saline to replace salt and volume losses, ± fludrocortisone
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Natriuresis with negative balance and haemoconcentration suggests cerebral salt wasting. After SAH, hypovolaemia increases the risk of delayed cerebral ischaemia, so salt and volume are replaced (isotonic/hypertonic saline); fludrocortisone can reduce natriuresis.

**Why not the others:**
- A – fluid restriction in SAH increases delayed cerebral ischaemia.
- B – aquaresis would worsen hypovolaemia.
- C – both measures worsen volume depletion.
- D – she is not losing free water but salt; desmopressin would worsen hyponatraemia.

**Ref:** Spasovski G, Eur J Endocrinol 2014.

questions.stem: Regarding water disorders after transsphenoidal pituitary surgery:
options: Transient diabetes insipidus is common in the first postoperative days.
Delayed hyponatraemia typically occurs around day 5–10.
In the triphasic response, the second phase is due to uncontrolled release of stored AVP.
Permanent diabetes insipidus develops in most patients.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – about 15–30 % on days 1–2.
- B (True) – SIADH-type hyponatraemia around day 5–10; patients are advised to limit fluid intake after discharge.
- C (True) – release from degenerating posterior pituitary neurons.
- D (False) – permanent DI occurs only when > 80–90 % of AVP neurons are lost – a minority.

**Ref:** Christ-Crain M, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2019.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with small-cell lung cancer has asymptomatic chronic hyponatraemia (Na⁺ 126 mmol/L) due to SIADH; urine osmolality 620 mOsm/kg, urine Na⁺ 90, urine K⁺ 50, serum Na⁺ 126 mmol/L. All of the following are reasonable EXCEPT:
options: Recognising that fluid restriction is likely to fail
Oral urea 0.25–0.5 g/kg/day
Low-dose loop diuretic with oral salt
Treating the underlying tumour
Demeclocycline as first-line therapy
questions.expl:
**Why E:** The European guideline recommends against lithium and demeclocycline (nephrotoxicity, unpredictable effect) for SIADH.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Furst ratio (90 + 50)/126 > 1 and Uosm > 500 predict failure of fluid restriction.
- B – urea is an effective second-line therapy (osmotic diuresis).
- C – an accepted second-line option.
- D – chemotherapy for SCLC may resolve ectopic AVP secretion.

**Ref:** Spasovski G, Eur J Endocrinol 2014.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman has been in the ICU for 5 days with Na⁺ 162 mmol/L after aggressive diuresis; she weighs 60 kg. What is the safest correction plan?
options: Lower Na⁺ by 20 mmol/L within 12 hours
Correct the free-water deficit (≈ 0.5 × 60 × [162/140 − 1] ≈ 4.7 L) plus ongoing losses, aiming for ≤ 10–12 mmol/L per 24 h
Give 0.9 % saline until Na⁺ normalises
Haemodialysis to normalise Na⁺ within 6 hours
Withhold water because hypernatraemia is self-limiting
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In chronic (> 48 h) hypernatraemia, the brain has adapted with organic osmolytes; rapid lowering risks cerebral oedema. The water deficit is replaced (enteral water or 5 % dextrose) plus ongoing losses, lowering Na⁺ by about 0.5 mmol/L/h (≤ 10–12 mmol/L per day).

**Why not the others:**
- A – 20 mmol/L in 12 h is far too fast for chronic hypernatraemia.
- C – isotonic saline does not correct a free-water deficit (only if hypovolaemic shock).
- D – dialysis would correct far too fast and is not indicated.
- E – ICU hypernatraemia is associated with mortality and must be treated.

**Ref:** Christ-Crain M, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2019; Spasovski G, Eur J Endocrinol 2014.

open.q: Outline the diagnostic approach to hyponatraemia in the ICU and the criteria for SIADH.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Assess symptoms (severe → treat first with 3 % saline 150 mL over 20 min ×2–3, aim + 5 mmol/L).
- Serum osmolality: exclude pseudohyponatraemia (lipids, protein) and hypertonic hyponatraemia (glucose, mannitol).
- Urine osmolality: ≤ 100 → excess water intake; > 100 → AVP activity.
- Urine Na⁺: ≤ 30 → low effective volume (hypovolaemia, heart failure, cirrhosis); > 30 → diuretics, SIADH, adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, CSW, renal salt loss.
- SIADH criteria: Posm < 275, Uosm > 100, euvolaemia, UNa > 30, normal thyroid/adrenal/renal function, no diuretics; causes CNS, lung, cancer, drugs, pain/nausea.
- Correction limits ≤ 10 mmol/L first 24 h, ≤ 8 thereafter; re-lower with D5W + desmopressin if overcorrected; ODS risk factors.

title: W19 · Saturday – weekly review: Endocrine (DKA and HHS, ICU glucose control, thyroid emergencies, adrenal insufficiency and CIRCI, pituitary, DI and SIADH)

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with type 1 diabetes has glucose 31 mmol/L, venous pH 7.04, HCO₃⁻ 6 mmol/L, β-hydroxybutyrate 6.8 mmol/L and K⁺ 4.6 mmol/L. After the first litre of crystalloid, which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol IV
Insulin bolus 10 units IV, then subcutaneous insulin
Fixed-rate IV insulin 0.1 U/kg/h with potassium 20–40 mmol per litre of fluid
Withhold potassium until K⁺ falls below 3.5 mmol/L
Fixed-rate insulin 0.05 U/kg/h without potassium
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Severe DKA is treated with fixed-rate IV insulin 0.1 U/kg/h (no bolus needed). With K⁺ between 3.5 and 5.0–5.5 mmol/L, 20–40 mmol K⁺ is added to each litre to prevent insulin-induced hypokalaemia.

**Why not the others:**
- A – bicarbonate is not routine; the 2024 consensus allows it only for pH < 7.0.
- B – subcutaneous insulin is for mild or uncomplicated moderate DKA, not severe DKA.
- D – waiting for hypokalaemia is dangerous; replacement starts below 5.0–5.5 mmol/L.
- E – 0.05 U/kg/h is the HHS dose; omitting K⁺ is dangerous.

**Ref:** Umpierrez GE, Diabetes Care 2024; Dhatariya KK, Diabet Med 2022. → [D1](D1.md)
