questions.stem: Regarding the hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state:
options: Insulin at 0.1 U/kg/h should be started before any fluid is given.
Sodium should fall by no more than about 10 mmol/L in 24 hours.
Effective osmolality is calculated as 2 × Na⁺ + glucose + urea.
Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis is recommended.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – fluids come first; insulin is started at 0.05 U/kg/h when glucose stops falling with fluids (JBDS), unless there is significant ketonaemia.
- B (True) – rapid changes risk cerebral oedema and osmotic demyelination.
- C (False) – urea is an ineffective osmole; effective osmolality = 2 × Na⁺ + glucose.
- D (True) – LMWH for all unless contraindicated.

**Ref:** Mustafa OG, Diabet Med 2023. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with DKA has been treated for 10 hours. Glucose is 8.5 mmol/L, β-hydroxybutyrate 2.4 mmol/L, pH 7.24. The nurse proposes stopping the insulin infusion because glucose is normal. What is the best response?
options: Stop insulin and restart if glucose rises
Continue fixed-rate insulin and add 10 % dextrose
Switch to subcutaneous insulin now
Give bicarbonate and stop insulin
Halve the insulin rate and stop dextrose
questions.expl:
**Why B:** The target of treatment is ketone clearance and correction of acidosis (BHB < 0.6 mmol/L and pH ≥ 7.30), not a normal glucose. Dextrose is added (from glucose < 13.9–14 mmol/L) so that insulin can continue.

**Why not the others:**
- A – stopping insulin with BHB 2.4 mmol/L allows ketoacidosis to worsen.
- C – DKA has not resolved; transition is made only after resolution, with overlap.
- D – bicarbonate is not indicated and insulin is still needed.
- E – reducing insulin and stopping dextrose slows ketone clearance and risks hypoglycaemia.

**Ref:** Umpierrez GE, Diabetes Care 2024. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man after cardiac surgery is on an insulin infusion. Which glucose target is best supported by the current evidence and guidelines?
options: Below 12 mmol/L without insulin
7.8–10 mmol/L
10–14 mmol/L
questions.expl:
**Why D:** After NICE-SUGAR (increased mortality with 4.5–6.0 mmol/L) and TGC-fast (no benefit of 4.4–6.1 mmol/L without early PN), guidelines start insulin at ≥ 10 mmol/L and target about 7.8–10 mmol/L; SCCM 2024 suggests against an intensive 4.4–7.7 mmol/L range.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the Leuven target; not beneficial in multicentre trials and increases hypoglycaemia.
- B – also within the intensive range the SCCM 2024 guideline suggests against.
- C – leaving glucose up to 12 mmol/L untreated is above the insulin threshold.
- E – sustained values > 10 mmol/L are associated with infection after cardiac surgery.

**Ref:** NICE-SUGAR Investigators, N Engl J Med 2009; Honarmand K, Crit Care Med 2024. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: Regarding glucose control trials in the ICU:
options: In NICE-SUGAR, intensive control increased 90-day mortality.
VISEP was stopped early because of hypoglycaemia.
TGC-fast reduced ICU length of stay with tight glucose control.
In Leuven I, patients commonly received early parenteral nutrition.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 27.5 vs 24.9 %.
- B (True) – severe hypoglycaemia 17.0 vs 4.1 %.
- C (False) – HR 1.00 for ICU discharge; no difference in 90-day mortality.
- D (True) – early IV glucose/PN made the control arm very hyperglycaemic.

**Ref:** NICE-SUGAR Investigators, N Engl J Med 2009; Gunst J, N Engl J Med 2023; Van den Berghe G, N Engl J Med 2001. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman in septic shock on noradrenaline has a fingerstick glucose of 2.9 mmol/L; she has marked peripheral oedema and Hb 70 g/L. Her enteral feed was stopped 2 hours ago for a CT scan while her insulin infusion continued. All of the following are appropriate EXCEPT:
options: Stopping the insulin infusion
Checking glucose on arterial blood with a blood-gas analyser
Giving IV dextrose if hypoglycaemia is confirmed
Increasing the insulin infusion because capillary values are unreliable
Revising the protocol to couple insulin with nutrition
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Capillary errors can go either way; a low reading with insulin running and nutrition stopped is very likely true hypoglycaemia. Increasing insulin is dangerous.

**Why not the others:**
- A – insulin is stopped while hypoglycaemia is confirmed and treated.
- B – arterial blood on a blood-gas analyser is more reliable in shock, oedema and anaemia.
- C – IV dextrose is the treatment of choice.
- E – interrupting nutrition with insulin running is a classic preventable cause.

**Ref:** Honarmand K, Crit Care Med 2024; NICE-SUGAR Investigators, N Engl J Med 2012. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman with Graves' disease has a Burch–Wartofsky score of 55. Methimazole 20 mg has just been given orally. When should iodide be started?
options: Before the methimazole
At least 1 hour after the thionamide
Only after 2 weeks of thionamide
Never – iodide is contraindicated in Graves' disease
Only if radioiodine is planned the same week
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Iodide blocks the release of preformed hormone; it is given at least 1 hour after a thionamide, so that the iodine cannot be used as substrate for new hormone synthesis. (In storm the thionamide dose should be high – methimazole 60–80 mg/day or PTU.)

**Why not the others:**
- A – iodide first may fuel synthesis and worsen thyrotoxicosis.
- C – a 2-week delay is inappropriate in a storm.
- D – iodide is part of standard storm treatment.
- E – iodide reduces radioiodine uptake for weeks; it is not given to prepare for radioiodine.

**Ref:** Ross DS, Thyroid 2016; Taylor P, Eur Thyroid J 2026. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: Regarding thyroid emergencies:
options: Aspirin is the preferred antipyretic in thyroid storm.
In myxoedema coma, hydrocortisone should be started with or before thyroid hormone.
Type 2 amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis is treated mainly with thionamides.
In non-thyroidal illness syndrome, T3 is low and reverse T3 is raised.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – salicylates displace T4 from binding proteins; paracetamol and cooling are used.
- B (True) – thyroid hormone increases cortisol clearance and may precipitate adrenal crisis.
- C (False) – type 2 (destructive thyroiditis) is treated with glucocorticoids; type 1 with thionamides.
- D (True) – altered deiodinase activity; thyroid hormone treatment is not recommended.

**Ref:** Ross DS, Thyroid 2016; Jonklaas J, Thyroid 2014; Bartalena L, Eur Thyroid J 2018; Fliers E, Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2015. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman is admitted in winter with GCS 9, temperature 31.8 °C, HR 40/min, PaCO₂ 10 kPa, Na⁺ 118 mmol/L. TSH 90 mU/L, free T4 very low. What is the most important element of rewarming?
options: Forced-air active external rewarming to 37 °C within 2 hours
Warm-water immersion
Immediate VA-ECMO
No rewarming until thyroid hormone has normalised
Passive rewarming, with thyroid hormone and hydrocortisone, avoiding aggressive active external rewarming
questions.expl:
**Why E:** In myxoedema coma, aggressive active external rewarming causes peripheral vasodilatation and cardiovascular collapse. Passive rewarming (blankets, warm room) is used while IV levothyroxine (200–400 µg load), hydrocortisone and ventilatory support correct the underlying hypometabolism.

**Why not the others:**
- A – rapid active external rewarming risks collapse.
- B – immersion is impractical and causes vasodilatation.
- C – ECMO is reserved for refractory cardiovascular collapse, not first-line.
- D – hypothermia must be addressed; thyroid hormone takes days to normalise.

**Ref:** Jonklaas J, Thyroid 2014. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with faecal peritonitis has septic shock requiring noradrenaline 0.4 µg/kg/min for 5 hours despite fluids and source control. What is the most appropriate corticosteroid strategy?
options: Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (infusion or 50 mg every 6 h), ± fludrocortisone 50 µg/day
Methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg once
No corticosteroids until a short Synacthen test is available
Dexamethasone 20 mg/day
Prednisolone 5 mg/day orally
questions.expl:
**Why A:** For septic shock with ongoing vasopressor need (noradrenaline ≥ 0.25 µg/kg/min ≥ 4 h), the SSC suggests IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day; APROCCHSS added fludrocortisone 50 µg/day and showed lower 90-day mortality (43.0 vs 49.1 %).

**Why not the others:**
- B – high-dose short courses are recommended against (SCCM 2024).
- C – test results do not guide steroid use in septic shock.
- D – high-dose dexamethasone has no evidence in septic shock and no mineralocorticoid effect.
- E – a physiological oral dose is insufficient and unreliable in shock.

**Ref:** Prescott HC (SSC 2026), Crit Care Med 2026; Annane D, N Engl J Med 2018; Chaudhuri D, Crit Care Med 2024. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: Regarding adrenal insufficiency:
options: Hyperkalaemia suggests primary rather than secondary adrenal insufficiency.
Dexamethasone provides adequate mineralocorticoid replacement in adrenal crisis.
Hydrocortisone above 50 mg/day has sufficient mineralocorticoid activity.
A short Synacthen test must be performed before treating suspected adrenal crisis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – aldosterone is lost only in primary disease.
- B (False) – dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity.
- C (True) – fludrocortisone is not needed during stress dosing.
- D (False) – take cortisol/ACTH if possible, but never delay hydrocortisone 100 mg IV.

**Ref:** Bornstein SR, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2016. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with severe community-acquired pneumococcal pneumonia on high-flow oxygen (no shock, no influenza) is admitted to the ICU. According to the SCCM 2024 focused update, which statement is correct?
options: Corticosteroids are recommended (strong recommendation)
Corticosteroids are recommended against
There is no recommendation for severe CAP
Only fludrocortisone is suggested
Steroids are indicated only after a positive Synacthen test
questions.expl:
**Why A:** SCCM 2024 recommends corticosteroids for hospitalised adults with severe bacterial CAP (strong, moderate certainty), largely based on CAPE COD (hydrocortisone 200 mg/day: 28-day mortality 6.2 vs 11.9 %). REMAP-CAP (2025) later found no evidence of a large benefit, so the debate continues.

**Why not the others:**
- B – the recommendation is in favour.
- C – "no recommendation" applies to *less severe* CAP.
- D – fludrocortisone has no role in CAP.
- E – the effect is anti-inflammatory, not replacement.

**Ref:** Chaudhuri D, Crit Care Med 2024; Dequin PF, N Engl J Med 2023; REMAP-CAP, Intensive Care Med 2025. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has a serum Na⁺ of 120 mmol/L, serum osmolality 252 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg and urine Na⁺ 60 mmol/L. She is clinically euvolaemic, takes no diuretics and has only mild headache. Which investigation must be completed before diagnosing SIADH?
options: Water deprivation test
Morning cortisol (or Synacthen test) and TSH/free T4
Arginine-stimulated copeptin
MRI of the pituitary
Renal biopsy
questions.expl:
**Why B:** The SIADH criteria require exclusion of adrenal insufficiency (especially secondary) and hypothyroidism, which produce an identical biochemical picture (euvolaemia, Uosm > 100, UNa > 30).

**Why not the others:**
- A – the water deprivation test is for polyuria, and is dangerous in hyponatraemia.
- C – copeptin stimulation tests are for the polyuria–polydipsia syndrome.
- D – MRI may follow if hypopituitarism is found, but is not a criterion.
- E – there is no indication for biopsy.

**Ref:** Spasovski G, Eur J Endocrinol 2014. → [D5](D5.md)

questions.stem: Regarding diabetes insipidus (AVP deficiency/resistance):
options: Central diabetes insipidus is common after brain death.
Polyuria with a urine osmolality of 600 mOsm/kg after mannitol is diabetes insipidus.
Hypercalcaemia can cause AVP resistance.
Chronic hypernatraemia should be corrected by no more than about 10–12 mmol/L per 24 hours.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – in up to 80–90 % of brain-dead donors; desmopressin/vasopressin are used.
- B (False) – Uosm > 300 with mannitol is an osmotic diuresis.
- C (True) – hypercalcaemia (and hypokalaemia, lithium) cause nephrogenic DI.
- D (True) – rapid correction risks cerebral oedema.

**Ref:** Christ-Crain M, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2019. → [D5](D5.md)

questions.stem: Regarding the treatment of hyponatraemia (European guideline 2014):
options: Severe symptoms are treated with 150 mL of 3 % saline over 20 minutes, repeated if needed.
The initial goal is a 5 mmol/L rise in serum sodium.
Fluid restriction is the first-line treatment of hyponatraemia after subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Vasopressin receptor antagonists are recommended first-line for profound hyponatraemia.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – up to two or three boluses, checking Na⁺ between them.
- B (True) – a 5 mmol/L rise usually controls symptoms; then ≤ 10 mmol/L in 24 h and ≤ 8 mmol/L per subsequent day.
- C (False) – fluid restriction after SAH increases delayed cerebral ischaemia; salt and volume are replaced.
- D (False) – the guideline does not recommend vasopressin antagonists for moderate or profound hyponatraemia (overcorrection, hepatotoxicity).

**Ref:** Spasovski G, Eur J Endocrinol 2014. → [D5](D5.md)

title: W20 · D1 – Upper GI bleeding: non-variceal and variceal haemorrhage

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child–Pugh C, 11 points) is admitted with haematemesis. After terlipressin, ceftriaxone and band ligation of an actively bleeding oesophageal varix 6 hours ago, he is haemodynamically stable. What is the best next step?
options: Repeat endoscopy at 24 hours to confirm haemostasis
Continue terlipressin for 5 days and start carvedilol at discharge
Insert a Sengstaken–Blakemore tube prophylactically for 24 hours
Placement of a covered TIPS within 72 hours
Start propranolol immediately while continuing terlipressin
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Child–Pugh C 10–13 points (or Child B > 7 with active bleeding) identifies high risk of treatment failure and death. Pre-emptive covered TIPS within 72 h (ideally < 24 h) improved 1-year survival (86 vs 61 %) in García-Pagán's trial and is recommended by Baveno VII/VIII.

**Why not the others:**
- A – routine second-look endoscopy is not recommended.
- B – drugs + EVL alone are inferior to p-TIPS in this high-risk group.
- C – balloon tamponade is reserved as a temporary bridge for refractory bleeding (SEMS preferred).
- E – NSBB are started after the vasoactive drug is stopped, and do not replace p-TIPS.

**EDIC trap:** high bilirubin, HE or ACLF are not absolute contraindications to p-TIPS (Baveno VIII).

**Ref:** García-Pagán JC, N Engl J Med 2010; Baveno VIII, J Hepatol 2026.

questions.stem: Regarding red cell transfusion in acute upper GI bleeding:
options: In the Villanueva trial, a restrictive threshold of 7 g/dL improved 6-week survival compared with 9 g/dL.
A liberal transfusion strategy lowers the hepatic venous pressure gradient in cirrhosis.
ESGE recommends a post-transfusion target of at least 10 g/dL in patients with acute coronary syndrome.
Fresh frozen plasma should be given to cirrhotic patients with an INR > 1.5 before variceal ligation.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – survival 95 vs 91 % (HR 0.55), with less rebleeding and fewer adverse events.
- B (False) – liberal transfusion **increased** HVPG in the first days, promoting rebleeding.
- C (True) – with cardiovascular disease ESGE transfuses at ≤ 8 g/dL with a target ≥ 10 g/dL.
- D (False) – INR does not reflect bleeding risk in cirrhosis; FFP is not recommended (Baveno VIII).

**Ref:** Villanueva C, N Engl J Med 2013; Gralnek IM, Endoscopy 2021; Baveno VIII, J Hepatol 2026.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after one episode of melaena. HR 82/min, BP 128/76 mmHg, Hb 13.6 g/dL, urea 5.0 mmol/L, no syncope, no comorbidities. Her Glasgow–Blatchford score is 1. What is the most appropriate management?
options: ICU admission and endoscopy within 6 hours
Outpatient management with outpatient endoscopy
Admission and IV pantoprazole infusion for 72 hours
CT angiography
Transfusion of 1 unit of red cells
questions.expl:
**Why B:** A Glasgow–Blatchford score ≤ 1 identifies very low risk of needing intervention or of death; ESGE strongly recommends outpatient management without urgent inpatient endoscopy.

**Why not the others:**
- A – emergent endoscopy is not recommended even in high-risk NVUGIB.
- C – high-dose PPI infusion is for high-risk stigmata after endoscopic therapy.
- D – CTA is for active bleeding not localised at endoscopy.
- E – Hb 13.6 g/dL is far above any transfusion threshold.

**Ref:** Gralnek IM, Endoscopy 2021.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with known cirrhosis presents with haematemesis, HR 118/min and BP 92/55 mmHg. All of the following are recommended in the first hours EXCEPT:
options: Terlipressin or somatostatin started before endoscopy
Intravenous ceftriaxone
Erythromycin 250 mg IV before endoscopy
Lactulose to prevent hepatic encephalopathy
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV followed by an infusion
questions.expl:
**Why E:** HALT-IT (n = 12,009, many with liver disease and suspected variceal bleeding) showed no reduction in death due to bleeding (4 % in both arms) and more venous thromboembolism with TXA. Baveno VIII and ESGE recommend against it.

**Why not the others:**
- A – vasoactive drugs should be started as soon as variceal bleeding is suspected.
- B – antibiotic prophylaxis reduces infection, rebleeding and mortality.
- C – erythromycin 30–90 min before endoscopy improves visualisation (new Baveno VIII statement).
- D – lactulose is recommended to prevent or treat overt HE.

**Ref:** HALT-IT, Lancet 2020; Baveno VIII, J Hepatol 2026.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man has a 1.5-cm duodenal ulcer at endoscopy. Regarding endoscopic findings and therapy:
options: A non-bleeding visible vessel (Forrest IIa) should be treated endoscopically.
Adrenaline injection alone is adequate therapy for an actively spurting ulcer.
A clean-based ulcer (Forrest III) does not need endoscopic therapy.
Routine second-look endoscopy at 24 h is not recommended after successful haemostasis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Forrest IIa carries ~40–50 % rebleeding risk; thermal, mechanical or sclerosant therapy ± adrenaline is recommended.
- B (False) – adrenaline must be combined with a second modality (thermal or clips).
- C (True) – Forrest IIc and III have low rebleeding risk.
- D (True) – second look is reserved for clinical evidence of rebleeding.

**Ref:** Gralnek IM, Endoscopy 2021.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with melaena has a Glasgow–Blatchford score of 13. After 2 L of crystalloid and 2 units of red cells, HR is 88/min and BP 118/70 mmHg. When should endoscopy be performed?
options: Within 24 hours of presentation
Immediately, within 2 hours, irrespective of haemodynamics
Within 6 hours, because urgent endoscopy reduces mortality in high-risk patients
After 48 hours of PPI infusion
Only if bleeding recurs
questions.expl:
**Why A:** ESGE recommends early endoscopy (≤ 24 h) after haemodynamic resuscitation. In Lau's trial (GBS ≥ 12), endoscopy ≤ 6 h did not reduce 30-day mortality compared with 6–24 h (8.9 vs 6.6 %).

**Why not the others:**
- B – endoscopy before resuscitation is unsafe; she is now stable.
- C – urgent endoscopy did not improve mortality or rebleeding.
- D – delaying beyond 24 h increases risk; PPI does not replace endoscopy.
- E – all patients with GBS > 1 need inpatient endoscopy.

**Ref:** Lau JYW, N Engl J Med 2020; Gralnek IM, Endoscopy 2021.

questions.stem: Regarding the HALT-IT trial of tranexamic acid in gastrointestinal bleeding:
options: It showed a 30 % reduction in death due to bleeding at 5 days.
The rate of venous thromboembolic events was higher with tranexamic acid.
It enrolled fewer than 1,000 patients.
Benefit was confined to patients with variceal bleeding.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – death due to bleeding was 4 % in both groups (RR 0.99).
- B (True) – VTE 0.8 vs 0.4 % (RR 1.85); seizures were also more frequent.
- C (False) – 12,009 patients were randomised.
- D (False) – no subgroup benefited, including suspected variceal bleeding.

**Ref:** HALT-IT Trial Collaborators, Lancet 2020.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man with cirrhosis continues to bleed from oesophageal varices despite terlipressin and two attempts at band ligation. He is intubated; the TIPS team is unavailable until tomorrow. What is the preferred bridging measure?
options: Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg
Recombinant factor VIIa
A covered self-expanding oesophageal metal stent
Emergency surgical portocaval shunt
Increase terlipressin and wait for TIPS
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Baveno VIII prefers a covered self-expanding metal stent over balloon tamponade as a bridge to TIPS or transplantation in refractory oesophageal variceal bleeding. In Escorsell's RCT the stent controlled bleeding without rebleeding more often (66 vs 20 %) with fewer serious adverse events.

**Why not the others:**
- A – FFP does not correct the coagulopathy of cirrhosis and expands volume.
- B – rFVIIa is not recommended.
- D – surgical shunts carry very high mortality and have been replaced by TIPS.
- E – ongoing bleeding requires a mechanical bridge; escalation of drugs alone fails.

**Ref:** Escorsell À, Hepatology 2016; Baveno VIII, J Hepatol 2026.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman on apixaban for atrial fibrillation presents with haematemesis, HR 124/min and BP 84/50 mmHg despite initial fluids. What is the most appropriate approach to her anticoagulation?
options: Continue apixaban and perform endoscopy when anti-Xa activity is undetectable
Withhold apixaban, resuscitate and consider andexanet alfa or PCC, without delaying endoscopy
Give vitamin K 10 mg IV and FFP 4 units
Give idarucizumab 5 g IV
Delay endoscopy for 48 hours until the drug has been eliminated
questions.expl:
**Why B:** ESGE recommends withholding DOACs, and in severe ongoing bleeding considering a reversal agent (andexanet alfa for factor Xa inhibitors) or IV PCC; endoscopy should not be delayed by antithrombotic use.

**Why not the others:**
- A – continuing anticoagulation during life-threatening bleeding is inappropriate.
- C – vitamin K and FFP do not reverse factor Xa inhibitors.
- D – idarucizumab reverses dabigatran only.
- E – timing of endoscopy should not depend on anticoagulant clearance.

**Ref:** Gralnek IM, Endoscopy 2021.

questions.stem: Regarding pharmacological therapy in acute variceal bleeding according to Baveno VIII:
options: Vasoactive drugs should be started only after endoscopy has confirmed variceal bleeding.
A third-generation cephalosporin is generally preferred for antibiotic prophylaxis.
After successful band ligation, a vasoactive course as short as 24 hours can be considered if a non-selective beta-blocker is started.
Proton pump inhibitors should be continued for 14 days after band ligation to prevent post-ligation ulcer bleeding.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – start as soon as possible, before endoscopy.
- B (True) – e.g. ceftriaxone 1 g/24 h, adapted to local resistance.
- C (True) – new in Baveno VIII; standard duration remains 2–5 days.
- D (False) – PPIs started before endoscopy should be stopped once a portal-hypertensive source is confirmed; routine PPI after EVL is not recommended.

**Ref:** Baveno VIII, J Hepatol 2026.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has a gastric ulcer with a spurting vessel (Forrest Ia) treated with adrenaline injection and clips. Which PPI regimen is recommended afterwards?
options: Oral omeprazole 20 mg once daily
No PPI is needed after successful endoscopic therapy
IV pantoprazole 40 mg once daily for 24 hours
Ranitidine 50 mg IV every 8 hours
High-dose PPI: 80 mg IV bolus then 8 mg/h for 72 hours (or high-dose intermittent dosing)
questions.expl:
**Why E:** After endoscopic haemostasis of high-risk stigmata, ESGE recommends high-dose PPI for 72 h, preferably 80 mg bolus + 8 mg/h, or high-dose intermittent IV/oral twice daily, then twice-daily oral PPI.

**Why not the others:**
- A – standard-dose once daily is insufficient in the first 72 h.
- B – PPI reduces rebleeding after endoscopic therapy.
- C – dose and duration are inadequate.
- D – H₂ blockers are inferior to PPIs.

**Ref:** Gralnek IM, Endoscopy 2021.

open.q: Outline the management of a patient with cirrhosis and suspected acute variceal bleeding during the first 24 hours.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- ABC: intubation if altered consciousness or massive haematemesis; large-bore access; ICU/intermediate care.
- Restrictive transfusion (Hb target 7–8 g/dL); avoid over-expansion; no FFP, routine platelets, rFVIIa or TXA.
- Vasoactive drug immediately (terlipressin, somatostatin or octreotide) for 2–5 days (shorter possible after EVL + NSBB).
- Antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone 1 g/day), lactulose; stop pre-endoscopy PPI once a variceal source is confirmed.
- Erythromycin 250 mg 30–90 min before endoscopy; endoscopy ≤ 12 h with EVL (cyanoacrylate/TIPS for GOV2/IGV1).
- Risk stratification (Child–Pugh, MELD, HVPG ≥ 20): p-TIPS within 72 h for Child C 10–13 or Child B > 7 with active bleeding.
- Refractory bleeding: SEMS (preferred) or balloon tamponade as bridge → rescue TIPS.

open.q: A patient rebleeds 2 days after endoscopic treatment of a duodenal ulcer. Describe the escalation pathway.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Resuscitate, restrictive transfusion, high-dose PPI, review antithrombotics.
- Repeat endoscopy with haemostasis (consider over-the-scope clip or haemostatic powder).
- If the second endoscopic attempt fails → CT angiography and transcatheter angiographic embolisation (TAE).
- Surgery if TAE fails or is unavailable.
- Test and treat H. pylori; plan antiplatelet restart.

title: W20 · D2 – Acute pancreatitis: severity, fluids (WATERFALL), nutrition, necrosis

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with alcohol-related acute pancreatitis develops hypoxaemia (PaO₂/FiO₂ 220) on day 1, which resolves within 36 hours. CT on day 4 shows no necrosis or collections. According to the revised Atlanta classification, his pancreatitis is:
options: Mild
Severe
Moderately severe
Critical
Cannot be classified until day 7
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Transient organ failure (modified Marshall ≥ 2, resolving < 48 h) defines moderately severe acute pancreatitis, even without local complications.

**Why not the others:**
- A – mild requires no organ failure at all.
- B – severe requires persistent organ failure > 48 h.
- D – "critical" is a category of the determinant-based classification (persistent OF + infected necrosis), not Atlanta.
- E – classification is dynamic and possible once the 48-h window has passed.

**Ref:** Banks PA, Gut 2013.

questions.stem: Regarding the WATERFALL trial:
options: Both arms received Lactated Ringer's solution.
The aggressive arm received a 20 mL/kg bolus followed by 3 mL/kg/h.
Aggressive resuscitation reduced progression to moderately severe or severe pancreatitis.
The trial was stopped early because of more fluid overload in the aggressive arm.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – LR in both arms.
- B (True) – vs 1.5 mL/kg/h (10 mL/kg bolus only if hypovolaemic) in the moderate arm.
- C (False) – 22.1 vs 17.3 % (aRR 1.30, NS) – numerically worse.
- D (True) – fluid overload 20.5 vs 6.3 %; stopped at the first interim analysis for harm.

**Ref:** de-Madaria E, N Engl J Med 2022.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman is admitted with mild gallstone pancreatitis (no organ failure). Her pain is controlled with opioids on day 2 and she is hungry. Lipase is still 4 × ULN. What is the best nutritional plan?
options: Start a low-fat solid oral diet now
Keep nil by mouth until lipase normalises
Start clear liquids only for 48 hours
Insert a nasojejunal tube and start enteral feeding
Start parenteral nutrition to rest the pancreas
questions.expl:
**Why A:** In mild AP, early oral feeding within 24–48 h as tolerated is recommended, starting with a low-fat solid diet; normalisation of lipase is not required.

**Why not the others:**
- B – "resting the pancreas" increases infection and length of stay.
- C – stepwise liquid diets offer no advantage over solid low-fat diet.
- D – tube feeding is for patients who cannot eat (usually severe AP).
- E – PN is reserved for failure of enteral nutrition.

**Ref:** Tenner S, Am J Gastroenterol 2024; Párniczky A, Pancreatology 2025.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with severe necrotising pancreatitis is in the ICU on day 5. All of the following are appropriate EXCEPT:
options: Measuring intra-abdominal pressure via the bladder
Enteral nutrition via a nasogastric tube
Opioid analgesia
Goal-directed fluid therapy with Lactated Ringer's
Prophylactic meropenem to prevent infection of the necrosis
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Prophylactic antibiotics do not reduce infected necrosis or mortality in severe or necrotising AP and are recommended against (ACG 2024, IAP 2025). Antibiotics are given for documented or strongly suspected infection.

**Why not the others:**
- A – IAH is common in severe AP; IAP should be monitored when risk factors are present.
- B – NG feeding is as safe as NJ in severe AP.
- C – opioids are safe and effective.
- D – moderate, goal-directed LR is recommended.

**Ref:** Tenner S, Am J Gastroenterol 2024; Párniczky A, Pancreatology 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding local complications of acute pancreatitis (revised Atlanta):
options: A pseudocyst can be diagnosed 10 days after onset if a fluid collection is present.
Walled-off necrosis develops more than 4 weeks after onset of necrotising pancreatitis.
Gas within a necrotic collection on CT suggests infection.
An acute necrotic collection by definition contains no solid material.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – pseudocysts are encapsulated collections > 4 weeks after interstitial AP; before that it is an APFC.
- B (True) – WON = mature encapsulated necrosis, usually > 4 weeks.
- C (True) – gas (in the absence of recent intervention) is a sign of infected necrosis.
- D (False) – ANC contains fluid and necrotic (solid) tissue.

**Ref:** Banks PA, Gut 2013.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with necrotising pancreatitis develops fever and rising CRP on day 14. CT shows gas in a 10-cm heterogeneous acute necrotic collection. She is haemodynamically stable on room air. What is the best initial management?
options: Immediate percutaneous drainage within 24 hours
Open surgical necrosectomy
CT-guided fine-needle aspiration before any treatment
Broad-spectrum antibiotics with penetration into necrosis, postponing drainage until the collection is walled off
Urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy
questions.expl:
**Why D:** POINTER showed that postponing intervention until walled-off necrosis (with antibiotics meanwhile) was not inferior to immediate drainage, required fewer interventions, and 39 % of patients needed no intervention. Step-up intervention follows if she fails to improve.

**Why not the others:**
- A – immediate drainage offered no benefit and more procedures.
- B – primary open necrosectomy has more major complications and death (PANTER 69 vs 40 %).
- C – routine FNA is not recommended; gas on CT already indicates infection.
- E – ERCP is not a treatment for infected necrosis.

**Ref:** Boxhoorn L, N Engl J Med 2021; van Santvoort HC, N Engl J Med 2010.

questions.stem: Regarding the evidence for interventions in acute pancreatitis:
options: In PANTER, a step-up approach reduced major complications or death compared with primary open necrosectomy.
In TENSION, an endoscopic step-up approach caused fewer pancreatic fistulae than a surgical step-up approach.
In PYTHON, early nasoenteric feeding within 24 h did not reduce major infection or death compared with an on-demand oral diet.
In APEC, urgent ERCP did not improve outcome in predicted severe gallstone pancreatitis without cholangitis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 40 vs 69 %; 35 % needed drainage only.
- B (True) – 5 vs 32 %, shorter stay; primary endpoint not different (43 vs 45 %).
- C (True) – 30 vs 27 %.
- D (True) – 38 vs 44 %, NS.

**Ref:** van Santvoort HC, N Engl J Med 2010; van Brunschot S, Lancet 2018; Bakker OJ, N Engl J Med 2014; Schepens NJ, Lancet 2020.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with gallstone pancreatitis has fever 39.2 °C, rigors, jaundice (bilirubin 85 µmol/L) and a dilated common bile duct. What is the most appropriate intervention?
options: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 24 hours
ERCP with sphincterotomy within 24 hours
ERCP after 2 weeks of antibiotics
Percutaneous drainage of the peripancreatic fluid
MRCP followed by conservative management
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Acute cholangitis complicating gallstone pancreatitis is an indication for urgent ERCP (< 24 h) with biliary drainage, in addition to antibiotics.

**Why not the others:**
- A – cholecystectomy does not drain the infected bile duct and is deferred.
- C – delayed drainage in cholangitis increases mortality.
- D – the source is biliary, not a collection.
- E – MRCP delays treatment; conservative care is for patients without cholangitis (APEC).

**Ref:** Tenner S, Am J Gastroenterol 2024; Schepens NJ, Lancet 2020.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes presents with acute pancreatitis. Serum is lipaemic; triglycerides are 28 mmol/L. Glucose is 16 mmol/L; there is no organ failure. Which initial treatment is most appropriate to lower triglycerides?
options: Oral fenofibrate only
Prophylactic imipenem
Unfractionated heparin bolus to activate lipoprotein lipase
Urgent ERCP
Intravenous insulin infusion with glucose as needed
questions.expl:
**Why E:** IV insulin activates lipoprotein lipase and lowers triglycerides rapidly; glucose is added to avoid hypoglycaemia. Plasmapheresis is reserved for selected severe cases.

**Why not the others:**
- A – oral agents are for long-term prevention, not acute lowering.
- B – prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated.
- C – heparin causes only transient lipolysis followed by depletion of lipoprotein lipase, and risks haemorrhagic pancreatitis.
- D – there is no biliary indication.

**Ref:** Párniczky A, Pancreatology 2025; Tenner S, Am J Gastroenterol 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding diagnosis and severity assessment in acute pancreatitis:
options: A lipase of 20 × ULN predicts severe disease better than a lipase of 4 × ULN.
Contrast-enhanced CT is recommended within 12 hours of admission in all patients.
Persistent SIRS for more than 48 hours is associated with increased mortality.
Amylase is more specific than lipase for pancreatitis.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – enzyme level does not correlate with severity.
- B (False) – early CT is only for diagnostic doubt; necrosis is assessed at 72–96 h.
- C (True) – persistent SIRS is a marker of persistent organ failure and death.
- D (False) – lipase is more specific and remains elevated longer.

**Ref:** Banks PA, Gut 2013; Tenner S, Am J Gastroenterol 2024.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with mild biliary pancreatitis has recovered by day 4 and is tolerating a normal diet. What is the best management of her gallbladder?
options: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the same admission
Cholecystectomy after 3 months
No intervention unless symptoms recur
Ursodeoxycholic acid long term
Elective ERCP and sphincterotomy before discharge in all patients
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Same-admission cholecystectomy in mild biliary pancreatitis reduces readmission for gallstone-related complications or death (PONCHO: 5 vs 17 %).

**Why not the others:**
- B – interval cholecystectomy exposes the patient to recurrent pancreatitis, cholangitis and colic.
- C – recurrence risk is high without cholecystectomy.
- D – ursodeoxycholic acid does not prevent recurrence.
- E – ERCP is for persistent CBD stones or cholangitis; sphincterotomy alone is an option only for patients unfit for surgery.

**Ref:** da Costa DW, Lancet 2015; Tenner S, Am J Gastroenterol 2024.

open.q: Describe your approach to fluid resuscitation in a patient with predicted severe acute pancreatitis, and justify it with trial evidence.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Early hypovolaemia from capillary leak, but excess fluids cause fluid overload, IAH/ACS, ARDS.
- WATERFALL (NEJM 2022): aggressive LR (20 mL/kg bolus + 3 mL/kg/h) vs moderate (1.5 mL/kg/h, 10 mL/kg bolus if hypovolaemic) – fluid overload 20.5 vs 6.3 %, no reduction in moderately severe/severe AP (22.1 vs 17.3 %).
- Moderate, goal-directed fluid therapy (ACG 2024, IAP 2025) with Lactated Ringer's rather than saline; no starches.
- Endpoints: HR, MAP ≥ 65, urine output ≥ 0.5 mL/kg/h, falling haematocrit/urea, lactate; dynamic tests of fluid responsiveness; stop when unresponsive.
- Monitor IAP and fluid balance; vasopressors rather than further fluids once preload-unresponsive.

title: W20 · D3 – Acute liver failure: aetiology, King's criteria, neuroprotection, plasma exchange

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman is admitted 3 days after a staggered paracetamol overdose. After 3 L of crystalloid her arterial pH is 7.24, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, INR 4.8, creatinine 190 µmol/L and she has grade II encephalopathy. Which statement is correct?
options: She does not meet King's College Criteria because INR is < 6.5
She meets King's College Criteria for emergency liver transplantation
NAC is no longer indicated because more than 24 h have passed
Transplant criteria cannot be applied in staggered overdoses
She should first receive FFP to correct the INR before reassessment
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In paracetamol ALF, an arterial pH < 7.30 after adequate fluid resuscitation is sufficient on its own (the lactate modification also applies: > 3.0 mmol/L after resuscitation).

**Why not the others:**
- A – the INR/creatinine/HE triad is an alternative criterion, not a requirement.
- C – NAC is given in established paracetamol ALF regardless of the time since ingestion.
- D – KCC are applied to staggered overdoses (nomograms are not).
- E – FFP obscures the INR as a prognostic marker and is not indicated without bleeding.

**Ref:** O'Grady JG, Gastroenterology 1989; EASL, J Hepatol 2017.

questions.stem: Regarding the classification of acute liver failure (O'Grady):
options: Hyperacute liver failure has an interval of ≤ 7 days between jaundice and encephalopathy.
Cerebral oedema is most frequent in subacute liver failure.
Paracetamol typically causes hyperacute liver failure.
Subacute liver failure has the best transplant-free survival.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – acute 8–28 days, subacute 29 days–12 weeks.
- B (False) – cerebral oedema is most common in hyperacute ALF.
- C (True) – also HAV and HEV.
- D (False) – subacute ALF has the worst spontaneous survival; hyperacute the best.

**Ref:** EASL, J Hepatol 2017.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with hyperacute ALF is intubated for grade IV encephalopathy. Arterial ammonia is 240 µmol/L, Na 136 mmol/L, creatinine 160 µmol/L, MAP 70 mmHg on norepinephrine. Which intervention is most appropriate to reduce the risk of intracranial hypertension?
options: Hypertonic saline to a sodium of 145–150 mmol/L and early continuous renal replacement therapy
Lactulose via nasogastric tube
Cooling to 33 °C
Prophylactic hyperventilation to PaCO₂ 3.5 kPa
Dexamethasone 4 mg IV every 6 hours
questions.expl:
**Why A:** With ammonia > 150–200 µmol/L, grade IV HE and AKI, prophylactic hypernatraemia (Na 145–150 mmol/L) reduces ICP surges, and early high-dose CRRT lowers ammonia and was associated with better transplant-free survival.

**Why not the others:**
- B – lactulose is not recommended in ALF (distension, no benefit).
- C – moderate hypothermia did not prevent ICH in an RCT.
- D – sustained hyperventilation causes cerebral vasoconstriction/ischaemia; only as brief rescue.
- E – steroids do not treat cytotoxic cerebral oedema.

**Ref:** EASL, J Hepatol 2017; Cardoso FS, Hepatology 2018; Bernal W, J Hepatol 2016.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman develops ALF 6 weeks after starting isoniazid. She has grade I encephalopathy and INR 2.8. Paracetamol is undetectable. Besides stopping the drug and contacting a transplant centre, which therapy is supported by randomised evidence?
options: Prednisolone 60 mg/day
Molecular adsorbent recirculating system (MARS)
Lactulose
Intravenous N-acetylcysteine
Fresh frozen plasma to keep INR < 1.5
questions.expl:
**Why D:** In non-paracetamol ALF, NAC improved transplant-free survival in patients with early (grade I–II) coma (52 vs 30 %), but not in grade III–IV.

**Why not the others:**
- A – steroids are for autoimmune hepatitis, not idiosyncratic DILI in general.
- B – albumin dialysis showed no survival benefit (FULMAR).
- C – not recommended in ALF.
- E – prophylactic FFP is not indicated and masks prognosis.

**Ref:** Lee WM, Gastroenterology 2009.

questions.stem: Regarding high-volume plasma exchange (HVP) in acute liver failure (Larsen 2016):
options: Each session exchanged about 15 % of ideal body weight (8–12 L) daily for 3 days.
HVP improved hospital survival, mainly in patients who did not undergo transplantation.
HVP reduced vasopressor requirements.
HVP was associated with a higher rate of cerebral oedema.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – exchanged against fresh frozen plasma.
- B (True) – transplant-free survival 58.7 vs 47.8 % (HR 0.56).
- C (True) – MAP rose and SIRS/SOFA scores fell.
- D (False) – no increase in cerebral oedema was reported.

**Ref:** Larsen FS, J Hepatol 2016.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man presents with jaundice, INR 3.1, grade II encephalopathy, haemoglobin 82 g/L with a negative Coombs test, ALT 280 IU/L, ALP 30 IU/L and bilirubin 420 µmol/L. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Paracetamol toxicity
Wilson disease
Acute hepatitis A
Ischaemic hepatitis
Amanita phalloides poisoning
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Fulminant Wilson disease classically presents in young patients with Coombs-negative haemolysis, modest transaminases, very low ALP and an ALP:bilirubin ratio < 4 (here < 0.1). It requires emergency transplantation.

**Why not the others:**
- A – paracetamol causes very high transaminases (> 3,000 IU/L) with relatively low bilirubin early.
- C – HAV usually gives very high transaminases and no haemolysis.
- D – ischaemic hepatitis follows shock, with very high ALT and rapid fall.
- E – Amanita causes severe GI symptoms then very high transaminases.

**Ref:** EASL, J Hepatol 2017.

questions.stem: Regarding coagulation in acute liver failure:
options: An INR of 6 indicates a high risk of spontaneous major bleeding that requires FFP correction.
Thrombin generation is usually severely reduced in proportion to the INR.
Prophylactic correction of INR is recommended before any intubation.
Platelets above 100 × 10⁹/L should be targeted in all patients.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – spontaneous bleeding is uncommon; pro- and anticoagulant factors are both reduced.
- B (False) – thrombin generation is often preserved (rebalanced haemostasis).
- C (False) – correction is only for bleeding or high-risk procedures, ideally viscoelastic-guided.
- D (False) – no routine platelet target; transfuse for bleeding or procedures.

**Ref:** EASL, J Hepatol 2017; Nanchal R, Crit Care Med 2020.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman at 35 weeks' gestation presents with vomiting, jaundice, glucose 2.4 mmol/L, INR 2.2 and confusion. Blood pressure is 145/92 mmHg. Which is the most important definitive treatment?
options: Prompt delivery of the fetus
N-acetylcysteine infusion
Emergency liver transplant listing
IV aciclovir
High-volume plasma exchange
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (or HELLP) causing liver failure is treated by prompt delivery after maternal stabilisation (glucose, coagulation support); most patients recover.

**Why not the others:**
- B – NAC does not treat AFLP.
- C – transplantation is reserved for those who deteriorate after delivery.
- D – aciclovir is for HSV hepatitis (fever, very high ALT, low bilirubin); delivery remains the key here.
- E – plasma exchange may be used as an adjunct but is not definitive.

**Ref:** EASL, J Hepatol 2017.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings is LEAST consistent with the King's College Criteria for transplantation in non-paracetamol acute liver failure?
options: INR 7.0 with grade I encephalopathy
Age 45 years
Jaundice for 10 days before encephalopathy
Bilirubin 350 µmol/L
Arterial pH 7.28 after fluid resuscitation
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Arterial pH < 7.30 is a criterion for **paracetamol**-induced ALF only. Non-paracetamol criteria are INR > 6.5, or three of: age < 10 or > 40, unfavourable aetiology, jaundice-to-HE > 7 days, INR > 3.5, bilirubin > 300 µmol/L.

**Why not the others:**
- A – INR > 6.5 alone suffices, irrespective of HE grade.
- B – age > 40 is a minor criterion.
- C – jaundice-to-HE > 7 days is a minor criterion.
- D – bilirubin > 300 µmol/L is a minor criterion.

**Ref:** O'Grady JG, Gastroenterology 1989.

questions.stem: Regarding organ support in acute liver failure:
options: Benzodiazepines are the sedatives of choice after intubation.
Continuous renal replacement therapy is preferred to intermittent haemodialysis.
Prophylactic moderate hypothermia (33–34 °C) is recommended to prevent intracranial hypertension.
Hypoglycaemia is common and requires frequent glucose monitoring.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – propofol (short-acting) is preferred; benzodiazepines accumulate.
- B (True) – better haemodynamic and ICP stability; also lowers ammonia.
- C (False) – no benefit in an RCT; avoid fever instead.
- D (True) – impaired gluconeogenesis; continuous dextrose often needed.

**Ref:** EASL, J Hepatol 2017; Bernal W, J Hepatol 2016.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman receiving tacrolimus after a renal transplant presents with fever, ALT 4,800 IU/L, bilirubin 50 µmol/L, INR 2.5 and confusion. Paracetamol is undetectable. Which empirical treatment should be started immediately?
options: Entecavir
Prednisolone
Intravenous aciclovir
Silibinin
Penicillin G
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Fever, very high transaminases with low bilirubin in an immunosuppressed patient strongly suggest HSV (or VZV) hepatitis; IV aciclovir should be started empirically while PCR results are awaited.

**Why not the others:**
- A – antivirals for HBV are given after serology confirms HBV.
- B – steroids may worsen viral hepatitis.
- D – silibinin is used for Amanita phalloides poisoning.
- E – penicillin G is an adjunct for Amanita poisoning, not for viral hepatitis.

**Ref:** EASL, J Hepatol 2017.

open.q: Describe the measures to prevent and treat intracranial hypertension in a patient with hyperacute liver failure.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Risk factors: hyperacute course, young age, grade III–IV HE, arterial ammonia > 150–200 µmol/L, AKI, vasopressors.
- Intubate at grade III–IV; propofol; head-up 30°, neutral neck; normocapnia; normothermia; normoglycaemia; treat seizures.
- Hypertonic saline to Na 145–150 mmol/L; early high-dose CRRT for ammonia; avoid lactulose.
- Monitoring: pupils, ONSD, TCD; invasive ICP in selected listed patients (target ICP < 20–25, CPP > 50–60).
- Surges: mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg (osmolality < 320) or hypertonic bolus, brief hyperventilation as rescue; consider HVP; urgent transplant.
- Prophylactic hypothermia not recommended.

title: W20 · D4 – Cirrhosis and acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) in the ICU

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and pneumonia has creatinine 2.4 mg/dL (212 µmol/L), bilirubin 4 mg/dL, INR 1.9, no encephalopathy, MAP 72 mmHg without vasopressors and PaO₂/FiO₂ 280. What is his EASL-CLIF ACLF grade?
options: No ACLF
ACLF-2
ACLF-3
Cannot be graded without the MELD score
ACLF-1
questions.expl:
**Why E:** He has a single organ failure – kidney (creatinine ≥ 2.0 mg/dL). Single kidney failure defines ACLF-1 (28-day mortality ~22 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – single kidney failure is ACLF, unlike most single non-kidney failures without renal dysfunction or HE.
- B – only one organ fails (bilirubin < 12, INR < 2.5, P/F > 200, no vasopressors).
- C – ACLF-3 needs ≥ 3 organ failures.
- D – the EASL-CLIF grade uses CLIF-C OF criteria, not MELD.

**Ref:** Moreau R, Gastroenterology 2013; EASL, J Hepatol 2023.

questions.stem: Regarding acute-on-chronic liver failure (EASL-CLIF definition):
options: Respiratory failure is defined as a PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 200 or mechanical ventilation for non-neurological reasons.
Coagulation failure is defined as an INR ≥ 2.5.
28-day mortality in ACLF-3 is approximately 30 %.
The grade at days 3–7 predicts outcome better than the grade at diagnosis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – or SpO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 214.
- B (True) – CLIF-C OF threshold.
- C (False) – ~77 % in CANONIC; ~32 % is ACLF-2.
- D (True) – ACLF is dynamic; the course over the first week is most prognostic.

**Ref:** Moreau R, Gastroenterology 2013; EASL, J Hepatol 2023.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with cirrhosis and tense ascites is admitted with fever and confusion. Ascitic fluid neutrophil count is 620/mm³; creatinine is 1.3 mg/dL. Besides cefotaxime, which treatment reduces renal failure and mortality?
options: Furosemide 40 mg IV
Daily 20 % albumin to keep serum albumin ≥ 30 g/L
Albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3
Hydroxyethyl starch 500 mL
Large-volume paracentesis of 8 L without albumin
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In SBP, albumin 1.5 g/kg at diagnosis and 1 g/kg on day 3 reduced renal impairment (10 vs 33 %) and hospital mortality (10 vs 29 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – diuretics should be stopped in infection/AKI risk.
- B – ATTIRE showed no benefit and more fluid overload with targeted albumin.
- D – starches are nephrotoxic.
- E – large-volume paracentesis requires 8 g albumin per litre removed, and is not the priority in SBP.

**Ref:** Sort P, N Engl J Med 1999; EASL, J Hepatol 2018.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with cirrhosis has AKI with creatinine rising from 1.0 to 2.6 mg/dL over 3 days. All of the following are appropriate initial steps EXCEPT:
options: Start terlipressin immediately, before excluding hypovolaemia or other causes
Stop diuretics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Screen for infection, including diagnostic paracentesis
Assess volume status and give albumin if hypovolaemic
Reduce or stop the non-selective beta-blocker if he is hypotensive
questions.expl:
**Why A:** HRS-AKI is diagnosed only after lack of response to adequate volume resuscitation (within 24 h) and exclusion of alternative causes (shock, nephrotoxins, obstruction, structural injury). Vasoconstrictors are started once HRS-AKI is diagnosed.

**Why not the others:**
- B – removal of precipitating drugs is the first step.
- C – infection is the commonest precipitant.
- D – volume replacement as clinically indicated (albumin 1–1.5 g/kg or crystalloid).
- E – NSBB worsen renal perfusion in hypotension/AKI.

**Ref:** Francoz C, J Hepatol 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding the 2024 ADQI-ICA criteria for hepatorenal syndrome–AKI:
options: A 48-hour albumin challenge of 1 g/kg/day is mandatory before diagnosis.
Pre-existing chronic kidney disease excludes HRS-AKI.
The presence of ascites is required.
Septic shock requiring vasopressors is compatible with the diagnosis of HRS-AKI.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – the panel recommended against a systematic 48-h albumin requirement; non-response within 24 h of adequate volume resuscitation suffices.
- B (False) – HRS-AKI can occur on top of CKD.
- C (True) – cirrhosis with ascites is required.
- D (False) – septic shock is a strong alternative cause and excludes the diagnosis.

**Ref:** Francoz C, J Hepatol 2024.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with HRS-AKI (creatinine 3.1 mg/dL) is being considered for terlipressin. SpO₂ is 88 % on room air with bilateral crackles after several albumin infusions. Which is the best course of action?
options: Start terlipressin 1 mg every 4 h and increase albumin to 1 g/kg/day
Withhold terlipressin and albumin, treat volume overload; consider norepinephrine in ICU once oxygenation improves
Start terlipressin by continuous infusion; hypoxaemia is not relevant
Start midodrine and octreotide as the most effective option
Start haemodialysis immediately regardless of indications
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In CONFIRM, terlipressin increased deaths from respiratory disorders (11 vs 2 %); it should be avoided with SpO₂ < 90 % or volume overload. Albumin should be withheld in fluid overload/pulmonary oedema.

**Why not the others:**
- A – more albumin and terlipressin would worsen pulmonary oedema.
- C – continuous infusion reduces ischaemic events but not this contraindication.
- D – midodrine/octreotide is the least effective regimen.
- E – KRT is indicated for conventional indications or as bridge to transplant, not routinely.

**Ref:** Wong F, N Engl J Med 2021; Francoz C, J Hepatol 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding albumin use in decompensated cirrhosis:
options: ATTIRE showed that targeting a serum albumin ≥ 30 g/L reduced infection, renal dysfunction and death.
Albumin 8 g per litre of ascites removed is recommended after paracentesis > 5 L.
Albumin is the preferred fluid for volume expansion in suspected HRS-AKI.
Albumin should be given to every hospitalised cirrhotic patient with serum albumin < 25 g/L.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – composite 29.7 vs 30.2 %, with more pulmonary oedema.
- B (True) – prevents post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction.
- C (True) – 20–25 % albumin, with terlipressin once HRS-AKI is diagnosed.
- D (False) – albumin to correct hypoalbuminaemia alone is not recommended.

**Ref:** China L, N Engl J Med 2021; EASL, J Hepatol 2018.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man with cirrhosis has been in the ICU for 6 days with septic shock, KRT, mechanical ventilation, grade IV encephalopathy and INR 3.2. His CLIF-C ACLF score is 74. Active alcohol use excludes transplantation. Which is the most appropriate approach?
options: Continue full organ support for at least another 4 weeks
Start prednisolone 40 mg/day for presumed alcohol-related hepatitis
Start G-CSF
Discuss limitation or withdrawal of organ support with the family as futile care
Start MARS albumin dialysis
questions.expl:
**Why D:** After 3–7 days of full organ support, ≥ 4 organ failures or a CLIF-C ACLF score > 70 in a patient without a transplant option indicates very high mortality; EASL suggests considering withdrawal of organ support.

**Why not the others:**
- A – prolonged support without a transplant option is futile in this setting.
- B – steroids are not recommended in ACLF-3 or uncontrolled infection.
- C – G-CSF is not recommended (GRAFT).
- E – extracorporeal liver support does not improve survival.

**Ref:** EASL, J Hepatol 2023.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with cirrhosis is confused and drowsy (West Haven grade II) on day 2 of a urinary tract infection. Glucose and sodium are normal. Which treatment is first line?
options: Protein restriction to 0.5 g/kg/day
Rifaximin monotherapy
Lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools per day, plus treatment of the infection
Flumazenil infusion
Intubation and sedation with midazolam
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Treat the precipitant and give lactulose (oral or enema) titrated to 2–3 soft stools/day; rifaximin is an add-on mainly to prevent recurrence.

**Why not the others:**
- A – protein restriction worsens sarcopenia; 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day is recommended.
- B – rifaximin is added to lactulose, not used alone first line.
- D – flumazenil only if benzodiazepine toxicity is suspected.
- E – grade II HE does not require intubation; benzodiazepines worsen HE.

**Ref:** EASL, J Hepatol 2018; Nadim MK, J Hepatol 2016.

questions.stem: Regarding the CONFIRM trial of terlipressin in hepatorenal syndrome:
options: Terlipressin plus albumin increased verified HRS reversal compared with placebo plus albumin.
Deaths due to respiratory disorders were more frequent with terlipressin.
Terlipressin improved 90-day overall survival.
Patients with a serum creatinine ≥ 5 mg/dL are less likely to benefit.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 32 vs 17 %.
- B (True) – 11 vs 2 % within 90 days.
- C (False) – no survival benefit was shown.
- D (True) – advanced kidney dysfunction (and ACLF-3) predicts poor response and more toxicity.

**Ref:** Wong F, N Engl J Med 2021.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old man with alcohol-related hepatitis (Maddrey 54, no infection, ACLF-1) received prednisolone 40 mg/day. On day 7 his Lille score is 0.62. What should be done?
options: Double the prednisolone dose
Stop prednisolone
Continue prednisolone to complete 28 days
Add pentoxifylline and continue steroids
Switch to budesonide
questions.expl:
**Why B:** A Lille score > 0.45 at day 7 indicates non-response; continuing steroids increases infection risk without benefit. Non-responders should be evaluated for early transplantation where appropriate.

**Why not the others:**
- A – higher doses do not help and increase infection.
- C – continuation is for responders (Lille ≤ 0.45).
- D – pentoxifylline adds no benefit (STOPAH).
- E – budesonide has no role in severe alcohol-related hepatitis.

**Ref:** EASL, J Hepatol 2023; EASL, J Hepatol 2018.

open.q: Define ACLF according to EASL-CLIF and outline the principles of ICU management, including when to consider limitation of treatment.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Acute decompensation of cirrhosis + organ failure(s) (CLIF-C OF: kidney creatinine ≥ 2 mg/dL or KRT; liver bilirubin ≥ 12 mg/dL; INR ≥ 2.5; HE III–IV; vasopressors; PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 200) + 28-day mortality ≥ 20 %.
- Grades: ACLF-1 (single kidney failure, or single other OF + creatinine 1.5–1.9 and/or HE I–II), ACLF-2 (2 OF), ACLF-3 (≥ 3 OF); 28-day mortality ~22/32/77 %.
- Find and treat precipitants (infection – early broad-spectrum antibiotics; alcohol hepatitis; bleeding; HBV flare).
- Organ support: norepinephrine, albumin for SBP/LVP/HRS, terlipressin or norepinephrine + albumin for HRS-AKI, KRT, intubation for HE III–IV, lactulose, nutrition without protein restriction.
- Early transplant referral (ACLF-3 early LT ~80 % 6-month survival).
- Reassess at days 3–7; consider withdrawal with ≥ 4 OF or CLIF-C ACLF > 70 if no transplant option.
- Not recommended: G-CSF, routine extracorporeal liver support; plasma exchange promising (APACHE 2026).

title: W20 · D5 – Intra-abdominal hypertension and abdominal compartment syndrome

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man with 45 % total body surface area burns received 18 L of crystalloid in 24 hours. Bladder pressure is 26 mmHg, urine output 0.1 mL/kg/h and peak airway pressure is rising. He has no abdominal injury. Which term best describes his condition?
options: Primary abdominal compartment syndrome
Grade II intra-abdominal hypertension
Recurrent abdominal compartment syndrome
Secondary abdominal compartment syndrome
Polycompartment syndrome by definition
questions.expl:
**Why D:** IAP > 20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction (oliguria, respiratory failure) is ACS; it is **secondary** because it arises from conditions outside the abdominopelvic region (burns, massive resuscitation, capillary leak).

**Why not the others:**
- A – primary ACS results from abdominopelvic injury or disease.
- B – 26 mmHg is grade IV IAH, and with organ dysfunction it is ACS.
- C – recurrent ACS follows previous treatment of IAH/ACS.
- E – polycompartment syndrome requires ≥ 2 compartments with raised pressure (not shown).

**Ref:** Kirkpatrick AW, Intensive Care Med 2013.

questions.stem: Regarding the measurement of intra-abdominal pressure via the bladder:
options: The transducer should be zeroed at the mid-axillary line.
Instilling 100 mL of saline improves accuracy.
The measurement is taken at end-expiration in the supine position.
The value is reported in cmH₂O.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – at the level of the iliac crest in the mid-axillary line.
- B (False) – maximum 25 mL; larger volumes overestimate IAP.
- C (True) – without abdominal muscle contraction.
- D (False) – IAP is expressed in mmHg.

**Ref:** Kirkpatrick AW, Intensive Care Med 2013.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is on day 2 after a laparotomy for perforated sigmoid diverticulitis. MAP is 70 mmHg and IAP 18 mmHg. What is his abdominal perfusion pressure?
options: 34 mmHg
52 mmHg
70 mmHg
88 mmHg
18 mmHg
questions.expl:
**Why B:** APP = MAP − IAP = 70 − 18 = 52 mmHg, below the commonly used target of ≥ 60 mmHg.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 34 mmHg is the filtration gradient (MAP − 2 × IAP).
- C – this is the MAP alone.
- D – MAP + IAP has no physiological meaning.
- E – this is the IAP.

**Ref:** Kirkpatrick AW, Intensive Care Med 2013.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman with severe acute pancreatitis has an IAP of 23 mmHg, rising creatinine and worsening oxygenation. All of the following are reasonable medical measures EXCEPT:
options: Nasogastric decompression and a rectal tube
Ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage of a large volume of ascites
Optimising analgesia and sedation, with a brief trial of neuromuscular blockade
Avoiding further positive fluid balance
Elevating the head of the bed to 45° to improve oxygenation
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Head-of-bed elevation increases IAP; WSACS suggests considering the contribution of body position, and in severe IAH flatter positioning (or reverse Trendelenburg) is preferred.

**Why not the others:**
- A – enteral decompression of a dilated stomach/colon is recommended.
- B – percutaneous catheter drainage of intraperitoneal fluid may avoid laparotomy.
- C – analgesia/sedation and short NMB trials improve abdominal wall compliance.
- D – a positive cumulative balance worsens IAH.

**Ref:** Kirkpatrick AW, Intensive Care Med 2013; De Laet IE, Crit Care 2020.

questions.stem: Regarding the physiological effects of raised intra-abdominal pressure:
options: Central venous pressure may be elevated despite reduced intravascular volume.
Respiratory system compliance falls mainly because chest-wall compliance falls.
Oliguria is an early sign, related to renal venous congestion and a fall in filtration gradient.
Intracranial pressure can rise.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – pressure transmission to the thorax raises CVP/PAOP.
- B (True) – cranial displacement of the diaphragm stiffens the chest wall; high Pplat does not mean stiff lungs.
- C (True) – FG = MAP − 2 × IAP; oliguria ~15 mmHg, anuria ~30 mmHg.
- D (True) – via increased intrathoracic and jugular venous pressures.

**Ref:** De Laet IE, Crit Care 2020; Kirkpatrick AW, Intensive Care Med 2013.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man after damage-control laparotomy for liver trauma has IAP 28 mmHg, anuria, peak airway pressure 42 cmH₂O and rising lactate despite sedation, neuromuscular blockade and nasogastric decompression. There is no drainable fluid on ultrasound. What is the next step?
options: Decompressive laparotomy
Furosemide infusion
Albumin 20 % with furosemide
Continue observation and repeat IAP in 6 hours
Increase PEEP to 20 cmH₂O
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Overt ACS refractory to medical measures is an indication for decompressive laparotomy (WSACS 1D), followed by an open abdomen with NPWT and early fascial closure.

**Why not the others:**
- B – diuretics have no recommendation in ACS and would be too slow and ineffective in anuria.
- C – albumin with furosemide likewise has no recommendation and does not decompress the abdomen.
- D – delay worsens organ failure and mortality.
- E – high PEEP does not treat the cause and further impairs venous return.

**Ref:** Kirkpatrick AW, Intensive Care Med 2013.

questions.stem: Regarding definitions of intra-abdominal hypertension (WSACS 2013):
options: Normal intra-abdominal pressure in critically ill adults is 12–15 mmHg.
An IAP of 18 mmHg corresponds to grade II IAH.
ACS is defined as an IAP > 25 mmHg, regardless of organ function.
In children, the bladder instillation volume is 5 mL/kg.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – normal is ~5–7 mmHg; 12–15 is grade I IAH.
- B (True) – grade II is 16–20 mmHg.
- C (False) – ACS = sustained IAP > 20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction.
- D (False) – 1 mL/kg (minimum 3 mL, maximum 25 mL).

**Ref:** Kirkpatrick AW, Intensive Care Med 2013.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man on day 4 in the ICU after hip surgery has massive colonic dilatation (caecum 11 cm) without obstruction, IAP 19 mmHg and new oliguria. Rectal tube, electrolyte correction and stopping opioids have not helped. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Immediate decompressive laparotomy
Increase enteral feeding to full target
Neostigmine IV with cardiac monitoring
Start metoclopramide and wait 72 hours
Insert a peritoneal drain
questions.expl:
**Why C:** WSACS suggests neostigmine for established colonic ileus (Ogilvie's syndrome) not responding to simple measures and associated with IAH (2D); colonoscopic decompression is the next option.

**Why not the others:**
- A – laparotomy is for refractory overt ACS or perforation.
- B – feeding should be reduced in GI dysfunction with IAH.
- D – metoclopramide acts mainly on the upper GI tract; waiting risks caecal perforation.
- E – there is no free intraperitoneal fluid to drain.

**Ref:** Kirkpatrick AW, Intensive Care Med 2013.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old woman with septic shock has an IAP of 22 mmHg, persistent feeding intolerance and new oliguria. What does the ESICM guideline recommend about enteral nutrition?
options: Start full-target enteral nutrition to protect the mucosa
Switch to post-pyloric feeding at full rate
Continue the current rate and recheck IAP in 24 hours
Withhold enteral nutrition and reassess
Give parenteral nutrition at 35 kcal/kg/day immediately
questions.expl:
**Why D:** ESICM suggests delaying EN when IAP > 20 mmHg or ACS is present, and reassessing as IAP falls (low-rate EN is acceptable with IAP 12–20 mmHg, with monitoring).

**Why not the others:**
- A – full EN may increase luminal contents and IAP.
- B – post-pyloric feeding does not solve the problem at full rate.
- C – rising IAP with organ dysfunction requires action.
- E – early full PN overfeeds and is not recommended in the first days.

**Ref:** Reintam Blaser A, Intensive Care Med 2017.

questions.stem: Regarding WSACS 2013 recommendations and the open abdomen:
options: Negative pressure wound therapy is recommended for the open abdomen.
Efforts should be made to achieve early or same-hospital-stay fascial closure.
A prophylactic open abdomen is routinely recommended after laparotomy for intra-abdominal sepsis.
Damage-control resuscitation with a high plasma:red cell ratio is suggested in massive haemorrhage.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – GRADE 1C.
- B (True) – GRADE 1D; delayed closure increases fistulae and hernias.
- C (False) – suggested against routine use in sepsis/contamination unless IAH is a concern (2B).
- D (True) – GRADE 2D; reduces crystalloid load and IAH.

**Ref:** Kirkpatrick AW, Intensive Care Med 2013; Coccolini F, World J Emerg Surg 2018.

questions.stem: In the IROI study of 491 mixed ICU patients, which factor was independently associated with the development of intra-abdominal hypertension?
options: Female sex
PEEP ≥ 7 cmH₂O
Early enteral nutrition
Low body mass index
Use of propofol for sedation
questions.expl:
**Why B:** IROI identified BMI, APACHE II ≥ 18, abdominal distension, absent bowel sounds and PEEP ≥ 7 cmH₂O as risk factors; positive daily fluid balance predicted new IAH during the first week.

**Why not the others:**
- A – sex was not a risk factor.
- C – early EN was not identified as a risk factor.
- D – **high** BMI, not low, increases risk.
- E – sedation was not associated; adequate sedation improves abdominal wall compliance.

**Ref:** Reintam Blaser A, Crit Care Med 2019.

open.q: A patient develops IAP of 24 mmHg with oliguria after massive resuscitation for septic shock. Describe your step-wise management.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Confirm measurement (≤ 25 mL, supine, end-expiration, mid-axillary zero); diagnose secondary ACS (IAP > 20 + new organ dysfunction).
- Evacuate intraluminal contents: NG and rectal tubes, stop/reduce EN, prokinetics, neostigmine for colonic ileus.
- Evacuate intra-abdominal fluid: ultrasound, percutaneous catheter drainage of ascites.
- Improve wall compliance: analgesia, sedation, short NMB trial, avoid head-up > 30°, remove tight dressings.
- Optimise fluids: stop further fluids, aim neutral/negative balance (diuretics, ultrafiltration once stable – no formal recommendation), vasopressors to APP ≥ 60.
- If refractory → decompressive laparotomy (anticipate reperfusion syndrome), open abdomen with NPWT, early fascial closure.
- Monitor IAP 4–6-hourly; interpret CVP/Pplat with caution.

title: W20 · Saturday – weekly review: GI I (upper GI bleeding and varices, acute pancreatitis, acute liver failure, cirrhosis and ACLF, abdominal compartment syndrome)

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease presents with melaena from a duodenal ulcer. Hb is 7.8 g/dL; he is haemodynamically stable after fluids. According to ESGE, what is the appropriate transfusion strategy?
options: No transfusion until Hb < 7 g/dL
Transfuse to a target of 7–8 g/dL
Transfuse now (Hb ≤ 8 g/dL) with a target of ≥ 10 g/dL
Transfuse to a target of 14 g/dL
Give FFP before red cells
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In patients with acute or chronic cardiovascular disease, ESGE recommends transfusion at Hb ≤ 8 g/dL with a post-transfusion target of ≥ 10 g/dL; without cardiovascular disease the threshold is ≤ 7 g/dL (target 7–9).

**Why not the others:**
- A – the 7 g/dL threshold applies to patients without cardiovascular disease.
- B – 7–8 g/dL is the Baveno VIII target for variceal bleeding.
- D – liberal targets increase rebleeding and mortality.
- E – FFP has no role without a specific coagulopathy.

**Ref:** Gralnek IM, Endoscopy 2021. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: Regarding the management of acute variceal bleeding (Baveno VIII):
options: Upper endoscopy should be performed within 12 hours of presentation once the patient is resuscitated.
A covered oesophageal stent is preferred over balloon tamponade as a bridge in refractory bleeding.
Tranexamic acid is recommended to reduce rebleeding.
Child–Pugh A patients always require 7 days of antibiotic prophylaxis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – sooner if unstable.
- B (True) – more effective and safer (Escorsell 2016).
- C (False) – TXA and rFVIIa are not recommended (HALT-IT: no benefit, more VTE).
- D (False) – duration is individualised; Child A may need a shorter course or none.

**Ref:** Baveno VIII, J Hepatol 2026. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with cirrhosis (Child–Pugh B, 9 points) has an actively bleeding oesophageal varix at endoscopy, treated with band ligation. She is on terlipressin and ceftriaxone. What further measure improves survival?
options: Balloon tamponade for 24 hours
Continuous PPI infusion for 72 hours
Liberal transfusion to Hb 10 g/dL
FFP to INR < 1.5
Pre-emptive covered TIPS within 72 hours
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Child–Pugh B > 7 with active bleeding at endoscopy (or Child C 10–13, or HVPG ≥ 20 mmHg) is an indication for p-TIPS within 72 h (ideally < 24 h), which reduces treatment failure and mortality.

**Why not the others:**
- A – tamponade is only a bridge for refractory bleeding.
- B – PPIs are stopped once a variceal source is confirmed.
- C – liberal transfusion raises portal pressure and mortality.
- D – FFP does not correct the rebalanced coagulopathy.

**Ref:** García-Pagán JC, N Engl J Med 2010; Baveno VIII, J Hepatol 2026. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with acute pancreatitis and no organ failure is randomised in a trial like WATERFALL. Compared with moderate fluid therapy, aggressive resuscitation (20 mL/kg bolus then 3 mL/kg/h) most likely results in:
options: More fluid overload without reduction in severe pancreatitis
Less necrosis
Shorter hospital stay
Lower mortality
Less persistent SIRS
questions.expl:
**Why A:** WATERFALL was stopped early: fluid overload 20.5 vs 6.3 % and moderately severe/severe AP 22.1 vs 17.3 % (NS) with aggressive therapy.

**Why not the others:**
- B – no reduction in necrosis.
- C – hospital stay was not shorter (numerically longer).
- D – no mortality benefit.
- E – SIRS was not reduced.

**Ref:** de-Madaria E, N Engl J Med 2022. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: Regarding necrotising pancreatitis:
options: Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended.
In POINTER, postponing drainage of infected necrosis until it was walled off reduced the number of interventions.
The step-up approach starts with percutaneous or endoscopic drainage.
Contrast-enhanced CT on the day of admission accurately quantifies necrosis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – no effect on infected necrosis or mortality.
- B (True) – 2.6 vs 4.4 interventions; 39 % needed antibiotics only.
- C (True) – PANTER: major complications/death 40 vs 69 %.
- D (False) – necrosis is best assessed at 72–96 h.

**Ref:** Boxhoorn L, N Engl J Med 2021; van Santvoort HC, N Engl J Med 2010; Banks PA, Gut 2013. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with predicted severe gallstone pancreatitis is in the ICU. Bilirubin is 32 µmol/L, there is no fever and no cholangitis. All of the following are appropriate EXCEPT:
options: Moderate goal-directed resuscitation with Lactated Ringer's
Enteral nutrition via a nasogastric tube if oral intake fails
Monitoring of intra-abdominal pressure
Urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy within 24 hours
Cholecystectomy once the collections have resolved
questions.expl:
**Why D:** APEC showed no benefit of urgent ERCP in predicted severe gallstone pancreatitis without cholangitis (38 vs 44 %); ERCP is reserved for cholangitis or persistent obstruction.

**Why not the others:**
- A – recommended (ACG 2024, IAP 2025).
- B – NG feeding is safe and effective.
- C – IAH is common in severe AP.
- E – in necrotising/severe AP, cholecystectomy is delayed until collections resolve (~6 weeks).

**Ref:** Schepens NJ, Lancet 2020. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: Regarding acute liver failure:
options: Lactulose is recommended to lower ammonia in hyperacute liver failure.
Moderate hypothermia (34 °C) prevents intracranial hypertension.
An arterial ammonia > 150–200 µmol/L is associated with intracranial hypertension.
FFP should be given to keep the INR < 2 to prevent spontaneous bleeding.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – lactulose is not recommended in ALF.
- B (False) – no benefit in the RCT by Bernal (2016).
- C (True) – with high-grade HE, AKI, vasopressors and young age.
- D (False) – bleeding is uncommon; INR is prognostic; correct only for bleeding/procedures.

**Ref:** EASL, J Hepatol 2017; Bernal W, J Hepatol 2016. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man with non-paracetamol acute liver failure has INR 7.2 and grade I encephalopathy. Other parameters are unremarkable. Which statement is correct?
options: He does not meet King's College Criteria because encephalopathy is only grade I
He meets King's College Criteria for emergency liver transplantation
Arterial pH < 7.30 is required for him to meet the criteria
He needs three additional minor criteria
NAC is contraindicated because INR is > 6.5
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In non-paracetamol ALF, an INR > 6.5 (PT > 100 s) fulfils King's College Criteria on its own, irrespective of HE grade.

**Why not the others:**
- A – HE grade is not part of the INR > 6.5 criterion.
- C – pH applies to paracetamol ALF.
- D – three of five minor criteria are an alternative pathway.
- E – NAC benefits early (grade I–II) non-paracetamol ALF.

**Ref:** O'Grady JG, Gastroenterology 1989. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has paracetamol-induced acute liver failure with grade III encephalopathy, vasopressor-dependent shock and AKI while awaiting a transplant offer. Which extracorporeal therapy has shown improved transplant-free survival in a randomised trial?
options: MARS albumin dialysis
Haemoperfusion with charcoal
Intermittent haemodialysis
Bioartificial liver support
High-volume plasma exchange
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Larsen's RCT (n = 182) showed that HVP (15 % of ideal body weight, 8–12 L/day for 3 days) improved hospital transplant-free survival (58.7 vs 47.8 %), with less vasopressor need and inflammation.

**Why not the others:**
- A – MARS (FULMAR) did not improve survival.
- B – charcoal haemoperfusion was abandoned (no benefit, complications).
- C – intermittent HD destabilises haemodynamics and ICP; CRRT is preferred.
- D – bioartificial devices have not shown survival benefit.

**Ref:** Larsen FS, J Hepatol 2016. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis has creatinine 2.3 mg/dL, bilirubin 13 mg/dL, INR 2.7, grade I encephalopathy, no vasopressors and PaO₂/FiO₂ 320. What is his EASL-CLIF ACLF grade?
options: No ACLF
ACLF-1
ACLF-3
ACLF-2
APASL-ACLF only
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Three organ failures – kidney (creatinine ≥ 2 mg/dL), liver (bilirubin ≥ 12 mg/dL) and coagulation (INR ≥ 2.5) – define ACLF-3 (28-day mortality ~77 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – multiple organ failures are present.
- B – ACLF-1 has a single organ failure.
- D – ACLF-2 has exactly two organ failures.
- E – EASL-CLIF criteria are fulfilled; the APASL definition uses different criteria.

**Ref:** Moreau R, Gastroenterology 2013. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: Regarding kidney dysfunction in cirrhosis:
options: HRS-AKI requires the absence of ascites.
Terlipressin increased respiratory failure deaths in CONFIRM.
Albumin 1.5 g/kg at diagnosis of SBP reduces renal failure and mortality.
Norepinephrine is ineffective for HRS-AKI.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – cirrhosis **with** ascites is required.
- B (True) – 11 vs 2 % within 90 days.
- C (True) – Sort 1999: renal impairment 10 vs 33 %, mortality 10 vs 29 % (1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3).
- D (False) – norepinephrine + albumin is an effective alternative in ICU.

**Ref:** Francoz C, J Hepatol 2024; Wong F, N Engl J Med 2021; Sort P, N Engl J Med 1999. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with decompensated cirrhosis has a serum albumin of 24 g/L but no infection, AKI or paracentesis. The team considers daily albumin infusions to raise it to ≥ 30 g/L. What did the ATTIRE trial show for this strategy?
options: No reduction in infection, renal dysfunction or death, and more pulmonary oedema
Fewer infections
Lower 28-day mortality
Less hepatic encephalopathy
Fewer episodes of hepatorenal syndrome
questions.expl:
**Why A:** ATTIRE (n = 777) found no difference in the composite of infection, renal dysfunction or death (29.7 vs 30.2 %), and more severe adverse events, notably pulmonary oedema/fluid overload.

**Why not the others:**
- B – infection rates were not reduced.
- C – mortality was not lower.
- D – hepatic encephalopathy was not reduced.
- E – renal dysfunction (including HRS) was not reduced.

**Ref:** China L, N Engl J Med 2021. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: Regarding intra-abdominal hypertension and abdominal compartment syndrome (WSACS 2013):
options: IAH is defined as a sustained or repeated IAP ≥ 12 mmHg.
ACS is defined as sustained IAP > 20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction.
Abdominal perfusion pressure is calculated as MAP − 2 × IAP.
Percutaneous catheter drainage of intraperitoneal fluid may avoid decompressive laparotomy.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – grades I 12–15, II 16–20, III 21–25, IV > 25 mmHg.
- B (True) – with or without APP < 60 mmHg.
