- C (False) – APP = MAP − IAP; MAP − 2 × IAP is the filtration gradient.
- D (True) – suggested (2C/2D) when technically feasible.

**Ref:** Kirkpatrick AW, Intensive Care Med 2013. → [D5](D5.md)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with severe pancreatitis has IAP 24 mmHg, plateau pressure 34 cmH₂O, CVP 18 mmHg and oliguria. His echocardiogram shows a small, hyperdynamic left ventricle. How should the CVP be interpreted?
options: It confirms fluid overload, so diuretics are indicated
It is falsely elevated by transmitted intra-abdominal pressure and does not reflect preload
It excludes hypovolaemia
It indicates right ventricular failure requiring inotropes
It accurately reflects transmural filling pressure
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Raised IAP is transmitted to the thorax (~50 %), raising CVP and PAOP despite reduced intravascular volume and venous return. Volumetric or dynamic indices and echocardiography are more reliable.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the echo suggests underfilling, not overload.
- C – a high CVP does not exclude hypovolaemia in IAH.
- D – there is no evidence of RV failure.
- E – transmural pressure is CVP minus intrathoracic pressure, which is elevated here.

**Ref:** De Laet IE, Crit Care 2020; Kirkpatrick AW, Intensive Care Med 2013. → [D5](D5.md)

questions.stem: Regarding the surgical management of abdominal compartment syndrome:
options: Decompressive laparotomy is recommended for overt ACS refractory to medical treatment.
After decompression the fascia should be closed immediately in all patients.
Bioprosthetic mesh is routinely recommended for early closure of the open abdomen.
Reperfusion after decompression can cause hypotension, arrhythmias and hyperkalaemia.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – WSACS 1D.
- B (False) – the abdomen is left open with NPWT; early (same-hospital-stay) fascial closure is the goal once IAP allows.
- C (False) – WSACS suggests against routine bioprosthetic mesh (2D).
- D (True) – washout of acidotic, potassium-rich blood; volume load and correct K⁺ beforehand.

**Ref:** Kirkpatrick AW, Intensive Care Med 2013. → [D5](D5.md)

title: W21 · D1 – Nutrition in the ICU: timing, route and calories (NUTRIREA-3)

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man (75 kg) has been ventilated for 24 hours for faecal peritonitis after Hartmann's procedure. Noradrenaline has been stable at 0.15 µg/kg/min for 8 hours and lactate fell from 5.2 to 1.6 mmol/L. Bowel sounds are absent. What is the most appropriate nutritional strategy?
options: Withhold nutrition until bowel sounds return
Start low-dose enteral nutrition via a nasogastric tube and advance progressively
Start full-target parenteral nutrition (25 kcal/kg/day) today
Start full-target enteral nutrition at 25 kcal/kg/day immediately
Withhold all nutrition until noradrenaline is stopped
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Shock is controlled (stable dose, falling lactate), so ESICM and ESPEN recommend starting low-dose EN within 48 h and advancing over days. Absent bowel sounds are not a contraindication to EN.

**Why not the others:**
- A – bowel sounds are a poor marker of gut function; waiting for them delays EN unnecessarily.
- C – early full PN offers no benefit and early PN was harmful in EPaNIC (more infections).
- D – full-dose early EN in shock increased bowel ischaemia and GI intolerance (NUTRIREA-2) and standard-dose feeding was not better than low-dose (NUTRIREA-3).
- E – EN can be started once shock is controlled, even on vasopressors.

**EDIC trap:** "Uncontrolled shock" (escalating doses, rising lactate) is the contraindication, not vasopressors per se.

**Ref:** Reintam Blaser A, Intensive Care Med 2017; Singer P, Clin Nutr 2023.

questions.stem: Regarding the NUTRIREA-3 trial (ventilated adults with shock):
options: Patients in the low-intake arm received about 6 kcal/kg/day and 0.2–0.4 g/kg/day of protein during the first week.
Low intake reduced day-90 mortality significantly.
Time to readiness for ICU discharge was shorter with low intake.
Only parenteral nutrition was allowed in both arms.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – low arm 6 kcal/kg and 0.2–0.4 g/kg protein vs standard 25 kcal/kg and 1.0–1.3 g/kg, for 7 days.
- B (False) – day-90 mortality was 41.3 vs 42.8 %, not significantly different.
- C (True) – median 8 vs 9 days; there were also fewer vomiting, diarrhoea, bowel ischaemia and liver dysfunction episodes.
- D (False) – both EN and PN were allowed; the trial compared dose, not route.

**Ref:** Reignier J (NUTRIREA-3), Lancet Respir Med 2023.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman (70 kg) with ARDS on day 3 is sedated with propofol 1 % at 25 mL/h and receives enteral nutrition. Indirect calorimetry measures 1,700 kcal/day. Approximately how many kilocalories per day does the propofol provide?
options: 100 kcal
250 kcal
660 kcal
1,100 kcal
None – propofol has no caloric value
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Propofol 1 % in a lipid emulsion provides ~1.1 kcal/mL; 25 mL/h × 24 h = 600 mL × 1.1 ≈ 660 kcal/day – almost 40 % of her measured expenditure. It must be subtracted from the EN target to avoid overfeeding.

**Why not the others:**
- A, B – underestimate the lipid load (10 % emulsion = 0.1 g fat/mL).
- D – would correspond to ~1,000 mL/day.
- E – the soybean-oil emulsion is a real energy source and can also cause hypertriglyceridaemia.

**Ref:** Singer P, Clin Nutr 2019; Singer P, Clin Nutr 2023.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man is mechanically ventilated after a cardiac arrest. All of the following are reasons to DELAY enteral nutrition according to the ESICM 2017 guideline EXCEPT:
options: Gastric residual volume of 650 mL over 6 hours
Overt mesenteric ischaemia on CT
Active upper gastrointestinal bleeding
Targeted temperature management at 36 °C
Uncontrolled shock with rising lactate and escalating vasopressor doses
questions.expl:
**Why D:** ESICM suggests low-dose EN during therapeutic hypothermia/TTM, with advancement after rewarming. Temperature control is not a reason to withhold EN.

**Why not the others:**
- A – GRV > 500 mL/6 h is a reason to delay EN (and start prokinetics).
- B – overt bowel ischaemia is a contraindication.
- C – active upper GI bleeding delays EN until haemostasis.
- E – uncontrolled shock is the main contraindication.

**Ref:** Reintam Blaser A, Intensive Care Med 2017.

questions.stem: Regarding energy expenditure and energy targets in ICU patients:
options: Indirect calorimetry is the recommended method to determine energy expenditure in ventilated patients.
When indirect calorimetry is not available, VCO₂ from the ventilator is preferable to predictive equations.
During the early acute phase, ESPEN recommends providing more than 100 % of measured energy expenditure to prevent an energy deficit.
Predictive equations such as 25 kcal/kg/day are accurate within ±10 % in most ICU patients.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ESPEN grade B; IC measures VO₂ and VCO₂ (Weir equation).
- B (True) – EE ≈ VCO₂ × 8.19; VO₂ from a pulmonary artery catheter is another option.
- C (False) – early hypocaloric nutrition ≤ 70 % of EE; progress to 80–100 % after day 3; overfeeding is harmful.
- D (False) – equations are inaccurate in a large proportion of patients (over- and underestimation).

**Ref:** Singer P, Clin Nutr 2019; Singer P, Clin Nutr 2023.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with alcohol use disorder and a BMI of 16 kg/m² is admitted with aspiration pneumonia. On day 2 of enteral feeding her phosphate falls from 1.0 to 0.45 mmol/L. Which management is best supported by randomised evidence?
options: Continue full feeding and give phosphate only if the level falls below 0.3 mmol/L
Stop feeding completely for 5 days
Switch to parenteral nutrition at the same dose
Increase the caloric target to correct the malnutrition faster
Restrict caloric intake for 48 hours, replace phosphate, then increase gradually
questions.expl:
**Why E:** This is refeeding hypophosphataemia. In Doig's RCT (n = 339), protocolised caloric restriction for 48 h, with electrolyte replacement and then gradual return to target, reduced 60-day mortality compared with continued standard intake.

**Why not the others:**
- A – waiting for severe hypophosphataemia risks respiratory muscle weakness, arrhythmias and haemolysis.
- B – prolonged starvation worsens the deficit; restriction is temporary.
- C – the route does not prevent refeeding; PN can cause it as well.
- D – increasing intake aggravates the intracellular shift of phosphate.

**Ref:** Doig GS, Lancet Respir Med 2015.

questions.stem: Regarding the route of nutrition in critically ill adults:
options: In the CALORIES trial, early parenteral nutrition increased infectious complications compared with early enteral nutrition.
In NUTRIREA-2, early full-dose enteral nutrition in ventilated patients with shock was associated with more bowel ischaemia than parenteral nutrition.
In EPaNIC, starting supplemental parenteral nutrition on day 8 rather than within 48 hours led to fewer ICU infections.
Commercial parenteral nutrition bags contain all required trace elements and vitamins.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – at similar calories, infections and 30-day mortality (33.1 vs 34.1 %) did not differ.
- B (True) – bowel ischaemia 2 vs < 1 %; also more vomiting, diarrhoea and colonic pseudo-obstruction with EN.
- C (True) – infections 22.8 vs 26.2 %, and faster discharge alive with late PN.
- D (False) – vitamins and trace elements must be added daily.

**Ref:** Harvey SE, NEJM 2014; Reignier J, Lancet 2018; Casaer MP, NEJM 2011.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has been in the ICU for 5 days after polytrauma. He tolerates nasogastric feeding at 40 mL/h; gastric residual volume is 200 mL over 4 hours. What should be done with the feeding?
options: Stop EN and start parenteral nutrition
Continue and advance EN towards target
Switch to post-pyloric feeding immediately
Stop EN for 24 hours
Start erythromycin and metoclopramide for 7 days
questions.expl:
**Why B:** The ESPEN/ESICM threshold for gastric intolerance is a GRV > 500 mL/6 h; 200 mL/4 h is acceptable, so EN should be continued and advanced.

**Why not the others:**
- A – there is no EN failure; switching to PN is unnecessary.
- C – post-pyloric feeding is reserved for persistent intolerance despite prokinetics or high aspiration risk.
- D – stopping feeding for a normal residual adds to the energy deficit.
- E – prokinetics are not indicated; when used, limit them to 24–72 h because of tachyphylaxis and QT effects.

**Ref:** Reintam Blaser A, Intensive Care Med 2017; Singer P, Clin Nutr 2019.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has been ventilated for 4 days in a medical ICU. Enteral feeding meets only 30 % of the target despite prokinetics, and she was well nourished before admission. According to ESPEN, what is the most appropriate next step regarding parenteral nutrition?
options: Start full-dose parenteral nutrition from day 1 of admission in all patients
Never use supplemental parenteral nutrition in the ICU
Consider supplemental parenteral nutrition, weighed on a case-by-case basis, after day 3–7 if EN remains insufficient
Start parenteral glutamine to improve gut tolerance
Give supplemental PN only once albumin falls below 25 g/L
questions.expl:
**Why C:** ESPEN suggests supplemental PN when EN fails to cover the target after day 3–7, assessed individually. Early supplemental PN in well-nourished patients is not beneficial (EPaNIC).

**Why not the others:**
- A – early PN increased infections and delayed recovery in EPaNIC.
- B – PN is appropriate when EN is persistently insufficient or contraindicated.
- D – glutamine is not recommended in unstable/complex ICU patients (REDOXS harm).
- E – albumin reflects inflammation and capillary leak, not nutritional status.

**Ref:** Singer P, Clin Nutr 2019; Singer P, Clin Nutr 2023; Casaer MP, NEJM 2011.

questions.stem: Regarding the metabolic response to critical illness:
options: Endogenous glucose production in the early phase is not fully suppressed by exogenous nutrition.
Overfeeding increases CO₂ production and may prolong weaning.
Serum albumin is a reliable marker of nutritional status in the ICU.
Hypertriglyceridaemia may result from high-dose propofol and parenteral lipids.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – stress hormones and insulin resistance maintain gluconeogenesis, so feeding adds to endogenous energy (risk of overfeeding).
- B (True) – carbohydrate excess and lipogenesis raise VCO₂ and minute ventilation demand.
- C (False) – albumin falls with inflammation, dilution and capillary leak; it is not a nutrition marker.
- D (True) – monitor triglycerides with propofol and IV lipid emulsions.

**Ref:** Singer P, Clin Nutr 2019; Casaer MP, NEJM 2011.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with severe traumatic brain injury has been ventilated for 36 hours and is haemodynamically stable. He has vomited twice on nasogastric feeding at 20 mL/h, with gastric residual volumes of 600 mL over 6 hours despite 48 hours of IV erythromycin. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Stop all nutrition for 7 days
Increase the gastric feeding rate to overcome the ileus
Switch to total parenteral nutrition at full target
Continue erythromycin indefinitely
Insert a post-pyloric feeding tube and continue enteral nutrition
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Persistent gastric intolerance (GRV > 500 mL/6 h, vomiting) despite prokinetics is the indication for post-pyloric feeding (ESPEN/ESICM), which preserves enteral nutrition and reduces aspiration risk.

**Why not the others:**
- A – prolonged starvation is harmful; EN can usually continue post-pylorically.
- B – increasing the gastric rate increases aspiration risk.
- C – PN is considered if EN fails by any route; early full-target PN is not beneficial.
- D – prokinetics lose efficacy after 48–72 h (tachyphylaxis) and prolong QT.

**Ref:** Singer P, Clin Nutr 2019; Reintam Blaser A, Intensive Care Med 2017.

open.q: Describe how you would plan nutrition during the first week for a 60-year-old ventilated patient with septic shock who is now stabilised on noradrenaline.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **Screening/assessment:** risk of malnutrition after 48 h (NUTRIC, GLIM), weight history, muscle mass; baseline phosphate, K⁺, Mg²⁺.
- **Timing:** start **low-dose gastric EN within 48 h** once shock is controlled (stable or falling vasopressor dose, falling lactate); delay only in uncontrolled shock, hypoxaemia/acidosis, active upper GI bleed, bowel ischaemia, ACS, GRV > 500 mL/6 h.
- **Energy:** ≤ 70 % of EE in days 1–2, then 80–100 % of **measured EE** (indirect calorimetry; VCO₂ × 8.19 if unavailable); count propofol, citrate, glucose. NUTRIREA-3: low early intake (6 kcal/kg, low protein) shortened time to ICU discharge readiness with fewer GI complications.
- **Protein:** progressive increase towards ~1.2–1.3 g/kg/day (see D2).
- **Intolerance:** GRV > 500 mL/6 h → erythromycin ± metoclopramide 24–72 h → post-pyloric tube.
- **PN:** not early in well-nourished patients (EPaNIC); supplemental PN if EN < 60 % after day 3–7; early progressive PN only if severely malnourished and EN impossible.
- **Monitoring:** glucose (insulin > 10 mmol/L), phosphate daily (refeeding → restrict calories 48 h), triglycerides, liver tests, GI symptoms.

open.q: Summarise the key randomised trials that have shaped current recommendations on early calorie intake in the ICU.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **EPaNIC (2011):** late (day 8) vs early (48 h) supplemental PN – late PN: fewer infections (22.8 vs 26.2 %), faster discharge, less KRT.
- **EDEN (2012)/PermiT (2015):** trophic or permissive underfeeding vs full feeding – no difference in mortality.
- **CALORIES (2014)/NUTRIREA-2 (2018):** EN vs PN – equal mortality; PN not more infectious if not overfed; full early EN in shock → more bowel ischaemia, vomiting, diarrhoea.
- **TARGET (2018):** energy-dense EN delivered more calories without benefit.
- **NUTRIREA-3 (2023):** low vs standard calorie/protein in shock – same mortality (41.3 vs 42.8 %), faster readiness for discharge, fewer GI and liver complications.
- **Synthesis:** early progressive EN, hypocaloric in the acute phase, avoid overfeeding, measure EE (ESPEN 2023).

title: W21 · D2 – Protein in critical illness: EFFORT Protein, PRECISe, TARGET Protein

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man (80 kg) with pneumonia and septic shock is ventilated on day 4. He has KDIGO stage 2 AKI (not on KRT) with urea rising from 12 to 24 mmol/L. The dietitian proposes increasing protein to 2.0 g/kg/day. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Agree – high protein reduces mortality in AKI
Stop all protein until kidney function recovers
Restrict protein to 0.6 g/kg/day to delay the need for dialysis
Aim for about 1.0–1.3 g/kg/day, increased progressively, and avoid high-dose protein
Start CRRT so that 2.0 g/kg/day can be given
questions.expl:
**Why D:** In the EFFORT Protein AKI analysis, high protein in patients with AKI not on KRT was associated with higher mortality, and the 2026 synthesis of protein trials suggests a progressive increase to ~1.2 g/kg/day. ESPEN advises against restricting protein to avoid KRT.

**Why not the others:**
- A – no trial shows benefit; EFFORT suggested harm in AKI.
- B – stopping protein worsens the catabolic deficit.
- C – protein restriction to delay dialysis is not recommended.
- E – KRT is not started to allow a nutritional target.

**Ref:** Stoppe C, Crit Care 2023; Chapple LS, Crit Care 2026; Fiaccadori E, Clin Nutr 2021.

questions.stem: Regarding the EFFORT Protein trial:
options: It compared prescribed protein of ≥ 2.2 g/kg/day with ≤ 1.2 g/kg/day in ventilated patients with high nutritional risk.
High protein significantly shortened the time to discharge alive.
Patients with acute kidney injury at baseline appeared to be harmed by higher protein.
The trial was double-blinded with isocaloric formulas.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – delivered 1.6 vs 0.9 g/kg/day; 1,329 patients in 85 ICUs.
- B (False) – 46.1 vs 50.2 % discharged alive by day 60 (HR 0.91, 95 % CI 0.77–1.07).
- C (True) – the AKI and SOFA ≥ 9 subgroups had slower discharge and (AKI) higher mortality with high protein.
- D (False) – it was pragmatic, open-label and registry-based; PRECISe was the double-blind trial.

**Ref:** Heyland DK, Lancet 2023; Stoppe C, Crit Care 2023.

questions.stem: In the double-blind PRECISe trial, ventilated patients received isocaloric enteral nutrition with either 2.0 or 1.3 g/kg/day of protein. What was the main finding?
options: High protein improved 6-minute walk distance and was adopted as standard
High protein reduced 180-day mortality
High protein reduced ICU-acquired weakness measured by MRC sum score
There was no difference in any outcome, including GI tolerance
High protein led to worse health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L) over 180 days
questions.expl:
**Why E:** The primary outcome, EQ-5D-5L health utility over 180 days, was lower with high protein (mean difference −0.05; 95 % CI −0.10 to −0.01). GI intolerance was also more frequent (9 vs 6 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – the 6-minute walk difference was not adjusted for multiplicity and the trial did not support high protein.
- B – 180-day mortality was 42 vs 38 % (not significant, numerically worse).
- C – muscle strength was not improved.
- D – GI intolerance and quality of life differed.

**Ref:** Bels JLM (PRECISe), Lancet 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding muscle wasting and protein metabolism in critical illness:
options: Rectus femoris cross-sectional area may decrease by almost 20 % within the first 10 days.
Muscle loss is greater in patients with multiorgan failure.
A positive nitrogen balance can usually be achieved in the first days of septic shock by giving 2.5 g/kg/day of protein.
Amino acids in excess of what can be used for synthesis are oxidised, increasing urea production.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 17.7 % by day 10 (Puthucheary, JAMA 2013).
- B (True) – wasting was faster with more organ failures.
- C (False) – anabolic resistance means nitrogen balance remains negative in the acute phase regardless of intake.
- D (True) – rising urea and urea:creatinine ratio occur with high protein (seen in EFFORT and PRECISe).

**Ref:** Puthucheary ZA, JAMA 2013; Heyland DK, Lancet 2023.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman (90 kg) with septic shock and AKI is on continuous veno-venous haemodiafiltration with an effluent dose of 25 mL/kg/h. Her shock has resolved by day 5. What daily protein intake is best supported by the ESPEN renal guideline?
options: 0.6 g/kg/day to limit urea generation
0.8 g/kg/day
3.0 g/kg/day
Up to 1.7 g/kg/day to compensate for amino acid losses
Protein should be withheld while on CRRT
questions.expl:
**Why D:** CRRT removes ~10–20 g of amino acids per day. ESPEN recommends 1.0–1.5 g/kg/day on KRT and up to 1.7 g/kg/day for hypercatabolic patients on CRRT; in EFFORT patients already on KRT were not harmed by higher protein.

**Why not the others:**
- A, B – protein restriction is not recommended in AKI, and even less on CRRT.
- C – 3.0 g/kg exceeds any recommendation.
- E – withholding protein aggravates catabolism.

**Ref:** Fiaccadori E, Clin Nutr 2021; Stoppe C, Crit Care 2023.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man (height 175 cm, weight 130 kg, BMI 42 kg/m²) is ventilated for pneumonia. Ideal body weight is ~71 kg. According to ESPEN, what is the appropriate daily protein target once he is stable?
options: About 1.3 g/kg of adjusted body weight (~120 g/day)
1.3 g/kg of actual body weight (~170 g/day)
2.5 g/kg of actual body weight
0.5 g/kg of ideal body weight
Protein should be avoided in obesity to promote fat loss
questions.expl:
**Why A:** ESPEN uses adjusted body weight in obesity: IBW + ⅓ × (actual − IBW) = 71 + ⅓ × 59 ≈ 91 kg, and 1.3 × 91 ≈ 118 g/day – well below dosing by actual weight. ASPEN instead uses 2.0–2.5 g/kg IBW with hypocaloric energy.

**Why not the others:**
- B – actual weight overestimates lean mass and protein needs.
- C – 2.5 g/kg applies to ideal (not actual) body weight in ASPEN.
- D – too low; worsens muscle loss.
- E – obese patients lose lean mass and need protein.

**EDIC trap:** In obesity, adjust the **weight** you use, not just the dose per kg.

**Ref:** Singer P, Clin Nutr 2023; Compher C, JPEN 2022.

questions.stem: Regarding the TARGET Protein trial (2025):
options: It was a cluster-randomised crossover trial in Australian and New Zealand ICUs.
Augmented protein increased days alive and free of hospital at day 90.
The intervention arms differed markedly in energy delivery.
Augmented protein shortened ICU length of stay.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 8 ICUs alternated between formulas; 3,397 patients analysed.
- B (False) – median 62 vs 64 days; no benefit (and ICU stay slightly longer).
- C (False) – both arms received ~14 kcal/kg IBW/day; only protein differed (1.12 vs 0.69 g/kg IBW).
- D (False) – ICU stay was slightly longer with augmented protein (6.6 vs 6.2 days); harm signals appeared in the ventilated and new-KRT subgroups.

**Ref:** Summers MJ (TARGET Protein), JAMA 2025.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman is admitted with septic shock and is ventilated. Which protein strategy for the first week best reflects the evidence available in 2026?
options: Give 2.0–2.5 g/kg/day from day 1 to prevent muscle wasting
Start low once haemodynamically stable and increase progressively over about 5 days to ~1.2–1.3 g/kg/day
Give no protein for the first 7 days
Give IV amino acids 2 g/kg/day for kidney protection
Titrate protein to achieve a positive nitrogen balance by day 2
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Three RCTs (EFFORT Protein, PRECISe, TARGET Protein) found no benefit and possible harm with higher protein; ESPEN 2023 recommends 1.3 g/kg/day delivered progressively, and a 2026 synthesis suggests a ceiling of ~1.2 g/kg/day during the acute phase.

**Why not the others:**
- A – high early doses did not improve outcomes and worsened quality of life in PRECISe.
- C – prolonged protein deprivation is not recommended; NUTRIREA-3 restricted only for 7 days at 0.2–0.4 g/kg.
- D – IV amino acids reduced AKI after cardiac surgery (PROTECTION) but are not a nutrition strategy in sepsis.
- E – a positive nitrogen balance is not achievable early (anabolic resistance).

**Ref:** Singer P, Clin Nutr 2023; Chapple LS, Crit Care 2026.

questions.stem: Regarding protein and nutrition calculations:
options: One gram of urinary nitrogen corresponds to about 6.25 g of protein.
Protein provides about 9 kcal/g.
Patients on CRRT lose clinically relevant amounts of amino acids in the effluent.
A rising urea:creatinine ratio may indicate catabolism or excess protein intake.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – protein is ~16 % nitrogen.
- B (False) – protein and carbohydrate ~4 kcal/g; fat ~9 kcal/g.
- C (True) – ~10–20 g/day, higher with higher effluent doses.
- D (True) – urea rises when amino acids are oxidised.

**Ref:** Fiaccadori E, Clin Nutr 2021; Singer P, Clin Nutr 2019.

questions.stem: Which statement about the EFFORT Protein, PRECISe and TARGET Protein trials is LEAST accurate?
options: None of them showed a benefit of higher protein on its primary outcome
PRECISe was the only double-blinded trial of the three
EFFORT Protein enrolled patients at high nutritional risk
TARGET Protein was the largest of the three
All three showed that higher protein significantly reduced mortality in patients with AKI
questions.expl:
**Why E:** No trial showed lower mortality with higher protein in AKI; the EFFORT AKI analysis suggested higher mortality (HR ≈ 1.4), and TARGET Protein showed harm signals in patients needing new KRT.

**Why not the others:**
- A – all primary outcomes were neutral or worse with high protein.
- B – PRECISe used blinded isocaloric formulas.
- C – EFFORT selected NUTRIC ≥ 5, BMI < 18.5 or > 35, frailty or other high-risk features.
- D – ~3,400 patients vs 1,329 (EFFORT) and 935 (PRECISe).

**Ref:** Heyland DK, Lancet 2023; Bels JLM, Lancet 2024; Summers MJ, JAMA 2025.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with cirrhosis (Child–Pugh C) and grade 2 hepatic encephalopathy is admitted to the ICU with variceal bleeding, now controlled. Enteral feeding is planned. What protein intake is recommended?
options: Protein restriction to < 0.5 g/kg/day until encephalopathy resolves
No protein for 72 hours
About 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day without restriction for encephalopathy
3 g/kg/day to reverse sarcopenia
Only branched-chain amino acids parenterally
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Protein restriction worsens sarcopenia and does not improve encephalopathy; liver guidelines (ESPEN/EASL) recommend 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day in cirrhosis, using enteral feeding once bleeding is controlled.

**Why not the others:**
- A, B – protein restriction is no longer recommended in hepatic encephalopathy.
- D – excessive and unsupported.
- E – BCAA-enriched formulas may be used in protein-intolerant patients but are not the standard route or sole source.

**Ref:** Singer P, Clin Nutr 2019; Fiaccadori E, Clin Nutr 2021.

open.q: Summarise the evidence from the large randomised trials of protein dose in critical illness and give a practical recommendation for 2026.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **Rationale:** rapid muscle wasting (−17.7 % rectus femoris by day 10), observational associations of higher protein with survival – confounded by illness severity; anabolic resistance, ureagenesis, autophagy suppression as counter-arguments.
- **EFFORT Protein (2023, n = 1,329):** 1.6 vs 0.9 g/kg – no difference in time to discharge alive (46.1 vs 50.2 %), 60-day mortality 34.6 vs 32.1 %; harm in AKI and SOFA ≥ 9.
- **PRECISe (2024, n = 935, double-blind):** 2.0 vs 1.3 g/kg – worse EQ-5D-5L over 180 days, more GI intolerance.
- **TARGET Protein (2025, n ≈ 3,400):** 1.12 vs 0.69 g/kg IBW – no difference in days alive and out of hospital.
- **Recommendation:** start low once stable, increase over ~5 days to ~1.2–1.3 g/kg/day (ESPEN 2023; Chapple 2026); use adjusted BW in obesity; AKI without KRT – avoid high doses but do not restrict; CRRT up to 1.7 g/kg; reassess in recovery with rehabilitation.

title: W21 · D3 – Stress-ulcer prophylaxis: SUP-ICU, PEPTIC, REVISE and the 2024 guideline

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman has been ventilated for 3 days for community-acquired pneumonia and remains in septic shock on noradrenaline 0.3 µg/kg/min. She tolerates full enteral nutrition. Platelets are 180 × 10⁹/L and INR 1.1. What is the most appropriate approach to stress-ulcer prophylaxis?
options: Start a PPI (e.g. pantoprazole 40 mg daily) or an H₂-receptor antagonist
No prophylaxis, because full enteral nutrition is sufficient protection
Start sucralfate 1 g four times daily
Start high-dose pantoprazole infusion 8 mg/h
Start prophylaxis only if coffee-ground aspirates appear
questions.expl:
**Why A:** She has shock and is ventilated, so she is at risk of clinically important bleeding. The SCCM/ASHP 2024 guideline suggests SUP with a PPI or H₂RA for at-risk patients, including those receiving enteral nutrition.

**Why not the others:**
- B – EN reduces bleeding but is not a substitute for SUP in at-risk patients; SUP is withheld only in low-risk fed patients.
- C – sucralfate is less effective than H₂RA (Cook 1998) and PPI/H₂RA are preferred.
- D – low-dose rather than high-dose SUP is recommended; the infusion is for treating bleeding ulcers.
- E – waiting for overt bleeding defeats prophylaxis.

**Ref:** MacLaren R, Crit Care Med 2024; Cook D (REVISE), NEJM 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding the REVISE trial (2024):
options: It enrolled invasively ventilated adults and compared IV pantoprazole 40 mg daily with placebo.
Pantoprazole reduced clinically important upper GI bleeding from about 3.5 % to 1.0 %.
Pantoprazole significantly reduced 90-day mortality.
Ventilator-associated pneumonia was significantly more frequent with pantoprazole.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 4,821 patients in 68 ICUs.
- B (True) – HR 0.30 (95 % CI 0.19–0.47).
- C (False) – 90-day mortality 29.1 vs 30.9 % (HR 0.94, 0.85–1.04).
- D (False) – no significant difference in pneumonia or *C. difficile* infection.

**Ref:** Cook D (REVISE), NEJM 2024.

questions.stem: In the cohort study by Cook et al. (1994) of 2,252 ICU patients, which risk factors were the strongest independent predictors of clinically important GI bleeding?
options: Age > 65 years and male sex
Enteral nutrition and sedation
Mechanical ventilation for > 48 hours and coagulopathy
Diabetes and hypertension
Use of corticosteroids and NSAIDs
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Respiratory failure requiring ventilation > 48 h (OR 15.6) and coagulopathy (OR 4.3) were the two independent risk factors; without either, the bleeding rate was ~0.1 %.

**Why not the others:**
- A, D – not independent predictors.
- B – EN is protective, and sedation was not a risk factor.
- E – corticosteroids were not independent predictors in this cohort.

**Ref:** Cook DJ, NEJM 1994.

questions.stem: Regarding the definition and epidemiology of stress-related GI bleeding:
options: Endoscopic mucosal erosions are found in the majority of critically ill patients within days of admission.
Clinically important bleeding requires overt bleeding plus haemodynamic compromise, transfusion or need for intervention.
Stress ulcers are typically solitary, deep ulcers in the duodenal bulb.
In recent trials, clinically important bleeding without prophylaxis occurred in more than 20 % of ventilated patients.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – erosions in 75–100 % of patients, usually clinically silent.
- B (True) – Cook's definition, used in SUP-ICU and REVISE.
- C (False) – lesions are typically multiple, superficial erosions in the fundus and body of the stomach.
- D (False) – placebo arms had ~3.5–4.2 %.

**Ref:** Cook DJ, NEJM 1994; Krag M, NEJM 2018; Cook D, NEJM 2024.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is in the ICU on day 6 after elective spine surgery for observation of a post-operative respiratory complication. He is extubated, eating, haemodynamically stable, with normal coagulation. He has been on IV pantoprazole since admission and has no pre-admission indication. What should be done?
options: Continue pantoprazole until hospital discharge
Switch to oral omeprazole for 8 weeks
Switch to sucralfate
Add famotidine for dual protection
Stop the PPI, because risk factors have resolved
questions.expl:
**Why E:** The 2024 guideline good practice statement: discontinue SUP when risk factors are no longer present and before ICU discharge, to avoid inappropriate long-term PPI use and its harms.

**Why not the others:**
- A, B – continuing without indication exposes him to *C. difficile*, pneumonia, interactions and hypomagnesaemia.
- C – there is no indication for any prophylaxis.
- D – dual acid suppression has no role.

**Ref:** MacLaren R, Crit Care Med 2024; Amer M, Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2026.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man on clopidogrel after a recent coronary stent is ventilated in septic shock. Stress-ulcer prophylaxis is indicated. Which agent is most appropriate?
options: Omeprazole 40 mg daily
Pantoprazole 40 mg daily
Esomeprazole 80 mg bolus then 8 mg/h
Sucralfate 1 g four times daily
Misoprostol 200 µg four times daily
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19 and reduce clopidogrel activation; pantoprazole has the weakest interaction. Low-dose PPI (or H₂RA) is the recommended SUP regimen.

**Why not the others:**
- A – CYP2C19 interaction with clopidogrel.
- C – high-dose infusion is treatment for bleeding ulcers, not prophylaxis, and esomeprazole interacts with clopidogrel.
- D – less effective than acid suppression.
- E – no role in ICU SUP; causes diarrhoea.

**Ref:** MacLaren R, Crit Care Med 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding trials of stress-ulcer prophylaxis:
options: In SUP-ICU, pantoprazole reduced clinically important GI bleeding compared with placebo.
In SUP-ICU, 90-day mortality was similar with pantoprazole and placebo.
In PEPTIC, a PPI strategy resulted in fewer GI bleeds but numerically higher in-hospital mortality than an H₂RA strategy.
In the 1998 trial by Cook et al., sucralfate was more effective than ranitidine in preventing clinically important bleeding.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 2.5 vs 4.2 %.
- B (True) – 31.1 vs 30.4 %.
- C (True) – bleeding 1.3 vs 1.8 %; mortality 18.3 vs 17.5 % (RR 1.05, 95 % CI 1.00–1.10).
- D (False) – ranitidine was more effective (CIB 1.7 vs 3.8 %), with no difference in VAP.

**Ref:** Krag M, NEJM 2018; Young PJ, JAMA 2020; Cook D, NEJM 1998.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child–Pugh B) is admitted to the ICU with community-acquired pneumonia requiring high-flow oxygen. She is not ventilated and eats normally. Platelets 85 × 10⁹/L, INR 1.6. What is the best approach to stress-ulcer prophylaxis?
options: No prophylaxis because she is not ventilated
No prophylaxis because she is eating
Start a PPI or H₂RA at low dose, because chronic liver disease and coagulopathy are risk factors
Start high-dose PPI infusion
Give tranexamic acid instead
questions.expl:
**Why C:** The 2024 guideline identifies coagulopathy, shock and chronic liver disease as risk factors; SUP is suggested for at-risk patients regardless of ventilation status, using a low dose.

**Why not the others:**
- A – ventilation is one, but not the only, risk factor.
- B – eating does not remove her risk factors.
- D – high-dose infusion is not prophylaxis.
- E – tranexamic acid is not used for SUP and increased VTE in GI bleeding (HALT-IT).

**Ref:** MacLaren R, Crit Care Med 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding the 2024 SCCM/ASHP stress-ulcer prophylaxis guideline:
options: It recommends a PPI rather than an H₂RA as the only acceptable first-line agent.
It suggests against SUP in enterally fed patients at low risk of bleeding.
It recommends high-dose rather than low-dose acid suppression.
It suggests intravenous administration only, because enteral absorption is unreliable.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – either a PPI or an H₂RA is suggested as first line (moderate certainty).
- B (True) – low-risk, enterally fed patients should not receive SUP.
- C (False) – low-dose (e.g. pantoprazole ≤ 40 mg/day, famotidine ≤ 40 mg/day) is preferred.
- D (False) – enteral or IV routes are both acceptable.

**Ref:** MacLaren R, Crit Care Med 2024.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with septic shock (APACHE II 31) and multiorgan failure is ventilated. The team discusses stress-ulcer prophylaxis. Which statement best reflects current evidence?
options: PPIs clearly reduce mortality in this group
PPIs reduce bleeding, but subgroup data raise uncertainty about mortality in the most severely ill; an H₂RA is a reasonable alternative
SUP is contraindicated in patients with APACHE II > 25
Sucralfate is preferred in the most severely ill
Prophylaxis increases *C. difficile* infection threefold in randomised trials
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In REVISE, SUP-ICU and PEPTIC, PPIs reduced bleeding, but subgroups hinted at possible mortality harm in the sickest patients. Guidelines still suggest SUP for shock; some panels (SSAI 2026) note that H₂RAs may be preferred in the highest illness acuity.

**Why not the others:**
- A – no trial showed a mortality benefit.
- C – subgroup findings are hypothesis-generating, not contraindications.
- D – sucralfate is less effective.
- E – RCTs did not show a significant increase (meta-analysis RR 1.20, 0.66–2.16).

**Ref:** Cook D, NEJM 2024; Amer M, Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2026.

questions.stem: All of the following are recognised adverse effects or interactions of acid-suppressive therapy EXCEPT:
options: Hypomagnesaemia with long-term proton pump inhibitors
Thrombocytopenia with H₂-receptor antagonists
Reduced clopidogrel activation with omeprazole
Increased risk of hepatic encephalopathy with sucralfate
Acute interstitial nephritis with proton pump inhibitors
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Sucralfate's concerns are aluminium accumulation in renal failure, drug binding (e.g. fluoroquinolones, phenytoin) and tube occlusion; it is not associated with hepatic encephalopathy.

**Why not the others:**
- A – PPIs reduce intestinal magnesium absorption.
- B – H₂RAs can cause thrombocytopenia (and delirium).
- C – CYP2C19 inhibition.
- E – PPIs are a recognised cause of AIN.

**Ref:** MacLaren R, Crit Care Med 2024.

open.q: Outline the evidence and current recommendations for stress-ulcer prophylaxis in ventilated ICU patients.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **Pathophysiology:** splanchnic hypoperfusion, impaired mucosal defence; erosions very common, clinically important bleeding (overt + haemodynamic change/transfusion/intervention) ~1–4 %.
- **Risk factors:** ventilation > 48 h, coagulopathy (Cook 1994); shock, coagulopathy, chronic liver disease (2024 guideline).
- **Trials:** SUP-ICU (2018) – pantoprazole ↓ CIB 4.2 → 2.5 %, mortality unchanged; PEPTIC (2020) – PPI vs H₂RA: fewer bleeds, borderline ↑ mortality; REVISE (2024) – pantoprazole ↓ CIB 3.5 → 1.0 %, mortality 29.1 vs 30.9 %, no ↑ VAP/*C. difficile*; possible harm in APACHE II ≥ 25.
- **Recommendations:** SUP for at-risk patients (including on EN), not in low-risk fed patients; PPI or H₂RA, low dose, IV or enteral; avoid sucralfate; stop when risk resolves and before ICU discharge; deprescribe.
- **Harms:** pneumonia, *C. difficile*, interactions (clopidogrel), hypomagnesaemia, AIN, thrombocytopenia (H₂RA).

title: W21 · D4 – Acute mesenteric ischaemia and peritonitis

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation (anticoagulation stopped 2 weeks ago for a dental procedure) presents with sudden, severe periumbilical pain. Her abdomen is soft and minimally tender. Lactate is 1.4 mmol/L, creatinine 160 µmol/L (baseline 90), D-dimer 4,800 µg/L. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Abdominal ultrasound and review in 6 hours
Repeat lactate in 2 hours; image only if it rises
Non-contrast CT to protect the kidneys
Diagnostic laparoscopy in 24 hours if pain persists
Immediate biphasic CT angiography and unfractionated heparin
questions.expl:
**Why E:** This is a classic embolic SMA occlusion (AF, pain out of proportion, high D-dimer). ESVS recommends immediate CT angiography even with impaired renal function, and therapeutic heparin as soon as AMI is suspected.

**Why not the others:**
- A – ultrasound is inadequate and delay costs bowel.
- B – lactate is often normal in early AMI.
- C – non-contrast CT cannot show the vascular occlusion; the risk of missing AMI outweighs contrast-associated AKI.
- D – delay leads to transmural necrosis.

**Ref:** Koelemay MJW (ESVS), Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 2025; Bala M, World J Emerg Surg 2022.

questions.stem: Regarding the types of acute mesenteric ischaemia:
options: An SMA embolus typically lodges a few centimetres distal to the origin, so the proximal jejunum may be spared.
Acute SMA thrombosis often occurs on a pre-existing ostial atherosclerotic stenosis.
Non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia is associated with low cardiac output, vasopressors and haemodialysis.
Mesenteric venous thrombosis is primarily treated with anticoagulation.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – the embolus usually stops beyond the middle colic artery origin (3–10 cm).
- B (True) – often with a history of post-prandial pain and weight loss; the whole midgut is at risk.
- C (True) – splanchnic vasoconstriction in low-flow states, after cardiac surgery, with digoxin or cocaine.
- D (True) – heparin, then oral anticoagulation; surgery only for peritonitis/necrosis.

**Ref:** Koelemay MJW (ESVS), Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 2025.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is on day 2 after aortic valve replacement with low cardiac output (cardiac index 1.8 L/min/m²) on noradrenaline 0.4 µg/kg/min and adrenaline. Lactate has risen to 7 mmol/L and he has a distended abdomen. CT angiography shows patent mesenteric arteries with diffuse narrowing of SMA branches and no free air. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Immediate laparotomy with extensive small-bowel resection
Surgical SMA embolectomy
Optimise cardiac output, minimise vasoconstrictors, and consider selective intra-arterial vasodilator infusion
Systemic thrombolysis
Increase noradrenaline to MAP 85 mmHg
questions.expl:
**Why C:** This is non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia. Treatment targets the low-flow state and vasospasm: improve cardiac output, reduce vasoconstrictors where possible, and infuse papaverine or prostaglandin via a selective SMA catheter; laparotomy only for peritonitis/necrosis.

**Why not the others:**
- A – no evidence of necrosis or perforation yet; resection without treating the cause fails.
- B – there is no embolus.
- D – there is no thrombus.
- E – more vasoconstrictor aggravates splanchnic vasospasm.

**Ref:** Koelemay MJW (ESVS), Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 2025; Bala M, World J Emerg Surg 2022.

questions.stem: Regarding the diagnosis of acute mesenteric ischaemia:
options: A normal serum lactate reliably excludes acute mesenteric ischaemia.
D-dimer has high sensitivity, so a normal value makes AMI unlikely.
Pneumatosis intestinalis and portal venous gas on CT suggest transmural ischaemia.
CT angiography should include an arterial and a portal venous phase.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – lactate rises late, with necrosis.
- B (True) – sensitivity ~95 % but low specificity.
- C (True) – late signs of advanced ischaemia.
- D (True) – the venous phase identifies mesenteric venous thrombosis and bowel wall enhancement.

**Ref:** Koelemay MJW (ESVS), Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 2025.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man undergoes laparotomy for embolic SMA occlusion. After successful embolectomy, 60 cm of ileum appears dusky but not frankly necrotic. What is the best surgical strategy?
options: Resect the dusky segment with primary anastomosis and close the abdomen
Leave the dusky bowel, close the abdomen temporarily and perform a planned second-look laparotomy at 24–48 hours
Resect all small bowel distal to the SMA origin
Close the abdomen and repeat CT in 7 days
Create an end-ileostomy and close the abdomen definitively
questions.expl:
**Why B:** After revascularisation, questionable bowel may recover. Damage-control surgery with temporary closure and a planned second look at 24–48 h preserves bowel length and allows resection of only non-viable segments.

**Why not the others:**
- A – premature resection of potentially viable bowel risks short bowel syndrome; anastomosis in ischaemia risks leak.
- C – massive resection is unnecessary and causes intestinal failure.
- D – a 7-day delay misses progressive necrosis.
- E – definitive closure prevents reassessment.

**Ref:** Bala M, World J Emerg Surg 2022; Koelemay MJW (ESVS), Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 2025.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man has faecal peritonitis from a perforated sigmoid diverticulum. He undergoes Hartmann's procedure with adequate source control and is extubated on day 2. Which antibiotic duration is best supported by randomised evidence?
options: About 4 days
10 days
14 days
Until CRP normalises
21 days
questions.expl:
**Why A:** STOP-IT randomised 518 patients with complicated IAI and adequate source control: a fixed ~4-day course was as effective as treatment until resolution of physiological abnormalities (median 8 days) – composite outcome 21.8 vs 22.3 %.

**Why not the others:**
- B, C, E – longer courses add resistance and toxicity without benefit.
- D – CRP-guided therapy was not tested and prolongs exposure.

**EDIC trap:** Short courses apply only when **source control is adequate**; for postoperative IAI in ICU patients, DURAPOP showed 8 days non-inferior to 15.

**Ref:** Sawyer RG (STOP-IT), NEJM 2015.

questions.stem: Regarding peritonitis in critically ill patients:
options: Secondary peritonitis is typically monomicrobial.
Tertiary peritonitis is often caused by enterococci, *Candida* and coagulase-negative staphylococci.
In the RELAP trial, planned relaparotomy reduced mortality compared with on-demand relaparotomy.
Anaerobic cover is unnecessary in secondary peritonitis from colonic perforation.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – secondary peritonitis is polymicrobial (Enterobacterales, anaerobes, enterococci); SBP is monomicrobial.
- B (True) – resistant, low-virulence organisms persisting after source control.
- C (False) – no difference in death/major morbidity (57 vs 65 %); on-demand meant fewer laparotomies and lower costs.
- D (False) – *Bacteroides fragilis* must be covered (e.g. metronidazole, piperacillin–tazobactam, carbapenem).

**Ref:** Sartelli M, World J Emerg Surg 2021; van Ruler O (RELAP), JAMA 2007.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites is admitted with fever and confusion. Ascitic fluid shows 620 neutrophils/mm³; Gram stain shows Gram-negative rods only. Creatinine is 130 µmol/L. Besides cefotaxime, which intervention reduces renal failure and mortality?
options: Urgent laparotomy
Large-volume paracentesis of 8 litres without albumin
IV albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3
Terlipressin from day 1 in all patients
Furosemide infusion
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In SBP, albumin plus cefotaxime reduced renal impairment (10 vs 33 %) and hospital mortality (10 vs 29 %) in Sort's RCT; benefit is greatest with raised creatinine or bilirubin.

**Why not the others:**
- A – monomicrobial SBP is treated medically; laparotomy only for secondary peritonitis.
- B – large-volume paracentesis without albumin precipitates circulatory dysfunction and AKI.
- D – terlipressin is for hepatorenal syndrome–AKI, not routine SBP.
- E – diuretics worsen renal function in SBP.

**Ref:** Sort P, NEJM 1999.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman is in the ICU with septic shock on day 6 after anterior resection; CT shows an anastomotic leak with generalised peritonitis. Regarding her management:
options: Empirical antifungal therapy (e.g. an echinocandin) should be considered.
Empirical antibiotics should cover Enterobacterales, anaerobes and enterococci.
Antibiotics alone, without source control, are adequate if she is started on a carbapenem.
Intra-operative peritoneal fluid cultures should be obtained.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – healthcare-associated IAI with anastomotic leak and septic shock is a recognised risk for *Candida* peritonitis.
- B (True) – postoperative IAI carries enterococci and MDR organisms; piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem ± glycopeptide.
- C (False) – generalised peritonitis requires urgent source control.
- D (True) – to guide de-escalation in healthcare-associated infection.

**Ref:** Sartelli M, World J Emerg Surg 2021; Blot S (AbSeS), Intensive Care Med 2019.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman taking combined oral contraceptives presents with 4 days of increasing abdominal pain and nausea. CT shows superior mesenteric vein thrombosis with bowel wall thickening but no signs of necrosis or perforation. She is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Therapeutic anticoagulation with heparin and close clinical monitoring
Immediate laparotomy and small-bowel resection
Antiplatelet therapy only
Surgical SMA embolectomy
Observation without anticoagulation
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Mesenteric venous thrombosis without peritonitis is treated with immediate therapeutic anticoagulation, which recanalises the vein and prevents extension; surgery is reserved for peritonitis or necrosis, and catheter-directed thrombolysis for deterioration.

**Why not the others:**
- B – no necrosis; surgery is not first line.
- C – antiplatelets do not treat venous thrombosis.
- D – the arteries are patent.
- E – untreated MVT risks progression to infarction.

**Ref:** Koelemay MJW (ESVS), Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 2025.

questions.stem: All of the following are independent risk factors for death in critically ill patients with intra-abdominal infection (AbSeS study) EXCEPT:
options: Late-onset hospital-acquired infection
Secondary peritonitis with septic shock
Failed source control
Community-acquired localised appendiceal abscess drained percutaneously
Diffuse peritonitis
questions.expl:
**Why D:** A localised community-acquired infection with successful percutaneous source control is the lowest-risk scenario. AbSeS (n = 2,621; mortality 29 %) identified late-onset hospital-acquired IAI, secondary peritonitis with septic shock, diffuse peritonitis and failed source control as risk factors.

**Why not the others:**
- A, B, C, E – all were associated with higher mortality in AbSeS.

**Ref:** Blot S (AbSeS), Intensive Care Med 2019.

open.q: Describe the diagnosis and management of acute arterial mesenteric ischaemia.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **Suspicion:** pain out of proportion, AF/embolic source or vascular history; in ICU – unexplained lactate rise, distension, GI intolerance.
- **Tests:** lactate and WBC may be normal early; D-dimer sensitive (normal → unlikely); **immediate biphasic CTA**, even with AKI.
- **Treatment:** resuscitation, **IV heparin**, broad-spectrum antibiotics, NG decompression; **revascularisation first** (embolectomy, bypass, ROMS or endovascular), then laparotomy with resection of non-viable bowel only; **second-look at 24–48 h**; avoid high-dose vasoconstrictors.
- **NOMI:** improve cardiac output, reduce vasoconstrictors, intra-arterial papaverine/prostaglandin; **MVT:** anticoagulation.
- **Outcome:** mortality 50–70 %, better in intestinal stroke centres; risk of short bowel syndrome.

open.q: What are the principles of managing secondary peritonitis with septic shock in the ICU?
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Sepsis bundle: cultures, **empirical antibiotics within 1 h** covering Enterobacterales and anaerobes (pip–tazo; carbapenem if ESBL risk), plus enterococci/MDR ± echinocandin in healthcare-associated IAI with leak, recurrent surgery or upper GI perforation.
- **Source control as soon as practical** (surgery, percutaneous drainage); intra-operative cultures; on-demand rather than planned relaparotomy (RELAP); open abdomen when needed; monitor IAP.
- **Short antibiotic duration** after adequate source control: ~4 days (STOP-IT), 8 days for postoperative IAI in ICU (DURAPOP); de-escalate.
- Recognise tertiary peritonitis; AbSeS risk factors (hospital-acquired, septic shock, diffuse peritonitis, failed source control).

title: W21 · D5 – Diarrhoea, *Clostridioides difficile* and ileus in the ICU

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man on day 9 of ICU stay for pneumonia (treated with ceftriaxone and clarithromycin) develops 6 watery stools per day. WBC is 18 × 10⁹/L, creatinine 150 µmol/L (baseline 80). Stool GDH and toxin A/B EIA are both positive. He is haemodynamically stable without ileus. What is the preferred treatment?
options: Oral metronidazole 500 mg tds for 10 days
IV vancomycin 1 g bd
Loperamide and probiotics
Oral fidaxomicin 200 mg bd for 10 days
Immediate subtotal colectomy
questions.expl:
**Why D:** This is severe (not fulminant) CDI (WBC > 15, creatinine > 133 µmol/L). ESCMID 2021 and IDSA/SHEA 2021 recommend fidaxomicin as first-line therapy, with oral vancomycin 125 mg qds as an alternative.

**Why not the others:**
- A – metronidazole is inferior and no longer recommended for severe CDI.
- B – IV vancomycin is not excreted into the colon lumen.
- C – antimotility agents are avoided in severe CDI; probiotics are not a treatment.
- E – surgery is for fulminant disease (perforation, toxic megacolon, refractory shock).

**Ref:** van Prehn J, Clin Microbiol Infect 2021; Johnson S, Clin Infect Dis 2021.

questions.stem: Regarding the laboratory diagnosis of *Clostridioides difficile* infection:
options: Stool culture is the recommended first-line test because it is specific for toxin-producing disease.
Formed stools should be tested in all ICU patients receiving antibiotics.
A repeat test should be sent after treatment to document cure.
A positive NAAT/PCR alone reliably distinguishes active infection from colonisation.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – culture is slow and detects non-toxigenic strains and colonisation; a two-step algorithm (GDH or NAAT, then toxin EIA) is recommended.
- B (False) – only unformed stool from patients with ≥ 3 unexplained loose stools in 24 h should be tested.
- C (False) – there is no test of cure; spores and toxin may persist.
- D (False) – NAAT detects the toxin gene and is positive in carriers; toxin EIA confirms active disease.

**Ref:** Crobach MJT, Clin Microbiol Infect 2016.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman with known *C. difficile* infection becomes hypotensive (MAP 58 mmHg on noradrenaline), her abdomen is distended with absent stool output, and CT shows colonic dilatation to 8 cm without perforation. Lactate is 3.8 mmol/L. Besides resuscitation and urgent surgical review, which antimicrobial regimen is recommended?
options: Oral metronidazole 500 mg tds alone
IV vancomycin plus IV metronidazole
Oral fidaxomicin 200 mg bd alone
IV meropenem
Vancomycin 500 mg qds via NG tube plus rectal vancomycin and IV metronidazole 500 mg tds
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Fulminant CDI with ileus and toxic megacolon: high-dose enteral vancomycin, rectal vancomycin (because ileus prevents delivery to the colon) and IV metronidazole (which reaches the colon via bile and inflamed mucosa). Surgery (subtotal colectomy or loop ileostomy with lavage) is considered early, before lactate exceeds 5 mmol/L.

**Why not the others:**
- A – oral metronidazole alone is inadequate and absorption/delivery is unreliable in ileus.
- B – IV vancomycin does not reach the colonic lumen.
- C – evidence for fidaxomicin alone in fulminant CDI with ileus is limited.
- D – meropenem does not treat CDI.

**Ref:** McDonald LC, Clin Infect Dis 2018; van Prehn J, Clin Microbiol Infect 2021.

questions.stem: Regarding *Clostridioides difficile*:
options: It is a spore-forming anaerobic Gram-positive bacillus.
Alcohol-based hand rub reliably inactivates its spores.
Clindamycin, cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones are high-risk antibiotics.
Proton pump inhibitors are associated with increased risk of infection.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – disease is mediated by toxins A and B.
- B (False) – spores resist alcohol; wash hands with soap and water and clean surfaces with chlorine-based agents.
- C (True) – risk persists for weeks to months after exposure.
- D (True) – an association repeatedly found in observational studies; review PPI indications.

**Ref:** McDonald LC, Clin Infect Dis 2018; van Prehn J, Clin Microbiol Infect 2021.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man ventilated for 6 days after polytrauma has 5 liquid stools per day for 48 hours. He receives enteral nutrition at 70 mL/h, paracetamol syrup, potassium chloride syrup, IV piperacillin–tazobactam and metoclopramide. *C. difficile* testing is negative. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Stop enteral nutrition and start parenteral nutrition
Start loperamide and continue all drugs
Review and change sorbitol-containing liquid drugs and prokinetics, and continue EN
Start empirical oral vancomycin
Order colonoscopy
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Drugs are the commonest cause of ICU diarrhoea; sorbitol-containing syrups (paracetamol, KCl) and prokinetics are classic culprits. EN should not be stopped routinely; adjust rate or formula if needed.

**Why not the others:**
- A – stopping EN deprives the gut and patient of nutrition and rarely resolves the cause.
- B – loperamide may be used once infection is excluded, but the reversible causes should be addressed first.
- D – CDI has been excluded.
- E – colonoscopy is not a first-line test for ICU diarrhoea.

**Ref:** Reintam Blaser A, Intensive Care Med 2012; Reintam Blaser A, Crit Care 2020.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman is on day 4 after hip replacement. She has abdominal distension, no stool for 4 days and no peritonism. CT shows dilatation of the caecum (11 cm) and right colon without mechanical obstruction. Potassium and magnesium have been corrected; 36 hours of conservative treatment (NG and rectal tube, opioid reduction) have failed. Heart rate is 82/min. What is the next step?
options: Neostigmine 2 mg IV over 3–5 minutes with ECG monitoring and atropine available
Emergency right hemicolectomy
Erythromycin 250 mg IV
Increase opioids for pain
Water-soluble contrast enema followed by observation for 7 days
questions.expl:
**Why A:** This is acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie) refractory to conservative care. Neostigmine produced rapid decompression in 10 of 11 patients vs 0 of 10 with placebo (Ponec 1999); monitor for bradycardia and bronchospasm with atropine ready.

**Why not the others:**
- B – surgery is for perforation, ischaemia or failure of medical/endoscopic decompression.
- C – erythromycin is an upper GI prokinetic; it is not the treatment for colonic pseudo-obstruction.
- D – opioids worsen colonic dysmotility.
- E – prolonged observation with a caecum approaching 12 cm risks perforation.

**Ref:** Ponec RJ, NEJM 1999.

questions.stem: Regarding the ESICM definitions of gastrointestinal dysfunction:
options: Lower GI paralysis is defined as no stool for at least 3 consecutive days without mechanical obstruction.
Feeding intolerance is defined as failure to reach 20 kcal/kg/day enterally within 24 hours of ICU admission.
Absent bowel sounds alone define AGI grade III.
Abdominal compartment syndrome is classified as AGI grade II.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – synonymous with paralytic ileus.
- B (False) – the threshold is < 20 kcal/kg/day within **72 h** of feeding attempts.
- C (False) – absent bowel sounds are grade I at most; grade III is GI failure persisting despite interventions.
- D (False) – ACS is AGI grade IV (immediately life-threatening); IAH grade I is grade II.

**Ref:** Reintam Blaser A, Intensive Care Med 2012.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman has her third episode of *C. difficile* infection within 4 months. Previous episodes were treated with oral vancomycin and then fidaxomicin. She is now clinically stable. What is the most effective strategy to prevent further recurrence?
options: Oral metronidazole for 6 weeks
Lifelong oral vancomycin 125 mg qds
Probiotics alone
Faecal microbiota transplantation after a course of anti-CDI antibiotics
Colectomy
questions.expl:
**Why D:** For multiple recurrences, ESCMID and IDSA/SHEA recommend FMT, which resolved recurrent CDI in ~81 % vs 31 % with vancomycin alone (van Nood, NEJM 2013).

**Why not the others:**
- A – metronidazole is not recommended for recurrence and causes neurotoxicity with prolonged use.
- B – long-term suppression is reserved for patients unsuitable for FMT.
- C – probiotics have insufficient evidence.
- E – surgery is for fulminant disease, not recurrence.

**Ref:** van Prehn J, Clin Microbiol Infect 2021; Johnson S, Clin Infect Dis 2021; van Nood E, NEJM 2013.

questions.stem: Regarding infection control and severity assessment in *C. difficile* infection:
options: Patients should be isolated with contact precautions (gloves and gowns).
Sporicidal, chlorine-based agents are recommended for environmental cleaning.
A white cell count > 15 × 10⁹/L is a marker of severe disease.
Hypotension, ileus or toxic megacolon define fulminant (severe-complicated) disease.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – single room or cohorting, gloves and gowns.
- B (True) – spores persist on surfaces for months.
- C (True) – together with creatinine > 133 µmol/L (IDSA) or > 50 % rise and fever > 38.5 °C (ESCMID).
- D (True) – also shock, perforation and raised lactate.

**Ref:** McDonald LC, Clin Infect Dis 2018; van Prehn J, Clin Microbiol Infect 2021.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man ventilated for septic shock has not passed stool for 5 days. He receives fentanyl, enteral nutrition at target and noradrenaline. There is no distension and CT is not indicated. All of the following are appropriate measures EXCEPT:
options: Correcting hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia
Starting an osmotic laxative (e.g. macrogol)
Reducing opioid exposure with multimodal analgesia where possible
A rectal examination to exclude faecal impaction
Stopping enteral nutrition until the patient passes stool
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Lower GI paralysis (no stool ≥ 3 days) is not by itself a reason to stop EN; feeding helps restore motility. EN is withheld only for obstruction, ischaemia, ACS or large GRV.

**Why not the others:**
- A – electrolyte disturbances impair motility.
- B – laxative protocols are standard.
- C – opioids are a major cause of ICU constipation.
- D – impaction must be excluded (also a cause of overflow diarrhoea).

**Ref:** Reintam Blaser A, Intensive Care Med 2012; Reintam Blaser A, Crit Care 2020.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman develops 4 watery stools per day on day 5 of ICU stay. She has a WBC of 9 × 10⁹/L, normal creatinine and no fever. GDH is positive, toxin EIA negative and PCR for the toxin B gene positive. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options: Definite severe CDI requiring IV metronidazole
False-positive result; *C. difficile* is not present
Toxin-producing strain present – possible CDI or colonisation; decide on clinical grounds (alternative causes, risk factors)
Fulminant colitis
The test must be repeated daily until negative
questions.expl:
**Why C:** GDH+/NAAT+ with a negative toxin EIA indicates a toxigenic strain without detectable free toxin – it may be colonisation or CDI with low toxin levels. ESCMID advises clinical evaluation; treat if CDI is likely and no other cause is found.

**Why not the others:**
- A – she has no severity criteria, and IV metronidazole is not first-line.
- B – both screen tests confirm the organism is present.
- D – no features of fulminant disease.
- E – repeat testing within 7 days and tests of cure are discouraged.

**Ref:** Crobach MJT, Clin Microbiol Infect 2016.

open.q: Outline the diagnosis and management of *Clostridioides difficile* infection in an ICU patient, including fulminant disease.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **Risk factors:** antibiotics (clindamycin, cephalosporins, quinolones), age, hospitalisation, PPIs, immunosuppression.
- **Diagnosis:** unformed stool, ≥ 3 in 24 h; two-step (GDH/NAAT then toxin EIA); no test of cure; CT for complications (toxic megacolon > 6 cm).
- **Severity:** severe – WBC > 15 × 10⁹/L, creatinine > 133 µmol/L or > 50 % rise, fever > 38.5 °C; fulminant – shock, ileus, megacolon, perforation.
- **Treatment:** stop inciting antibiotics/PPIs; fidaxomicin 200 mg bd × 10 days (or oral vancomycin 125 mg qds); fulminant – vancomycin 500 mg qds enterally + rectal vancomycin if ileus + IV metronidazole; early surgery (subtotal colectomy or loop ileostomy with lavage) for perforation, megacolon, refractory shock, lactate approaching 5 mmol/L.
- **Recurrence:** fidaxomicin/vancomycin taper; FMT for multiple recurrences.
- **Infection control:** contact precautions, soap and water, chlorine cleaning, stewardship.

title: W21 · Saturday – weekly review: GI II (nutrition timing and calories, protein, stress-ulcer prophylaxis, mesenteric ischaemia and peritonitis, diarrhoea, C. difficile and ileus)

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man (80 kg) is ventilated on day 1 for septic shock from cholangitis. Noradrenaline has risen from 0.2 to 0.6 µg/kg/min over the last 4 hours and lactate from 4 to 7 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate nutritional plan for now?
options: Start full-dose enteral nutrition at 25 kcal/kg/day
Start full-dose parenteral nutrition
Start trophic enteral nutrition at 10 mL/h
Delay nutrition until shock is controlled, then start low-dose enteral nutrition
Give IV glutamine to protect the gut
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Uncontrolled shock (escalating vasopressor dose, rising lactate) is the main ESICM indication to delay EN. Once shock is controlled, low-dose EN is started and advanced progressively.

**Why not the others:**
- A – full-dose early EN in shock increased bowel ischaemia (NUTRIREA-2), and low early intake was at least as safe (NUTRIREA-3).
- B – early full PN adds no benefit (EPaNIC, CALORIES) and risks overfeeding.
- C – even trophic EN is withheld while shock is uncontrolled.
- E – glutamine is harmful in shock and multiple organ failure (REDOXS).

**Ref:** Reintam Blaser A, Intensive Care Med 2017; Reignier J, Lancet 2018. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: Regarding trials of early nutrition in the ICU:
options: In EPaNIC, late parenteral nutrition (from day 8) resulted in fewer infections than early parenteral nutrition.
In NUTRIREA-3, low calorie and protein intake during the first week reduced day-90 mortality.
In TARGET (2018), energy-dense enteral nutrition reduced 90-day mortality.
In CALORIES, 30-day mortality did not differ between early parenteral and early enteral nutrition.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 22.8 vs 26.2 %, with faster discharge alive.
- B (False) – mortality 41.3 vs 42.8 % (not significant); the benefit was a shorter time to readiness for ICU discharge and fewer GI complications.
- C (False) – 26.8 vs 25.7 % – more calories, no benefit.
- D (True) – 33.1 vs 34.1 %.

**Ref:** Casaer MP, NEJM 2011; Reignier J, Lancet Respir Med 2023; TARGET Investigators, NEJM 2018; Harvey SE, NEJM 2014. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with chronic pancreatitis and a BMI of 17 kg/m² is ventilated after a laparotomy. On day 3 of enteral feeding, serum phosphate is 0.4 mmol/L (from 1.1 on admission), potassium 3.1 mmol/L. What should be done with the feeding?
options: Increase feeding to 30 kcal/kg/day
Reduce caloric intake for about 48 hours, replace phosphate, potassium and thiamine, then increase gradually
Stop feeding for one week
Continue unchanged and recheck phosphate in 3 days
Switch to parenteral nutrition at the same calories
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Refeeding hypophosphataemia. In Doig's RCT, temporary caloric restriction for 48 h with electrolyte replacement reduced 60-day mortality.

**Why not the others:**
- A – more calories aggravate the intracellular shift.
- C – prolonged starvation worsens malnutrition.
- D – severe hypophosphataemia needs immediate action (respiratory muscle weakness, arrhythmias).
- E – PN causes refeeding as well.

**Ref:** Doig GS, Lancet Respir Med 2015. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man ventilated for 6 days for septic shock has new stage 3 AKI (not on KRT). Which protein strategy is best supported by recent randomised evidence?
options: Moderate protein (~1.0–1.3 g/kg/day), avoiding high doses
2.2 g/kg/day to counter muscle wasting
Stop protein until creatinine falls
0.5 g/kg/day to delay dialysis
IV amino acids 2 g/kg/day for kidney protection
questions.expl:
**Why A:** In EFFORT Protein, high protein in patients with baseline AKI (not on KRT) was associated with higher 60-day mortality (HR ≈ 1.4); current synthesis supports a progressive increase to ~1.2–1.3 g/kg/day, without restriction.

**Why not the others:**
- B – high doses showed no benefit and possible harm (EFFORT, PRECISe, TARGET Protein).
- C, D – protein restriction to avoid KRT is not recommended.
- E – PROTECTION tested IV amino acids for AKI prevention in cardiac surgery, not as treatment in septic AKI.

**Ref:** Stoppe C, Crit Care 2023; Chapple LS, Crit Care 2026. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: Regarding the large protein-dose trials in critical illness:
options: PRECISe was double-blinded and compared isocaloric formulas providing 2.0 vs 1.3 g/kg/day of protein.
In PRECISe, high protein improved health-related quality of life at 180 days.
TARGET Protein was a cluster-randomised crossover trial with more than 3,000 patients.
In EFFORT Protein, high protein significantly reduced 60-day mortality.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 935 ventilated patients in the Netherlands and Belgium.
- B (False) – EQ-5D-5L utility was worse (mean difference −0.05) with more GI intolerance.
- C (True) – 3,397 analysed, 8 ICUs in Australia and New Zealand; no benefit in days alive and out of hospital.
- D (False) – 34.6 vs 32.1 % (RR 1.08, not significant).

**Ref:** Bels JLM, Lancet 2024; Summers MJ, JAMA 2025; Heyland DK, Lancet 2023. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is on day 7 of continuous veno-venous haemodiafiltration for septic AKI. His shock has resolved and he tolerates enteral nutrition. What protein intake is recommended by the ESPEN renal guideline?
options: 0.6 g/kg/day
0.8 g/kg/day
No protein while on CRRT
3.0 g/kg/day
Up to 1.7 g/kg/day
questions.expl:
**Why E:** CRRT removes ~10–20 g of amino acids daily; ESPEN suggests 1.0–1.5 g/kg/day on KRT and up to 1.7 g/kg/day on CRRT in hypercatabolic patients. In EFFORT, patients already on KRT were not harmed by higher protein.

**Why not the others:**
- A, B – protein restriction is not recommended.
- C – withholding protein worsens catabolism.
- D – exceeds any recommendation.

**Ref:** Fiaccadori E, Clin Nutr 2021. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman is ventilated on day 2 for ARDS. She is haemodynamically stable without vasopressors, platelets 210 × 10⁹/L, INR 1.0, no liver disease, and is fully enterally fed. Mechanical ventilation is expected to continue for several days. Which statement about stress-ulcer prophylaxis is best supported by REVISE?
options: Pantoprazole would reduce her risk of clinically important upper GI bleeding without a clear effect on mortality
Pantoprazole would reduce 90-day mortality
Pantoprazole would significantly increase ventilator-associated pneumonia
Enteral nutrition makes pantoprazole ineffective
Sucralfate is superior to pantoprazole
questions.expl:
**Why A:** REVISE enrolled invasively ventilated adults: pantoprazole reduced clinically important upper GI bleeding (1.0 vs 3.5 %, HR 0.30) with no significant difference in 90-day mortality (29.1 vs 30.9 %), pneumonia or *C. difficile*.

**Why not the others:**
- B – mortality was not reduced.
- C – no significant increase in VAP.
- D – most REVISE patients were enterally fed, and the effect on bleeding was consistent.
- E – sucralfate is less effective than acid suppression.

**Ref:** Cook D (REVISE), NEJM 2024. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: Regarding the 2024 SCCM/ASHP stress-ulcer prophylaxis guideline:
options: Shock, coagulopathy and chronic liver disease are considered risk factors for clinically important bleeding.
SUP should be stopped when risk factors resolve and before ICU discharge.
SUP is suggested for enterally fed patients who have risk factors.
High-dose PPI infusion is the preferred prophylactic regimen.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – low to moderate certainty.
- B (True) – good practice statement to avoid inappropriate continuation.
- C (True) – conditional recommendation, very low certainty; low-risk fed patients should not receive SUP.
- D (False) – low-dose PPI or H₂RA is recommended; infusions treat bleeding ulcers.

**Ref:** MacLaren R, Crit Care Med 2024. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: In the PEPTIC cluster-crossover trial of 26,982 ventilated ICU patients, what did a PPI-based prophylaxis strategy show compared with an H₂-receptor antagonist strategy?
options: Lower in-hospital mortality
Fewer GI bleeds but numerically higher in-hospital mortality (18.3 vs 17.5 %)
More GI bleeding and more *C. difficile* infection
No difference in any outcome, including bleeding
A significant reduction in ventilator-associated pneumonia
questions.expl:
**Why B:** GI bleeding was lower with PPIs (1.3 vs 1.8 %), but in-hospital mortality was 18.3 vs 17.5 % (RR 1.05, 95 % CI 1.00–1.10) – a borderline signal that later fed the debate about PPIs in the sickest patients.

**Why not the others:**
- A – mortality was numerically higher with PPIs.
- C – bleeding was lower; *C. difficile* did not differ significantly.
- D – bleeding differed.
- E – pneumonia was not reduced.

**Ref:** Young PJ (PEPTIC), JAMA 2020. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man with atrial fibrillation not on anticoagulation presents with sudden abdominal pain out of proportion to examination. Regarding his management:
options: A normal lactate makes acute mesenteric ischaemia very unlikely.
CT angiography should be delayed until renal function is known.
Intravenous unfractionated heparin should be started as soon as AMI is suspected.
After revascularisation, bowel of doubtful viability should be resected immediately to avoid a second operation.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – lactate is often normal early; D-dimer is more sensitive.
- B (False) – CTA should be done immediately, even with impaired renal function.
- C (True) – heparin limits thrombus propagation.
- D (False) – questionable bowel is reassessed at a planned second-look laparotomy at 24–48 h.

**Ref:** Koelemay MJW (ESVS), Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 2025; Bala M, World J Emerg Surg 2022. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a perforated appendix and localised peritonitis undergoes laparoscopic appendicectomy with adequate source control. Which antibiotic course is most appropriate?
options: A fixed course of about 4 days
14 days of IV therapy
Antibiotics until WBC normalises, regardless of duration
21 days to prevent abscess formation
No antibiotics after surgery in any case
questions.expl:
**Why A:** STOP-IT showed that ~4 days after adequate source control were as effective as longer, physiology-guided courses (median 8 days): composite outcome 21.8 vs 22.3 %.

**Why not the others:**
- B, D – longer courses increase resistance and adverse effects without benefit.
- C – laboratory normalisation prolongs exposure unnecessarily.
- E – complicated intra-abdominal infection with perforation requires a short course.

**Ref:** Sawyer RG (STOP-IT), NEJM 2015. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with cirrhosis and ascites has spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (ascitic neutrophils 900/mm³). Which ascitic finding would most strongly suggest secondary peritonitis instead?
options: Neutrophil count of 300/mm³
Ascitic total protein of 8 g/L
Monomicrobial *E. coli* growth
Polymicrobial culture with ascitic glucose < 2.8 mmol/L and LDH above the serum upper limit
Serum-ascites albumin gradient > 11 g/L
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Polymicrobial growth and Runyon criteria (glucose < 2.8 mmol/L, protein > 10 g/L, LDH > upper limit of serum) suggest a surgical source (perforation) and require urgent CT.

**Why not the others:**
- A – a neutrophil count ≥ 250/mm³ defines SBP.
- B – low protein (< 10 g/L) is typical of cirrhotic ascites and SBP risk.
- C – monomicrobial Gram-negative growth is typical of SBP.
- E – a high SAAG indicates portal hypertension.

**Ref:** Sort P, NEJM 1999; Sartelli M, World J Emerg Surg 2021. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: Regarding *Clostridioides difficile* infection:
options: Fidaxomicin is the preferred first-line agent in ESCMID and IDSA/SHEA guidelines.
IV vancomycin is effective because it achieves high colonic concentrations.
Metronidazole is the preferred treatment for severe disease.
Diagnosis should use a two-step algorithm, such as GDH or NAAT followed by a toxin immunoassay.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – oral vancomycin 125 mg qds is the alternative.
- B (False) – IV vancomycin is not excreted into the colon; only oral/rectal vancomycin works.
- C (False) – metronidazole is inferior; it is used IV only as an adjunct in fulminant disease.
- D (True) – NAAT alone overdiagnoses colonisation.

**Ref:** van Prehn J, Clin Microbiol Infect 2021; Crobach MJT, Clin Microbiol Infect 2016. → [D5](D5.md)

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman develops massive caecal dilatation (13 cm) on day 3 after open pelvic surgery. CT shows no mechanical obstruction or perforation. All of the following are appropriate EXCEPT:
options: Stopping opioids and anticholinergic drugs where possible
Correcting potassium and magnesium
Neostigmine 2 mg IV with ECG monitoring if conservative measures fail
Colonoscopic decompression if neostigmine fails
Metoclopramide infusion as the definitive treatment for 7 days
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Metoclopramide acts on the upper GI tract and is not a treatment for acute colonic pseudo-obstruction; 7 days of observation with a caecum > 12 cm risks perforation.

**Why not the others:**
- A, B – reversible contributors to Ogilvie syndrome.
- C – neostigmine decompressed 10/11 vs 0/10 with placebo; monitor for bradycardia.
- D – colonoscopic decompression is the next step after failed neostigmine.

**Ref:** Ponec RJ, NEJM 1999; Reintam Blaser A, Intensive Care Med 2012. → [D5](D5.md)

questions.stem: Regarding diarrhoea and GI dysfunction in the ICU:
options: Diarrhoea is defined as ≥ 3 loose or liquid stools per day.
Sorbitol-containing liquid medications are a recognised cause of diarrhoea.
Enteral nutrition should not routinely be stopped because of diarrhoea.
Faecal impaction can present with overflow diarrhoea.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – with stool weight > 200–250 g/day (ESICM 2012).
- B (True) – e.g. paracetamol and potassium syrups.
- C (True) – review drugs, exclude *C. difficile* and adjust the rate or formula instead.
- D (True) – rectal examination is part of the work-up.

**Ref:** Reintam Blaser A, Intensive Care Med 2012. → [D5](D5.md)

title: W22 · D1 – Red cell transfusion thresholds: TRICC to TRICS-III, MINT and TRAIN

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is on day 4 in ICU with septic shock from pneumonia, now on noradrenaline 0.08 µg/kg/min. Lactate is 1.6 mmol/L, Hb 7.6 g/dL and there is no bleeding. What is the most appropriate transfusion approach?
options: Transfuse 2 units to reach Hb ≥ 10 g/dL
Transfuse 1 unit to keep haematocrit ≥ 30 %
Do not transfuse now; transfuse if Hb falls below 7 g/dL
Transfuse if ScvO₂ is below 70 %
Start erythropoietin and IV iron instead of transfusion
questions.expl:
