With an IAP of 12–20 mmHg, low-rate EN may be started or continued with IAP monitoring; EN is delayed when IAP exceeds 20 mmHg or ACS develops.
In hepatic encephalopathy due to cirrhosis, protein should not be restricted.
In refeeding hypophosphataemia, restricting calories for 48 h with phosphate replacement reduced mortality (Doig 2015).
questions.expl:
- A (True) – EN is preferred over PN in severe AP. Use nasojejunal feeding only if gastric feeding is not tolerated. In mild AP, start a low-fat oral diet within 24–48 h.
- B (True) – This is ESICM 2017. IAH grade I corresponds to AGI II, IAH grades II–III to AGI III, and ACS to AGI IV.
- C (True) – Give 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day, up to 2 g/kg in the critically ill. Protein is also not restricted in ALF, where ammonia is monitored.
- D (True) – Calories were restricted to about 20 kcal/h for 48 h, which lowered 60-day mortality. Check phosphate daily in the first week, along with K⁺, Mg²⁺ and thiamine.

**Ref:** Reintam Blaser A, et al. ESICM early EN. *Intensive Care Med* 2017;43:380–398; Tenner S, et al. ACG. *Am J Gastroenterol* 2024;119:419–437; Doig GS, et al. *Lancet Respir Med* 2015;3:943–952.

Review: [W20/D2](#W20-D2), [W20/D5](#W20-D5), [W20/D4](#W20-D4), [W21/D1](#W21-D1)

title: W22 · Saturday – weekly review: Haematology (transfusion thresholds, DIC and coagulopathy, TTP/HUS and HIT, VTE, massive transfusion and viscoelastic testing)

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man is on day 5 in ICU after an emergency laparotomy for perforated diverticulitis. He is off vasopressors, not bleeding, and has no cardiac history. Hb is 7.3 g/dL. The surgical team requests 2 units of red cells "to aid healing". What is the most appropriate response?
options: Transfuse 2 units to reach Hb 9 g/dL
Transfuse 1 unit and recheck
Give IV iron and erythropoietin instead
Transfuse to Hb 10 g/dL because he is elderly
No transfusion now; transfuse if Hb falls below 7 g/dL or he develops signs of inadequate oxygen delivery
questions.expl:
**Why E:** ESICM 2020 strongly recommends a restrictive threshold of 7 g/dL in non-bleeding critically ill adults (TRICC; Cochrane – no mortality difference with ~40 % fewer patients transfused). There is no evidence that transfusion improves wound healing.

**Why not the others:**
- A – liberal transfusion adds risk (TACO, infection) without benefit.
- B – single-unit transfusion is good practice, but Hb 7.3 g/dL is above the threshold.
- C – ESICM 2020 suggests against iron/EPO to prevent transfusion in non-bleeding ICU patients.
- D – ESICM 2020 makes no recommendation for a higher threshold in elderly patients.

**Ref:** Vlaar AP, Intensive Care Med 2020; Hébert PC, N Engl J Med 1999. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: Regarding red cell transfusion thresholds in specific populations:
options: In TRICS-III, a threshold of 7.5 g/dL after cardiac surgery was non-inferior to a liberal threshold.
In MINT, a restrictive strategy in acute MI significantly reduced death or re-infarction at 30 days.
In TRISS, a threshold of 7 g/dL in septic shock gave similar 90-day mortality to 9 g/dL.
In upper GI bleeding, a liberal threshold of 9 g/dL reduced rebleeding compared with 7 g/dL.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – composite 11.4 vs 12.5 %.
- B (False) – 16.9 % restrictive vs 14.5 % liberal (RR 1.15, 0.99–1.34); the point estimates favoured liberal.
- C (True) – 43.0 vs 45.0 %.
- D (False) – the restrictive strategy reduced rebleeding and 6-week mortality (5 vs 9 %).

**Ref:** Mazer CD, N Engl J Med 2017; Carson JL, N Engl J Med 2023; Holst LB, N Engl J Med 2014. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with AML (platelets 22 × 10⁹/L, INR 1.3) needs an ultrasound-guided internal jugular CVC for chemotherapy. She is not bleeding. Based on the PACER trial, what is the most appropriate approach?
options: Transfuse plasma 15 mL/kg before insertion
Transfuse one unit of platelets before insertion
No platelets – ultrasound guidance makes bleeding negligible
Postpone the line until platelets exceed 100 × 10⁹/L
Give tranexamic acid instead of platelets
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In PACER (platelets 10–50 × 10⁹/L, ultrasound-guided CVC), withholding prophylactic platelets was not non-inferior: grade 2–4 bleeding 11.9 vs 4.8 % with one unit of platelets. A single unit before insertion is reasonable.

**Why not the others:**
- A – prophylactic plasma is not recommended for a mildly raised INR.
- C – PACER showed more bleeding without transfusion, despite ultrasound.
- D – a count of 100 × 10⁹/L is unnecessary, and the delay harms treatment.
- E – TXA was not tested and is not a substitute.

**Ref:** van Baarle FLF, N Engl J Med 2023; Vlaar AP, Intensive Care Med 2020. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man on dabigatran 150 mg twice daily (last dose 6 hours ago) has a ruptured spleen after a fall. Creatinine clearance is 45 mL/min. What is the most appropriate reversal while preparing for laparotomy?
options: Idarucizumab 5 g IV
Andexanet alfa
Vitamin K 10 mg IV
Protamine 50 mg IV
FFP 15 mL/kg alone
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Idarucizumab is a humanised antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with very high affinity. RE-VERSE AD showed a median maximal reversal of 100 % within minutes. Haemodialysis is an alternative if idarucizumab is unavailable.

**Why not the others:**
- B – andexanet reverses factor Xa inhibitors, not thrombin inhibitors.
- C – vitamin K reverses VKAs.
- D – protamine reverses heparin.
- E – FFP does not reverse dabigatran.

**Ref:** Pollack CV, N Engl J Med 2017. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman with meningococcal sepsis has purpura fulminans, platelets 35 × 10⁹/L, PT prolonged by 7 s, fibrinogen 0.9 g/L and very high D-dimer. Regarding her coagulopathy:
options: Her ISTH overt DIC score is at least 5.
Routine tranexamic acid is indicated to treat the purpura.
Therapeutic heparin may be considered for a predominantly thrombotic DIC phenotype such as purpura fulminans.
Platelet and fibrinogen replacement is indicated if she bleeds or needs an invasive procedure.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – platelets < 50 (2) + strong D-dimer (3) + PT > 6 s (2) + fibrinogen < 1 g/L (1) = 8.
- B (False) – antifibrinolytics worsen microthrombosis in septic DIC.
- C (True) – heparin may be considered, with careful replacement of products if bleeding occurs; protein C concentrate is also used.
- D (True) – products are given for bleeding or procedures (platelets > 50 × 10⁹/L, fibrinogen > 1.5 g/L), not to correct numbers alone.

**Ref:** Taylor FB, Thromb Haemost 2001; Iba T, J Thromb Haemost 2025. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man has a prolonged aPTT (54 s) with a normal PT before an elective percutaneous tracheostomy. He has no history of bleeding. The aPTT corrects fully on a 1:1 mixing study. Which explanation is most consistent?
options: Acquired haemophilia A
Lupus anticoagulant
Factor XII deficiency
Unfractionated heparin contamination
Disseminated intravascular coagulation
questions.expl:
**Why C:** An isolated prolonged aPTT that corrects on mixing indicates a factor deficiency. FXII deficiency is the classic incidental finding without bleeding; mild FVIII, FIX or FXI deficiency should also be excluded with specific factor assays.

**Why not the others:**
- A – an FVIII inhibitor does not correct on mixing, and patients bleed.
- B – lupus anticoagulant does not correct on mixing.
- D – heparin, an inhibitor, does not correct on mixing (check the thrombin time and anti-Xa).
- E – DIC would prolong the PT and lower platelets and fibrinogen.

**Ref:** Vlaar AP, Intensive Care Med 2021. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: Regarding immune thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura:
options: ADAMTS13 activity below 10 % supports the diagnosis.
Platelet transfusion is routinely given before inserting the plasma exchange catheter.
A PLASMIC score of 6–7 indicates a high probability of severe ADAMTS13 deficiency.
Adding caplacizumab to plasma exchange and immunosuppression reduced TTP recurrence in HERCULES.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ISTH 2020.
- B (False) – platelets are avoided unless there is life-threatening bleeding; use ultrasound and a compressible site.
- C (True) – about 80 % have ADAMTS13 < 10 %.
- D (True) – recurrence 12 vs 38 %; composite of TTP-related death, recurrence or major thromboembolism 12 vs 49 %.

**Ref:** Zheng XL, J Thromb Haemost 2020; Bendapudi PK, Lancet Haematol 2017; Scully M, N Engl J Med 2019. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman on day 8 of UFH prophylaxis after hip surgery has platelets that have fallen from 310 to 120 × 10⁹/L. She has a new arterial thrombosis of the left leg. PF4–heparin ELISA is strongly positive (OD 2.4). She has CrCl 22 mL/min and normal liver function. What is the most appropriate anticoagulant?
options: Switch UFH to enoxaparin
Warfarin, INR 2–3
Fondaparinux at prophylactic dose
Platelet transfusion and continue UFH
Argatroban infusion
questions.expl:
**Why E:** This is HIT with thrombosis (4Ts high, strongly positive ELISA). All heparin must be stopped and a therapeutic non-heparin anticoagulant started. Argatroban is cleared by the liver, so it suits severe renal impairment, and it can be titrated quickly for possible vascular surgery.

**Why not the others:**
- A – LMWH cross-reacts with HIT antibodies.
- B – early warfarin causes venous limb gangrene; delay it until platelets ≥ 150 × 10⁹/L.
- C – a prophylactic dose is inadequate, and fondaparinux accumulates at CrCl < 30 mL/min.
- D – platelet transfusion and continued heparin worsen thrombosis.

**Ref:** Cuker A, Blood Adv 2018. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: All of the following are typical of a thrombotic microangiopathy EXCEPT:
options: Schistocytes on the blood film
Strongly positive direct antiglobulin test
Raised LDH
Undetectable haptoglobin
Thrombocytopenia
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Haemolysis in TMA is mechanical (shearing on microthrombi), so the direct antiglobulin test is negative. A positive DAT points to autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, or Evans syndrome if combined with immune thrombocytopenia.

**Why not the others:**
- A – schistocytes (> 1 %) are typical.
- C – LDH rises from haemolysis and tissue ischaemia.
- D – haptoglobin is consumed by free haemoglobin.
- E – thrombocytopenia from platelet consumption is required for the diagnosis.

**Ref:** Zheng XL, J Thromb Haemost 2020; Fakhouri F, Lancet 2017. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman presents with syncope and a large bilateral PE. In the emergency department, BP is 108/70 mmHg, HR 120/min, lactate 4.1 mmol/L and creatinine is rising. Echo shows severe RV dilatation. According to the 2026 AHA/ACC classification, which category best describes her?
options: Category B
Category C1
Category E2
Category D (incipient cardiopulmonary failure – normotensive shock, D2)
Category A
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Category D is incipient cardiopulmonary failure: D1 is transient hypotension or syncope, and D2 is normotensive shock with hypoperfusion (raised lactate, AKI) despite normal BP. With both syncope and hypoperfusion she is in the higher subcategory, D2. Advanced therapies (systemic lysis, CDT or mechanical thrombectomy) carry a class 2b recommendation in D, via a PERT.

**Why not the others:**
- A – B is symptomatic PE with low clinical severity.
- B – C has raised severity scores without hypoperfusion or haemodynamic compromise.
- C – E2 is refractory cardiogenic shock or cardiac arrest.
- E – A is asymptomatic, incidental PE.

**Ref:** Creager MA, Circulation 2026. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: Regarding VTE prophylaxis and filters in the ICU:
options: In PROTECT, dalteparin reduced pulmonary embolism compared with UFH.
A retrievable IVC filter added to anticoagulation reduced recurrent PE in PREPIC2.
Adding IPC to pharmacological prophylaxis reduced proximal DVT in PREVENT.
A raised INR in cirrhosis is not a reason to withhold thromboprophylaxis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 1.3 vs 2.3 %, with similar proximal DVT rates.
- B (False) – 3.0 vs 1.5 %, NS; no benefit.
- C (False) – 3.9 vs 4.2 %.
- D (True) – rebalanced haemostasis; patients remain at thrombotic risk.

**Ref:** Cook D, N Engl J Med 2011; Mismetti P, JAMA 2015; Arabi YM, N Engl J Med 2019. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with a first unprovoked PE has completed 6 months of apixaban 5 mg twice daily. He has no bleeding risk factors. What is the most appropriate long-term plan?
options: Extended anticoagulation, e.g. apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily
Stop anticoagulation and start aspirin
Stop anticoagulation now
Switch to warfarin indefinitely
Insert a permanent IVC filter
questions.expl:
**Why A:** After a first PE without a major reversible risk factor, recurrence risk is high (> 5 %/year) if anticoagulation stops. Extended anticoagulation is recommended, and reduced-dose apixaban (2.5 mg bid) or rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) after 6 months is effective with low bleeding risk (AHA/ACC 2026 class 1; ESC 2019).

**Why not the others:**
- B – aspirin is much less effective than a DOAC.
- C – stopping is appropriate only for PE provoked by a major transient risk factor.
- D – VKAs give more bleeding than DOACs, without APS or another indication.
- E – filters are only for patients with a contraindication to anticoagulation.

**Ref:** Konstantinides SV, Eur Heart J 2020; Creager MA, Circulation 2026. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: A 24-year-old motorcyclist has a femoral fracture and haemorrhagic shock. He arrives 4 hours after injury because of a long extrication and has not received tranexamic acid. Which statement about TXA is most accurate?
options: TXA should be given at double dose because of the delay
TXA is most effective when given 3–8 hours after injury
Beyond 3 hours, TXA increased the risk of death from bleeding in CRASH-2, so routine initiation is not recommended
TXA should be given only if fibrinogen is below 1 g/L
TXA is contraindicated in trauma because it increases arterial thrombosis
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In CRASH-2 the benefit of TXA was greatest within 1 hour and present up to 3 hours. Given after 3 hours it increased bleeding deaths, probably because coagulopathy shifts toward fibrinolytic shutdown. The European guideline recommends TXA within 3 h. Later use is reserved for documented hyperfibrinolysis (e.g. LY30 > 3 %, ML > 15 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – the dose is not increased.
- B – effectiveness decreases with time.
- D – TXA is not guided by fibrinogen level.
- E – CRASH-2 showed no increase in vascular occlusive events.

**Ref:** CRASH-2 collaborators, Lancet 2010; Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023. → [D5](D5.md)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is bleeding after a liver resection. ROTEM shows EXTEM CT 95 s (prolonged), EXTEM A5 36 mm (normal), FIBTEM A5 12 mm (normal) and EXTEM ML 6 %. INTEM and HEPTEM CT are both equally prolonged. Which of the following are appropriate interpretations?
options: The pattern suggests deficiency of coagulation factors.
Fibrinogen concentrate is the priority.
There is evidence of hyperfibrinolysis requiring TXA.
Protamine is indicated.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – a prolonged CT with normal clot firmness suggests a factor deficit, which can be treated with plasma or PCC.
- B (False) – FIBTEM A5 12 mm is adequate.
- C (False) – ML 6 % is below the 15 % threshold.
- D (False) – INTEM and HEPTEM are equally prolonged, so there is no heparin effect.

**Ref:** Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023; Kietaibl S, Eur J Anaesthesiol 2023. → [D5](D5.md)

questions.stem: Regarding massive transfusion in trauma:
options: Permissive hypotension with SBP 80–90 mmHg is recommended in patients with severe TBI.
Ionised calcium should be kept within the normal range during massive transfusion.
Platelets should be kept above 100 × 10⁹/L in ongoing bleeding with TBI.
In PROPPR, a 1:1:1 ratio significantly reduced 30-day mortality.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – MAP ≥ 80 mmHg is recommended in severe TBI; permissive hypotension applies only without TBI.
- B (True) – citrate causes hypocalcaemia, which impairs coagulation and cardiac function.
- C (True) – the European guideline 2023 (2C).
- D (False) – 22.4 vs 26.1 %, NS; it improved haemostasis and reduced exsanguination at 24 h.

**Ref:** Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023; Holcomb JB, JAMA 2015. → [D5](D5.md)

title: W23 · D1 – Primary survey and damage-control resuscitation

questions.stem: A 28-year-old motorcyclist arrives with a near-amputation of the right thigh spurting blood, GCS 13, RR 28/min and HR 140/min. According to ATLS 11, what is the first action?
options: Rapid sequence intubation with video laryngoscopy
Application of a cervical collar
Tourniquet or direct pressure on the thigh wound
Bilateral needle decompression of the chest
Two large-bore cannulas and 1 L of warm crystalloid
questions.expl:
**Why C:** ATLS 11 introduced the xABCDE sequence: exsanguinating external haemorrhage is controlled first, before the airway. A tourniquet for life-threatening open extremity bleeding is a 1B recommendation in the European 2023 guideline.

**Why not the others:**
- A – airway follows control of catastrophic bleeding, and induction in profound shock without resuscitation risks arrest.
- B – spinal motion restriction is now selective and never precedes haemorrhage control.
- D – there are no signs of tension pneumothorax.
- E – crystalloid is only a bridge; the source of loss must be stopped first.

**Ref:** ATLS 11th ed., ACS 2025; Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023.

questions.stem: Regarding haemorrhagic shock classification and recognition in adults:
options: Systolic hypotension typically appears only after loss of more than 30 % of blood volume.
A base deficit of −8 mmol/L corresponds to ATLS class III shock.
A normal haemoglobin on arrival makes major haemorrhage unlikely.
Beta-blockade can mask the tachycardic response to blood loss.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – SBP falls in class III (31–40 % loss); classes I–II are compensated.
- B (True) – class III corresponds to base deficit −6 to −10.
- C (False) – Hb falls only after haemodilution; serial measurement is recommended.
- D (True) – age, beta-blockers, pacemakers and athletic training blunt tachycardia.

**Ref:** ATLS 11th ed., ACS 2025; Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with a stab wound to the abdomen has HR 125/min and BP 78/45 mmHg; there is no head injury. The surgeons are preparing the theatre. What blood-pressure target should guide fluid and blood administration until bleeding is controlled?
options: MAP ≥ 80 mmHg
SBP 120–140 mmHg
MAP ≥ 65 mmHg with noradrenaline if needed
Normal urine output of 0.5 mL/kg/h
SBP 80–90 mmHg (MAP 50–60 mmHg)
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Without TBI, the European guideline recommends restricted volume replacement with a target SBP of 80–90 mmHg (MAP 50–60) until major bleeding has been stopped (1B). Bickell's trial in penetrating torso injury showed better survival with delayed fluid resuscitation (70 vs 62 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – MAP ≥ 80 mmHg is the target in severe TBI.
- B – normotension before haemorrhage control increases bleeding ("popping the clot") and dilution.
- C – MAP 65 is the sepsis target, not for uncontrolled bleeding.
- D – urine output is too slow and unreliable a target in the hyperacute phase.

**Ref:** Bickell WH, N Engl J Med 1994; Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023.

questions.stem: Regarding the PROPPR trial of transfusion ratios in severe trauma:
options: 1:1:1 plasma:platelets:red cells significantly reduced 30-day all-cause mortality compared with 1:1:2.
More patients achieved haemostasis in the 1:1:1 group.
Death from exsanguination within 24 hours was lower in the 1:1:1 group.
The 1:1:1 strategy significantly increased ARDS and thromboembolic complications.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – 30-day mortality 22.4 vs 26.1 % and 24-h mortality 12.7 vs 17.0 % were not significantly different.
- B (True) – haemostasis 86 vs 78 %.
- C (True) – exsanguination deaths at 24 h 9.2 vs 14.6 %.
- D (False) – complications did not differ.

**Ref:** Holcomb JB, JAMA 2015.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman is admitted after a fall from height with a severe head injury (GCS 6), a pelvic fracture and HR 120/min. All of the following are appropriate during initial resuscitation EXCEPT:
options: Target MAP ≥ 80 mmHg
Ringer's lactate as the main resuscitation fluid
Pelvic binder centred over the greater trochanters
Tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 min followed by 1 g over 8 h
Keeping ionised calcium in the normal range
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Ringer's lactate is hypotonic and the European guideline recommends avoiding hypotonic solutions in severe head trauma (1B); 0.9 % saline or a balanced isotonic crystalloid (and blood products) should be used.

**Why not the others:**
- A – with severe TBI, MAP ≥ 80 mmHg is recommended instead of permissive hypotension.
- C – a binder at the level of the greater trochanters closes the pelvic ring.
- D – TXA within 3 h is recommended in bleeding trauma (1A).
- E – hypocalcaemia worsens coagulopathy; keep iCa²⁺ 1.1–1.3 mmol/L.

**Ref:** Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023.

questions.stem: Regarding acute traumatic coagulopathy:
options: It is present on hospital arrival in a substantial proportion of severely injured patients, before major fluid administration.
Activation of protein C by hypoperfusion contributes to its development.
Platelet count is the first haemostatic parameter to reach critically low levels.
Standard laboratory coagulation tests run at 37 °C underestimate the effect of hypothermia.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – about a quarter to a third of major trauma patients are coagulopathic on arrival; it is endogenous, not only dilutional.
- B (True) – thrombomodulin–activated protein C causes anticoagulation and hyperfibrinolysis via PAI-1 consumption.
- C (False) – fibrinogen is the first factor to fall to critical levels.
- D (True) – samples are warmed to 37 °C, masking hypothermic enzyme slowing.

**Ref:** Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man in a motor-vehicle collision has AIS 4 for a head injury, AIS 3 for a lung contusion, AIS 2 for a second chest injury (rib fractures) and AIS 3 for a femoral fracture. What is his Injury Severity Score?
questions.expl:
**Why A:** ISS is the sum of the squares of the highest AIS in the three most severely injured body regions: head 4² (16) + chest 3² (9) + extremities 3² (9) = 34. Only the highest AIS in each region counts.

**Why not the others:**
- B – this would mis-sum the regions (e.g. 16 + 9 + 4 using the second chest injury).
- C – 38 adds both chest injuries (16 + 9 + 4 + 9), counting one region twice.
- D – there is no combination of the three regions giving 41.
- E – AIS values must be squared, not summed.

**EDIC trap:** the New ISS (NISS) uses the three highest AIS regardless of region; here NISS would also be 34.

**Ref:** ATLS 11th ed., ACS 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding prehospital and in-hospital adjuncts in haemorrhagic trauma:
options: In PAMPer, prehospital plasma during air transport reduced 30-day mortality.
In SWiFT, prehospital whole blood reduced death or massive transfusion at 24 hours compared with red cells and plasma.
In UK-REBOA, emergency department REBOA reduced 90-day mortality.
In REACT-2, immediate whole-body CT reduced in-hospital mortality compared with selective CT.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 23.2 vs 33.0 %; the ground-transport COMBAT trial was neutral.
- B (False) – 48.7 vs 47.7 %, no benefit.
- C (False) – 54 vs 42 % mortality, with an 86.9 % probability of harm.
- D (False) – in-hospital mortality 16 % in both groups.

**Ref:** Sperry JL, N Engl J Med 2018; Smith JE, N Engl J Med 2026; Jansen JO, JAMA 2023; Sierink JC, Lancet 2016.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman is ventilated after a crush injury to the chest. Ten minutes after intubation her SpO₂ falls to 78 %, BP to 70/40 mmHg, airway pressures rise and breath sounds are absent on the right. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Urgent chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis
eFAST before any intervention
Increase PEEP and FiO₂
Decompression of the right chest (finger thoracostomy or needle) followed by a chest drain
Fluid bolus and noradrenaline
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and needs immediate decompression; in a ventilated patient a finger thoracostomy (4th/5th intercostal space, anterior to the mid-axillary line) is effective, followed by a chest drain.

**Why not the others:**
- A – waiting for imaging delays life-saving treatment.
- B – ultrasound may support but must not delay decompression in obstructive shock.
- C – higher PEEP worsens tension physiology.
- E – fluids/vasopressors do not treat obstructive shock.

**Ref:** ATLS 11th ed., ACS 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding damage-control surgery and the ICU phase:
options: Damage-control surgery is indicated in haemorrhagic shock with coagulopathy, hypothermia and acidosis.
The ICU phase aims to rewarm the patient and correct coagulopathy and acidosis before definitive repair.
Planned re-look surgery is typically performed 24–48 hours after the index operation.
Abdominal compartment syndrome is a recognised complication during the ICU phase.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – European 2023 recommends damage-control surgery in deep shock, ongoing bleeding and coagulopathy, with hypothermia and acidosis as further triggers.
- B (True) – restoring physiology is the purpose of stage 2.
- C (True) – definitive repair once physiology is normalised, usually at 24–48 h.
- D (True) – packing, visceral oedema and massive resuscitation raise IAP; monitor bladder pressure.

**Ref:** Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man after a motorcycle crash receives 6 units of red cells in the first hour through a massive transfusion protocol. Ionised calcium is 0.82 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Calcium chloride IV, aiming for ionised calcium 1.1–1.3 mmol/L
No treatment; hypocalcaemia resolves when transfusion stops
Sodium bicarbonate to correct acidosis, which will raise ionised calcium
Switch to whole blood, which contains no citrate
Recombinant factor VIIa
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Citrate in blood products chelates calcium; hypocalcaemia impairs coagulation and contractility and is associated with mortality. The European guideline recommends monitoring and keeping ionised calcium in the normal range with calcium chloride (1C).

**Why not the others:**
- B – ongoing hypocalcaemia worsens bleeding and haemodynamics.
- C – alkalinisation actually **lowers** ionised calcium.
- D – whole blood is also citrated.
- E – rFVIIa is not recommended first line (1B) and does not treat hypocalcaemia.

**Ref:** Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023.

open.q: List the principles of damage-control resuscitation in a bleeding trauma patient without head injury.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Minimise time to haemorrhage control (surgery/angioembolisation), tourniquets, pelvic binder.
- Permissive hypotension SBP 80–90 / MAP 50–60 mmHg until bleeding stops; noradrenaline if needed.
- Minimise crystalloid (isotonic only), avoid colloids; early MTP with plasma:RBC ≥ 1:2 (1:1:1) or factor concentrates; Hb 70–90 g/L.
- TXA 1 g + 1 g within 3 h; fibrinogen when < 1.5 g/L; platelets > 50 × 10⁹/L.
- Ionised calcium 1.1–1.3 mmol/L; prevent hypothermia; correct acidosis by restoring perfusion.
- Repeated lactate/base deficit and coagulation (standard or VEM) monitoring with goal-directed therapy.
- Damage-control surgery when physiology is deranged.

open.q: Explain the mechanisms of acute traumatic coagulopathy.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Endogenous coagulopathy driven by tissue injury plus hypoperfusion, present on arrival.
- Thrombomodulin–thrombin complex activates protein C → inactivation of factors Va/VIIIa and consumption of PAI-1 → hyperfibrinolysis.
- Endothelial glycocalyx shedding (autoheparinisation), platelet dysfunction, early fibrinogen depletion.
- Amplified by hypothermia, acidosis, hypocalcaemia and dilution (crystalloids, red cells only).
- Fibrinolytic phenotypes: hyperfibrinolysis, physiological, shutdown.

title: W23 · D2 – Haemorrhagic shock and tranexamic acid (CRASH-2, CRASH-3, PATCH-Trauma)

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with a crush injury of the pelvis arrives 4.5 hours after injury because of a prolonged extrication. He is bleeding with BP 85/50 mmHg and has not received tranexamic acid. What is the most appropriate approach to TXA?
options: Give 1 g over 10 min followed by 1 g over 8 h
Give a 2 g bolus because of the delay
Do not start TXA now
Give TXA only if ROTEM shows a maximum lysis > 3 %
Give 3 g over 24 h
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In the CRASH-2 exploratory analysis, TXA given more than 3 h after injury increased death due to bleeding (RR 1.44). The European guideline recommends TXA within 3 h of injury only.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the standard regimen, but only within 3 h.
- B – a larger dose does not compensate for the time window.
- D – ROTEM-guided late TXA is not evidence-based; hyperfibrinolysis is rare by this time and shutdown is more common.
- E – this is the HALT-IT (GI bleeding) regimen, which was ineffective.

**Ref:** CRASH-2 collaborators, Lancet 2011; Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023.

questions.stem: Regarding the CRASH-2 trial:
options: It randomised more than 20,000 bleeding trauma patients.
Tranexamic acid reduced all-cause mortality at 28 days.
Tranexamic acid significantly increased vascular occlusive events.
Tranexamic acid significantly reduced the number of red cell units transfused.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 20,211 patients in 40 countries.
- B (True) – 14.5 vs 16.0 % (RR 0.91).
- C (False) – vascular occlusive events 1.7 vs 2.0 %.
- D (False) – transfusion requirements did not differ.

**Ref:** CRASH-2 trial collaborators, Lancet 2010.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman is admitted 1 hour after a fall with an isolated head injury (GCS 11) and a small subdural haematoma on CT. There is no extracranial bleeding. What does CRASH-3 suggest about tranexamic acid in her case?
options: It reduces head-injury death in mild-to-moderate TBI when given within 3 hours
It is contraindicated because it increases thrombotic events in TBI
Benefit is greatest in patients with bilateral unreactive pupils
It should only be given after a repeat CT shows haematoma expansion
It reduces death only when given more than 3 hours after injury
questions.expl:
**Why A:** CRASH-3's primary outcome was neutral overall, but in mild-to-moderate TBI (GCS 9–15) head-injury death fell from 7.5 to 5.8 % (RR 0.78), with greater benefit the earlier TXA was given.

**Why not the others:**
- B – vascular occlusive events were 1.6 % in both groups.
- C – no benefit was seen in severe TBI or with unreactive pupils.
- D – benefit is time-dependent; waiting for expansion loses it.
- E – the trial included only patients treated within 3 h.

**Ref:** CRASH-3 trial collaborators, Lancet 2019.

questions.stem: Regarding PATCH-Trauma (prehospital tranexamic acid):
options: Survival with a favourable functional outcome at 6 months was improved.
Mortality at 24 hours was lower with tranexamic acid.
Patients were selected by a score predicting trauma-induced coagulopathy.
Vascular occlusive events were significantly increased with tranexamic acid.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – 53.7 vs 53.5 % (RR 1.00).
- B (True) – 9.7 vs 14.1 %; 28-day mortality was also lower (17.3 vs 21.8 %).
- C (True) – COAST score ≥ 3.
- D (False) – no significant difference.

**Ref:** Gruen RL, N Engl J Med 2023.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man on warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve has a splenic laceration with active bleeding and an INR of 3.4. Angioembolisation is being arranged. Which is the most appropriate reversal?
options: FFP 15 mL/kg alone
Vitamin K 10 mg orally
Recombinant factor VIIa
Idarucizumab 5 g
Four-factor PCC 25–50 U/kg plus vitamin K 5–10 mg IV
questions.expl:
**Why E:** For bleeding trauma patients on VKA the European guideline recommends early PCC with 5–10 mg IV vitamin K (1A). PCC corrects INR within minutes; vitamin K sustains the effect. A mechanical valve does not change the need for reversal in life-threatening bleeding.

**Why not the others:**
- A – FFP is slower, needs large volumes and corrects INR incompletely.
- B – oral vitamin K takes hours and is insufficient alone.
- C – rFVIIa is not recommended for VKA reversal.
- D – idarucizumab reverses dabigatran only.

**Ref:** Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023.

questions.stem: Regarding fibrinogen supplementation in bleeding trauma patients:
options: Treatment is recommended when plasma fibrinogen is ≤ 1.5 g/L with major bleeding.
An initial dose of 3–4 g fibrinogen is suggested.
In CRYOSTAT-2, early empirical high-dose cryoprecipitate reduced 28-day mortality.
FFP is the preferred product to correct hypofibrinogenaemia when concentrate is available.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – or a functional fibrinogen deficit on VEM (1C).
- B (True) – 3–4 g concentrate or 15–20 single-donor units of cryoprecipitate (2C).
- C (False) – 25.3 vs 26.1 % (NS), with a signal of harm in penetrating trauma.
- D (False) – the fibrinogen content of FFP is too low; use concentrate or cryoprecipitate (1C).

**Ref:** Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023; Davenport R, JAMA 2023.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman taking apixaban is admitted after a fall with an expanding intracerebral contusion and a femoral fracture. Which agent does the European trauma guideline suggest for reversal?
options: Protamine sulphate
Andexanet alfa, or PCC 25–50 U/kg if unavailable
Idarucizumab
Vitamin K
Platelet transfusion
questions.expl:
**Why B:** For life-threatening bleeding with apixaban or rivaroxaban, especially in TBI, the guideline suggests andexanet alfa; if it is unavailable, PCC 25–50 U/kg (2C).

**Why not the others:**
- A – protamine reverses heparin (partially LMWH).
- C – idarucizumab is specific for dabigatran.
- D – vitamin K has no effect on factor Xa inhibitors.
- E – platelets do not reverse anticoagulants.

**Ref:** Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023.

questions.stem: Regarding tranexamic acid pharmacology:
options: It is a lysine analogue that blocks the binding of plasminogen to fibrin.
It is mainly eliminated by hepatic metabolism.
High doses can cause seizures.
Dose reduction is needed for prolonged infusions in severe renal failure.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – it occupies the lysine-binding sites of plasminogen.
- B (False) – ~95 % is excreted unchanged in urine; accumulates in renal failure.
- C (True) – via GABA-A and glycine receptor antagonism, mainly with high cardiac surgical doses.
- D (True) – it accumulates when GFR is low; the bolus is unchanged but infusions should be reduced.

**Ref:** CRASH-2 trial collaborators, Lancet 2010.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man with a gunshot wound to the abdomen arrives in shock. A colleague suggests giving 4-factor PCC 25 IU/kg early to reduce transfusion. What did the PROCOAG trial show for this approach?
options: Reduced 24-hour blood product use
Reduced 28-day mortality
No reduction in blood product use and more thromboembolic events
Benefit only in penetrating trauma
Benefit only when combined with rFVIIa
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In PROCOAG (n = 324) early 4F-PCC on top of an FFP-based MTP did not reduce 24-h blood product consumption and thromboembolic events were more frequent (35 vs 24 %). Routine empirical PCC is not recommended.

**Why not the others:**
- A – blood product use was not reduced.
- B – mortality did not differ.
- D – no subgroup benefit was shown.
- E – rFVIIa was not part of the trial and is not recommended first line.

**Ref:** Bouzat P, JAMA 2023; Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man is admitted with haemorrhagic shock after a motorcycle crash; he takes aspirin and clopidogrel after a coronary stent. According to the European guideline:
options: Routine platelet transfusion is recommended because of dual antiplatelet therapy.
Platelet count should be maintained above 50 × 10⁹/L while bleeding continues.
Point-of-care platelet function testing should be used routinely.
Desmopressin is strongly recommended.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – routine platelet transfusion is not recommended in patients on antiplatelet agents (1C).
- B (True) – > 50 × 10⁹/L with ongoing bleeding; > 100 × 10⁹/L with TBI (2C).
- C (False) – routine POC platelet function testing is not recommended (1C).
- D (False) – no recommendation was made because of scarce data.

**Ref:** Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is in the ICU 18 hours after damage-control laparotomy for liver injury. Bleeding has stopped and haemoglobin is stable. Which approach to VTE prophylaxis is most appropriate?
options: Inferior vena cava filter
Graduated compression stockings only
No prophylaxis for 7 days because of bleeding risk
Intermittent pneumatic compression and LMWH within 24 hours of bleeding control
Therapeutic unfractionated heparin
questions.expl:
**Why D:** European 2023 recommends early IPC (1C) and pharmacological prophylaxis combined with IPC within 24 h after bleeding control (1B). Trauma patients are highly prothrombotic after the early phase (fibrinolytic shutdown).

**Why not the others:**
- A – routine IVC filters are not recommended.
- B – stockings are not recommended.
- C – delay increases VTE without reducing bleeding once haemostasis is achieved.
- E – therapeutic anticoagulation is not prophylaxis and increases rebleeding.

**Ref:** Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023.

open.q: Summarise the evidence for tranexamic acid in trauma, including timing and traumatic brain injury.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Mechanism: lysine analogue, antifibrinolytic.
- CRASH-2 (n = 20,211): all-cause mortality 14.5 vs 16.0 %, bleeding death ↓, no ↑ thrombosis; benefit ≤ 3 h, harm > 3 h; ~10 % less benefit per 15 min delay.
- CRASH-3 (n = 12,737, TBI ≤ 3 h): primary outcome neutral (RR 0.94); benefit in mild–moderate TBI (RR 0.78); no harm.
- PATCH-Trauma: prehospital TXA – no improvement in survival with good function at 6 months, lower 24-h/28-day mortality.
- Dose 1 g over 10 min + 1 g over 8 h (2 g bolus accepted in TBI by ATLS 11); give en route, do not wait for VEM; not for GI bleeding.

title: W23 · D3 – Thoracic and abdominal trauma

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man with a stab wound to the left chest has a chest drain inserted; 1,700 mL of blood drains immediately and he remains hypotensive despite transfusion. What is the next step?
options: Clamp the drain to tamponade the bleeding
Thoracotomy
Insert a second chest drain
CT angiography of the chest
Observe drainage for the next 4 hours
questions.expl:
**Why B:** An initial drainage of ≥ 1,500 mL, ongoing loss > 200 mL/h for 2–4 h, or persistent transfusion requirement indicates massive haemothorax requiring surgical control.

**Why not the others:**
- A – clamping does not stop bleeding and risks tension haemothorax.
- C – a second drain does not address the source.
- D – CT in an unstable patient delays haemorrhage control.
- E – observation is appropriate only when initial loss is small and the patient is stable.

**Ref:** ATLS 11th ed., ACS 2025; Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023.

questions.stem: Regarding emergency department (resuscitative) thoracotomy according to EAST 2015:
options: It is strongly recommended in pulseless patients with signs of life after penetrating thoracic injury.
It is recommended in blunt trauma patients without signs of life.
Cross-clamping of the descending aorta is one of its aims.
Survival after blunt trauma is similar to that after penetrating thoracic trauma.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – the only strong recommendation; survival ~ 20 %.
- B (False) – conditionally recommended against (survival ~ 0.1 %).
- C (True) – together with release of tamponade, haemorrhage control and internal massage.
- D (False) – outcome after blunt trauma is much worse.

**Ref:** Seamon MJ, J Trauma Acute Care Surg 2015.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old driver involved in a high-speed frontal collision has a sternal fracture. He is haemodynamically stable, the ECG shows sinus rhythm without abnormalities and troponin I is normal. What is the most appropriate management regarding blunt cardiac injury?
options: Transthoracic echocardiography before discharge
Telemetry for 48 hours
Serial CK-MB measurements
No further cardiac investigation for blunt cardiac injury
Coronary angiography
questions.expl:
**Why D:** EAST 2012: a normal ECG combined with a normal troponin I rules out blunt cardiac injury. A sternal fracture alone does not predict BCI.

**Why not the others:**
- A – echocardiography is reserved for haemodynamic instability or abnormal findings.
- B – monitoring is indicated for an abnormal ECG or rising troponin.
- C – CK-MB has no role in BCI screening.
- E – angiography is only for suspected coronary dissection/ACS.

**Ref:** Clancy K, J Trauma Acute Care Surg 2012.

questions.stem: Regarding rib fractures and chest wall injury:
options: Pulmonary contusion is usually maximal on the admission chest X-ray.
Prophylactic antibiotics are recommended for pulmonary contusion.
Corticosteroids reduce progression of pulmonary contusion to ARDS.
In elderly patients, rib fractures carry a lower mortality than in younger patients with the same number of fractures.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – it is often absent initially and worsens over 24–72 h.
- B (False) – no prophylactic antibiotics.
- C (False) – steroids are not recommended.
- D (False) – elderly patients have about twice the mortality, rising 19 % per additional rib fracture.

**Ref:** Bulger EM, J Trauma 2000.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman on apixaban for atrial fibrillation has six unilateral rib fractures after a fall. She is hypoxaemic on 4 L/min O₂ because of pain and poor cough. Apixaban was last taken 10 hours ago. Which analgesic technique is most appropriate?
options: Thoracic epidural catheter now
Intramuscular morphine as needed
Paravertebral catheter now
Intercostal blocks repeated every 4 hours
Erector spinae or serratus anterior plane catheter as part of multimodal analgesia
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Fascial plane blocks are superficial and compressible and can be used in anticoagulated patients, providing effective analgesia for rib fractures within a multimodal regimen.

**Why not the others:**
- A – neuraxial block is contraindicated within the apixaban window (risk of epidural haematoma).
- B – IM opioids alone give poor analgesia and respiratory depression.
- C – paravertebral blocks are deep blocks and share the anticoagulation restrictions of neuraxial techniques.
- D – repeated multilevel injections are impractical and carry pneumothorax risk.

**Ref:** Bulger EM, J Trauma 2000; Kasotakis G, J Trauma Acute Care Surg 2017.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has a blunt thoracic aortic injury with a pseudoaneurysm at the isthmus, a severe TBI and a splenic laceration. Regarding management:
options: Endovascular repair is preferred over open repair.
Repair can be delayed in a stable patient until other injuries are stabilised.
Anti-impulse therapy with a short-acting beta-blocker is used while awaiting repair, if cerebral perfusion allows.
The injury most commonly occurs at the aortic root.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – TEVAR has lower mortality and paraplegia rates (EAST 2015).
- B (True) – delayed repair is suggested in stable patients.
- C (True) – lowering HR and dP/dt reduces the risk of rupture; balance with CPP in TBI.
- D (False) – the isthmus just distal to the left subclavian artery is typical.

**Ref:** Fox N, J Trauma Acute Care Surg 2015.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman is admitted after a car crash. BP 112/70 mmHg, HR 92/min, stable after 1 L of fluid. CT shows a grade IV splenic laceration with a contrast blush; there are no other injuries. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Angioembolisation as part of non-operative management
Immediate splenectomy because of the high grade
Observation alone without intervention
Diagnostic peritoneal lavage
Laparoscopic splenorrhaphy
questions.expl:
**Why A:** WSES recommends NOM in haemodynamically stable patients regardless of grade, with angioembolisation for a contrast blush, provided monitoring, angiography and theatre are available.

**Why not the others:**
- B – the grade alone does not mandate surgery in a stable patient.
- C – an active blush predicts NOM failure without embolisation.
- D – DPL is obsolete in a stable patient with a CT diagnosis.
- E – splenorrhaphy is not the first choice in a stable patient.

**Ref:** Coccolini F, World J Emerg Surg 2017.

questions.stem: Regarding pelvic fractures with haemodynamic instability:
options: Most bleeding is venous or from fracture surfaces.
A pelvic binder should be centred over the iliac crests.
Preperitoneal pelvic packing is an option when FAST is negative.
A urinary catheter should be inserted immediately when there is blood at the urethral meatus.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – about 85 %; arterial bleeding ~ 10–15 %.
- B (False) – it should be placed over the greater trochanters.
- C (True) – with external fixation and/or angioembolisation.
- D (False) – suspect urethral injury; avoid blind catheterisation before imaging.

**Ref:** Coccolini F, World J Emerg Surg 2017 (pelvic); Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man is hypotensive (BP 75/40 mmHg) after blunt abdominal trauma despite 2 units of blood. FAST shows free fluid in Morison's pouch. All of the following are appropriate EXCEPT:
options: Activation of the massive transfusion protocol
Tranexamic acid within 3 hours of injury
CT abdomen to grade the injuries before deciding on surgery
Permissive hypotension in the absence of TBI
Damage-control laparotomy
questions.expl:
**Why C:** A haemodynamically unstable patient with a positive FAST needs immediate surgical haemorrhage control; transfer to CT delays it and is dangerous.

**Why not the others:**
- A – MTP for ongoing haemorrhagic shock.
- B – TXA within 3 h is recommended.
- D – SBP 80–90 mmHg until bleeding control without TBI.
- E – the physiology (shock, transfusion) favours damage control.

**Ref:** Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023; ATLS 11th ed., ACS 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding the CT findings in blunt abdominal trauma:
options: Free intraperitoneal fluid without solid-organ injury raises suspicion of a hollow-viscus injury.
FAST reliably excludes retroperitoneal haemorrhage.
A seat-belt sign is associated with small-bowel and mesenteric injury.
A pancreatic duct injury is always visible on the initial CT.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – especially in males without pelvic fracture.
- B (False) – FAST is poor for the retroperitoneum.
- C (True) – also with Chance fractures.
- D (False) – early CT can miss pancreatic injury; MRCP/ERCP may be needed.

**Ref:** Coccolini F, World J Emerg Surg 2020; ATLS 11th ed., ACS 2025.

questions.stem: At a damage-control laparotomy after a fall from height, the surgeon finds a non-expanding haematoma in the pelvic retroperitoneum (zone 3) in a patient with a pelvic fracture. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Open the haematoma and ligate the internal iliac arteries
Leave it unopened and control pelvic bleeding with packing, fixation or angioembolisation
Open it to exclude a ureteric injury
Explore it because all retroperitoneal haematomas must be explored
Insert a REBOA catheter in zone I
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In blunt trauma, zone 3 (pelvic) haematomas should not be opened – this releases tamponade of venous bleeding; preperitoneal packing, external fixation and angioembolisation are used.

**Why not the others:**
- A – opening a pelvic haematoma causes uncontrollable bleeding.
- C – a ureteric injury is assessed with imaging, not exploration.
- D – only zone 1 haematomas are always explored.
- E – zone I REBOA occludes the thoracic aorta and is not indicated for a contained pelvic haematoma.

**Ref:** Coccolini F, World J Emerg Surg 2017 (pelvic).

open.q: Outline the ICU management of an 80-year-old with seven rib fractures and a flail segment.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- High risk: mortality and pneumonia increase per fracture in the elderly; ICU/HDU monitoring.
- Multimodal analgesia: paracetamol, ketamine, opioids; regional – epidural or paravertebral if no anticoagulation, otherwise erector spinae/serratus anterior catheters.
- Respiratory support: physiotherapy, incentive spirometry, HFNC/NIV if alert; lung-protective ventilation if intubated.
- Consider SSRF within 72 h (EAST 2017 conditional recommendation for flail chest).
- Treat contusion: avoid fluid overload, no steroids or prophylactic antibiotics; monitor for pneumonia; VTE prophylaxis; review anticoagulants.

open.q: What are the requirements for non-operative management of a splenic injury?
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Haemodynamic stability (or rapid responder) regardless of grade; no peritonitis or other indication for laparotomy.
- CT with contrast; angioembolisation for blush, pseudoaneurysm or AV fistula.
- ICU/HDU monitoring with serial examination and Hb; immediate access to theatre and angiography.
- Most failures in the first days; early LMWH is safe once stable; vaccination after splenectomy or extensive embolisation.

title: W23 · D4 – Burns: fluid resuscitation, inhalation injury and CO/cyanide poisoning

questions.stem: A 70-kg man has partial- and full-thickness burns of the whole anterior trunk and the whole of both upper limbs, plus erythema of the face. What is his %TBSA for fluid calculation?
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Anterior trunk 18 % + each upper limb 9 % × 2 = 36 %. Superficial (erythema-only) burns are not included in the TBSA.

**Why not the others:**
- A – adds 9 % for the face, which has only erythema.
- B – counts only one arm.
- C – adds the posterior trunk, which is not burned.
- E – counts only the anterior trunk.

**Ref:** ISBI Practice Guidelines, Burns 2016.

questions.stem: Regarding initial fluid resuscitation in a 70-kg adult with a 40 % TBSA burn:
options: The Parkland formula gives 11.2 L over the first 24 hours.
Half of the Parkland volume is given in the first 8 hours from hospital arrival.
The ABA 2024 guideline suggests starting at 2 mL/kg/%TBSA and titrating.
The urine output target is 0.5 mL/kg/h.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 4 × 70 × 40 = 11,200 mL.
- B (False) – timing starts from the time of injury, not arrival.
- C (True) – to limit total volume and fluid creep.
- D (True) – ~ 35 mL/h; titrate hourly.

**Ref:** Cartotto R, J Burn Care Res 2024.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a 55 % TBSA burn has received 9 mL/kg/%TBSA over 20 hours. She now has a tense abdomen, oliguria, peak airway pressure 42 cmH₂O and bladder pressure 28 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Abdominal compartment syndrome due to fluid creep
Inhalation injury with ARDS
Septic shock from burn wound infection
Acute kidney injury from myoglobinuria
Tension pneumothorax
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Excess resuscitation volume (Ivy index > 250 mL/kg) causes visceral and abdominal wall oedema; IAP > 20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction (oliguria, high airway pressures) defines abdominal compartment syndrome.

**Why not the others:**
- B – would not explain the tense abdomen and high bladder pressure.
- C – sepsis typically occurs after the first days.
- D – myoglobinuria is mainly an electrical/crush issue and does not raise IAP.
- E – would cause unilateral absent breath sounds and obstructive shock, not raised IAP.

**Ref:** Cartotto R, J Burn Care Res 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding colloids and adjuncts in burn resuscitation (ABA 2024):
options: Albumin may be considered within the first 24 hours to reduce total fluid volume.
Albumin may be used as rescue when resuscitation is failing despite increasing crystalloid.
Routine fresh frozen plasma is recommended against.
Invasive haemodynamic monitoring with transpulmonary thermodilution is not recommended to guide routine resuscitation.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – especially in larger burns.
- B (True) – "rescue" albumin.
- C (True) – insufficient benefit and TRALI risk.
- D (True) – urine output remains the primary end-point.

**Ref:** Cartotto R, J Burn Care Res 2024.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man is rescued from a house fire. He is confused, SpO₂ 98 % on a non-rebreather mask, lactate 12 mmol/L, BP 85/50 mmHg, COHb 18 %. Burns are minor. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment besides 100 % O₂?
options: Sodium nitrite 300 mg IV
Hyperbaric oxygen before any other treatment
Sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol
Methylene blue 1 mg/kg
Hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Smoke inhalation with shock and lactate > 8–10 mmol/L strongly suggests cyanide toxicity (Baud 1991). Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to cyanocobalamin and does not impair oxygen carriage.

**Why not the others:**
- A – nitrites cause methaemoglobinaemia, worsening hypoxia in combined CO poisoning.
- B – HBO may be considered for CO but must not delay antidote and resuscitation.
- C – bicarbonate does not treat the cause.
- D – methylene blue treats methaemoglobinaemia.

**Ref:** Baud FJ, N Engl J Med 1991; Jeschke MG, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2020.

questions.stem: Regarding carbon monoxide poisoning:
options: Standard pulse oximetry overestimates oxygen saturation.
The half-life of COHb is about 4–6 hours when breathing 100 % oxygen.
CO shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the right.
Delayed neurological sequelae may appear weeks after apparent recovery.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – COHb is read as O₂Hb; co-oximetry is needed.
- B (False) – 4–6 h on air; ~ 60–90 min on 100 % O₂; ~ 20–30 min with HBO.
- C (False) – it shifts the curve to the left, impairing O₂ unloading.
- D (True) – 2–40 days; Weaver showed fewer cognitive sequelae with HBO.

**Ref:** Hampson NB, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2012; Weaver LK, N Engl J Med 2002.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man with 45 % TBSA burns is taken to theatre for excision on day 5 after injury. Which neuromuscular blocker should be AVOIDED?
options: Rocuronium
Suxamethonium
Cisatracurium
Atracurium
Vecuronium
questions.expl:
**Why B:** After the first 24–48 h extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors proliferate; suxamethonium can then cause life-threatening hyperkalaemia, a risk lasting up to a year.

**Why not the others:**
- A, C, D, E – non-depolarising agents are safe, although burn patients are resistant and need higher doses.

**Ref:** Jeschke MG, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2020.

questions.stem: Regarding inhalation injury:
options: Supraglottic oedema may progress over the first 12–24 hours.
Prophylactic systemic corticosteroids are recommended.
Prophylactic antibiotics reduce pneumonia and are recommended.
A small (6.0 mm) tube should be preferred to limit laryngeal injury.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – hence early intubation in high-risk patients.
- B (False) – no steroids.
- C (False) – no prophylactic antibiotics.
- D (False) – use a large uncut tube (≥ 7.5–8.0) to allow bronchoscopy and clearance of casts.

**Ref:** ISBI Practice Guidelines, Burns 2016.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old electrician sustains an 11,000-V injury with small entry and exit wounds on the hand and foot. Urine is dark brown and CK is 48,000 U/L. All of the following are appropriate EXCEPT:
options: Calculating fluid by the Parkland formula from the small visible burns only
Continuous ECG monitoring
Fluid titrated to a urine output of ~ 1–1.5 mL/kg/h until the urine clears
Serial assessment for compartment syndrome
Monitoring of potassium and renal function
questions.expl:
**Why A:** In high-voltage injury the skin wounds grossly underestimate deep muscle necrosis; fluid needs are driven by rhabdomyolysis and are titrated to a higher urine output, not calculated from visible TBSA.

**Why not the others:**
- B – high voltage mandates cardiac monitoring.
- C – higher UO targets for myoglobinuria.
- D – muscle oedema causes compartment syndrome needing fasciotomy.
- E – hyperkalaemia and AKI are major risks.

**Ref:** Jeschke MG, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2020.

questions.stem: Regarding nutrition and metabolism after major burns:
options: Enteral glutamine reduced time to discharge alive in RE-ENERGIZE.
Propranolol reduces resting energy expenditure and muscle catabolism.
Enteral feeding should be delayed until resuscitation is complete at 72 hours.
Fever is a reliable sign of infection in burn patients.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – no difference; 6-month mortality 17.2 vs 16.2 %.
- B (True) – Herndon, NEJM 2001.
- C (False) – early enteral feeding (< 24 h) is recommended.
- D (False) – hypermetabolism resets the thermoregulatory set point; burn-specific sepsis criteria are used.

**Ref:** Heyland DK, N Engl J Med 2022; Herndon DN, N Engl J Med 2001.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman is rescued from a closed-space fire with 30 % TBSA partial- and full-thickness burns and bronchoscopy-confirmed inhalation injury. What is her revised Baux score?
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Revised Baux = age + %TBSA + 17 for inhalation injury: 60 + 30 + 17 = 107. Age, %TBSA and inhalation injury are the main predictors of burn mortality.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the classic Baux score without the inhalation adjustment.
- B – adds 10 instead of 17 points for inhalation injury.
- D – adds 27 points, which is not part of the score.
- E – age + 17 only; the %TBSA has been omitted.

**Ref:** Jeschke MG, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2020.

open.q: Describe the first 24 hours of ICU management of a 40 % TBSA burn with suspected inhalation injury.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Airway assessment (fibre-optic), early intubation with a large uncut tube if stridor, hoarseness or deep facial burns; lung-protective ventilation, bronchoscopy, pulmonary toilet.
- COHb by co-oximetry; 100 % O₂; consider cyanide (lactate > 8–10) → hydroxocobalamin 5 g.
- Accurate TBSA (Lund–Browder, no erythema); crystalloid 2–4 mL/kg/%TBSA from the time of injury, titrated hourly to UO 0.5 mL/kg/h; albumin if escalating; avoid fluid creep; monitor bladder pressure.
- Escharotomy for circumferential burns; warming; analgesia.
- Early enteral feeding, glucose control, VTE prophylaxis, tetanus, no systemic antibiotic prophylaxis, avoid suxamethonium after 24 h, early excision planning.

title: W23 · D5 – Crush injury, compartment syndrome, mass casualties and triage

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man has been trapped under a collapsed wall for 6 hours with both legs compressed. Rescue teams expect extrication within 30 minutes; IV access is obtained. What is the most appropriate fluid strategy?
options: Withhold fluids until the patient is extricated to avoid pulmonary oedema
Ringer's lactate 250 mL/h
Isotonic saline about 1,000 mL/h started now, before extrication
5 % glucose 1 L/h
Hydroxyethyl starch 500 mL bolus at extrication
questions.expl:
**Why C:** The Renal Disaster Relief Task Force recommends isotonic saline at ~ 1 L/h in adults before and during extrication (reduced to ~ 500 mL/h if > 2 h), to restore volume and protect the kidneys before reperfusion releases potassium and myoglobin.

**Why not the others:**
- A – delaying fluids until release increases hyperkalaemic arrest and AKI.
- B – potassium-containing solutions are avoided and the rate is too low.
- D – hypotonic glucose does not expand the intravascular volume.
- E – starches cause AKI and coagulopathy.

**Ref:** Sever MS, Nephrol Dial Transplant 2012.

questions.stem: Regarding rhabdomyolysis-induced acute kidney injury:
options: Renal vasoconstriction, tubular cast obstruction and haem-iron toxicity all contribute.
Alkaline urine favours myoglobin cast formation.
A urine dipstick positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy suggests myoglobinuria.
Randomised trials have shown that sodium bicarbonate with mannitol reduces the need for dialysis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – the three main mechanisms.
- B (False) – acidic urine favours precipitation of myoglobin with Tamm–Horsfall protein.
- C (True) – the orthotoluidine reaction detects haem in myoglobin.
- D (False) – there are no RCTs showing benefit; retrospective trauma data were negative.

**Ref:** Bosch X, N Engl J Med 2009.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has a closed tibial shaft fracture treated with an intramedullary nail. Twelve hours later he is sedated and ventilated because of a chest injury. The leg is tense; BP is 120/62 mmHg and anterior compartment pressure is 40 mmHg. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Urgent four-compartment fasciotomy
Elevate the leg above heart level and re-measure in 4 hours
Mannitol infusion
Wait for loss of the dorsalis pedis pulse
Measure CK and fasciotomy only if > 20,000 U/L
questions.expl:
**Why A:** ΔP = diastolic pressure − compartment pressure = 62 − 40 = 22 mmHg, below the 30 mmHg threshold (McQueen) – in a sedated patient the pressure measurement is decisive. Fasciotomy of all four compartments via two incisions is required.

**Why not the others:**
- B – elevation reduces arterial inflow; keep the leg at heart level.
- C – mannitol does not treat compartment syndrome.
- D – pulses are lost late, after irreversible muscle injury.
- E – CK is non-specific and delays treatment.

**Ref:** McQueen MM, J Bone Joint Surg Br 1996; von Keudell AG, Lancet 2015.

questions.stem: Regarding the clinical features of acute extremity compartment syndrome:
options: Pain on passive stretch of the compartment muscles is an early sign.
Distal pulses are usually lost early in the course.
The anterior compartment of the leg is the most commonly affected after tibial fracture.
Irreversible muscle necrosis can occur after about 6–8 hours of ischaemia.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – with pain out of proportion to the injury.
- B (False) – compartment pressure rarely exceeds arterial pressure; pulses usually persist until late.
- C (True) – paraesthesia of the first web space (deep peroneal nerve).
- D (True) – hence urgency of fasciotomy.

**Ref:** von Keudell AG, Lancet 2015.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman is admitted after an earthquake with crush injury of the thigh. K⁺ 5.4 mmol/L, ionised calcium 0.95 mmol/L, ECG normal, no tetany. CK 62,000 U/L. Which of the following is most appropriate?
options: Prophylactic fasciotomy of the thigh
Calcium gluconate to normalise ionised calcium
Ringer's lactate 2 L/h
Furosemide to maintain urine output
Isotonic saline titrated to a urine output of ~ 200–300 mL/h and close K⁺ monitoring
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Aggressive isotonic volume expansion to a high urine output until myoglobinuria clears is the main AKI-protective measure, with close potassium monitoring and readiness for dialysis.

**Why not the others:**
- A – fasciotomy only for established compartment syndrome; prophylactic fasciotomy increases infection.
- B – asymptomatic hypocalcaemia should not be treated (calcium deposits in muscle, rebound hypercalcaemia later), unless hyperkalaemic ECG changes appear.
- C – avoid potassium-containing fluids.
- D – loop diuretics do not prevent AKI and may worsen volume depletion.

**Ref:** Sever MS, Nephrol Dial Transplant 2012; Bosch X, N Engl J Med 2009.

questions.stem: Using the START triage system at a train crash, the following assignments are correct:
options: A man walking with a forearm laceration – minor (green).
A woman with RR 36/min who obeys commands and has a radial pulse – immediate (red).
An apnoeic man who does not breathe after airway repositioning – immediate (red).
A man with RR 22/min, capillary refill 4 s, obeying commands – delayed (yellow).
questions.expl:
- A (True) – all walking casualties are initially green.
- B (True) – RR > 30/min = immediate.
- C (False) – no breathing after airway repositioning = dead/expectant (black).
- D (False) – capillary refill > 2 s = immediate (red).

**Ref:** Frykberg ER, J Trauma 2002.

questions.stem: During a major incident, the ICU is full and two more ventilated patients are waiting in the emergency department. According to the ESICM Task Force, which approach to ICU triage is most appropriate?
options: First come, first served without any criteria
Transparent, publicly disclosed criteria applied equitably by a triage officer, with regular reassessment
The treating physician decides at the bedside for each patient
Priority for hospital staff and their families
Age above 65 years as a single exclusion criterion
questions.expl:
**Why B:** The Task Force recommends maximal surge first, then triage based on transparent, ethical criteria, applied equitably and disclosed publicly, prioritising patients most likely to benefit; triage is performed by a dedicated officer and reassessed (e.g. SOFA-based at 48 and 120 h).

**Why not the others:**
- A – first come, first served without criteria is not the preferred approach once capacity is exceeded.
- C – the treating clinician has a conflict of roles; a separate triage officer is recommended.
- D – priority for staff is not part of the recommendations.
- E – age alone is not an ethical criterion.

**Ref:** Sprung CL, Intensive Care Med 2010; Christian MD, CMAJ 2006.

questions.stem: Regarding blast injuries:
options: Primary blast injury predominantly affects air-filled organs.
An intact tympanic membrane excludes blast lung.
Explosions in enclosed spaces cause more primary blast injury than those in open air.
Penetrating fragment injuries are classified as tertiary blast injuries.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – lungs, ears, bowel.
- B (False) – TM rupture is not a reliable marker of other primary blast injury.
- C (True) – reflection of the blast wave increases overpressure.
- D (False) – fragments cause secondary injury; tertiary = displacement of the body.

**Ref:** Wolf SJ, Lancet 2009.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman injured by an explosion in a metro station 6 hours ago develops dyspnoea, haemoptysis and bilateral infiltrates. She is intubated for hypoxaemia. All of the following are appropriate EXCEPT:
options: Low tidal volumes and plateau pressures
Vigilance for pneumothorax
Considering arterial air embolism if neurological deficits or arrhythmias appear after starting ventilation
Liberal fluids at 4 mL/kg/%TBSA to prevent blast lung progression
Judicious fluid administration guided by perfusion
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Blast lung is a pulmonary contusion-like injury; excess fluid worsens oedema. Burn formulae are irrelevant without burns, and fluids should be judicious.

**Why not the others:**
- A – lung-protective ventilation limits barotrauma.
- B – positive pressure may cause or enlarge pneumothoraces.
- C – alveolar–venous fistulae can cause systemic air embolism after starting PPV.
- E – perfusion-guided fluid therapy is appropriate.

**Ref:** Wolf SJ, Lancet 2009.

questions.stem: Regarding hospital organisation in a mass casualty incident:
options: The first patients to arrive are usually the most severely injured.
"Reverse triage" refers to early discharge or transfer of stable inpatients to create capacity.
Over-triage is harmless because it ensures critical patients are not missed.
Decontamination should take place after admission to the ICU in a chemical incident.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – walking, minor casualties usually self-present first at the nearest hospital.
- B (True) – a key surge strategy.
- C (False) – over-triage correlates linearly with critical mortality (Frykberg).
- D (False) – decontamination must happen before entering the hospital.

**Ref:** Frykberg ER, J Trauma 2002; Sprung CL, Intensive Care Med 2010.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man is found unconscious after an opioid overdose, having lain on his left arm for an estimated 14 hours. CK is 38,000 U/L, creatinine 210 µmol/L, K⁺ 6.8 mmol/L with peaked T waves. What is the immediate priority?
options: Forearm fasciotomy
IV calcium and insulin–glucose, followed by urgent renal replacement therapy if refractory
Sodium bicarbonate infusion to a urine pH > 6.5 as the only treatment
Furosemide 80 mg IV
Repeat potassium measurement in 4 hours
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is immediately life-threatening: membrane stabilisation with calcium, shift with insulin–glucose (± salbutamol), then removal – in rhabdomyolysis with AKI, potassium is continuously released and early dialysis is often needed.

**Why not the others:**
- A – compartment syndrome must be assessed, but hyperkalaemia with ECG changes comes first.
- C – bicarbonate alone is insufficient and unproven.
- D – furosemide is ineffective in oliguric AKI and may worsen volume depletion.
- E – delay risks cardiac arrest.

**Ref:** Bosch X, N Engl J Med 2009.

open.q: Outline the medical management of a crush victim from entrapment to the ICU.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Pre-extrication isotonic saline ~ 1 L/h (500 mL/h if > 2 h), no K⁺-containing fluids; anticipate hyperkalaemic arrest on release (ECG, calcium, insulin–glucose, binders).
- After extrication 3–6 L in the first 6 h, then titrate to UO ~ 200–300 mL/h; catheterise; monitor for overload, especially if anuric.
- Labs: K⁺, CK, creatinine, Ca²⁺, phosphate, pH; dipstick (blood without RBC).
- Bicarbonate/mannitol optional, unproven; treat hypocalcaemia only if symptomatic/hyperkalaemic.
- Early RRT for refractory K⁺, acidosis, overload; triage dialysis resources in disasters.
- Fasciotomy only for established compartment syndrome; wound care, tetanus, antibiotics for open wounds.

open.q: How should an ICU prepare for and run a mass casualty incident?
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Major incident plan with incident command, communication (METHANE), staff call-in and inventory.
- Surge: cancel electives, reverse triage, expand ICU into PACU/theatres, ventilators, oxygen, drugs, blood products.
- Damage-control approach, selective imaging, streamlined patient flow.
- Ethical triage when capacity is exceeded: transparent criteria, triage officer, SOFA-based reassessment, palliative care.
- Staff safety, PPE/decontamination for CBRN, psychological support, debriefing.

title: W23 · Saturday – weekly review: Trauma, burns, mass casualties (primary survey and DCR, haemorrhagic shock and TXA, thoracic and abdominal trauma, burns, crush and triage)

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man is shot in the groin; bright red blood is pouring from the wound. He is agitated, RR 30/min, HR 150/min. Which intervention comes first in the ATLS 11 sequence?
options: Oxygen via non-rebreather mask
Cervical spine protection
Intraosseous access and 1 L of crystalloid
Direct pressure and haemostatic packing of the junctional wound
Endotracheal intubation
questions.expl:
**Why D:** ATLS 11 uses xABCDE: catastrophic external haemorrhage (including junctional bleeding not amenable to a tourniquet) is controlled first by direct pressure and wound packing.

**Why not the others:**
- A – airway/breathing follow control of exsanguination.
- B – spinal motion restriction is selective and not indicated for an isolated penetrating wound.
- C – volume without haemorrhage control is futile; crystalloid is minimised.
- E – intubation in profound shock before haemorrhage control and resuscitation risks arrest.

**Ref:** ATLS 11th ed., ACS 2025. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: Regarding damage-control resuscitation according to the European guideline 2023:
options: The target SBP without TBI is 80–90 mmHg until major bleeding is stopped.
The Hb target is 70–90 g/L.
Colloids are preferred over crystalloids to limit fluid volume.
Hypotonic solutions such as Ringer's lactate should be avoided in severe head injury.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – MAP 50–60 mmHg (1B).
- B (True) – 1C.
- C (False) – colloids should be restricted because of their adverse effects on haemostasis (1C).
- D (True) – 1B.

**Ref:** Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman with polytrauma has AIS 5 for a liver laceration, AIS 4 for a splenic injury, AIS 3 for a lung contusion and AIS 2 for a forearm fracture. What is her Injury Severity Score?
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Liver and spleen are both in the abdominal region, so only the highest (AIS 5) counts: abdomen 25 + chest 9 + extremity 4 = 38.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 25 + 16 + 9 + 4 counts two abdominal injuries and four regions.
- C – 16 + 9 + 4 ignores the highest AIS.
- D – 25 + 9 is only two regions.
- E – 25 + 16 + 9 counts the abdomen twice (that would be the NISS).

**Ref:** ATLS 11th ed., ACS 2025. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: Regarding tranexamic acid in trauma:
options: In CRASH-2, TXA given more than 3 hours after injury increased the risk of death due to bleeding.
In CRASH-3, the primary outcome (head-injury death in patients treated within 3 h) was significantly reduced.
The European guideline recommends waiting for viscoelastic evidence of hyperfibrinolysis before giving TXA.
PATCH-Trauma showed improved survival with a favourable functional outcome at 6 months.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – RR 1.44 for bleeding death when given > 3 h.
- B (False) – 18.5 vs 19.8 % (RR 0.94, NS); benefit only in mild–moderate TBI.
- C (False) – do not await VEM results (1B).
- D (False) – 53.7 vs 53.5 %; mortality at 24 h and 28 days was lower.

**Ref:** CRASH-2 collaborators, Lancet 2011; CRASH-3 collaborators, Lancet 2019; Gruen RL, N Engl J Med 2023. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is bleeding after a motorcycle crash. ROTEM shows a low FIBTEM amplitude and Clauss fibrinogen is 1.1 g/L. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Four-factor PCC 25 IU/kg
Platelet transfusion
Fibrinogen concentrate 3–4 g (or 15–20 single-donor units of cryoprecipitate)
Recombinant factor VIIa
FFP 15 mL/kg as the sole fibrinogen source
questions.expl:
**Why C:** With major bleeding and fibrinogen ≤ 1.5 g/L or a functional deficit on VEM, fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate is recommended (1C), with an initial 3–4 g (2C).

**Why not the others:**
- A – PCC is suggested only when fibrinogen is normal and VEM shows delayed initiation; PROCOAG showed more thrombosis.
- B – there is no indication of thrombocytopenia.
- D – rFVIIa is not first line.
- E – FFP contains too little fibrinogen to correct hypofibrinogenaemia.

**Ref:** Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man on dabigatran has a traumatic subdural haematoma and pelvic fracture with ongoing bleeding. Which reversal agent is recommended?
options: Andexanet alfa
Vitamin K 10 mg IV
Protamine
Desmopressin
Idarucizumab 5 g IV
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Idarucizumab, a monoclonal antibody fragment, specifically and rapidly reverses dabigatran (European 2023, 1C).

**Why not the others:**
- A – andexanet alfa reverses factor Xa inhibitors.
- B – vitamin K reverses VKA only.
- C – protamine reverses heparin.
- D – desmopressin has no role in DOAC reversal.

**Ref:** Rossaint R, Crit Care 2023. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: Regarding chest trauma:
options: Tracheal deviation is an early and reliable sign of tension pneumothorax.
Blunt cardiac injury is ruled out when both the ECG and troponin I are normal.
Blunt aortic injury most commonly occurs at the isthmus distal to the left subclavian artery.
Pulmonary contusion typically worsens over the first 24–72 hours.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – it is a late and unreliable sign; diagnosis is clinical (distress, hypotension, absent breath sounds).
- B (True) – EAST 2012.
- C (True) – at the ligamentum arteriosum.
- D (True) – often absent on the initial chest X-ray.

**Ref:** Clancy K, J Trauma Acute Care Surg 2012; Fox N, J Trauma Acute Care Surg 2015. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has a grade III liver laceration after a fall from a horse. She is haemodynamically stable with no peritonitis; CT shows no contrast blush. All of the following are appropriate EXCEPT:
options: Admission to ICU/HDU with serial examinations and Hb
Immediate laparotomy because of the injury grade
Availability of angiography and an operating theatre
LMWH prophylaxis once the injury is stable
Monitoring for bile leak or biloma in the following days
questions.expl:
**Why B:** WSES recommends non-operative management in haemodynamically stable patients regardless of grade if there is no other indication for laparotomy; grade alone does not mandate surgery.

**Why not the others:**
- A – monitoring is an integral part of NOM.
- C – NOM requires immediate access to angiography and theatre.
- D – early pharmacological prophylaxis is safe in stable NOM.
- E – bile leak, biloma and haemobilia are recognised complications.

**Ref:** Coccolini F, World J Emerg Surg 2020. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: Regarding pelvic trauma with haemorrhagic shock:
options: A pelvic binder should be centred over the greater trochanters.
Arterial bleeding accounts for most pelvic fracture haemorrhage.
Preperitoneal pelvic packing is an option when the patient remains unstable with a negative FAST.
Zone 3 retroperitoneal haematoma found at laparotomy after blunt trauma should be opened and explored.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – not over the iliac crests.
- B (False) – ~ 85 % is venous or from fracture surfaces.
- C (True) – with external fixation and/or angioembolisation.
- D (False) – opening releases tamponade; pack/embolise instead.

**Ref:** Coccolini F, World J Emerg Surg 2017 (pelvic). → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: An 80-kg man has 50 % TBSA burns sustained 2 hours before hospital arrival; no fluid was given prehospital. Using the Parkland formula, how much fluid should he receive in the next 6 hours?
options: 4 L
6 L
8 L
2 L
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Parkland 4 × 80 × 50 = 16 L/24 h; half (8 L) is due in the first 8 h from the time of burn. Two hours have passed without fluid, so 8 L should be given over the remaining 6 h, then titrated to urine output (ABA 2024 suggests starting lower, at 2 mL/kg/%TBSA).

**Why not the others:**
- A – this is a quarter of the 24-h volume.
- B – this would assume proportional delivery over 8 h, ignoring the missed 2 h.
- D – this is the full 24-h volume.
- E – far too little.

**Ref:** Cartotto R, J Burn Care Res 2024. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: Regarding carbon monoxide and cyanide poisoning in smoke inhalation:
options: Pulse oximetry underestimates the true oxygen saturation in CO poisoning.
Hydroxocobalamin is the preferred cyanide antidote in fire victims.
Sodium nitrite is preferred when CO poisoning coexists.
A plasma lactate > 10 mmol/L in a fire victim suggests significant cyanide poisoning.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – it overestimates (reads COHb as O₂Hb).
- B (True) – 5 g IV over 15 min.
- C (False) – nitrites produce methaemoglobin and worsen oxygen carriage.
- D (True) – Baud 1991 (sensitivity 87 %, specificity 94 %).

**Ref:** Baud FJ, N Engl J Med 1991; Hampson NB, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2012. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with 40 % TBSA burns needs re-intubation on day 6 after injury. Which drug choice is most appropriate?
options: Rocuronium in an adequate (often increased) dose
Suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg
No neuromuscular blocker because burns increase sensitivity to all of them
Suxamethonium after pre-treatment with calcium
Mivacurium because of its short duration
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Non-depolarising blockers are safe; burn patients are resistant (up-regulated receptors), so higher doses may be needed.

**Why not the others:**
- B – contraindicated after ~ 24–48 h (hyperkalaemia).
- C – burn patients are resistant to non-depolarisers, not more sensitive.
- D – calcium pre-treatment does not make suxamethonium safe.
