- E – mivacurium offers no advantage and is not the standard RSI drug.

**Ref:** Jeschke MG, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2020. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: Regarding crush syndrome:
options: Isotonic saline should be started before extrication.
Hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest can occur at the moment of release.
Asymptomatic hypocalcaemia should be corrected promptly.
Prophylactic fasciotomy is recommended for all crushed limbs.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ~ 1 L/h in adults.
- B (True) – reperfusion washes out potassium and acid.
- C (False) – risk of calcium deposition and rebound hypercalcaemia; treat only if symptomatic or hyperkalaemic.
- D (False) – only for established compartment syndrome.

**Ref:** Sever MS, Nephrol Dial Transplant 2012. → [D5](D5.md)

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man is sedated in the ICU after a femoral and tibial fracture. His leg is swollen; diastolic BP is 58 mmHg and anterior compartment pressure 34 mmHg. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Normal – compartment pressure is below 40 mmHg
Compartment syndrome – ΔP 24 mmHg, fasciotomy indicated
Repeat the measurement after elevating the leg
Diagnosis requires loss of distal pulses
Diagnosis requires CK > 20,000 U/L
questions.expl:
**Why B:** ΔP = 58 − 34 = 24 mmHg, below the 30 mmHg threshold (McQueen). In a sedated patient the pressure measurement guides urgent fasciotomy.

**Why not the others:**
- A – absolute thresholds are less accurate than ΔP.
- C – elevation reduces perfusion; keep the leg at heart level.
- D – pulses are lost late.
- E – CK is non-specific.

**Ref:** McQueen MM, J Bone Joint Surg Br 1996. → [D5](D5.md)

questions.stem: Regarding mass casualty incidents:
options: In START triage, all patients who can walk are initially labelled minor (green).
Over-triage correlates with higher critical mortality.
Primary blast injury mainly affects air-filled organs.
ICU triage criteria should be transparent and applied by a dedicated triage officer.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – re-triage later.
- B (True) – Frykberg 2002.
- C (True) – ears, lungs, bowel.
- D (True) – ESICM Task Force 2010.

**Ref:** Frykberg ER, J Trauma 2002; Wolf SJ, Lancet 2009; Sprung CL, Intensive Care Med 2010. → [D5](D5.md)

title: W24 · D1 – Toxidromes and the general approach to the poisoned patient (NICO)

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department agitated and hallucinating after a party. HR 132/min, BP 150/90 mmHg, temperature 38.6 °C, pupils 7 mm. Which additional finding would best support an anticholinergic rather than a sympathomimetic toxidrome?
options: Seizure
Hypertension
Dry axillae and a palpable bladder
Tachycardia
Hyperthermia
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Both toxidromes cause agitation, mydriasis, tachycardia, hypertension and hyperthermia. Anticholinergic agents block sweating and detrusor/gut muscarinic tone, so dry skin, urinary retention and absent bowel sounds point to anticholinergic poisoning, whereas sympathomimetics cause profuse sweating.

**Why not the others:**
- A – seizures occur in both (cocaine, amphetamines, TCA, diphenhydramine).
- B – hypertension is common to both.
- D – tachycardia is common to both.
- E – hyperthermia occurs in both and does not discriminate.

**EDIC trap:** "Wet or dry?" – the axilla is the quickest discriminator.

**Ref:** Boyer EW, NEJM 2005; Chyka PA, Clin Toxicol 2005.

questions.stem: Regarding single-dose activated charcoal in acute poisoning:
options: It is most effective when given within 1 hour of ingestion.
It adsorbs lithium and iron effectively.
It may be given to a drowsy patient with an unprotected airway if a nasogastric tube is used.
Its main serious complication is aspiration pneumonitis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – AACT/EAPCCT: benefit is greatest within 1 h; later use is considered for modified-release drugs or agents slowing gastric emptying.
- B (False) – metals (iron, lithium), alcohols, hydrocarbons and corrosives are poorly adsorbed.
- C (False) – an unprotected airway is a contraindication; a nasogastric tube does not protect against aspiration.
- D (True) – aspiration of charcoal causes severe pneumonitis.

**Ref:** Chyka PA, Clin Toxicol 2005.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman on sertraline 200 mg/day was given tramadol for back pain. Six hours later she is agitated and sweating, temperature 38.4 °C, HR 118/min, with inducible ankle clonus, ocular clonus and hyperreflexia in the lower limbs. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV
Bromocriptine via nasogastric tube
Paracetamol 1 g IV for the fever and observation
Haloperidol 5 mg IV for agitation
Stop serotonergic drugs, give benzodiazepines and cyproheptadine, and cool
questions.expl:
**Why E:** She fulfils the Hunter criteria (inducible clonus with agitation and diaphoresis, ocular clonus) for serotonin toxicity from SSRI plus tramadol. Treatment is removal of the drugs, benzodiazepines, the 5-HT2A antagonist cyproheptadine (oral/NG) and cooling; paralysis and ventilation if temperature exceeds ~41 °C.

**Why not the others:**
- A – dantrolene is the treatment of malignant hyperthermia, not serotonin toxicity.
- B – bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist used in NMS and may worsen serotonin toxicity.
- C – hyperthermia is due to muscle activity; antipyretics are ineffective.
- D – antipsychotics may worsen hyperthermia and confuse the picture with NMS.

**Ref:** Dunkley EJC, QJM 2003; Boyer EW, NEJM 2005.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents 90 minutes after an intentional overdose and is alert and cooperative. All of the following substances are poorly adsorbed by activated charcoal EXCEPT:
options: Lithium carbonate
Carbamazepine
Ferrous sulfate
Ethylene glycol
Methanol
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Carbamazepine is well adsorbed by charcoal, and multiple-dose activated charcoal is recommended in life-threatening carbamazepine poisoning because it also interrupts enteric recirculation.

**Why not the others:**
- A – lithium (a metal ion) is not adsorbed; WBI and haemodialysis are the options.
- C – iron is not adsorbed; use WBI if tablets are seen on X-ray.
- D – ethylene glycol (an alcohol) is rapidly absorbed and not bound.
- E – methanol is not bound; fomepizole and haemodialysis are the treatments.

**Ref:** Chyka PA, Clin Toxicol 2005; AACT/EAPCCT, J Toxicol Clin Toxicol 1999.

questions.stem: Regarding the NICO trial of airway management in comatose poisoned patients:
options: Patients with a Glasgow Coma Scale score below 9 were included.
The conservative strategy reduced the rate of intubation to under 20 %.
In-hospital mortality was significantly lower in the conservative arm.
Patients with suspected cardiotoxic or seizure-inducing poisons were excluded.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – adults with suspected acute poisoning and GCS < 9 in French EDs and one ICU.
- B (True) – intubation 16.4 vs 57.8 %; pneumonia 6.9 vs 14.7 %.
- C (False) – there were no deaths in either arm; benefit came from shorter ICU and hospital stay (win ratio 1.85).
- D (True) – so the results do not apply to TCA, beta-blocker or calcium-channel blocker poisoning.

**Ref:** Freund Y (NICO), JAMA 2023.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman ingested about 60 ferrous sulfate tablets (65 mg elemental iron each) 5 hours ago. She weighs 55 kg, has vomited blood, BP 85/50 mmHg, pH 7.18, lactate 6 mmol/L; abdominal X-ray shows multiple radio-opaque tablets. Serum iron is pending. Besides resuscitation, what is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube
Wait for the serum iron level before giving any antidote
Gastric lavage with sodium bicarbonate
Intravenous desferrioxamine 15 mg/kg/h and whole-bowel irrigation once haemodynamically stable
Oral desferrioxamine
questions.expl:
**Why D:** She took ~70 mg/kg of elemental iron and has systemic toxicity (shock, metabolic acidosis), which is an indication for IV desferrioxamine regardless of the serum iron. Radio-opaque tablets in the gut can be removed with WBI, which is contraindicated while she is haemodynamically unstable.

**Why not the others:**
- A – charcoal does not bind iron.
- B – desferrioxamine is given for clinical toxicity irrespective of the level; waiting delays treatment.
- C – lavage is not routine; bicarbonate lavage is obsolete.
- E – oral desferrioxamine may increase absorption of the chelate; it has no role.

**EDIC trap:** Desferrioxamine infusions beyond 24 h are associated with ARDS.

**Ref:** Thanacoody R, Clin Toxicol 2015; Chyka PA, Clin Toxicol 2005.

questions.stem: Regarding toxidromes and calculated gaps:
options: Organophosphate poisoning typically causes mydriasis and dry skin.
A normal osmolal gap excludes methanol poisoning.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is characterised by hyperreflexia and clonus.
Methaemoglobinaemia produces a gap between pulse oximetry and arterial oxygen tension–derived saturation.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – cholinergic excess causes miosis, sweating, salivation and bronchorrhoea.
- B (False) – in late presentation methanol has been metabolised to formate: the osmolal gap falls while the anion gap rises.
- C (False) – NMS causes lead-pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia; clonus and hyperreflexia suggest serotonin toxicity.
- D (True) – SpO₂ reads ~ 85 % while calculated SaO₂ from a normal PaO₂ is high ("saturation gap"); co-oximetry confirms.

**Ref:** Eddleston M, Lancet 2008; Boyer EW, NEJM 2005.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old farmer drank an organophosphate insecticide 2 hours ago. He is drowsy with pinpoint pupils, profuse salivation, wheeze and crackles over both lungs, HR 48/min, BP 80/45 mmHg, and fasciculations. Which is the best end point for atropine titration?
options: Clear chest on auscultation with resolution of bronchorrhoea, HR > 80/min and SBP > 80 mmHg
Pupils dilated to 6 mm
Heart rate above 120/min
Disappearance of fasciculations
Normalisation of red-cell acetylcholinesterase activity
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Atropine is given in doubling doses every 5 min until atropinisation: clear chest (no bronchorrhoea), HR > 80/min, SBP > 80 mmHg, dry axillae and pupils no longer pinpoint. Bronchorrhoea and bronchospasm are what kill, so a clear chest is the key target.

**Why not the others:**
- B – pupil size is a late and unreliable target; aiming for mydriasis leads to atropine toxicity.
- C – excessive tachycardia indicates over-atropinisation; tachycardia is not a target.
- D – fasciculations are nicotinic and do not respond to atropine.
- E – enzyme activity is not available in real time and recovers slowly.

**EDIC trap:** Avoid suxamethonium for intubation – plasma cholinesterase is inhibited, causing prolonged paralysis.

**Ref:** Eddleston M, Lancet 2008.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man on a methadone programme is found apnoeic with pinpoint pupils. After naloxone 0.4 mg IV he wakes and breathes 14/min. Forty minutes later his respiratory rate falls to 6/min. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Flumazenil 0.5 mg IV
Discharge after 1 hour if awake
Immediate intubation and admission to ICU without further naloxone
Activated charcoal via nasogastric tube
Repeat the naloxone bolus and start a naloxone infusion with monitoring
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Naloxone has a half-life of ~60–90 min, much shorter than methadone (> 24 h), so re-narcotisation is expected. Repeat the effective bolus and start an infusion (about two-thirds of the reversing dose per hour), titrated to respiratory rate, in a monitored setting.

**Why not the others:**
- A – flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids, and may provoke seizures.
- B – early discharge after long-acting opioid overdose is dangerous.
- C – intubation is reserved for failure of naloxone or aspiration; naloxone is effective here.
- D – the airway is unprotected and charcoal is not useful for methadone at this stage.

**Ref:** Chyka PA, Clin Toxicol 2005; Boyer EW, NEJM 2005.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with schizophrenia, started on high-dose haloperidol 5 days ago, develops temperature 40.1 °C, generalised rigidity, fluctuating BP and CK 28,000 U/L. Regarding his condition:
options: Hyporeflexia and lead-pipe rigidity are typical.
Cyproheptadine is the first-line specific treatment.
Dantrolene and bromocriptine may be used in severe cases.
Onset within a few hours of the first dose is required for the diagnosis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – NMS causes bradykinesia, lead-pipe rigidity and diminished reflexes (in contrast to serotonin toxicity).
- B (False) – cyproheptadine is used in serotonin toxicity; NMS is a dopamine-blockade syndrome.
- C (True) – plus stopping the antipsychotic, cooling, benzodiazepines, fluids for rhabdomyolysis.
- D (False) – NMS develops over days to weeks; rapid onset (< 24 h) suggests serotonin toxicity.

**Ref:** Boyer EW, NEJM 2005.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman receives 30 mL of bupivacaine 0.5 % for an interscalene block. Within 2 minutes she seizes and then develops broad-complex bradycardia progressing to pulseless electrical activity. CPR is started. What specific treatment should be given now?
options: Lidocaine 1 mg/kg IV
20 % lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus followed by an infusion
Vasopressin 40 units IV
Phenytoin 15 mg/kg IV
Propofol 2 mg/kg IV as a lipid source
questions.expl:
**Why B:** This is local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST). The Lipid Emulsion Workgroup recommends 20 % lipid emulsion for bupivacaine cardiotoxicity: 1.5 mL/kg bolus, then 0.25 mL/kg/min, with repeat boluses for persistent instability, alongside CPR with reduced adrenaline doses.

**Why not the others:**
- A – lidocaine is another sodium-channel blocking local anaesthetic and worsens toxicity.
- C – vasopressin is not recommended in LAST.
- D – phenytoin is a sodium-channel blocker and ineffective for toxic seizures.
- E – propofol contains too little lipid and is a myocardial depressant.

**Ref:** Gosselin S, Clin Toxicol 2016.

open.q: Outline your initial assessment and management of a 30-year-old found unconscious at home with empty packets of several unknown tablets.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **ABC and immediate checks:** airway position, SpO₂, RR, BP, HR, temperature, **capillary glucose**; naloxone trial if miosis and bradypnoea.
- **Airway decision:** intubate for emergency criteria (hypoxaemia, respiratory failure, vomiting/aspiration, seizures, shock) or when cardiotoxic/proconvulsant poisoning is likely; otherwise close observation even with GCS < 9 (NICO).
- **History** from witnesses, packets, prescriptions: agents, amount, time, modified-release, co-ingestion.
- **Toxidrome examination:** pupils, skin, bowel sounds, bladder, tone, reflexes, clonus.
- **Investigations:** ECG (QRS, QTc, aVR), paracetamol and salicylate levels, blood gas, lactate, electrolytes, anion and osmolal gap, CK, renal and liver tests, specific levels as indicated; co-oximetry if CO/methaemoglobin suspected.
- **Decontamination:** SDAC 50 g within 1 h only if airway protected and agent adsorbable; WBI for iron/lithium/MR drugs; MDAC for carbamazepine, dapsone, phenobarbital, quinine, theophylline; no routine lavage.
- **Antidotes** guided by findings; **enhanced elimination** (alkalinisation, ECTR per EXTRIP).
- **Supportive care:** seizures (benzodiazepines), hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, VA-ECMO for refractory cardiogenic shock; poison centre advice; psychiatric review.

title: W24 · D2 – Paracetamol and salicylate poisoning (SNAP, EXTRIP)

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman (60 kg) took 16 g of immediate-release paracetamol at a single known time. She is asymptomatic; the 4-hour paracetamol concentration is 180 mg/L and ALT is normal. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Repeat the level at 8 hours and treat only if it remains above the line
Activated charcoal only, as she presented after 1 hour
Fomepizole 15 mg/kg IV
Start intravenous acetylcysteine now
Urgent haemodialysis
questions.expl:
**Why D:** A single acute ingestion of ~ 270 mg/kg with a 4-h level of 180 mg/L lies above every treatment line (UK 100 mg/L, US/ANZ 150 mg/L). NAC is nearly fully hepatoprotective when started within 8 h of ingestion.

**Why not the others:**
- A – waiting loses the most effective window; a valid 4-h level is already above the line.
- B – charcoal is an adjunct and does not replace NAC; its benefit is greatest within 1–2 h.
- C – fomepizole has no standard role; data are insufficient outside very high-risk ingestions.
- E – ECTR is reserved for extreme levels (> 700–1,000 mg/L) with metabolic failure.

**Ref:** Dart RC, JAMA Netw Open 2023; Chiew AL, Med J Aust 2020.

questions.stem: Regarding the mechanism of paracetamol hepatotoxicity:
options: The toxic metabolite NAPQI is produced mainly by CYP2E1.
Hepatocellular necrosis predominantly affects the centrilobular (zone 3) region.
Chronic alcohol use, malnutrition and enzyme-inducing drugs are recognised susceptibility factors.
Current UK guidance uses a lower nomogram treatment line for patients with these susceptibility factors.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – CYP2E1 (and CYP3A4) oxidise ~ 5–10 % of a therapeutic dose to NAPQI, normally conjugated with glutathione.
- B (True) – zone 3 has the most CYP2E1 and the lowest oxygen tension.
- C (True) – they increase NAPQI production (induction) or reduce glutathione stores.
- D (False) – since 2012 the UK uses a single line (100 mg/L at 4 h) for all patients.

**Ref:** Dart RC, JAMA Netw Open 2023; Chiew AL, Med J Aust 2020.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man took 2 g of paracetamol every few hours over the past day for toothache, about 14 g in total (75 kg). He presents 30 hours after the first dose. Paracetamol concentration is 25 mg/L and ALT 120 U/L (normal < 40). What is the most appropriate management?
options: Start acetylcysteine without using the nomogram
Plot the level on the nomogram from the time of the first dose and treat if above the line
Discharge, because the level is below 100 mg/L
Activated charcoal and repeat ALT in 24 hours
Refer for liver transplant assessment
questions.expl:
**Why A:** This is a staggered/repeated supratherapeutic ingestion – the nomogram is invalid. A potentially toxic dose with detectable paracetamol and a raised ALT mandates NAC, then reassessment of ALT, INR and paracetamol at the end of the regimen.

**Why not the others:**
- B – the nomogram applies only to single acute ingestions at a known time.
- C – a "low" level after staggered ingestion does not exclude toxicity.
- D – charcoal is useless 30 h after ingestion; delaying NAC worsens outcome.
- E – there is no evidence of liver failure (normal INR, no encephalopathy).

**Ref:** Dart RC, JAMA Netw Open 2023; Chiew AL, Med J Aust 2020.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is in the ICU on day 3 after a paracetamol overdose that presented late. She is receiving acetylcysteine. After adequate fluid resuscitation, which single finding fulfils the King's College criteria for liver transplant listing?
options: ALT 12,000 U/L
INR 4.0
Arterial pH 7.25
Bilirubin 150 µmol/L
Grade II encephalopathy
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In paracetamol ALF, arterial pH < 7.30 after adequate fluid resuscitation is a stand-alone King's criterion. Otherwise all three of INR > 6.5, creatinine > 300 µmol/L and grade III–IV encephalopathy within 24 h are required.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the height of ALT does not predict outcome.
- B – INR must exceed 6.5 and be combined with renal failure and grade III–IV encephalopathy.
- D – bilirubin is part of the non-paracetamol criteria only.
- E – grade III–IV encephalopathy is needed, and only in combination.

**EDIC trap:** Lactate > 3.5 mmol/L at 4 h or > 3.0 mmol/L at 12 h after resuscitation is the modified criterion.

**Ref:** O'Grady JG, Gastroenterology 1989; Wendon J, J Hepatol 2017.

questions.stem: Regarding intravenous acetylcysteine regimens:
options: The SNAP regimen gives 100 mg/kg over 2 hours followed by 200 mg/kg over 10 hours.
In the SNAP trial the 12-hour regimen caused less vomiting and fewer anaphylactoid reactions than the 21-hour regimen.
Anaphylactoid reactions are IgE-mediated, and acetylcysteine must not be restarted after a reaction.
Acetylcysteine is ineffective if started more than 24 hours after ingestion and should then be withheld.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – total 300 mg/kg over 12 h, with a slower initial rate.
- B (True) – vomiting/retching 36 vs 65 %, anaphylactoid reactions 5 vs 28 %, with no difference in ALT rises.
- C (False) – reactions are non-IgE, rate-related; stop, give antihistamine and restart at a slower rate.
- D (False) – NAC improves survival in established paracetamol ALF and is given whenever there is ongoing toxicity.

**Ref:** Bateman DN (SNAP), Lancet 2014; Dart RC, JAMA Netw Open 2023.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presents 3 hours after ingesting 100 aspirin tablets of 300 mg. All of the following are typical features of acute salicylate poisoning in an adult EXCEPT:
options: Tinnitus and deafness
A primary respiratory acidosis as the earliest acid–base disturbance
High anion gap metabolic acidosis
Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
Hyperthermia and sweating
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Salicylates directly stimulate the respiratory centre, so the earliest disturbance in adults is a primary respiratory alkalosis, followed by a high anion gap metabolic acidosis from uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation. Respiratory acidosis appears only with exhaustion, CNS depression or co-ingested sedatives, and is ominous.

**Why not the others:**
- A – tinnitus and deafness are classic early symptoms.
- C – lactate and ketoacids accumulate (mixed disorder).
- D – increased capillary permeability causes non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, more often in chronic toxicity and the elderly.
- E – uncoupling generates heat.

**Ref:** Juurlink DN, Ann Emerg Med 2015.

questions.stem: Regarding management of salicylate poisoning:
options: EXTRIP recommends extracorporeal treatment when the salicylate concentration exceeds 7.2 mmol/L (100 mg/dL).
Altered mental status is an indication for extracorporeal treatment irrespective of the salicylate concentration.
Urine alkalinisation aims for a urine pH of about 7.5–8.5.
Hypokalaemia should be corrected because it impairs urine alkalinisation.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – also > 6.5 mmol/L (90 mg/dL) with impaired kidney function.
- B (True) – altered mental status, new hypoxaemia requiring O₂ and failure of standard therapy are clinical indications (recommended).
- C (True) – ion trapping increases renal salicylate clearance many-fold; keep serum pH ≤ 7.55–7.60.
- D (True) – with hypokalaemia the distal tubule reabsorbs K⁺ in exchange for H⁺, acidifying the urine.

**Ref:** Juurlink DN, Ann Emerg Med 2015.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man with acute salicylate poisoning (level 820 mg/L) becomes increasingly drowsy. RR 36/min, pH 7.41, PaCO₂ 2.4 kPa (18 mmHg), HCO₃⁻ 11 mmol/L. His GCS falls to 8 and he vomits. Intubation is judged necessary. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Rapid sequence induction followed by standard ventilation of 6 mL/kg at 14 breaths/min
Delay intubation and give flumazenil to improve consciousness
Perform intubation without sedation to preserve respiratory drive
Stop the bicarbonate infusion before induction to avoid alkalaemia
Bicarbonate bolus before induction, intubation by an experienced operator, high minute ventilation to match the pre-intubation PaCO₂, and urgent haemodialysis
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Loss of compensatory hyperventilation after induction causes acute acidaemia, increasing non-ionised salicylate and its entry into the brain, with seizures and cardiac arrest. A bicarbonate bolus, rapid intubation, high minute ventilation with frequent gases and haemodialysis (altered mental status is an EXTRIP indication) mitigate this.

**Why not the others:**
- A – "normal" ventilation will produce severe respiratory acidosis in this patient.
- B – flumazenil is not indicated and may cause seizures.
- C – awake intubation without sedation is not appropriate in a vomiting, drowsy patient; the issue is ventilation afterwards.
- D – alkalaemia is protective; stopping bicarbonate worsens CNS salicylate penetration.

**Ref:** Juurlink DN, Ann Emerg Med 2015.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man (70 kg) ingested 40 g of immediate-release paracetamol 4 hours ago. He is alert; the 4-hour paracetamol concentration is 520 mg/L, lactate 3.5 mmol/L, pH 7.34. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Start acetylcysteine with an increased dose for a high-risk ingestion, consider activated charcoal and seek toxicology advice
Standard acetylcysteine only, with no further action
Immediate liver transplant listing
Haemodialysis as the first-line therapy instead of acetylcysteine
Wait for a repeat level at 8 hours to confirm absorption
questions.expl:
**Why A:** A 40 g ingestion and a level above the high-risk line (300 mg/L at 4 h) define a high-risk ingestion; guidelines support increased NAC dosing (e.g. doubling the second bag in ANZ) with toxicology advice, and charcoal up to 4 h for ingestions ≥ 30 g in a cooperative patient. Early lactic acidosis reflects mitochondrial toxicity of very high concentrations.

**Why not the others:**
- B – standard dosing may be insufficient at very high concentrations.
- C – he has no liver failure; King's criteria apply to established ALF.
- D – ECTR is suggested only above ~ 700 mg/L with altered mental status or acidosis (without NAC) and never replaces NAC.
- E – he is already far above the line; delay is harmful.

**Ref:** Dart RC, JAMA Netw Open 2023; Chiew AL, Med J Aust 2020; Gosselin S, Clin Toxicol 2014.

questions.stem: Regarding paracetamol poisoning:
options: A paracetamol concentration taken 2 hours after an acute ingestion can be plotted on the nomogram to decide on treatment.
Fresh frozen plasma should be given routinely to correct the INR in paracetamol-induced acute liver failure.
The 2023 US/Canada consensus recommends stopping acetylcysteine after exactly 21 hours regardless of laboratory results.
Acetylcysteine should be given in established paracetamol-induced acute liver failure, even when started more than 24 hours after ingestion.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – absorption and distribution are incomplete before 4 h; the level cannot be interpreted.
- B (False) – INR is a key prognostic marker; correct only for bleeding or procedures (EASL).
- C (False) – the consensus states that NAC should continue until stopping criteria (falling paracetamol, ALT/INR) are met.
- D (True) – late NAC improves survival in established ALF.

**Ref:** Dart RC, JAMA Netw Open 2023; Wendon J, J Hepatol 2017.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman taking regular high-dose aspirin for arthritis is admitted confused and tachypnoeic. pH 7.38, PaCO₂ 3.1 kPa (23 mmHg), HCO₃⁻ 13 mmol/L, anion gap 24 mmol/L, creatinine 190 µmol/L (baseline 80), salicylate 450 mg/L (3.3 mmol/L). What is the most appropriate management?
options: Treat empirically for sepsis and recheck salicylate in 24 hours
Urine alkalinisation alone, because the level is below 500 mg/L
Intubate and ventilate to protect the airway
Urgent haemodialysis in addition to supportive care
Multiple-dose activated charcoal alone
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Chronic salicylate toxicity causes serious toxicity at lower levels. EXTRIP recommends ECTR for altered mental status regardless of concentration, and AKI both limits salicylate excretion and makes alkalinisation hazardous; intermittent haemodialysis also corrects the acidosis.

**Why not the others:**
- A – chronic salicylism is often mistaken for sepsis; the diagnosis is already made.
- B – the level does not reflect tissue toxicity in chronic poisoning, and confusion is an indication for HD.
- C – intubation removes compensatory hyperventilation and is dangerous; it is not needed for airway protection here.
- E – charcoal has little role in chronic ingestion.

**Ref:** Juurlink DN, Ann Emerg Med 2015.

open.q: Describe the risk assessment and treatment of a patient who presents 6 hours after an acute paracetamol overdose.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **History:** dose (mg/kg; ≥ 150 mg/kg toxic, ≥ 30 g high-risk), single vs staggered, immediate vs modified-release, co-ingestants, susceptibility factors.
- **Investigations:** paracetamol level (≥ 4 h), ALT, INR, creatinine, glucose, gas and lactate, salicylate level.
- **Nomogram** valid for single acute known-time ingestion: treat if above the line (UK 100 mg/L, US/ANZ 150 mg/L at 4 h); high-risk line 300 mg/L.
- **Charcoal** not useful at 6 h unless ≥ 30 g or modified-release (up to 4 h or later).
- **NAC:** start now if the level will not be back before 8 h or if above the line; SNAP 12 h (100 mg/kg/2 h + 200 mg/kg/10 h) or two-bag/three-bag regimens; increased dose for high-risk ingestions; manage anaphylactoid reactions and restart.
- **End of treatment:** repeat paracetamol, ALT, INR, creatinine; continue NAC if ongoing injury.
- **ALF:** King's criteria, early transplant-centre contact, avoid FFP, glucose, ammonia, ECTR only for extreme levels with metabolic failure (EXTRIP).
- **Psychiatric assessment** before discharge.

open.q: Explain the acid–base disturbance of acute salicylate poisoning and how it influences ICU management.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **Respiratory alkalosis** (direct medullary stimulation) early, then **HAGMA** (uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation → lactate, ketones; salicylate anion itself contributes little).
- **Acidaemia increases non-ionised salicylate**, which enters the CNS → seizures, cerebral oedema, death; therefore keep the patient alkalaemic.
- **Sodium bicarbonate** for urine alkalinisation (urine pH 7.5–8.5) and serum alkalinisation; correct **K⁺**.
- **Avoid intubation**; if necessary, bicarbonate bolus, high minute ventilation matching PaCO₂, frequent gases.
- **Haemodialysis** (EXTRIP): > 100 mg/dL, > 90 with renal impairment, altered mental status, new hypoxaemia, failure of therapy; pH ≤ 7.20 suggested.
- Watch for **neuroglycopenia** (give glucose), pulmonary and cerebral oedema, hyperthermia.

title: W24 · D3 – Cardiotoxic drugs: tricyclic antidepressants, beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, digoxin

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman took an unknown number of amitriptyline 50 mg tablets 2 hours ago. GCS 9, HR 128/min, BP 82/50 mmHg, QRS 140 ms with a terminal R wave of 5 mm in aVR. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Amiodarone 300 mg IV
Sodium bicarbonate 8.4 % 1–2 mmol/kg IV bolus, repeated to narrow the QRS
Physostigmine 1 mg IV
Flumazenil 0.5 mg IV
Urgent haemodialysis
questions.expl:
**Why B:** QRS > 100 ms and hypotension indicate fast sodium-channel blockade. Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate overcomes the block (sodium load) and reduces drug binding (alkalaemia); repeat boluses until the QRS narrows and BP improves, then maintain pH 7.45–7.55.

**Why not the others:**
- A – amiodarone (class III, also Na⁺-blocking) may worsen conduction and hypotension.
- C – physostigmine can cause bradyasystole in TCA poisoning.
- D – flumazenil can precipitate seizures in TCA overdose.
- E – TCA have a large Vd and high protein binding; EXTRIP recommends against ECTR.

**Ref:** Boehnert MT, NEJM 1985; Yates C, Semin Dial 2014.

questions.stem: Regarding the prognostic value of investigations in tricyclic antidepressant poisoning:
options: A limb-lead QRS duration of 100 ms or more is associated with an increased risk of seizures.
A terminal R wave of 3 mm or more in lead aVR predicts seizures or arrhythmias.
The serum TCA concentration predicts complications better than the QRS duration.
Haemodialysis is recommended by EXTRIP in severe TCA poisoning with QRS > 160 ms.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – seizures in 34 % with QRS ≥ 100 ms vs none below; ventricular arrhythmias in 50 % with QRS ≥ 160 ms.
- B (True) – Liebelt 1995; also R/S ratio in aVR > 0.7.
- C (False) – Boehnert and Lovejoy showed the QRS was superior to the serum level.
- D (False) – EXTRIP recommends against ECTR because of the large Vd and protein binding.

**Ref:** Boehnert MT, NEJM 1985; Liebelt EL, Ann Emerg Med 1995; Yates C, Semin Dial 2014.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man intubated after a dosulepin overdose has received 300 mmol of sodium bicarbonate and is hyperventilated to pH 7.52, yet develops recurrent haemodynamically unstable broad-complex tachycardia after synchronised cardioversion. Which antiarrhythmic is most appropriate?
options: Flecainide
Procainamide
Amiodarone
Lidocaine
Esmolol
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Lidocaine is a class IB agent with fast on–off kinetics that competes with the TCA at the sodium channel and is the antiarrhythmic of choice for VT refractory to bicarbonate. Correct hypoxia, acidosis and hyperthermia simultaneously.

**Why not the others:**
- A – class IC agents worsen Na⁺-channel blockade.
- B – class IA agents prolong QRS and QT further.
- C – amiodarone prolongs QT, has Na⁺-blocking and vasodilating effects – avoid.
- E – beta-blockade worsens hypotension and myocardial depression.

**Ref:** Boehnert MT, NEJM 1985; Gosselin S, Clin Toxicol 2016.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man ingested sustained-release verapamil 6 hours ago. HR 38/min (junctional), BP 70/40 mmHg, glucose 16 mmol/L. All of the following are recommended treatments by the 2017 expert consensus EXCEPT:
options: Haemodialysis to remove verapamil
Intravenous calcium
High-dose insulin euglycaemia therapy if myocardial dysfunction is present
Noradrenaline or adrenaline for shock
Atropine for symptomatic bradycardia
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Verapamil is highly protein-bound with a large Vd; EXTRIP recommends against ECTR for amlodipine, diltiazem and verapamil (strong recommendation, very low quality evidence).

**Why not the others:**
- B – IV calcium is first line.
- C – HIET is first line when myocardial dysfunction is present, and is escalated in refractory shock.
- D – catecholamines are first-line vasopressors/inotropes.
- E – atropine is recommended for symptomatic bradycardia, although often ineffective.

**Ref:** St-Onge M, Crit Care Med 2017; Wong A, Clin Toxicol 2021.

questions.stem: Regarding high-dose insulin euglycaemia therapy (HIET) in calcium-channel blocker poisoning:
options: A typical regimen is a 1 U/kg bolus of regular insulin followed by 1 U/kg/h.
Dextrose infusion and frequent glucose and potassium monitoring are required.
The degree of hyperglycaemia at presentation correlates with the severity of poisoning.
Its haemodynamic effect is maximal within 1–2 minutes of the bolus, so it is reserved for cardiac arrest.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – titrated up to 10 U/kg/h in refractory shock.
- B (True) – dextrose ~ 0.5 g/kg/h, glucose every 15–30 min initially; insulin shifts K⁺ intracellularly.
- C (True) – β-cell L-type channel block reduces insulin release; hyperglycaemia reflects severity.
- D (False) – onset takes 15–60 min, so HIET should be started early in symptomatic patients, not only in arrest.

**Ref:** St-Onge M, Crit Care Med 2017.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman ingested 40 of her grandmother's digoxin 250 µg tablets 4 hours ago. She is vomiting, HR 36/min with second-degree AV block, BP 85/50 mmHg, K⁺ 6.4 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Haemodialysis to remove digoxin and potassium
Calcium chloride 10 mL IV and observation
Temporary transvenous pacing as definitive therapy
Wait for a 6-hour digoxin level before any specific treatment
Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (e.g. 10 vials)
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Acute digoxin poisoning with life-threatening bradyarrhythmia, hypotension and hyperkalaemia (> 5–6 mmol/L) is an indication for Fab; a 10-mg ingestion corresponds to ~ 20 vials if fully neutralised, and an empirical 5–10 vials is a typical starting dose, repeated according to response.

**Why not the others:**
- A – digoxin has a large Vd (5–7 L/kg) and is not dialysable.
- B – calcium does not treat digoxin toxicity and is usually avoided when Fab is available.
- C – pacing may be a bridge but does not reverse toxicity and can trigger arrhythmias.
- D – treatment is based on clinical severity; delay is dangerous.

**Ref:** Chan BS, Clin Toxicol 2014.

questions.stem: Regarding beta-blocker poisoning:
options: Propranolol may cause QRS widening and seizures because of sodium-channel blockade.
Sotalol poisoning may cause QT prolongation and torsade de pointes.
EXTRIP recommends extracorporeal treatment for severe propranolol poisoning.
Glucagon acts by directly stimulating cardiac β₁-receptors.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – propranolol is lipophilic and membrane-stabilising; treat QRS widening with bicarbonate.
- B (True) – class III (K⁺-channel) effect; magnesium and overdrive pacing.
- C (False) – EXTRIP recommends against ECTR for propranolol; ECTR is suggested only for atenolol/sotalol with impaired kidney function.
- D (False) – glucagon acts on its own G-protein-coupled receptor, raising cAMP independently of β-receptors.

**Ref:** Bouchard J, Crit Care 2021.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is ventilated after a diltiazem overdose. Despite calcium, adrenaline 1 µg/kg/min, noradrenaline 1 µg/kg/min and insulin 10 U/kg/h, he has lactate 9 mmol/L, BP 60/35 mmHg and echocardiography shows severe global LV hypokinesia. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Methylene blue as the only additional therapy
Haemodialysis
Veno-arterial ECMO
Increase insulin to 20 U/kg/h
Glucagon infusion as the only additional therapy
questions.expl:
**Why C:** This is refractory cardiogenic shock from a reversible poison. The expert consensus recommends VA-ECMO as rescue therapy; observational data show markedly higher survival with ECLS in refractory toxic shock (86 vs 48 % in Masson 2012), and ECMO maintains organ perfusion and drug clearance.

**Why not the others:**
- A – methylene blue targets vasoplegia, not severe LV failure.
- B – diltiazem is not dialysable (EXTRIP: against ECTR).
- D – 10 U/kg/h is the upper titration limit in the consensus; further escalation is unproven.
- E – glucagon has limited efficacy in CCB poisoning and will not reverse established cardiogenic shock.

**Ref:** St-Onge M, Crit Care Med 2017; Masson R, Resuscitation 2012.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman took 300 mg of amlodipine 8 hours ago. HR 115/min, BP 70/30 mmHg, warm peripheries; echocardiography shows a hyperdynamic left ventricle. Shock persists despite calcium, high-dose insulin and noradrenaline 1.2 µg/kg/min. Which additional therapy is supported by the expert consensus for this situation?
options: Transvenous pacing
Veno-arterial ECMO as first choice
Haemodialysis
Atropine 3 mg IV
Methylene blue
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Dihydropyridine poisoning produces vasoplegic shock with preserved or hyperdynamic contractility. The consensus suggests methylene blue (inhibition of the NO–cGMP pathway) for refractory vasodilatory shock.

**Why not the others:**
- A – pacing helps bradycardia/AV block, but she is tachycardic.
- B – VA-ECMO supports the failing heart; it does little for isolated vasoplegia with a hyperdynamic ventricle.
- C – amlodipine is not dialysable (EXTRIP: against ECTR).
- D – atropine treats bradycardia, which is absent.

**Ref:** St-Onge M, Crit Care Med 2017; Wong A, Clin Toxicol 2021.

questions.stem: Regarding digoxin toxicity:
options: Digoxin is effectively removed by haemodialysis.
Hypokalaemia protects against digoxin toxicity.
A serum digoxin level taken 1 hour after an oral dose reliably reflects tissue toxicity.
After administration of Fab fragments, the total serum digoxin concentration falls immediately and should guide redosing.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Vd 5–7 L/kg; not dialysable.
- B (False) – hypokalaemia (and hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia) increases toxicity, especially in chronic poisoning.
- C (False) – levels must be drawn ≥ 6 h after the dose, after distribution.
- D (False) – total digoxin rises after Fab (bound complexes); only free digoxin is interpretable; redosing is clinical.

**Ref:** Chan BS, Clin Toxicol 2014.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman took 10 tablets of amitriptyline 25 mg (immediate-release, 60 kg) 6 hours ago. She has been alert throughout, with HR 92/min, BP 118/70 mmHg and serial ECGs showing QRS 84 ms and a normal aVR. What is the most appropriate disposition?
options: ICU admission for 24 hours of monitoring
Medically fit for psychiatric assessment
Prophylactic sodium bicarbonate infusion for 12 hours
Haemodialysis before discharge
Elective intubation because deterioration can be sudden
questions.expl:
**Why B:** She ingested ~ 4 mg/kg (< 10 mg/kg) of an immediate-release TCA and remains asymptomatic with a normal ECG 6 h after ingestion; serious toxicity is then very unlikely. She can proceed to psychiatric assessment.

**Why not the others:**
- A – prolonged ICU monitoring is not needed for asymptomatic patients with a normal ECG at 6 h.
- C – bicarbonate is given for QRS widening, arrhythmia or hypotension, not prophylactically.
- D – ECTR is not effective for TCA.
- E – intubation is indicated for falling GCS, seizures or instability, which are absent.

**Ref:** Boehnert MT, NEJM 1985; Liebelt EL, Ann Emerg Med 1995.

open.q: Outline a stepwise approach to a patient in shock after an overdose of a calcium-channel blocker.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **Assessment:** agent (DHP vs non-DHP), modified-release, time, co-ingestants (beta-blockers); ECG (bradycardia, AV block), glucose (hyperglycaemia = severity), lactate, K⁺, echocardiography to distinguish **cardiogenic vs vasoplegic** shock.
- **Decontamination:** charcoal with protected airway; WBI for large sustained-release ingestions in stable patients.
- **First line:** IV calcium (bolus ± infusion), fluids, atropine for bradycardia, **noradrenaline/adrenaline**, **HIET** 1 U/kg bolus + 1 U/kg/h with dextrose and K⁺ monitoring (early – onset 15–60 min).
- **Refractory:** escalate HIET to 10 U/kg/h, lipid emulsion, pacing for unstable bradycardia/AV block, **methylene blue** for vasoplegia, **VA-ECMO** for refractory cardiogenic shock or arrest.
- **Not useful:** ECTR (EXTRIP: against for amlodipine, diltiazem, verapamil).
- Monitor for delayed toxicity (12–24 h), non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (amlodipine), and hypoglycaemia/hypokalaemia when HIET is weaned.

title: W24 · D4 – Toxic alcohols, carbon monoxide and cyanide

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man is found confused 18 hours after drinking from a bottle in his garage. pH 7.08, HCO₃⁻ 6 mmol/L, anion gap 32 mmol/L, osmolal gap 38 mOsm/kg, ionised calcium 0.85 mmol/L, creatinine 290 µmol/L (normal previously); the urine contains needle-shaped crystals. Ethanol is undetectable. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Fomepizole alone and repeat the anion gap in 12 hours
Folinic acid and ethanol infusion only
Fomepizole plus intermittent haemodialysis, with thiamine and pyridoxine
Continuous kidney replacement therapy without an antidote
Urine alkalinisation to pH 8
questions.expl:
**Why C:** This is ethylene glycol poisoning (HAGMA, raised osmolal gap, hypocalcaemia, oxalate crystals, AKI). EXTRIP recommends ECTR for AKI and an anion gap > 27 mmol/L; intermittent HD is the preferred modality, combined with ADH blockade (fomepizole, dosed every 4 h during HD) and the cofactors thiamine and pyridoxine.

**Why not the others:**
- A – fomepizole stops further glycolate formation but does not remove accumulated glycolate; HD is indicated.
- B – folinic acid is the methanol cofactor; ethanol without HD is inadequate.
- D – CKRT is less efficient and is the second choice only if HD is unavailable; an antidote is still needed.
- E – alkalinisation enhances elimination of salicylates, not EG.

**Ref:** Ghannoum M, Crit Care 2023; Brent J, NEJM 1999.

questions.stem: Regarding ethylene glycol poisoning:
options: Glycolic acid is the main contributor to the metabolic acidosis.
Calcium oxalate deposition causes acute kidney injury and hypocalcaemia.
Thiamine and pyridoxine are recommended cofactors.
Folinic acid is the key cofactor to enhance elimination of the toxic metabolite.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – glycolate accumulates (glycolate → glyoxylate is rate-limiting) and causes the anion gap.
- B (True) – oxalate precipitates with calcium in renal tubules and tissues.
- C (True) – they divert glyoxylate to glycine and α-hydroxy-β-ketoadipate rather than oxalate.
- D (False) – folinic acid accelerates formate metabolism in methanol poisoning.

**Ref:** Ghannoum M, Crit Care 2023; Brent J, NEJM 1999.

questions.stem: During a methanol outbreak, a 38-year-old man presents with blurred vision 30 hours after drinking illicit spirits. GCS 14, pH 7.05, anion gap 30 mmol/L, serum methanol 900 mg/L. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Fomepizole, intermittent haemodialysis, folinic acid and sodium bicarbonate
Fomepizole alone, because haemodialysis also removes the antidote
Ethanol infusion alone until vision improves
Thiamine and pyridoxine with continuous haemofiltration
Observation – visual symptoms indicate irreversible damage, so treatment is futile
questions.expl:
**Why A:** New visual deficits, pH ≤ 7.15, anion gap > 24 mmol/L and methanol > 700 mg/L are all EXTRIP indications for ECTR; intermittent HD removes methanol and formate. Fomepizole (every 4 h during HD) stops further formate production, folinic acid enhances formate clearance, and bicarbonate corrects acidaemia.

**Why not the others:**
- B – fomepizole alone prolongs methanol half-life to ~ 50 h and does not remove formate; the dose is simply adjusted during HD.
- C – ethanol alone is inadequate in severe poisoning.
- D – thiamine/pyridoxine are EG cofactors; intermittent HD is preferred.
- E – vision may improve with prompt treatment; severe poisoning has a high mortality without HD.

**Ref:** Roberts DM, Crit Care Med 2015; Brent J, NEJM 2001.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman is found drowsy in a closed garage with the car engine running. She had transient loss of consciousness, now GCS 15 with headache; SpO₂ 99 % on air, venous COHb 28 %, ECG normal, troponin normal. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Reassure, because the oxygen saturation is normal
Low-flow oxygen 2 L/min to avoid hyperoxia
Discharge home once the headache resolves
Hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV
High-flow 100 % oxygen immediately and discussion with a hyperbaric centre
questions.expl:
**Why E:** 100 % O₂ shortens COHb half-life from ~ 4–5 h to ~ 60–90 min and is the standard of care. Loss of consciousness and COHb > 25 % are common criteria for considering HBO (ACEP 2025: may benefit selected patients, Level C), so contact the hyperbaric centre while giving normobaric O₂.

**Why not the others:**
- A – pulse oximetry cannot distinguish COHb from O₂Hb and is falsely normal.
- B – low-flow O₂ slows CO elimination.
- C – she needs O₂ for several hours, assessment for HBO and follow-up for delayed neurological sequelae.
- D – there is no smoke exposure or severe lactic acidosis to suggest cyanide.

**Ref:** ACEP, Ann Emerg Med 2025; Weaver LK, NEJM 2002.

questions.stem: Regarding the physiology of carbon monoxide poisoning:
options: CO shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the right.
Standard pulse oximetry overestimates oxygen saturation in CO poisoning.
The COHb concentration correlates closely with neurological outcome.
The elimination half-life of COHb while breathing 100 % normobaric oxygen is about 5 hours.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – CO shifts the curve to the left, impairing O₂ release to tissues.
- B (True) – two-wavelength oximeters read COHb as O₂Hb; co-oximetry is required.
- C (False) – COHb reflects exposure and time since exposure/O₂, not tissue injury; DNS occur even with modest levels.
- D (False) – ~ 4–5 h is the half-life on room air; on 100 % O₂ it is ~ 60–90 min, and ~ 20–30 min with HBO.

**Ref:** Weaver LK, NEJM 2002; ACEP, Ann Emerg Med 2025.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man is rescued from a house fire after 20 minutes. He is unconscious, BP 75/40 mmHg, lactate 14 mmol/L, COHb 18 %, central venous O₂ saturation 88 %. He is intubated and ventilated with FiO₂ 1.0. Which additional treatment is most appropriate now?
options: Sodium nitrite 300 mg IV
Hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV over 15 minutes
Dicobalt edetate 300 mg IV
Methylene blue 1 mg/kg IV
No antidote until the blood cyanide level is available
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Coma, shock, lactate > 10 mmol/L and a high venous saturation after smoke inhalation indicate cyanide poisoning (Baud 1991: lactate > 10 mmol/L had 87 % sensitivity and 94 % specificity). Hydroxocobalamin is first line, acts rapidly and does not impair O₂ carriage.

**Why not the others:**
- A – nitrites induce methaemoglobinaemia, which, with COHb, further reduces O₂ content.
- C – dicobalt edetate is very toxic if cyanide is absent and is reserved for confirmed severe poisoning.
- D – methylene blue treats methaemoglobinaemia and is not a cyanide antidote.
- E – cyanide levels take hours; empirical treatment is required.

**Ref:** Baud FJ, NEJM 1991; Borron SW, Ann Emerg Med 2007.

questions.stem: Regarding hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) for carbon monoxide poisoning:
options: In Weaver's 2002 trial, three HBO sessions within 24 hours reduced cognitive sequelae at 6 weeks.
In Annane's 2011 trials, two HBO sessions improved outcome compared with one in comatose patients.
The 2025 ACEP clinical policy gives a Level A recommendation for HBO in all patients with CO poisoning.
Delayed neurological sequelae may appear days to weeks after apparent recovery.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 25.0 vs 46.1 % (double-blind, n = 152), with benefit persisting at 12 months.
- B (False) – two sessions were associated with worse outcomes than one in comatose patients.
- C (False) – Level C: HBO may benefit selected symptomatic patients; normobaric O₂ is standard.
- D (True) – DNS (cognitive deficits, parkinsonism, mood change) occur 2–40 days after exposure.

**Ref:** Weaver LK, NEJM 2002; Annane D, Intensive Care Med 2011; ACEP, Ann Emerg Med 2025.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with smoke inhalation received hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV and is now in the ICU. All of the following are expected consequences of hydroxocobalamin EXCEPT:
options: Red discolouration of skin and urine
Interference with colorimetric laboratory assays
False blood-leak alarms on haemodialysis machines
Methaemoglobinaemia
Transient hypertension
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin; it does not oxidise haemoglobin. Methaemoglobinaemia is the intended effect of nitrites, which is why nitrites are avoided in fire victims with CO poisoning.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the red colour lasts days (skin) to weeks (urine).
- B – creatinine, bilirubin, magnesium and CO-oximetry results can be affected.
- C – red plasma triggers optical blood-leak detectors, which can stop dialysis.
- E – a transient rise in BP is common (NO scavenging).

**EDIC trap:** Hydroxocobalamin has also been associated with oxalate nephropathy and AKI after smoke inhalation.

**Ref:** Borron SW, Ann Emerg Med 2007.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is admitted drowsy after a suspected ingestion. Na⁺ 140 mmol/L, glucose 5 mmol/L, urea 5 mmol/L, measured serum osmolality 330 mOsm/kg; ethanol is undetectable. What is his osmolal gap?
options: 10 mOsm/kg
20 mOsm/kg
30 mOsm/kg
50 mOsm/kg
40 mOsm/kg
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Calculated osmolality = 2 × 140 + 5 + 5 = 290 mOsm/kg; gap = 330 − 290 = 40 mOsm/kg. This strongly suggests an unmeasured osmole such as methanol, ethylene glycol or isopropanol, and with a compatible history justifies ADH blockade.

**Why not the others:**
- A – a gap ≤ 10 is normal.
- B, C – arithmetic errors (e.g. forgetting to double Na⁺ correctly or adding urea twice).
- D – would require a measured osmolality of 340 mOsm/kg.

**EDIC trap:** Late presenters may have a normal osmolal gap with a high anion gap, as the parent alcohol has been metabolised.

**Ref:** Ghannoum M, Crit Care 2023; Roberts DM, Crit Care Med 2015.

questions.stem: Regarding the EXTRIP recommendations for ethylene glycol poisoning:
options: Extracorporeal treatment is recommended when the anion gap exceeds 27 mmol/L.
Intermittent haemodialysis is the preferred modality.
Fomepizole dosing frequency must be increased during haemodialysis.
Extracorporeal treatment can be stopped as soon as the EG concentration is below 25 mmol/L, regardless of the anion gap.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – or glycolate > 12 mmol/L; also coma, seizures or AKI.
- B (True) – CKRT is recommended only when intermittent HD is unavailable.
- C (True) – fomepizole is dialysed (e.g. every 4 h or continuous infusion during HD).
- D (False) – stopping is recommended when the anion gap is < 18 mmol/L and suggested when EG is < 4 mmol/L.

**Ref:** Ghannoum M, Crit Care 2023.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man drank a bottle of rubbing alcohol. He is drowsy but protecting his airway; BP 105/65 mmHg, pH 7.38, anion gap 12 mmol/L, osmolal gap 45 mOsm/kg, serum and urine ketones strongly positive, glucose 6 mmol/L, no urinary crystals. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Supportive care without fomepizole
Fomepizole and urgent haemodialysis
Ethanol infusion to a level of 1 g/L
Insulin–dextrose infusion for ketoacidosis
Folinic acid
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Isopropanol is metabolised by ADH to acetone, a ketone that is not an acid: the result is a raised osmolal gap with ketosis but no acidosis. Treatment is supportive; ADH blockade would only prolong the effect of the more sedating parent alcohol. HD is reserved for refractory hypotension or very high levels.

**Why not the others:**
- B – fomepizole is not indicated, and HD is not needed in a stable patient.
- C – ethanol blockade is not indicated and adds CNS depression.
- D – there is no acidosis or hyperglycaemia.
- E – folinic acid is for methanol.

**Ref:** Roberts DM, Crit Care Med 2015.

open.q: A patient presents with a severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis of unknown cause. How would you assess and treat a suspected toxic alcohol ingestion?
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **History:** source (antifreeze, windscreen fluid, illicit spirits), time, co-ingested ethanol (delays toxicity), visual symptoms.
- **Labs:** anion gap, **osmolal gap** (measured − [2 Na⁺ + glucose + urea], correct for ethanol), lactate (laboratory vs gas analyser – "lactate gap" in EG), calcium, creatinine, urine crystals, ketones, salicylate/paracetamol; methanol/EG levels if available.
- **Interpretation:** early high osmolal gap, late high anion gap; normal osmolal gap does not exclude.
- **Antidote:** fomepizole 15 mg/kg then 10 mg/kg q12h (q4h on HD) or ethanol 1–1.5 g/L when level > 20 mg/dL, or history + gap, or suspicion + acidosis.
- **Cofactors:** folinic acid (methanol), thiamine + pyridoxine (EG); bicarbonate for pH < 7.3.
- **ECTR (intermittent HD)** per EXTRIP: EG – AG > 27, glycolate > 12, coma, seizures, AKI, EG > 50 mmol/L; methanol – coma, seizures, visual loss, pH ≤ 7.15, AG > 24, levels > 500–700 mg/L; stop when AG < 18 (EG) or methanol < 200 mg/L.
- **Supportive care:** airway, seizures, hypocalcaemia only if symptomatic, ophthalmology review, KRT for AKI.

title: W24 · D5 – Extracorporeal removal of poisons (EXTRIP)

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman on long-term lithium for bipolar disorder was started on a thiazide 2 weeks ago. She has had diarrhoea for 3 days and is now drowsy (GCS 11) with coarse tremor and myoclonus. Creatinine 280 µmol/L (baseline 90), lithium 3.2 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate management in addition to stopping lithium and giving isotonic fluids?
options: Activated charcoal 50 g
Forced diuresis with furosemide
Observation – the level is below 4.0 mmol/L
Intermittent haemodialysis, with a repeat lithium level about 6 hours after the session
Urine alkalinisation
questions.expl:
**Why D:** EXTRIP recommends ECTR for decreased consciousness, seizures or life-threatening dysrhythmias irrespective of the lithium level, and for levels > 4.0 mmol/L with impaired kidney function. Chronic toxicity causes neurotoxicity at lower levels. Intermittent HD is preferred, and the level should be rechecked because of rebound from tissue stores.

**Why not the others:**
- A – charcoal does not bind lithium.
- B – diuretics worsen sodium/volume depletion and lithium retention.
- C – the level threshold applies only in the absence of severe neurotoxicity; her reduced consciousness is a stand-alone indication.
- E – alkalinisation does not increase lithium excretion meaningfully and adds sodium bicarbonate risks.

**Ref:** Decker BS, Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2015.

questions.stem: Regarding the properties that determine whether a poison is removed by haemodialysis:
options: A volume of distribution below about 1 L/kg favours removal.
Protein binding above 80 % favours removal by haemodialysis.
ECTR adds little when the endogenous clearance of the poison is already high.
Molecules larger than 5,000 Da cannot be removed by any extracorporeal technique.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – most of the drug must be in plasma to be accessible to the filter.
- B (False) – only unbound drug crosses the membrane; high protein binding prevents removal (unless binding saturates in overdose).
- C (True) – ECTR is useful when it substantially increases total clearance (e.g. > 4 mL/kg/min endogenous clearance argues against).
- D (False) – high-flux membranes remove molecules up to ~ 10–15 kDa, and haemoperfusion/plasma exchange remove larger or protein-bound compounds.

**Ref:** Lavergne V, Clin Toxicol 2012; Ghannoum M, Kidney Int 2018.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin 1 g twice daily presents with vomiting and AKI (creatinine 520 µmol/L). pH 6.92, lactate 22 mmol/L, BP 95/60 mmHg on low-dose noradrenaline. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Sodium bicarbonate infusion alone until pH > 7.2
Intermittent haemodialysis, continued until lactate < 3 mmol/L and pH > 7.35
Haemoperfusion with a charcoal cartridge
Insulin–dextrose infusion
Multiple-dose activated charcoal
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Metformin-associated lactic acidosis with lactate > 20 mmol/L and pH ≤ 7.0 meets EXTRIP recommended criteria. Metformin (MW 129 Da, negligible protein binding) is dialysable and HD also corrects acidosis and AKI; CKRT is the alternative if he cannot tolerate IHD.

**Why not the others:**
- A – bicarbonate alone does not remove metformin or treat the cause, and adds sodium and CO₂.
- C – haemoperfusion offers no advantage for a non-protein-bound drug and has more complications.
- D – insulin does not treat MALA.
- E – charcoal has no role in chronic accumulation.

**Ref:** Calello DP, Crit Care Med 2015.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man is admitted after a mixed overdose. EXTRIP recommends against extracorporeal treatment, or does not recommend it, for each of the following agents EXCEPT:
options: Amitriptyline
Digoxin
Verapamil
Propranolol
Valproic acid
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Valproate protein binding (90 %) saturates in overdose, so the free fraction becomes dialysable; ECTR is recommended for levels > 1,300 mg/L, cerebral oedema or shock.

**Why not the others:**
- A – TCA: large Vd, high protein binding – ECTR not recommended.
- B – digoxin: Vd 5–7 L/kg; Fab fragments are the treatment.
- C – EXTRIP recommends against ECTR for verapamil, diltiazem and amlodipine.
- D – EXTRIP recommends against ECTR for propranolol.

**Ref:** Ghannoum M, Clin Toxicol 2015; Wong A, Clin Toxicol 2021.

questions.stem: Regarding extracorporeal modalities in poisoning:
options: Intermittent haemodialysis is the preferred modality for most poisons in EXTRIP recommendations.
Lithium levels may rebound after intermittent haemodialysis because of redistribution from tissues.
Charcoal haemoperfusion can cause thrombocytopenia and hypocalcaemia.
Continuous kidney replacement therapy is an acceptable alternative when intermittent haemodialysis is unavailable.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – highest clearance for small water-soluble molecules, rapid correction of acidosis.
- B (True) – recheck levels ~ 6 h after the session; repeat HD or continue with CKRT.
- C (True) – also leucopenia, hypoglycaemia and hypothermia; HP has largely been replaced by high-flux HD.
- D (True) – lower clearance, but useful in unstable patients and to limit rebound.

**Ref:** Ghannoum M, Kidney Int 2018; Decker BS, Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2015.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman ingested a large amount of sodium valproate. She is comatose and ventilated; valproate concentration 1,500 mg/L, ammonia 210 µmol/L, pH 7.15, BP stable. What is the most appropriate management?
options: High-flux intermittent haemodialysis and intravenous L-carnitine
Urine alkalinisation
Charcoal haemoperfusion only after levels have fallen below 900 mg/L
Therapeutic plasma exchange
Supportive care only, because valproate is 90 % protein-bound
questions.expl:
**Why A:** A valproate level > 1,300 mg/L is an EXTRIP "recommended" criterion (coma requiring ventilation, hyperammonaemia and pH ≤ 7.10 are further suggested criteria). Protein binding saturates in overdose, making high-flux HD effective; L-carnitine treats valproate-induced hyperammonaemia.

**Why not the others:**
- B – alkalinisation does not meaningfully enhance valproate elimination.
- C – waiting is inappropriate; HD is preferred over HP.
- D – plasma exchange has low clearance and no advantage.
- E – protein binding falls in overdose, so ECTR is effective.

**Ref:** Ghannoum M, Clin Toxicol 2015.

questions.stem: Regarding lithium poisoning:
options: Lithium is not adsorbed by activated charcoal.
Chronic toxicity can cause severe neurotoxicity at lower serum levels than acute ingestion.
Thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs can increase lithium concentrations.
Lithium is highly protein-bound, which limits its removal by haemodialysis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – metal ions are not adsorbed; WBI is an option for large sustained-release ingestions.
- B (True) – in chronic toxicity tissue (brain) concentrations are already high; in acute ingestion the level may be very high with little early neurotoxicity.
- C (True) – they reduce renal lithium clearance.
- D (False) – lithium is not protein-bound; MW 7 Da and Vd ~ 0.7 L/kg make it highly dialysable.

**Ref:** Decker BS, Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2015.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with asthma ingested sustained-release theophylline 5 hours ago. She has had two generalised seizures, HR 160/min with frequent ventricular ectopics, and K⁺ 2.6 mmol/L; theophylline concentration is 120 mg/L. What is the most appropriate elimination strategy?
options: Multiple-dose activated charcoal alone
Urine alkalinisation
Intermittent haemodialysis, with multiple-dose activated charcoal if tolerated
Phenytoin and observation
Continuous venovenous haemofiltration at low effluent dose
questions.expl:
**Why C:** EXTRIP recommends ECTR for acute theophylline levels > 100 mg/L, seizures, life-threatening dysrhythmias or shock. Intermittent HD is preferred (haemoperfusion if unavailable), and MDAC can be continued as it interrupts enteral recirculation.

**Why not the others:**
- A – MDAC alone is insufficient with seizures and a level > 100 mg/L.
- B – alkalinisation does not enhance theophylline elimination.
- D – phenytoin is ineffective for theophylline seizures (benzodiazepines, then barbiturates/propofol).
- E – low-dose CKRT provides far lower clearance than IHD.

**Ref:** Ghannoum M, Clin Toxicol 2015 (theophylline).

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is ventilated on day 2 after a large carbamazepine overdose. He remains comatose with intermittent broad-complex tachycardia; carbamazepine concentrations are rising despite multiple-dose activated charcoal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Urine alkalinisation
Forced diuresis
Therapeutic plasma exchange
Stop charcoal and wait for spontaneous elimination
Intermittent haemodialysis while continuing multiple-dose activated charcoal
questions.expl:
**Why E:** EXTRIP recommends ECTR for life-threatening dysrhythmias and refractory seizures, and suggests it for prolonged coma or rising concentrations despite MDAC. High-flux intermittent HD is preferred (carbamazepine is ~ 75 % protein-bound, and binding saturates at high levels), with MDAC continued.

**Why not the others:**
- A – alkalinisation has no effect on carbamazepine.
- B – forced diuresis is obsolete and not effective.
- C – plasma exchange has a lower clearance than high-flux HD.
- D – rising levels (delayed absorption, bezoar) and arrhythmias require active elimination.

**Ref:** Ghannoum M, Clin Toxicol 2014.

questions.stem: Regarding the EXTRIP workgroup and its recommendations:
options: A grade "1" recommendation denotes a strong recommendation ("we recommend").
Most EXTRIP recommendations are based on high-quality randomised controlled trials.
ECMO is classified as an extracorporeal treatment for poison removal.
ECTR is never indicated in phenobarbital poisoning because multiple-dose activated charcoal is always sufficient.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – "2" = weak ("suggest"), "3" = neutral; quality A–D.
- B (False) – evidence is mostly case reports, series and toxicokinetic data; most grades are 1D/2D.
- C (False) – ECMO supports the circulation and oxygenation; it does not remove the poison.
- D (False) – ECTR is recommended in severe long-acting barbiturate poisoning (prolonged coma, ventilation, shock, rising levels despite MDAC).

**Ref:** Lavergne V, Clin Toxicol 2012; Mactier R, Am J Kidney Dis 2014.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man with methanol poisoning (methanol 800 mg/L, pH 7.10) is started on intermittent haemodialysis. He received a fomepizole loading dose of 15 mg/kg 2 hours earlier. How should fomepizole be continued during haemodialysis?
options: Stop fomepizole – haemodialysis alone is sufficient
Continue 10 mg/kg every 12 hours unchanged
Give fomepizole every 4 hours (or as a continuous infusion) during dialysis
Switch to oral ethanol at a fixed dose without monitoring
Double the loading dose and give no maintenance doses
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Fomepizole is a small, dialysable molecule; during HD it is given every 4 h (or by continuous infusion ~ 1–1.5 mg/kg/h) to maintain ADH blockade, with the usual schedule resumed after dialysis.

**Why not the others:**
- A – without ADH blockade, residual methanol continues to be converted to formate, especially between sessions.
- B – a 12-hourly schedule leads to subtherapeutic concentrations during HD.
- D – ethanol is also dialysed and requires an increased, monitored infusion.
- E – a single large dose does not maintain blockade over the course of treatment.

**Ref:** Roberts DM, Crit Care Med 2015; Ghannoum M, Crit Care 2023.

open.q: Explain the principles used to decide whether a poisoned patient should receive extracorporeal treatment, and give examples of poisons for and against.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- **Toxicokinetics:** small MW (< 500 Da conventional, ≤ 10–15 kDa high-flux), low protein binding (< 80 %, or saturable in overdose), low Vd (< 1 L/kg), low endogenous clearance, single-compartment kinetics.
- **Clinical:** severe toxicity or predicted severe toxicity (levels, clinical features), impaired elimination organ (AKI), no effective antidote, benefit outweighing risks (catheter, anticoagulation, hypotension, antidote removal).
- **EXTRIP framework:** systematic reviews + Delphi; recommendations 1/2/3 or against, evidence A–D (mostly D).
- **Modality:** intermittent high-flux HD preferred; CKRT if unavailable/unstable; HP for protein-bound drugs where available; TPE rarely; monitor rebound and adjust antidotes.
- **For:** lithium, metformin, salicylates, methanol, ethylene glycol, valproate, theophylline, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, thallium (paracetamol rarely; atenolol/sotalol only with renal impairment).
- **Against:** TCA, digoxin, amlodipine/diltiazem/verapamil, propranolol – use antidotes and ECMO.
- **Stopping criteria** are poison-specific (e.g. lithium < 1.0 mmol/L, metformin lactate < 3 mmol/L and pH > 7.35, EG anion gap < 18).

title: W24 · Saturday – weekly review: Toxicology (toxidromes and general approach, paracetamol and salicylates, cardiotoxic drugs, toxic alcohols, CO and cyanide, extracorporeal removal)

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man ingested 30 tablets of sustained-release lithium carbonate 400 mg 2 hours ago. He is alert, haemodynamically stable, with normal bowel sounds and renal function. Which gastrointestinal decontamination is most appropriate?
options: Activated charcoal 50 g
Whole-bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol
Gastric lavage
Syrup of ipecac
Multiple-dose activated charcoal
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Lithium is not adsorbed by charcoal, and sustained-release preparations continue to be absorbed for hours. Whole-bowel irrigation (PEG 1.5–2 L/h) is indicated for metals (iron, lithium) and modified-release drugs in a stable patient with a protected airway and a functioning gut.

**Why not the others:**
- A – charcoal does not bind lithium.
- C – lavage is not routine and is ineffective for large sustained-release tablets.
- D – ipecac is obsolete.
- E – MDAC is for carbamazepine, dapsone, phenobarbital, quinine and theophylline, not lithium.

**Ref:** Thanacoody R, Clin Toxicol 2015; Chyka PA, Clin Toxicol 2005. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: Regarding antidotes:
options: Methylene blue is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.
Pyridoxine is the antidote for isoniazid-induced seizures.
Octreotide is used to reverse opioid-induced respiratory depression.
Flumazenil should be given routinely to comatose patients with an unknown mixed overdose.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – it can cause haemolysis and is ineffective without NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway.
- B (True) – about 1 g per g of isoniazid ingested (max 5 g), as isoniazid depletes GABA via pyridoxine antagonism.
- C (False) – octreotide prevents recurrent hypoglycaemia in sulfonylurea poisoning; naloxone reverses opioids.
- D (False) – flumazenil can precipitate seizures and arrhythmias in benzodiazepine-dependent patients or with co-ingested TCA.

**Ref:** Boyer EW, NEJM 2005; Chyka PA, Clin Toxicol 2005. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after drinking alcohol and taking GHB at a party. GCS 7 (E1 V2 M4), RR 12/min, SpO₂ 97 % on air, BP 115/70 mmHg, no vomiting, ECG normal; no cardiotoxic drug is suspected. Based on the NICO trial, what is the most appropriate airway strategy?
options: Immediate rapid sequence intubation because GCS is below 9
Flumazenil to avoid intubation
Gastric lavage after insertion of an oropharyngeal airway
Close monitoring in the lateral position, with intubation only if emergency criteria develop
Non-invasive ventilation
questions.expl:
**Why D:** In NICO (GCS < 9, acute poisoning), withholding intubation unless emergency criteria developed (seizure, vomiting, respiratory distress, hypoxaemia, shock) reduced intubation (16 vs 58 %), pneumonia (7 vs 15 %) and ICU stay, with no deaths. GHB coma typically resolves within hours.

**Why not the others:**
- A – GCS alone is a poor marker of airway risk in poisoning.
- B – flumazenil does not reverse GHB or alcohol and risks seizures.
- C – lavage is not indicated and is dangerous in a comatose patient.
- E – NIV is inappropriate in a comatose patient with an unprotected airway and she is not hypoxaemic.

**Ref:** Freund Y (NICO), JAMA 2023. → [D1](D1.md)

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man is found drowsy at home with empty paracetamol packets; the time of ingestion is unknown. Paracetamol concentration is 60 mg/L, ALT 45 U/L (normal < 40), INR 1.1. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Discharge, because the level is below the treatment line at 4 hours
Repeat the level in 4 hours and decide then
Activated charcoal only
Plot the level assuming ingestion occurred 4 hours earlier
Start intravenous acetylcysteine now
questions.expl:
**Why E:** With an unknown time of ingestion the nomogram cannot be used; a detectable paracetamol concentration (and here a slightly raised ALT) after an overdose of unknown timing mandates NAC, with reassessment of paracetamol, ALT and INR at the end of the regimen.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the level cannot be interpreted without a known time of ingestion.
- B – delay reduces NAC efficacy if ingestion was > 8 h ago.
- C – charcoal is of no proven benefit beyond 1–4 h and does not replace NAC.
- D – assumptions about timing are unsafe.

**Ref:** Dart RC, JAMA Netw Open 2023; Chiew AL, Med J Aust 2020. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: Regarding salicylate poisoning:
options: Small volumes of methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen) can be lethal.
CNS glucose may be low despite normal blood glucose concentrations.
Serial salicylate levels are needed because absorption may be delayed.
EXTRIP recommends stopping haemodialysis once the salicylate concentration falls below 5.8 mmol/L (80 mg/dL).
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 1 teaspoon (5 mL) contains about 7 g of salicylate equivalent.
- B (True) – neuroglycopenia; give glucose to patients with altered mental status.
- C (True) – enteric-coated tablets and bezoars delay the peak; repeat every 2–4 h until falling.
- D (False) – stop when clinically improved and salicylate < 1.4 mmol/L (19 mg/dL), or after 4–6 h if levels are unavailable.

**Ref:** Juurlink DN, Ann Emerg Med 2015. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with asthma develops flushing, urticaria and mild wheeze 30 minutes into the first bag of intravenous acetylcysteine for a paracetamol overdose above the treatment line. BP 120/75 mmHg, SpO₂ 96 %. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Stop acetylcysteine permanently and switch to oral methionine
Give adrenaline 0.5 mg IM and stop all further acetylcysteine
Pause the infusion, give an antihistamine (± bronchodilator) and restart at a slower rate
Continue at the same rate – the reaction is harmless
Switch to fomepizole
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Anaphylactoid reactions to NAC are non-IgE, rate- and concentration-dependent and most frequent during the loading phase, particularly in asthmatics. Treat symptomatically and restart, because the patient still needs NAC; slower regimens (SNAP 12 h: 5 vs 28 % reactions) reduce the risk.

**Why not the others:**
- A – stopping NAC exposes her to hepatotoxicity; methionine is inferior and not suitable here.
- B – IM adrenaline is reserved for life-threatening anaphylaxis with hypotension or severe bronchospasm; NAC need not be abandoned.
- D – symptoms should be treated and the infusion slowed.
- E – fomepizole is not a substitute for NAC.

**Ref:** Bateman DN (SNAP), Lancet 2014; Dart RC, JAMA Netw Open 2023. → [D2](D2.md)

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man with an amitriptyline overdose develops a generalised tonic–clonic seizure in the emergency department. QRS 118 ms, BP 100/60 mmHg. Which is the most appropriate first-line anticonvulsant?
options: Intravenous benzodiazepine (e.g. lorazepam or midazolam)
Phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV
Physostigmine 2 mg IV
Flumazenil 0.5 mg IV
Carbamazepine via nasogastric tube
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Benzodiazepines are first-line for toxic seizures; propofol or barbiturates follow. Seizures produce acidosis, which worsens sodium-channel blockade, so the QRS widening should also be treated with sodium bicarbonate.

**Why not the others:**
- B – phenytoin is a sodium-channel blocker, ineffective in toxic seizures and may worsen cardiotoxicity.
- C – physostigmine may cause bradyasystole in TCA poisoning.
- D – flumazenil lowers the seizure threshold.
- E – carbamazepine is itself a sodium-channel blocker and not an acute treatment.

**Ref:** Boehnert MT, NEJM 1985; Yates C, Semin Dial 2014. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: Regarding calcium-channel blocker poisoning:
options: Verapamil and diltiazem typically cause bradycardia and AV block.
Hypoglycaemia is a characteristic early finding.
Amlodipine poisoning may be complicated by non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
Delayed toxicity is unlikely with sustained-release preparations if the patient is asymptomatic 2 hours after ingestion.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – non-dihydropyridines act on the SA and AV nodes and depress contractility.
- B (False) – hyperglycaemia (β-cell L-type channel block) is typical and correlates with severity.
- C (True) – capillary leak after dihydropyridine overdose.
- D (False) – toxicity may be delayed 12–24 h with sustained-release preparations; prolonged monitoring is required.

**Ref:** St-Onge M, Crit Care Med 2017. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman on digoxin is admitted to the ICU. Digoxin-specific Fab fragments are indicated in each of the following situations EXCEPT:
options: Ventricular tachycardia attributed to digoxin
Serum K⁺ of 6.3 mmol/L after an acute digoxin overdose
High-grade AV block with hypotension attributed to digoxin
An asymptomatic patient on therapeutic digoxin with "reverse tick" ST depression on the ECG
Digoxin toxicity with signs of end-organ hypoperfusion
questions.expl:
**Why D:** "Reverse tick" (sagging) ST depression reflects digoxin effect at therapeutic levels, not toxicity; it requires no antidote.

**Why not the others:**
- A – life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias are a key indication.
- B – hyperkalaemia > 5–6 mmol/L in acute poisoning predicts mortality and is an indication.
- C – haemodynamically significant bradyarrhythmias are an indication.
- E – end-organ hypoperfusion due to toxicity is an indication.

**Ref:** Chan BS, Clin Toxicol 2014. → [D3](D3.md)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presents 24 hours after drinking homemade spirits with blurred "snowstorm" vision, pH 7.12 and an anion gap of 28 mmol/L. MRI shows bilateral putaminal lesions. Besides fomepizole and haemodialysis, which cofactor should be given?
options: Thiamine and pyridoxine
Folinic acid
N-acetylcysteine
Vitamin K
Hydroxocobalamin
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Visual disturbance and putaminal necrosis are characteristic of methanol poisoning (formate toxicity). Folinic acid (1 mg/kg, max 50 mg, every 4–6 h) accelerates the folate-dependent oxidation of formate to CO₂.

**Why not the others:**
- A – thiamine and pyridoxine are the cofactors for ethylene glycol.
- C – NAC is the paracetamol antidote.
- D – vitamin K is for coumarin anticoagulants.
- E – hydroxocobalamin is the cyanide antidote.

**Ref:** Roberts DM, Crit Care Med 2015; Brent J, NEJM 2001. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: Regarding carbon monoxide and cyanide poisoning:
options: Hyperbaric oxygen is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.
Fetal carboxyhaemoglobin may exceed the maternal level.
A normal PaO₂ excludes tissue hypoxia in CO poisoning.
Sodium nitrite is the preferred cyanide antidote in fire victims.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – pregnancy is a common indication for considering HBO because of fetal vulnerability.
- B (True) – fetal Hb has higher affinity for CO, and fetal COHb peaks later and higher.
- C (False) – PaO₂ reflects dissolved O₂; O₂ content and delivery are reduced by COHb and the left-shifted curve.
- D (False) – nitrites induce methaemoglobinaemia, which compounds CO-related hypoxia; hydroxocobalamin is preferred.

**Ref:** Weaver LK, NEJM 2002; ACEP, Ann Emerg Med 2025; Borron SW, Ann Emerg Med 2007. → [D4](D4.md)
