questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is admitted confused with Kussmaul breathing. A point-of-care blood gas shows pH 7.10 and lactate 14 mmol/L, but the central laboratory lactate on a simultaneous sample is 2.5 mmol/L. Which poison is most likely?
options: Methanol
Metformin
Cyanide
Salicylate
Ethylene glycol
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Glycolate, the main acidic metabolite of ethylene glycol, is misread as lactate by some point-of-care analysers (lactate oxidase methods), producing a "lactate gap" between gas-analyser and laboratory results.

**Why not the others:**
- A – methanol causes formate accumulation, without this assay interference.
- B – metformin causes true lactic acidosis on both analysers.
- C – cyanide causes true lactic acidosis.
- D – salicylates cause a mixed disorder with a modest true lactate rise.

**Ref:** Ghannoum M, Crit Care 2023. → [D4](D4.md)

questions.stem: Regarding EXTRIP recommendations:
options: In metformin poisoning, ECTR is continued until lactate is below 3 mmol/L and pH above 7.35.
In valproate poisoning with hyperammonaemia, L-carnitine is given alongside ECTR.
For atenolol poisoning, ECTR is suggested when kidney function is impaired.
Continuous kidney replacement therapy is preferred over intermittent haemodialysis for lithium poisoning in a haemodynamically stable patient.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – stopping criteria in the metformin recommendation.
- B (True) – L-carnitine treats valproate-induced hyperammonaemia and hepatotoxicity.
- C (True) – with refractory bradycardia/hypotension (and recurrent torsade for sotalol).
- D (False) – intermittent HD is preferred; CKRT is an acceptable alternative when IHD is unavailable.

**Ref:** Calello DP, Crit Care Med 2015; Ghannoum M, Clin Toxicol 2015; Bouchard J, Crit Care 2021; Decker BS, Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2015. → [D5](D5.md)

questions.stem: When deciding whether haemodialysis will enhance elimination of a poison, each of the following properties favours removal EXCEPT:
options: Volume of distribution below 1 L/kg
Protein binding below 80 %
High endogenous (hepatic and renal) clearance
Molecular weight below 500 Da
Rapid equilibration between tissue and plasma (single-compartment kinetics)
questions.expl:
**Why C:** If the body already clears the poison efficiently, ECTR adds little to total clearance; ECTR is most useful when endogenous clearance is low (e.g. lithium in AKI, methanol under fomepizole).

**Why not the others:**
- A – a small Vd means most of the drug is in plasma, accessible to the filter.
- B – only unbound drug crosses the membrane.
- D – small molecules diffuse readily across dialysis membranes.
- E – rapid equilibration limits rebound and allows efficient removal.

**Ref:** Lavergne V, Clin Toxicol 2012; Ghannoum M, Kidney Int 2018. → [D5](D5.md)

questions.stem: Regarding extracorporeal treatment in poisoning:
options: Antidotes such as fomepizole and acetylcysteine are removed by haemodialysis, requiring dose adjustment.
Haemodialysis corrects the metabolic acidosis as well as removing metformin.
Lithium concentrations may rebound after a session of intermittent haemodialysis.
Most EXTRIP recommendations are based on very low quality evidence.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – e.g. fomepizole every 4 h during HD; increase NAC dosing during ECTR.
- B (True) – bicarbonate-buffered dialysate corrects acidaemia, an added benefit in MALA.
- C (True) – redistribution from tissue stores; recheck ~ 6 h after the session.
- D (True) – mostly 1D/2D grades based on case series and toxicokinetics.

**Ref:** Lavergne V, Clin Toxicol 2012; Calello DP, Crit Care Med 2015; Decker BS, Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2015. → [D5](D5.md)

title: Case-style practice · W01-D1 · Sepsis-3, SOFA and SOFA-2

questions.stem: Five patients have received adequate fluid resuscitation. Which one meets the Sepsis-3 criteria for septic shock?
options: Acute cholangitis; MAP 58 mmHg after 30 mL/kg crystalloid, noradrenaline 0.12 µg/kg/min started, MAP now 67 mmHg, lactate 2.9 mmol/L
Pneumonia; noradrenaline 0.08 µg/kg/min needed to keep MAP 66 mmHg, lactate 1.5 mmol/L
Faecal peritonitis; MAP 72 mmHg without vasopressors, lactate 4.6 mmol/L
Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm; noradrenaline 0.3 µg/kg/min, lactate 6.0 mmol/L
Pyelonephritis; SBP 88 mmHg on arrival, MAP 75 mmHg after 1 L crystalloid, lactate 2.4 mmol/L
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Cholangitis is an infection with organ dysfunction (sepsis). Despite 30 mL/kg crystalloid he needs noradrenaline to keep MAP ≥ 65 mmHg **and** his lactate is > 2 mmol/L – both Sepsis-3 criteria for septic shock are met.

**Why not the others:**
- B – Vasopressor-dependent, but lactate 1.5 mmol/L is ≤ 2: sepsis with hypotension, not septic shock.
- C – Hyperlactataemia, but MAP is maintained without any vasopressor.
- D – Haemorrhagic shock from aneurysm rupture; there is no infection, so it is not sepsis.
- E – Hypotension corrected with fluids alone; there is no vasopressor requirement.

**EDIC trap:** Hyperlactataemia alone, or a vasopressor alone, is not septic shock.

**Ref:** Singer M, et al. Sepsis-3. *JAMA* 2016;315:801–810.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old nursing-home resident on the ward has fever, new confusion, RR 24/min, SBP 104 mmHg and SpO₂ 93 % on air. Regarding screening and the diagnosis of sepsis:
options: Her qSOFA score is 2.
SSC 2026 recommends qSOFA rather than NEWS/NEWS2 as the single screening tool for sepsis.
Had her qSOFA been < 2, sepsis would have been excluded.
If her baseline SOFA is unknown and she has no known pre-existing organ dysfunction, the baseline is assumed to be 0.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – RR ≥ 22 (1) + altered mentation (1); SBP ≤ 100 is not met (0) → qSOFA 2.
- B (False) – SSC 2026 recommends **against** qSOFA as a single screening tool compared with NEWS/NEWS2, MEWS or SIRS (strong, moderate certainty).
- C (False) – qSOFA is prognostic, not diagnostic; a low score does not rule sepsis out.
- D (True) – Sepsis-3 convention – sepsis = acute rise in SOFA ≥ 2 attributable to infection.

**EDIC trap:** qSOFA predicts poor outcome; it neither defines nor excludes sepsis.

**Ref:** Singer M, et al. Sepsis-3. *JAMA* 2016; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with septic shock is on noradrenaline 0.3 µg/kg/min plus vasopressin, invasive ventilation with P/F 140 mmHg, continuous RRT and platelets 70 × 10⁹/L. Scoring him with SOFA-2 (JAMA 2025):
options: His kidney score is 4 because he is receiving RRT.
Platelets of 70 × 10⁹/L give the maximum haemostasis score of 4.
SOFA-2 adds a sixth, gastrointestinal organ system.
In the cardiovascular system, noradrenaline 0.3 µg/kg/min plus a second vasopressor scores higher than noradrenaline 0.3 µg/kg/min alone.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Receiving (or meeting criteria for) RRT = 4 kidney points.
- B (False) – SOFA-2 platelet cut-offs are 150 / 100 / 80 / 50; 4 points only at ≤ 50 × 10⁹/L, so 70 scores 3.
- C (False) – SOFA-2 keeps 6 systems – brain, respiratory, cardiovascular, liver, kidney, haemostasis; GI and immune dysfunction were not included.
- D (True) – Combined NA + adrenaline 0.2–0.4 µg/kg/min = 3; any other vasopressor or inotrope adds a level (→ 4).

**EDIC trap:** SOFA-2 has the same 6 systems with new names and modern organ support – no GI system.

**Ref:** Ranzani OT, et al. SOFA-2. *JAMA* 2025.

title: Case-style practice · W01-D2 · Initial septic shock resuscitation

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman arrives in the emergency department with obstructive pyelonephritis. BP 78/42 mmHg (MAP 54), HR 124/min, capillary refill time 5 s, lactate 5.1 mmol/L. Regarding her initial management according to the Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026:
options: A balanced crystalloid is suggested in preference to 0.9 % saline for the initial fluid resuscitation.

After the initial fluid, the decision to give more should be guided by dynamic measures (e.g. passive leg raising with stroke-volume measurement) and capillary refill time rather than by a CVP target of 8–12 mmHg.
Antimicrobials may reasonably be delayed until two sets of blood cultures have been obtained, even if this takes 90 minutes.
Noradrenaline should not be started until a central venous catheter has been inserted.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – SSC 2026 suggests balanced crystalloids over 0.9 % saline (conditional, moderate certainty); the exception is TBI.
- B (True) – Static CVP targets came from early goal-directed therapy, which ProCESS, ARISE and ProMISe did not support; dynamic measures and capillary refill time (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK) are suggested to guide further fluid.
- C (False) – In possible septic shock antimicrobials are recommended immediately, ideally within 1 h; cultures are drawn first only if this causes no substantial delay.
- D (False) – Noradrenaline may be started peripherally rather than delaying for central access (conditional, very low certainty).

**EDIC trap:** "CVP 8–12 mmHg" is an outdated EGDT target.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026; PRISM investigators. *N Engl J Med* 2017;376:2223–2234.

title: Case-style practice · W01-D3 · Resuscitation fluids and early vasopressors

questions.stem: Concerning landmark trials of resuscitation fluids in critically ill adults:
options: In ALBIOS, giving 20 % albumin to keep serum albumin ≥ 30 g/L reduced 90-day mortality in severe sepsis.
In 6S, hydroxyethyl starch 130/0.42 increased 90-day mortality and the need for renal replacement therapy compared with Ringer's acetate in severe sepsis.
In CLASSIC, restricting IV fluid after initial resuscitation of septic shock reduced 90-day mortality.
In the traumatic brain injury subgroup of SAFE, 4 % albumin was associated with higher mortality than saline.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – ALBIOS showed no difference in 28- or 90-day mortality (only a post-hoc signal in septic shock).
- B (True) – 6S: more deaths and more RRT with HES 130/0.42 than with Ringer's acetate; HES licences were suspended in the EU in 2022.
- C (False) – CLASSIC: no mortality difference (42.3 % vs 42.1 %); SSC 2026 therefore suggests either a liberal or a restrictive approach after the initial 30 mL/kg.
- D (True) – SAFE-TBI: higher 24-month mortality with 4 % albumin, probably via raised ICP.

**Ref:** Caironi P, et al. ALBIOS. *N Engl J Med* 2014;370:1412–1421; Perner A, et al. 6S. *N Engl J Med* 2012;367:124–134; Meyhoff TS, et al. CLASSIC. *N Engl J Med* 2022;386:2459–2470; SAFE Study Investigators. *N Engl J Med* 2007;357:874–884.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman (60 kg) with pyelonephritis has received 2 L of balanced crystalloid over 90 minutes. MAP is 56 mmHg, HR 128/min, capillary refill time 5 s and lactate 4.6 mmol/L. A passive leg raising test increases stroke volume by only 4 %. Antibiotics were given within the first hour. A central venous catheter is not yet in place. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: A further 1000 mL of 0.9 % saline over 30 minutes
Start noradrenaline through a well-sited large peripheral cannula now
Wait for ultrasound-guided central venous access before starting any vasopressor
Give 400 mL of 20 % albumin
Start dobutamine 5 µg/kg/min
questions.expl:
**Why B:** She has received > 30 mL/kg, remains hypotensive with hypoperfusion, and a PLR rise in SV of only 4 % (< 10 %) shows she is unlikely to respond to more fluid. SSC 2026 recommends noradrenaline first line and suggests starting it peripherally rather than delaying for a central line (large proximal vein, extravasation checks, switch to central access if prolonged).

**Why not the others:**

- A – More saline is unlikely to raise SV in a fluid non-responder and adds chloride and oedema.
- C – Waiting for central access needlessly prolongs hypotension.
- D – Albumin is only suggested after large crystalloid volumes and would not help a fluid non-responder.
- E – Dobutamine is for proven cardiac dysfunction with hypoperfusion despite adequate MAP.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026; Monnet X, et al. *Crit Care* 2015;19:18.

title: Case-style practice · W01-D4 · Vasopressors in septic shock

questions.stem: Regarding vasopressin in adult septic shock:
options: Its vasoconstrictor effect is relatively preserved in acidaemia, unlike that of catecholamines.
Its pressor effect is mediated mainly by V2 receptors in the renal collecting duct.
SSC 2026 suggests titrating vasopressin upwards like noradrenaline, to doses of about 0.1 U/min.
In VANISH, early vasopressin significantly increased kidney failure–free days compared with noradrenaline.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – V1a signalling (Gq → IP3 → Ca²⁺, plus K-ATP channel inhibition) is less affected by acidosis than adrenergic receptors – one rationale for its catecholamine-sparing role.
- B (False) – V2 receptors mediate antidiuresis; vasoconstriction is via **V1a** receptors.
- C (False) – Vasopressin is added at a fixed dose, usually up to 0.03 U/min (sometimes 0.04); higher doses cause digital, mesenteric and myocardial ischaemia. SSC 2026 suggests adding it when noradrenaline requirements escalate.
- D (False) – VANISH found no difference in kidney failure–free days; less RRT use with vasopressin was a secondary finding.

**Ref:** Gordon AC, et al. VANISH. *JAMA* 2016;316:509–518; Russell JA, et al. VASST. *N Engl J Med* 2008;358:877–887; Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with severe community-acquired pneumonia has received 40 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid and appropriate antibiotics. MAP is 57 mmHg, HR 118/min, lactate 3.8 mmol/L. Bedside echocardiography shows a small, hyperdynamic left ventricle with a collapsible IVC variation that has disappeared after the fluid. Which is the most appropriate initial vasopressor strategy?
options: Noradrenaline titrated to a MAP of 65 mmHg
Dopamine titrated to a MAP of 65 mmHg
Vasopressin monotherapy at 0.03 U/min
Phenylephrine titrated to a MAP of 80 mmHg
Adrenaline titrated to a MAP of 80 mmHg
questions.expl:
**Why A:** SSC 2026 recommends noradrenaline as the first-line vasopressor, with an initial MAP target of 65 mmHg (strong; 60–65 mmHg suggested if ≥ 65 years). He is 52, adequately filled (IVC no longer collapsible) and vasoplegic with a hyperdynamic LV.

**Why not the others:**

- B – Dopamine causes more arrhythmias than noradrenaline (SOAP II) and is recommended against.
- C – Vasopressin is an add-on when noradrenaline requirements escalate, not monotherapy.
- D – Phenylephrine is not a recommended agent, and 80 mmHg gave no survival benefit in SEPSISPAM.
- E – Adrenaline is a second agent (raises lactate, tachycardia), and the 80 mmHg target is too high.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026; De Backer D, et al. SOAP II. *N Engl J Med* 2010;362:779–789; Asfar P, et al. SEPSISPAM. *N Engl J Med* 2014;370:1583–1593.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman with acute cholangitis has received 35 mL/kg of crystalloid and piperacillin–tazobactam. MAP remains 55 mmHg, CVP 13 mmHg, ScvO2 62 %, haemoglobin 82 g/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L. An ERCP slot is available in 2 hours. Her capillary refill time is 4 s and urine output 0.2 mL/kg/h. Each of the following is appropriate EXCEPT:
options: Starting noradrenaline with an initial MAP target of 60–65 mmHg
Arranging biliary decompression as soon as she is stabilised enough to travel
Transfusing red cells to a haemoglobin above 100 g/L to raise ScvO2 above 70 %
Inserting an arterial line for continuous blood pressure monitoring
Reassessing perfusion with capillary refill time and serial lactate
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Transfusion to a haematocrit > 30 % (and dobutamine) to reach ScvO2 ≥ 70 % were elements of early goal-directed therapy; ProCESS, ARISE and ProMISe found no benefit. TRISS showed a threshold of 70 g/L is as safe as 90 g/L in septic shock, and SSC recommends a restrictive transfusion strategy – so this is the inappropriate action.

**Why the others are appropriate:**

- A – Noradrenaline with an initial MAP target of 60–65 mmHg is suggested for age ≥ 65 years.
- B – Timely biliary decompression is source control, ideally within 6 h.
- D – An arterial line is reasonable once vasopressors are needed and doses may escalate.
- E – Capillary refill time and serial lactate are the suggested perfusion markers.

**Ref:** Holst LB, et al. TRISS. *N Engl J Med* 2014;371:1381–1391; PRISM investigators. *N Engl J Med* 2017;376:2223–2234; Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026.

title: Case-style practice · W01-D5 · Corticosteroids and adjuncts in septic shock

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with faecal peritonitis has had source control. Despite adequate fluids she has needed noradrenaline 0.35 µg/kg/min for 5 hours to keep MAP 66 mmHg. Regarding corticosteroids:
options: Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day is indicated.
A short Synacthen (ACTH) test should be done first to select patients who will benefit.
In APROCCHSS, hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone reduced 90-day mortality.
In ADRENAL, hydrocortisone reduced 90-day mortality.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – SSC: septic shock with NA/adrenaline ≥ 0.25 µg/kg/min for ≥ 4 h → IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day.
- B (False) – No ACTH test – it does not identify responders.
- C (True) – APROCCHSS (with fludrocortisone 50 µg) – lower 90-day mortality.
- D (False) – ADRENAL – no mortality difference, but faster shock resolution and shorter ventilation.

**EDIC trap:** ADRENAL = faster shock reversal, not lower mortality.

**Ref:** Venkatesh B, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2018;378:797–808; Annane D, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2018;378:809–818.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with severe community-acquired pneumonia (no influenza) is admitted to the ICU on high-flow nasal oxygen, FiO₂ 0.6. He needs no vasopressors. Which statement about corticosteroids is best supported?
options: Corticosteroids are contraindicated because he is not in shock
Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day can be considered; in CAPE COD it reduced 28-day mortality in severe CAP without shock
Give fludrocortisone alone
Measure a random cortisol and treat only if it is < 10 µg/dL
Give methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3 days
questions.expl:
**Why B:** CAPE COD enrolled ICU patients with severe CAP (HFNO/NIV/ventilation, high FiO₂) and excluded septic shock and influenza. Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (tapered, 8–14 days) reduced 28-day mortality (6.2 vs 11.9 %), and current guidelines suggest corticosteroids in severe CAP.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Shock is not required; the benefit was shown precisely in patients without shock.
- C – Fludrocortisone alone has never been studied in CAP; it is given only with hydrocortisone in septic shock (APROCCHSS).
- D – A random cortisol does not identify who benefits and is not used to select patients.
- E – Pulse methylprednisolone 1 g/day is not the studied regimen and adds hyperglycaemia and infection risk.

**EDIC trap:** Corticosteroids are for septic **shock** (NA ≥ 0.25 for ≥ 4 h) and for severe CAP **without** shock – not for sepsis without shock in general.

**Ref:** Dequin PF, et al. CAPE COD. *N Engl J Med* 2023;388:1931–1941.

questions.stem: Regarding adjunctive therapies in septic shock (SSC 2026):
options: High-dose IV vitamin C is suggested.
Sodium bicarbonate is suggested for patients with pH ≤ 7.2 and AKI stage 2–3.
Sodium bicarbonate is suggested to improve haemodynamics in hypoperfusion-induced lactic acidaemia.
Intravenous immunoglobulins are suggested in adult septic shock.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Suggested against (LOVIT – harm signal).
- B (True) – BICAR-ICU subgroup – fewer deaths and less RRT with pH ≤ 7.2 and AKI 2–3.
- C (False) – Not to improve haemodynamics or reduce vasopressor dose.
- D (False) – Suggested against.

**EDIC trap:** Bicarbonate only for pH ≤ 7.2 **with** AKI 2–3 – never "for the blood pressure".

**Ref:** Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026; Jaber S, et al. BICAR-ICU. *Lancet* 2018;392:31–40.

title: Case-style practice · W02-D1 · Antimicrobial dosing and microbiology basics

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man with an estimated creatinine clearance of 40 mL/min (CKD stage 3b) is admitted with sepsis. Regarding his antimicrobial dosing:
options: Linezolid requires no dose reduction for his renal function.
Ceftriaxone requires no dose adjustment at this level of renal function.
If gentamicin is used, the dosing interval should be extended and guided by drug levels.
Flucloxacillin must be halved at this creatinine clearance.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – linezolid is cleared mainly by non-renal oxidation; metabolites accumulate in severe CKD, but the dose is unchanged.
- B (True) – ceftriaxone has dual biliary and renal elimination and needs no adjustment unless hepatic and renal failure coexist.
- C (True) – aminoglycosides are renally cleared and nephrotoxic: give a full weight-based dose and extend the interval according to trough levels.
- D (False) – flucloxacillin needs reduction only in severe impairment (CrCl < 10 mL/min).

**EDIC trap:** in sepsis the first (loading) dose of any hydrophilic agent is never reduced, because Vd is increased.

**Ref:** Roberts JA et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2014;14:498–509; Abdul-Aziz MH et al., Intensive Care Med 2020;46:1127–1153.

questions.stem: Regarding Gram-stain classification of clinically important organisms:
options: Enterococcus faecium is a Gram-positive coccus.
Corynebacterium diphtheriae is a Gram-positive rod.
Neisseria meningitidis is a Gram-positive diplococcus.
Legionella pneumophila is a Gram-positive rod.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – enterococci are Gram-positive cocci in pairs/chains, intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins.
- B (True) – corynebacteria are Gram-positive "club-shaped" rods.
- C (False) – *Neisseria* species are Gram-negative diplococci.
- D (False) – *Legionella* is a Gram-negative rod that stains poorly; diagnosis is by urinary antigen (serogroup 1) or PCR rather than Gram stain.

**Ref:** Murray PR, Rosenthal KS, Pfaller MA. *Medical Microbiology*, 9th ed. Elsevier 2020; Martin-Loeches I et al., ERS/ESICM/ESCMID/ALAT severe CAP guidelines, Intensive Care Med 2023;49:615–632.

title: Case-style practice · W02-D2 · De-escalation, duration of therapy and procalcitonin

questions.stem: A 70-year-old ventilated man developed VAP. BAL grew *Klebsiella pneumoniae* susceptible to ceftriaxone. On day 3 of meropenem plus amikacin he is afebrile and his oxygenation is improving.
options: Switching to ceftriaxone monotherapy is de-escalation.
A total course of 8 days is reasonable.
In PneumA, 8 days of treatment increased mortality compared with 15 days.
A procalcitonin fall of ≥ 80 % from its peak supports stopping antibiotics.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Narrower spectrum and fewer drugs = de-escalation (SSC 2026: strong recommendation to reassess and de-escalate daily).
- B (True) – PneumA – 8 days as good as 15 days for mortality.
- C (False) – No mortality difference; only recurrence was higher with non-fermenting Gram-negatives.
- D (True) – Stopping rule: PCT < 0.5 µg/L or ≥ 80 % fall from peak.

**EDIC trap:** The non-fermenter recurrence signal in PneumA applies to *Pseudomonas*/*Acinetobacter*, not to *Klebsiella*.

**Ref:** Chastre J, et al. PneumA. *JAMA* 2003;290:2588–2598.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman has *E. coli* bacteraemia from obstructive pyelonephritis. The obstruction was drained, she is afebrile by day 4 and not immunosuppressed. What is the shortest total duration of antibiotics supported by trial evidence?
options: 3 days
5 days
7 days
14 days
Until CRP has normalised
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In BALANCE (hospitalised and ICU patients with bloodstream infection), 7 days was non-inferior to 14 days for 90-day mortality (14.5 vs 16.1 %). This patient fits: source controlled, clinically improved, not immunosuppressed and not *S. aureus* or *Candida*.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 3 days has not been tested in Gram-negative bacteraemia.
- B – 5 days lacks randomised evidence in bacteraemia; the shortest proven course is 7 days.
- D – 14 days gave no mortality benefit over 7 days and only adds antibiotic exposure.
- E – CRP-guided stopping is not supported; in ADAPT-Sepsis only procalcitonin guidance safely shortened therapy.

**EDIC trap:** 7 days does **not** apply to *S. aureus* bacteraemia (≥ 14 days).

**Ref:** Daneman N, et al. BALANCE. *N Engl J Med* 2025;392:1065–1078; Dark P, et al. ADAPT-Sepsis. *JAMA* 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding biomarker-guided antibiotic therapy:
options: Procalcitonin is best used to decide when to stop antibiotics rather than whether to start them in suspected septic shock.
In ADAPT-Sepsis, CRP-guided stopping shortened antibiotic duration as well as PCT-guided stopping.
In PRORATA, PCT guidance gave more antibiotic-free days without a significant increase in mortality.
In SAPS, PCT guidance shortened antibiotic duration and was associated with lower mortality.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Do not delay antibiotics waiting for PCT in septic shock.
- B (False) – Only PCT reduced duration; CRP did not.
- C (True) – PRORATA – +2.7 antibiotic-free days, mortality non-inferior.
- D (True) – SAPS – shorter duration and lower mortality.

**EDIC trap:** PCT is a **stopping** tool; CRP is not.

**Ref:** Bouadma L, et al. PRORATA. *Lancet* 2010; de Jong E, et al. SAPS. *Lancet Infect Dis* 2016; ADAPT-Sepsis. *JAMA* 2025.

title: Case-style practice · W02-D3 · Multidrug resistance and anti-MRSA therapy

questions.stem: Regarding antimicrobial resistance and MRSA treatment:
options: Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) means non-susceptibility to at least one agent in all but two or fewer antimicrobial categories.
Daptomycin is an appropriate first-line agent for MRSA pneumonia.
Ceftaroline is a β-lactam with activity against MRSA.
Oral vancomycin is well absorbed and can be used to complete treatment of MRSA bacteraemia.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – international consensus definitions: MDR = non-susceptible to ≥ 1 agent in ≥ 3 categories; XDR = non-susceptible to ≥ 1 agent in all but ≤ 2 categories; PDR = non-susceptible to all agents in all categories.
- B (False) – daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant and must not be used for pneumonia; use linezolid or vancomycin.
- C (True) – ceftaroline (and ceftobiprole) bind PBP2a and are the only β-lactams active against MRSA.
- D (False) – oral vancomycin is essentially not absorbed (used only for *C. difficile*); linezolid, by contrast, has ~100 % oral bioavailability.

**Ref:** Magiorakos AP et al., Clin Microbiol Infect 2012;18:268–281; Silverman JA et al., J Infect Dis 2005;191:2149–2152.

title: Case-style practice · W02-D4 · Candidaemia and aspergillosis in the ICU

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man, 9 days after bowel surgery and with a central venous catheter, has *Candida albicans* in two blood cultures.
options: An echinocandin is the first-line treatment.
The central venous catheter should be removed.
An ophthalmological examination should be done within the first week.
Treatment should last 14 days from the first positive blood culture.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Echinocandin first line; step down to fluconazole after 5–7 days if stable, cultures negative and the isolate is susceptible.
- B (True) – Remove the CVC.
- C (True) – Look for endophthalmitis within the first week.
- D (False) – 14 days from the **first negative** blood culture (clearance), not from the first positive.

**EDIC trap:** Duration counts from blood-culture clearance.

**Ref:** Pappas PG, et al. IDSA candidiasis guideline. *Clin Infect Dis* 2016;62:e1–e50.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old ventilated man is being investigated for VAP. Endotracheal aspirate grows *Candida albicans* (moderate growth) and *Staphylococcus aureus*. He has no other risk factors for invasive candidiasis and blood cultures are negative. Regarding *Candida*:
options: Start fluconazole
Start an echinocandin
No antifungal treatment – this is colonisation
Start liposomal amphotericin B
Treat if serum β-D-glucan is positive in 1 hour
questions.expl:
**Why C:** *Candida* in respiratory secretions of ventilated patients is almost always colonisation; true *Candida* pneumonia is exceptionally rare and needs histological proof. With negative blood cultures and no risk factors, no antifungal is given – treat the *S. aureus* VAP.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Fluconazole for airway colonisation adds toxicity and resistance without benefit.
- B – Echinocandins are for candidaemia/invasive candidiasis, not respiratory isolates.
- D – Liposomal amphotericin B is not indicated without invasive infection.
- E – β-D-glucan has poor positive predictive value in ICU patients and does not make airway *Candida* pathogenic.

**EDIC trap:** *Candida* in the airway ≠ *Candida* pneumonia.

**Ref:** Pappas PG, et al. *Clin Infect Dis* 2016.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman with severe influenza A pneumonia on invasive ventilation has BAL galactomannan 1.4 (ODI) on day 3 in the ICU. She has no classical host factors.
options: A diagnosis of influenza-associated pulmonary aspergillosis (IAPA) requires classical host factors (e.g. neutropenia, transplant).
BAL galactomannan ≥ 1.0 supports a diagnosis of probable aspergillosis in this setting.
Voriconazole or isavuconazole is first-line treatment.
*Aspergillus* in BAL in influenza ICU patients is almost always colonisation and need not be treated.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – The IAPA definition does not require host factors (~19 % of ICU influenza patients develop IAPA).
- B (True) – BAL GM ≥ 1.0 (or serum GM > 0.5, or positive BAL culture) = probable.
- C (True) – Voriconazole/isavuconazole first line; liposomal amphotericin B if azole resistance.
- D (False) – IAPA carries high mortality and should be treated.

**EDIC trap:** Severe influenza is itself a risk factor – no host factors needed.

**Ref:** Verweij PE, et al. IAPA consensus. *Intensive Care Med* 2020;46:1524–1535.

title: Case-style practice · W02-D5 · Ventilator-associated pneumonia

questions.stem: Regarding ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP):
options: A pneumonia first appearing 24 hours after intubation meets the usual definition of VAP.
Subglottic secretion drainage reduces the incidence of VAP.
Scheduled routine changes of the ventilator circuit reduce VAP.
In a patient without risk factors for resistance, early-onset VAP is more likely than late-onset VAP to be caused by S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae or MSSA.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – VAP requires > 48 h of invasive ventilation (ATS/IDSA 2016; ERS/ESICM/ESCMID/ALAT 2017).
- B (True) – meta-analyses show fewer VAP episodes with subglottic secretion drainage, without a clear mortality effect.
- C (False) – circuits should be changed only when visibly soiled or malfunctioning; routine changes do not reduce VAP.
- D (True) – early-onset VAP (< 5 days) more often involves community flora; late onset and prior antibiotics increase the risk of *Pseudomonas*, *Acinetobacter*, ESBL Enterobacterales and MRSA.

**Ref:** Kalil AC et al., ATS/IDSA HAP/VAP guidelines, Clin Infect Dis 2016;63:e61–e111; Torres A et al., Eur Respir J 2017;50:1700582.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man has been ventilated for 5 days after a motorcycle collision with pulmonary contusions that had been resolving. Today he has a temperature of 38.9 °C, purulent tracheal secretions, a WBC of 17 × 10⁹/L and a new right lower-lobe consolidation on chest X-ray. His PaO2/FiO2 has fallen from 280 to 170 mmHg. Echocardiography shows normal LV function. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Ventilator-associated tracheobronchitis
Acute pulmonary embolism
Ventilator-associated pneumonia
Lobar atelectasis from a mucus plug
Worsening of the pulmonary contusions
questions.expl:
**Why C:** A new, persistent infiltrate after > 48 h of ventilation plus fever, purulent secretions, leucocytosis and worsening oxygenation is clinical VAP; his CPIS would exceed 6. CPIS has only moderate sensitivity and specificity, so guidelines rely on clinical diagnosis supported by (semi-)quantitative respiratory cultures rather than CPIS alone.

**Why not the others:**
- A – ventilator-associated tracheobronchitis has no new infiltrate.
- B – pulmonary embolism does not cause purulent secretions or a new consolidation with leucocytosis.
- D – atelectasis from a mucus plug does not explain fever and purulence.
- E – contusions appear within 24 h of injury and resolve over days; these had been resolving.

**Ref:** Kalil AC et al., ATS/IDSA HAP/VAP guidelines, Clin Infect Dis 2016;63:e61–e111; Torres A et al., Eur Respir J 2017;50:1700582.

title: Case-style practice · W03-D1 · CRBSI/CLABSI

questions.stem: A ventilated patient with a 9-day-old jugular CVC develops fever. Paired blood cultures grow *Enterobacter cloacae*: the CVC sample becomes positive after 10 h, the peripheral sample after 13 h. No other source is found.
options: This is a CLABSI, but CRBSI cannot be diagnosed without culturing the catheter tip
CRBSI is confirmed: the differential time to positivity is ≥ 2 h
The result most likely represents contamination
CRBSI requires a differential time to positivity of ≥ 5 h
CRBSI is excluded because the peripheral culture is also positive
questions.expl:
**Why B:** The CVC culture turned positive 3 h before the peripheral one; a differential time to positivity ≥ 2 h confirms the catheter as the source (CRBSI). Alternatives are a tip culture ≥ 15 CFU with the same organism, or a quantitative ratio ≥ 3:1.

**Why not the others:**
- A – Tip culture is only one option; DTP diagnoses CRBSI with the catheter in situ.
- C – The same Gram-negative in both sets with a clear DTP is true infection, not contamination.
- D – The validated DTP threshold is 2 h, not 5 h.
- E – A positive peripheral culture is required for CRBSI; it confirms bacteraemia rather than excluding it.

**EDIC trap:** CLABSI = surveillance; CRBSI = proof the catheter is the source.

**Ref:** Mermel LA, et al. IDSA CRBSI guideline. *Clin Infect Dis* 2009;49:1–45.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman has *Staphylococcus aureus* (MSSA) bacteraemia from a 6-day-old jugular CVC.
options: The catheter must be removed.
She needs at least 14 days of IV therapy after the first negative blood culture.
Transoesophageal echocardiography should be performed.
Antibiotic lock therapy with catheter retention is an acceptable alternative.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – *S. aureus* = always remove.
- B (True) – ≥ 14 days for uncomplicated infection, longer if complicated.
- C (True) – TEE to exclude endocarditis.
- D (False) – Lock therapy/retention is not acceptable for *S. aureus*.

**EDIC trap:** *S. aureus*: remove, ≥ 14 days, TEE.

**Ref:** Mermel LA, et al. *Clin Infect Dis* 2009.

questions.stem: Regarding the prevention of CVC infections:
options: Chlorhexidine–alcohol skin antisepsis is superior to povidone-iodine–alcohol.
The subclavian site has the lowest rates of infection and thrombosis but more pneumothorax.
Transparent dressings must be changed every 48 hours.
The femoral site is preferred to reduce infection risk.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – CLEAN – HR 0.21 for CRBSI.
- B (True) – 3SITES.
- C (False) – Transparent/CHG dressings every 7 days (or if soiled or loose).
- D (False) – Avoid femoral when possible.

**EDIC trap:** Fewest infections = subclavian; most = femoral.

**Ref:** Mimoz O, et al. CLEAN. *Lancet* 2015; Parienti JJ, et al. 3SITES. *N Engl J Med* 2015.

title: Case-style practice · W03-D2 · CNS infection

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman presents with 2 days of fever, word-finding difficulty and a focal seizure. Herpes simplex encephalitis is suspected. Regarding her management:
options: IV aciclovir should be started before MRI or lumbar puncture results are available.
A CSF HSV PCR obtained within the first 72 hours can be falsely negative, so a repeat sample is advised if suspicion persists.
CT is more sensitive than MRI for early temporal lobe changes.
The usual aciclovir dose with normal renal function is 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Delay in aciclovir is the main modifiable determinant of poor outcome; start it empirically within hours of presentation, before MRI or LP results.
- B (True) – CSF HSV PCR in the first 72 h may be falsely negative; repeat 3–7 days later if HSE remains likely, continuing aciclovir meanwhile.
- C (False) – **MRI** (FLAIR/DWI hyperintensity of the medial temporal lobes and insula) is far more sensitive than CT, which is often normal early.
- D (True) – 10 mg/kg IV 8-hourly for 14–21 days, reduced in renal impairment; ensure hydration to avoid crystal nephropathy.

**EDIC trap:** A negative day-1 PCR never justifies stopping aciclovir when the clinical picture fits.

**Ref:** Solomon et al., ABN/BIA viral encephalitis guidelines, J Infect 2012; Tunkel et al., IDSA encephalitis guidelines, Clin Infect Dis 2008.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with a renal transplant, on tacrolimus and prednisolone, presents with 3 days of fever, headache, unsteadiness and new diplopia with a right facial palsy. CSF: WBC 450/µL (60 % neutrophils), protein 1.4 g/L, CSF/serum glucose ratio 0.35; Gram stain shows no organisms. Which empirical regimen should be started, together with dexamethasone?
options: Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin
Ceftriaxone plus ciprofloxacin
Ceftriaxone alone
Ceftriaxone plus high-dose amoxicillin
Liposomal amphotericin plus flucytosine
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Immunosuppression (and age > 50) is a risk factor for *Listeria monocytogenes*, which typically causes rhombencephalitis – brainstem signs, cranial nerve palsies, ataxia – and the Gram stain is often negative or misread. Cephalosporins have no activity against *Listeria*, so high-dose amoxicillin/ampicillin must be added to a third-generation cephalosporin (co-trimoxazole if severe penicillin allergy).

**Why not the others:**

- A – Vancomycin covers penicillin-resistant pneumococci but not *Listeria*.
- B – Ciprofloxacin is not a recommended anti-*Listeria* agent for meningitis.
- C – Ceftriaxone alone leaves *Listeria* uncovered.
- E – Amphotericin + flucytosine fits cryptococcal meningitis (lymphocytic CSF, raised opening pressure), not this neutrophilic picture.

**EDIC trap:** *Listeria* meningitis is treated for ≥ 21 days.

**Ref:** van de Beek et al., ESCMID guideline, Clin Microbiol Infect 2016; Charlier et al., MONALISA, Lancet Infect Dis 2017.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV (CD4 90 cells/µL) has a 3-week history of headache, night sweats and weight loss, and now a left sixth nerve palsy. Sodium is 127 mmol/L. CSF: lymphocytes 220/µL, protein 2.1 g/L, CSF/serum glucose ratio 0.3; Gram stain and cryptococcal antigen are negative. MRI shows basal meningeal enhancement and mild hydrocephalus. Which test is most likely to confirm the diagnosis rapidly?
options: CSF India ink stain
Serum Toxoplasma IgG
CSF VDRL
CSF cytology for lymphoma
Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra on a large-volume CSF sample
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Subacute lymphocytic meningitis with very high protein, low glucose, basal meningeal enhancement, hydrocephalus, sixth nerve palsy and hyponatraemia in advanced HIV points to tuberculous meningitis. WHO recommends Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra as the initial CSF test (sensitivity improves with ≥ 6 mL of CSF); a negative result does not exclude TBM.

**Why not the others:**

- A – India ink is less sensitive than cryptococcal antigen, which is already negative.
- B – Serum *Toxoplasma* IgG shows prior exposure and does not diagnose meningitis; toxoplasmosis causes ring-enhancing lesions.
- C – CSF VDRL tests for neurosyphilis, which does not explain this subacute basal picture with hydrocephalus.
- D – CSF cytology for lymphoma has low sensitivity and is not the most likely diagnosis.

**EDIC trap:** In TBM, ART is deferred ~4–8 weeks (early ART increased severe adverse events), and adjunctive dexamethasone did not improve survival in HIV-positive adults (ACT HIV).

**Ref:** WHO consolidated TB guidelines, Module 3: diagnosis, 2024; Donovan et al., ACT HIV, N Engl J Med 2023.

title: Case-style practice · W03-D3 · Necrotising soft-tissue infection and toxic shock

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with diabetes presents with severe thigh pain, fever and hypotension 2 days after a minor abrasion. The overlying skin shows only mild erythema. Regarding suspected necrotising fasciitis:
options: Surgical exploration should not wait for cross-sectional imaging when clinical suspicion is high.
Crepitus is present in most patients at presentation.
Clindamycin is added to broad-spectrum therapy mainly for suppression of toxin production.
Near-normal overlying skin makes necrotising fasciitis unlikely.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Delay to debridement is the strongest modifiable predictor of death; imaging must not delay surgery in an unstable patient.
- B (False) – Crepitus and gas are **late** signs present in a minority – specific but insensitive.
- C (True) – Clindamycin inhibits ribosomal toxin synthesis and is unaffected by the inoculum (Eagle) effect; it is combined with a broad-spectrum β-lactam (piperacillin–tazobactam or a carbapenem) ± MRSA cover.
- D (False) – Infection spreads along the fascia beneath initially normal-looking skin; **pain out of proportion** to findings is the classic early clue.

**EDIC trap:** Hypotension plus disproportionate pain after minor trauma = NSTI until surgical exploration proves otherwise.

**Ref:** Stevens et al., IDSA SSTI guidelines, Clin Infect Dis 2014; Sartelli et al., WSES/SIS-E consensus, World J Emerg Surg 2022.

questions.stem: Regarding toxic shock syndromes (TSS):
options: Blood cultures are positive more often in streptococcal than in staphylococcal TSS.
Desquamation, particularly of the palms and soles, typically appears 1–2 weeks after onset.
TSST-1 acts as a superantigen, cross-linking MHC class II molecules and T-cell receptors outside the antigen-binding groove.
Positive blood cultures for S. aureus are required for the diagnosis of staphylococcal TSS.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Streptococcal TSS is bacteraemic in ~60% of cases, staphylococcal TSS in < 5%.
- B (True) – Late desquamation (palms and soles, 1–2 weeks after onset) is a CDC criterion for confirmed staphylococcal TSS.
- C (True) – TSST-1 is a superantigen that cross-links MHC class II and the TCR Vβ chain outside the antigen-binding groove, activating up to 20% of T cells non-specifically and producing a cytokine storm.
- D (False) – Staphylococcal TSS is toxin-mediated; the CDC definition requires fever, rash, hypotension, ≥ 3 organ systems and negative tests for alternatives – **not** positive *S. aureus* blood cultures.

**EDIC trap:** Negative blood cultures in a shocked woman with erythroderma favour staphylococcal TSS.

**Ref:** Lappin & Ferguson, Lancet Infect Dis 2009; CDC TSS (other than streptococcal) case definition 2011.

questions.stem: Regarding the classification and assessment of necrotising soft-tissue infection (NSTI):
options: Type 1 NSTI is polymicrobial with anaerobes and is typical of perineal (Fournier's) infection in diabetic patients.
Type 2 NSTI is most commonly caused by Clostridium perfringens.
A LRINEC score below 6 reliably excludes NSTI.
NSTI due to Vibrio vulnificus is associated with seawater exposure and chronic liver disease.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Type 1 (the most common) is polymicrobial – anaerobes, Enterobacterales, streptococci – and typical of Fournier's gangrene in diabetics.
- B (False) – Type 2 is monomicrobial, usually **group A streptococcus** (± *S. aureus*); clostridial myonecrosis is classed separately as gas gangrene (or with type 1).
- C (False) – LRINEC has poor sensitivity (~68% in meta-analysis) and must **not** be used to rule out NSTI.
- D (True) – *Vibrio vulnificus* (type 3, with *Aeromonas*) is linked to marine wounds, raw shellfish and cirrhosis; type 4 is fungal.

**EDIC trap:** Type 2 GAS NSTI affects healthy people of any age, often without a portal of entry.

**Ref:** Fernando et al., Ann Surg 2019; Stevens & Bryant, N Engl J Med 2017.

questions.stem: Concerning the diagnosis and treatment of necrotising fasciitis:
options: Gas in the soft tissues on CT is required to make the diagnosis.
Antibiotics alone are adequate for early type 1 infection in a haemodynamically stable patient.
Pain is usually proportionate to the visible skin changes.
Necrosis of muscle with intact fascia is the defining lesion.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Gas is absent in many cases; CT findings (fascial thickening, fluid) support but cannot exclude the diagnosis. Surgical exploration ("finger test": easy dissection, dishwater fluid, no bleeding) is diagnostic.
- B (False) – Surgical debridement is the cornerstone regardless of type or stability; antibiotics are adjunctive.
- C (False) – Pain is classically **out of proportion** to the visible skin changes.
- D (False) – Necrotising fasciitis is defined by necrosis of the superficial/deep **fascia**; myonecrosis may coexist but does not define it.

**EDIC trap:** Plan a second-look operation within 24 h.

**Ref:** Stevens & Bryant, N Engl J Med 2017; Sartelli et al., WSES/SIS-E consensus, World J Emerg Surg 2022.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents 3 days after septorhinoplasty with nasal packing in situ. She has a temperature of 39.6 °C, diffuse macular erythroderma, BP 78/40 mmHg, diarrhoea, confusion, creatine kinase 2400 U/L, creatinine 190 µmol/L and platelets 85 × 10⁹/L. Her conjunctivae are injected. Alongside fluid resuscitation, which is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: IV immunoglobulin as the sole specific treatment
Ceftriaxone, leaving the packing in place to protect the surgical result
CT of the sinuses before any antibiotic is given
Remove the nasal packing and give an anti-staphylococcal β-lactam plus clindamycin
Meropenem monotherapy
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Fever, erythroderma, shock and multi-organ involvement (GI, CNS, muscle, platelets, kidney) after nasal packing is staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome. Priorities: remove the toxin source and give a bactericidal anti-staphylococcal agent (flucloxacillin/cefazolin; vancomycin or linezolid if MRSA risk) plus a protein-synthesis inhibitor (clindamycin or linezolid) to suppress toxin production.

**Why not the others:**

- A – IVIG is an adjunct in refractory cases, not a substitute for source control and antibiotics.
- B – Leaving the packing leaves the toxin source in place; ceftriaxone also lacks an antitoxin effect.
- C – Delaying antibiotics for imaging is wrong in shock.
- E – Meropenem alone lacks an antitoxin effect and is unnecessarily broad.

**EDIC trap:** Non-menstrual TSS follows nasal packing, surgical wounds, burns.

**Ref:** Lappin & Ferguson, Lancet Infect Dis 2009; Stevens et al., IDSA SSTI guidelines, Clin Infect Dis 2014.

title: Case-style practice · W03-D4 · Immunocompromised patient: neutropenia and HIV

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman on chemotherapy for breast cancer presents with a temperature of 38.6 °C, BP 84/50 mmHg and a neutrophil count of 0.2 × 10⁹/L. She has a tunnelled central venous catheter without signs of exit-site infection. Regarding her initial management:
options: An empirical antipseudomonal β-lactam should be given within 1 hour.
Febrile neutropenia is defined using a neutrophil count < 0.5 × 10⁹/L, or one expected to fall below this.
Vancomycin should be added routinely because she has a central venous catheter.
Given her septic shock, adding an aminoglycoside (or escalating to a carbapenem, depending on local resistance) is reasonable.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – An antipseudomonal β-lactam (piperacillin–tazobactam, cefepime or meropenem) within 1 h; delays increase mortality.
- B (True) – Standard ESMO/IDSA definition: ANC < 0.5 × 10⁹/L or expected to fall below this within 48 h, with fever ≥ 38.3 °C (or ≥ 38.0 °C for 1 h).
- C (False) – Glycopeptides are added only for specific indications (suspected serious catheter-related infection, skin/soft-tissue infection, pneumonia, MRSA colonisation, haemodynamic instability) – not for the mere presence of a CVC.
- D (True) – Septic shock is a complicated presentation: ECIL-4 recommends a **de-escalation** approach (carbapenem, or β-lactam + aminoglycoside, ± anti-MRSA cover), narrowing at 72–96 h.

**EDIC trap:** The line need not be removed immediately unless tunnel/pocket infection or *S. aureus*, *Pseudomonas* or *Candida* bacteraemia.

**Ref:** Averbuch et al., ECIL-4, Haematologica 2013; Klastersky et al., ESMO guideline, Ann Oncol 2016.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with HIV infection after presenting with weight loss and painful swallowing; her CD4 count is 260 cells/µL and HIV viral load 85 000 copies/mL. She has not yet started antiretroviral therapy, and further investigations are under way. Which one of the following conditions, if present, would by itself establish a diagnosis of AIDS?
options: Multidermatomal herpes zoster
Oral hairy leukoplakia
Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2
Oesophageal candidiasis
Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura
questions.expl:
**Why D:** With a CD4 count > 200 cells/µL, AIDS (CDC stage 3) is defined by an AIDS-defining illness. Candidiasis of the oesophagus, trachea, bronchi or lungs is AIDS-defining; oral candidiasis is not. Odynophagia and weight loss fit oesophageal candidiasis.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Multidermatomal herpes zoster is a "category B" indicator condition, not AIDS-defining.
- B – Oral hairy leukoplakia is a category B condition.
- C – Cervical dysplasia/carcinoma in situ is category B; only invasive cervical carcinoma is AIDS-defining.
- E – ITP is an HIV-associated condition but not AIDS-defining.

**EDIC trap:** AIDS-defining conditions relevant to ICU include *Pneumocystis* pneumonia, cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, tuberculosis, recurrent bacterial pneumonia and CMV retinitis.

**Ref:** Selik et al., CDC revised surveillance case definition, MMWR Recomm Rep 2014.

title: Case-style practice · W03-D5 · Infection prevention and control

questions.stem: Regarding selective digestive decontamination (SDD) in ventilated ICU patients:
options: It aims to eradicate carriage of aerobic Gram-negative bacilli, S. aureus and yeasts while preserving the anaerobic flora.
It uses non-absorbable antimicrobials applied as an oropharyngeal paste and an enteral suspension.
SuDDICU (JAMA 2022) showed a significant reduction in hospital mortality.
Enteral vancomycin is a routine component in all ICUs.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – SDD targets aerobic Gram-negative bacilli, *S. aureus* and yeasts while sparing anaerobes, which maintain colonisation resistance.
- B (True) – Non-absorbable topical agents (classically colistin, tobramycin and amphotericin B/nystatin) are given as oropharyngeal paste and enteral suspension throughout ventilation, plus a short IV cephalosporin course.
- C (False) – SuDDICU (5982 patients, 19 Australian ICUs) found hospital mortality 27.0% vs 29.1%, OR 0.91 (0.82–1.02) – **not significant**.
- D (False) – Enteral vancomycin is added only in units with endemic MRSA, not routinely.

**EDIC trap:** The pooled evidence (Hammond 2022) suggests a small benefit that depends on the IV component.

**Ref:** Myburgh et al., SuDDICU, JAMA 2022; Hammond et al., JAMA 2022.

questions.stem: Regarding hand hygiene, decontamination of equipment and central-line infection programmes:
options: "Before an aseptic procedure" and "after body fluid exposure risk" are two of the WHO five moments for hand hygiene.
In the Spaulding classification, items that enter sterile tissue or the vascular system require sterilisation.
An alcohol-based hand rub is preferred to soap and water when hands are visibly soiled.
The Matching Michigan programme in English ICUs targeted central venous catheter–associated bloodstream infection.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – The WHO five moments: before touching a patient, before a clean/aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, after touching patient surroundings.
- B (True) – Spaulding: critical items (sterile tissue, vascular system) → sterilisation; semi-critical (mucous membranes, e.g. laryngoscope blades, bronchoscopes) → high-level disinfection; non-critical (intact skin) → low-level disinfection/cleaning.
- C (False) – Visibly soiled hands (and *C. difficile*/norovirus exposure) require **soap and water**; alcohol rub is preferred otherwise.
- D (True) – Matching Michigan adapted the Keystone CVC bundle to 215 English ICUs; CVC-BSI rates fell, partly in line with a pre-existing downward trend.

**EDIC trap:** Alcohol does not kill *C. difficile* spores.

**Ref:** WHO guidelines on hand hygiene in health care, 2009; Bion et al., Matching Michigan, BMJ Qual Saf 2013.

questions.stem: Under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010 in England, which of the following must be notified by the attending clinician on clinical suspicion?
options: Legionnaires' disease
Botulism
Uncomplicated seasonal influenza A in an adult
Invasive group A streptococcal disease
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Legionnaires' disease is listed in Schedule 1.
- B (True) – Botulism is listed in Schedule 1.
- C (False) – Seasonal influenza is monitored through laboratory surveillance and is **not** clinician-notifiable.
- D (True) – Invasive group A streptococcal disease (and scarlet fever) is notifiable.

Schedule 1 also includes acute meningitis, acute encephalitis, meningococcal septicaemia, tuberculosis, tetanus, HUS, measles, diphtheria and viral haemorrhagic fevers. Notification is on **clinical suspicion**, without waiting for laboratory confirmation. Other European countries have analogous national lists under the EU decision on communicable disease surveillance.

**Ref:** Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010, SI 2010/659 (as amended); UKHSA, Notifiable diseases and causative organisms: how to report, 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding prevention of device-associated infection in the ICU:
options: 2 % chlorhexidine in 70 % alcohol is preferred to povidone-iodine for skin antisepsis before CVC insertion.
The subclavian site is associated with a lower risk of catheter-related bloodstream infection than the femoral site.
Routine replacement of CVCs every 7 days reduces catheter-related bloodstream infection.
The risk of bacteriuria with an indwelling urinary catheter is roughly 3–7 % per day of catheterisation.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – In CLEAN, chlorhexidine–alcohol reduced CRBSI by about 80% vs povidone iodine–alcohol (0.28 vs 1.32/1000 catheter-days, HR 0.21).
- B (True) – In 3SITES the subclavian site had the lowest rate of CRBSI + symptomatic DVT (1.5 vs 4.6/1000 catheter-days for femoral), at the cost of more pneumothorax.
- C (False) – Scheduled replacement (over a guidewire or at a new site) does **not** reduce infection and adds mechanical risk; remove catheters when no longer needed.
- D (True) – Bacteriuria risk is roughly 3–7% per catheter-day, which is why daily review and early removal are the key CAUTI-prevention measures.

**EDIC trap:** Keystone's fifth bundle element is removal of unnecessary lines, not routine replacement.

**Ref:** Mimoz et al., CLEAN, Lancet 2015; Parienti et al., 3SITES, N Engl J Med 2015; Gould et al., CDC CAUTI guideline 2009 (updated 2019).

questions.stem: Regarding the evidence on selective decontamination strategies:
options: SDD is primarily intended for patients expected to require mechanical ventilation for more than 48 hours.
Selective oropharyngeal decontamination (SOD) omits the enteral component of SDD.
A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis found SDD to be associated with lower hospital mortality in ventilated patients.
SDD markedly increases the incidence of Clostridioides difficile infection.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Trials enrolled patients expected to be ventilated beyond the next day or two (SuDDICU: > 48 h).
- B (True) – SOD uses only the oropharyngeal paste, without the enteral suspension or IV component; de Smet (NEJM 2009) compared SDD, SOD and standard care.
- C (True) – Hammond et al. (32 RCTs, 24,389 patients) estimated hospital mortality RR 0.91 (95% CrI 0.82–0.99), moderate certainty.
- D (False) – *C. difficile* infection is not increased; SuDDICU's ecological analysis showed non-inferiority for *C. difficile*.

**EDIC trap:** SuDDICU itself was neutral, unit-level non-inferiority for resistant organisms was not confirmed, and data from high-resistance settings (R-GNOSIS) are not reassuring.

**Ref:** Hammond et al., JAMA 2022; Myburgh et al., SuDDICU, JAMA 2022; de Smet et al., N Engl J Med 2009.

title: Case-style practice · W04-D1 · Physiology of shock

questions.stem: A patient has a cardiac output of 5 L/min, haemoglobin 100 g/L (10 g/dL) and SaO₂ 90 %. Ignoring dissolved oxygen, what is his oxygen delivery (DO₂)?
options: ≈ 300 mL/min
≈ 450 mL/min
≈ 600 mL/min
≈ 800 mL/min
≈ 1,000 mL/min
questions.expl:
**Why C:** CaO₂ = 1.34 × Hb (g/dL) × SaO₂ = 1.34 × 10 × 0.90 ≈ 12.1 mL/dL = 121 mL/L. DO₂ = CO × CaO₂ = 5 × 121 ≈ 600 mL/min; dissolved oxygen (0.003 × PaO₂) would add very little.

**Why not the others:**
- A – ≈ 300 mL/min would need roughly half the cardiac output or haemoglobin.
- B – ≈ 450 mL/min corresponds to an SaO₂ of about 67 %.
- D – ≈ 800 mL/min would need Hb ≈ 13 g/dL at the same CO and SaO₂.
- E – ≈ 1,000 mL/min is normal resting DO₂ (Hb 15 g/dL, SaO₂ ~98 %).

**EDIC trap:** Remember × 10 to convert mL/dL to mL/L.

**Ref:** Vincent JL, De Backer D. Circulatory shock. *N Engl J Med* 2013;369:1726–1734.

questions.stem: Regarding venous oxygen saturation and oxygen delivery:
options: A low SvO₂ is typical of cardiogenic and hypovolaemic shock.
A normal or high SvO₂ in septic shock confirms adequate tissue oxygenation.
Below the critical DO₂, VO₂ becomes delivery-dependent and lactate rises.
At constant VO₂ and cardiac output, anaemia lowers SvO₂.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Low flow → high extraction → low SvO₂.
- B (False) – Normal or high SvO₂ in distributive shock can coexist with tissue hypoxia (impaired extraction, shunting).
- C (True) – Supply dependency below DO₂crit.
- D (True) – Lower CaO₂ → more extraction → lower SvO₂.

**EDIC trap:** A "good" SvO₂ in sepsis is not reassurance.

**Ref:** Cecconi M, et al. ESICM shock consensus. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815.

questions.stem: According to the ESICM 2014 consensus on circulatory shock:
options: Hypotension is required for the diagnosis of shock.
Routine use of a pulmonary artery catheter is recommended.
Echocardiography is the preferred modality to evaluate the type of shock.
An initial MAP target of ≥ 65 mmHg is recommended, individualised thereafter.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Shock = inadequate cellular O₂ utilisation; hypotension is not required.
- B (False) – Recommended **against** routine PAC (1A).
- C (True) – Echo preferred (2B).
- D (True) – Initial MAP ≥ 65, then individualise.

**EDIC trap:** Shock can exist with a normal blood pressure.

**Ref:** Cecconi M, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2014.

title: Case-style practice · W04-D2 · Fluid responsiveness

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man on day 2 after laparotomy for faecal peritonitis is ventilated on pressure support 10 cmH2O and PEEP 6 cmH2O, triggering every breath at 24/min. He is in sinus rhythm with MAP 61 mmHg on low-dose noradrenaline. Which finding best indicates that he will increase his cardiac output with a fluid bolus?
options: Pulse pressure variation of 16 % on the radial arterial line
Central venous pressure of 4 mmHg
Inferior vena cava collapsibility of 50 % on ultrasound
A small left-ventricular end-diastolic area on transthoracic echocardiography
A 15 % rise in left-ventricular outflow tract VTI during passive leg raising
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Passive leg raising transfers ~300 mL of venous blood from the legs and splanchnic bed and, when measured with real-time CO or LVOT VTI (threshold ≈ 10 %), predicts fluid responsiveness regardless of spontaneous breathing, arrhythmia or tidal volume (pooled AUROC 0.95). A 15 % rise in VTI is well above the threshold and above the ~12 % precision limit of echo VTI.

**Why not the others:**

- A – PPV is valid only with fully controlled ventilation, VT ≥ 8 mL/kg, sinus rhythm and a closed chest; triggering every breath invalidates it.
- B – CVP is a static measure and predicts responsiveness poorly, even when low.
- C – IVC collapsibility during spontaneous or assisted breathing has only modest accuracy and is confounded by inspiratory effort.
- D – LV end-diastolic area is a static preload index with poor predictive value.

**Ref:** Monnet X, et al. Passive leg raising for predicting fluid responsiveness: a systematic review and meta-analysis. *Intensive Care Med* 2016;42:1935–1947. Monnet X, Shi R, Teboul JL. Prediction of fluid responsiveness. What's new? *Ann Intensive Care* 2022;12:46.

title: Case-style practice · W04-D3 · Haemodynamic monitoring

questions.stem: Regarding interpretation of the arterial pressure waveform in an ICU patient:
options: The maximum slope of the systolic upstroke (dP/dt max) from a peripheral line is a rough index of LV contractility but is influenced by arterial compliance.
A pulse pressure variation of 18 % in a patient ventilated with a tidal volume of 6 mL/kg who is triggering breaths reliably indicates preload responsiveness.
Systolic pressure measured in the radial artery is normally lower than in the ascending aorta.
A dicrotic notch positioned low on the descending limb suggests a high systemic vascular resistance.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Peripheral dP/dt max tracks LV contractility directionally but is affected by vascular tone, compliance and pulse amplification.
- B (False) – With triggering and VT 6 mL/kg PPV is uninterpretable – irregular efforts can create false positives and low VT false negatives; use PLR or EEO.
- C (False) – Distal pulse amplification by reflected waves makes radial systolic pressure **higher** than aortic; MAP is similar.
- D (False) – A low dicrotic notch suggests vasodilatation and low SVR; a high notch suggests vasoconstriction.

**Ref:** Saugel B, et al. Cardiac output estimation using pulse wave analysis. *Br J Anaesth* 2021;126:67–76. Michard F, et al. Applicability of pulse pressure variation. *Crit Care* 2015;19:144.

questions.stem: Concerning variables obtained with a pulmonary artery catheter:
options: Thermodilution cardiac output is a measured variable, calculated from the area under the temperature–time curve (Stewart–Hamilton equation).
Pulmonary vascular resistance is calculated from mean pulmonary artery pressure, PAOP and cardiac output.
Mixed venous oxygen saturation is measured from blood sampled at the catheter tip in the pulmonary artery.
Oxygen consumption can be derived (reverse Fick) from cardiac output and the arterial and mixed venous oxygen contents.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Thermodilution CO is measured with the Stewart–Hamilton equation (CO inversely proportional to the area under the curve); accuracy falls with severe TR, shunts and very low output.
- B (True) – PVR = 80 × (mPAP − PAOP) / CO in dyn·s·cm⁻⁵, or without the factor 80 in Wood units.
- C (True) – SvO2 comes from blood sampled at the PA tip or from fibreoptic oximetry – true mixed venous blood.
- D (True) – Reverse Fick: VO2 = CO × (CaO2 − CvO2) × 10; likewise DO2 = CO × CaO2 × 10.

**EDIC trap:** Measured: pressures, PAOP, thermodilution CO, SvO2. Derived: CI, SV, SVR, PVR, DO2, VO2.

**Ref:** Rajaram SS, et al. Pulmonary artery catheters for adult patients in intensive care. *Cochrane Database Syst Rev* 2013;(2):CD003408. Cecconi M, et al. ESICM consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815.

questions.stem: Regarding oesophageal Doppler monitoring:
options: It measures blood flow velocity in the descending thoracic aorta and estimates stroke volume using a nomogram-derived aortic cross-sectional area.
A corrected flow time (FTc) below 330 ms is specific for hypovolaemia.
Its velocity measurement is accurate regardless of the angle between the beam and the direction of flow.
It is poorly tolerated by awake patients and is used mainly in sedated, intubated patients.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Only descending aortic flow (~70 % of CO) is measured and scaled by a nomogram; altered flow distribution (cross-clamp, pregnancy) causes error.
- B (False) – A short FTc reflects low preload but also high afterload (vasoconstriction, mitral stenosis); interpret it with the SV response to fluid.
- C (False) – The Doppler equation contains cos θ; angles > 20° underestimate velocity, so probe position matters.
- D (True) – It is poorly tolerated awake and suits theatre and sedated, intubated ICU patients.

**Ref:** Singer M. Oesophageal Doppler. *Curr Opin Crit Care* 2009;15:244–248. Cecconi M, et al. ESICM consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman with septic shock is ventilated and triggering the ventilator. She is in permanent atrial fibrillation (ventricular rate 110–140/min) and echocardiography shows severe tricuspid regurgitation with a dilated right ventricle. She has received 2 L of crystalloid and remains on noradrenaline 0.3 µg/kg/min. You want to track her response to fluid and dobutamine. Which method is most appropriate?
options: Serial transthoracic echocardiographic LVOT VTI averaged over several beats
Pulse pressure variation from the radial arterial line
Bolus thermodilution via a pulmonary artery catheter
Trend of central venous pressure
Uncalibrated pulse-contour analysis of beat-to-beat stroke volume variation
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Echocardiographic LVOT VTI (× LVOT area = SV), **averaged over 5–10 cardiac cycles**, copes with the irregular rhythm and can be repeated after each fluid bolus or dobutamine change. Because LVOT area is constant, changes in VTI alone track changes in stroke volume.

**Why not the others:**

- B – PPV requires sinus rhythm and controlled ventilation; both conditions fail here.
- C – Severe TR recirculates the cold indicator and makes PAC thermodilution unreliable.
- D – CVP is not a measure of flow and is raised by TR.
- E – SVV has the same limitations as PPV, and uncalibrated pulse contour is unreliable with high-dose vasopressors.

**Ref:** Cecconi M, et al. ESICM consensus on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring. *Intensive Care Med* 2014;40:1795–1815. Vieillard-Baron A, et al. A decade of progress in critical care echocardiography. *Intensive Care Med* 2019;45:770–788.

questions.stem: Regarding the physics of invasive arterial pressure measurement:
options: An underdamped system overestimates systolic and underestimates diastolic pressure.
Long, compliant tubing lowers the natural frequency of the system.
If the transducer is raised 10 cm above the phlebostatic axis, the displayed pressure will be about 7 mmHg lower than the true value.
A fast-flush test producing one or two oscillations before returning to baseline indicates appropriate damping.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Resonance (ringing) exaggerates systolic peaks and lowers diastolic pressure; MAP is relatively preserved.
- B (True) – Natural frequency falls with long, compliant tubing, air bubbles and extra stopcocks, and rises with short, stiff, wide-bore tubing.
- C (True) – 10 cmH2O ≈ 7.4 mmHg; levelling to the phlebostatic axis is distinct from zeroing to atmosphere.
- D (True) – 1.5–2 oscillations indicate optimal damping; none suggests overdamping, many suggest underdamping.

**Ref:** Saugel B, et al. How to measure blood pressure using an arterial catheter: a systematic 5-step approach. *Crit Care* 2020;24:172.

questions.stem: Which of the following typically raise the pulmonary artery occlusion pressure (PAOP)?
options: Severe idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension with a normal left heart
Acute massive pulmonary embolism
Acute severe mitral regurgitation
Aggressive diuresis in a patient with normal cardiac function
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Pulmonary arterial hypertension is pre-capillary: high mPAP and PVR with PAOP ≤ 15 mmHg.
- B (False) – PE is a pre-capillary obstruction; PAOP is normal or low because LV filling falls.
- C (True) – Acute severe MR produces large v waves and a raised PAOP.
- D (False) – Diuresis lowers PAOP.

**EDIC trap:** High PEEP or a catheter tip outside West zone 3 can falsely elevate PAOP.

**Ref:** Humbert M, et al. 2022 ESC/ERS pulmonary hypertension guidelines. *Eur Heart J* 2022;43:3618–3731. Magder S. *Chest* 2017;151:908–916.

title: Case-style practice · W04-D4 · Lactate

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin presents with vomiting, AKI (creatinine 520 µmol/L), pH 6.98 and lactate 18 mmol/L, with normal blood pressure. Regarding lactate and lactic acidosis:
options: Hyperlactataemia in sepsis always indicates tissue hypoxia.
Metformin accumulation can cause type B lactic acidosis.
The kidney is the main organ of lactate clearance.
D-lactate (e.g. in short-bowel syndrome) is detected by standard blood gas lactate analysers.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Much septic hyperlactataemia comes from β2-stimulated aerobic glycolysis and reduced hepatic clearance; lactate marks severity, not proof of anaerobiosis.
- B (True) – Metformin inhibits mitochondrial respiration and hepatic gluconeogenesis from lactate; accumulation in AKI causes MALA, and EXTRIP recommends dialysis in severe cases (e.g. lactate > 20 mmol/L, pH ≤ 7.0).
- C (False) – The liver clears ~60–70 % (Cori cycle); the kidneys ~20–30 %.
- D (False) – Analysers use L-lactate oxidase; D-lactic acidosis causes a raised anion gap and encephalopathy with a normal measured lactate.

**Ref:** Garcia-Alvarez M, Marik P, Bellomo R. Sepsis-associated hyperlactatemia. *Crit Care* 2014;18:503. Calello DP, et al. EXTRIP metformin. *Crit Care Med* 2015;43:1716–1730. Kraut JA, Madias NE. Lactic acidosis. *N Engl J Med* 2014;371:2309–2319.

title: Case-style practice · W04-D5 · Echocardiography and POCUS in shock

questions.stem: A ventilated patient in shock has an LVOT VTI of 16 cm. During passive leg raising it rises to 18.5 cm. How should this be interpreted?
options: Not fluid responsive – the change is < 25 %
Fluid responsive – VTI rose by ≥ 10 %
Uninterpretable without an IVC measurement
Uninterpretable because the patient is ventilated
Fluid responsive only if CVP also rises by ≥ 2 mmHg
questions.expl:
**Why B:** (18.5 − 16)/16 ≈ +16 %, above the ≥ 10 % rise in VTI/cardiac output that defines a positive passive leg raise. It also exceeds the least significant change of VTI (~12 %), and PLR remains valid in ventilated patients.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 25 % is not the PLR threshold; a ≥ 10 % rise is.
- C – IVC size is unreliable in ventilated patients and is not needed to interpret PLR.
- D – PLR is valid regardless of ventilation or spontaneous breathing, unlike pulse pressure variation.
- E – CVP changes do not predict fluid responsiveness; PLR is judged on a flow variable.

**EDIC trap:** PLR threshold 10 %; EEO + EIO 13 %.

**Ref:** Robba C, et al. ESICM POCUS consensus. *Intensive Care Med* 2021;47:1347–1367.

questions.stem: A patient with moderate ARDS on PEEP 14 becomes hypotensive. TTE shows RV/LV end-diastolic area ratio 1.1 and paradoxical septal motion.
options: The RV is severely dilated.
A fluid bolus is the first step.
Noradrenaline to maintain RV perfusion pressure is appropriate.
Prone positioning can unload the RV.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – RV/LV > 0.6 = dilated, ≥ 1 = severe; with septal dyskinesia = acute cor pulmonale (~22 % in ARDS).
- B (False) – Fluids worsen RV dilatation and septal shift.
- C (True) – Restore RV coronary perfusion.
- D (True) – Proning lowers pulmonary vascular resistance and is part of RV-protective ventilation.

**EDIC trap:** In ACP, fluids harm.

**Ref:** Mekontso Dessap A, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2016;42:862–870.

questions.stem: Regarding the inferior vena cava (IVC) in shock:
options: A small IVC that collapses on inspiration in a spontaneously breathing hypotensive patient suggests hypovolaemia.
A plethoric IVC in a patient on high PEEP reliably excludes fluid responsiveness.
A non-dilated IVC makes cardiac tamponade very unlikely.
ESICM 2021 recommends using ultrasound to predict fluid responsiveness in all patients with shock.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Small collapsing IVC = hypovolaemia.
- B (False) – PEEP is one of the ~10 situations where the IVC fails.
- C (True) – Tamponade almost always produces a plethoric IVC.
- D (False) – Recommended against for basic ultrasound in shock without hypovolaemia.

**EDIC trap:** IVC size has many confounders – PEEP, RV failure, TR, intra-abdominal hypertension.

**Ref:** Robba C, et al. *Intensive Care Med* 2021.

title: Case-style practice · W05-D1 · Acid–base: anion gap and blood gas analysis

questions.stem: Which of the following typically cause a normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis?
options: Ureterosigmoidostomy
Distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis
Toluene inhalation (glue sniffing)
Moderate chronic kidney disease (GFR 20–50 mL/min)
questions.expl:
- A (True) – with urine in the colon, Cl⁻ is absorbed in exchange for HCO₃⁻ (and NH₄⁺ is reabsorbed), causing a hyperchloraemic acidosis.
- B (True) – impaired distal H⁺ secretion gives a urine pH > 5.5 and a positive urinary anion gap, often with hypokalaemia.
- C (True) – toluene is metabolised to hippuric acid; hippurate is rapidly excreted in urine with Na⁺/K⁺, so the AG is often normal and hypokalaemia is prominent.
- D (True) – moderate CKD reduces ammoniagenesis, causing a hyperchloraemic acidosis. The gap rises only when GFR falls further and phosphate and sulphate accumulate.

**EDIC trap:** CKD moves from a normal-AG to a high-AG acidosis as GFR declines.

**Ref:** Kraut JA, Madias NE, Metabolic acidosis: pathophysiology, diagnosis and management, Nat Rev Nephrol 2010;6:274–285; Berend K, de Vries AP, Gans RO, N Engl J Med 2014;371:1434–1445.

questions.stem: A patient is cooled to 32 °C. Blood gases are analysed in a standard analyser. Regarding blood gas analysis:
options: The PaO2 reported at 37 °C is higher than the true in vivo value at 32 °C.
Alpha-stat management uses temperature-corrected values.
pH-stat management requires increasing minute ventilation to remove CO2.
A sample with a very high leucocyte count left at room temperature for an hour will show a falsely high PaO2.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – when blood is warmed to 37 °C in the analyser, gas solubility falls and partial pressures rise, so uncorrected PO₂ and PCO₂ overestimate in vivo values in hypothermia.
- B (False) – alpha-stat uses values measured at 37 °C (**uncorrected**), preserving the ionisation state of histidine imidazole groups.
- C (False) – pH-stat targets a temperature-corrected PaCO₂ of ~5.3 kPa, i.e. relative hypercapnia, achieved by adding CO₂ or **reducing** ventilation.
- D (False) – metabolising leucocytes (and platelets) consume O₂ in the syringe ("leucocyte larceny"), so PaO₂ is falsely **low**.

**EDIC trap:** alpha-stat = uncorrected (37 °C) values; pH-stat = temperature-corrected values.

**Ref:** Ashwood ER, Kost G, Kenny M, Clin Chem 1983;29:1877–1885; Fox MJ, Brody JS, Weintraub LR, Am J Med 1979;67:742–746.

questions.stem: Regarding causes and interpretation of a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis:
options: Pyroglutamic acidosis (5-oxoprolinuria) may occur with regular paracetamol in malnourished patients, especially when combined with flucloxacillin.
Propylene glycol, a solvent in high-dose IV lorazepam infusions, can cause a raised anion gap and osmolar gap.
Hypoalbuminaemia lowers the anion gap and can mask a raised-gap acidosis unless the gap is corrected.
Large-volume 0.9 % saline administration causes a raised anion gap acidosis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – glutathione depletion leads to 5-oxoproline accumulation, and flucloxacillin inhibits 5-oxoprolinase; malnutrition, sepsis and CKD increase the risk.
- B (True) – propylene glycol is metabolised to L- and D-lactate, causing a raised anion gap together with a raised osmolar gap.
- C (True) – albumin is the main unmeasured anion; corrected AG ≈ AG + 0.25 × (40 − albumin g/L).
- D (False) – saline lowers the SID through hyperchloraemia, causing a **normal** anion gap acidosis.

**Ref:** Berend K et al., N Engl J Med 2014;371:1434–1445; Emmett M, Acetaminophen toxicity and 5-oxoproline (pyroglutamic acid): a tale of two cycles, Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2014;9:191–200.

title: Case-style practice · W05-D2 · Stewart approach to acid–base

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman with decompensated cirrhosis has: pH 7.40, PaCO2 5.3 kPa, HCO3⁻ 24 mmol/L, Na⁺ 138, K⁺ 4.0, Cl⁻ 110, lactate 1.0 mmol/L, albumin 18 g/L. Regarding her acid–base status:
options: Her apparent strong ion difference is about 31 mEq/L, which is reduced.
Her low albumin produces a metabolic alkalosis that offsets an acidifying process.
The normal pH and bicarbonate exclude a metabolic acid–base disorder.
Infusing 20 % albumin is the appropriate treatment for this acid–base disturbance.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – SIDa = (Na⁺ + K⁺) − (Cl⁻ + lactate) = 142 − 111 = 31 mEq/L (normal ~40–42, ignoring Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺): a hyperchloraemic (low-SID) acidosis.
- B (True) – albumin is the main component of ATOT; a low ATOT is alkalinising (~+6–7 mmol/L BE at 18 g/L), which is why her pH is normal.
- C (False) – two opposing metabolic disorders cancel out; Stewart or albumin-corrected anion gap analysis reveals them.
- D (False) – acid–base values are not a target for albumin; treat the cause (chloride load, underlying illness).

**EDIC trap:** a normal pH and HCO₃⁻ ≠ normal acid–base status in hypoalbuminaemia (Fencl: ~1/6 of ICU patients).

**Ref:** Kellum JA, Determinants of blood pH in health and disease, Crit Care 2000;4:6–14; Fencl V et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2000;162:2246–2251.

questions.stem: In the Stewart (physicochemical) approach:
options: Bicarbonate concentration is an independent variable.
The total concentration of weak acids (ATOT), mainly albumin and phosphate, is an independent variable.
Lactate is a dependent variable.
The hydroxide ion concentration is an independent variable.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – bicarbonate is a **dependent** variable, determined by PaCO₂, SID and ATOT.
- B (True) – ATOT (mainly albumin and phosphate) is one of the three independent variables, with PaCO₂ and SID.
- C (False) – lactate is a strong (fully dissociated) anion and therefore a component of the SID: it changes the independent variables rather than being determined by them.
- D (False) – OH⁻, like H⁺, HCO₃⁻, A⁻ and CO₃²⁻, is a dependent variable.

**Ref:** Stewart PA, Modern quantitative acid–base chemistry, Can J Physiol Pharmacol 1983;61:1444–1461; Kellum JA, Crit Care 2000;4:6–14.

title: Case-style practice · W05-D3 · Metabolic alkalosis, mixed disorders, ketoacidoses and toxic alcohols

questions.stem: After 5 days of vomiting, a 40-year-old woman has pH 7.52, HCO₃⁻ 38 mmol/L, PaCO₂ 6.4 kPa (48 mmHg), K⁺ 2.9 mmol/L and urine chloride 8 mmol/L. The best treatment is:
options: Acetazolamide
0.9 % NaCl with KCl
Spironolactone
Hydrochloric acid infusion as first line
Haemodialysis
questions.expl:
